name: Stanley Uttley
title: Mr
place_of_death: the Abraham Ormerod Medical Centre, Todmorden
conclusion:
The circumstances of this death are well documented in the contemporaneous records. The post-mortem findings were entirely consistent with a death from myocardial infarction or heart attack. It appears that Shipman had already discovered that Mr Uttley has ischaemic heart disease.
Shipman last saw Mr Uttley on the day before he died, when he took a blood sample. After that, Mr Uttley appeared to be well until he collapsed suddenly in the market hall. There can be no possible suspicion that Shipman played any part in this death.
I am quite sure that Mr Uttley died a natural death.

name: Edith Brock
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, Flat 4 Carter Place, Hyde
conclusion:
This is an obvious case of unlawful killing. Everything points to that conclusion. Shipman was barely out of Mrs Brock's flat when Mrs Duckworth found her dead. When he left, she must have been dead or very nearly so.
Mrs Brock did not have a history of heart disease or high blood pressure. Her only cardiac symptoms were palpitations and these do not appear to have been thought serious in the past. In fact, Mrs Brock was in good physical condition, as evidenced by her active lifestyle.
Shipman's notes of his consultations with Mrs Brock on the day of her death are inadequate and reveal a standard of care which no doctor would wish to admit to. I am satisfied that Shipman made up the records for that day in order to provide an explanation for the sudden death which would satisfy a confirming doctor and a medical referee. He claimed that Mrs Brock was suffering from supraventricular arrhythmia, which could be associated with ischaemic heart disease. A person with those conditions might have a coronary thrombosis. But if he suspected supraventricular arrhythmia, he should have arranged speedy treatment for Mrs Brock.
Shipman lied to the family about Mrs Brock's medical history, suggesting there was a history of heart disease. He lied on Form B, suggesting that there was an interval of two hours between his departure and the time of death.
I have no doubt whatever that Shipman killed Mrs Brock. The most likely cause of her death was an overdose of opiate, probably diamorphine. Mrs Brock's appearance in death was entirely typical of that of a large number of Shipman's victims.

name: Lavinia Robinson
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 46 Chartist House, Mount Street, Hyde
conclusion:
There is one highly suspicious factor relating to this death. It is that the death occurred in Shipman's presence. There can be no doubt of that, as Shipman admitted as much in the medical records and on the MCCD. As Dr John Grenville has said and, as common sense and experience would suggest, it is most unusual for a sudden death to occur in the presence of a general practitioner. The chances of a sudden death occurring within the ten to fifteen minutes that a visit would usually last must be very small indeed. However, patients often died in Shipman's presence and when this occurs it gives rise to a very high degree of suspicion.
Shipman's explanation for this death would be that Mrs Robinson was suffering from CHF and was therefore at a high risk of sudden death from heart attack. Her death from heart attack was not unexpected. Her sons say that they were quite unaware that their mother had had any symptoms of heart failure or had been on any treatment for it. However, as Mr Albert Henshall said, his mother did not like to bother her sons with details of her health and I think it likely that she kept such matters to herself. It appears to me that Mrs Robinson did have recurring episodes of CHF and was therefore at some increased risk of heart attack.
On the face of it, there is evidence in the records of a quite severe episode of CHF in the week before the death. If Mrs Robinson really had had a severe episode of CHF that week, the risk of her having a heart attack would be raised. However, the evidence that she had that episode is limited to the medical records and is not supported by the witness evidence. I must consider the possibility that Shipman fabricated those records. It is known that Shipman often did fabricate records after killing a patient. There are some signs that these records could have been fabricated. When Shipman visited Mrs Robinson on 9th
February, he recorded that she had a cold, which her sons accept as accurate. The note then went on to deal exclusively with signs of CHF. Shipman did not record any symptoms of a cold or cough. That is slightly strange, as is the fact that he did not record as thorough an examination as one would expect if he were concerned about CHF. There is no record of pulse rate or blood pressure or heart sounds. On the Friday, Shipman visited again but the note is extremely brief. It records only that Mrs Robinson felt better. There is no record of any examination at all.
I accept the evidence of Mr James Henshall that, when he saw his mother in the early afternoon of 16th
February, he had no immediate cause for concern about her health. I am less certain of the accuracy of the sons' recollections about her state of health in the week before her death. It may be that Mrs Robinson did not tell her sons everything about her health. It is possible that their recollections have faded over the years. Having said that, if she was in quite severe heart failure, it is strange that none of them had an inkling of it.
The crucial point is that, when one compares Mr James Henshall's account of his mother at 2pm (which I accept as accurate) with the account suggested by Shipman about 45 minutes later, I am driven to conclude that Shipman's account for that day must be false. I cannot believe that if Mrs Robinson had been suffering from chest pain on and off, as Shipman recorded, her son would have been wholly unaware of it when he visited at 2pm. If Shipman made a false record on that day, he might well have made a false record for the previous days. I conclude that there are sensible grounds to suspect that all three entries for the week of the death might have been fabricated.
The record for the day of the death is typical of many I have seen in cases where Shipman has killed a patient. Here, he records a complaint of chest pain, which might indicate angina. He finds signs of heart failure. Then suddenly, while he is with her, Mrs Robinson collapses. That Mrs Robinson should appear well at 2pm and go into cardiac arrest shortly afterwards, at the very moment Shipman was with her, is just too much of a coincidence. It is beyond belief. I suspect that Shipman's claim that he made a 999 call is false. There is no evidence that an ambulance attended. It is possible that Shipman did indeed attempt resuscitation as he claimed in his note. However, there is no independent confirmation that he did. If the patient were dead as the result of a lethal injection of opiate, there would be no point in calling an ambulance or attempting resuscitation. I am suspicious also of Shipman's claim that a home help and neighbour were present at the death. It is possible that they were, but Shipman often claimed that people were present when they were not and when the truth was that he was alone with the patient throughout the process of dying. In my view, the record describing the death does not ring true.
Taking these factors together, I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Robinson when he visited her in the early afternoon of 16th
February. There is no reason to think that he used any other method than his usual one, a lethal injection of strong opiate.

name: Joyce Woodhead
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 1 Sawyer Brow, Newton, Hyde
conclusion:
I am satisfied that Shipman killed Mrs Woodhead.
Mrs Woodhead was alive when Shipman arrived at some time after 10.30am on the day of her death. No one saw her alive or spoke to her after his visit. There is evidence from which I infer that she was probably dead at the time of Shipman's conversation with Miss Coe at 11.52am. First, I think Mrs Woodhead would have spoken to Miss Coe herself at that time had she been alive. I think Shipman's claim that Mrs Woodhead was resting was just an excuse and the truth was that she could not come to the telephone. Shipman tried to encourage Miss Coe not to come to the house for some time. I am sure he did not want Miss Coe to discover the death too soon. Shipman left soon after that conversation. Had she then been alive, Mrs Woodhead would have telephoned her sister and Miss Coe as soon as Shipman had gone. Shipman gave inconsistent accounts of Mrs Woodhead's condition when he left. To Miss Coe, he said that Mrs Woodhead was resting and that she should not come round. To Mrs Hibbs, he said that Mrs Woodhead had waved him off. Another factor, which makes me think that Mrs Woodhead was already dead when Shipman left, is that, when he spoke to Miss Coe, he asked her for Mrs Hibbs' telephone number. Had Mrs Woodhead been alive, he would have asked her for the number, even if she were having a rest. Finally, Miss Coe went to Mrs Woodhead's house within a few minutes of Shipman's departure. There was no reply at the door. I conclude that Mrs Woodhead was already dead and had died while Shipman was at the house. Shipman lied about this, which points compellingly to his guilt.
There are many other factors which confirm my view that Shipman killed Mrs Woodhead. I am satisfied that Shipman's medical notes are false. He paints a picture of a constellation of symptoms which could indicate that Mrs Woodhead had had a heart attack. However, the symptoms do not closely resemble those which she had mentioned to her sister and Miss Coe. To them she had spoken of having a cold and of having caught a bug. She mentioned stomach ache. Shipman's notes speak of sternal or chest pain radiating into the neck. I suspect that this reference to sternal or chest pain was an attempt to create the impression that Mrs Woodhead had had a heart attack. As Dr Grenville has said, any doctor who was really presented with this constellation of symptoms would wish to admit the patient to hospital for further tests in order to establish a diagnosis. Shipman did not suggest any further tests or offer any treatment at all.
Shipman's explanation to Mrs Hibbs that he had left Mrs Woodhead alone while she decided whether she was prepared to go into hospital, is a variant on the explanation he has given in many other cases. It does not bear examination. First, he wrote in the notes that hospital admission was not necessary. He told Miss Coe that it was not necessary. Had he really suggested hospital admission and had Mrs Woodhead refused, Shipman would have recorded that in the notes. Had Mrs Woodhead refused, and suggested care by her sister as an alternative, either she or Shipman would have telephoned Mrs Hibbs there and then. Instead, Shipman's accounts of why he left Mrs Woodhead, wished to return to see her again and wished to contact Mrs Hibbs, became more elaborate and less plausible as he spoke first to Miss Coe, then to Mrs Stott and then to Mrs Hibbs.
The manner of Mrs Woodhead's death, lying on her bed, looking peaceful, is not at all typical of a death by heart attack or any of the other common causes of sudden death. It is, however, typical of other deaths caused by Shipman, by the administration of diamorphine.
Form B contains a number of demonstrable lies. Mrs Hibbs was not present at the moment of death and could not have contributed any information as to the time or manner of death. The whole document is a fabrication designed to distance Shipman from the death and place another person at the scene. The intention was obviously to allay suspicion.
It is possible that Mrs Woodhead might have had a minor coronary thrombosis during the few days before her death. However, in the light of her previous medical history, no honest medical practitioner could have stated that he had no doubt as to the cause of death. This case should have been reported to the coroner.
All the evidence points to this being a case of an unlawful killing and I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Woodhead.

name: Frances Elaine Oswald
title: Mrs
conclusion:
It seems clear from the contemporaneous documents that an incident did indeed occur on 21st
August 1974, when Mrs Oswald collapsed in Shipman's presence and required resuscitation and hospitalisation. It seems highly likely that the collapse was due to the administration of a drug. It is theoretically possible that it occurred as a result of an overdose of opiates taken recreationally or in an attempt to do harm to herself and that she concealed this in her 'journal entry' and in the account given to her employers. There is no evidence that this was the case and Professor Oswald has denied it. I accept her evidence that she had taken only the Diconal and only as Shipman had instructed. I also accept that the essentials of the account set out in her journal entry are true.
The first issue for me to decide is whether this was a reaction to a painkiller innocently prescribed or the result of the deliberate injection of an opiate by Shipman or a reaction to both drugs combined. If I conclude that Shipman did inject a drug into Mrs Oswald's arm under the guise of taking a blood sample, I must also consider what his intention was in so doing.
What caused Mrs Oswald to collapse? It appears from the pharmacological evidence that it is possible, although unlikely, that Mrs Oswald's collapse was caused by an anaphylactoid reaction or respiratory depression resulting from 20mg Diconal. However, it would have been a remarkable coincidence for such a collapse to occur so soon after Shipman arrived at Mrs Oswald's house. That the collapse occurred in his presence gives rise to suspicion that he caused it. There are other factors which increase my suspicion.
First, there seems no good reason for Shipman to have been at Mrs Oswald's house at all. According to Dr Grenville, blood tests of the type proposed would not assist in diagnosis of a kidney stone. The appropriate diagnostic test was to take a urine sample and examine it for microscopic haematuria. Even if Shipman had thought that a blood test was necessary, there was no apparent reason why this should not have been done at the surgery earlier in the morning. It seems that Shipman was seeking an excuse to visit Mrs Oswald, which is in itself suspicious.
Second, the journal entry describes how the collapse occurred just after Shipman had been using a needle, as Mrs Oswald believed, to take blood from her left arm. In later years Shipman often injected his patients with opiates under the pretext of taking a blood sample. In the light of that, it would seem unlikely that, at the very moment when Shipman 'took a blood sample', Mrs Oswald would collapse from some other unrelated cause. She probably collapsed because the 'taking of the blood sample' was, in truth, an injection in disguise.
It seems likely that Mrs Oswald's collapse followed the giving of an injection of opiate by Shipman. That she had already taken two Diconal tablets must inevitably have increased the risk that she might suffer respiratory arrest and collapse if a further dose of opiate were injected. I think it likely that the collapse was caused by the combination of the Diconal and the additional injected drug.
In my view, the injected drug was probably pethidine. The Inquiry has evidence that Shipman began to acquire pethidine unlawfully from April 1974, only one month after his arrival in Todmorden in March 1974 as a young doctor starting his first job in general practice. It appears highly likely that he was taking pethidine himself at this time. There is no clear evidence that Shipman was obtaining morphine or diamorphine illicitly in 1974, although the possibility must exist.
The question of Shipman's intention then arises. In the light of what is now known of Shipman's later activities, the possibility that he intended to kill Mrs Oswald must be a real one. However, there are several factors which have led me to the conclusion that he almost certainly did not intend to kill her or even to cause her serious harm.
The first is that at this time Shipman was not an established killer and did not become one for some time. If Shipman did try to kill Mrs Oswald, it was his first venture.
Examination of my decisions will show that there was not one among his victims who was young and in good health. In my view, it is clear that if Shipman did try to kill Mrs Oswald, it would have been atypical behaviour, not only at that time but for the rest of his medical career.
Second, an attempt by Shipman to kill Mrs Oswald would have involved a massive risk of discovery. She was a healthy young woman and her death or serious injury would have attracted considerable local attention. It would have inevitably been followed by a post-mortem examination, almost certainly with toxicological tests. The fact that Shipman had seen Mrs Oswald in his surgery that morning and had visited her at home would have become known and his activities would have been subjected to scrutiny. His own use of pethidine and his illegal obtaining of the drug would probably have emerged, together with the fact that he had killed or seriously injured Mrs Oswald. As it was, he faced some risk of investigation. It seems to me that Shipman's attempts to make Mrs Oswald think he had saved her life were designed to prevent her from wondering whether he had done anything to her that he should not have done. I think he was probably terrified that she would make some sort of complaint and the truth would come out.
Third, it is clear that Shipman resuscitated Mrs Oswald. Why he would have done that if he intended to kill her is hard to imagine unless one embarks on the kind of speculation in which Professor Oswald indulged when she suggested that Mrs Shipman had entered the house unexpectedly. A much more obvious reason why he resuscitated her is that he was horrified at her collapse and hastened to do all he could to bring her round.
I think Shipman gave Mrs Oswald an excessive dose of pethidine by mistake and was shocked by its effect. In assessing the dose, he might have failed to take account of the two Diconal tablets she had already taken orally. He might have based his calculation of the pethidine dose on his own usage, forgetting that while he was accustomed to pethidine, Mrs Oswald was opiate-naïve.
If Shipman did not intend to kill Mrs Oswald, what were his intentions? I am sure they were not honourable ones. His conduct afterwards in seeking to placate Mrs Oswald by paying her much attention and being unusually hospitable is compatible with a desire to gloss over the incident. His failure to report the adverse reaction to the drug manufacturer would suggest that he did not want the incident to be investigated. Counsel has suggested that Shipman intended merely to experiment in some way by involving Mrs Oswald in his habit of abusing pethidine. That is possible. Another possibility is that he hoped that, while she was under the influence of the drug, she might agree to indulge in some sexual activity, although to embark on such conduct while his wife was outside in the car seems foolhardy.
My conclusion is that Shipman probably did inject Mrs Oswald with an opiate and caused her to suffer respiratory arrest. I do not feel able to reach any positive conclusion as to his motive. However, I think it is highly unlikely that he had any intention to kill her or to cause her serious harm.
I hope and intend that this decision leaves no one in doubt as to the truth of Professor Oswald's account to the Inquiry of what Shipman did on 21st
August 1974. I have accepted it as true.

name: Lily Higgins
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 352 Stockport Road, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
Mrs Higgins was fit and well only two hours before she was found dead. Her medical history gives no indication that she was at risk of a sudden death, whether from cardiovascular accident or any other cause. Her death on that day is not explicable. There should most certainly have been a post-mortem examination.
Mrs Higgins' appearance after death is not what would be expected if she had suffered a sudden death from cardiovascular accident or a cardiac cause. However, it is entirely typical of the appearance of many victims who had been killed by Shipman by means of a lethal injection of diamorphine.
The MCCD and Form B contain a number of lies. I am satisfied that Shipman had not seen Mrs Higgins 11 days before her death. He said that he had because, if the truth had been stated, that he had not seen her for over a year, the death would certainly have been referred to the coroner.
The lies on Form B are, in my judgement, plainly designed to give the impression that Mrs Higgins had been ill for some time (so that her death would not be unexpected) and that responsible and experienced paramedics had been present at the death and would have been able to give a reliable account of what had occurred. A wholly false picture was presented, designed to ensure that the medical referee would authorise cremation.
There is no direct evidence that Shipman had visited Mrs Higgins that afternoon. There is evidence that he had the time to visit her and that he was in the area. That he was not seen visiting her does not mean that he did not do so. He was not seen even when it is known that he visited, after the death. Stockport Road is very busy. He could have visited her before her death.
I am more influenced by the strange entry in the computerised medical records made by Shipman at 3pm on the afternoon of the death. Shipman had not seen Mrs Higgins for over a year. He had not signed a repeat prescription for her for many months. Yet, on the very afternoon of her death, he made an entry in her notes, backdated by about seven weeks, suggesting that he had seen her in the market and had reminded her that she had had a letter from him and was due to come in for a check-up. If, on the afternoon of 17th March, he had suddenly remembered that, seven weeks earlier, he had seen Mrs Higgins and spoken to her in the market and had decided to make a note in the records, it would be the most remarkable coincidence that that thought should have occurred to him, out of the blue, on the afternoon of her death. In my view, coincidences of that kind do not occur. There must be another explanation for Shipman making that entry. If he had been to her house and had killed her, it would be expected that he would take out her medical records on his return to the surgery. I have found that he has done that on many occasions. Here, I think he must have been at a loss to think of anything that he could enter into the records to provide a plausible explanation for her death. There was no chronic illness on which to base an explanation. It seems to me that he must have decided that the best he could do was to suggest that Mrs Higgins had neglected to come in for a check-up, so that her state of health might have deteriorated, without any record having been made.
In my judgement, the evidence of the wristwatch and this false entry in the records provide a sufficient link to Shipman for me to say that I am satisfied that he did visit Mrs Higgins on the afternoon of her death. Notwithstanding the absence of direct evidence of his presence, I am satisfied, so as to be sure, that Shipman killed Mrs Higgins.

name: Moira Kelly
title: Miss
place_of_death: the Fielden Hospital, Todmorden
conclusion: I am quite sure that Miss Kelly died as the result of natural causes. There is no evidence whatsoever to suggest that Shipman was in any way involved in her death.

name: Annie Nash
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion:
In the absence of any medical records, it is not possible to be certain about Mrs Nash’s condition in the days before her death. However, from the description given by Mrs Higgins, it appears that Mrs Nash suffered a stroke on 9th
May and that she never fully regained consciousness after that time. Dr Aneez Esmail, Medical Advisor to the Inquiry, has advised me that the fact that Mrs Nash was unconscious and did not regain consciousness is a sign of the severity of the stroke that she suffered. The prognosis in such situations is invariably poor and patients are at risk of dying either from a further extension of the stroke or from the risk of other sequelae such as bronchopneumonia. The restlessness was almost certainly a sign of cerebral irritation and was not an indication that she was going to recover. It is therefore entirely possible that Mrs Nash died a natural death on the evening of 12th
May.
Having said that, it must be recognised that Shipman was on duty that evening. If the nurse to whom Mrs Higgins spoke at about 8pm did indeed call a doctor to see Mrs Nash, that doctor would almost certainly have been Shipman. We do not know whether she did call him. It does not seem likely that she would call a doctor just because Mrs Nash needed some water. It is possible that the nurse had noticed some deterioration in Mrs Nash’s condition that the family was unaware of. Cremation Form B suggests that Shipman was called to see her. Shipman claims that he knew, from his own observation, that Mrs Nash had been in a coma for one to two hours. If the death occurred at 8.45pm, that entry suggests that Shipman must have seen Mrs Nash either immediately before visiting time at 7pm or soon after the end of visiting time at 8pm. In the light of the nurse’s indication that she intended to call the doctor, it is more likely that Shipman saw Mrs Nash after 8pm. I infer that he probably did see her soon after 8pm.
It would be usual for a nurse to remain with the doctor while s/he examined and treated the patient. However, I believe that, on occasion, doctors were left alone with patients. I do not know whether this was one such occasion. Nor do I know whether Shipman administered any drug to Mrs Nash. He could have done. She might then have been found dead some time later by the nursing staff and Shipman would have been called back to certify the fact that she had died.
Professor Richard Baker’s review has shown that an unusually high proportion of the deaths whose cause was certified by Shipman took place during the evening. That gives rise to a suspicion that he killed some patients during that time. I cannot say whether or not Mrs Nash was one of those. All I can say is that it appears that Shipman saw Mrs Nash shortly before her death and may have had the opportunity to give her something which hastened her death. There are grounds for some suspicion but that is all.
I very much regret that I have had to raise these doubts so many years after the death and I am sorry for the distress this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: John Howcroft
title: Mr
conclusion:
There are two suspicious features connected with this death. First, Mr Howcroft's position after death is not wholly consistent with a death from natural causes. If he had had a heart attack, Mr Howcroft would have been likely to fall from his upright chair. Second, Shipman has given a time of death on Form B which cannot possibly be a genuine estimate. It was not possible for him to make an accurate estimate with the information available to him. If he had visited Mr Howcroft and feared that he might have been seen, he might have advanced this spurious time of death to deflect suspicion from himself.
On the other hand, Mr Peter Howcroft's recollection that he received a telephone call on the evening of 1st
January, in which someone seemed to breathe heavily in a distressed manner, is consistent with Mr Howcroft having made an attempt to contact his grandson while in the throes of death. The observation by Shipman that, when found, Mr Howcroft had the telephone in his hand and a pad of numbers on his knee, tends to support that theory. However, it is possible that that telephone call did come from Mr Howcroft while in the throes of death but that it was made in the presence of Shipman. So I do not think I can draw any firm conclusion from that circumstance.
As there are no medical records, I cannot form any view as to the likelihood that Mr Howcroft might have suffered a sudden cardiac death.
It is with regret that I feel obliged to say that I am unable to reach a conclusion one way or the other about the true cause of Mr Howcroft's death, although I am suspicious about it.

name: Harold Edward Jackman
title: Mr
place_of_death: Halifax General Hospital
conclusion:
The post-mortem examination revealed physical findings sufficient to account for death. In the opinions of both Professor Whitwell and Dr Grenville, Mr Jackman would have suffered a degree of renal failure and this was the most likely explanation for his death.
There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman saw Mr Jackman on the day of his death. It is quite possible that he did and that it was he who arranged the admission to hospital. We do not know. If he did, it is quite possible that he gave Mr Jackman an injection of some kind of opiate. If he was in pain, as seems very likely, some pain relief would seem appropriate for the journey. It is not always easy to assess what dose is appropriate for a patient who is suffering severe pain, especially if the patient has been receiving opiates over a period of time. It will usually be necessary to increase the dosage as the pain worsens and the patient becomes accustomed to the effect of the drug. If Shipman gave an injection, we do not know how much he gave.
It seems unlikely (although not impossible) that any dose given to Mr Jackman could have been the principal cause of his death. Professor Henry McQuay and Dr Grenville say that an intramuscular injection of an opiate reaches its maximal effect within between 30 and 60 minutes from the time of the injection. Therefore, if Shipman had administered a lethal injection before Mr Jackman left home, one might have expected him to die either during the journey or very soon after arrival at hospital. Although there are elements of speculation in this calculation (as the times given by the experts are subject to some variability, the journey time is not known and it is not clear how long after arrival Mr Jackman died), it rather looks as though Mr Jackman could not have died as the direct result of a lethal injection of opiate.
Bearing in mind the findings at post-mortem examination and the opinions of the experts, it seems to me highly likely that Mr Jackman died a natural death. There is no positive evidence that Shipman played any part in events. It is possible that Shipman was present shortly before Mr Jackman was put into the ambulance and that he gave a pain-relieving injection before the journey. If he did, it is likely that the injection was intended only to relieve pain, although it might have had the unintended effect of hastening the death. I cannot absolutely rule out the possibility that he gave an injection of opiate before Mr Jackman left home and that the dose was excessive and intended to hasten Mr Jackman's end. However, I stress that there is no evidence that this occurred.

name: William Givens
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 27 Waverley Road, Hyde
certified_cause: respiratory failure due to chronic bronchitis and emphysema
conclusion:
There is no evidence that Shipman murdered Mr Givens in the way that he killed many other patients, by giving him a lethal dose of an opiate. Mr Givens lived for about five or six hours after Shipman had given him the second injection. Had that injection been of a lethal dose, Mr Givens would have died within about an hour. It is possible that Shipman gave a sub-lethal dose of opiate or other narcotic drug, which caused respiratory depression and contributed to the death.
It is entirely possible that the intramuscular injections, said by Shipman to be Largactil, were in fact Largactil. However, we do not know what dosage was given. Mr Givens appears to have gone to sleep soon afterwards and the evidence suggests that he never awoke. It is not clear whether he was in distress at the time of the second injection. I suspect that Shipman might have over-sedated Mr Givens. There would be a risk attached to giving Mr Givens a drug such as Largactil, as it can cause respiratory depression. As Mr Givens' respiratory function was already poor, it would be important not to risk over-sedating him. If Mr Givens were over-sedated, he would become more vulnerable to bronchopneumonia, a common mechanism of death in elderly patients with poor respiratory function. The administration of two doses within a few hours gives rise to a suspicion that Shipman might have intended not to relieve distress but to hasten the death.
Concern also arises because it appears that Shipman might have taken a deliberate decision to allow Mr Givens to die. Mr Givens was not seriously ill until the morning of 28th
September. It sounds as though he had a chest infection, probably an infective exacerbation of his chronic bronchitis. The standard treatment would be to prescribe an antibiotic but it appears that this was not done. Usually a seriously ill patient would be admitted to hospital. Shipman gave only an injection of something to make Mr Givens more comfortable. He did not discuss the available options with the family but announced that Mr Givens had not long to live. If this is what really happened, Shipman's actions were, at the very least, negligent. If his decision to withhold antibiotic treatment were taken deliberately, it would be quite unethical and might be unlawful. If Shipman, who owed a duty to Mr Givens, had consciously decided not to give the standard treatment without which he realised Mr Givens would probably die, Shipman would have shown so complete a disregard for Mr Givens' welfare as might well amount to the offence of manslaughter. However, it is not possible for me to make a positive decision on this issue. Shipman might have genuinely believed that nothing could save Mr Givens' life and he might have been right. I am left with a real suspicion that Shipman may have taken it upon himself to decide, without discussion with the patient or family, that the best thing to do was to let Mr Givens die. This would be consistent with Shipman's philosophy that, with elderly or sick patients, he did not approve of keeping them going.
I regret to say that I am unable to reach a positive conclusion on this case. There are grounds to suspect that Shipman might have decided to ensure that Mr Givens died, by a combination of a decision not to give an antibiotic which might have extended his life and by over-sedating him and hastening the end.

name: Gladys Roberts
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 25 Shaw Hall Avenue, Hyde
certified_cause: pulmonary embolus due to right deep vein thrombosis
conclusion:
There are a number of suspicious features surrounding this death.
Although her medical records are unavailable, the witness evidence suggests that, apart from her ulcerated leg, Mrs Roberts was in reasonably good health. On the morning of her death, Mrs Ashton thought that she looked well. The nurse who attended to dress Mrs Roberts' leg thought that a visit by Shipman was needed to assess whether Mrs Roberts might benefit from hospital treatment. We do not know why the nurse formed this view. There are many possibilities. One is that the ulcer was not healing as rapidly as it should. It might have become infected. It is possible that the nurse thought that Mrs Roberts might have a deep vein thrombosis. As Dr John Grenville explained when giving evidence to the Inquiry in the case of Mrs Elizabeth Battersby, it can sometimes be difficult to diagnose a deep vein thrombosis in an ulcerated leg. The presence of the ulcer creates an increased risk of deep vein thrombosis. The nurse would know that, if Mrs Roberts had a deep vein thrombosis, she ought to be admitted to hospital, as an emergency, as she was at risk of suffering a pulmonary embolism. However, it seems unlikely that the nurse thought Mrs Roberts was acutely ill, otherwise she would almost certainly have called an ambulance. It does not appear that Mrs Roberts thought that she might be admitted to hospital that day, rather that she might be referred to the hospital. I think it doubtful that the nurse thought that there was a deep vein thrombosis, although it is possible that she did. I am quite sure that Mrs Roberts was not at that stage suffering from a pulmonary embolism.
It must be accepted that there is a possibility that Mrs Roberts had a deep vein thrombosis in her right leg. If so, she was at risk of suffering a pulmonary embolism. However, most pulmonary emboli do not result in death. Only a very large embolus will kill. Before a large embolus breaks off, one would expect the leg with the deep vein thrombosis to be very swollen, hot and painful. One might have expected Mrs Roberts to have noticed such symptoms for herself and mentioned them to her family. I conclude that, even though it is possible that Mrs Roberts might have been developing a deep vein thrombosis, this was unlikely to have been of the severity usually necessary to cause a sudden death by pulmonary embolus.
Shipman's account of the death is frankly unbelievable. First, there is the remarkable coincidence that the death occurred during the few minutes that Shipman was in Mrs Roberts' house. That in itself is an extraordinary coincidence and I find it hard to believe that Mrs Roberts' embolus (if she had one) could have chosen the very moment of Shipman's presence to reach her lungs and kill her. In any event, death by pulmonary embolism is a very painful and frightening event. If the embolus is large enough to be fatal, it will have blocked the flow of blood to the lungs. The patient will be gasping for breath. If Mrs Roberts died in those circumstances, she would be unlikely to look peaceful in death.
Shipman claimed that Mrs Roberts simply coughed and died. That would not be typical of a death by pulmonary embolus. I could understand that a doctor might wish to understate the pain and distress suffered when describing the death to relatives. I note that Shipman did not give this extraordinary account when completing Form B. His medical colleagues would surely have known it was false. To them, he said that he found Mrs Roberts dead when he returned from making a telephone call to arrange admission to hospital. In fact, the telephone was in the living room where Mrs Roberts died.
If, as is entirely possible, Shipman was summoned because the nurse suspected that Mrs Roberts might have a deep vein thrombosis, I would have expected him to undo her bandage to examine her leg. It appears that he probably did not do so.
Mrs Roberts was found with her dress partly undone and her arm out of the sleeve. A possible explanation for that is that Shipman might have wished to examine the back of her chest with his stethoscope. It seems to me that that is a rather more plausible explanation for her state of partial undress than the explanation Shipman gave. I cannot think that it would help with resuscitation to take one arm out of a dress. There are other signs that resuscitation did not take place. It would be impossible to carry it out while Mrs Roberts' spectacles were on her nose. If Shipman did attempt resuscitation, he would need a firm surface and would have had to put Mrs Roberts on the floor. Why he would then wish to move her onto the settee and leave her as he did is hard to understand.
I am puzzled by Shipman's claim on Form B that he had attended Mrs Roberts during her last illness for a period of 12 hours. It is highly unlikely to be true, but is probably not a deliberate lie.
Mrs Roberts' peaceful appearance in death is not consistent with death caused by a pulmonary embolism, as Dr Grenville explained when he gave evidence in the case of Mrs Elizabeth Battersby on 13th
November 2001. However, it is wholly consistent with death by a lethal injection of opiates.
Taking all the factors together, I think I can safely rule out the possibility that Mrs Roberts really did die suddenly as the result of massive pulmonary embolism. I am driven to the conclusion that Shipman must have killed her. There is no reason to think that he used any other than his usual method, the administration of a lethal dose of strong opiate. I am sure of this conclusion.

name: Mary Gaunt
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her daughter's home, in Hyde
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to carcinoma of the stomach
conclusion:
It is clear that Mrs Gaunt was extremely ill shortly before her death and was in great pain. It seems likely that Shipman gave Mrs Gaunt an injection on the Sunday morning to relieve her pain. We do not know exactly what the injection was. It might have been morphine from her own supply or it might have been diamorphine supplied by Shipman. In any event, we do not know how much was given. Nor do we know to what extent Mrs Gaunt had become accustomed to morphine during the terminal stage of her illness.
It is not clear how long after the injection Mrs Gaunt died. Shipman himself said she died two hours after he saw her. However, Shipman was frequently careless or deceitful when completing cremation forms. It is entirely possible that he wrote two hours on the form because it was two hours since he had seen Mrs Gaunt, rather than two hours before she died. Mrs Ollerenshaw initially told the Inquiry that her mother died 'a few hours' after the injection was given. Later, she said that the death occurred about 30 minutes to an hour afterwards.
Professor Henry McQuay and Dr John Grenville have told the Inquiry that if a lethal dose of opiate is given intramuscularly, the patient will die within about an hour of administration. It is possible (but by no means clear) that Mrs Gaunt died within about an hour after the injection. Accordingly, it is possible that Shipman had given her an excessive dose of opiate, intending to end her life that day. However, it is also entirely possible that she died after two or more hours had elapsed, in which case the injection cannot have been a lethal dose. At whatever time Mrs Gaunt died, it is quite possible that Shipman gave a dose that he honestly intended should only relieve her pain. Dr Grenville has said that it can be very difficult to assess the right amount of opiate to give a terminally ill patient. In seeking to relieve the pain, the doctor might unintentionally hasten the patient's death. I cannot say whether or not Shipman deliberately hastened Mrs Gaunt's end.

name: Frederick King
title: Mr
place_of_death: on Ward 2, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: haemorrhagic pneumonia of the right lung
conclusion:
Having considered the material before the Inquiry, I am satisfied that Mr King had generally enjoyed good health but that this changed in early 1972. It can never be known whether the lump that he developed in his neck was or was not connected with his later symptoms of extreme tiredness. However, the absence of any reference to the lump in the mortuary record of the post-mortem examination suggests that the lump was not considered to be germane to the cause of death.
The post-mortem record shows that Mr King had pneumonia. After Mr King was admitted to hospital, his wife was told that he had a severe chest infection. The two pieces of information are consistent. Mr King’s extreme tiredness in the period before his admission is also consistent with the development of a chest infection of increasing seriousness. The development of confusion in the last day or so before the death is also consistent with the diagnosis of pneumonia. It seems to me that the diagnosis of pneumonia is as clear as one could hope for in the absence of medical records. I think I can reassure the King family that Mr King’s underlying illness was pneumonia and was not connected with the lump in his neck. I am also of the view that Mr King could well have died of pneumonia without any intervention on the part of Shipman.
However, Mr Howard King remains concerned that Shipman might have played some part in causing his father’s death. That is certainly a possibility. Shipman was the SHO on the ward at the time and was involved in Mr King’s treatment. Mr Howard King is concerned about some of the entries on cremation Form B. Shipman stated that Mr King was in a coma for two days and Mr Howard King says that he was not. I understand Mr Howard King’s concern but do not think that this inconsistency suggests that Shipman did anything wrong. I think it entirely possible that Shipman used the expression ‘coma’ loosely, meaning only that Mr King’s level of consciousness was depressed, which it clearly was. Of potentially greater significance is Shipman’s assertion that Mr King’s wife and one of his sons were present at the death when they were not. That entry is puzzling. It may be that Shipman saw members of the family at the hospital and assumed that they had been present at the time of death. It is possible that Shipman deliberately lied when making that entry. I cannot say that he did but, if he did, then that would increase any suspicion about his involvement.
Perhaps the most troubling feature is that the family was advised to leave the hospital and that Mr King died very soon afterwards. I can understand why the family is concerned about that. However, there is no evidence that the advice to leave was given by Shipman or on his instructions. There is no reason to suspect that it was given in order to get the family out of the way. It might have been given because the nurse thought that Mrs King was looking tired (she had been at the hospital for about five days) and genuinely believed that there would be no change in Mr King’s condition for some time. It may have been pure mischance that Mr King died so soon after the family’s departure. That said, I cannot rule out the possibility that Shipman gave instructions intended to get the family out of the way and that he then gave Mr King something which hastened his death. If he did, I think the death was advanced by only a very short period. However, I stress that there is no evidence that Shipman played any sinister part in this death and my opinion is that the death was very probably natural.

name: Tom Redfern
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 9 Carter Street, Hyde
conclusion:
The evidence strongly suggests that Mr Redfern was very ill as a result of respiratory failure in the days leading up to his death and that his mental faculties were compromised by impairment of the oxygen supply to his brain. There was grave concern about his prospects of survival on the morning of 29th
October. His death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
There is inevitably some concern when the evidence suggests that Shipman gave an injection shortly before the death. Mr Peter Redfern does not say what the injection was, but his sister recalls that she was told it was Largactil. As she is a nurse, I think she is likely to have remembered the name of the drug accurately. I think it probably was Largactil and not an opiate.
If an opiate had been given, it would certainly have hastened Mr Redfern's death, as opiates depress respiration and Mr Redfern's respiratory function was already severely compromised. However, I can be almost certain that Shipman did not give Mr Redfern a lethal dose of opiate. It appears that the injection was given at about lunchtime and that Mr Redfern did not die until shortly before 6pm. Had the injection been of a lethal dose, capable of directly causing the death, Mr Redfern would have died within an hour.
In a suitable dose, Largactil would have been an appropriate drug to give for Mr Redfern's confusion and distress. As I do not know what dose was given, I cannot say with complete confidence that Mr Redfern's death was not deliberately hastened by the giving of an excessive dose.
In the light of all the evidence, I feel able to conclude that it is highly likely that Mr Redfern died of the natural causes certified by Shipman.

name: Sarah Ann Thomas
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 7 Ridgefoot, Todmorden
conclusion:
This death was investigated because Shipman certified the cause of death.
In the absence of the medical records or any evidence from those who cared for Mrs Thomas in the days before her death, it is not possible to reach any firm conclusion as to whether Shipman might have caused the death. In the absence of the MCCD or a cremation certificate, there is no evidence of when Shipman last visited Mrs Thomas.

name: George Fisher
title: Mr
place_of_death: on Ward 2, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
Without the benefit of medical records, it is impossible to reach any firm conclusion about Mr Fisher’s death. As Mr Fisher retired early owing to angina, it seems very likely that he was suffering from ischaemic heart disease. He would be vulnerable to a coronary thrombosis and it seems likely that this is what had happened to precipitate his admission to hospital on 14th
April. Dr Aneez Esmail, Medical Advisor to the Inquiry, has told me that Mr Fisher, having been admitted to hospital following a coronary thrombosis, was at very high risk of suffering another in the 48 hours following admission. Therefore, it is entirely possible that Mr Fisher had a further cardiac episode late in the evening of 16th
April and died naturally as a result.
That said, there are reasons to suspect that Shipman might have caused Mr Fisher’s death. The most striking feature of the information on cremation Form B is that Shipman claims that he was present when Mr Fisher went into cardiac arrest, apparently at about 10.40pm. How and why Shipman should have been present at that moment is not clear. We have neither medical nor nursing records which might have explained it. Shipman might have been summoned by a nurse who had found Mr Fisher to be suffering chest pain and apparently having another heart attack. If so, Shipman might have arrived before Mr Fisher went into cardiac arrest and might have witnessed it as he claimed to have done. However, if that were so, one would have expected that a member of the nursing staff would have stayed with Mr Fisher and that Shipman would have mentioned that person as having been present with him at the death. If Shipman had found Mr Fisher in pain as he was passing by his bed, one would have expected him to call a nurse and that she would have remained at the bedside until death. It was very unusual for other doctors to be present alone at the deaths of their patients. It was not unusual for Shipman to imply on Form B that he had been present alone although, as I have explained in
Chapter Seven
, claims made by Shipman on cremation Forms B that he was present or present alone at a death cannot always be relied on as being accurate. It is possible that Shipman decided to engineer an opportunity to be alone with Mr Fisher so as to end his life. It would have been very easy for Shipman to give Mr Fisher a drug which would lead to cardiac arrest.
The proportion of deaths certified by Shipman that occurred between the hours of 6pm and midnight was abnormal and far greater than for other doctors. This death occurred during that period. For that reason and because Shipman claims to have been alone with Mr Fisher at the moment of death, I have some suspicion that Shipman may have caused the death. However, the evidence is not sufficiently clear for me to reach a definite conclusion.
I very much regret that I have had to raise these doubts so many years after the death and I am sorry for the distress this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Ethel Follon
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion:
Although Mrs Smalley does not have a detailed recollection of her aunt’s admission to hospital, her evidence about her aunt’s final illness is very helpful. She is able to confirm that Mrs Follon was terminally ill with a brain tumour. The cause of death certified by Shipman is exactly what one would have expected. The death came as no surprise to the family. But for the fact that Shipman was involved in her care and claimed to have been present at the time of her death, there would be no reason to suspect that her death resulted from anything other than natural causes.
However, Shipman was involved in Mrs Follon’s treatment and said on Form B that he was present, apparently alone, at the death. For reasons that I have explained in this Report, and for reasons that are acknowledged by Mrs Burchill, it was very unusual for a doctor to be alone at the death of a patient, although, as I have explained in
Chapter Seven
, there are several reasons to doubt that he was always present or present alone when he claimed to have been. Whenever Shipman implied that he had been present alone at a death, there would be cause for suspicion that he might have given something to the patient to cause or hasten the death. In this case, suspicion is heightened because there would be no reason for Shipman to be called to see Mrs Follon. She had been in a coma for two days, according to Shipman, and that is supported by Mrs Smalley. She would have been receiving only general nursing care. It is hard to imagine why Shipman would have been called to see her by a nurse until the death had occurred. How and why he could legitimately have been present at the death is puzzling. As the death took place during the evening, there is further cause for suspicion. There were fewer staff on duty during the evening and it would be easier for Shipman to be alone with a patient if he wished to be. If he wished to do so, he could easily slip into a cubicle unobserved and no one would have realised that he was there. Professor Richard Baker has observed that a disproportionately large number of deaths of patients whose deaths were certified by Shipman occurred in the period between 6pm and midnight.
I have already said that Mrs Follon was terminally ill as a result of her brain tumour and had not long to live. Even without any intervention from Shipman, she was likely to die very soon. That said, there are some grounds to suspect, on the basis of what he wrote on Form B, that Shipman may have entered her room alone, late in the evening, and, knowing that she was likely to die soon, given her something which hastened her death.
I very much regret that I have had to raise these doubts so many years after the death and I am sorry for the distress this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI, once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Arthur Henderson Stopford
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 17 Rydal Avenue, Hyde
conclusion:
There are highly suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. The first and most obvious is the temporal connection between Shipman's visit and the discovery of Mr Stopford's death. Although Shipman sought to establish that an unidentified neighbour had seen Mr Stopford alive after he, Shipman, had left, there is no evidence that such a neighbour existed. As there was no neighbour present in the house when Shipman came to see the body, it is hard to imagine how he could have discovered this information. There must be a very strong suspicion that this neighbour is an invention of Shipman, designed to avoid any suspicion that he was associated with the death.
There is no evidence that Mr Stopford was seriously ill. He had not seen Shipman for about three months before 26th
August. He appears to have had a very unpleasant attack of gastroenteritis. However, the results of the tests taken on the day of the death do not indicate that Mr Stopford was very ill. It is hard to imagine how Mr Stopford could have died a natural death three days later. It unfortunately seems that Shipman planned to kill Mr Stopford some time before he died, which would explain why he told Mr Stopford's daughter that he had cancer.
As Dr Grenville said, it was not acceptable for Shipman to ascribe Mr Stopford's death to old age. Dr Grenville told the Inquiry that old age is justifiable as a cause of death in an elderly person who has been ill for some considerable time and where there has been multiple organ failure and a gradual deterioration to the point of death. In those circumstances, if the doctor is unsure of the precise mechanism of death, it is acceptable to say that the cause of death is old age. Clearly, this did not apply in Mr Stopford's case.
Taking these factors together, I am driven to the clear conclusion that Shipman killed Mr Stopford. It was particularly easy for Shipman to kill a patient from whom he wished to take blood samples. Shipman had an opportunity to introduce a needle into a patient's veins. Many patients do not watch when their doctor takes a blood sample. Shipman had an opportunity to give a lethal injection of opiate when he had taken the blood samples. I have no doubt that is what happened with Mr Stopford.

name: Beatrice Lowe
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 34 Baron Road, Hyde
conclusion:
Although the medical records are no longer available and have probably been destroyed, the witness evidence suggests that Mrs Lowe's health had gradually deteriorated in the months leading up to her death. In the last few weeks of her life she spent most of her time confined to bed. Towards the end, she seems to have slept a great deal. The death was neither sudden nor unexpected. The picture presented by the witness evidence is consistent with the gradual failure of one or more of her vital organs.
There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman saw Mrs Lowe in the hours before her death and I therefore rule out the possibility that Shipman unlawfully killed her by administering a lethal dose of opiates which directly caused her death. However, I cannot rule out the possibility that Shipman administered a sub-lethal dose of opiates or a large dose of a sedative when he visited on 15th
October, two days before Mrs Lowe died. If sedated, Mrs Lowe would be vulnerable to bronchopneumonia, a common mechanism of death in elderly people. If Shipman did this, it would not be possible to say whether he had done it with the intention of keeping Mrs Lowe comfortable or whether he used it as an indirect way of hastening her death.
I regret that I cannot reach a positive decision in this case. There are grounds to suspect that Shipman might have hastened Mrs Lowe's death. All I can say is that it would appear that, if Shipman did hasten Mrs Lowe's end, he shortened her life by only a short period.

name: Esther Hannah Roberts
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 11 Bryce Street, Hyde
conclusion:
Mrs Platt's description of the development of her aunt's symptoms is entirely consistent with developing bronchopneumonia. Dr John Grenville has described the usual course of this condition in his generic evidence. The range of treatments available for bronchopneumonia includes an intravenous injection of antibiotics. It is entirely possible that Shipman gave Mrs Roberts an antibiotic on 19th
December.
Shipman's visit took place several hours before Mrs Roberts' death, probably over 12 hours. In his evidence to the Inquiry, Professor Henry McQuay said that an intravenous dose of opiate would reach maximal effect within a few minutes. If the dose were lethal, the patient would die within minutes. An intramuscular dose would reach maximal effect within about an hour and, if the dose were lethal, the patient would die within that time. After a few hours, the effect of the drug would be wearing off. That Mrs Roberts lived for several hours after Shipman's visit demonstrates that he cannot have given her a lethal dose of opiate. As she remained conscious for some time after Shipman's departure, it appears very unlikely that the injection was of an opiate or a sedative. It seems likely that the injection was an antibiotic.
Mrs Platt has provided a clear account of her aunt's symptoms, which were entirely typical of bronchopneumonia. As there is no reason to suppose that Shipman played any sinister part in this death, I am able to say that I am quite satisfied that Mrs Roberts died a natural death.

name: Agnes Davidson
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: left ventricular failure due to ischaemic heart disease and hypertensive disease
conclusion:
It is clear that Mrs Davidson had a sudden episode of illness, which resulted in her admission to hospital as an emergency. It seems likely that the sudden episode was due to a problem with her heart. It also appears, however, that she made a reasonable recovery over the following days and that her condition on the afternoon of the day of her death was reasonable. Nevertheless, the fact that she had suffered a recent heart problem put her at increased risk of suffering a further episode. It is entirely possible that she suffered a second, more serious, episode on the evening of 14th
April and that this resulted in her death. However, Mrs Davidson’s death does give rise to some cause for suspicion that Shipman might have been involved. He suggested on Form B that he was alone with Mrs Davidson at the time of her death. That is an unusual circumstance with other doctors. If he was present alone, this is sufficient to make me suspicious about the death although, as I explained in
Chapter Seven
, the fact that Shipman stated that he was present alone at the moment of death does not necessarily mean that he was. That suspicion is increased because the death took place in the late evening. As Professor Baker has pointed out, deaths certified by other doctors at PGI were evenly spread throughout the 24 hour day. However, an abnormal proportion of deaths certified by Shipman took place in the late evening. At that time, there would be little activity on the ward. It would be relatively easy for Shipman to gain access to a patient in the absence of a nurse.
For these reasons, I feel unable to say with confidence that Mrs Davidson’s death was natural. It may have been, but the factors I have outlined above give rise to some suspicion that Shipman might have caused it.
I very much regret that I have had to raise these doubts so many years after the death and I am sorry for the distress this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI, once those concerns had been communicated to th Inquiry.

name: Ernest Gummerson
title: Mr
place_of_death: on Ward 5, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: acute peritonitis due to a perforated duodenal ulcer
conclusion: Very little information is available about the circumstances of Mr Gummerson’s death. However, that which is known suggests that the death was natural and due to the perforation of a duodenal ulcer. There is no reason to suspect that Shipman caused or contributed to the death.

name: Peter Lewis
title: Mr
certified_cause: congestive heart failure and that he died on 2nd January
conclusion:
It is clear that Mr Lewis was severely and terminally ill when he died. It is also clear that he was in severe pain despite the medication that was being given, which included an opiate, probably diamorphine. If Shipman hastened his death, he can only have done so by a very short period.
It seems clear that Shipman gave Mr Lewis an intravenous injection not long before he died. It is highly likely that this was diamorphine. Mr Lewis had probably been taking diamorphine regularly for some time for pain relief and would be accustomed to its effects. It is not known how large a dose he had been receiving at each injection. Nor is it known how much Shipman gave that night. A further injection would have been appropriate treatment, provided that the dose was estimated in good faith as being that which was necessary to relieve Mr Lewis' pain. Doctors in this position may face a difficult decision. They may realise that the dose they think will be necessary to relieve pain will also have the effect of shortening that patient's life. If the dose is given with the primary intention of relieving pain, the act is not only lawful, it is entirely proper. If, on the other hand, the doctor deliberately gives a dose which is larger than that necessary for the relief of pain, with the primary objective of bringing life to an end, that would be unlawful.
It would have been entirely proper for Shipman to give an injection on the evening of New Year's Day to relieve Mr Lewis' pain. We do not know how much he gave or how much would have been appropriate as pain relief. It follows that the only evidence from which I can infer Shipman's intention is evidence of his words and actions that evening and the period of time which elapsed between the injection and the death.
Professor Henry McQuay and Dr John Grenville agree that if an intravenous injection of diamorphine contains a lethal dose, the death will occur within a few minutes of the injection. There is a conflict of evidence between the two witnesses as to how much time elapsed between the injection and the death. On Mrs Gee's account, death occurred very soon after the injection. On Mrs Hamilton's account, it did not occur for an appreciable time. If the death occurred within a few minutes of the injection, this would suggest that Shipman might have intended to hasten death. However, I could not safely conclude, on this evidence alone, that it had been so intended, as the dose might have been intended only to relieve pain but had had the unintended effect of hastening the death.
I am puzzled by the evidence of timing. The only documentary evidence still available is the death certificate. It records that the death took place on 2nd
January. Unless Shipman made a mistake and wrote 2nd
when he meant 1st
January (which seems an unlikely error on New Year's Day) he seems to have been saying that the death took place just after midnight. Shipman was often both careless and dishonest in his completion of the official documents connected with death certification but I doubt if he would have deliberately entered a false date of death when the death had taken place in his own presence and that of the deceased's family. So I incline to the view that Mr Lewis did indeed die after midnight on 2nd
January. If that is so, I think both Mrs Hamilton and Mrs Gee must be mistaken about the time at which Shipman was summoned and the time of his arrival. I think it must have been later than they recall. If he came much later, say at some time around 11pm, it would more readily explain why Mrs Shipman was with him. Possibly they had been out together to a social occasion or possibly Shipman had had a drink at home and did not want to drive.
Even if this theory explains the time given on the death certificate, it does not help me to decide whether the death occurred a few minutes after the injection was given or considerably longer. I am inclined to doubt the accuracy of Mrs Hamilton's recollection about the passage of time on this evening. I think that these events were so traumatic that events which took only a few minutes seemed to her to have taken a long time. Although I have reservations about some aspects of Mrs Gee's evidence, I do think it likely that her estimate of the time between the start of the injection, Mrs Hamilton's hurried exit from the bedroom, Mrs Gee's entry into the bedroom, her return to the living room, Mrs Hamilton's return to the bedroom and the moment of death is more likely to be accurate than Mrs Hamilton's. I think the likely course of events is that Mrs Hamilton went in with Shipman and stayed until Shipman was giving the injection. She then ran out in distress, having seen blood in the needle. Mrs Gee went into the bedroom and saw Shipman doing something with a pillow. She heard Mr Lewis' 'rattly' breathing and realised that he was close to death. She returned to the living room and told her daughter to go into the bedroom; she probably assured her that the injection was over. When Mrs Hamilton went back into the bedroom, she saw Shipman with his hand at her husband's mouth or throat. Something was said which made her realise that her husband was about to die. She felt unable to remain and returned to the living room. When Shipman came out of the bedroom, he advised her to sit with her husband's body for a while, so that, in her own mind, she would accept that he had died. I think all of those events probably took place almost continuously. I also think it highly unlikely that, if Shipman had not known how long it would take for Mr Lewis to die, he would have waited at the house with his wife. Accordingly, I conclude, not without some hesitation, that the death probably occurred quite quickly after the giving of the injection.
The other evidence which helps me to judge Shipman's intention is that relating to his behaviour and comments. If Mrs Hamilton were right in her impression that Shipman was trying to strangle her husband, that would be an indication of his intention. However, as I have indicated, I think her first recollection on that issue is probably correct and that she saw him with his fingers in Mr Lewis' throat. That was something that Shipman has been seen doing on other occasions when he had killed a patient. If asked, he would say he was keeping the airway open. I think he did that (in cases where he had killed) in order to stop the patient gagging on his or her tongue, an event which might well cause the patient to struggle, which might interfere with the otherwise smooth progress towards death following an overdose of opiate. So, I infer that what Mrs Hamilton saw was probably not an attempt at strangulation but might well have been designed to ensure that the diamorphine had its expected and intended effect. I bear in mind Mrs Hamilton's evidence that she had the impression from what Shipman said that he was willing her husband to give up and die.
If Mrs Gee is correct in her impression that Shipman attempted to smother Mr Lewis, this would suggest an attempt to hasten the death. However, Mrs Gee's description did not sound like a very determined attempt to smother and it is quite possible that Shipman was rearranging the pillows. Mrs Gee did not mention the episode with the pillow until very recently. I regard Mrs Gee as an honest witness, although her recollection of some events is not clear.
There is another factor which I must take into account. By 1985, Shipman had killed a number of patients. I am quite sure that he had no moral or ethical scruples about hastening the death of a terminally ill patient. Indeed, I think it likely that he thought that when he did so he was doing the best thing for everyone concerned. I think that this visit took place very late at night. I think Shipman believed that Mr Lewis would not survive until morning. I think there is a real possibility that he wished to hasten Mr Lewis' end, as he would not wish to be called out again during the night.
The evidence is not entirely clear. If these circumstances had arisen with any doctor other than Shipman, I would say that it was probable that nature had taken its course. However, knowing what I do of Shipman, I have come to the conclusion Shipman probably intended to ensure that Mr Lewis died that night, whether or not he might otherwise have survived for a little longer. My conclusion is that Shipman probably hastened Mr Lewis' death by the administration of a dose of opiate, which was deliberately assessed as larger than was appropriate for the relief of pain.

name: Norman Deyes
title: Mr
place_of_death: Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI), probably on Ward 2
certified_cause: obstruction of the small bowel due to peritonitis and perforation of a gangrenous appendix
conclusion:
From the documentary evidence and Mrs Campsell’s recollection, I am satisfied that Mr Deyes was severely ill at the time of his admission to PGI. The symptoms described and the result of the post-mortem examination make it clear that Mr Deyes had suffered an obstruction of his small bowel. This condition will be fatal unless it can be corrected by emergency surgery. The decision was taken not to undertake surgery apparently on account of Mr Deyes’ general condition. The decision not to operate is unlikely to have been Shipman’s. If there was to be no operation, Mr Deyes’ death was inevitable.
It was, in my view, very likely that it was Shipman with whom the family had contact on the afternoon of Mr Deyes’ death. He appears to have been the SHO on call on Ward 2 that weekend. The details provided on the cremation certificate suggest that he was responsible for Mr Deyes’ treatment that day. Any case in which Shipman was involved at or around the time of the patient’s death inevitably gives rise to some concern, particularly when the patient was in a side room in which Shipman would be able to act unobserved. However, Mr Deyes was plainly very ill when seen by his relatives on the Sunday afternoon. Given the nature of his condition, as revealed by post-mortem examination, he must have been receiving strong analgesia, quite possibly morphine or diamorphine. It was inevitable that he would die within a fairly short time. Yet Shipman advised Mrs Deyes and Mrs Campsell to go home and, very soon afterwards, Mr Deyes was dead. Shipman might have given this advice because he could not see the point of the family remaining there. Alternatively, he might have wanted the family out of the way, so that he could administer something that would hasten Mr Deyes’ death. By the end of May 1972, Shipman had killed at least three patients at PGI and it is entirely possible that he had decided that Mr Deyes’ life should end sooner rather than later.
Shipman’s Form B account of his contact with Mr Deyes around the time of death suggests that he was not present either just before or shortly after the death. However, Mrs Campsell thinks that the entries on Form B are not accurate. She may well be right. In any event, no reliance can be placed on the timings giving by Shipman; they might have been accurate; they might have been completely fabricated. The contents of Form B do not arouse particular suspicion but nor do they allay suspicion.
One factor which tends to reduce the level of suspicion I feel in this case is that there was a post-mortem examination. I do not know who decided that there should be one. If Shipman made the decision, that would suggest that he had not hastened Mr Deyes’ death. On the other hand, he might have killed Mr Deyes in the expectation that he would be able to certify the death without the need for a post-mortem examination. It is quite possible that the consultant, Dr Watson, decided that one was necessary the following day. The fact that there was a post-mortem examination does not rule out the possibility that Shipman killed the patient.
The evidence in this case does not enable me to reach a clear conclusion. It may well be that Mr Deyes’ death was natural. However, there are some worrying features which give rise to some suspicion that Shipman might have hastened the death.
I very much regret that I have had to raise these doubts so many years after the death and I am sorry for the distress this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI, once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Florence May Griffiths
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: myocardial infarction due to coronary thrombosis due to atherosclerosis
conclusion: There is no reason to suspect that Mrs Griffiths’ death was other than entirely natural. A post-mortem examination was carried out and there must have been pathological evidence that she had suffered a myocardial infarction or heart attack. The information provided by Shipman on cremation Form B appears to me to be consistent with that provided by Mrs Kew. He did not record that he was present at the moment of death. Indeed, he suggested that he did not see Mrs Griffiths’ body until 30 minutes after her death. I am quite satisfied that Mrs Griffiths died a natural death.

name: Martha Parkes
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion:
Since it was Shipman who certified the cause of Mrs Parkes’ death, it is very likely that he was involved in her treatment following admission. I know from the documentation in the case of Mr Norman Deyes that Shipman was on call on the medical wards that weekend. In the absence of any medical records, it is impossible for me to report on Mrs Parkes’ physical condition or on Shipman’s involvement in her care. Senile dementia used to be acceptable as a certified cause of death but the material before me is insufficient to say whether it was appropriate in Mrs Parkes’ case. As there is no cremation documentation, I know nothing of the circumstances of the death or Shipman’s presence at or near the time of death. Accordingly, I am unable to reach any conclusion about Mrs Parkes’ death.
I very much regret that the Inquiry has had to make these enquiries so many years after the death, and I am sorry for the disturbance this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI, once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Elizabeth Thwaites
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: congestive heart failure due to anaemia due to uraemia and a chronic duodenal ulcer
conclusion:
Although Mrs Grayson’s recollection is that her mother’s condition had not changed markedly by the evening of 14th
April, the nursing notes suggest that she had deteriorated quite suddenly late in the evening of 12th
April. Precisely why is not clear. In any event, Mrs Thwaites did not die that night, although she never improved to her previous state.
On the evening of 14th
April, Shipman attended Mrs Thwaites but the nursing notes do not confirm that he was called to see her. That arouses in my mind the suspicion that he attended of his own volition and might have been alone with her at the time when he claimed to have administered the Lasix and digoxin. He was on the ward during the late evening, dealing with other patients. He might have done what he claims to have done, which would have been appropriate treatment and quite incapable of hastening Mrs Thwaites’ death. However, he might have done something quite different and have caused or hastened her death; for example, he might have given more digoxin than he claimed to have given or he might have given another drug entirely.
