A further cause for suspicion is that Mrs Grayson was not advised that her mother was close to death. It was common for relatives to be warned if the end was near so that they could stay at the patient’s bedside. A yet further cause for suspicion arises because this death occurred in the late evening. A high proportion of the deaths certified by Shipman occurred between 6pm and midnight. Finally, Shipman noted in terms that the death was not reported to the coroner. I suspect that he made the note because the death followed immediately the giving of the injections. I suspect that he did not refer the death to the coroner because he did not want the facts to be investigated.
It seems to me that Mrs Thwaites was very poorly and had not long to live. Having said that, I entertain very strong suspicions that Shipman hastened her death.
I very much regret that I have had to raise these doubts so many years after the death and I am sorry for the distress this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI, once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Joseph Green
title: Mr
place_of_death: on Ward 2, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion:
Despite Mr Robert Green’s recollection that his father was much improved on the afternoon of the day of his death, it seems to me that his underlying condition was very serious and that he was unlikely to live long. It is, in my view, entirely possible that Mr Green died a natural death in the late evening of 20th
April 1972. However, the fact that Shipman suggested on cremation Form B that he was alone with Mr Green at the time of the death gives rise to some suspicion that he might have caused the death although, as I have explained in
Chapter Seven
, the fact that he implied on Form B that he was present alone does not necessarily mean that he was. Shipman would not normally be on the ward late in the evening although if he was ‘on call’ he might well be summoned to the ward if a nurse thought it necessary. If a nurse had called him to see Mr Green, I would have expected the nurse to stay with him while he examined the patient and gave any necessary treatment. I accept that it is possible that Shipman might have been in the company of a nurse at the time of the death but omitted to say so on cremation Form B. Also, Mr Green’s death occurred in the period between 6pm and midnight. As I have explained in
Chapter Seven
of the Report, an unusually large proportion of deaths certified by Shipman occurred during this quarter of the day. In my view, the facts that Shipman may have been alone with Mr Green at the time of his death and that the death occurred in the late evening give rise to some suspicion that he may have caused the death.
I very much regret that I have had to raise these doubts so many years after the death and I am sorry for the distress this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI, once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Martha Ann Phelps
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: left ventricular failure, due to congestive heart failure
conclusion:
In the absence of any medical records relating to Mrs Phelps’ admission to hospital before her death, it is not possible to reach any conclusion about the cause or circumstances of her death. It may well be that the frailty noticed by her granddaughters was a sign that Mrs Phelps was suffering from heart trouble and that she deteriorated suddenly on 18th
July. It is likely that Mrs Phelps was admitted to Ward 1 at PGI and was probably treated by Shipman. I regret to say that I cannot throw any further light on the circumstances of the death. There is no evidence, however, that Shipman played any sinister part in it.
I very much regret that the Inquiry has had to make these enquiries so many years after the death, and I am sorry for the disturbance this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Susan Garfitt
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion:
It is difficult to provide a decision in this case because of the lack of contemporaneous documentation. The only such documentation that survives is the copy entry in the register of deaths (‘death certificate’) which confirms that the cause of death was certified by Shipman.
Given that it was Shipman who certified the cause of death, I think it almost certain that he was the doctor with whom Mrs Garfitt spoke shortly before Susie’s death. That was an important conversation. I acknowledge the danger of complete reliance on Mrs Garfitt’s recollection of the words used or the sequence in which they were spoken. Even as she recollects it, the conversation is susceptible to more than one interpretation. Shipman may have been asking Mrs Garfitt to give her tacit consent that no further active steps should be taken to keep Susie alive if the only effect of those steps would be to prolong her daughter’s suffering. I think that is, broadly speaking, what Mrs Garfitt understood. He may, alternatively, have been trying to suggest (although this was not Mrs Garfitt’s understanding) that active steps should be taken to hasten Susie’s (inevitable) death. He may have been trying to tell Mrs Garfitt that Susie’s death was imminent.
It may be that Shipman played no part in Susie’s death. As I have sought to emphasise, she was gravely ill and she could not have been expected to survive for long. However, the fact that the death occurred so very shortly after the conversation between Mrs Garfitt and Shipman, combined with what I know about Shipman, gives rise to a significant degree of suspicion that he entered Susie’s room after the conversation and gave her a lethal injection.
I very much regret that I have had to raise these doubts so many years after the death and I am sorry for the inevitable distress this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI, once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Mary Ellen Price
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion:
In the absence of any medical records, it is not possible to assess the seriousness of Mrs Price’s condition in the few days following her stroke and admission to hospital. The fact that she was put into a side room or cubicle suggests that she was more seriously ill than Mr Price now recalls. It is possible that Mrs Price’s condition deteriorated gradually during her stay and that she was unconscious for the last 24 to 36 hours of her life. If so, it would seem likely that her death was natural.
However, Mr Price claims to have a clear recollection of speaking to his mother not long before her death, at which time she was coherent and talking about the possibility of returning home. Of course, it might not have been realistic for her to hope that she would return home but the very fact that she was able to talk at all shows that she was not in a coma. It is possible that Mr Price is mistaken and that he did not visit his mother during the last 24 hours of her life. It is easy to make mistakes of recollection about events so long ago. I conclude that it is entirely possible that Mrs Price deteriorated gradually after her stroke and died after a period of unconsciousness of 24 to 36 hours.
That said, there are reasons to suspect that that did not happen. Although it is quite possible for Mr Price’s recollection of the time of his visits to be mistaken, he is, in my view, far less likely to be mistaken when he avers that no one in the family was warned that Mrs Price was in danger of dying. Mrs Price had three adult children and other relations and, in my view, it is most unlikely that not one of them would have attended if they had been warned that her life was in danger or that she had entered a coma. I infer from that that it is likely that Mrs Price’s death was quite sudden. That raises the suspicion that Shipman might have done something to hasten her death. If the death was quite sudden, there is ground for suspicion in that Shipman stated that Mrs Price had been in a coma for 24 to 36 hours. If that was untrue, it was a fabrication designed to give the appearance that the death was expected and consistent with the stated cause. A further ground for suspicion is that Shipman has implied on cremation Form B that he was alone with Mrs Price at the time of her death. For most doctors, it would be quite unusual to be present at the death of a patient and very unusual indeed to be alone with the patient at the death. As I have explained in
Chapter Seven
, however, I am satisfied that there were occasions when Shipman suggested on Form B that he had been present alone at the moment of death of a patient when that was not so.
My conclusion is that I am unable to say whether or not Mrs Price died a natural death. She probably did but there are some grounds to suspect that Shipman might have caused or hastened her end.
I very much regret that I have had to raise these doubts so many years after the death and I am sorry for the distress this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Donald Taylor
title: Mr
place_of_death: on Ward 2, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: myocardial infarction due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion: Although there are no hospital records available to the Inquiry, it seems quite clear that Mr Taylor was suffering from ischaemic heart disease and was admitted to hospital after suffering a heart attack. It is also clear from the family’s evidence that he improved for a while and then suffered another coronary episode. Thereafter, he remained poorly and he must have been at severe risk of suffering a further, fatal, heart attack. Mrs Hepworth was called to the hospital in the early hours of the morning. She believed that her husband had indeed had a further attack. She could hear sounds suggesting that a team was attempting to save her husband’s life. Then she was told that he had died. Although Shipman was involved in her husband’s treatment, there is no suggestion that he was alone with Mr Taylor. Also, the cause of death given by Shipman is consistent with the information available to the family. It appears to me that this death was entirely natural. I do not think Mr Taylor’s family need have any cause for concern.

name: Colin Whitham
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 21 Poplar Avenue, Todmorden
conclusion:
This death was investigated only because Shipman had certified the cause of death.
In the absence of the medical records, it is not possible to discover what medication Mr Whitham was taking before his death. If, as Mrs McNicholas remembers, the cancer had spread, it is likely that Mr Whitham was in pain and would have required pain-relieving drugs. It would not be unusual in circumstances of this kind for a doctor to attend daily to give an injection. It is possible that this was so in Mr Whitham's case but that Mrs McNicholas has forgotten. It is also possible that tablets provided sufficient pain relief.
There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman visited Mr Whitham shortly before his death. However, Mrs McNicholas' recollection is understandably hazy and I do not feel able to rule out the possibility that Shipman was at the house in the period before death. It follows that, although the death was expected, and, although the family has never had any cause for concern about this death, I cannot rule out the possibility that Shipman might have hastened Mr Whitham's death by injecting him with an excessive dose of opiate. If one were dealing with any doctor other than Shipman, I would say that I was quite sure that Mr Whitham's death was natural. But Shipman did become a serial murderer and used injected opiates as his method of killing. It seems to me, however, that, if Shipman did hasten the death, he could only have shortened Mr Whitham's life by a very little.
My conclusion is that Mr Whitham almost certainly died solely as the result of his cancer but I cannot rule out the possibility that Shipman might have hastened his death by a short period.

name: Henry William Garnham
title: Mr
place_of_death: on Ward 2, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion:
There is very little information available in this case. However, that which is available suggests that Mr Garnham’s death was caused by a stroke that occurred on the morning of the day of his death. The only slightly worrying feature of the case is that Shipman claimed to have attended Mr Garnham for 24 hours when he clearly had not. Mr Garnham had been in hospital for less than 12 hours when he died. I have seen other cremation forms on which Shipman has exaggerated the length of time for which he had attended the patient. I believe that he sometimes did this in order to avoid reporting the death to the coroner and he appears to have done that here. A wish to avoid reporting a death to the coroner sometimes arouses suspicion that Shipman might have caused the death. However, as I have explained in
Chapter Seven
, I believe that he sometimes sought to avoid reporting a death even when it was entirely natural, possibly for selfish financial reasons, possibly so as to avoid the need for further formalities. In this case, there is no other reason to suspect that Shipman was responsible for the death. My conclusion is that this was almost certainly a natural death.

name: William Turner
title: Mr
place_of_death: on Ward 2, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: myocardial infarction, due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
The course of Mr Turner’s final illness and death is well chronicled in the medical and nursing notes. Although any record made by Shipman must be viewed with caution, the nursing notes in this case, made independently of him, paint a similar picture to that painted by him. It is clear that Mr Turner had heart disease and suffered a myocardial infarction shortly before his admission to hospital. He was given appropriate treatment. However, he was at severe risk of suffering another, possibly fatal, cardiac episode. It appears from the medical and nursing records that this is what happened at 2.35pm on 6th
March. It also appears that the treatment given following the arrest was appropriate. It is likely that Mr Turner suffered a cardiac arrest, was given appropriate treatment but died shortly afterwards, from completely natural causes.
The only reason why Professor Baker expressed any concern about this death was that Shipman suggested that he was the only person present at the time of Mr Turner’s death. As I have explained in
Chapter Seven
, however, I am satisfied that there were several occasions when Shipman suggested that he alone was present at the moment of death when that was not the case. In this case, if by
‘the moment of death’
, Shipman meant the end of the attempt to resuscitate, when it was clear that Mr Turner was indeed dead, it is hard to see how Shipman could have been alone. At least one nurse would have been present and possibly another doctor. If, on the other hand, Shipman took the view that Mr Turner was dead before the resuscitation attempts began, it is possible that he was alone with him at that time. However, Shipman gave the time of death as 3.05pm, at the end of the attempts at resuscitation. How Shipman could ever have come to write that the duration of death was
‘seconds’
is hard to imagine, when the attempts at resuscitation had lasted nearly 30 minutes.
I cannot completely rule out the possibility that Shipman was alone with Mr Turner at about 2.35pm, did something which caused Mr Turner to go into cardiac arrest and then took part in the attempts to resuscitate. However, this is speculation and my view is that Mr Turner very probably died a natural death.

name: Hena Cheetham
title: Mrs
place_of_death: an ambulance on the way to Halifax Royal Infirmary
conclusion:
Following post-mortem examination, the cause of Mrs Cheetham's death was certified to be superior mesenteric artery thrombosis. Gangrene of the small intestine was noted on post-mortem as was the thrombosis of the superior mesenteric artery. These are both physical findings which, according to Professor Whitwell and Dr Grenville, would properly account for Mrs Cheetham's death. The history of Mrs Cheetham's condition in the two weeks prior to death is also consistent with the certified cause of death.
It is not known at what time Shipman visited in the afternoon of 9th
October. Mrs Crossley was almost certainly present. It appears from the Report of Death that some time had elapsed between Shipman's visit and the arrival of the ambulance at 5.15pm. According to Dr David Bunn, a former partner of Shipman, the majority of the practice's home visits were carried out between 11am and 3pm. It seems likely that Shipman last saw Mrs Cheetham alive at least two hours before the ambulance arrived. Mrs Cheetham probably died at about 5.30pm. There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman gave Mrs Cheetham an injection that afternoon. If one supposes that Shipman might have given Mrs Cheetham an injection of opiate that afternoon, it would seem very unlikely that it had any effect upon her subsequent death. Professor Henry McQuay and Dr Grenville agree that an opiate injected intramuscularly reaches maximal effect within 30-60 minutes. Therefore, if a lethal injection were administered, death would be expected to occur within one hour. Although I cannot say with certainty that Shipman could not have given Mrs Cheetham a lethal injection of opiate shortly before the ambulance arrived, there is no reason to suppose that he did. Further, the mechanism of death described in the Report, where Mrs Cheetham was said to be gasping for breath, would be inconsistent with death caused by a lethal injection of an opiate.
I conclude that, although Shipman was involved in the treatment of Mrs Cheetham shortly before she died and it is possible that he administered a lethal injection of opiate to her, it is unlikely that he did so. It is highly likely that her death was natural.

name: Tom Goodliffe
title: Mr
place_of_death: on Ward 2, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion: Although there is some confusion about the identity of the nurse who was present with Shipman at the moment of the death, there is really no reason to doubt that a nurse was present with Shipman at that moment. That accords with the recollection of Mr Kevin Goodliffe. There is also no doubt that Mr Goodliffe was very close to death when his relatives arrived at the hospital at about 3am. Mr Kevin Goodliffe plainly recognised the breathing pattern which indicated to him that the end was near. Although there are some features of cremation Form B which appear to be of questionable accuracy, none of them gives rise to any suspicion that Shipman might have caused or hastened Mr Goodliffe’s death. I am satisfied that the death was natural.

name: Ruth Highley
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 5 Maitland Street, Walsden, Todmorden
conclusion:
Mrs Highley had terminal cancer and was extremely unwell. She was suffering much pain and it is likely that Shipman visited her daily to give her pain-relieving drugs. There is no evidence to show whether Shipman saw Mrs Highley alive on the day of her death. We do not even know at what time of day Mrs Highley died. It may be that Shipman's only visit on that day was after the death. We do not know.
It is possible that Shipman visited Mrs Highley shortly before her death or was with her at the moment of death. It is possible that Shipman administered a lethal injection of opiate with the intention, not of relieving her pain, but of hastening her death. Bearing in mind that Shipman was to become a serial killer, that his known means of killing was to inject opiate and that many of his victims were in poor health, it is not fanciful to postulate that he might have killed Mrs Highley.
However, the fact that Mr Highley did not mention to Mrs Lever that there was a close temporal association between Shipman's visit, an injection and the death probably indicates that there was no such close association. I think it is unlikely that Shipman did anything unlawful that had the effect of causing or hastening Mrs Highley's death. I conclude therefore that the death was probably natural. I cannot, however, rule out the possibility of foul play.

name: Mary Elizabeth Roper
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: status epilepticus due to idiopathic epilepsy
conclusion:
The circumstances of Mrs Roper’s admission to PGI are far from clear. The implication of the cremation form that was completed by Shipman is that she was admitted because of her epilepsy, although her sons deny that this is the case. Although Mr Geoffrey Roper’s recollection is that the admission was for routine monitoring of her inhaler use, this would not normally require an overnight admission. That said, if the reason for her admission was that she had suffered a severe epileptic fit, then I am sure her sons would remember this.
It is entirely understandable that her sons should not have visited Mrs Roper in hospital, given that they thought she would be in hospital for only a day or two. Their absence means, however, that they have only a limited amount of information to offer about the circumstances of her stay in hospital. In particular, they do not know whether their mother was on the main ward or in a side room.
One matter that gives rise to some concern is the fact that Shipman recorded on Form B that he was present at the time of the death, although he suggested that a nurse was also present. However, in the case of a sudden death from a violent epileptic fit it would not be entirely unexpected for a doctor and nurse to be present, as Shipman suggests.
My conclusion is that the evidence overall is insufficient to allow me to reach a decision as to whether Shipman did or did not have any unlawful involvement in Mrs Roper’s death. Nor can I say that I am suspicious that he did so.
I very much regret that the Inquiry has had to make these enquiries so many years after the death, and I am sorry for the disturbance this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI, once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Margaret Thompson
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion:
It is not possible to be confident about any of the facts in this case, because most of them are provided in documents of which Shipman was the author. It seems probable, however, that Mrs Thompson had been in PGI for about four weeks before she died, having suffered a stroke. She was probably diabetic and suffering from long-term kidney problems.
I do not know whether Mrs Thompson was nursed in one of the main areas of the ward, or whether she was admitted to, or at some later stage transferred to, one of the cubicles which were used to accommodate patients who were seriously ill or whose death was imminent.
I do not know whether Mrs Thompson was seriously ill shortly before she died or whether her death was expected. It is entirely possible, even likely, that her death was the result of the natural progression of her illness. However, some features of the information provided on Form B give rise to concern that Shipman might have been involved in the death.
Shipman claimed that he was present at the death and implied that he had been present at the bedside shortly before the death occurred. He said that he knew from his own observation that Mrs Thompson had been in a coma for ten minutes before she died. He implied that he was alone with her at the moment of death although, as I have explained in
Chapter Seven
, it does not necessarily follow that he was. Presence alone at the death of a patient is a most unusual occurrence for a doctor. In the ordinary course of events, it is most unlikely that it should have been a doctor, rather than a nurse, who first observed that Mrs Thompson had deteriorated and was unconscious. The usual course would be for a nurse to notice any change in the patient’s condition and to summon a doctor if necessary. Usually, the nurse would then stay at the bedside while the doctor examined the patient and gave or ordered any necessary treatment. It would be unusual for the doctor to remain after that time and most unusual for the doctor to remain at the bedside in the absence of a nurse. Yet this is what Shipman implied had happened in this case.
There might be a perfectly innocent explanation for what Shipman wrote on Form B. It is possible that, although such an occurrence would be unusual for most doctors, Shipman was indeed present before, during and after the death and was administering such appropriate treatment as he could. I cannot say.
I also have some concern about the cause of death certified by Shipman. He ascribed the death to a myocardial infarction (heart attack) and yet did not state that there was any underlying heart disease. A heart attack often results in a rapid death, lasting only a few minutes. Professor Richard Baker reported that Shipman certified more deaths than other doctors as being due to cardiac or cerebrovascular causes and often stated that the duration of the death was much shorter than other doctors usually did. These were also common features of the cremation certificates of patients he killed in later years.
The degree of suspicion that I entertain is reduced to some extent because, at the time, Shipman was still very inexperienced. He was not yet fully qualified and had worked on the medical wards for only just over a month. I am doubtful that he would have had the confidence to kill so soon after his arrival. That said, in the light of Shipman’s subsequent history, the unusual pattern of entries on Form B must give rise to some suspicion that he caused or hastened Mrs Thompson’s death.
I very much regret that I have had to raise these doubts so many years after the death and I am sorry for the distress this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI, once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Sean Stuart Callaghan
title: Mr
place_of_death: the Fielden Hospital, Todmorden
conclusion:
I am quite sure that Mr Callaghan died from natural causes. His progressive deterioration is clearly recorded in the nursing notes, which are of a very high quality and give me confidence in their accuracy.
The death was investigated only because Shipman certified the cause of death. From the records, it appears that Shipman did not visit Mr Callaghan until after his death and there is no reason to suspect that Shipman had any involvement beyond certifying the cause of death.

name: Hannah Rider
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 5 Monument Lane, Pontefract
conclusion:
Although I cannot be certain about it, it is likely that Shipman attended Mrs Rider during the evening before her death. It is quite likely that he gave her a pain-relieving injection. Cancer of the larynx can be very painful and, in the 1970s, the most common form of relief for severe pain would have been an intramuscular injection of an opiate drug. There is no reason to think that Shipman gave an excessive dose of the drug; if he had done so, Mrs Rider would have been dead within about an hour. In fact, she lived until the following morning.
It is likely that Shipman attended again the following day and confirmed that Mrs Rider had died. He would also have completed the MCCD either then or later. The cause of death must have been given as cancer of the larynx and I am sure that Mrs Rider had that condition. Dr Hessel would not have given that as the cause of death on cremation Form B if he had not known of the diagnosis.
I note that, before he signed cremation Form B, Dr Hessel spoke to Mrs Rider’s daughter-in-law and confirmed with her that Mrs Rider had died at about 8.45am and that she had been in a coma for two hours before then. Mrs Burrow was best placed to provide such information and it is likely to have been correct.
In my view, there is no reason to doubt that this death was a natural death and that Mrs Rider had been suffering from cancer of the larynx. I am quite satisfied that Shipman played no sinister part in events.

name: James Rhodes
title: Mr
place_of_death: on Ward 2, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
Mr Rhodes had suffered a coronary thrombosis in the past and probably had another shortly before his admission. He may well have had another a few hours after admission. He was certainly at serious risk of suffering a further cardiac episode and of dying as a result. His death may well have been completely natural. That is so, even though his daughter and son-in-law had found him to be quite well only three hours before his death. There are inconsistencies between the medical notes and the contents of cremation Form B but these may indicate only that Shipman was cavalier about his duties of certification. A natural death is a real possibility.
That said, inconsistencies between the medical records and the contents of Form B could have a more sinister explanation. One possible explanation for the inconsistencies is that Shipman was on the ward at about 9pm, went into Mr Rhodes’ room alone and gave him an injection of something which caused his death, but did not make any entry in the medical notes. Shipman could then have left Mr Rhodes to be found dead by the nursing staff some time later. It would have appeared to them that Mr Rhodes had died ‘in his sleep’. If Shipman did not see Mr Rhodes in a coma, he could not have relied on ‘his own observations’ about the mode of death.
On Form B, Shipman claimed that he knew that Mr Rhodes went into a coma some 20 to 30 minutes before he died. Although I recognise that standards of note-keeping were not uniformly good in the early 1970s, if Shipman was called to see Mr Rhodes by a nurse at about 9pm and found him in a coma, one would expect to see a note to that effect in the medical records and some statement as to his condition. One would also expect to find some entry in the nursing records. If Shipman had been passing Mr Rhodes’ room and happened to notice that he was in a coma, one would expect to see an entry in the medical records and some indication that he had alerted the nursing staff to this deterioration. There are no such notes. I do not think that either of those things can have happened.
As I have said, one possibility is that Shipman made a secret visit to Mr Rhodes’ room for a sinister purpose. That theory fits the known facts. The other possibility is that Shipman did not see Mr Rhodes at all that evening until after his death but believed the death to have been due to a coronary thrombosis and falsely reported that he had seen Mr Rhodes in a coma in order to provide a plausible firsthand account of the death. That theory could also fit the known facts. It is possible that Shipman wished to create such an account of the death so that he could be responsible for certification and avoid reporting the death to the coroner. The only motives I can think of for him wishing to do that are, first, a desire to save the family from the ‘unnecessary’ stress (and himself from the possible inconvenience) of a coroner’s investigation with post-mortem examination (and, possibly, an inquest) or, second, to give himself the opportunity (if the family decided on cremation) to earn a few pounds by completing cremation Form B.
Of the two possibilities, I have come to the conclusion that the sinister explanation is more likely to be correct and that Shipman secretly visited Mr Rhodes in his room and killed him there. I am satisfied that there were times, especially in the evening, when visiting time was over and fewer nursing staff were on duty, when Shipman was able to gain access to patients unobserved by the nursing staff. This would be particularly easy if the patient was in a side room. Professor Baker’s statistical analysis of the deaths certified by Shipman shows that a higher proportion of deaths certified by Shipman occurred during this part of the day than for any other doctor working at PGI. I think it likely that this was one of the unnatural deaths that account for Professor Baker’s finding.
As I have said, this death may well have been natural but there are strong grounds to suspect that Shipman caused it and I have come to the conclusion that it is more likely than not that he did so.

name: Thomas Henry Ridge
title: Mr
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion:
Very little is known about Mr Ridge or the circumstances of his admission to PGI in 1972. It is quite likely that he was very ill and that he died a completely natural death. However, the information provided by Shipman on cremation Form B gives rise to some suspicion that Shipman might have been involved in Mr Ridge’s death. The death took place during the evening. As Professor Richard Baker has observed, an unusual proportion of deaths certified by Shipman took place between the hours of 6pm and midnight. Further, if Mr Ridge was admitted only that day, his death ought to have been reported to the coroner. I have explained in
Chapter Seven
that there may have been more than one reason why Shipman did not report cases that ought to have been reported. I am suspicious in this case, however, that the reason why he did not report the death is that he did not want it to be investigated. Also, Shipman appears to have been present shortly before, at and immediately after the death. That is quite unusual for other doctors but not for Shipman. It is a factor which gives rise to some concern. Shipman did not claim to have been alone at the death; he said that Sister Byford was also present. However, the statement that she was present at the moment of death does not completely allay my concern. During the evening, it would be very easy for Shipman to go to a patient’s bedside without having a nurse in attendance. He could easily give the patient something which would lead to death. He could then call a nurse who would come and would then be present at the moment of death. There is no evidence that this is what happened in this case. However, as an unusual number of deaths occurred during the evenings in this six-month period, it appears to me that some suspicion must attach to this death.
I very much regret that I have had to raise these doubts so many years after the death and I am sorry for the disturbance this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI, once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Cissie Macfarlane
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: renal failure due to chronic pyelonephritis
conclusion:
There can be no doubt that Mrs Macfarlane was very seriously ill at the time of her admission to hospital and that it was inevitable that she would die quite soon. It is quite likely that her death was entirely natural and unaffected by any treatment given.
The second point that must be made is that there can be no certainty that the doctor who prescribed Valium and who was present when Mrs Macfarlane was given an injection of Valium on the night before her death was in fact Shipman. I appreciate that Mrs Steward feels confident that it was he but she met the doctor only once. I accept entirely that it could have been he and would go as far as to say that it very probably was he, but I cannot be sure of it.
Mrs Macfarlane was given 40mg Valium at a time when she was very poorly and her respiratory and renal functions were severely compromised. I think it highly likely that the injection was given intramuscularly by Mrs Naylor, on Shipman’s instruction; if it had been given intravenously, Mrs Macfarlane would have died within a few minutes. Even if given intramuscularly, 40mg is a very large dose to give and, for a patient in Mrs Macfarlane’s condition, would expose the patient to the risk of death. It is entirely possible that Shipman acted in bad faith, with the intention that Mrs Macfarlane’s death would be accelerated. It is also quite possible that he acted as he did, being reckless as to whether or not the prescribed dose would accelerate Mrs MacFarlane’s death. It is far less likely that Shipman acted in good faith, believing that that amount was appropriate and necessary to relieve distress; the dose was very large and Mrs Macfarlane was very poorly. This is one of the cases that I regard as entailing potentially dangerous treatment that directly caused or hastened the death of the patient but in which I cannot say whether Shipman acted deliberately, recklessly or in good faith. This causes me to have some suspicion about it.
I very much regret that I have had to raise these doubts so many years after the death and I am sorry for the distress this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI, once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Clare Louise Matthews
title: Mr
place_of_death: Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: cerebral haemorrhage resulting from deformity of the head during delivery
conclusion:
There is an abundance of evidence to suggest that Clare’s death resulted from natural causes. Clare became extremely ill with meningitis when she was between two and three weeks old. Although it appeared that she was treated successfully for that, her condition remained poor and she went on to suffer an intestinal blockage. Such illnesses would be worrying in the case of an adult but they would be that much more serious in the case of a young baby. Clare was at severe risk of cerebral haemorrhage. Mrs Dunn’s recollection is that she was told that Clare had died whilst she was being fed by a nurse (quite possibly a junior nurse rather than Sister White) and she observed a nurse crying on the ward when she arrived there. The hospital ordered a post-mortem examination, the result of which definitely indicated that the cause of death was cerebral haemorrhage, and the description of Clare’s sudden death is, as I have explained, consistent with that cause.
It is understandable that Mrs Dunn should be concerned now that she knows that Shipman was involved in Clare’s treatment and certified the cause of her death. However, in my view, there is no real cause for concern about Shipman’s involvement. I have explained that Dr Esmail thinks it unlikely that the nurse who was holding Clare was actually feeding her at the time. Mrs Dunn remembers otherwise. I cannot resolve this conflict but it does not alter my view about the cause of death.
To my mind, the only possible remaining cause for concern is that Shipman stated that he was present at the death and implied that no other person was present. Why Shipman should have said that, I cannot imagine. However, it is most unlikely and it is inconsistent with Mrs Dunn’s recollection. It is likely that a baby as seriously ill as Clare would be under almost constant supervision by the nursing staff. If Clare became suddenly worse, there would have been an emergency and the most senior medical and nursing staff available would have attended to her. I cannot explain why Shipman wrote that on Form B but, in this case, it does not suggest to me that he had done anything to harm Clare.
If Dr Esmail’s explanation for Clare’s death is correct - and I believe that it probably is - it means that the causes of death given by Shipman are not strictly correct. The primary cause - cerebral haemorrhage - is correct but the underlying causes are not correctly stated. This is of no great importance.
This is a tragic case and I greatly regret that the Inquiry has reopened Mrs Dunn’s sad memories. However, I hope that she will now feel reassured that Clare’s death was completely natural.

name: Bernadette McCourt
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion:
There is, by reason of the passage of time, very little independent evidence available in this case. However, the hospital notes provide sufficient information for me to be able to say that Bernadette was very vulnerable at birth by reason of her prematurity, low birth weight and unexpanded lungs. She received care that was typical of that provided at the time. As Professor Baker has pointed out, both Bernadette’s progress and her eventual death are consistent with what would be expected in the case of a child born at about 31 weeks’ gestation in the early 1970s. What gives rise to concern, of course, is the fact that the only medical record that exists was made by Shipman who may have been present, possibly alone, at the death. I do not, however, think that I should infer that Shipman did anything to imperil Bernadette’s tenuous hold on life. The entries he made in her notes on the days before her death suggest that he was giving her appropriate treatment. On the day of the death, he recorded signs of breathing difficulties. There are no suspicious features in the medical records.
Where Shipman was involved in treating a patient who died, I cannot rule out the possibility that he did something to cause the death. However, in this case, there is no evidence to suggest that he did. My conclusion is that Bernadette’s death was almost certainly natural and was due to her extreme prematurity.

name: Gertrude Millicent Shepherd
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion:
Were it not for the fact that Shipman was involved in treating Mrs Shepherd before her death and were it not for the fact that he certified the cause of her death, there would be absolutely no reason to suspect that she died as a result of anything other than natural causes. Mrs Shepherd had a long history of asthma and cardiac problems and she clearly suffered a very severe myocardial infarction three days before she died. Even though she made a partial recovery from this severe episode she was at very high risk indeed of suffering a further episode over the ensuing days.
Although Shipman was involved in Mrs Shepherd’s treatment, there is nothing to suggest that he played a sinister role in her death. The note recording her death is very brief. It does not suggest that Shipman saw Mrs Shepherd alive on the day of her death. It is consistent with his having been called to her after the death had already occurred. I cannot say with complete confidence that that is what happened. However, there are two reasons why I feel able to give Mrs Shepherd’s family reassurance that the death was almost certainly natural. First, Mrs Shepherd’s previous history of heart problems was such that she was at grave risk of suffering a further, fatal, heart attack. Second, this death occurred during the late morning, at a time when there would be several members of the nursing staff about. It is unlikely that, at that time of day, Shipman would have had the opportunity of seeing Mrs Shepherd alone, without the presence of a nurse, or that he would have been able to give her any drug that might have caused her death. In the circumstances, I am able to reassure Mrs Shepherd’s family that the death was almost certainly natural.

name: Thomas Cullumbine
title: Mr
place_of_death: on Ward 2, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion:
I am satisfied that, at the time of his admission on 8th
April 1972, Mr Cullumbine was suffering quite severe respiratory illness. It appears that his condition did not improve thereafter and probably became worse. On the night of 11th
April, it seems that there may have been concern for his life, as some members of the family stayed with him. Shipman was on duty on 12th
April and appears to have been in charge of Mr Cullumbine’s treatment. It seems that the family was given the impression that Mr Cullumbine’s life was not in immediate danger. Yet, he died late that evening, in Shipman’s presence.
Shipman entered an elaborate account of the decline before death in the medical records. I have formed the view that that account was probably false. First, if Mr Cullumbine had deteriorated as Shipman claimed, it would be usual for a nurse to be present with the doctor who was giving treatment. If a nurse had been present, I would have expected a note to have been made in the nursing records. The nursing records contain no description of the deterioration leading to the death. I infer that there was no nurse present and that Shipman was alone with the patient before the death. Shipman not only had the opportunity to kill Mr Cullumbine but was also free to write a false account of his death. Second, Shipman’s elaborate note of Mr Cullumbine’s decline towards death and the treatment he claims to have administered is reminiscent of entries that he made later in the notes of patients he had killed. I am particularly suspicious of the deletions and the way in which he stressed that aminophylline had been given
‘
very slowly
’
. Third, I suspect that Shipman did not give aminophylline at all, although he claimed to have given two separate injections of it. No aminophylline was prescribed that day. The last prescription for that drug was written up by Dr Bowden on 8th
April. The only drug Shipman prescribed on 12th
April, was 10mg morphine. I think it likely that Shipman wrote in the medical record that he had given 10mg morphine at 23.10hrs but then deleted the reference to morphine and substituted aminophylline.
A further cause for concern is Shipman’s unconcealed irritation with Mr Cullumbine. In the First Report, I drew attention to the fact that Shipman sometimes killed patients who had irritated or annoyed him in some way. One example was Miss Beatrice Clee, about whom I have added some further relevant information in
Appendix E
to this Report.
Finally, I feel some suspicion that Shipman may have been responsible for ensuring that Mr Cullumbine’s family did not stay with him on the night of 12th
April, although they had stayed throughout the previous night.
For all these reasons, I have come to the conclusion that Shipman probably killed Mr Cullumbine. I think it likely that he did so by giving morphine intravenously. Although 10mg morphine would not usually be a lethal dose, it would be lethal for a patient such as Mr Cullumbine, with severely compromised respiratory function. I think it very likely that, even with the best of treatment, Mr Cullumbine would have died quite soon; he was very poorly and seemed to be deteriorating. In later years, Shipman is known to have hastened the deaths of patients whose quality of life was poor and for whom there was no real prospect of recovery.

name: Ann Cartwright
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion:
The witnesses in this case, who have only a remote connection with Mrs Cartwright, have provided helpful, but inevitably limited, evidence. As I have suggested, it is quite possible that Mrs Cartwright was suffering from lung cancer with secondary deposits and that this did not become known either to her or to those treating her until around the time of her death. It may be that her daughter became aware of it and chose not to discuss it. I find myself unable to say whether Mrs Cartwright did suffer from that condition, but it is certainly likely that she did. It is highly improbable that Shipman would openly record that Mrs Cartwight had cancer if in fact she did not. Whether she did or did not, however, does not answer the question whether or not Shipman played any sinister role in her death.
The only reason to suspect that Shipman might have had a hand in causing Mrs Cartwright’s death is that he implied on cremation Form B that he was alone with her at the time of the death. It is unusual for a doctor to be present at the death of a patient and most unusual for one to be alone with the patient at the moment of death. Yet Shipman often said that he was alone with dying patients. However, this factor alone is not sufficient for me to say that I am suspicious about his involvement in the death. As I have explained in
Chapter Seven
, Shipman had a very cavalier attitude towards his duties of certification. I consider that it is quite possible that others were present at the death but that he either chose not to mention their presence or simply did not take the trouble to do so. Also, the time when Mrs Cartwright died was a busy time on the ward when the opportunity for Shipman to act unobserved would be less than at other times of the day.
The evidence in this case is so limited that I am afraid that I am unable to express any concluded view about Shipman’s involvement in Mrs Cartwright’s death.
I very much regret that the Inquiry has had to make these enquiries so many years after the death, and I am sorry for the disturbance this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI, once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Marian Siemiernik
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
In the absence of the medical records, it is not possible to know how serious Mrs Siemiernik’s condition was before her death. However, she had plainly suffered more than one heart attack and was at risk of suffering another which might well be fatal. Were it not for the fact that Shipman was involved in Mrs Siemiernik’s treatment, there would be no reason to suspect that her death was other than natural. However, Shipman was involved in her treatment and claimed that he had been present at the moment of death. He implied that he had been alone with her. That is a feature which usually gives rise to suspicion although, as I have explained in
Chapter Seven
, there were occasions when Shipman was not present alone at the moment of death, even though he had suggested to the contrary on Form B. I am satisfied that this is such a case. Mr Siemiernik’s evidence suggests that several people were attending his mother shortly before her death and were trying to save her life. As she was only 59 and as she was not suffering respiratory illness as well as heart disease, I would have expected that the staff would have tried to resuscitate her if she suffered a heart attack with cardiac arrest.
Although Shipman’s claimed presence at the death does not allow me to rule out the possibility that he played some sinister part in the death, there is no evidence to suggest that he did and I think it very likely that Mrs Siemiernik’s death was natural.

name: Ada Wandless
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: hypertensive encephalopathy, caused by hypertension, and that congestive heart failure contributed to the death
conclusion:
In the absence of any medical records, it is not possible to form a clear view about Mrs Wandless’ illness. However, Miss Wandless recalls that her mother was unconscious for about a week before her death and this is not dissimilar to the information provided by Shipman. It seems entirely likely that Mrs Wandless suffered from very severely raised blood pressure which affected her brain and resulted in loss of consciousness. It seems likely that Mrs Wandless’ death was imminent and it is entirely possible that the death was completely natural.
The only cause for concern is that Shipman stated on Form B that he was present at Mrs Wandless’ death and did not state that any other person was present with him. It was most unusual for other doctors to be alone with a patient at death and quite hard to imagine how that could come about in the ordinary course of hospital life. If a nurse had asked Shipman to attend to a patient and he formed the view that the patient was close to death, he might stay at the bedside but I would expect that a nurse would also stay. It would not be expected that the nurse would leave the bedside and that the doctor would stay awaiting the death. If Shipman had not been asked by a nurse to attend Mrs Wandless, and if he was indeed present at the death, it seems that he must have entered the cubicle alone and in the absence of a nurse. It that was so, it would be surprising and potentially suspicious. Shipman would have had the opportunity to administer something to Mrs Wandless that could have had the effect of hastening her death. However, as I have explained in
Chapter Seven
, there were occasions when Shipman said that he was present alone at the death of a patient when that was not so. In this case, I am far from sure that he was present alone at the moment of death, although he might have been.
It seems to me that, on 12th
April 1972, Mrs Wandless was gravely ill and had not long to live. Her death in the late afternoon may well have been natural but I cannot rule out the possibility that Shipman administered something that hastened her death. Indeed, I have some suspicion that he did so.
I very much regret that I have had to raise these doubts so many years after the death and I am sorry for the distress this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI, once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Margery Bateman
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI), probably on Ward 6
certified_cause: secondary carcinoma of the liver, ‘Probably due to’ melanoma in the right eye, which had been excised six years before
conclusion:
In the absence of any medical records relating to the period preceding Mrs Bateman’s death, it is impossible to reach any definite conclusion about the nature of her last illness. However, the existence of records dating back to 1964, which record the removal of her right eye and the histology result showing the presence of a melanoma, suggest that the cause of death might well have been carcinoma of the liver, secondary to the earlier melanoma. Mr Bateman’s understanding that his mother died of
‘yellow jaundice’
is not inconsistent with this cause of death. Because the relevant medical records have not survived and there never were any cremation certificates, there is no information available to the Inquiry which sheds light on the part Shipman played in the treatment of Mrs Bateman before her death. However, on the basis of the evidence available to the Inquiry, I feel able to reassure Mr Bateman that there is no reason to suspect that Shipman played any sinister role in his mother’s death.

name: Ada Hardacre
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Ward 6, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: acute peritonitis due to right pyonephrosis
conclusion:
From the evidence of Mr John Hardacre and from the hospital records, I am quite satisfied that Mrs Hardacre developed a significant infection in her abdomen following her left above-knee amputation. I am also satisfied that her condition became very grave in the 24 hours before she died. She was in severe pain and it was appropriate that she should have been prescribed pethidine and morphine.
The only causes for concern in this case are that Shipman was the doctor who last saw Mrs Hardacre alive and that he administered morphine just a few hours before she died. It is recorded that Mrs Hardacre was given 10mg morphine, an entirely appropriate dose. It is most unlikely that Shipman gave more than that. He would not have been allowed unrestricted access to the controlled drugs cupboard and a record had to be kept of all controlled drugs used. Moreover, at this time, Shipman was not yet qualified as a doctor and was in his first six-month post as a junior house officer. It is likely that the nursing staff would have watched the giving of this injection with particular care. In any event, if Shipman had given a lethal overdose of morphine, Mrs Hardacre would have died far more quickly than she did. In the light of all the information before me, I am satisfied that Mrs Hardacre died a natural death. I think it almost inconceivable that Shipman would have had the confidence to give a lethal dose of morphine at this stage in his career.

name: Ernest Sheard
title: Mr
place_of_death: on Ward 2, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: left ventricular failure due to bronchopneumonia
conclusion:
In the absence of any medical records or cremation certificates, there is very little evidence on which to base a conclusion. Mrs Birkby’s recollection of her mother’s description of Mr Sheard’s sudden collapse suggests that the problem was either a cardiac episode (as the GP suspected) or a stroke. However, Mrs Birkby’s recollection of events after her father’s admission does not fit well with Shipman’s certification of the cause of death. Once in hospital, Mrs Birkby recalls that her father made a gradual recovery and, by the evening before his death, was ready to come home. So eager was he to do so that he had been getting out of bed to telephone his wife and he was distressed, apparently because the nurses had sought to prevent him from doing so. Mrs Birkby’s recollection is that her father improved in hospital rather than deteriorated. An alternative explanation for his distress is that his condition had in fact deteriorated; he had developed bronchopneumonia and was becoming confused due to impairment of the oxygen supply to his brain. If this is what had happened, Mr Sheard would have been at risk of sudden death due to ventricular failure, as his cardiac status was already compromised. The following day, Mr Sheard died quite suddenly and Shipman certified the cause of death as left ventricular failure (a cardiac problem) due to bronchopneumonia.
On the evidence available, I am unable to make a judgement about what happened. If Mr Sheard was suffering from bronchopneumonia, he would not have been fit to be discharged the following day; he would have been very poorly and he might well have been confused. Mrs Birkby says that her father was to be discharged the following day. The causes of death given by Shipman and Mrs Birkby’s recollection of events are inconsistent with each other. As there are no medical records or other contemporaneous documents from which I can find out about the nature and course of Mr Sheard’s illness, I find myself unable to reach any conclusion about Shipman’s involvement in his death.
I very much regret that the Inquiry has had to make these enquiries so many years after the death, and I am sorry for the disturbance this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI, once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Wilfred Arnold Sanderson
title: Mr
place_of_death: on Ward 2, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion:
It is clear from the available evidence that Mr Sanderson was gravely ill at the time of his admission to PGI, that his condition did not improve during the course of that admission and that there was no realistic prospect of improvement or recovery. But for the fact that Shipman was involved in his treatment, there would be no reason to suspect that his death was anything other than the natural consequence of a stroke resulting from a chronic history of raised blood pressure.
However, Shipman was involved in Mr Sanderson’s care. Moreover, according to what Shipman wrote on Form B, he alone was present at the time of Mr Sanderson’s death. That death occurred late at night. That was a time when there would have been few nurses on the ward and when Shipman might have had the opportunity to go unobserved into a side room where a patient was lying. As Mrs Patrick has observed, there would be no obvious reason for him to have gone into Mr Sanderson’s room that night.
I cannot say whether Shipman did in fact go into Mr Sanderson’s room shortly before his death. Shipman’s claim that he was present at the death may not have been true. He might have been summoned only after the death. However, the fact that he claimed to have been present leaves some suspicion in my mind that he might have seen Mr Sanderson shortly before the death and have given him something that hastened the death. However, I am quite satisfied that, if Shipman did do anything to hasten Mr Sanderson’s death, the effect could only have been to bring forward the death by a short period. There can have been no realistic prospect of recovery.
I very much regret that I have had to raise these doubts so many years after the death and I am sorry for the distress this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI, once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Charles Lyndon Bailey
title: Mr
place_of_death: Ackton Hospital, an annexe of Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion: On the basis of the evidence before me, a fairly clear picture emerges that Mr Bailey had a history of heart disease which had already given rise to one quite serious heart attack. After that, he was being successfully treated with warfarin but it was thought advisable to attempt to end that treatment. After a period of in-patient assessment, Mr Bailey suddenly collapsed and died, just before he was about to go home. This death was particularly sudden and shocking for the family and I can well understand their concern, particularly after learning that Shipman had certified the cause of death. I hope that this decision will serve to reassure them that it is highly likely that Mr Bailey’s death was entirely natural.

name: John Auty Harrison
title: Mr
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion:
In the absence of hospital records, I cannot say whether Mr Harrison’s death was sudden and unexpected. He was plainly quite poorly. However, Mrs Woolley did not remain with her parents when her father was about to be admitted to hospital and Mrs Harrison did not accompany her husband to hospital. These facts suggest that they did not expect him to die so soon. That said, it is entirely possible that Mr Harrison was gravely ill on arrival at hospital and died from natural causes later that day.
There are, however, some grounds for suspecting that Shipman caused Mr Harrison’s death. The first and most obvious ground is that Shipman stated on Form B that he had seen Mr Harrison alive five minutes before his death and that he was also present, impliedly alone, at the moment of death. I have explained in
Chapter Seven
that the fact that Shipman claimed on Form B to have been present alone at a death did not necessarily mean that he was. The claim does give rise to suspicion, however, and, if he was present, it means that Shipman had the opportunity to administer something that could have caused Mr Harrison’s death.
Second, Shipman did not report the case to the coroner even though a report was required in any case where death occurred within 24 hours of hospital admission. As I have explained in
Chapter Seven
, I believe that Shipman sometimes sought to avoiding reporting a death to the coroner even when it was entirely natural, possibly for selfish financial reasons, possibly to avoid the need for further formalities. In this case, however, the need to report to the coroner was quite clear and Shipman exaggerated the period of time for which he had attended Mr Harrison. Very recently, in connection with death of Mr John Brewster on 28th April 1972, Shipman had expressly noted that he would not report the death to the coroner and this causes me to feel significant suspicion about Mr Brewster’s death. It is quite plain to me that by the time of Mr Harrison’s death, Shipman was well aware of the circumstances in which a report to the coroner was required.
There is a third ground for suspicion in this case. The death occurred in the evening, when, in general, there would be fewer members of the nursing staff on duty and when it would be easier for Shipman to gain sole access to patients. A higher proportion of deaths certified by Shipman took place between 6pm and midnight than for any other doctor working at PGI. My conclusion is there are significant grounds for suspecting that Shipman may have killed Mr Harrison.
I very much regret that I have had to raise these doubts so many years after the death and I am sorry for the distress this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI, once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Walter Martin Hodgson
title: Mr
place_of_death: on Ward 2, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion:
Even in the absence of medical records, it seems clear that Mr Hodgson was quite seriously ill at the time of his admission to PGI. Although Mrs Anderson was told that her father’s condition was improving, I am not sure that this was in fact the case. First, he had not been moved from the cubicle, as would have been the usual practice if he had improved. Second, the fact that he was being given oxygen is suggestive of a deterioration in his condition. It is entirely possible, even likely, that Mr Hodgson’s condition deteriorated further shortly before his death and that his death was natural and due to the causes given by Shipman on Form B. The mode of death described by Shipman is also consistent with what is known about Mr Hodgson’s condition. My only concern is that Shipman’s statements on cremation certificates cannot be trusted as being truthful and accurate. It appears from Form B that Shipman was on the ward during the period immediately before Mr Hodgson’s death and I cannot rule out the possibility that he gave Mr Hodgson something which hastened his death. However, I stress that there is no evidence that he did. I regret to say that there is insufficient evidence for me to provide a more definite opinion about Mr Hodgson’s death.
I very much regret that the Inquiry has had to make these enquiries so many years after the death, and I am sorry for the distress this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Walter Spence
title: Mr
place_of_death: on Ward 2, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: myocardial infarction due to coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease and that a left pleural effusion and cancer of the left bronchus had contributed to the death
conclusion:
It appears from Mrs Hodgson’s recollection of events that Mr Spence was very ill when she saw him on 23rd
April and that he probably did not have long to live. It is entirely possible, even likely, that Mr Spence died a natural death at about 10pm on that day. However, the fact that Shipman appears to have been with Mr Spence very shortly before the death gives rise to some concern. According to Form B, Shipman observed Mr Spence suffering a cardiac arrest only two minutes before he died. That suggests that Shipman was present at Mr Spence’s bedside only two minutes before the death. There may be a perfectly innocent explanation for Shipman’s presence at the bedside at that moment; he might have been summoned by a nurse who had observed a deterioration in Mr Spence’s condition. However, it is also entirely possible that Shipman was at the bedside without a nurse, gave something to Mr Spence to induce cardiac arrest and then went to find a nurse. That would explain why the nurse was present at the moment of death but Shipman himself was not, although he had been there two minutes earlier. I am not saying that that is what happened; I am saying only that that is a possibility. Such possibilities have to be considered where Shipman was involved, particularly in respect of deaths that occurred between the hours of 6pm and midnight. Professor Richard Baker has established that an abnormal proportion of deaths certified by Shipman occurred during this part of the day. It is possible that Mr Spence’s death was one of those that contributed to this abnormal finding. I stress that Mr Spence’s death may well have been natural. I regret to have to leave this suspicion in the minds of Mr Spence’s relatives so many years after his death. However I am quite satisfied that, if Shipman did do anything to hasten the death, it is likely that Mr Spence’s life was shortened only by a few hours. As I explained in
Chapter One
, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Mary Jane Binns
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: cerebrovascular accident due to diabetes mellitus
conclusion:
In the absence of any medical records or any evidence from a witness who visited her shortly before her death, it is impossible to say with any confidence what Mrs Binns’ medical condition was. It is quite possible that her fall occurred because she had had a stroke but that her level of consciousness had not been affected. It is also possible that the stroke progressed during the next few days and that she died a natural death on 20th
April.
In the absence of cremation forms, nothing is known of the circumstances of the death. I regret to say that there is insufficient information for me to reach any conclusion at all about this death.
I very much regret that the Inquiry has had to make these enquiries so many years after the death, and I am sorry for the distress this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI, once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: James Sullivan
title: Mr
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: myocardial failure due to thrombosis of the right pulmonary artery
conclusion: If it were not for the fact that Shipman made an entry in Mr Sullivan’s hospital records on the day when he died, there would be no evidence to give rise to any cause for concern in this case. The hospital records confirm that his condition deteriorated quite significantly in the months before he died. They also show that there had been a further deterioration in the period immediately before his hospital admission. The entry that Shipman made was made after Mr Sullivan’s death, probably after Shipman had been summoned to confirm that Mr Sullivan was dead. As Professor Baker has observed, the post-mortem examination findings, which are consistent with the symptoms reported before the death, are sufficiently serious to account for Mr Sullivan’s death. He had a blockage of an important artery. The fact that Shipman appeared not to know the cause of death when it occurred and arranged for a post-mortem examination to be undertaken strongly suggests that this death was entirely natural. Taking all of these matters into account, I conclude that it is highly unlikely that Shipman played any sinister part in this death.

name: Louis Bastow
title: Mr
place_of_death: on Ward 2, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied on the basis of all the evidence in this case that Mr Bastow’s condition at the time of his admission to PGI was very grave and that his death was imminent. But for the fact that Shipman was present on Ward 2 around the time of his death, there would be no cause for concern about it. However, on the basis of what Shipman wrote on cremation Form B, he was not only present on the ward that evening, but he also claimed to have observed Mr Bastow suffering a cardiac arrest. Yet he claimed that he was not present at the death and that no nurse was present either.
No reliance can be placed on the truthfulness or accuracy of the contents of Forms B completed by Shipman. They might be accurate; they might be completely untrue. I am always suspicious when I see alterations by Shipman on a Form B. Here, Shipman altered his statement that Mr Bastow had been in cardiac arrest for one to two hours to a statement that the arrest had lasted minutes. That seems to me to be a very odd mistake to make for someone who was supposed to have witnessed it. It occurs to me that Shipman may have realised that his original story would not hold water because Mr Bastow had had visitors until 8pm who would have known that he had not been in arrest when they left. I suspect that the story given on Form B might not be true. If it is not, I suspect Shipman’s motives for telling lies.
However, on the assumption that the account in Form B might be true, it is worth considering what could have happened that evening to account for that set of circumstances. If Shipman had been called by a nurse to see Mr Bastow, because he had suddenly gone into cardiac arrest, the nurse would have stayed at the bedside. Indeed, one might have expected both Shipman and the nurse to stay if the arrest lasted only
‘minutes’
. It is possible that Shipman might have chanced to find Mr Bastow suffering a cardiac arrest and have gone to find a nurse, only to find that Mr Bastow had already died when they returned. However, that would be something of a coincidence. It was not Shipman’s job to go around the beds checking patients and Mr Bastow was in a side room, not on the main ward. On the other hand, if Shipman was not called out by a nurse but slipped into Mr Bastow’s room without a nurse being present, the speed with which the death occurred gives rise to some suspicion. He might well have administered something to hasten the death before going in search of a nurse. In short, he had the opportunity to kill Mr Bastow and I suspect that he may have done. A further cause for concern is the time when Mr Bastow died. After visiting time was over, the ward would be quiet and Shipman would be able to move around unnoticed. Certainly, he would be unobserved if he went into a side room. As Professor Richard Baker has found, a disproportionately high number of deaths certified by Shipman occurred between 6pm and midnight. Taking all these matters into account, I am very suspicious that Shipman hastened Mr Bastow’s death, although I am not in a position to say that he probably did so.
I very much regret that I have had to raise these doubts so many years after the death and I am sorry for the distress this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the conerns that were raised about Shipman's conduct at PGI once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Ruth Margaret Harrison
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Hydes Medical Ward, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: anaemia; hypogammaglobulinaemia was said to have contributed to the death
conclusion:
Mr and Mrs Harrison are naturally concerned now that they know that the cause of their daughter’s death was certified by Shipman. In the absence of any medical records, it is not known what part he played in looking after and treating Ruth during her stay on the paediatric ward. He was the registrar at the time and he is bound to have been involved. In the absence of the records, it is not possible to discover what steps the medical staff were taking to try to find out the cause of Ruth’s disorder or to treat it.
Because Shipman worked on the ward, it must be accepted that it is possible that Shipman had formed the view that Ruth’s death was inevitable and took advantage of the absence of her mother to give her something which hastened her death. However, I think that is unlikely. There would be nursing staff about on the ward on a weekday afternoon and it would not be easy for Shipman to have private access to Ruth. I do not think he would have harmed Ruth in the sight of a member of the nursing staff. I think that it is far more likely that Ruth died a natural death as the result of her very serious blood disorder.
I very much regret the fact that this Inquiry has reopened memories of a tragic episode in the lives of Mr and Mrs Harrison. It must have been very worrying for them to think that Shipman might have been involved in the care of their daughter, especially as they have never fully understood the nature of her illness. I hope that they will now have at least some better understanding of what probably happened and I hope too that they will feel able to accept my reassurance that there is no reason to think that Shipman did anything to hasten Ruth’s death.

name: Agnes Scott
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: cerebrovascular accident due to coronary thrombosis
conclusion:
Mrs More and Mrs Haigh would like to think that Mrs Scott died peacefully on her own. However, the apparent inaccuracies on cremation Form B and the fact that Shipman stated that he was present at the time of death (albeit with Sister Byford) have planted seeds of doubt in their minds. I understand their concerns but feel able to put their minds at rest. There can be no doubt of the seriousness of the episode, at which Mrs More was present, during which her mother suddenly became unconscious. The lumbar puncture test result confirms that this episode was a cerebral haemorrhage. The death should have been reported to the coroner because it occurred within 24 hours of Mrs Scott's admission to hospital and, in some cases, I am suspicious when no report was made in such circumstances. However, I have explained in
Chapter Seven
that Shipman sometimes sought to avoid reporting a death even when it was entirely natural, possibly for selfish financial reasons, possibly so as to avoid the need for further formalities. In this case, I suspect that he thought no useful purpose would be served by reporting the case, since the lumbar puncture had provided a clear cause of death.
