In conclusion, although there are inaccuracies in cremation Form B and although the death should have been reported to the coroner but was not, I do not think that Mrs More and Mrs Haigh need feel any concern about Shipman’s role in their mother’s death. I am satisfied that it was natural.

name: John Brewster
title: Mr
place_of_death: on Ward 2, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion:
Mr Brewster was an elderly man whose GP arranged for his prompt admission to hospital when he showed symptoms suggesting a myocardial infarction in the presence of left ventricular failure. Shipman agreed to the admission after discussing the case with the GP over the telephone and, on the afternoon of that day, having assessed Mr Brewster, organised the administration of initial treatment.
So far as Mr Brewster’s family was aware, Mr Brewster’s condition was giving no cause for concern when they left the hospital at about 6pm. He was awake and alert. However, Dr Esmail has advised me that Mr Brewster was at high risk of suffering another cardiac episode which could well have been fatal. In my view, it is quite possible that Mr Brewster died a natural death during the evening of 28th
April.
That said, there are reasons to suspect that Shipman might deliberately have caused Mr Brewster’s death. According to Shipman’s entry in Form B, Mr Brewster deteriorated into a coma shortly after 8pm. Shipman claims to have known that of his own knowledge. However, there is no entry in the medical notes to confirm that deterioration. To my mind, that is suspicious. If Shipman was called to see Mr Brewster, he should have recorded the fact, together with his findings on examination and any treatment given or prescribed. He did not. If he had happened by chance to notice that Mr Brewster’s condition had deteriorated, he should have summoned a nurse and should have made notes of his observations and any treatment given. He did not. If Mr Brewster had deteriorated and if Shipman was aware of it, I would expect not only that there would be an entry to that effect in the medical records, but also that a nurse would stay close by Mr Brewster’s bed. I would not expect Shipman to stay with Mr Brewster, unless there was some purpose in doing so, such as giving treatment. Yet Shipman recorded in Form B that he alone was present at the moment of death. As I have explained in
Chapter Seven
, the fact that Shipman claimed on Form B to have been present or present alone at a death does not necessarily mean that he was. There is, however, nothing in this case to indicate that others were or must have been present and I think it is likely that Shipman was present alone.
The brevity of Shipman’s entry in the medical notes, recording only that Mr Brewster had died, also gives rise to suspicion. This note is very reminiscent of notes I have seen in cases where I am satisfied that Shipman had killed the patient. Shipman gave causes of death which were compatible with the condition for which Mr Brewster was admitted, but also recorded expressly - and I regard this as suspicious - that there was no need for the case to be reported to the coroner. This comment, in what was otherwise an extremely brief note, gives me cause for concern, particularly when I know of his subsequent reluctance for cases to be referred to the coroner. This case should have been reported because Mr Brewster’s death had occurred within 24 hours of his admission. I have explained in
Chapter Seven
that there were several reasons why Shipman might have sought to avoid reporting a death to the coroner. In this case, however, taking into account the clear need for a report and Shipman’s explicit reference to the fact that none was needed, I strongly suspect that he wished to avoid any investigation of the circumstances of the death.
I have explained in
Chapters Six and Seven
and earlier in this Chapter that a high proportion of deaths certified by Shipman occurred between the hours of 6pm and midnight. That this death took place during that period raises the level of suspicion against Shipman. It is also suspicious that the coma is said by Shipman to have begun shortly after 8pm, which was the end of normal visiting time. In suggesting that it began at that time, Shipman was avoiding the risk that the family (whom he might have expected to have been on the ward until 8pm) would contradict the assertion that Mr Brewster was in a coma before he died.
I am also concerned that, in the letter that he wrote to Mr Brewster’s GP, Shipman suggested that there had been some deterioration in Mr Brewster’s condition on the way to the hospital. The GP had seen and assessed Mr Brewster on the day of his death and would presumably not have expected him to die if he reached the hospital in the same condition in which he was at the time of the GP’s examination. The very full admission note does not mention any deterioration. The fact that the family left the bedside suggests that, at about 6pm, Mr Brewster was stable, although vulnerable to a further episode. By suggesting that there had been a deterioration en route, it appears to me that Shipman might well have been lying in order to make the rather sudden death more explicable.
These suspicious features of the death have driven me to the conclusion that Shipman probably killed Mr Brewster. How he did so, I do not know. Nor am I certain that he did so. I stress that Mr Brewster was vulnerable to a fatal cardiac episode. However, in the end, I think it likely that Shipman killed him.

name: Edith Mary Swift
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion:
It is clear from the hospital records and the report of the post-mortem examination that Mrs Swift was suffering from bronchopneumonia and was still very poorly on 8th
May, despite the recorded improvement in her condition that day. It is entirely possible that Mrs Swift died only as the result of bronchopneumonia and that her treatment did not hasten her death. On the other hand, there is some cause for suspicion that Mrs Swift’s treatment may have caused or accelerated her death.
On 8th
May, Shipman prescribed Mogadon and phenobarbitone for Mrs Swift. It appears to me that the most likely course of events was that Mrs Swift was given a Mogadon tablet at bedtime but that she remained confused and unsettled and kept getting out of bed. It appears likely that, in the small hours, the nurses gave Mrs Swift a cup of tea and the phenobarbitone tablet that Shipman had prescribed. That had the desired effect of helping her to sleep but may also have had the effect of depressing her respiration and causing her death, which was regarded as sudden by Mr Jordan.
There is no evidence that Shipman gave the phenobarbitone himself, only that he prescribed it. I cannot say with complete confidence whether he knew that phenobarbitone was dangerous for a patient suffering from impaired respiratory function. That danger was not generally recognised at the time. The fact that he prescribed both drugs quite openly suggests that he was not aware of the danger although I suspect that, even in 1971, Shipman was more aware than most of the properties of such drugs. There is certainly no evidence to suggest that the nursing staff were aware of any risk. They gave Mrs Swift the phenobarbitone, no doubt believing that it would help to settle her down to sleep. It seems to me quite likely that the phenobarbitone depressed Mrs Swift’s already impaired respiratory function and contributed to her death. My conclusion is that there is some cause to suspect that Shipman prescribed phenobarbitone for Mrs Swift, being reckless as to its likely effect upon her.
I very much regret that I have had to raise these doubts so many years after the death and I am sorry for the distress this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI, once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Butterfield Hammill
title: Mr
place_of_death: Ackton Hospital, Ackton, Pontefract
certified_cause: ventilatory failure due to chronic bronchitis
conclusion:
Mr Hammill was admitted to PGI in circumstances that did not amount to an emergency. According to a letter written by Dr Meikle, consultant physician, to Mr Hammill’s GP after his death, Mr Hammill appears to have had a chest infection. Whether Shipman ever realised that is not clear. In any event, Mr Hammill was transferred to Ackton Hospital on 31st
March. He was not given any treatment for his chest infection and he was started on a high dose of Largactil. Thereafter, very little was noted in the medical records until Shipman recorded that Mr Hammill had died. That is not entirely surprising, as there was no resident doctor at Ackton. It is entirely possible that Shipman did not see Mr Hammill alive after he left PGI. There is no cremation documentation to provide information about the circumstances of death. In my view, there is no evidence to suggest that Shipman deliberately did anything which directly caused Mr Hammill’s death. However, in the light of Professor Baker’s observations, it seems to me that it is entirely possible that Shipman decided to hasten Mr Hammill’s death by withholding antibiotic treatment and by suggesting large doses of Largactil at night. These two factors combined would increase the risk that Mr Hammill would succumb to bronchopneumonia. That said, Shipman did not expressly record that Mr Hammill had a chest infection and it is possible that he overlooked that fact and that his failure to prescribe an antibiotic was negligent rather than deliberate. I cannot say whether Shipman suggested that Mr Hammill be given very large doses of Largactil deliberately intending to hasten his death. He might have done or he might have been reckless as to the effect of a large dose. In short, I find it impossible to say whether or not Shipman hastened Mr Hammill’s death, although I suspect that he did so, either deliberately or recklessly.
I very much regret that I have had to raise these doubts so many years after the death and I am sorry for the distress this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman's conduct at PGI once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Albert Hewitt
title: Mr
place_of_death: on Ward 2, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion: It is clear from the first entry in the hospital records, which was not made by Shipman, that Mr Hewitt was very poorly at the time of his admission to PGI. He was suffering from heart failure. On the day before the death, Mr Peter Hewitt and his wife realised that Mr Hewitt was close to death. Shipman may have seen Mr Hewitt at some time during that day, although there is no record of him doing so. It may well be that, by that time, Mr Hewitt was receiving only general nursing care. There is no evidence that Shipman saw Mr Hewitt at or around the time of death. In my view, there is every reason to believe that Mr Hewitt’s death was natural and no reason at all to suspect that Shipman was involved in it.

name: Eunice Holbrook
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion: From the evidence of Mrs Thompson, it is clear that that Mrs Holbrook’s leukaemia had reached a terminal stage. From Mrs Thompson’s description of Mrs Holbrook’s appearance and her evidence of Mr Holbrook’s distress, I am satisfied that Mrs Holbrook was close to death at the time of the last visit. It is highly likely that Mrs Holbrook’s death was due to natural causes. I cannot absolutely rule out the possibility that Shipman did something to hasten Mrs Holbrook’s death but there is no evidence that he did so.

name: Dorothy Mary Andrew
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 156 Sheffield Road, Godley, Hyde
certified_cause: renal failure due to uraemia and old age
conclusion:
Mrs Andrew was quite well on the day of her death, although she had plainly suffered from some sort of infection in the few days before her death. The evidence was that she was feeling much better by 12th
September 1996.
The death took place in Shipman's presence. That in itself arouses suspicion. Dr Grenville has told the Inquiry that it is most unusual for a patient to die during a visit by the general practitioner, unless the patient is known to be terminally ill or the doctor has attended as an emergency in response to the onset of severe symptoms, which might, for example, indicate that the patient was having a heart attack or stroke. Mrs Andrew was not terminally ill and Shipman had not been summoned as an emergency. Mrs Andrew's death during his visit is highly suspicious.
Shipman's note of his visit on the day of the death gives rise to further suspicion. First, there is no clear account of the signs or symptoms on which Shipman based his supposed decision that Mrs Andrew ought to be admitted to hospital. He could not have relied on the urea and creatinine results as they were clearly fabricated. They were probably inserted in the records when the registrar had rejected the certificate which gave the cause of death as old age. Second, Shipman claimed to have called an ambulance and arranged a hospital bed. In fact, he did neither. Third, the note suggests that Mrs Andrew's daughter and a neighbour were present at the death. They were not and it seems clear that Mrs Andrew was dead before Mrs Ramsden was able to go into the house to see her. In short, this note is pure fabrication. It has been created in an attempt to provide a plausible explanation for Mrs Andrew's death. It gives rise to the grave suspicion that Shipman killed Mrs Andrew.
Shipman also made false entries in cremation Form B, which were designed to create the impression that this death had followed a three day illness and that Mrs Andrew's daughter and her neighbour were with her, as they would have been at a death which was not sudden. This death was very sudden and only Shipman was present when it occurred.
These factors leave me in no doubt that Shipman must have killed Mrs Andrew, almost certainly by administering a lethal dose of diamorphine. The possibility that she died suddenly from a natural cause is only theoretical and I can safely rule it out.
In my view, the possibility that Mrs Andrew might have died suddenly from natural causes is only theoretical. The overwhelming likelihood is that she was killed by lethal injection. She was almost certainly dead by the time Mrs Ramsden entered the house. She noticed that Mrs Andrew's lips were purple.
I am sure that this was an unlawful killing.

name: Irene Berry
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 12a Rufford Avenue, Hyde
conclusion:
Shipman's account of this death, as reconstructed from his completion of Form B, is that he first called on Mrs Berry at 11.30am and left her alive, although suffering from chest pain. He went to fetch an ECG monitor. If that had happened, it is inconceivable that Mrs Berry would not have telephoned Mrs Darlington, her daughter, who lived not far away, to tell her what the doctor had said. No one spoke to Mrs Berry or saw her alive after Shipman had left. I think it is unlikely that she was alive when he left. Shipman claims in Form B that he returned to the house at 3pm. That must be wrong by at least a small margin as he telephoned Mr and Mrs Darlington at 2.45pm to tell them that Mrs Berry had died. However, in my view, Shipman's estimate is probably wrong by much more than 15 minutes. Mrs Sandiford says that he returned to the house only some 20 minutes after she had seen him leave, in the morning. It appears from the evidence that Shipman probably visited Mrs Berry's house three times that day. The first time was the occasion when he was seen leaving by Mrs Sandiford. The second time Mrs Sandiford saw him arriving about 20 minutes after he had left. The third time he came in the afternoon and 'found' Mrs Berry dead. I am satisfied that his account of events in Form B is untrue. I am also satisfied that his statement that a neighbour had seen Mrs Berry alive after his first visit is untrue, as is the statement that a neighbour was present when the body was found.
Although Mrs Berry was at some risk of suffering a heart attack, there is no reliable evidence that she did so. Shipman's account of events cannot be accepted at face value and should not be accepted unless it is consistent with established facts. Here, his account is inconsistent with established facts, as shown above. Moreover, Mrs Berry's appearance in death was not consistent with a sudden cardiac death.
Shipman plainly avoided referring this case to the coroner in circumstances where any honest doctor would have been bound to do so.
I am driven to the conclusion that Shipman must have killed Mrs Berry during his first visit of the day. It may be that he had to leave urgently before he had ascertained that she was dead. That may well be why he returned briefly soon after his first departure. He then returned later in the afternoon to stage a discovery of the body. Thereafter, he created a wholly false picture of events in order to pass off the killing as a natural death. I am sure that this was an unlawful killing.

name: Lilian Cullen
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 96 Foxholes Road, Hyde
certified_cause: right cerebrovascular accident due to hypertension
conclusion:
This death took place in Shipman's presence. That in itself is a highly suspicious factor. Other doctors report that it is extremely rare for a patient to die in their presence. If Shipman is to be believed, such events took place very frequently when his patients were involved. Although Mrs Cullen was at some risk of suffering a stroke, it would be a remarkable coincidence if she had done so very shortly before Shipman arrived to discuss the vertigo from which she had been suffering for some time.
I do not think Mrs Cullen was unconscious when Shipman arrived. I think she let him in. I think the medical record which he made is a fabrication and that events did not occur as he has described. I think that Shipman must have made some excuse to give Mrs Cullen an injection or take a blood sample. I think he gave her an opiate, almost certainly a lethal dose of diamorphine. Soon afterwards she would have lapsed into unconsciousness. Why Shipman did not follow his usual course of leaving the patient on the chair or sofa on which he had administered the injection, I do not know. For some reason he put her on the floor near the telephone in the recovery position. Possibly this was so as to make it appear that she was seeking help at the time of her collapse.
Shipman then telephoned Mr Cullen. I think he might well have said that there was no need for him to hurry round. Shipman usually waited until his victim was dead. According to his entry on Form B, Shipman was with Mrs Cullen for 20 minutes before she died. Apart from putting her in the recovery position, he seems to have done nothing to help her. He made a note in the records, which purported to diagnose a right-sided stroke, but there is no information on which he could have reached that diagnosis. That record is a fabrication, as are the contents of the MCCD and Form B.
I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Cullen.

name: Elsie Lorna Dean
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 4 Wood Street, Hyde
conclusion:
In my view, this death is highly suspicious. First, it appears that Shipman has lied about his movements on 8th
January. Mr and Mrs Mellish both say that Shipman told them he had found Mrs Dean dead when making a routine visit. He had telephoned them at about 1.30pm to tell them of his discovery. However, on Form B, he says that a neighbour discovered the death. This was not true. That Shipman did not wish to admit that it was he who discovered the body must indicate that he wished to distance himself from the death. An intention to create the impression of an interval of time between his presence and the death is a common feature of many Shipman killings. It appears to me highly likely that Shipman did visit at about lunchtime on 8th
January. He must have gained access to the house, as he telephoned the Mellish number from there. Usually the door would have been locked. It seems to me that the likely explanation is that Mrs Dean was not dead when he arrived, that she let him in, that he killed her in his usual way and then telephoned her daughter.
This theory fits all the known facts. Mrs Dean was not seriously ill after Shipman's visit on the 6th
. Mrs Lester was not worried about her. Shipman created an entry in the computerised medical records, which suggested that she had a viral illness. However, there are no findings to support the diagnosis. Nor was Mrs Dean seriously ill when Mr Hadfield spoke to her on the doorstep in the early evening of 7th
January. Dr Grenville says that if she had been suffering from bronchopneumonia on 7th
January, as Shipman claimed, she would have been growing steadily more ill. It is inconceivable that she would not have contacted her daughter if she had felt ill. There is nothing in the evidence which convincingly supports Shipman's claim to have visited on the 7th
. However, by the evening of the 7th
, he had created a record on the computer, which implied that he had seen her. Yet its terms were so vague as to be almost meaningless. The entries for the 6th
and 7th
taken together would just about adequately correspond with Mrs Dean's true condition, but would also provide Shipman with an explanation for her death if Shipman had the opportunity to kill her on the 8th
. That opportunity arose when Mrs Dean was alone when he visited on the 8th
January. Her peaceful appearance in death was entirely typical of many of Shipman's victims. After her death, Shipman's entries on the MCCD and Form B support a version of events (now seen to be untruthful) which he had previously decided to advance, namely that he had called on Mrs Dean on 6th
and 7th
January but not on the 8th
. The entry in the written records could have been written at any time and seems to be a mixture of the complaints Mrs Dean probably did make at the visit on the 6th
, combined with signs of a more serious situation not recorded anywhere on the computer.
I am driven to the conclusions, not only that Shipman killed Mrs Dean, but also that he planned to do so in advance. I think he laid his plans possibly on 6th
January but certainly by the late afternoon of 7th
January, when he made what I am sure was a false entry on the computer records. Like the coroner, I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Dean.

name: Doris Earls
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 35 Brabyns Road, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of highly suspicious factors surrounding this death. First and most obvious, Mrs Earls was found dead a short time after Shipman visited her house. No one spoke to her or saw her alive after Shipman had left. That in itself raises a high degree of suspicion. Mrs Earls was fit and well at 2.50pm when Mrs Ewing last saw her alive. Shipman implies that she was not unwell when he saw her. It would have been the most remarkable coincidence for Mrs Earls to suffer a sudden fatal stroke after Shipman had left and before she was found. The period of time would have been very short, as Mrs Earls appears to have been dead by about 3.30pm when Mr Blezard telephoned her. The chances of Mrs Earls having a sudden fatal stroke in the short period between Shipman's departure and Mr Blezard's telephone call are so remote that I can dismiss that possibility. Other doctors find that the death of a patient during or very soon after a visit is an extremely rare occurrence. If Shipman is to be believed, it happened very frequently to him. Coincidences such as this do not happen. There must be another explanation.
I think Shipman told a number of lies on Form B. First he sought to suggest that the death occurred at about 5pm. I am satisfied that it did not; it occurred much earlier. Shipman claimed that he saw Mrs Earls three hours before her death, which would have been 2pm. However, I think it very unlikely that he was there as early as that, as Mrs Ewing spoke to Mrs Earls at 1.30pm and again at about 2.50pm and Mrs Earls did not say that Shipman was expected or that he had been. In my view, the telephone call from Mrs Earls' house to Shipman's surgery probably gives the best clue as to when Shipman was there. Although it is possible that Mrs Earls telephoned the surgery at that time to say that her husband had fallen over again, I think it is more likely that the 3.17pm call was made by Shipman from her house. If the 3.17pm call were made by Mrs Earls, there would have been insufficient time for Shipman to go to her house, see Mr and Mrs Earls and then leave before the time when Mr Blezard obtained no reply to his telephone call. I think it is likely that Shipman went to the house at about 3pm and left soon after he had telephoned the surgery at 3.17pm.
The evidence indicates that Shipman went to the Earls' house because Mr Earls kept falling over. There is no evidence that Mrs Earls was suffering any ill health. However, I believe he must have suggested to Mrs Earls that she should allow him either to give her an injection or take a blood sample. Shipman made at least two false entries in Mrs Earls' medical records at 4.20pm that afternoon. There can be no doubt that the entries for 13th
April 1994 and 4th
February 1995 are false and designed to create the impression that Mrs Earls had a long-standing problem of raised blood pressure for which she refused treatment. This condition would, if it had existed, place Mrs Earls at risk of suffering a cerebrovascular accident. That afternoon, Shipman created a third entry, which I think was also false, in which he suggested that Mrs Earls was unwell (which she was not), had high blood pressure and had provided a blood sample. This entry was designed to provide a plausible explanation for her sudden death that afternoon.
Mrs Earls' appearance in death was not consistent with the appearance of one who had died of a cerebrovascular accident. It was, however, entirely typical of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of diamorphine.
I am sure that Shipman must have killed Mrs Earls. In my view, the overwhelming likelihood is that he did it by giving her a lethal injection, while pretending to take a blood sample.

name: Elizabeth Fletcher
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 40 St John's Drive, Godley, Hyde
conclusion:
Very little is known about Mrs Fletcher's health in the days before her death. As her medical records are not available, I cannot say whether she was suffering from hypertension or, if she was, how serious it was. I must approach this case on the basis that she was probably suffering from hypertension and was at increased risk of suffering a sudden death from cardiovascular accident. Even approached on that basis, there is substantial evidence that Shipman killed Mrs Fletcher.
Mrs Fletcher was not terminally ill and Shipman was not visiting her regularly on account of any condition requiring treatment or supervision. He told Mrs Mellor that he called because he happened to be passing. That rules out the possibility that Mrs Fletcher had asked for a visit on account of the sudden onset of illness. That she should die suddenly while he was with her is just too much of a coincidence. If this were the only case in which such a coincidence had occurred, I would accept it as such. If Shipman is to be believed, such coincidences occurred quite frequently. In fact, these deaths were not the result of coincidence, they were killings. This case has Shipman's hallmark on it.
There are other features which point to the same conclusion. Shipman made no attempt to call an ambulance or to summon Mrs Harrop, as any reasonable doctor would have done if he had found Mrs Fletcher in the throes of a stroke. As I have already observed, Shipman probably lied when he claimed that another person was present with him at the moment of death. This is something he often did, in an attempt to make it appear that the death was not wholly unexpected and that relatives or friends were aware of what was happening. Finally, Mrs Fletcher's position and appearance in death were not typical of those seen after a stroke but were entirely typical of those seen in many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of opiate.
I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Fletcher, using his usual method, an intravenous injection of opiate.

name: Kathleen Grundy
title: Mrs
conclusion:
This was a clear case of morphine poisoning, proved by the post-mortem results. Even leaving that evidence out of account, there are a number of noteworthy features:
This was a very sudden death of an elderly person in good health. It was discovered shortly after a visit from Shipman during which he was alone with her.
Shipman claimed or implied that Mrs Grundy must have left the door unlocked after letting him out. This is a feature of other cases where Shipman has been unable to leave the security system in the condition in which relatives would have expected.
The medical records had been falsified to show that Mrs Grundy was unwell just before her death and that Shipman had suspected her of drug abuse. Even so, they still showed that Mrs Grundy had been in good general health and had no potentially fatal conditions or increased risk factors.
The cause of death, 'old age', was quite inappropriate for a person who had been in such good health.

name: Elsie Hannible
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 36 Rydal Avenue, Hyde
conclusion:
The circumstances of this death are highly suspicious. The fact that Shipman was present at the death gives rise to suspicion. Dr Grenville says that it is extremely unusual for a patient to die during a general practitioner's visit, unless the patient is terminally ill or the doctor has been called out as an emergency, in response to a report of symptoms suggesting a life-threatening event such as a heart attack or stroke. Mrs Hannible was not suffering from a terminal illness and she had not called Shipman out in an emergency. Her request appears to relate to the long-standing problem with her legs. It would, therefore, be something of a coincidence if Mrs Hannible had suffered a stroke in the period between telephoning the surgery and Shipman's arrival at her house and that the stroke proved fatal while he was there. Other doctors find that such coincidences do not happen. If Shipman is to be believed, this kind of coincidence happened to him very frequently. I regard the happening of a sudden death in Shipman's presence as highly suspicious.
Although Mrs Hannible was elderly and at some increased risk of suffering a stroke, there had been no sign that she would do so on that day. I accept that elderly people can suffer strokes without any warning. So, it is possible that Mrs Hannible could have died from a stroke on that day. However, Shipman's account of the death, as set out in the medical records and Form B, does not make medical sense. If she was unconscious when he arrived, he could not have diagnosed a right-sided stroke.
Form B contains at least one demonstrable lie. The grandson was not present
'through'
the stroke. He arrived after Mrs Hannible had died. Shipman often claimed that others were present at the death when in fact he was alone with his patient. I am sure he did this to make it appear that the death was not unexpected. I think it highly likely that Shipman also lied in stating that he had seen Mrs Hannible alive on 17th
July, a week before her death. The surgery records do not show either a visit or a surgery appointment. The acute prescriptions book does not contain any reference to her. The medical records show a request for zopiclone on that day. I suspect that entry might have been inserted after the death but that cannot be checked as at this time the audit trail facility had not been installed on the computer. Even if the entry in the medical record were genuine, it would not suggest a face to face meeting but implies a telephone request. I suspect that Shipman wished to say that he had seen Mrs Hannible more recently than he had, so as to give the impression that she had recently been in need of medical attention and that he was in a good position to diagnose the cause of death.
Mrs Hannible's appearance in death was typical of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of diamorphine.
I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Hannible.

name: Jozef Iwanina
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 3 Clough Fold Road, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
It is possible that Mr Iwanina died a natural death from a cause related to heart disease. The family believed that Mr Iwanina had been diagnosed as having angina and was to be assessed for suitability for bypass surgery. I infer from this that Mr Iwanina must have had ischaemic heart disease. He would therefore be at a significantly increased risk of a heart attack. If it is right that he was doing strenuous work in his garden, as opposed to 'pottering about', it may be that this put additional strain on his heart and precipitated a heart attack.
At some time during the afternoon, Mr Iwanina stopped gardening and went indoors. He might have done so simply to have lunch and a cup of coffee but he might have gone in because he had chest pains. It is even possible that he went in to answer the door to Shipman. However, there is no evidence to suggest that Shipman visited on the day of the death, and Shipman was not in the habit of visiting any member of the family.
So far, everything points to a natural death. There are, however, some unexplained features. Mr Iwanina's position and appearance in death are not typical of those found after a death from heart attack. The generic evidence of Dr John Grenville suggests that this peaceful appearance would be rare after any sudden death, especially one with a cardiac cause. However, this factor is far from conclusive. The index for suspicion is increased because it seems that Shipman falsely claimed that he had seen Mr Iwanina within 14 days before his death. Whether or not Mrs Iwanina is right when she recalls that Shipman said he had seen her husband only the previous day, it does seem likely that Shipman was anxious to avoid a referral to the coroner and a post-mortem examination. Shipman seems to have thought that if he had not seen a patient within 14 days before death, the certificate would be rejected by the registrar, who would refer the case to the coroner. In fact this should not necessarily follow, but there appears to be a common belief among doctors that it does. However, it is possible that this apparent untruth was a 'white lie', told by Shipman in order to avoid the trouble of a referral to the coroner. The Inquiry is aware of several cases in which Shipman made similar false statements in relation to deceased persons whom he did not kill.
It is surprising that Shipman stated that his answers as to mode and cause of death were based on his own observations of the position in which Mr Iwanina's body was found. The position in which the body was found was not suggestive of a sudden cardiac death, although the position in which Shipman first saw the body might have been.
In some ways Mr Iwanina would have been an improbable victim for Shipman to choose. He was quite young and active and lived with his wife. However, it appears that he was to be assessed for suitability for by-pass surgery and it is quite possible that Shipman would have wished to forestall the expensive heart surgery.
I regret to say that I an unable to reach a positive conclusion in this case. There is evidence to suggest that the death was natural but there are factors which arouse my suspicion that Shipman might have killed Mr Iwanina.

name: Hannah Jones
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 24 Chartist House, Hyde
conclusion:
In the absence of medical records, it is very difficult to form any reliable view of the circumstances of Mrs Jones' death. I regret to say that I do not find Mrs Foden a reliable witness. Where it has been possible to make a check on her recollection, it has been found that she is not always right. I am, for example, quite satisfied that Shipman visited Mrs Jones on 9th
and 10th
as well as on Monday, 8th
July. I am also satisfied that Mrs Jones had been unwell for some days before 8th
July and that Shipman had visited on 4th
and 6th
July. It follows that I do not accept that Mrs Jones was well until she developed some breathlessness on Monday, 8th
July. These matters reveal important inaccuracies in Mrs Foden's evidence. I cannot rely on her account of the events of the Monday afternoon. I regret to add that I think that Mrs Foden's account has been coloured by her strong dislike of Shipman. Whether that dislike is justified is not for me to say. I believe it has affected her view of him and she has persuaded herself that he was responsible for her mother's death.
I regret that I will be unable to reach any conclusion in this case. The circumstances are not sufficiently clear. In the absence of the medical records, I cannot have confidence in Mrs Foden's assertion that her mother was reasonably well until 8th
July. Nor am I confident in the accuracy of Mrs Foden's account of the events of that day or the two succeeding days.

name: Charles Henry Killan
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 12 Bagshaw Street, Newton, Hyde
conclusion:
This case is highly suspicious. First, the death occurred when Shipman was alone with the patient. This is a most unusual and highly suspicious circumstance.
Second, although the symptoms reported to the surgery through Ms Lawrence are not inconsistent with acute left ventricular failure, they are not diagnostic of it. Mr Killan's medical history was not such as would give rise to an expectation that he would die suddenly of acute left ventricular failure. Shipman claimed he had ordered an ambulance, which would have been the appropriate thing to do if Mr Killan was in acute left ventricular failure. However, he had not ordered one.
Third, it appears likely that Shipman administered an injection of some sort to Mr Killan. In the records he claimed to have given Lasix, which would have been appropriate for acute left ventricular failure, but the dose was inappropriately large. Shipman could properly have given a small dose of diamorphine, but there is no record that he did. No reliance can be placed on the accuracy or honesty of Shipman's records.
Fourth, the mode of death was not consistent with death due to heart failure, but was entirely consistent with death by morphine poisoning.
Fifth, Shipman did not make any proper examination before declaring Mr Killan dead. Unless he already knew Mr Killan was dead, he would have had to examine his eyes, pulse and heart in order to establish death.
Taking all these factors into account, I consider that the overwhelming likelihood is that Shipman killed Mr Killan. I am sure he did so.

name: Ivy Lomas
title: Mrs
conclusion:
This was a clear case of murder, as the jury found, but it was clear only because of the morphine level found in the body tissues. Were it not for that evidence, this death might well have been passed off as natural, even at a post-mortem examination. The noteworthy features are:
This was a sudden death behind closed doors in Shipman's surgery. This is a very rare event in the experience of other doctors. Such an event gives rise to a high degree of suspicion. If a patient collapses at a surgery, the doctor should call for assistance and ask for an ambulance to be summoned. Shipman did not call an ambulance or request the assistance of the staff in his claimed attempt to resuscitate Mrs Lomas. In fact, there is little doubt that no such attempt was made.
Shipman chose an explanation for the death which was plausible in that Mrs Lomas had been complaining of chest pain and pain in the arm on the day of her death. It rather looks as though Shipman realised that this was pain of cardiac origin and took the opportunity to kill Mrs Lomas.
Shipman gave inconsistent accounts of events to others. To Mrs Dalpiaz, he had said he had tried resuscitation. To PC Reade, he said he had not. To Mrs Chapman, he did not say that he had. To Mrs Chapman, he said that Mrs Lomas had died in his presence, as he was trying to use the ECG machine. To PC Reade and Mrs Dalpiaz, he said Mrs Lomas had died while he was attending to another patient in another room.

name: Winifred Mellor
title: Mrs
conclusion:
This was a clear case of morphine poisoning as the post-mortem results showed. Apart from that evidence, the case contains a number of features worthy of note:
This was a sudden death of a woman who lived alone and which was discovered shortly after a visit from Shipman, at a time when she was alone. No one saw Mrs Mellor alive or spoke to her after Shipman had visited.
Shipman altered medical records to create a history of angina, which was supportive of his diagnosis of the cause of death, namely coronary thrombosis.
There are important conflicts between the accounts Shipman gave at the time of the death and the evidence given at trial. Shipman told the family that he had visited Mrs Mellor at home at about 3pm. He told them that Mrs Mellor had been suffering from angina for about a year. At the trial, he said that Mrs Mellor saw him at the surgery in the afternoon and told him for the first time about the angina symptoms she had supposedly been suffering. This was a complete volte-face, rendered necessary by the realisation that the police had been able to trace and time the false records.
Shipman claimed that the patient had refused treatment shortly before death. This is one of his regular excuses for leaving a supposedly sick patient alone when the truth was that the patient had not been ill and had not required treatment but had been killed by Shipman. He would then have an explanation for the death when it was discovered.
Shipman was ready to give the impression that a daughter and neighbour had been present at the time of death, when they had not.

name: Norah Nuttall
title: Mrs
conclusion:
This was a cremation case in which there were no remains to be examined. Nonetheless, the jury convicted Shipman of murder. The case bore a number of the hallmarks of a Shipman killing:
Shipman had no proper reason for his decision to call upon the patient. He lied in claiming that the patient had requested a visit. He knew that she was not well because she had called at the surgery that morning. In describing her condition just before death, he exaggerated it, claiming that she was seriously ill when she was not.
The death was extremely sudden and quite unexpected. It occurred while the patient was alone with Shipman. That is an extremely rare event in the experience of most general practitioners.
Shipman chose a cause of death which was plausible, in that Mrs Nuttall had been suffering from heart disease for some time.
Shipman's description of the manner of death was not typical of a death from the cause he diagnosed. Nor was the appearance of the body (sitting in a chair as if asleep) such as would have been expected after a death from heart failure. It was what would be expected from a death from diamorphine.
Shipman did not attempt resuscitation in circumstances in which that would have been the appropriate course if Mrs Nuttall really had gone into acute heart failure.
Shipman lied when he claimed to have rung for an ambulance and pretended to cancel it. This is a feature that occurs in other cases.
Shipman's examination of the body was perfunctory. It was not sufficient to have diagnosed the fact of death. It was as if he already knew that Mrs Nuttall was dead.

name: Enid Otter
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 21 Waverley Road, Hyde
certified_cause: congestive heart failure due to hypertension
conclusion:
There are a number of highly suspicious factors surrounding this death. The first is that the death was discovered not long after a visit by Shipman. There is a close temporal link between his visit and her death. Shipman visited Mrs Otter at approximately midday on 29th
September. He was the last person to speak to or see Mrs Otter alive. It appears that Mrs Shedwick was unable to attract her attention at about 4pm and, when Mrs Heywood visited just before 7pm, there was no answer at the door. Mrs Otter did not make telephone contact with her son, as she would have done had she been feeling unwell. According to Dr Grenville, had Mrs Otter suffered severe cardiac failure it is likely that she still would have had an opportunity to do so. Her telephone was not used after 10.40am on the day of the death. The temporal link excites a high degree of suspicion.
Although Shipman certified that the death was due to congestive heart failure, there is little independent evidence that she had that condition. In the week before she died, but not before, Mrs Otter exhibited some of the signs and symptoms of heart failure. However, the doctor in Rhos-on-Sea thought she had phlebitis and the record of that consultation does not refer to chest pain. In her statement to the police, Mrs Heywood said that Mrs Otter had told her that while away, she suffered from chest pains and very swollen feet. She did not repeat that, assertion in her statement to the Inquiry. Mr Otter does not remember his mother saying that she had had chest pain while on holiday. Dr Grenville is of the opinion that, as Mrs Otter requested a visit because her legs were swollen, painful and inflamed, the swelling was consistent with a recurrence of phlebitis, and not necessarily indicative of congestive heart failure. If Mrs Otter were not showing clear signs of congestive heart failure on 28th
September, when Mrs Heywood last saw her, she would have been unlikely to die of it the following day.
Shortly before her death, it appears that Mrs Otter felt well enough to eat, as she had left a pasty in the oven. This factor does not necessarily assist in a determination of the time of death, as Mrs Otter might have planned to eat a pasty for lunch or in the mid-afternoon or for her evening meal. However, it is not consistent with a death at 10pm, as suggested by Shipman, even if the death had been preceded by a coma of two hours. That the curtains were open and the pasty in the oven suggests, but does not prove, that the death occurred much earlier than 10pm.
Mrs Heywood says that she noticed that the front door was unlocked when Shipman arrived on 30th
September. It would appear that she herself had not tried the front door when she called on Mrs Otter at about 9.45am. At the surgery, Shipman had suggested to her that she should try to gain access via the back doors, which suggests either that Mrs Heywood had told Shipman that she had tried the door and could not gain access or that Shipman was anxious to suggest that entry be made by the back doors as he knew that Mrs Heywood might be puzzled if the front door was insecure. If the front door were unlocked, as Mrs Heywood says, it would suggest that someone had left the house after Mrs Otter's death.
The entry in the Lloyd George notes is startlingly similar to many I have seen in cases where Shipman has killed his patient. He starts by recording the true reason for the visit, and then switches to recording findings which he wishes to present in order to explain the death which is about to be discovered. Here, he presented a picture of severe heart failure. There are several suspicious features in this record, in particular the suggestion that Shipman had discussed hospital admission with Mrs Otter, but she preferred to stay at home and would 'let him know' if matters deteriorated. Mrs Heywood is of the opinion that, had Shipman advised Mrs Otter to go to hospital, then she would have done so without hesitation, as she held him in such high regard. Further doubt is cast on this version of events by Shipman's reaction to the news that Mrs Otter was not answering the door when Mrs Heywood called at the surgery the following day. If, on the previous day, Mrs Otter had genuinely presented with symptoms of heart failure serious enough to warrant hospital admission, then the fact that she was not answering her door would have given real cause for concern. His reaction was more consistent with his knowledge that she was dead, than a belief that she might need urgent medical attention. It appears to me highly likely that Shipman's record of the consultation on 29th
September was fabricated for the purpose of explaining her death.
Shipman recorded on Form B of the cremation certificate that Mrs Heywood was present at the moment of Mrs Otter's death. It is clear from her statement that she was not. Whilst it is possible that this was a genuinely mistaken entry, the far more plausible explanation is that it was an attempt by Shipman to deflect any suspicion that the countersigning doctor and medical referee might have had when examining cremation Form B.
The position in which Mrs Otter was found is inconsistent with the stated cause of death but consistent with the administration of a lethal dose of opiates.
Taking all these factors into account, I am sure that Shipman was responsible for Mrs Otter's death. I think it highly likely that he killed her using his usual method, a lethal injection of diamorphine.

name: Bianka Pomfret
title: Mrs
conclusion:
The death is a clear case of morphine poisoning but, even if the evidence of morphine in the body is taken out of account, there remain a number of significant factors:
This was a sudden death, which was discovered shortly after a visit from Shipman at which he saw the patient alone. No one saw or spoke to Mrs Pomfret after Shipman's visit.
Shipman told the family that Mrs Pomfret had refused treatment that he had advised. Shipman often said this of patients whom he had killed.
Shipman gave a quite different account to Dr Tait from that which he had given to the family.
Mrs Pomfret's position and peaceful appearance in death were not typical of those seen in a patient who has suffered a heart attack. They were entirely typical of those seen in many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by diamorphine injection.
When the falsified entries were excluded, the medical records did not support Shipman's stated opinion of the medical cause of death.
The family says that Shipman did not offer a post-mortem but Shipman said that he had offered the family a post-mortem but they had refused it. This particular conflict of evidence is found again and again in cases where Shipman is suspected of killing a patient. In any event, it was not for Shipman to offer the family a post-mortem examination. It was his duty to decline to sign the MCCD if he was not sufficiently confident that he knew the cause of death. On his story, he could not have been sufficiently sure that Mrs Pomfret had had a heart attack and the death should have been reported to the coroner.

name: Marie Quinn
title: Mrs
conclusion:
The evidence in this case is overwhelming, as with all the cases where morphine was found in the body. Even without that evidence the case would have been strong and there are a number of noteworthy features:
This was a sudden death, wholly unexpected to those who knew Mrs Quinn.
The death was closely associated in time with Shipman's presence. He claimed to have found Mrs Quinn on the verge of death. There are a number of other cases where Shipman has claimed to have found a patient already dead or dying, when the truth is that they were alive when he arrived but dead when he left.
Shipman claimed that the patient had telephoned, requesting a visit. This was a proven lie as no call had been made from Mrs Quinn's house to the surgery. Shipman sometimes said this to the families of victims as an excuse for a visit, when the truth was that he had made his own decision to call.
Shipman also claimed that he had told Mrs Quinn to leave the door on the latch. He sometimes said this to families of victims when he needed an explanation for his means of entry, when he was claiming that on arrival he found the patient already dead.
Despite his attempts at falsification, the cause of death given by Shipman was not borne out by examination of the records.

name: Dorothea Hill Renwick
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 148 Dowson Road, Gee Cross, Hyde
certified_cause: cardiac failure, due to ischaemic heart disease caused by hypertension
conclusion:
Mrs Renwick was alive when Shipman arrived for the visit. I think it likely that he arrived while she was still eating her lunch, soon after Mrs Morgan left. On Form B, he estimates the time of his visit at about noon. I think that would be about right. From the entry he made at some stage in the medical records, Shipman would have us think that he examined Mrs Renwick, gave her a prescription and left her alive and well. Had he done so, I think it likely she would have either finished her lunch or at least taken the dishes to the kitchen and washed them up. Shipman suggests that Mrs Renwick died at about 2pm, although how he is supposed to know that is hard to understand, if he was not there. On the evidence, I infer that Shipman arrived at about noon and that Mrs Renwick was never able to finish her pudding. So this was a very sudden death which took place extremely close to the time of a visit by Shipman. When Mrs Morgan left the house, her mother was in good health, relaxed and eating a healthy lunch. It is too much of a coincidence to accept that Mrs Renwick could have died a natural death so soon after Shipman's departure that she had not had time to finish her pudding. It is far more likely that Shipman administered an injection to Mrs Renwick and that she lapsed into sleep, unconsciousness and died while he was there. In my view, the medical note is a fabrication, designed to suggest that Mrs Renwick was alive and well when Shipman left.
The gas fire, which had been left on a high setting, is also a cause for suspicion. This is a feature of a number of suspicious deaths in which Shipman had left the body to be found by others. Leaving the body wrapped up and in a warm room would make the task of estimating the time of death even more difficult than usual.
The contents of Form B, in particular the claim that the information about the cause and mode of death had come from Dr Moysey and Mrs Morgan, are plainly false and are designed to create a feasible account and to allay any possible suspicion.
It appears that Shipman was prepared to run the risk that, if the body was not found during surgery hours, the duty doctor called to the death might refer the case to the coroner. However, one of the Donneybrook doctors or a deputising doctor would have been on call that night and that doctor would have left the matter of certification to Shipman, as the patient's regular doctor. In any event, a routine post-mortem examination would not reveal the presence of morphine and Shipman might well have believed that the death was likely to be ascribed to heart disease. This indicates a degree of confidence on Shipman's part that the normal course of events following the death would not raise suspicions.
I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Renwick.

name: Mabel Shawcross
title: Miss
place_of_death: her home, 105 Stockport Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I regard the circumstances of this case as highly suspicious, even though there is no direct evidence that Shipman visited Miss Shawcross on the day of her death.
The medical evidence suggests that Miss Shawcross was in good health up to the day of her death. This death should have been referred to the coroner and Shipman's failure to refer it must be seen as a suspicious feature.
The entry in the computerised notes relating to the 20th
January was entered on the day before the death was discovered. There is no reference to Mrs Shawcross in either the practice appointments sheets or the visits book for the whole month of January 1998. In my view, it is likely that Shipman has made up the supposed consultations of 20th
January. If it were known that Shipman had not seen Miss Shawcross since September 1997, the registrar would almost certainly have referred the case to the coroner, with a view to post-mortem examination. What is so remarkable and, in my view, very highly suspicious, is that Shipman made those entries on the afternoon of 22nd
January. That was before Miss Shawcross' body had been found. In my view, this suggests that Shipman knew that Miss Shawcross was dead at a time when no one else did. Otherwise, it is an extraordinary coincidence that he should have made an entry in her records just a few hours before her death. Thus, although there is no direct evidence that Shipman visited Miss Shawcross on the day of her death, the 22nd
January, this entry in the medical record convinces me that he must have done.
The time of death, stated with apparent precision, as
'19.00'
hours on 22nd January, must in my view be a false entry. There is absolutely no basis on which Shipman could properly have assessed that as the time of death. No one had seen Miss Shawcross on 22nd January, unless Shipman had. The fact that the milk bottle was still on the door step and that the dining room curtains were open, suggests that Miss Shawcross had died during the daylight hours of the previous day. Nothing more could be said with any confidence. The police officer does not record Shipman having taken the body temperature when he came to see the body. Dr Grenville has explained, in connection with other cases, that it is not possible for a doctor to estimate the time of death with precision. He considers Shipman's claims to be able to do so to be pure charlatanism. Any honest doctor called out to see a body in these circumstances could do no more than give a very broad bracket within which the death had occurred. Why would Shipman wish to advance a precise time of death? If Miss Shawcross had died a natural death, it is hard to imagine why Shipman would not be content to say that he did not know the time of death. However, if he had visited the house and had killed Miss Shawcross in the afternoon, he would not know whether he had been seen. He would wish to establish that the death had occurred a considerable time after he had visited. I regard this feature as highly suspicious.
An additional factor, which increases the index of suspicion, is that Miss Shawcross' appearance in death was not typical of that seen in stroke victims. It was, however, entirely typical of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of diamorphine.
My conclusion is that Shipman killed Miss Shawcross, almost certainly by administering a lethal injection of opiate. Although there is a theoretical possibility that she could have suffered a fatal stroke, I regard that as so unlikely that I feel able to say that I am sure of my conclusion.

name: Irene Turner
title: Mrs
conclusion:
This was a proven case of morphine poisoning. However, if one takes that factor out of the equation, there remain several factors which are common to other cases:
This was a very sudden death of a patient who did not appear to others to be seriously ill on the day of death. However, she had underlying conditions which could have resulted in her sudden death at any time. Shipman's victims often had potentially fatal conditions, which he relied on as a plausible cause of death.
Shipman claimed that he found Mrs Turner to be seriously ill and that she refused admission to hospital. This is a common feature in many Shipman killings. Shipman left her alone, supposedly in a serious condition. She was found dead very shortly afterwards. It would have been a remarkable coincidence if she had died naturally during the few intervening minutes.
Shipman's account of his treatment of Mrs Turner was inappropriate. In order to explain the course of events, he was driven to give an account of his actions which, if true, would have shown him to be seriously incompetent. This is a common feature of Shipman killings.
Shipman's two sets of records of the events preceding the death were woefully inadequate and were mutually inconsistent. It was accepted that Shipman was a poor record keeper and this is amply demonstrated in very many cases.
The body gave the appearance of having been 'laid out'. So neat and tidy an appearance is not typical of an unattended death from natural causes. Other examples of this feature have emerged from the Inquiry's investigations.

name: Lucy Virgin
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 24 Carter Place, Newton, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis caused by ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
There are a number of suspicious features about this death.
The cause of death given by Shipman gives rise to suspicion. Although it is theoretically possible that Mrs Virgin could have died suddenly from a heart attack or some other cause of sudden death, a death from such a cause was unlikely. There was nothing in her general or recent medical history to suggest that she was at risk from a cardiac death or any other type of sudden death. Shipman told a lie on the MCCD when he said that Mrs Virgin had been suffering from ischaemic heart disease for 11 years. This was not supported by the medical records. Mrs Virgin's appearance in death was not what would be expected following a sudden natural death. I find it unlikely that Mrs Virgin died of a heart attack or any other of the common causes of sudden natural death.
There is clear evidence that Mrs Virgin was alive after Shipman's visit at about noon on 1st
March. There is evidence to suggest that she was dead by about 2.45pm. She was certainly dead by 4pm. If Shipman did not visit Mrs Virgin again that day, the only rational conclusion is that she died a sudden but natural death, unlikely though such a death might be. Although there is no direct evidence that Shipman visited for a second time on 1st
March, there is evidence from which it may be inferred that he did visit again. He had the opportunity, although that does not prove anything. There is evidence that Mrs Virgin was on Shipman's mind that day. He asked Mrs Smith whether she had seen her aunt. She could have been on his mind because he had just visited her but the comment is strange even so. The most powerful evidence in favour of a second visit by Shipman is that Mrs Virgin's door was unlocked when Mr Booth arrived at about 4pm, although it was securely locked when he arrived and when he left earlier that day. Mrs Virgin was conscious of the need for security. She usually kept her door bolted and chained. It seems to me likely that, if she were able to do so, she would secure the door after any visitor had departed. Had she died a natural death, I would have expected the door to be locked from within. That Mrs Virgin had not locked her door on an occasion during the afternoon of the day of her death suggests that she was unable to do so.
Shipman made a number of misleading statements on Form B. I have already discussed those statements and the reasons why I think they were made. I regard these statements as highly suspicious.
As Dr Grenville observed, if this were a natural death, Shipman could not honestly have certified the cause of death on the information available to him. Any honest doctor in his supposed position would have referred the case to the coroner.
Mrs Virgin's appearance in death was entirely typical of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of diamorphine.
I am sure that Shipman did visit Mrs Virgin again, at some time between 1pm and 2pm, and that he injected her with a lethal dose of diamorphine, thereby causing her death.

name: Ada Warburton
title: Miss
place_of_death: her home, 55 Grange Road North, Hyde
conclusion:
It appears that Shipman's version of events, as taken from the medical records, the MCCD and Form B, is that Miss Warburton began to suffer a stroke during the morning, some six to eight hours before her death; that would be between 9.30am and 11.30am. She telephoned the surgery at about lunchtime to say that she thought she might be having a stroke. Shipman seems to time his attendance during the last illness from that time. He visited her at about 3pm according to the medical note but at 5.30pm according to Form B. He then found no reason to think she was having a stroke but promised to return later on. He returned later at 6.15pm and found that she had died about 45 minutes earlier.
This account can be shown to be false in some respects. First, the evidence shows that there was no neighbour (whether from number 79 or at all) who could have provided Shipman with any information about the mode of death. Nor was a neighbour (whether from number 79 or at all) present at the moment of death. Further, there is no evidence to support Shipman's claim that Miss Warburton was concerned about slurred speech in the morning. Nor is there any evidence to support his claim that Miss Warburton telephoned the surgery to ask him to visit. I think it is highly unlikely that she did so. Had she been concerned about herself in the morning she would almost certainly have told Mrs Cooper when they met. Also, when Mrs Cooper returned home, Miss Warburton would probably have told her that she was expecting the doctor. Shipman told PC Hodkinson that Miss Warburton had come in to the surgery in the morning but he told Mrs Creasey that she had telephoned to ask for a visit. Shipman told Mrs Creasey that there was nothing apparently wrong with Miss Warburton when he visited in the afternoon; yet he told Mrs Cooper that she was very poorly. Shipman was either present at the death or, if not actually in the room at the moment of death, he was near the house. Yet he has pretended that the death occurred after he had departed. The death must have occurred much sooner than Shipman claims. Mrs Cooper is not certain of the time but her first recollection, which I believe is likely to be the more accurate, is that she first saw Shipman at about 3.30-3.45pm and that Miss Warburton was dead within about 15 minutes after that. I think it likely that Mr Catlow is right in implying that he learned of the death while he was outside in his garden. Although I cannot be sure of the timings of events, I am sure that Shipman's various statements are full of inconsistencies and I am sure that his account is a tissue of lies.
Miss Warburton was fit and well in the late morning of 20th
March. She did not seek a visit from Shipman and Shipman lied in suggesting that she had. I am satisfied that he paid an unsolicited visit, probably at about 3pm. I think he found some excuse to give her an injection of diamorphine. Possibly he told her he would take a blood sample. He then waited a while and went to speak to Mrs Cooper. He virtually forbad Mrs Cooper to visit her friend. When Mrs Cooper looked through the window and saw Miss Warburton apparently watching television, she was almost certainly unconscious and close to death. I think Shipman remained in the vicinity, possibly returning to his car before coming back to the house to check that Miss Warburton was dead. I think he then told Mrs Cooper of the death and Mr Catlow learned of it as well. I think Mrs Cooper is probably mistaken when she says that she stayed with the body until the police and undertakers arrived. It is possible that the death was not 'discovered' by Shipman until the early evening, in which case the recollections of both Mrs Cooper and Mr Catlow are inaccurate in any event.
Shipman gave inconsistent accounts of the events of the day and made false entries on Form B. If Miss Warburton's death had been natural, Shipman could not possibly have known what had caused it and he would, if honest, have referred it to the coroner.
Miss Warburton's appearance in death was very similar to that of many of Shipman's victims and was consistent with death from opiate overdose.
Despite the uncertainty as to the time of the discovery of the body, I am sure that Shipman killed Miss Warburton, by injecting her with a large dose of opiate, almost certainly diamorphine.

name: Lizzie Adams
title: Mrs
conclusion:
The following significant points arise in this case:
The death took place in Mrs Adams' home and in Shipman's presence. This is a factor which gives rise to a high degree of suspicion. A natural death at home during a doctor's visit is an extremely rare event in the experience of most general practitioners. If Shipman were to be believed, natural deaths occurred frequently during his home visits.
The death was extremely sudden. As Dr Grenville has explained, death from bronchopneumonia is not as sudden as this. The patient is very ill for at least a few hours before death. Mrs Adams had been out shopping the previous day. That morning she had done her usual household jobs.
Shipman's treatment of the condition he claimed to have found was inappropriate, according to Dr Grenville. If Mrs Adams had been truly as ill as Shipman later claimed, he should have summoned an ambulance immediately. If she had been unwilling to go to hospital, he should have spoken to Mrs Thorley. If Mrs Adams really had collapsed, he should have tried to resuscitate her. As it was obvious that he had not made any attempt to do so, he made an untenable attempt to justify his decision. He should have made a complete and thorough note of the consultation, Mrs Adams' reluctance to go to hospital, the steps he had taken in the face of that reluctance and the events leading to the death. He did not.
Mrs Adams was found sitting in a chair as though asleep. This position and appearance are not typical of a death following bronchopneumonia but are entirely typical of those observed at the deaths of many of Shipman's victims.
Shipman told others that the patient had been advised she needed hospital admission but that she was reluctant to agree. This is an explanation Shipman was to give on many other occasions.
Shipman told others he had called an ambulance and cancelled it but no such call was made. At trial, he denied having said this.
A witness says that Shipman did not carry out any examination to diagnose death whereas Shipman claimed he did. This is a feature common to many cases.
Shipman's claim on cremation Form B that Mr Catlow was present at the death is misleading.
Shipman claimed that he suggested a post-mortem examination but the witnesses said that Shipman told them this was not necessary. The death was not reported to the coroner although, as Dr Grenville said, such a report was plainly called for.

name: Valerie Cuthbert
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 38 Daisy Bank, Gee Cross, Hyde
certified_cause: left ventricular failure due to congestive heart failure and hypertension
conclusion:
Mrs Cuthbert was not in the best of health at the time of her death. Due to her raised blood pressure she was probably at a slightly increased risk of heart attack and stroke. However, she was only 54. There was nothing in her medical history which would give rise to concern that she might die suddenly. A sudden death at this time was possible but not likely. Certainly there was no reason to anticipate a death from left ventricular failure, a condition which rarely manifests itself without warning. The complete absence of any previous sign of congestive heart failure means that a sudden death from left ventricular failure was most unlikely.
I note that Mrs Cuthbert did not complain of feeling ill when she telephoned the surgery on the morning of her death. She only mentioned her painful toe. Nor had she told her sister or any friend that she was feeling unwell. I do not think she was unwell that day, apart from suffering pain in her bunion.
This death was discovered a short time after Shipman had visited Mrs Cuthbert and had been alone with her. No one apart from Shipman claims to have seen or spoken to Mrs Cuthbert after Shipman left. Shipman's claim to have telephoned Mrs Cuthbert from the surgery must be regarded with extreme suspicion. It was then Shipman who 'discovered' the death.
The record of Shipman's consultation with Mrs Cuthbert on 29th
May arouses very strong suspicion that it is not genuine. I have now seen many such entries, which begin with a reference to the condition for which the visit has been requested and then switch to signs of another condition to which Shipman will subsequently attribute the death. Here, the signs described are of congestive heart failure. There is no independent evidence that Mrs Cuthbert was suffering from this condition to a severe degree as suggested by the note. Shipman's claim that Mrs Cuthbert refused to go to hospital is highly unlikely to be true. Her relatives and friends regarded her as a sensible woman. She did not even telephone any friend or relative to tell them that Shipman had advised her to go into hospital. I am satisfied that this note was fabricated to provide an explanation for Mrs Cuthbert's death.
I am also satisfied that the tales Shipman told Mrs Wheatley and Mr Taylor were fabricated. I think he inserted a reference to a telephone call in the medical records and Form B in order to create the impression that Mrs Cuthbert had died later than she really had, and a considerable time after he had visited her.
Mrs Cuthbert's appearance in death was not consistent with the appearance of one who has died of left ventricular failure. It was, however, entirely typical of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of diamorphine. I am sure that such an injection was the cause of Mrs Cuthbert's death.

name: Joan Edwina Dean
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 58 Joel Lane, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
There is no evidence whatsoever that Shipman saw Mrs Dean on the day of her death. The Inquiry has made extensive efforts to find such evidence. Shipman had time to visit her, but that is all that can be said.
Mrs Dean had enjoyed very good health and was active at the time of her death. She had had raised blood pressure for many years, well controlled by medication. She was probably at an increased risk of suffering a stroke or a heart attack. It is possible that she could have suffered either a fatal heart attack or a fatal stroke on the day of her death. The presence of vomit in the lounge, on the stairs and in the bedroom is consistent with death from either of those natural causes.
If it were not for the false entries made on the surgery computer, in the MCCD and in Form B, there would be nothing to suggest that this was anything other than a sudden unexpected natural death. These false entries arouse real suspicion that Shipman visited Mrs Dean and killed her. It is hard to imagine why he would have gone to such trouble to fabricate a false medical history if Mrs Dean had died a natural death.
It has become clear to me from an examination of other cases, that Shipman frequently disregarded his duties in respect of the registration of deaths. A doctor is entitled to complete the MCCD if he or she has attended the deceased during the final illness and has either seen him or her within 14 days before death or has seen the body after death. There is some confusion about these requirements and some doctors and registrars are under the impression that the doctor cannot certify the cause of death unless he or she has seen the patient within 14 days before death. I think Shipman must have been under this impression, as he frequently made a false claim that he had seen a patient within 14 days of death in cases where the death was obviously natural. I assume that he did this so as to ensure that the registrar would not refer the case to the coroner. What his motives were for this, I do not know. It may be that he wished to spare the relatives the possible distress and inevitable delay resulting from a post-mortem examination. It may be, as the South Manchester Coroner suggested during the inquest in the present case, that Shipman simply did not want to be bothered with the processes involved in a coroner's referral. A desire to avoid a referral to the coroner, which the law plainly required in this case, would explain his decision to falsify the medical records so as create a consultation on 13th
February. I could not draw an inference that Shipman had killed Mrs Dean simply from the fact that he had made false entries that would enable him to sign the MCCD and avoid the risk of referral to the coroner.
A desire to avoid referral would not, however, require him to make other false entries. It was not necessary for him to claim to have already seen the body when he signed the MCCD on Monday 2nd
March. His claim, false though it was, to have seen Mrs Dean alive on 13th
February 1995 would have been enough to satisfy the coroner's liaison officer that Shipman was able to certify the cause of death. Nor did Shipman need to say that he had been Mrs Dean's doctor for far longer than he had been.
Shipman made other false entries, which at first sight appear to be quite pointless if he was not involved in the death and only wished to avoid the need for referral to the coroner. He did not need to create the false entries of 6th
and 30th
January. That he should fabricate so carefully the symptoms and signs of transient ischaemic attacks makes it appear that he was anxious to create a plausible background to a death from a stroke. Yet he certified the death as due to coronary thrombosis. He could easily have created false entries to indicate events that might presage a heart attack. Shipman was not ignorant of the relevant signs and symptoms and, in other cases, he has taken good care to create relevant false entries, helpful to the concealment of his unlawful killings. I find it strange that Shipman fabricated these entries tending to justify a death by stroke and then incompetently certified the death as due to coronary thrombosis.
Nor, if innocent but wishing to avoid a referral to the coroner, did Shipman need to make the false entries on Form B, in which he suggested that Mrs Dean had been alive when found and had died in the presence of several people. There are other cases in which Shipman has told this kind of lie, but in those cases the lie has been designed to create the impression that he was not alone with the patient at the time of death, when the truth was that he had been. Here, there is no evidence that he was alone with Mrs Dean on the day of her death, but if he was alone with her at the time of her death, it would help him to create the impression that others had been with her at the moment of death.
It is said that money and jewellery were missing from the house. Although it has been suggested in other cases that Shipman has stolen from victims he has just killed, the evidence has never been clear enough for me to make a positive finding that he has done so. There is no more than suspicion. Here, the evidence that valuables and money were missing raises a suspicion of theft but I could not possibly say that this suspicion amounted to evidence that Shipman was at the house on the day of the death.
So far in this analysis, I have only been able to say that there is no evidence that Shipman killed Mrs Dean but that there are some very odd and suspicious features to the case. I propose to test the alternative theories.
