If Shipman killed Mrs Dean, he must have visited her at some time after her return home from the bank and before 4pm. He could have done so. He was not seen but that does not mean he was not there. If he gave Mrs Dean an injection of diamorphine, it must have been administered intramuscularly. That was not his usual method of killing, although it is possible that he gave excessive doses of opiate, by the intramuscular route to some of his terminally ill patients. There are also a few cases in which I have concluded that the injection he gave probably entered the body subcutaneously, so that the drug did not act with the extreme rapidity characteristic of cases in which Shipman killed. But I know of no Shipman killing where a patient has moved so far and has left so extensive a trail of vomit as to be consistent only with intramuscular injection.
If Shipman did kill Mrs Dean, all the false entries in the MCCD and Form B are explicable as part of a plan to give the impression that the death occurred in the evening (in which he was innocently abetted by Dr Choudhury) and that it occurred in the presence of other people. However, the false entries in the medical records, presaging a death by stroke, are not explicable unless one assumes either that Shipman did not know how best to falsify the records, which I am sure he did, or that he had a mental block and certified the cause of death as heart attack when he meant to certify it as stroke.
If Shipman did not kill Mrs Dean, the circumstances of the death are wholly explicable, although the death was extremely sudden and unexpected. Shipman's desire to avoid a referral to the coroner, wrongful though it was in itself, explains some of the false records. However, I find myself unable to understand why he would have gone to such trouble to enter convincing details of transient ischaemic attacks and why he would have felt the need to give the impression that so many people were present at the death, when they were not. I can think of no satisfactory explanation for the fabrication of the records and the false entries in Form B consistent with innocence.
I have found this one of the most difficult cases to decide. In the end and after much hesitation I have come to the conclusion that Shipman probably killed Mrs Dean. I reach that conclusion mainly because I cannot believe that Shipman would have gone to such trouble to fabricate entries in Mrs Dean's medical records if he had nothing to hide in respect of her death. I think the most probable explanation is that he visited her during the afternoon of 27th
February and either gave her an intramuscular injection or attempted to give her an intravenous injection and failed to keep the needle in the vein so that at least part of the drug entered the body subcutaneously. If that happened, Mrs Dean might well have felt sick and might well have been able to walk about the house until she eventually collapsed on a bed in her spare bedroom. There are some strange and inexplicable features to the case and I am not sure of my conclusion but I am satisfied that Shipman probably killed Mrs Dean.

name: Harold Eddleston
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 25 Rufford Avenue, Hyde
conclusion:
Mr Eddleston was undoubtedly quite ill in March 1998, but to those about him he did not appear to be close to death. His lung cancer had not yet confined him to his bed. As Dr Grenville observed, the cancer was not at that time sufficiently advanced to provide a mechanism for the death. It seems to me highly unlikely that Mr Eddleston could have died suddenly of lung cancer on 4th
March.
It is possible that Mr Eddleston died a sudden death due to some other natural cause, not lung cancer. He was at an increased risk of sudden death from heart attack and stroke. It seems to me that a sudden death from one of those causes is a real possibility. However, as Dr Grenville has said, it would not be usual to find a person who has suffered a sudden death from stroke or heart attack sitting upright in a chair as if peacefully asleep.
In his report, Dr Grenville raised the possibility that Mr Eddleston might have taken an overdose of tablets, either accidentally or even deliberately. Shortly before his wife's death, he had told one of the wardens, Mrs Conley, that if his wife died he would want to go with her and would find a way of doing so. He had not said anything of that nature after Mrs Eddleston died. However, he was plainly very depressed. Mr and Mrs Dickson were both asked about the possibility of an overdose. They were both of the view that this was highly unlikely. Mr Eddleston did not like taking pills and they thought he would not have had the 'courage' to take his own life. The only drug in Mr Eddleston's possession, which could have caused his death, was the tramadol. As this made Mr Eddleston sick, it is highly unlikely he would have taken a large number, either accidentally or on purpose, and have died, without there being any sign of vomit. In any event, there were no signs of any tablets or a container near the body. I think I can safely discount the suggestion of overdose for those reasons.
Where a patient of Shipman has died suddenly, in circumstances where there is no clear cause of death, there is always a suspicion that he might have been involved. Here, there is no clear evidence that he was with Mr Eddleston at the material time, but there is some evidence from which I can infer that he was. Mr Eddleston was alone in the house for just over two hours in the early afternoon. This was at a time when Shipman would have been out on his visits. For what it is worth, he had to pay one visit not far from Rufford Avenue. Mrs Downs says that he called twice at the Eddleston house, once at about lunchtime and again later in the afternoon. We know that he did call in the mid to late afternoon. If Mrs Downs' evidence can be accepted as to the earlier visit, Shipman paid a visit to Mr Eddleston, after which he was not seen alive. If this earlier visit occurred, Shipman later sought to conceal it. Although Shipman often admitted and asserted that he had been with a patient at or shortly before death, he did not always make this admission. In the course of this Inquiry, I have come across other cases in which Shipman has visited and killed a patient, and has subsequently sought to conceal his presence at the material time. If Shipman did visit shortly after Mrs Dickson had left, we would have the usual pattern of a Shipman diamorphine killing: a visit with a patient alone in the house; no sighting of the patient alive after that visit; the body being found sitting in a chair as if asleep.
I have not had the benefit of seeing Mrs Downs in person. I am aware that she was initially unwilling to provide a statement for the Inquiry but I understand that this was on account of her extremely difficult personal circumstances. I found Mrs Marsden an impressive witness, whose evidence I accept as honest. I am conscious of the fact that both these women provided their evidence a long time after the event of which they were speaking and that, in the intervening period, Shipman has been exposed as a prolific serial killer who preyed on just such people as Mr Eddleston. I must recognise the possibility that both Mrs Downs and Mrs Marsden have become convinced that Shipman visited the Eddleston house twice on that day rather than once. Having said that, Mrs Downs' evidence puts him at the house at about the time when he would have had the opportunity to visit and when Mr Eddleston would have been alone. Mrs Downs would not have known when Mr Eddleston was alone and, not knowing Shipman, she would not have known the times at which he usually made his visits. Accordingly, I have come to accept that the evidence of Mrs Downs, supported as it is by Mrs Marsden, is right. I think Shipman visited at about 1pm.
In my view, all the natural causes of death that I have mentioned are unlikely, although theoretically possible. I discount the hypothesis of drug overdose. The suddenness of the death and manner of death is consistent with diamorphine poisoning. Having accepted that Shipman did visit Mr Eddleston at about 1pm, I can say that I am sure that Shipman unlawfully killed Mr Eddleston.

name: Dorothy Fletcher
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
In my view, there are several causes for suspicion in this case.
Mrs Fletcher was quite elderly and had been suffering from a chest infection for some time before her death. She was therefore at risk of developing bronchopneumonia. However, even if this condition develops rapidly, there is still some warning of the death. The decline towards death is noticeable over at least a few hours. I have been told by senior staff at Charnley House that it was their practice to warn relatives if a resident was critically ill. I have seen cases where this has been done. Yet here, there is no evidence that the staff foresaw Mrs Fletcher's death. The family was not warned. I regard that as a suspicious feature. It appears to me that Mrs Fletcher's death was rather sudden, especially as she is said to have eaten a full lunch.
My suspicions are further raised by the inconsistencies between the daily diary and Shipman's entries in Form B. First, there is Shipman's claim that Mrs Fletcher had been in a coma for 12 hours, which I am sure is untrue. Second, Shipman says that he was there shortly before the death and the diary says he did not attend until after the death. My concern is increased by the rather odd entry made by Mrs Meadows in the afternoon and evening report. She appears to have made an incomplete entry, leaving a blank space after Shipman's name. Someone else completed the time of his arrival, which probably reflects the time of his arrival after the death but implies that he had not been at the home before the death. Mrs Meadow's explanation for this odd entry is not satisfactory, not least because it appears that Shipman arrived before Mrs Meadows finished her shift at 8pm. There is a real suspicion that Shipman arrived at the home before Mrs Fletcher's death but that the time of his first arrival was not noted in the diary.
According to the daily diary, Shipman had not seen Mrs Fletcher for eight days before her death. She did not then have bronchopneumonia. Unless he had seen her after that, when the nature of her final illness could be diagnosed, Shipman would be unable to certify the cause of death and should have referred the case to the coroner.
Although this death occurred many years ago and the medical records have not survived, there are contemporaneous records kept by people who had a duty to be honest and careful. Where such records are available, it ought to be possible to piece together a clear picture of the circumstances preceding a death such as this, which occurred in an elderly persons' home. In general, the quality of note keeping at Charnley House is quite high and I usually feel a degree of confidence in its accuracy. I have seen many examples of diary notes that chart the decline before death, the attendance of the doctor and the warning of the relatives. This case seems to be something of an exception. If, during 23rd
April, Mrs Fletcher had been ill enough to die of bronchopneumonia in the early evening, I would have expected the death to be presaged in the notes. I would have expected to see a record of her condition, the summoning of the doctor (and concern if he did not attend), a note of the time of his arrival, the warning of the relatives and possibly a note of the watch being kept. In this case, there is nothing between the record that Mrs Fletcher ate a full lunch before 1pm and her death at 6pm. That Mrs Meadows noted that Mrs Fletcher 'passed away peacefully' does not give rise to suspicion. Her evidence is that she always put something like that, whatever the mode of death, and I have seen many entries to confirm the truth of that statement. Even so, the picture presented by the daily diary does not tally with a death from bronchopneumonia.
It is a matter of some concern that the daily diary does not provide me with a coherent account of the events leading to Mrs Fletcher's death. Whether deliberately or due to carelessness or overwork, it appears that Mrs Meadows, who made the afternoon and evening report, has failed to record important matters. It may be that it is only in recent years that the need for full and accurate notes has been stressed by those in charge at residential and nursing homes.
By 1986, Shipman had already killed a significant number of patients. It is therefore quite possible that he killed Mrs Fletcher. It seems quite possible to me that, having been unwell in the early morning (so that Shipman was asked to attend), Mrs Fletcher improved and was able to eat lunch. It seems quite likely that a member of staff might have cancelled the request for Shipman to visit. Otherwise I would have expected him to visit around lunchtime, as was his usual practice. I think he did not visit during the day. I think he visited in the evening, probably after surgery. He was on duty that evening. I think Mrs Fletcher died, rather suddenly, while he was there. I think it likely that he gave her a lethal injection of opiate. Although some of the Charnley House staff now say that there was always a rule that a doctor should not be left alone with a patient, I have the impression that that rule was not strictly observed in the 1980s. Indeed Ms Kilgariff, who worked there in 1979, was unaware of any such rule. I think it quite likely that, even if a care assistant was present at the start of a consultation, it would be very easy for Shipman to get rid of her. He would only need to ask her to collect an item of equipment or make him a cup of tea.
It is possible that Mrs Fletcher died naturally on 23rd
April 1986 although, if she did, I do not think it could have been from bronchopneumonia. Bearing in mind the suspicious factors to which I have referred, I have come to the conclusion that it is likely that Shipman killed her. The evidence falls a long way short of that which would be required before Shipman could be convicted of murder but I think it is likely that this was an unlawful killing.

name: Muriel Grimshaw
title: Mrs
conclusion:
This is a clear case of murder in which morphine was found in the body. Shipman must have made a completely unsolicited visit on 14th
July to a patient whom he had not seen since May and who was in completely normal health. He must have found some pretext for giving her an injection. The significant features are:
The sudden death of this healthy woman was discovered very soon after a visit at which Shipman saw her alone.
When Shipman was summoned, Mrs Brown said that he did not even examine the body sufficiently to establish that Mrs Grimshaw was dead. This is an observation made by many relatives in cases in which Shipman has killed. The inference to be drawn is that he already knew that the patient was dead.
There was no feasible natural explanation for the sudden death and Shipman was not in a position to certify the cause of death. Shipman should have refused to certify the cause of death and the death would then have had to be reported to the coroner. Shipman claimed that Mrs Brown had refused his suggestion that there should be a post-mortem examination. Shipman often said that relatives had refused or had 'not wanted' a post-mortem examination. It is not a matter for the relatives to decide. It is for the doctor to decide whether he or she is in a position to issue the MCCD. In any event, Mrs Brown says that Shipman made no such suggestion.

name: Pamela Marguerite Hillier
title: Mrs
conclusion:
The jury convicted although there was no direct evidence of morphine poisoning. The case contains a number of features typical of a Shipman killing:
The deceased was in apparently good health and death was very sudden and wholly unexpected.
The death was discovered shortly after a visit during which Shipman was alone with the patient. No one saw Mrs Hillier alive or spoke to her after Shipman's visit.
Shipman deterred the family from seeking a post-mortem examination (by applying some emotional pressure). He also dissuaded the paramedics from making a report to the police.
He falsified the records to lend credibility to his claimed cause of death. This is one of the cases where the audit trail enabled the prosecution to prove that there had been an elaborate falsification. Mrs Hillier was not suffering from any potentially fatal condition and Shipman found it necessary to create evidence that she was.

name: Nancy Jackson
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, Flat 1 Gower Court, King Edward Road, Hyde
conclusion:
There are highly suspicious circumstances surrounding this death.
Mrs Jackson was found dead shortly after a visit by Shipman. No one saw Mrs Jackson alive or spoke to her after that visit. The witness evidence suggests strongly that Shipman was the last person to see her alive. That, in itself, excites great suspicion.
Shipman lied on Form B. He said that Mrs Jackson was found dead by a neighbour who had seen her alive one hour beforehand. I am sure that is a lie. I am sure that if any neighbour had seen Mrs Jackson alive at about 5pm, Mrs Drew and Mrs Linda Jackson would have been told and the Inquiry would have learned about it. This lie was important because Shipman was seeking to create the impression that someone had seen Mrs Jackson alive well after his own visit.
On the same form, Shipman said that the mode of death was a coma of hours' duration. That statement is inconsistent with the claim that a neighbour saw Mrs Jackson alive an hour before death. It is also quite hard to reconcile with Shipman's presence at the house at about 2pm. Mrs Jackson was not in a coma then. She was alone. Shipman seems to imply that a neighbour had come into the house, seen Mrs Jackson in a coma, gone away again, leaving her completely alone and returned an hour later to find her dead. This account is not credible and the entries should have excited the concern of the doctor who signed Form C of the cremation certificate and the medical referee.
Mrs Jackson had been ill in the week before her death. Both the witnesses' evidence and Shipman's notes suggest that by the Friday she was greatly improved. The witnesses say that the improvement continued into the Monday. Shipman's note of his consultation on the Monday is confusing. He suggests that Mrs Jackson has right upper lobe pneumonia but does not suggest that anything needs to be done about it as a matter of urgency. Rather the reverse; he seems to be suggesting that Mrs Jackson has improved. Yet on his return to the surgery, he instructed Mrs Chapman to arrange a domiciliary visit. I think he also added the letters 'RUL' to a note he had made on the back of the visits slip on an earlier occasion. I think Shipman's request to Mrs Chapman was a diversionary tactic, designed to give the impression that Mrs Jackson was alive but unwell and in need of a specialist opinion. I think Shipman well knew at this time that she was dead. Shipman used this device in at least two other cases, those of Mrs Hilda Couzens and Mrs Olive Heginbotham, who died on the same day in February 1993.
As explained above, Mrs Jackson was not in such a moribund state as would justify ascribing her death to 'old age'. It was quite unacceptable to certify that her death was due to old age. Mrs Jackson's death was sudden and unexplained and should have been referred to the coroner.
Mrs Jackson's appearance in death was very similar to that of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of diamorphine.
I am quite sure that Shipman killed Mrs Jackson. I think he almost certainly decided to do so on Friday, 27th
August. That is why he was anxious to ensure that Mrs Drew went back to her own home, leaving Mrs Jackson alone in the house. That is why he said he would call again on the Monday to take blood samples. Patients who were to provide blood samples were particularly vulnerable to Shipman, as many patients do not watch while a blood sample is taken and would not realise that Shipman was giving an injection rather than taking blood. I am sure Shipman took some blood samples and then gave Mrs Jackson an intravenous lethal injection of opiate, almost certainly diamorphine, which would have killed her within a few minutes. He then left her and returned to the surgery where he asked Mrs Chapman to make an appointment for a domiciliary visit. When he was called out to see the body, he made up a story about a neighbour seeing Mrs Jackson alive at about 5pm. This lie was designed to distance himself from the death.

name: Alice Christine Kitchen
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 3 Kirkstone Road, Hyde
conclusion:
Mrs Kitchen was alive and apparently quite well during the afternoon of 17th
June when she spoke to Ms Raphael. Shipman visited and left at about 4pm. No one saw Mrs Kitchen alive or spoke to her after that time. That in itself is a highly suspicious factor.
Shipman's claim that Mrs Kitchen had had a mild stroke at the time when he saw her could be valid. It appears that she had told the receptionist that the nerves in her legs had gone. That might or might not have been an indication that she had had a stroke. However, she did not have high blood pressure and was not therefore at particular risk of suffering a stroke. If she had had a stroke, Shipman's response in leaving her alone in the house would have been inexcusable. She had a large family, any of whom could have been asked to sit with her. In my view, it is unlikely that Mrs Kitchen suffered a stroke that afternoon. Even if she had had a mild stroke, one would not expect her to die suddenly. The type of mild stroke that Shipman described does not usually lead to sudden death. As Dr Grenville said in his generic evidence to the Inquiry, if such strokes do progress to death, they usually do so over a period of two to three days. It would be highly improbable that Mrs Kitchen would suffer two different types of stroke on the same day.
I cannot attach much weight to the suspicion that there was morphine in the body, as there is a possibility that there could have been traces of an opiate drug taken for therapeutic purposes.
Taking all factors into account, I have reached the same conclusion as the coroner. Like him, I am satisfied so as to be sure that Shipman killed Mrs Kitchen.

name: Jean Lilley
title: Mrs
conclusion:
The following significant points arise from this case:
Because Mrs Lilley was in poor health, her sudden death would readily have been passed off as due to heart failure, had it not been for the finding of morphine in the body tissues. When Shipman had killed a patient, he usually attributed the death to a cause for which some foundation could be found in the medical records.
This was a sudden death which occurred in the patient's home, either while Shipman was present or very shortly indeed after he had been with her. If, as Mrs Hunter said, the body was cold by the time she found it, then Shipman had been present at the death. For a patient to die in the presence of his or her general practitioner during a home visit is a very rare event in the experience of most doctors.
Mrs Lilley was found sitting in a chair as though asleep. This appearance is typical of many of Shipman's victims who have been killed by diamorphine injection. This appearance would not be typical of a death from heart failure.
Shipman's explanation of events was not credible. It would have been most unlikely that Mrs Lilley would have rejected his advice to go into hospital. She would have contacted her husband on his mobile telephone to discuss the situation.
Shipman's account of his actions fell well below acceptable standards of medical practice. He claimed that Mrs Lilley rejected his advice to be admitted to hospital. If she were so ill as to require admission as an emergency, he should not have left her without making some efforts to find a relative who might persuade her to be sensible or without making some arrangements for her care.

name: Nellie Mullen
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 11 Lanegate, Hyde, a warden-controlled bungalow
conclusion:
Mrs Mullen's underlying medical condition put her at some increased risk of suffering a sudden cardiac death. It is therefore possible that she suffered a heart attack on 2nd
May, as Shipman claims she did in the note he made in the medical record. That is so, even though she was not displaying any signs of heart attack when visited by Ms Hillson. It is possible that the chest pain of the early morning was the effect of an attack of angina, which might have progressed to a myocardial infarction. However, the chances of her suffering a fatal occlusion during the short period of Shipman's visit are very low.
If Shipman really did find Mrs Mullen suffering a heart attack, he should have arranged admission to hospital and called an ambulance. He noted that he had done so and it has not been possible to find out whether or not he did. It does appear that, as he noted, Shipman called the warden. He should also have given Mrs Mullen some treatment for her pain, which, when speaking to Mrs Redfern, he claimed he had given. That treatment should have been a small dose of diamorphine, if available. He should also have given an aspirin to thin the blood. If, as is implied by the record, Mrs Mullen went into a state of cardiac arrest, Shipman should have attempted resuscitation. That he did not is obvious, as he could not have done anything useful while she was sitting in a chair. The fact that he cancelled the ambulance, which was, according to him, then on its way, rather than allow the paramedics to assist with resuscitation, gives rise to real suspicion. In other respects, the medical record for the day of the death is a feasible account of a cardiac death, but given Shipman's known record for creating false records, no reliance can be placed upon it.
In many other respects, this death appears highly suspicious. First, the death took place while Shipman was alone with the patient. A sudden death in the presence of a general practitioner is a rare event in the lives of most doctors but it happened frequently with Shipman. This factor is, of itself, enough to make me think that the death was probably unlawful. Second, Mrs Mullen's appearance in death, sitting peacefully in her chair, was not typical of a cardiac death but was entirely typical of a death by diamorphine injection. Third, if the evidence of the witnesses is accurate, Shipman gave a different account of the death to Mr Buckley from the one he later gave to the family. His completion of Form B of the cremation certificate is entirely typical of cases in which he has killed the patient and seeks, by his completion of this form, to draw other people into involvement and to make it appear he was not alone with the patient at the time of death.
I have come to the conclusion that Shipman must have killed Mrs Mullen. In my view, the chance that she suffered a fatal heart attack just as he arrived at the house is very unlikely. I think that, when Shipman arrived, Mrs Mullen probably did complain of chest pain. That is not to say she was having a heart attack, although she might have been. The chest pain of which she had been complaining earlier could have had many different causes. I think Shipman gave an injection of diamorphine, which he knew would kill her. He then telephoned for the warden and went next door to speak to Mrs Redfern. When Mr Buckley arrived, Mrs Mullen was recently dead and her body was still warm. Later, Shipman gave the relatives a different account of events from that which he had given to Mr Buckley. That account was, in itself, not implausible and tallied with the account which he wrote in the medical records. The lies he told in Form B were designed to make it appear that others had been involved with Mrs Mullen before and at the time of death. I am sure that Mrs Mullen was killed by Shipman.

name: Fanny Nichols
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 17 Ward Street, Hyde
certified_cause: congestive heart failure resulting from ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
There are a number of highly suspicious features in this case. First, the death was discovered shortly after a visit by Shipman, during which he was alone with the patient and had the opportunity to administer a drug. No one saw Mrs Nichols alive or spoke to her after his visit. Given what is known of Shipman's activities, that gives rise to grave suspicion.
Second, although Mrs Nichols may have been at some increased risk of a sudden cardiac death, it would be a coincidence if she succumbed to that risk within an hour or two of a visit by Shipman, particularly as he did not visit her regularly.
Shipman's account of the consultation does not make good medical sense, for all the reasons I outlined above. Although it is theoretically possible that Mrs Nichols could have gone into severe heart failure in the short time since her daughter-in-law and Mrs Nixon had seen her, it is most unlikely. Had she become ill after Mrs Nixon's departure, she would have telephoned her son or daughter-in-law. If she were ill, it is very unlikely that she would have refused hospital admission, at least without discussing her decision with the family. No sensible doctor would have behaved as Shipman suggests he did, advising the patient that she needed admission and then leaving her without immediate treatment when she rejected his advice. The account simply does not ring true. I am satisfied that it is a fabrication.
Mrs Nichols' appearance in death is not typical of a sudden death from heart failure which, as Dr Grenville has explained in his generic evidence, is invariably an extremely distressing process with the patient gasping for air and the secretions from the lungs apparent on the face or clothing. On the other hand, Mrs Nichols' appearance was entirely what would be expected following a death from morphine poisoning.
I am sure that Shipman was responsible for the death of Mrs Nichols.

name: Renate Eldtraude Overton
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Tameside General Hospital
conclusion:
Although Mrs Overton did not enjoy good health, her epilepsy and hypothyroidism were well controlled. There is no mention of any cardiac problem until 10th
February 1994, eight days before Shipman's last visit. She was, however, prone to asthma attacks and plainly suffered such an attack on the evening of 18th
February 1994. Shipman was summoned and applied the conventional treatment to such apparently good effect that Mrs Carrington felt able to retire to her room, no longer concerned about her mother's condition.
I have to consider what happened in the daughter's absence. Shipman claims that Mrs Overton had a heart attack and went into cardiac arrest. It is possible that Shipman decided to kill Mrs Overton and gave her an injection of opiate. If Mrs Carrington is correct and Shipman found her mother a nuisance, it would not be surprising in the light of what we now know about Shipman if he wished to kill her.
It is possible that Shipman believed that Mrs Overton had a recent history of chest pain indicative of angina. The possibility that Mrs Overton's symptoms on 10th
February 1994 were cardiac in origin cannot be definitively confirmed or refuted. Certainly, the symptoms recorded by someone other than Shipman of a heavy feeling in the chest, numbness in the left arm and shortness of breath are compatible with an episode of angina. It is, however, suspicious that Shipman seems not to have instigated any further investigation but jumped to the conclusion that Mrs Overton was suffering ischaemic heart disease. It may be, as Dr Grenville suggests, that Shipman used this chest pain as an excuse to build up a false history of ischaemic heart disease so that he could use it to explain her death when he had killed her. On the other hand, it is at least theoretically possible that Mrs Overton might have developed heart disease and might therefore have been at a substantially increased risk of suffering a heart attack. She was also a heavy smoker, which must have increased her risk of cardiac problems. However, the post-mortem findings suggest that Mrs Overton did not have ischaemic heart disease.
Even if, as Dr Grenville has said is possible, Mrs Overton complained of chest pain following her asthma attack that would not of itself cause her to lose consciousness. The possibility that she had a heart attack and went into cardiac arrest can to all intents and purposes be discounted in the light of the post-mortem examination findings. However, I shall assume for the moment that Mrs Overton either did have a heart attack and did go into cardiac arrest or that for some reason Shipman believed that this is what had happened. In those circumstances, one might expect Shipman to summon Mrs Carrington to help him carry out cardiopulmonary resuscitation. When Mrs Carrington entered the room, her mother was on the floor, unconscious and apparently gasping for breath. That is what one might expect to see in a patient who was in cardiac arrest. Shipman did not immediately tell her to call an ambulance. He told her to start mouth-to-mouth resuscitation while he gave cardiac massage. Mrs Carrington says that after about two minutes of this, Shipman gave an injection. However, Shipman's note suggests that before he called Mrs Carrington he had already given 10mg diamorphine intravenously for cardiac pain. His note does not say that he gave another injection after Mrs Carrington came in. Mrs Carrington does not know whether Shipman had already given one injection before she arrived or whether the one she saw was the only one he gave. Mrs Carrington is not sure whether Shipman said that the injection was of morphine or adrenaline. The effect of the injection was to cause Mrs Overton to stop gasping for breath and to stop breathing altogether. It is clear that that injection must have been morphine or diamorphine rather than adrenaline, although I think it quite likely that Shipman told Mrs Carrington that he had given adrenaline. Adrenaline would have been an appropriate drug for a patient in cardiac arrest. Morphine was completely inappropriate for several reasons. First, Mrs Overton was a known asthmatic just recovering from an acute attack and should not have been given any drug which might suppress her respiratory function. Second, if she was unconscious, as she was when Mrs Carrington saw her injected, Mrs Overton could not have been in pain, so no analgesic was called for. Third, Shipman believed Mrs Overton to be allergic to morphine. Whether she really was allergic, we do not know. Even if Mrs Overton had not been an asthmatic with a suspected allergy to morphine and in severe cardiac pain, the dose of diamorphine Shipman claimed to have given was excessive. Of course, we do not know whether the dose was of 10mg diamorphine. It would almost certainly not have been smaller but it might well have been greater, and the hospital notes suggest that 20mg morphine was given. A dose of 10mg diamorphine might have been lethal for Mrs Overton, although it would not be for most women of her age. There is a real possibility that Shipman gave more than 10mg. It would appear that by the time the paramedics arrived, seven minutes after the telephone call summoning them, Mrs Overton was almost dead. There can be no doubt that whatever happened before Mrs Carrington returned, Shipman's action in giving an injection of diamorphine when Mrs Overton was unconscious was grossly negligent and caused or materially contributed to her death. It was therefore probably unlawful even if Shipman did not intend to kill her.
I return to the two possible explanations for Mrs Overton's comatose state on the floor when her daughter returned to the room. The first is that Shipman decided to kill her and gave her an injection of opiate which rendered her unconscious. A factor that might point against that is Mrs Carrington's description of her mother 'gasping for air'. I am unsure what Mrs Carrington means by this. I note Mrs Carrington gave her mother mouth-to-mouth resuscitation which would seem inappropriate or even impossible if she was 'gasping' for breath. The effect of opiate would be to slow the breathing rate. If the breathing had slowed to a dangerous extent, mouth-to-mouth resuscitation would be appropriate. I think it likely that the breathing had slowed but that when Mrs Overton took a breath, it made a gasping sound.
The other possible explanation for Mrs Overton's comatose state is that she had had a heart attack and gone into cardiac arrest. That would account for her gasping for air. There are three reasons why I think she did not have a heart attack. The first is that the post-mortem examination did not reveal any sign that Mrs Overton had had a heart attack or that she had the underlying ischaemic heart disease which might have caused one. Second, the medical tests carried out after Mrs Overton's admission to hospital did not show the results which would have been expected if she had had a heart attack. Third, it would be something of a coincidence that Mrs Overton should have a heart attack in Shipman's presence, even though she had just had an asthma attack. Shipman would have us believe that many of his patients had heart attacks in his presence. Of course most of them did not; he had killed them. I conclude that Mrs Overton did not have a heart attack in Shipman's presence. I think the only sensible explanation for her unconscious state is that Shipman had injected her with diamorphine.
In summary, I think Shipman decided to kill Mrs Overton and gave her an injection of diamorphine which rendered her unconscious. I think he then called Mrs Carrington as he probably felt that he must involve her and make a show of trying to save her mother. She might be suspicious if Mrs Overton were already dead when he called her. It is possible that Shipman did not give as large a dose as he usually gave when killing a patient, or it is possible that Mrs Overton, being more robust than many of his elderly victims, did not die as quickly as he expected. I think he then decided to give a second injection to ensure death. I think he probably told Mrs Carrington that it was adrenaline. I think he delayed in instructing her to call an ambulance until he was satisfied that Mrs Overton would be dead before they arrived. In fact, she was not quite dead and was revived to a limited extent.
I am certain that Shipman caused Mrs Overton's death by an unlawful act and that he did so deliberately rather than negligently. I am almost certain that he killed her in two stages as I have described above.

name: Kenneth Pickup
title: Mr
place_of_death: whilst taking a walk next to Werneth Low Golf Course
certified_cause: left ventricular failure due to 'dilated heart with old myocardial fibrosis' due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
In my view, it is highly likely that Mr Pickup died of natural causes, as certified by Shipman.
Mr Pickup had a long history of heart disease and was at high risk of suffering a sudden cardiac death, notwithstanding the successful insertion of a cardiac pacemaker. The post- mortem examination findings confirm that Mr Pickup had severe ischaemic heart disease, although there was no sign of a thrombus which would prove beyond argument that a heart attack had been the cause of death. Dr Grenville says that the post-mortem examination signs were consistent with the theory that Mr Pickup had a fatal episode of ventricular fibrillation. Although Mr Pickup's death was sudden and was unexpected to his family, it was by no means unexpected from a medical viewpoint.
It is, however, entirely understandable that Mr Pickup's family should have great concern about his death, as it occurred so soon after Shipman had seen him. Their concern must be heightened by their suspicions, which I have now held were well founded, that Shipman killed Mrs Pickup a few weeks after her husband's death.
Shipman's preferred method of killing, which by August 1997 he had carried out very many times, was to give an intravenous injection of a lethal dose of diamorphine. He cannot have killed Mr Pickup in that way, as an intravenous injection of a lethal dose would render the patient unconscious within a minute or two and the patient would be dead within about five minutes. I have found that, on occasions, Shipman has probably killed a patient by giving an intramuscular injection. In general, I think he only did this deliberately to a patient who was terminally ill. The effect of an intramuscular lethal injection is, as Professor Henry McQuay and Dr Grenville have said in their joint report, much slower than an intravenous injection. In the immediate post-injection period, an onlooker might not notice anything strange, but probably after 15 minutes and certainly after 30 minutes it would be clear that something strange was happening. The drug would reach maximal effect within between 30 and 60 minutes and death would occur within about an hour. Dr Grenville said that he cannot think of any drug which would have a delayed effect which would allow Mr Pickup to go for a walk and collapse some time later. When he said that, Dr Grenville was not aware of the timing of Mr Pickup's movements on the afternoon on which he died. I am sure he would accept that it would be possible for a patient to walk about and behave normally for a short period, after being given an intramuscular injection of diamorphine. However, I do not think that the period could be more than 15 minutes. After that, I am sure the patient would become very sleepy and would be unable to continue to move.
Mr Pickup saw Shipman at some time on 27th
August. We do not know when, although I have indicated that there were two windows of opportunity. At some time after that visit, Mr Pickup's wife drove him to the top of Werneth Low and left him to walk home. Mr James Pickup says that the journey by car would take about five minutes. Mr Pickup probably collapsed and died about 10 to 15 minutes later, after walking about half a mile. On the face of it, it would seem possible that Mr Pickup might have had an intramuscular injection of a lethal dose of diamorphine, got straight into the car, been driven up to Werneth Lowe and walked for about 10 to 15 minutes before collapsing.
I say this is theoretically possible, but my view is that it is highly unlikely. First, the theory is dependent on the premise that Mr and Mrs Pickup left the house immediately after the injection had been given. Mr James Pickup can only report what his mother told him. He has given two accounts of what she told him. In December 1998, Mr James Pickup told the police that his mother had said that Shipman visited at about lunchtime and that she and her husband went up to Werneth Low at about 3pm. This suggests a time lapse between the visit and trip to Werneth Low. In 2001, Mr James Pickup told the Inquiry that his mother had said that Shipman had arrived at about 2pm and that they had left the house to go to Werneth Low immediately Shipman had gone. A visit at about 2pm is unlikely, as Shipman would have been busy in the surgery. If Shipman visited before 1.30pm and if Mr and Mrs Pickup went straight up to Werneth Low, Mr Pickup must have been left there by about 2pm and Mrs Pickup would surely have been extremely worried and have gone looking for her husband long before the police arrived some time after 5pm. If Shipman visited during the second window of opportunity and the Pickups left immediately for Werneth Low, Mr Pickup could have been dropped off soon after 3pm, at the earliest. He might have been dead within about 15 to 20 minutes. When the body was first examined at about 5pm, there were already signs of rigor mortis and venous pooling. Although venous pooling can appear within about half an hour, rigor mortis is not usually seen for at least two hours after death. If Mr Pickup died at about 3.15pm, the early signs of rigor mortis might have been discernible by 5pm, although the timing is very tight. It is puzzling that Mrs Pickup had not been more concerned about her husband's failure to return. It may be that she assumed he had met someone or called on someone.
In any event, I do not think Mrs Pickup had a very clear recollection of the events of that afternoon. This is not in any way surprising, as she was obviously very distressed. She told her son that the police came to the house at about 3.30pm or about 4pm to say that her husband had been found. She was becoming worried because she had expected him to be back by 3pm. We know that this account must be wrong, as the police did not arrive until after 5pm.
Even assuming that there is some explanation for those discrepancies, I do not take literally the assertion that Mr and Mrs Pickup left the house immediately after Shipman's departure. The Pickups would have had to say goodbye to Shipman, with whom they were on friendly terms. One would expect some sociable chat before he departed. Usually before going out for a walk there are last minute preparations such as changing shoes, going to the lavatory and locking the house. Mr and Mrs Pickup were not young and probably did not move very quickly. I do not believe that they could have left the house within five minutes of the injection. By the time Mr Pickup was ready to get out of the car, I think at least ten minutes would have passed and he would almost certainly have been aware of feeling different, probably a bit woozy and quite possibly feeling sick. I think it is highly unlikely that he would have got out of the car without saying anything to his wife. I also note that there is no suggestion that Mr Pickup told his wife that Shipman gave him an injection. One might have expected him to mention it.
There is another reason why I think it is most unlikely that Shipman would give Mr Pickup an intramuscular lethal injection. It would be highly dangerous for Shipman. The risk would be very great that Mr Pickup would feel ill and that his wife would call an ambulance and Mr Pickup would be brought round and would tell the doctors that Shipman had given him an injection. In short, I think it is most unlikely that Shipman gave Mr Pickup a lethal injection.
Taking the circumstances of this case as a whole, including Mr Pickup's cardiac problems and the post-mortem examination findings, I think it is highly likely that Mr Pickup died of natural causes.

name: Anne Lilian Ralphs
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 25 Baron Road, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
This death occurred in Shipman's presence. That is a highly suspicious circumstance.
At about noon, Mrs Ralphs was alive and feeling well enough to contemplate eating tea with her great-granddaughter. If Mrs Joan Ralphs' evidence about the lock on the door is right, Mrs Ralphs must have gone down the steps to let Shipman in. I say if that evidence is right, because in his Inquiry statement Mr Ralphs asserted that his mother had left the door open for Shipman. What made him think that is not clear. Mrs Joan Ralphs was the last person to leave the flat before Shipman arrived and she says the door was locked when she left. So I find that Mrs Ralphs came downstairs to let Shipman in. A short time later she was dead. For other doctors, this kind of sudden death in their presence hardly ever happens. For Shipman it happened frequently, if he is to be believed. That Mrs Ralphs should die a sudden natural death just after Shipman's arrival is quite incredible. It is too much of a coincidence. In my view, the only plausible explanation is that, on finding her alone, Shipman killed Mrs Ralphs by injecting her with opiate, probably diamorphine. She must then have fallen asleep and fallen backwards across the bed. Her peaceful appearance in death was consistent with death due to an overdose of opiate.
I have already said that Shipman's account of his consultation with Mrs Ralphs does not make good medical sense. Moreover, it appears to me that the entries in Form B were designed to allay suspicion and to provide a plausible explanation for the death, if one were called for.
I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Ralphs.

name: Gladys Saunders
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 24 Ogden Court, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that the only sensible inference which can be drawn from the circumstances is that Shipman must have killed Mrs Saunders, almost certainly by administering a lethal dose of diamorphine. The evidence shows that she was in reasonable health only half an hour before her death. When Shipman arrived, Mrs Saunders must have let him in. Soon afterwards, he fetched Mrs Simpson, telling her that Mrs Saunders was close to dying. When she was dead, he did not carry out the examination necessary to establish that death had occurred. He must have known when he went to fetch Mrs Simpson that Mrs Saunders' death was inevitable.
Old age was not an acceptable cause of death for someone who had been out and about the day before her death. But Shipman was not in a position to give any other cause of death, because, as the medical record reveals, Mrs Saunders had not been suffering from any potentially fatal condition. Shipman told lies on Form B to make it appear that he had not been present at the death and to distance himself from it.
I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Saunders.

name: Mary Tomlin
title: Mrs
conclusion:
The circumstances of Mrs Tomlin's death are very similar to those of Miss Mona White, whom Shipman had killed only three weeks earlier. The two women lived in the same road.
This death is plainly highly suspicious. Although Mrs Tomlin was unwell when the home helps visited her shortly before her death, she was chatting and smoking. Within an hour, Shipman had told Mrs Foley that she was dying. I recognise that people can and do suffer heart attacks without warning and may die suddenly. But, if Shipman is right, Mrs Tomlin must have suffered a heart attack within that short time. As with Miss Mona White and many others, the coincidence is utterly remarkable. In my view, it is so remarkable that it cannot be true. Further, Shipman's conduct was not appropriate in respect of a patient suffering from heart attack. He should have called an ambulance and if the patient went into cardiac arrest, he should have attempted resuscitation. Heart attack is usually a painful process but Mrs Tomlin appeared simply to have fallen asleep propped up in bed. This appearance in death is entirely typical of deaths caused by Shipman by means of morphine injection.
Despite the lack of medical records and my consequent inability to discover whether Mrs Tomlin was suffering from heart disease before her death, I am sure that this death was caused by Shipman. The circumstances allow no other plausible explanation.

name: Margaret Mary Vickers
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 41 Bennett Street, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of highly suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. First and most obvious, the death occurred during a visit by Shipman and almost certainly in his presence. Dr Grenville says that it is most unusual for a patient to die suddenly during a visit by a general practitioner, unless the patient is known to be terminally ill or the doctor has been called out in an emergency in response to a report of symptoms indicating a life-threatening event such as a heart attack or stroke. Shipman was not summoned to Mrs Vickers in an emergency on 25th
June. He was called before 9am and did not attend until, on his timings, about 1.45pm. Many of Shipman's patients died in his presence and I am satisfied that these deaths were not a series of coincidences. The temporal association between Shipman's visit and the death gives risk to grave suspicion that he killed Mrs Vickers.
Although Mrs Vickers was unwell in the days before her death, it does not appear that she was seriously ill. She looked pale and unwell on the day of death but was able to eat a small snack. Mrs Perry had not noticed any signs of a developing stroke. Dr Grenville said in his generic evidence that an occlusive stroke does not usually lead to sudden death. Most occlusive strokes are not fatal; the patient usually survives, with or without some residual disability. If the stroke is to be fatal, it develops over several hours or days. The patient gradually sinks into a coma, which deepens until eventually death supervenes. The type of stroke which can cause a sudden death is a haemorrhagic stroke which affects the brain stem. In such a stroke there is no one-sided weakness. Thus, Shipman's description appears to describe two different types of stroke: an occlusive stroke, giving rise to left-sided weakness and slurred speech, followed by a haemorrhagic stroke causing sudden death. It is most unlikely that a patient would have two strokes of a different type in different parts of the brain at the same time. It seems to me that Shipman has fabricated the history of a stroke.
Shipman lied when completing Form B. He claimed that a neighbour (which must be a reference to Mrs Campbell) was present at the death. She was not. Shipman often did this when he wished to create the impression that he had not been alone with his patient at the time of death.
This course of events is quite typical of cases in which Shipman killed. He often claimed to have visited an elderly patient, found him or her to be very ill, made arrangements to admit him or her to hospital and then made some pretext for involving a neighbour. When he returned with the neighbour (in this case Mrs Campbell), the patient would have died suddenly, supposedly in his absence. In the present case, Shipman knew that the back door would be left open for him. Yet, when he first went to Mrs Campbell's house, he told her that there was no reply at Mrs Vickers' front door. I suspect that he had already seen Mrs Vickers and had killed her, then went to fetch Mrs Campbell, intending that she would come inside with him and together they would find Mrs Vickers dead. Shipman would then have been able to pretend that Mrs Vickers had died before his arrival. When Mrs Campbell did not enter the house with him, he changed his plan and waited several minutes before going to fetch Mrs Campbell for a second time. During that time, I suspect that he tried to make a telephone call but was unsuccessful. I am quite satisfied that he did not call an ambulance during this period, as he claimed. When a suitable time had elapsed, he went back to fetch Mrs Campbell, supposedly to pack Mrs Vickers' clothes. Of course, when they returned, she was dead. He pretended to cancel the ambulance. It is possible that Shipman's first visit to Mrs Campbell was not a ruse and that he had genuinely forgotten that he was supposed to go in by the back door. If so, he must have killed Mrs Vickers in the interval between Mrs Campbell's first and second attendances.
This case has Shipman's hallmark on it. I am quite sure that Shipman killed Mrs Vickers, almost certainly in the usual way, by giving her a lethal injection of diamorphine.

name: Mary Walls
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 1 Werneth Avenue, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
Although Dr Grenville considered that it was theoretically possible that events might have occurred as Shipman claimed, in my view, such an occurrence is very unlikely. If this were the only time that Shipman had claimed that a patient of his had died suddenly in his presence, I might be inclined to accept the claim. But if Shipman is to be believed, his patients frequently died in his presence. He cannot be believed. Coincidences of this nature do not occur time and time again.
Mrs Walls was well on the evening before her death. There is no reason to think that she was ill the following morning. She went into Hyde to see Shipman for a routine appointment in connection with her cataracts. It is unlikely that she would not have spoken to a member of her family if she really had suffered from chest pain either during that night or during the previous week. I think it more likely that, when Shipman saw her that morning, he decided to kill her. He made a false entry in the computerised record suggesting that she had chest pain. This was to lay the ground for a supposed heart attack later in the day. I do not think there was ever any question of Mrs Walls going into hospital for chest pain. I think that was pure fabrication. Shipman often claimed that his patients had refused to go into hospital shortly before they were found dead. I do not know what excuse Shipman made to visit Mrs Walls later that day. He might have simply arrived unexpectedly. I think it likely that Mrs Walls let him in. He probably made an excuse to take a blood sample. I think he then gave her a lethal injection of a strong opiate, probably diamorphine. Mrs Walls would have soon slipped into unconsciousness and died. Her appearance in death was entirely consistent with a death from morphine overdose and not typical of a death from coronary thrombosis. Shipman then telephoned the names in Mrs Walls' address book until he found someone who would come and take over the practical problems.
His subsequent accounts to the family were fictional, as were many of the entries he made on Form B. His story to the family does not ring true. If Shipman had found Mrs Walls in cardiogenic shock, the first thing he would have done would be to telephone for an ambulance. He did not. As for Form B, it was not uncommon for him to claim falsely that another person had been present at the death. I am satisfied that he did that in order to create the impression that he was not alone with his patient throughout the process of death.
I am sure that Mrs Walls was killed by Shipman.

name: Sarah Ashworth
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 'Bella Vista', 8 Bowlacre Road, Hyde
conclusion:
There is no doubt that Mrs Ashworth's health had been deteriorating gradually for some months before her death and that her heart condition was serious. Death from heart failure was a real possibility. However, this death occurred in the presence of Shipman, at a time when Mrs Ashworth had appeared to be in quite good health. Other general practitioners find that patients very rarely die in their presence during a visit, unless the patient is terminally ill or the doctor has been called out in an emergency on account of acute symptoms of a serious nature, indicating for example a heart attack or stroke. Mrs Ashworth was not terminally ill and there is no evidence that Shipman was called out as an emergency on 17th
April. That Mrs Ashworth died suddenly in Shipman's presence gives rise to grave suspicion that he killed her.
There is some evidence that morphine was found in the tissues but the evidence is not conclusive because of the state of decomposition of the body. In any event, as Dr Rutherford pointed out, it would be acceptable practice for a doctor to administer morphine to a patient who was suffering from heart failure or a heart attack but great care should be taken in the administration of such a drug in all cases. The drug should be administered very slowly, the doctor observing the effect. In a patient with a history of chronic obstructive airways disease, the need for caution is even greater. If diamorphine had been administered in these circumstances, one would expect to see the fact recorded in the records. Here, Shipman was obliged to admit to having given an injection of some kind, because of the skin tear on the hand, but has not made any record of what he gave. The finding of morphine in the body, although uncertain, is a cause for suspicion, as is the absence of any record of drug administration.
The fact that Shipman obtained 30mg of diamorphine in Mrs Ashworth's name on the day of her death is significant but not conclusive. At his trial, Shipman said that he did not routinely carry diamorphine (or any controlled drug) in his bag, although this was proved to be a lie. He admitted that he was in the habit of prescribing a 30mg ampoule of diamorphine for patients who needed pain relief, although this is far more than would usually be given to a patient who is not accustomed to the effect of the drug. In this case, it is possible that Shipman obtained the prescription for Mrs Ashworth before the visit and equally possible that Shipman obtained it after her death. Police enquiries have shown that one way in which he obtained his illicit supplies of diamorphine was to prescribe for a patient who was already dead. This prescription is a cause for suspicion but is not conclusive.
Although none of the suspicious factors I have mentioned is in itself conclusive, when taken together they amount to strong circumstantial evidence that Shipman killed Mrs Ashworth. I am sure that he did so.

name: Edith Brady
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Shipman's surgery at 21 Market Street, Hyde
conclusion:
Everything about this death points to an unnatural death. Although a cardiac death was a theoretical possibility, it would have been a most remarkable coincidence that the attack should strike at the very moment when the patient was alone with Shipman in his consulting room. The suggestion on the MCCD that the attack had begun 12 hours earlier is a lie. Shipman did not react as any doctor would have reacted if Mrs Brady really had had a heart attack. He would have told the staff to call for an ambulance and would have summoned the most experienced member of staff into the room and instructed her to assist in resuscitation until the ambulance arrived. Shipman's suggestion to Mrs Massey that he could tell that Mrs Brady was brain dead by feeling the back of her neck is bizarre and can have been no more than mumbo-jumbo. His failure to make a proper note of what was supposed to have happened is a very suspicious feature. His account to the family was plainly untrue. Mrs Brady's neat and peaceful appearance was not consistent with a cardiac death involving a vigorous attempt at resuscitation. It was wholly consistent with a death by morphine poisoning.
Like the coroner, I am quite sure that Mrs Brady was killed by Shipman. She had attended for an injection of vitamin B
12
for her anaemia. I am satisfied that Shipman administered a lethal injection, almost certainly of diamorphine.

name: Erla Copeland
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 68 Grosvenor Crescent, Hyde
conclusion:
This is a clear case of unlawful killing. Mrs Copeland was not in the best of health in early January and had had an exacerbation of her diverticular disease. However, her condition was not serious, as is shown by the results of the blood tests taken on 4th
January. It appears that she was recovering from this episode by the day on which she died. There was no medical reason why she should have died on that day. This death should have been reported to the coroner.
Mrs Copeland was found dead within about 15 minutes of Shipman's departure following a visit. No one saw or spoke to her alive after he had left. That in itself is a highly suspicious feature.
Shipman's record of the consultation on the day of death is grossly inadequate. The suggestion that Mrs Copeland refused to go hospital is utterly incredible. She had been admitted a few weeks earlier without objection. There is no explanation as to why Shipman wanted her to go into hospital. She was clearly not very poorly, having enjoyed her lunch and a chat with Mrs Malone only an hour or two before. In my view, this entry in the record is a fabrication, designed to suggest that there was some natural cause for Mrs Copeland's death.
Following the death, it appears that Shipman himself was at a loss as to what he should put on the MCCD. He must have known that the records would reveal no plausible cause for the sudden death.
Shipman also gave inconsistent accounts of events to different people. He told Mrs Hamlett that he had seen her mother in the morning, whereas in fact he saw her in the afternoon just before her death was discovered. He must have done this in order to distance himself from the death. He did not say to Mrs Hamlett that he had found her mother in a very poorly state and that she had refused to go to hospital. He told her that he warned her that she might have to be admitted on account of something suspicious in the test results received from the hospital. It rather sounds to me as though he was trying to plant in Mrs Hamlett's mind the possibility that her mother might have taken her own life. He almost certainly knew that she was very much afraid of a diagnosis of cancer and the suggestion that 'they might have found something' would almost certainly have conveyed to Mrs Hamlett that there was a possibility that her mother had cancer. It is hardly surprising that Mrs Hamlett did not insist on a post-mortem examination.
I note that Shipman prescribed slow-release morphine on 4th
January in circumstances which both Dr Grenville and Dr Esmail consider inappropriate. He might well have done so for a sinister reason. If he had decided to kill Mrs Copeland by diamorphine injection and if the family were to have insisted on a post-mortem examination, he would have been able to explain the presence of morphine in the body.
For the reasons outlined above, I am quite satisfied that Mrs Copeland died as the result of an overdose of diamorphine administered by Shipman. Her appearance in death is entirely typical of that which would be expected after a lethal injection. Her appearance was very similar to a large number of victims of Shipman. Sickness is a well-recognised side effect of diamorphine. I agree with the coroner's verdict that this was an unlawful killing.

name: Frederick Dentith
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 12 Porlock Walk, Hattersley, Hyde
conclusion:
It is clear that Mr Dentith suffered from inoperable lung cancer, probably in the form of a Pancoast's tumour. This is extremely painful and it can be difficult to provide the patient with sufficient analgesia. Mr Dentith was probably receiving a high dose of analgesic and this will have caused or contributed to his comatose condition. I think it likely that the analgesic was of a strong opiate, either morphine or diamorphine, and was given by the district or Macmillan nurses and not by Shipman.
The evidence is conflicting as to whether Shipman administered an injection to Mr Dentith on the day of his death. Mr Morris Dentith suggests that he did and implies that this was intended to and did hasten his father's death. Mrs Shaw's evidence is to the contrary.
These events occurred a long time ago. Both witnesses have a firm view in their minds as to Shipman's integrity and attitude. I think that Mr Morris Dentith's attitude towards Shipman has been affected by his perception that Shipman was guilty of a delay in diagnosing his father's condition. This would be understandable. It would also be understandable if his recollection is affected by the passage of time and by what is now known about Shipman. He has plainly misunderstood the effect of what his sister-in-law told him. It is surprising that he can be '99 per cent certain' about the removal of all his father's medication, given that the events in question occurred so long ago and that he would have no real reason to remember an event which would then have had no obvious significance. Mrs Shaw's recollection may have been affected by her strong view that Shipman was supportive and compassionate. I consider that her view is probably the more reliable, as she was personally responsible for Mr Dentith's care in the terminal stage. He was in her house and she was always there. The family called from time to time, although Mrs Rossi was there a good deal towards the end. Mrs Shaw's recollection of the arrangements is more typical of what was usual at this time for a patient who required regular analgesia. Syringe drivers were not yet available in the community and it would be usual for the district or Macmillan nurses to attend regularly, possibly as much as three times a day, to give injections. It is likely that if Shipman had said that he would help Mr Dentith 'on his way' on the same day that he gave an injection, Mrs Shaw would have remembered this. I think it unlikely that Shipman gave an injection on the day of the death.
However, I recognise that it is possible that Shipman did visit in the late afternoon of the day of the death and it is possible that he gave an injection. If he did, I am quite sure that it did not have the effect described by Mr Morris Dentith of rendering his father unconscious. I am sure that Mr Dentith had been at least semi-conscious for several days. Dr Grenville says that it is possible that an injection at this time might have hastened the death by a small margin or might equally have lengthened life by relieving pain and distress. It appears, however, that any injection given at this time cannot have been the direct cause of the death. It seems that Mr Dentith lived for about two hours, possibly three, after Shipman's last visit. I can rule out the possibility that Shipman gave a lethal dose of opiate which directly caused the death. Had he done that, Mr Dentith would have been dead within the hour.
In Dr Grenville's view, the evidence suggests that Shipman's management of Mr Dentith's last illness was consistent with good practice.
My conclusion is that Mr Dentith's death was almost certainly due to natural causes.

name: Monica Eddleston
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Tameside General Hospital
conclusion: I, too, have examined the records from the hospital and the post-mortem report. I agree with Dr Grenville that Mrs Eddleston's death must have been due to natural causes. I am entirely satisfied that Shipman's involvement with Mrs Eddleston's death gives rise to no cause for suspicion. I should add that Shipman was sympathetic with and supportive of the Eddleston family on the day or so after the death. At that time, he behaved in an exemplary fashion.

name: Marie Antoinette Fernley
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 22 Darwin Street, Hyde
conclusion:
There are several highly suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. The first and most obvious is that the death was discovered very shortly after a visit by Shipman. Shipman's visit was made in response to a request by Mrs Fernley but was not an emergency visit. Mrs Fernley appeared to be in reasonable health when Mrs Armitage visited her on the morning of her death and when she spoke to her daughter at lunchtime. Mrs Fernley did not telephone her daughter after Shipman's visit, as she had promised to do. The probable explanation for that is that she was not able to make the telephone call. That suggests that Mrs Fernley died either in Shipman's presence (because she was murdered) or of natural causes very shortly after his departure. It appears to me that it would be a remarkable coincidence that she should die suddenly, of natural causes, so soon after Shipman's visit. If this were to happen in connection with another doctor, I would accept it as coincidence. With Shipman, this kind of 'coincidence' happened frequently. I cannot accept it as coincidence. The close temporal connection between Shipman's visit and Mrs Fernley's death is highly suspicious and persuades me that he almost certainly killed her.
All the other evidence points to the same conclusion. Although Mrs Fernley had a number of serious medical conditions, it would appear from the records that her cardiac and respiratory problems were satisfactorily controlled by medication and that her abdominal complaint was troublesome but not serious. Certainly, neither the hospital correspondence nor the general practitioner records would lead anyone to suspect that a sudden death was likely or imminent. Mrs Fernley's blood pressure was high and she must have been at an increased risk of suffering a stroke. However, there is no evidence that she had a stroke that day. Apart from Mrs Fernley's own statement to the surgery staff that she felt weak (a wholly non-specific complaint), there is nothing to suggest that she had a stroke. Even Shipman's own records (which must in any event be distrusted) do not suggest any signs of a stroke and none were observed by Mrs Armitage. If Mrs Fernley had died a natural death, any reasonable doctor would have referred the case to the coroner, as he or she would not have known the cause of death.
In Shipman's handwritten note, he claimed that Mrs Fernley had refused to go into hospital. That increases my suspicion for two reasons. First, it is a common feature of Shipman's killings that his patients are said to have rejected his advice to go into hospital shortly before their deaths. This is plainly a device which Shipman used as part of his explanation of the subsequent death. Second, in this case, it is manifest nonsense that Shipman should have advised Mrs Fernley to go into hospital. The only thing he recorded was wrong with her was her high blood pressure. While there might be cases in which a patient might be admitted simply for the treatment of high blood pressure, such a step would be unusual. The usual course would be for the general practitioner to treat the patient at home and, if appropriate, refer him or her to a consultant for advice on management of the problem. At this time, Mrs Fernley was taking a very small dose of enalapril and the most obvious course of action for Shipman, if he was worried about her blood pressure, would have been to increase her dosage, as he claimed to have done in the computerised medical records. The handwritten note is plainly false.
Finally, Mrs Fernley's appearance in death was not typical of that found following a massive stroke but it was entirely typical of that seen in many of Shipman's patients who had been killed by intravenous injection of opiate.
All the evidence points to the same conclusion. I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Fernley.

name: Alice Maude Gorton
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 2 Leigh Fold, Newton, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
There are a number of suspicious features surrounding this death. The first and most important is that Mrs Gorton was unconscious within a very short time after Shipman had arrived at her house, although she had been in her usual state of health when her daughter left not long before. Had Mrs Gorton been dead when Mrs O'Neill returned to the house, I would have said that that aroused strong suspicion that Shipman had killed her. The fact that she was unconscious rather than dead does not reduce the level of suspicion.
I find some aspects of Mrs O'Neill's evidence unreliable. First, I think she is probably mistaken when she says that Shipman used to visit her mother on a Tuesday. I also think she is probably mistaken when she says that her mother became unconscious on Tuesday, 7th
August and lay in that state for two and a half days. I find Mr Ian Moss' evidence on that issue more reliable. His evidence is consistent with Shipman's visits book. I am satisfied that Mrs Gorton was unconscious for about 24 hours before her death, as Mr Moss says. I think that Shipman had made a routine visit on Thursday, 9th
August.
Although I think Mrs O'Neill is mistaken about the day of the visit, in other respects I accept her evidence as truthful and reliable. I accept that Shipman came to her house and said that her mother had collapsed, that he had asked a neighbour to help to put her on the bed and asked Mrs O'Neill to return to her mother's house. I think she was right when she suspected that what Shipman said about a neighbour was untrue. I also accept that Shipman said that a post-mortem examination would not be necessary and that this was interrupted by a loud groan from the bedroom. This most unusual event might well have made a lasting impression on Shipman. Many years later, when Shipman had just killed Mrs Bessie Swann in 1997, Mrs Swann's son Barry Swann arrived at her house to meet Shipman. Shipman told Mr Swann that he thought Mrs Swann had died. Mr Swann felt his mother's hand and found it was still warm. Shipman then said,
'I'll wait a few minutes in case she wakes up and frightens us all'
. When I read that evidence, I wondered if there had been an earlier occasion when Shipman had had a fright when he had failed to kill someone he had intended to kill. I now think it possible that Mrs Gorton was that person.
Although Dr Grenville suggested that Mrs Gorton might have died a natural death, possibly from a stroke, the fact that she was unconscious so soon after Shipman's arrival leads me to believe that it is more likely that her loss of consciousness was connected with Shipman than that it was due to any natural cause. Dr Grenville explained that, if Shipman had given Mrs Gorton a dose of diamorphine which was just less than what would be required to kill her, she might well have suffered brain damage and might lie unconscious until she died, either as a result of the brain damage or from bronchopneumonia or a combination of the two.
Mrs Gorton's medical records are not available and I have been unable to assess the likelihood of her suffering a sudden fatal heart attack or some other natural event leading to unconsciousness and death. I accept that Mrs Gorton was almost certainly at some increased risk of heart attack because she had a history of angina. I am therefore unable to rule out the possibility that this was a natural death. However, I think it more likely that Mrs Gorton died as the result of Shipman injecting her with a sub-lethal dose of opiate. I cannot say that I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Gorton but I think he probably did.

name: Hilda Mary Hibbert
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 36 Joel Lane, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
Shipman's story here is that Mrs Hibbert had begun to suffer a stroke some considerable time before his visit. He told the administrator at Tameside General Hospital that it had started that morning. On the MCCD, he claimed it had started
'? 48 hours'
before death, which would be on 31st
December. Neither of these claims fits in with the evidence of the family, and in particular that of Mrs Ashton-Hibbert, who spent much of the day with her grandmother on 2nd
January. The notion of a woman playing hide-and-seek with young children while suffering from a developing stroke is frankly incredible. I think it is highly unlikely that Mrs Hibbert had a stroke either that morning or 48 hours earlier. I think the records are fabricated.
Mrs Hibbert was found dead very shortly after Shipman had visited her. No one saw her alive or spoke to her after he had left. That in itself is a cause for grave suspicion.
It is a common feature in cases where Shipman has killed a patient for him to claim that he had telephoned the hospital to book a bed or had called an ambulance but the patient had died before the ambulance had arrived. Investigation, where it is possible, has often shown that he did no such thing. It is an unusual feature of this case that Shipman did telephone the hospital, did ask for a bed to be booked and did request that an ambulance should attend. However, he asked that it should attend within the hour. If, at about 2.30pm, he had killed Mrs Hibbert by administering an injection of diamorphine, she would be found dead when the ambulance crew arrived.
