I consider that Shipman's request for an ambulance was no more than a variation upon a common theme.
Although Mrs Hibbert was at risk of having a stroke, I am satisfied that she did not in fact have one on 2nd
January. I am sure that this was an unlawful killing by Shipman.

name: Maureen Lamonnier Jackson
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 122 Mottram Road, Hyde
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to carcinoma of the breast
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Shipman killed Mrs Jackson on 7th
July. She was terminally ill but her death was not expected for some time. The circumstances of her death are entirely consistent with the administration of a large dose of diamorphine. Shipman engineered an opportunity to be alone with Mrs Jackson when he visited, and discouraged Mrs Hall from going to the bedroom when he left.
Shipman had retained 800mg diamorphine belonging to Mrs Jackson on 3rd
July. I am quite sure that he used some or all of that to kill her four days later. His explanation for the death is highly implausible and is inconsistent with the witness evidence of Mrs Jackson's condition on the morning of the day of her death. His medical note of that day was fabricated to support his implausible suggestion that Mrs Jackson had suffered a stroke. However, he did not mention this when completing the MCCD and Form B. Shipman lied on Form B in stating that Nurse Gilchrist and Mrs Hall were present at the moment of death. Everything points to the conclusion that Shipman killed Mrs Jackson.
It is true that Mrs Jackson did not have long to live. Shipman might have justified his actions to himself on the ground that he had saved her from further suffering. However, he also deprived Mrs Jackson and her family of their chance to prepare for the death.

name: Fred Kellett
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 26 Knott Lane, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
I accept the evidence of Mrs Wood that her uncle was in quite good health immediately before his death apart from suffering from a cold and cough. I accept that he was up and talking to her on the telephone a very short time before his death.
Dr Esmail has advised that it is highly improbable that Mr Kellett died from the causes stated by Shipman. It is most unusual for a person suffering a coronary thrombosis to sit down and die. For a very sudden death to occur during a visit from a general practitioner is obviously a most unusual occurrence and a remarkable coincidence. Yet, it is an event that Shipman claimed occurred quite frequently. Here, Shipman's account is quite incredible. He appears to claim that Mr Kellett suffered a fatal heart attack as he walked through the door. No attempt was made to resuscitate Mr Kellett and an ambulance was not called. Were an event really to occur such as Shipman claims, one would expect the doctor to decline to sign a certificate of cause of death and to report the death to the coroner. Instead, Shipman signed the certificate.
Mr Kellett's appearance in death is not typical of that seen after a sudden cardiac death. It is entirely typical of that seen in many of Shipman's victims who are known to have been killed by diamorphine injection.
In completing the cremation Form B, Shipman sought to suggest that he had not been alone with the patient at the moment of death. In my view, that was almost certainly a lie, designed to allay any possible suspicion in official quarters about the sudden death. Shipman is known to have told such lies on many occasions.
I am sure that Shipman was responsible for Mr Kellett's death. The overwhelming likelihood is that the death was caused by a lethal injection of diamorphine. Although there is no direct evidence of Shipman's illicit possession of diamorphine in 1985, there is evidence that he obtained opiates in the 1970s and in the 1990s. I infer that he was capable of acquiring morphine or diamorphine during the 1980s as well. I cannot say whether any property was taken from Mr Kellett's home after his death. The evidence is inconclusive.

name: Edna May Llewellyn
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 6 Carter Place, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
There can be no doubt from the established medical history that Mrs Llewellyn was at very high risk of suffering a sudden cardiac death.
On the day of her death, she had an episode which, in my view, was probably an angina attack. However, I am satisfied that the attack was short-lived and that her pain had eased while she was resting on the bed before Shipman arrived.
Shipman would then have us believe that Mrs Llewellyn suffered a massive heart attack, suffered great pain (for which he gave her a small dose of morphine) and went into cardiac arrest, which all his best efforts at resuscitation failed to resolve. That is a possible series of events. However, I agree with Dr Grenville that, if this happened, it was a remarkable coincidence that it should happen at the very moment that Shipman walked in. Such coincidences seemed to happen often in his professional life and they hardly ever seem to happen to other doctors. Several things point against this having happened, particularly Shipman's failure to call an ambulance or for assistance in his resuscitation attempt.
The lies told in Form B of the cremation certificate, which, as I have said, appear to me to be designed to give the impression that Shipman was not alone with the patient at the time of death, increase my suspicion. It seems to me that by far the most likely explanation for Mrs Llewellyn's death is that Shipman gave a much larger dose of diamorphine than he claimed, knowing and intending that it would cause death.
I was at one stage mystified by the evidence of Mrs Shaw, in which she describes Mrs Llewellyn's face as bloated and discoloured. The evidence of this appearance is not clear but I think there was probably some degree of bloating. Professor McQuay has suggested that this could have been caused by Mrs Llewellyn's tongue falling back and obstructing her airway. As I understand the position, this might well have happened when she lost consciousness, following an injection of opiate. I think this is the most likely explanation for the appearance noticed by Mrs Shaw. This does not affect my main conclusion which is that I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Llewellyn by means of lethal diamorphine overdose.

name: Bertha Moss
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Shipman's surgery, 21 Market Street, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to congestive heart failure and hypertension
conclusion:
Mrs Moss was at a high risk of suffering a heart attack. However, she was well while sitting in the waiting area of the surgery a few minutes before seeing Shipman. Although it is theoretically possible that she could have begun to suffer the pain of a heart attack as she entered the surgery, this would be something of a coincidence. If she had, and if she told Shipman about it, he might have taken an ECG. However, as Dr Grenville has explained, the trace would not have confirmed a heart attack which had occurred as recently as this one supposedly had. I suspect that Shipman's account was not true. The ECG trace has never been found. I suspect that it was never taken. I also find it odd that a woman who is supposed to be suffering a coronary thrombosis should be sufficiently unconcerned about the chest pain to mention her skin condition.
Shipman's conduct after Mrs Moss had her supposed heart attack was so inappropriate as to excite further suspicion that Shipman's account was fabricated. If a patient has a heart attack and collapses, any doctor would call an ambulance and would bring in help when trying to resuscitate. Single-handed resuscitation is much less likely to succeed. The process requires cardiac massage and assisted respiration using a bag and mask, which were available at the surgery. Also adrenaline should be given. Shipman probably did not call an ambulance and did not seek the help of the receptionist, although he told Mrs Joan Clayton that he had done. He also lied in Form B so as to make it appear that he was not the only person present at the death.
Taking these factors into account, I am driven to the conclusion that Shipman must have killed Mrs Moss. Like the coroner, I am sure that this was an unlawful killing.

name: Nora Needham
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, Coachman's Cottage, Oaklands, Godley, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to congestive heart failure
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Needham died a natural death.
Mrs Needham was at extremely high risk of suffering a heart attack at any time. Her death was sudden and was no doubt unexpected to her family but, from a medical viewpoint, it was certainly explicable.
There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman saw Mrs Needham shortly before her death was discovered. From her son's description of her usual habits and his account of the circumstances of her death, it seems likely that she died in the early morning. It is most unlikely that Shipman would have visited Mrs Needham at this time.
The position of her body was more suggestive of a sudden cardiac death than of death by a lethal injection of opiate.

name: Thomas O'Sullivan
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 12 Barleycroft Road, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis, due to ischaemic heart disease, resulting from diabetes mellitus
conclusion: It appears to me that Professor Baker was suspicious about this death because the entries in Form B are typical of those in many cases in which Shipman had killed his patient. As in so many of the unlawful killings, this was a sudden cardiac death at which Shipman appeared to be present. If Professor Baker had seen the medical records, I think his suspicions would have been further aroused. The records are scanty in the extreme and do not give an adequate background for the diagnosis of angina, which must have been the basis on which Shipman claimed to be satisfied that the cause of death was heart attack. Thus from the records, this case looks suspicious. However, the clear accounts of events given by the family and neighbour demonstrate that this was a natural death. There is no evidence that Shipman had had access to Mr O'Sullivan until he was already on the verge of death. I am quite satisfied that this was a natural death.

name: Mavis Mary Pickup
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 9 Spring Avenue, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
The evidence in this case is very clear and I am satisfied that Shipman must have killed Mrs Pickup.
Mrs Pickup was in good physical health when she last saw her doctor in August 1997 for a routine check. In particular, her blood pressure was and always had been within normal limits. There was no reason to suppose that she would have a stroke.
I find Shipman's suggestion that Mrs Pickup had had a stroke overnight or in the morning of 22nd
September to be quite incredible. Had she done so, she would have told a member of her family; she would have telephoned Shipman much earlier; she would not have gone out in the car; and the signs would have been apparent to Mrs Dyson. I am quite sure that Shipman's claim that she had had a stroke, as recorded in the medical notes, was false. I have already said that I have noticed that he would sometimes begin a record with genuine observations and would then move on to a fabricated account, designed to explain the death. That is clearly what he has done here.
Shipman's visit almost certainly took place in the early afternoon. Nobody saw Mrs Pickup alive or spoke to her after his visit. That in itself is a highly suspicious factor, especially when, as here, Shipman fabricated evidence that someone had seen her alive after his visit. In fact, there is nothing in the evidence which shows that she did not die at the time of his visit.
I have already said that Shipman's entries on Form B were a pack of lies, designed to make it appear that he had visited Mrs Pickup earlier than he did and that he was able to state that her death had occurred several hours later.
All the evidence points to the conclusion that Shipman killed Mrs Pickup, almost certainly by giving her an intravenous injection of diamorphine. I think it likely that he visited her in the early afternoon and that she told him that she felt very emotional and shaky. I have little doubt that he said that he would give her an injection to settle her nerves, which is what she wanted. She would have agreed without hesitation. After the injection, she would have been unconscious within a very short time. She was almost certainly sitting on her usual chair in the kitchen and would have fallen from it, as there were no supporting arms. She would have been dead within minutes.

name: Elizabeth Ann Rogers
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 132 Chartist House, Mount Street, Hyde
conclusion:
There is clear evidence that Mrs Rogers suffered from angina and congestive heart failure and must have been at risk of a sudden death from heart attack. There is also some evidence that she was not well on the day of her death. She had not dressed herself and seems to have telephoned the surgery to request a visit. It is therefore possible that she was suffering from some cardiac symptoms.
Having said that, it seems to me that this death is highly suspicious. The most obvious cause for suspicion is that it occurred during Shipman's visit. As Dr John Grenville has said, it is very rare indeed for a sudden death to occur during a doctor's home visit, unless the patient is terminally ill or has reported symptoms suggesting a life-threatening condition, such as a heart attack. Mrs Rogers was not terminally ill and I think it is most unlikely that she regarded herself as being seriously ill on the day of her death. First, if Mrs Rogers had been worried about her condition that morning, I think she would certainly have telephoned her daughter and might well have spoken to Mrs Unsworth. She did neither. Second, Shipman's visits book gives no indication that his proposed visit to Mrs Rogers was in the nature of an emergency. In general, Shipman used his visits book as a reminder of the names of the patients he was to see that day. Emergency requests were not usually entered.
Common sense would indicate that it must be very rare for a patient to die naturally during a routine visit by a general practitioner, as the visit usually lasts for only about 15 to 30 minutes. However, Shipman's patients often died during a visit and that feature gives rise to a high degree of suspicion.
There are other reasons for being suspicious about Shipman's role in this death. His account of the visit does not make sense. Shipman's note records signs and symptoms that are consistent with Mrs Rogers having a heart attack. If she were having a heart attack, one would expect Shipman to telephone immediately for an ambulance. He did not do so. According to Form B, he was with Mrs Rogers for half an hour during her last illness. I am bound to wonder what Shipman was doing for half an hour if he thought that Mrs Rogers was having a heart attack and ought to be admitted to hospital. Why did he not call for an ambulance? If he thought that her condition was not immediately life-threatening, why did he feel able to certify the cause of death without referral to the coroner? Why, if he needed the assistance of Mrs Unsworth, did he not telephone her rather than leave the patient and go down 13 floors to fetch her? Mrs Unsworth suggested that Shipman might not have known her telephone number. I think that is very unlikely. Shipman had many patients at Chartist House and Mrs Unsworth was in charge of some of them. Assuming that Mrs Rogers was alive when Shipman went downstairs, she could only recently have suffered a cardiac arrest when he returned. One would expect him then to commence resuscitation procedures, enlisting Mrs Unsworth's help, and to call for an ambulance. Instead he seems to have accepted that Mrs Rogers was beyond revival.
Form B also gives rise to suspicion. Shipman said that Mrs Unsworth was present at the moment of death and implied that she had contributed some information from which he had been able to diagnose the cause of death and describe the manner of its happening. I am quite sure that Mrs Unsworth was not present at the death and had no information to contribute. I note the inconsistency between the medical record and Form B on the issue of Mrs Unsworth's presence at the death.
Mrs Rogers' position and appearance in death were not consistent with death from coronary thrombosis. Dr Grenville has said that patients who begin to suffer the severe crushing pain which normally accompanies a heart attack usually try to get up to call help. They are not usually found sitting peacefully in a chair. On the other hand, Mrs Rogers' appearance was wholly consistent with that of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by a lethal injection of opiate.
I have come to the sure conclusion that Shipman must have killed Mrs Rogers by giving her a lethal injection. I think he then went downstairs and asked Mrs Unsworth to come upstairs with him under the pretence that he needed her help in packing a bag for Mrs Rogers to go to hospital.

name: Bessie Swann
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 2 Brooks Avenue, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
There are several suspicious circumstances surrounding this death.
The most suspicious feature is that the death occurred very suddenly within a matter of minutes of Shipman's arrival at the house. Before that day, Mrs Swann seems to have been well and certainly had no history of high blood pressure such as would put her at risk of sudden death by stroke. During the morning she went shopping. However, by 3pm, she had had a 'funny turn' and did not look well. She called the doctor, who came immediately. Within a short time of Shipman's arrival, Mr Avery found Shipman with his hand in Mrs Swann's mouth. Mrs Swann was unconscious or possibly already dead.
For the reasons given by Dr Esmail, I think it unlikely that the 'funny turn' was a cerebrovascular accident. In any event, even if the 'funny turn' was some sort of stroke, it is unlikely that Mrs Swann would have died so suddenly afterwards. As Dr John Grenville said in his generic evidence, sudden fatal strokes, due to a brain haemorrhage, are uncommon, certainly far less common than occlusive strokes, which do not result in sudden death. For a sudden death to occur naturally within such a short time of Shipman's arrival would have been a remarkable coincidence. On the other hand, if Shipman had given Mrs Swann a lethal injection of diamorphine she would have died very quickly. When Mr Avery arrived, Shipman appeared to have been waiting for her to die. He was disturbed by Mr Avery's return. For him to put his hand in Mrs Swann's mouth was not a proper method of keeping her airway open and, in my view, it must have been a pretence.
I also regard the contents of Form B as suspicious. First, Shipman suggests that he arrived 10 to 15 minutes before the death. On the MCCD, he stated that the interval between the onset of the stroke and death was 20 minutes. Shipman seems to be suggesting that Mrs Swann had already had a stroke when he arrived. If he found her suffering the signs of a stroke, he should have summoned an ambulance and have laid her down with her head back to keep her airway open. If she were already unconscious when he arrived, he would not know what had led to her loss of consciousness and would not have been able confidently to diagnose a stroke. Shipman did not do what any sensible doctor would have done in the circumstances. Second, Shipman has sought to involve Mr Avery and Mr Swann in the death by suggesting that they could have had some information to impart as to the manner or cause of death. Even if it might be said that they were present at the moment of death, they were not present during the stroke that is supposed to have preceded it and it is misleading to suggest that they could have imparted any information about it.
Mrs Swann was a usually healthy woman who had died very suddenly. Dr Esmail said that it would not have been proper for Shipman to certify the death as being due to a stroke unless he had been present when it happened and had seen the signs. It is not clear that he had done so; certainly no record was made in Mrs Swann's medical notes. In my view, a referral to the coroner was called for.
Shipman made a most unusual remark soon after he had told Mr Swann that his mother had died. He suggested that he would wait for a while 'in case she
(
Mrs Swann
)
wakens up and frightens us all'. This remark is resonant of an event that occurred shortly before the death in 1979 of Mrs Alice Maude Gorton, who was, as I have found, probably killed by Shipman. Shipman brought Mrs Gorton's daughter to her mother's house and was in the process of telling her that her mother was dead and that a post-mortem examination would not be necessary, when Mrs Gorton emitted a loud groan. She was unconscious but not yet dead. She died two days later, without recovering consciousness. I think this event must have remained on Shipman's mind and may well account for the remark he made to Mr Swann.
Mrs Swann's appearance in death was entirely typical of that of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of diamorphine.
These matters, taken together, drive me to the conclusion that Shipman must have killed Mrs Swann. I feel able to say that I am sure of this conclusion.

name: Beatrice Toft
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 24 Marler Road, Hyde
certified_cause: respiratory failure caused by chronic bronchitis with emphysema
conclusion:
Mrs Toft was plainly in poor health in the weeks and months before her death. It is possible that she had not long to live. I think it is likely (although I cannot be certain) that Mrs Toft had been more unwell than usual in the week before she died. I think it likely that Shipman visited her on the Tuesday and found her quite poorly, so poorly as to warrant a visit the following day. I think he must have then found her at least to some extent improved, as Mrs Toft was not admitted to hospital and Shipman did not consider it necessary to visit on the Thursday. I think he probably visited again on the Friday and found her improved. I infer that no admission was necessary and Shipman promised to come on the Monday. I think that, by the Monday, Mrs Toft was well enough to be left at home on her own while her daughters went about their usual business. Her daughters were very attentive to her needs and, had she been ill, one of them would have been with her. I am satisfied that she was alone that day, when Shipman visited. It is possible that I am wrong in my conclusion that Shipman probably did visit three times in the previous week. It is possible that the family is right when they assert that Mrs Toft was not more unwell than usual and the three visits did not take place. In the event, as I am satisfied that Mrs Toft was well enough to be left alone on the Monday, it does not matter greatly whether she had been unwell in the previous week.
Dr Grenville has said that a death from respiratory failure usually follows either an acute chest infection, heart attack or stroke. I am satisfied that, if Mrs Toft had a chest infection in the previous week, she had to all intents and purposes recovered from it by the Monday. I am satisfied too, that she had not undergone the kind of gradual decline described by Dr Grenville. It follows that I think it very unlikely that Mrs Toft died of respiratory failure as Shipman claimed.
I accept that Mrs Toft could have died suddenly from a heart attack. However, if she did, she could not have arranged herself in the bed in the position in which she was found. I rule that out as implausible.
This death is highly suspicious as it was discovered so shortly after a visit by Shipman. No one saw Mrs Toft alive after his visit. If Mrs Toft died a natural death in the short period that elapsed between Shipman's departure and the arrival of Mrs Clayton, this would be a real coincidence. This is the kind of coincidence that hardly ever happens to other doctors but, if he is to be believed, happened to Shipman very frequently.
Shipman's entries on Form B also give rise to suspicion. He has given the impression that the death was later than it really was. I am satisfied that he did this in order to increase the interval between his visit and the death. His suggestion that some information about the mode of death has come from a daughter must have been intended to create the impression that someone else had some knowledge of the circumstances, when, in truth, he was the only one who knew anything about the death.
I find the suggestion that Mrs Toft could have swallowed both dentures utterly incredible. It appears likely to me that someone removed them. I also think that Mrs Toft's position in bed must have been the result of someone arranging her. Shipman was the last person to see Mrs Toft alive. All the known facts are explicable if one considers what he might have done. He visited Mrs Toft; whether by arrangement or not, does not matter. He would have been able to gain access as the door was usually left unlocked. Mrs Toft would not be alarmed to see him, as she knew him well. It would not be difficult for him to persuade her that she needed an injection of some sort. Once she was unconscious, he could have arranged her body neatly with her arms on the covers and moved the pillows back. He could have removed her dentures. When he left, he must have switched the light off. He would not have known that Mrs Toft slept with her teeth in and the light on. I think this is what must have happened. Why he took the teeth out is something of a mystery, although Dr Grenville has suggested that Shipman might have had an alarming experience on another occasion, when a denture might possibly have become lodged in a patient's throat, so that on future occasions he thought it prudent to remove them. I have come across a number of Shipman killings in which the dentures of the deceased patient had been removed from the mouth, but none in which they had disappeared altogether.
Although Mrs Toft was not in good health at the time of her death and although a sudden cardiac death was possible, I am sure that Shipman was responsible for her death. Although the circumstances arouse a suspicion that Shipman took Mrs Toft's money, I do not feel able to reach a firm conclusion on that issue.

name: May Vizor
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 11 Goodier View, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Vizor died a natural death, almost certainly as the result of a coronary thrombosis, as certified by Shipman. All the evidence points to that conclusion.
I can understand why Professor Baker was suspicious when he saw the cremation forms. He would know that he could not trust Shipman's claims that Mrs Vizor had a history of heart problems and that her husband was present at the death. Now that Mr Vizor's account of events is known, all suspicions are laid to rest. In particular, there is clear evidence that Mrs Vizor suffered acute chest pain and that Shipman advised that the ambulance be called. Proper attempts to save Mrs Vizor had already been made by the paramedics before Shipman arrived at the house.

name: Maria West
title: Mrs
conclusion:
This was a cremation case with no direct evidence of morphine in the body tissues. There are a number of significant features about this case, all of which are common to other cases:
The death took place in Mrs West's home and while Shipman was alone with her. This is a highly suspicious factor, as other general practitioners say that this is an extremely rare event.
Death was extremely sudden, so sudden that it could not have happened as Shipman claimed.
Shipman made no attempt to resuscitate the patient and justified his decision by claiming that she would have been severely disabled if revived.
Mrs West's appearance in death, sitting peacefully in a chair as though asleep, was similar to the appearance of many of Shipman's other victims.
Shipman gave inconsistent accounts of the circumstances to different people. However, it must be borne in mind that the accounts of friends and relatives may not be wholly reliable due to the passage of time and the effect of shock and distress.
There was a dispute as to whether Shipman mentioned the possibility of a post-mortem examination. The relative said he did not. Shipman made no report to the coroner in a case in which such a report was plainly called for, as the death was sudden and unexplained.
To explain Mrs West's death, Shipman selected a moderately plausible cause, in that there were features of her medical history which put her at risk of a stroke.
Shipman wrote on cremation Form B that a neighbour was present at the death. Although she was in the house, Mrs Hadfield was not in the room at the moment of death and the statement that she was present is misleading. This is a typical example of the way in which Shipman would make false statements, seeking to distance himself from the death or to make it appear he had not been alone with the patient at the time of death.

name: Ada Ashworth
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 8 Spring Avenue, Hyde
conclusion:
Mrs Ashworth was a typical Shipman victim, an elderly woman living alone.
I am satisfied from the evidence of Mrs Wood that Mrs Ashworth was in reasonable general health at 1pm on the day of her death. I think it unlikely that she had asked Shipman to visit her. Had she been expecting him, she would have mentioned it to Mrs Wood. Shipman might have been making a routine visit to monitor Mrs Ashworth's progress after her fall but I think it more likely, in view of the explanation he gave to Mrs Wood and her husband, that he made an unsolicited visit to Mrs Ashworth some time during the afternoon. From what Shipman told Mrs Wood and Mr Mallinson, it appears that he had been inside Mrs Ashworth's house before he went to see them. He did not say he had seen Mrs Ashworth through the window. He could have gained access to the house, whether Mrs Ashworth was dead or alive at the time of his arrival, as the back door was left unlocked. It is possible that she was dead when he arrived, but it is also possible that she was alive and that he made an excuse to give her a lethal injection. My knowledge of cases in which Shipman has killed makes me highly sceptical of any claim by Shipman that he found a patient dead when he arrived at the house. Such an event is rare in practice, but with Shipman it apparently happened frequently.
Shipman's conduct after the death was typical of cases in which he had killed. Any reasonable doctor, on finding Mrs Ashworth unconscious, would either have examined her thoroughly in order to ascertain that she was dead or, if still unsure of death, would have called an ambulance. Instead, Shipman went to the neighbours' house and asked them to go in to Mrs Ashworth's while he confirmed that she was dead. Yet, when the three of them went back to Mrs Ashworth's house, he carried out only the most cursory examination. It appears to me highly likely that he well knew she was dead.
Shipman's subsequent conduct in respect of the MCCD also gives rise to suspicion. Whilst elderly, Mrs Ashworth was far from being so infirm that her death could reasonably be ascribed to old age. The circumstances in which Mrs Ashworth was found, sitting upright in her chair, dressed in her day clothes, are not typical of a death from old age but are entirely typical of death caused by the administration of a lethal dose of opiates. If Mrs Ashworth had died suddenly that afternoon, a reasonable doctor would have declined to certify a cause of death and would have reported the case to the coroner. At the very least, one would have expected a doctor to discuss the death with the next of kin. Here, Shipman avoided meeting the next of kin, who was a doctor and who might therefore be expected to be puzzled by the suddenness of the death.
I am also suspicious of Shipman's claim that he had last seen Mrs Ashworth alive on 20th
November. The visits book for that day contains no entry in her name. It is possible that he saw her in the surgery on that day. However, that is unlikely, given her restricted mobility. In any event, if she were fit to travel to the surgery a week before her death, this would be quite inconsistent with a death from old age so soon afterwards. I think it likely that Shipman's claim that he had seen Mrs Ashworth on 20th
November was false and was designed to avoid the risk that the registrar might refer the case to the coroner.
Taking all these factors into account, I have no doubt that Shipman was responsible for the death of Mrs Ashworth. I am sure that he gave her a lethal injection, almost certainly using diamorphine to which he had unrecorded and illicit access.

name: Elsie Barker
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 9 Green Street, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of suspicious features surrounding this death. Although there is no eyewitness evidence of Shipman's presence at Mrs Barker's house on the day of her death, I consider that the only inference which can be drawn from the computerised medical records is that he did in fact visit her. I say that, despite the fact that Shipman has not admitted or asserted that he was at the house, as he often did in other cases. It is hard to imagine why Shipman would have made entries in the medical records clearly stating that he had seen Mrs Barker on the day of her death if he had not done so. As with all medical records made by Shipman, these must be approached with caution, especially in this case as it has not been possible to check when they were made or whether they have been altered. The records could be a genuine account of a visit, at the end of which Mrs Barker was alive and well. However, they could be false and be part of Shipman's design to cover up his involvement in Mrs Barker's death. If Shipman had decided to visit Mrs Barker and kill her, one must ask why he would make entries in her records which showed he had visited her if his primary contention, as evidenced on the MCCD and Form B, was that he had not seen her since 24th
July.
In my view, it is entirely reasonable to suppose that, when Shipman visited and had killed Mrs Barker, he believed that he had not been observed at the house and therefore took the risk of asserting on the official forms that he had not seen her that day. That would be the best way of deflecting any possible suspicion that he had been involved in her death. However, he would wish to have some ready explanation if it transpired that he had been seen at her house. The medical records, as entered by him, would enable him to give a plausible explanation for him having visited her, even though she had not requested it. He could say that he had called in, as he was passing (as he said in other cases), in order to speak to Mrs Barker about her use of zopiclone and to take her blood pressure again as he was worried about it, having seen the result of the reading on the 24th
. The entry made on the day of death relating to blood pressure, which carries with it the (no doubt intended) implication that the reading was high but had to be
'accepted'
, would also provide support for the feasibility of a sudden death due to a stroke.
How likely is it that Mrs Barker had a sudden catastrophic cerebrovascular accident during the afternoon of 29th
July? Undoubtedly, her blood pressure was high. Whether it was as high as the record for the 24th
shows, we do not know. However, it is reasonable to assume that Mrs Barker was at some increased risk of a stroke. If she did die of a cerebrovascular accident that day, this must have been of sudden onset as she was well when she spoke to her granddaughter at about 2pm. But, as Dr Grenville has said, patients whose illness is due to sudden haemorrhage represent a very small proportion of all patients suffering a cerebrovascular accident. Much more common is the occlusive type of stroke, which evolves gradually and results in neurological signs, such as weakness and/or slurring of speech. In those circumstances, the victim can summon help. Also, a victim of sudden haemorrhagic stroke would not be expected to be found sitting upright in a chair looking peaceful and as if asleep. So, it appears to me that, although it is possible that Mrs Barker had a sudden fatal stroke, this is unlikely.
Form B contains a number of inconsistencies and untruths. First, Shipman claimed that he last saw Mrs Barker alive on 24th
July, when the medical records tend to show that he saw her on the day of her death. The statement that the 'nephew' had found the body at 6.45pm and had spoken to Mrs Barker at 4pm is a lie and in my view an important one. Shipman is here creating the impression that Mrs Barker was still alive after the time when he might have been seen at her house. Also, the statement that Mrs Barker had collapsed on furniture is, in my view, a lie, designed to add verisimilitude to Shipman's claim that this was a death from a sudden fatal stroke.
The appearance of Mrs Barker, sitting peacefully in her armchair, is entirely typical of a death from diamorphine poisoning.
Taking all these matters into account, I am quite satisfied that Shipman did visit Mrs Barker on the afternoon of her death, without prior arrangement. She trusted him and would have let him in without hesitation. I am sure that he then killed her, almost certainly by diamorphine injection, and left, believing, correctly as it transpired, that no one had seen him.

name: Thomas Cheetham
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 17 Garden Street, Newton, Hyde
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to adenocarcinoma of the rectum
conclusion:
There are many suspicious features surrounding this death.
Shipman sought to suggest that Mr Cheetham had been found dead when he arrived at the house, either when or shortly before Mrs Cheetham returned home. If the evidence of Mr Phelps can be accepted, that Mr Cheetham was alive and in Mr Kenneth Smith's house as Shipman arrived, then it would follow that Shipman has lied about the circumstances. Although Mr Phelps did not give oral evidence to the Inquiry in connection with this death, he did appear in connection with the deaths of his uncles, Mr Sidney Smith and Mr Kenneth Smith. I formed a favourable impression of Mr Phelps. He seemed to me an entirely reliable witness and I have no hesitation in accepting as accurate his recollection of what Mr Kenneth Smith told him at the time of Mr Cheetham's death. The timing may not be accurate (although I think the estimate that Shipman arrived at about 3pm probably is accurate) but I accept the core of his evidence, which is that Mr Kenneth Smith told him that Mr Cheetham was alive, and in his (Mr Smith's) house, when Shipman arrived. Mr Cheetham was dead shortly afterwards.
That finding alone is enough to enable me to reach a conclusion, but there are other factors which point in the same direction. Shipman certified the death as being due to carcinomatosis but, medically, that does not make sense. A person dying from carcinomatosis deteriorates gradually and is usually confined to bed in a state of extreme weakness for some time before death. It would be most unusual for a death from this cause to be as sudden as this. I note that Shipman said on the MCCD that the onset of the carcinomatosis was 18 months before death. The medical records show that there was no recognised spread of the cancer to the liver until about six months before the death. It appears to me that Shipman was trying to give the impression that the disease was at a more advanced stage than it was.
The position in which Mr Cheetham was found and his appearance in death were entirely typical of the appearance of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of diamorphine.
Finally, Shipman has fabricated the medical records and the entries on Form B in a way suggestive of guilt.
Taking all these factors together, I have no doubt that Mr Cheetham was killed by Shipman and I am sure that this is the case.

name: Cissie Davies
title: Mrs
conclusion:
Mrs Davies was well on the day of her death, save that she was recovering from a chest infection which was still troubling her to the extent that she sought a prescription from the surgery. Her level of activity that day is, however, totally inconsistent with her suffering bronchopneumonia. It is not feasible to suggest that she could have died so quickly from bronchopneumonia. In the unlikely event that her health had deteriorated suddenly later in the afternoon of 2nd
February, she would certainly have telephoned her son. I am quite sure Mrs Davies did not die of bronchopneumonia. Nor was there any other likely cause of a sudden death.
From the detailed picture that the Inquiry has been able to construct from the witnesses and from the computer audit trail, it would appear that Shipman's interest in Mrs Davies was aroused when he became aware of her request for a prescription for her chest infection. Having logged that request in the computer, he went on his rounds visiting several patients. I am satisfied that he visited Mrs Davies. I am also satisfied that he wished to make it appear that he had seen her at the surgery rather than at her own home. That afternoon, he had the opportunity to administer a lethal dose of diamorphine, which would have killed Mrs Davies in minutes.
It is right to point out that, unlike many of Shipman's victims, Mrs Davies was not found sitting in a chair or on a sofa. His usual method of killing was to administer the lethal injection in the patient's living room. It appears that if he gave Mrs Davies such an injection, he must have done so in her bedroom. She would not have been able to climb the stairs after receiving the dose. However, it is not hard to imagine circumstances in which it was decided that the consultation should take place in the bedroom. Mrs Davies may have been sitting on the bed while she was examined or received some treatment. Shipman could well have covered her over before leaving, making it appear that she had taken an afternoon nap with her clothes on. In fact she was not found until the next day.
When, next morning, Shipman made a computer entry recording a consultation the previous day, he did so presumably not knowing whether he had or had not been observed at the house. When he made that false entry he described symptoms such as chest pain and breathlessness, which are not mentioned by the witness who saw Mrs Davies that day. I am satisfied that Shipman fabricated that entry to lay the basis of the diagnosis he proposed to give for the death.
Finally, the lies and inconsistencies in the death certificate are compelling. Most telling is the assertion that Mr Davies had nursed his mother during her last illness. It appears that Shipman must have been confident that this assertion would not be checked.
Taking all these matters into account, I am driven to the conclusion that Shipman killed Mrs Davies during the afternoon of 2nd
February. There is no reason to think that his method would have been anything other than the usual injection of diamorphine.

name: Leah Fogg
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 133 Haughton Green Road, Denton
conclusion:
Although there is no direct evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Fogg on the day of her death, I think it is highly likely that he did so. He had promised to visit her when it was convenient. He noted an intention to do so on Tuesday, 11th
June. We do not know when that entry was made, but, if it was made genuinely, it must have been made before Shipman was officially told of Mrs Fogg's death at about 6.45pm on Monday, 10th
June. It is possible that he intended to visit Mrs Fogg on 11th June but found he had time on his hands on the afternoon of 10th
June, when he had only one visit to make. It is also possible that he made the entry for 11th
June dishonestly, at a time when he knew Mrs Fogg was dead, intending to create the impression that he did not know of her death.
Mrs Fogg was in good physical health at the time of her death. She was known to be well and active until shortly before 2pm on the day of her death. There was no history of any condition, apart from her age, that might put her at risk of sudden death. Certainly there was no reliable history of any factors that put her at risk of a stroke. Mrs Fogg's position and appearance in death were not typical of a death due to stroke. I think it is highly unlikely that Mrs Fogg died of a stroke. Although it is theoretically possible, there is no reason to suspect that she died of any other natural cause of sudden death.
Shipman could not possibly have made a genuine diagnosis of death due to cerebrovascular accident. There was no medical evidence to support the conclusion and no account of Mrs Fogg's condition shortly before the death from which he might have inferred the cause. If Shipman had acted honestly, he would have had to refer this death to the coroner. I believe that he told a deliberate lie in saying that he had seen Mrs Fogg on 1st
June in order to avoid a referral to the coroner. If he had told the truth, that he had not seen Mrs Fogg since 7th
May, the registrar would almost certainly have passed the case to the coroner.
The MCCD gives the false impression that Mrs Fogg had been suffering from cerebral arteriosclerotic vascular disease for two years. There was no proper basis on which Shipman could have said that. Form B reveals an attempt by Shipman to give the impression that he had attended Mrs Fogg, supposedly in connection with arteriosclerosis for nine days before her death. I am satisfied that that was a lie. This created the misleading impression that the death had not come as a complete surprise to all who knew her. I have little doubt that this impression was deliberately created in order to allay any possible concerns in the mind of the Form C doctor or the medical referee. Other entries sought to give the impression that others had provided him with information about the death, although not present at the actual moment, from which he had been able to infer how Mrs Fogg had died. This was misleading. No one was able to give any such information.
When the facts of this case are set against the background of Shipman's known activities, I am driven to the conclusion that he killed Mrs Fogg. Despite the absence of positive evidence of his presence, I feel sure of this conclusion.

name: Elsie Godfrey
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 61 Chartist House, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of suspicious features connected with this death. First, Mrs Godfrey does not appear to have been suffering from any potentially fatal condition. Although it is always possible for a person of her age to die suddenly, for example following a stroke or heart attack, there were no particular risk factors indicated by Mrs Godfrey's medical history. Although there is a reference to left ventricular failure on 25th
April 1996, there is nothing recorded in the notes to explain the basis of that diagnosis. The note merely says that Lasix was to be added to Mrs Godfrey's medication. I am deeply suspicious about that entry. Lasix is a powerful diuretic which Shipman usually prescribed in quite severe cases of congestive heart failure. There is no previous suggestion in Mrs Godfrey's notes that she had been suffering from heart failure. I think that entry is probably false.
Shipman gave a cause of death, old age, which was plainly not justified. Mrs Godfrey had been out for lunch that day. Old age is only appropriate as a cause of death where there has been a gradual failure of the bodily systems and it is not clear to the doctor exactly which organ failure has led immediately to death. In my view, there was no satisfactory explanation for Mrs Godfrey's death.
I accept the reasoning of Mrs Bowler when she explained why she thought that her mother probably died soon after her return to Chartist House after lunch. I accept that, had she been up and about after her unknown visitor had left, she would probably have telephoned Mr Schofield to finish their conversation. She would also have spoken to Mrs Unsworth to let her know of her return and she would probably have unpacked her bag. I infer that Mrs Godfrey probably died soon after the interrupted telephone call with Mr Schofield.
On Form B, Shipman gave a time of death that he could not have justified. If this death was natural and occurred some time between the telephone call with Mr Schofield and the discovery of the body the next day, it would not have been possible for Shipman to estimate the time of death with any precision. He would probably have been able to infer from the presence of rigor mortis that the death had not occurred within the last two or three hours. He might well have inferred, from the domestic circumstances, that it had occurred the previous day. But he purported to assess the time of death, with some precision, from the body temperature. This is something that he quite frequently purported to do and, as Dr John Grenville has explained, such attempts are wholly unscientific, as Shipman must have known. I infer that Shipman wished to give the impression that the death had occurred at 6.30pm because that would mean it was several hours after his visit, which someone might have noticed.
Mrs Godfrey's position and appearance in death were not typical of what is found following a sudden natural death. However, they were entirely typical of the position and appearance of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of diamorphine.
I have already mentioned that Shipman gave a cause of death that could not have been medically justified. If the death was natural, it was sudden and unexplained and should have been referred to the coroner.
The facts that Mrs Godfrey's television was on and a newspaper was on her knee do not seem to me to be probative one way or the other. Although these matters might indicate that Mrs Godfrey was alone at the time of her death, they do not prove that she was. If she had had the television on or had been reading her newspaper when Shipman arrived, and if she had put down her paper and switched her television off, it would have been a very simple matter for him to switch the television back on and put the newspaper on her knee before leaving.
Although there is no direct evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Godfrey on the day of the death, I think it is likely that he did so. I think it is likely that he was prompted to think of her because the results of her blood tests had arrived. Although there was no need for any repeat test, I think it likely that Shipman used the supposed need for a repeat test as an excuse to visit Mrs Godfrey and to give her a lethal injection under the guise of taking blood. It is known that he did this from time to time.
I have come to the conclusion that, despite the lack of any direct evidence of Shipman's visit, it is likely that he did visit Mrs Godfrey and killed her by giving a lethal injection of a strong opiate, probably diamorphine.

name: Irene Heathcote
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 3 Coronation Avenue, Hyde
conclusion:
This is a highly suspicious death. Mrs Heathcote was not seen alive after Shipman's afternoon visit. Nor did she answer her telephone when Mrs Thomson rang. These alone are factors from which I deduce that he killed her. All the other circumstances point to this conclusion.
Mrs Heathcote was well when she saw Mrs Thomson before going to the surgery on the morning of her death. If she had had a blackout in the night, I think it is highly likely that she would have told Mrs Thomson on that occasion. If Shipman's decision to visit her that afternoon had been on account of her report to him that she had had a blackout, I am certain she would have told Mrs Thomson afterwards. I suspect that Mrs Heathcote had her blood pressure taken, possibly by the practice nurse, and that Shipman spoke to her at some point. I do not think she made any complaint of a blackout. I think Shipman decided to visit her that afternoon to kill her and prepared the ground for his explanation for her death by making a false record showing that she had had a blackout.
When Shipman arrived in the afternoon, I think that he administered a lethal injection of opiate, almost certainly diamorphine. Mrs Heathcote would have lapsed into sleep and unconsciousness within a minute or two and I am sure she was dead by the time Shipman left at about 3.45pm, just in time for his afternoon surgery. All efforts to contact Mrs Heathcote after that were doomed to failure. Why the gas fire was on in both rooms is something of a mystery. It may be that Mrs Heathcote put the front room fire on in anticipation of Shipman's visit and he left both fires on when he left. It is just possible that he lit the front room fire and turned up the living room fire so as to keep the body warm. It does appear from some other cases that he has done this in case anyone other than he should try to assess the time of death from body temperature.
The next day, Shipman's claim to be able to assess the time of death by placing a thermometer under the armpit was pure charlatanism. His motive, however, is clear. He wished to create the impression that the death had occurred much later than it really did. Shipman's entries on Form B are inaccurate and deceitful. Mrs Heathcote did not have a final illness for which he attended her for 24 hours. She was well until Shipman arrived at her house. Nor did he last see her six hours before her death. Nor did he carry out a complete external examination of her body 12 hours after death. Nor were the police officer and neighbour able to shed any light on the mode of Mrs Heathcote's death. Finally, and most blatantly of all, he alleged that a neighbour had seen her alive at 7.45pm, which was not true. No one had seen her alive after he left. In short, the contents of this document are a pack of lies.
As Dr Grenville has observed, with this medical history, Shipman could not possibly have known what was the cause of death, unless he himself had caused it.
I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Heathcote.

name: Jane Jones
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 2 Leigh Fold, Hyde
conclusion:
There are some suspicious circumstances surrounding this death.
Although the medical records have not been found, it appears from the witness evidence that Mrs Jones was in relatively good health at 10.30am on the day of her death and yet, just over two hours later and within minutes after Shipman had visited her, she was dead. In giving his evidence in relation to the death of Mrs Beatrice Toft, Dr John Grenville provided a useful description of the likely pattern of events prior to a death caused by respiratory failure. He described a long, slow period of deterioration, perhaps over a period of weeks, leading to a patient becoming bed bound or chair bound, requiring either nursing care or admission to a hospital or nursing home. Often the patient would need to use an oxygen cylinder. The patient would become increasingly short of breath. In the later stages, it would be difficult for the patient to draw enough breath to speak more than a few words. Eventually the patient would lapse into unconsciousness due to hypoxia. This description does not accord with the evidence in this case. Mrs Jones was living alone and was not receiving nursing care. She had been talking to her niece only about two hours before her death. If Mrs Jones had been suffering from severe respiratory illness, such as might lead to death within days, one would have expected Shipman to be visiting her frequently. He was not. In my view, Shipman's certification as to the cause of Mrs Jones' death must be in real doubt. This was a sudden and unexplained death, which should have been referred to the coroner.
Shipman admitted that he had given Mrs Jones an injection, supposedly for her breathing difficulties. In the absence of the medical records, I cannot say whether he gave a drug that was or might have been appropriate treatment. However, there must be a real possibility that Shipman gave Mrs Jones an injection of strong opiate.
Shipman's conduct does not make sense. If he had really found Mrs Jones in a state of respiratory collapse, one would have expected him to call an ambulance and try to have her admitted to hospital as soon as possible. Instead, he left her alone and went to Mrs Panther's house, supposedly to fetch her to come and help. What Mrs Panther could usefully have done, if this was a real emergency, is hard to imagine. Shipman quite often left a body or a dying patient and enlisted the 'help' of a relative or neighbour who would be present when the death was 'discovered'. I think it likely that Shipman went to fetch Mrs Panther so that he would be able to involve her in the discovery of the death.
I am puzzled by Mrs Panther's assertion that her aunt was still alive when she entered the bedroom. If Shipman had given a lethal injection of diamorphine (his preferred method of killing) before he went to fetch Mrs Panther, I would have expected Mrs Jones to have died before Mrs Panther arrived. Usually, Shipman ensured that his murdered patients were already dead when his 'helper' arrived on the scene. Moreover, it would be very strange for Shipman to say that no one was present at the death if in fact Mrs Panther had arrived in time to witness the moment of death. I do wonder whether Mrs Panther's recollection is correct in this respect and think perhaps that she has misconstrued the exhalation of air. It is possible that Mrs Jones' body moved slightly and some air was expressed from the lungs as a result.
Shipman told at least one lie on Form B. He claimed that Mrs Jones had been nursed during her last illness. If Mrs Jones had died of respiratory failure, she would have needed nursing care. Shipman would have wished to give the impression that this death was not sudden or unexpected.
Mrs Jones' appearance in death was very similar to that of some of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of opiate. She was found sitting upright in bed, propped up on her pillows. The bed covers were pulled up to her waist with her left arm resting in her lap and her right arm by her side with the forearm exposed.
Mrs Jones had not declined gradually towards a death from respiratory failure but died quite suddenly. That sudden death occurred during a visit by Shipman. It seems to me that it is highly likely that she died as the result of a lethal injection of opiate. It would be so remarkable a coincidence that she should suddenly die naturally of some other cause during a visit by Shipman that I discount that possibility as fanciful. I am driven to the conclusion that Shipman killed Mrs Jones.

name: Ethel May Kellett
title: Mrs
conclusion:
There are some suspicious features surrounding this death. The most obvious is the temporal association between Shipman's visit and the discovery of Mrs Kellett's body. There is no evidence that anyone saw Mrs Kellett alive or spoke to her after Shipman's visit on 12th
May. Such evidence as there is, appears likely to have been fabricated by Shipman in Form B so as to create the impression that he had not been the last person to see Mrs Kellett alive. He said that a neighbour saw her alive at 6pm, whereas it seems very likely that Mrs Field tried but failed to make contact with her. He also said that a neighbour was with him when he found the body, which is inconsistent with the other evidence, including the telephone account he gave to the police.
It is clear that Mrs Kellett was at high risk of suffering from a cerebrovascular accident or heart attack. Further, the visits book and the visits request slip indicate that Mrs Kellett herself recognised that she was experiencing a stroke when she telephoned the surgery on the morning of 12th
May 1997. Shipman's detailed note, if true, does record a developing stroke. However, it is not at all clear that the note is a genuine record of Mrs Kellett's condition. If she had been worried about herself, as she would have been if she had had slurred speech and significant weakness on the right side, she would have telephoned her son just as Shipman told Mrs Janice Kellett that Mr Kellett had said he intended to. Also, I have learned to be suspicious of any medical record in which Shipman claims that his patient was reluctant to be admitted to hospital. Of course I accept that patients do sometimes refuse to go to hospital. However, I have seen so many such entries in cases where I have had to conclude that Shipman has killed his patient, that I now regard such a record as a suspicious feature. Shipman has repeatedly used this device as a means of explaining the death that is soon to be discovered.
Shipman's claim that Mrs Kellett had left her door unlocked, so that he was able to gain access on 13th
May, is also a highly suspicious factor especially had she been seen alive by a neighbour at 6pm. She would never, I am sure, have retired to bed with her door unlocked. Mrs Janice Kellett says her mother-in-law was safety conscious. I suspect that Mrs Kellett let Shipman in on 12th
May and that he either left the door unlocked when he left after killing her or that he took a key with him and let himself in again on the 13th
. He had certainly found a key by the time he reported the death to the police. He might well have found it the day before. This factor tends to suggest that Shipman was the last person to see Mrs Kellett alive and that her death occurred in his presence. When he did report the death to the police, he said he had visited over the weekend but made no mention of the visit on the Monday. This, again, is highly suspicious.
I cannot rule out the theoretical possibility that Mrs Kellett died of a stroke. She was certainly at high risk of doing so and she was exhibiting the signs and symptoms of a stroke on the morning of 12th
May. I believe, however, that Mrs Kellett was dead shortly after Shipman's departure on the afternoon of 12th
May. For her to have died naturally so soon after his departure would represent a remarkable coincidence, so remarkable in fact that I am sure she did not do so. I am sure that Shipman unlawfully killed her. She had been his patient for three months.

name: Renee Lacey
title: Mrs
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to carcinoma of the lung with carcinoma of the breast as a significant contributing condition
conclusion:
Mrs Lacey was very unwell in the months before she died although there was no definite evidence of secondary cancer in April 1996 when she was reviewed by Mr Logue. When she deteriorated towards the end of May, it appears that Shipman himself diagnosed her as suffering from malignant cancer and did not seek to confirm the diagnosis by referring her back to the Christie Hospital. When Shipman saw her on 30th
May, he told the family that he would arrange for Mrs Lacey to be admitted to a hospice. It is not known whether he tried to make arrangements for her to be admitted. Certainly the family was not given any further information in the remaining days of Mrs Lacey's life. On the day before Mrs Lacey's death, Shipman prescribed oral morphine although the family does not recall that Mrs Lacey was in pain. However, Shipman might quite properly have given oral morphine as a euphoric drug.
On 6th
June, Shipman acted in a very unusual manner. He prevented Mr Lacey from being present during his consultation with his wife. If Shipman had seen Mrs Lacey and she had asked to speak to Shipman alone, this action would be perfectly understandable. However, Shipman unilaterally decided that Mr Lacey should be absent before he had seen Mrs Lacey that day. During a previous consultation with Mrs Lacey, Shipman had had no objection to her daughter being present. The fact that Shipman engineered an opportunity to be alone with Mrs Lacey is a highly suspicious factor. He had an opportunity to inject her with diamorphine. A few minutes before Shipman arrived, she was speaking to her husband. A few minutes after Shipman's arrival, she was dead. That is sufficient to persuade me that he must have killed her. That he had prescribed oral morphine the day before suggests that he might well have decided that he would end Mrs Lacey's life when he had a suitable opportunity. If there should be a post-mortem examination, the morphine in her body would be readily explained.
The misleading entries made by Shipman on Form B of the cremation certificate were, in my view, designed to create the impression that Mrs Lacey had been close to death for some hours when he arrived; that this was a typical death from carcinomatosis; and that he and Mr Lacey were together at the bedside at the moment of death. I note also that Shipman did not carry out a full external examination and did no more than to feel for a pulse at Mrs Lacey's wrist. As Dr John Grenville has explained, such a brief examination is not sufficient to satisfy the doctor that the patient is really dead. That Shipman should make so brief an examination suggests that he already knew Mrs Lacey was dead and there was no need to examine her.
I am entirely satisfied that Shipman took Mrs Lacey's life on 6th
June 1996. It may well be that she would not have lived long, but he deprived her and her family of their proper opportunity to prepare themselves for her death.

name: Joan May Melia
title: Mrs
conclusion:
Had it not been for the finding of morphine in the body tissues, there would have been very little evidence of Shipman's involvement in the death:
First, there is no direct evidence of a visit by Shipman during the afternoon of 12th
June. No one saw Shipman arrive or leave; no one saw his car outside. There is no record of a visit in the surgery documents or on the computer. However, the jury must have been prepared to infer that Shipman had visited Mrs Melia and had administered a fatal dose, almost certainly of diamorphine.
Second, there are no false, exaggerated or backdated entries in the medical records. The record of the consultation of the morning of 12th
June appears to be a genuine one, properly reflecting the moderately severe chest infection from which Mrs Melia was actually suffering. Shipman does not appear to have created any false records to lend credibility to the cause of death he was to certify.
Third, Shipman did not spin any elaborate tale of Mrs Melia having refused treatment or hospital admission.
The only suspicious factors (apart from the finding of morphine) were that Shipman exaggerated the seriousness of her chest infection when speaking to Mrs Melia and certified a cause of death which was incompatible with her ability to walk about and eat a meal only a short time before death. If Mrs Melia had been cremated, there would have been no prospect of Shipman being convicted of her killing.

name: Hervey Nuttall
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 14 Chartist House, Hyde
conclusion:
It appears to me highly likely that Mr Nuttall died a natural death. Although he had enjoyed excellent health until not long before he died, the evidence is that he was seriously ill shortly before his death. He was bedridden and his breathing was noisy and rattly.
Although Mrs Jones does not suggest that her uncle had previously been debilitated and does not recall that he had suffered a stroke, it is quite possible that he had done. These events took place over 20 years ago and it would be wholly understandable if Mrs Jones had forgotten some of the background to her uncle's final illness. She does recall the final stages and her description of her uncle two days before his death is strongly suggestive of bronchopneumonia.
Although there is evidence that Shipman last saw Mr Nuttall alive on the day of his death, it would appear that his wife was present when he died and no concern has ever been expressed by the family. Mr Nuttall would have been an unlikely victim of Shipman. He was living with his wife and the death occurred very soon after Shipman had arrived in Hyde. Although I cannot rule out the possibility that Shipman caused or hastened Mr Nuttall's death by administering an injection during the visit when he last saw Mr Nuttall alive, I think it is far more likely that the death was entirely natural.

name: Mary Ogden
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 36 Grosvenor Crescent, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Ogden died as the result of her cancer and not as the result of any injection which Shipman might have given.
I cannot accept Mr Ogden's account of the last few days and weeks of his wife's life. It is all a very long time ago and it may be that Mr Ogden's memory of events has faded. His account does not accord with the contemporaneous records kept by the Christie Hospital, which must be more reliable than personal memory. In my view, Mrs Alexander's recollection is far more reliable and, insofar as there is conflict between her account and that of Mr Ogden, I accept hers as accurate. I am quite satisfied that Mrs Ogden was not well enough to go out on 15th
October. Nor was she capable of the other activities which Mr Ogden recalls. I do not accept that the photograph which Mr Ogden showed was taken in October 1985. I accept that it was taken during the late spring or early summer of that year.
As I have found that Mr Ogden's memory is unreliable, I would, in any event, be unable to accept his account of the events of 16th
October. It may be that Shipman did visit on that day, possibly in the late afternoon or early evening, while he was covering for Dr Moysey or performing his out of hours rota duty. It may well be that he gave Mrs Ogden an injection. If so, this was not because Mrs Ogden was suffering from discomfort from her hiatus hernia. At this time, she was suffering severe pain as the result of the spread of her cancer into her bones. It may well be that the oral medication which had hitherto controlled her pain was no longer adequate and it may be that Shipman gave her an injection of strong opiate to relieve her pain. If he did so, I am quite satisfied that that injection did not kill her or contribute to her death. If Shipman came in the early evening of 16th
October, the injection cannot have directly contributed to the death, as she lived for about a further 24 hours. In any event, her death appears to have been precipitated by the act of turning her over and does not seem to have resulted from respiratory depression, the mechanism by which an opiate can kill.
Mrs Ogden was a brave woman who bore her final illness with great fortitude. In so far as Shipman might have played any part in her terminal care, I am quite satisfied that he caused her no harm.

name: Elsie Platt
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 309 Stockport Road, Gee Cross, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to congestive heart failure and ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
There are a number of suspicious features surrounding this death.
Mrs Platt had a medical history of ischaemic heart disease and left ventricular failure. She must have faced a greater than normal risk of dying as the result of a heart attack. Although her cardiac conditions were well controlled by medication and she was well shortly before her death, a sudden cardiac death was a real possibility. Having said that, there is a good reason to think that this was not a cardiac death. Mrs Platt's appearance did not suggest such a death. On the contrary, her appearance was entirely typical of that of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of diamorphine.
There is no direct evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Platt while she was alive on 9th
February. However, there are a number of snippets of evidence, each of which suggests that he might have done. When considered together, they are suggestive of a visit, which, if it happened, took place in the early afternoon.
Shipman was due to visit Armitages, whose premises are very close to Mrs Platt's house.
Shipman knew that Mrs Platt was unwell, as she had cancelled her surgery appointment the previous day. This would put her into his mind and give him a reason, genuine or ulterior, to pay her a visit.
Mrs Platt's radio was off, which suggests that she might have put it off when a visitor arrived and have been unable to put it on when the visitor departed.
Shipman lied on Form B, claiming that he knew that Mrs Platt had died at 4pm and that someone had seen her alive at 3.30pm. If, as I suspect, Shipman visited some time before 3.30pm and did not know whether he had been observed, he would be anxious to create the impression that Mrs Platt was alive and well after he had left. In any event, Shipman could not have made a reliable estimate of the time of death, unless he had been present. That he should pretend to do so confirms my view that he was anxious to distance himself from the death.
This is not a straightforward case. The evidence falls short of that which would be required to convict Shipman of murder. Nonetheless, when this case is considered against the background of Shipman's proven behaviour, I am persuaded that it is likely that he did visit Mrs Platt on 9th
February and that her death was due to his administration of a lethal dose of opiate, almost certainly diamorphine.

name: Sidney Arthur Smith
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 15 Garden Street, Newton, Hyde
conclusion:
There is no doubt that Mr Smith was suffering from congestive heart failure during the months before his death and that he suffered an exacerbation of his symptoms in the last few days of his life. I think that he was having difficulty in walking on 27th
August and was only a little better on the following day. However, by 30th
August, I am satisfied that he was much better and was out and about in his usual way. I do not think he was in acute cardiac failure when Shipman arrived and Mr Kenneth Smith went into the kitchen. That he should have developed acute cardiac failure in the first few minutes of the consultation is theoretically possible but so unlikely that I regard the suggestion as fanciful. I am sure that Mr Sidney Smith did not have acute cardiac failure.
I am fortified in that view by the description given by Mr Kenneth Smith of Mr Smith's appearance in death, second-hand though that description is. Mr Kenneth Smith said that his brother was sitting upright in his chair, with his head to one side as if asleep. Dr John Grenville has said that a death from acute cardiac failure is a very distressing experience. The patient is gasping for breath and usually there are frothy secretions of blood and mucus coming from the mouth. Shipman's description of the death to Mr Stephen Phelps as 'simply dying' while his back was turned for a few moments does not ring true. As Dr Grenville has said, a cardiac death is not as easy as that. Mr Sidney Smith's appearance is entirely typical of Shipman's victims following death by diamorphine injection.
I am quite satisfied that Shipman's note in the medical records is a fabrication. It does not even ring true. If Shipman had indeed found Mr Smith in acute heart failure, he would have called for an ambulance and would have administered a strong diuretic. According to the note, he did not call an ambulance and he gave no treatment at all in the 20 minutes between his arrival and the death. This is not a credible account.
This death occurred while the patient was alone with Shipman. Shipman tried to conceal the fact that he was alone with Mr Smith by suggesting on Form B that Mr Kenneth Smith was present at the death. I do not think he was. Shipman made another false entry on Form B, claiming that Mr Smith had been nursed by his brother during his 'last illness'. On the evidence, there was no 'last illness'. These entries were designed to create the false impression that Mr Sidney Smith had been ill for some time and had required nursing. Shipman was giving the impression that this was not a sudden and unexpected death.
In my view, this was typical of cases in which Shipman has killed, almost certainly caused by the administration of a lethal dose of diamorphine. Shipman took advantage of Mr Kenneth Smith's absence in the kitchen to kill his brother. I am sure that this was an unlawful killing.

name: Angela Philomena Tierney
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 26 Commercial Street, Hyde
certified_cause: left ventricular failure due to congestive heart failure
conclusion:
In view of her medical history, Mrs Tierney must have been at risk of suffering a heart attack. She was not in good health on 10th
April and, during the morning, her daughter was concerned that she was having a heart attack. It seems more likely that she was suffering from angina, as the pain seemed to subside after she took a tablet. When Mrs Shenton left, Mrs Tierney was not in pain. Nor was she in pain when Shipman visited in the early afternoon. I think I can safely conclude that Mrs Tierney did not have a heart attack on the day of her death.
Shipman claimed that Mrs Tierney had been suffering from congestive heart failure for five years, although the medical records do not confirm this and certainly do not indicate that this condition, if present, was serious or increasing in severity. Having said that, congestive heart failure can lead to left ventricular failure, the condition from which Shipman said Mrs Tierney died. It seems to me that Mrs Tierney was at some risk of developing left ventricular failure.
Having recognised that risk, there are several features that point to this having been an unnatural death. First, the death was discovered quite shortly after a visit from Shipman. No one saw Mrs Tierney alive or spoke to her after Shipman's lunchtime visit. That is a highly suspicious factor. Second, that Mrs Tierney's tablets were still out on the kitchen table when her death was discovered tends to suggest that she died during or very shortly after Shipman's visit. Third, Mrs Tierney did not call any of her daughters after the visit. This was a very close family and it would have been natural for her to telephone one of them to report on the doctor's visit. That suggests that she might have been unable to do so.
The medical records suggest that Mrs Tierney had not been closely managed as a case of severe heart failure in the weeks before her death. It is highly unlikely that Mrs Tierney showed the classic signs of left ventricular failure as described in Shipman's note for the day of death. I can attach very little weight to that entry. It is well known that, when Shipman had just killed a patient, he would often make a false or exaggerated entry to provide a plausible explanation for the death and the cause that he gave.
The fact that the door was found ajar is not strongly probative. One might say that the fact that Shipman may have left the door open is as consistent with his having paid an ordinary visit as it is with his having murdered his patient before departing. It may be that if Mrs Tierney were alive when he left, she would have asked him to close the door, but one would have expected him to close the door in any event.
