Finally, Mrs Tierney's appearance in death was inconsistent with a death due to left ventricular failure. Her appearance was, however, entirely typical of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection, almost certainly of diamorphine.
It is curious that Mrs Caldecott found the telephone line engaged for such a long time in the afternoon and found the receiver on the cradle when she arrived at the house. I do not think I should attach any significance to this. There may have been a fault on the line. Mrs Caldecott may have been mistaken in recalling the engaged tone. It is extremely unlikely that Shipman or someone else entered the house and replaced the receiver in the late afternoon.
Taking the above factors into account, it appears to me that the overwhelming likelihood is that Mrs Tierney was killed by a lethal injection administered by Shipman. I have considered whether there is a real possibility that she died a natural death. Although she was at risk of a death following a heart attack, there is no convincing evidence that she had a heart attack that day. I feel able to rule out the possibility that this was a sudden death from acute ventricular failure. Accordingly I have come to the conclusion that I can properly say that I am sure that Shipman was responsible for Mrs Tierney's death.

name: George Edgar Vizor
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 15 Thorpe Hall Grove, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of highly suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. First and most obvious, Mr Vizor was found dead very shortly after Shipman had left his flat. The time interval might have been as little as 15 minutes or it might have been as much as an hour. In either case, it would be a startling coincidence if Mr Vizor had died suddenly, so shortly after Shipman's departure. If such an event were to occur with another doctor, I would accept it as coincidence, but with Shipman such apparent coincidences occurred very frequently. I cannot accept them as coincidence and I regard the temporal association between Shipman's visit and Mr Vizor's death as a highly suspicious factor.
Mr Vizor had had strokes in the past and was showing some signs of confusion, probably due to arteriosclerosis. He was therefore at significant risk of suffering a further stroke. Strokes do not usually give rise to very sudden death, although they can do, particularly in the case of a brain stem haemorrhage. Moreover, on the morning of the day of his death, Mrs Shawcross thought that Mr Vizor looked ill and asked for the doctor to visit. She did not consider his condition to be an emergency or needing supervision. In my view, a sudden death following a stroke was a real possibility.
On Shipman's account, as set out on Form B, he last saw Mr Vizor alive one hour before his death, although the witness evidence suggests that the time interval was rather less. He implies that he found Mr Vizor suffering from a stroke, as it is hard to see how else he could have known the cause of death. His condition at that stage must have been such that Shipman felt it appropriate to leave him alone and not, for example, to summon the warden or members of his family or to admit him to hospital. Then, according to Shipman, within one hour or less, Mr Vizor suffered a massive stroke, collapsed and died. Although this is a possibility, the coincidence would be remarkable.
Shipman lied on Form B in at least one respect. He claimed that Mr Vizor's daughter had provided him with some information upon which he had based his answers in respect of the cause and mode of death. Mrs Shepley did not arrive until some time after the death had been discovered. Apart from telling Shipman that her father had been found on the floor, which he must have known for himself, it is hard to see what else she could have told him. Shipman often told this type of lie on Form B as it helped to create the impression that he had not been the only person with any knowledge of the circumstances. I am also suspicious of Shipman's claim that Mr Vizor died at 2pm. If Shipman was not present at the death he could not have known when it had occurred. There was no way in which he could have made a proper assessment. If the death were to have been natural, it might have occurred within a few seconds of Shipman's departure or only a few seconds before the body was found. By suggesting a specific time, Shipman was distancing his visit from the death.
The position in which Mr Vizor was found is consistent with him having suffered a collapse, such as might occur during a massive stroke. In the great majority of cases in which Shipman has killed his patients, the body has been found sitting in a chair, looking peaceful, as if asleep. Mr Vizor's appearance therefore suggests that his death was natural. However, evidence of appearance is never conclusive. It is possible that Shipman gave him an injection of opiate and left quite quickly. Mr Vizor might have got up to show him out and collapsed on his way back to the living room. It is also possible that Mr Vizor got to his feet as soon as the injection had been given and collapsed quite quickly. Shipman could then have left him on the floor.
My conclusion is that Shipman probably killed Mr Vizor, by injecting him with a lethal dose of opiate. However, I stop short of saying that I am sure of that conclusion because Mr Vizor's medical history makes it quite possible that he could have suffered a fatal stroke and because his position in death was consistent with a death from that cause.

name: Laura Kathleen Wagstaff
title: Mrs
conclusion:
This was a cremation case so there was no direct evidence that the cause of death was morphine poisoning. Nonetheless, the jury convicted. The salient features of this case are:
Mrs Wagstaff was in good health and her death was wholly unexpected.
Shipman made an unsolicited visit to Mrs Wagstaff. His claim that she had summoned him was a lie. He must have made his mind up in advance that he was going to call on her and kill her.
The death took place in Shipman's presence. Most doctors say that it is extremely unusual for a patient to die suddenly during a home visit.
On Shipman's account of the sudden collapse, there was no excuse not to call an ambulance and to make a proper attempt to resuscitate. No doctor would behave as he did in the circumstances he described.
His two differing accounts both contained proven lies. In particular he had not telephoned the ambulance station.
Shipman chose to say that Mrs Wagstaff had died after a coronary thrombosis. However, her medical records showed that she was not likely to suffer such a death. Shipman usually chose a cause of death which would be plausible in the light of the medical history. However, Mrs Wagstaff was not suffering from any potentially fatal condition.

name: Netta Ashcroft
title: Mrs
conclusion:
There are several highly suspicious features in the circumstances of Mrs Ashcroft's death.
The death was discovered in the late afternoon following a visit by Shipman, which probably took place in the early afternoon. There is no evidence that Mrs Ashcroft was seen alive or spoken to by anyone after Shipman's visit. That factor, in itself, gives rise to a high degree of suspicion.
There is no reliable evidence that Mrs Ashcroft ever suffered from heart disease. All investigations of her chest pain had concluded that her problems related to her digestive system. Although it would have been possible for Mrs Ashcroft to have a heart attack in March 1995, such an event was unlikely.
Mrs Ashcroft had requested a visit from Shipman on the day of her death, complaining of a sore throat. Shipman recorded that she had flu or an upper respiratory tract infection, which conditions might well entail a sore throat. However, Shipman then claims that Mrs Ashcroft made complaints that might indicate an unstable heart condition. Shipman's records can never be accepted as honest and accurate unless their contents are in some way corroborated by evidence from another source. There is no such corroboration here.
Mrs Ashcroft was found in a position consistent with having received a lethal dose of opiates and inconsistent with having suffered a heart attack.
If Mrs Ashcroft had indeed waved Shipman off after his visit as he claimed, he should and would have been very surprised indeed to find her dead only a few hours later. In those circumstances, any honest doctor would examine the body carefully to ensure that the patient was indeed dead. Shipman did not examine Mrs Ashcroft at all, apart from touching her neck. A possible explanation for this is that he already knew Mrs Ashcroft was dead. Also, in those circumstances, any honest doctor would have felt unable to certify the cause of death and would have informed the coroner of that fact. Shipman did not do so. I infer from the fact that Dr Patel was prepared to confirm the cause of death that Shipman probably gave him a false, but convincing, account of a medical history of heart disease. These factors demonstrate that Shipman was probably anxious to avoid a post-mortem examination of Mrs Ashcroft's body.
Considering these factors and accepting, as I do, Dr Grenville's opinion on this death, I am driven to the conclusion that it is overwhelmingly likely that Shipman killed Mrs Ashcroft. I am satisfied so as to be sure of this.

name: Irene Brooder
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 53 St Johns Drive, Godley, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
It appears to me that Mrs Brooder probably suffered a heart attack over the weekend of 18th
to 19th
January. She still felt unwell when she called Shipman out on the Monday morning. When he arrived at about 2.45 or 3pm, she was still alive and had been able to speak to friends until 2pm. It appears that she was alive when Shipman arrived. However, it is only Shipman who claims that she was alive when he left. She was found dead within about half an hour of his departure and no one had been able to contact her on the telephone during that time. The occurrence of a natural death, so soon after Shipman's departure, would not be impossible. However, other doctors say that such an event is very rare. If Shipman is to be believed, it was commonplace in his practice. I regard the temporal connection between Shipman's visit and Mrs Brooder's death as highly suspicious.
Shipman's record of his visit must be viewed with extreme caution. It is in itself a remarkable account, suggesting that he was prepared to leave alone a patient who had suffered a heart attack and still had arrhythmia. On Shipman's own account, as inferred from the records, he was somewhat reckless of Mrs Brooder's safety. Although the Inquiry has received a number of allegations of incompetence on Shipman's part (which have not been fully investigated as they fall outside the Terms of Reference of this Inquiry), my general impression is that he was not so incompetent as to leave alone and untreated a woman who really had suffered a heart attack and really was still suffering arrhythmia. I think it is more likely that Mrs Brooder was recovering from a fairly minor heart attack and that Shipman invented the signs of arrhythmia so as to render feasible the sudden death soon afterwards.
Although Dr Grenville recognises the possibility of a sudden cardiac death, Mrs Brooder's peaceful appearance in death was not typical of such a death. It was, however, entirely consistent with death by morphine poisoning. I think it unlikely that Mrs Brooder's death was due to a sudden cardiac episode.
Shipman's account of events as given in Form B contains a highly suspicious feature. His claim that neighbours were with Mrs Brooder after he had visited and 20 minutes before she was found dead is not consistent with Mrs Dickinson's account of the events of the afternoon and is clearly designed to suggest falsely that someone had seen Mrs Brooder alive after Shipman's visit.
Shipman claimed that he had carried out a full external examination of the body. That was not true. He gave the body only a perfunctory examination and could not have been satisfied that Mrs Brooder was dead, unless he had already known that she was.
Taking all these factors into account, I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Brooder by giving an injection, almost certainly of diamorphine, and probably under the guise of taking a blood sample.

name: Elsie Cheetham
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 17 Garden Street, Hyde
conclusion:
This is an extremely suspicious death. Mrs Cheetham was physically fit and well until the morning of her death. She telephoned the surgery at some time that day to ask for a visit. The only record of her complaint is that she had had a 'funny do'. It is possible, although in my view unlikely, that she described symptoms from which the receptionist suspected a heart attack. I say that I think this is unlikely, as the practice, which I have observed from perusing many entries in the visits book, is that the receptionists usually wrote down every symptom the patient described. I think if Mrs Cheetham had described, for example, chest pain and sweating, that would have appeared in the book. I also think it unlikely that Mrs Cocker would have told Mrs Joyce Cheetham that she had suggested calling an ambulance but that Shipman had vetoed this. I think it is likely that, in a state of shock, as she must have been, Mrs Joyce Cheetham has misunderstood what Mrs Cocker has said about that.
In my view, bearing in mind Mrs Cheetham's previous health record, it is very unlikely that she suffered a heart attack on 25th
April. I accept that it is possible that she could have done so, even though there was no history of heart disease and no indication of any risk factors. I accept that a woman of Mrs Cheetham's age could have had a heart attack completely out of the blue. However, such an event was unlikely. Mrs Cheetham's complaint to the receptionist that she had had a 'funny do' was entirely non-specific and does not sound like a heart attack. It could have been a spell of dizziness with nausea, which might also have entailed a bout of sickness, which would have accounted for the finding of vomit in the sink and on the carpet. Mrs Cheetham's appearance in death was not consistent with a sudden cardiac death. Such deaths are usually painful and the patient does not usually look as though he or she has fallen asleep.
Mrs Cheetham died during a consultation while Shipman was alone with her. That in itself is a factor which arouses suspicion. Other doctors find that such an event hardly ever occurs. If Shipman is to be believed, it was a regular occurrence for him. That day, Shipman had an opportunity to administer a lethal dose of diamorphine.
In my view, the circumstances of Mrs Cheetham's death are more consistent with diamorphine injection than with coronary thrombosis.
Shipman's explanation as to why he did not call an ambulance is unacceptable. I am quite satisfied that it is not possible for a doctor to tell that the condition of a patient suffering a heart attack is hopeless. This woman had no history of heart disease. If she had suffered a coronary thrombosis and had gone into cardiac arrest, there would be every reason to hope for a satisfactory outcome if the ambulance had been called and Mrs Cheetham had been quickly conveyed to hospital for thrombolytic drug treatment.
That Shipman failed to give any proper account of the event and gave a false account in Form B (claiming that a neighbour was present) confirms my view that this must have been an unlawful killing. Like the coroner, I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Cheetham.
My decision in this case is one of a group of four cases in which I have found that Shipman killed the occupants of two adjacent houses in Garden Street. These victims were Sidney Smith who was killed in August 1996, Thomas Cheetham who was killed in December 1996, Kenneth Smith who was killed in the same month and Elsie Cheetham who, as I have just found, was killed in April 1997. It is not my duty to speculate on Shipman's motivation in killing his patients in the absence of evidence on the point. It has been suggested that Shipman killed Mrs Cheetham because she knew too much about Shipman's involvement in the deaths of her husband and her two neighbours. That is possible. However, it does not seem likely to me that Shipman would have killed her for that reason. If he were anxious to avoid detection, as one would expect him to be, I would have thought he would have been more likely to avoid further involvement with the Cheetham family. I would have thought that to kill Mrs Cheetham would have greatly increased the risk that the next generation would become suspicious. In fact they did not, but Elsie Cheetham's death must have increased the risk that they would. I think it more likely that Shipman killed Mrs Cheetham simply because he had the desire and the opportunity to do so.

name: Mary Rose Dudley
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 33 The Woodlands, Werneth Road, Hyde
conclusion:
The evidence in this case points strongly to an unlawful killing. The death took place in Shipman's presence. Dr Grenville has said that it is extremely unusual for a patient to die suddenly in the presence of a general practitioner, unless the patient is terminally ill or the doctor has been called out in an emergency, on account of symptoms indicating a life threatening condition such as a heart attack. Mrs Dudley was not terminally ill. The circumstances in which Shipman was called out on 30th
December are not entirely clear. However, it does not appear that there was an emergency. That the death should have occurred during his visit gives rise to grave suspicion that he killed Mrs Dudley.
Mrs Dudley had some history of heart disease and was at some risk of suffering a heart attack, which could be fatal. Her state of health on the day before her death is somewhat uncertain. At the oral hearing, I found the evidence of Mrs Dudley's sons and daughters-in-law entirely credible. They said that she was well on Saturday, 29th
December and went shopping to buy a new coat. Yet Shipman's visits book suggests that he intended to visit her on that day. If the family is right, she would not even have been at home. There are several possibilities. One is that the family members are correct and Mrs Dudley was perfectly well and not at home on 29th
December. Shipman's entry might have been intended to relate to a visit on the Sunday, although it is clearly written on Saturday's page. Shipman might have tried to visit Mrs Dudley on the Saturday, as a routine check, and found her not at home. The other possibility is that the family members are mistaken about Mrs Dudley's good health on the Saturday. Possibly they took her shopping on the Friday and returned her to her flat that evening. Possibly she was unwell the next morning and called Shipman out. If so, she cannot have been seriously ill as she was not admitted to hospital and her family was not summoned to look after her. Although there is something of a mystery about whether Shipman saw Mrs Dudley on the Saturday, I am quite sure he saw her on the Sunday, the day of the death.
Thus, although it is possible that she had been unwell for a little longer than the family recalls, I am satisfied that she was not so unwell as to think of cancelling her lunch arrangement or to prevent her from making her habitual visit to her neighbour. She was not apparently unwell when she left Mr and Mrs Murphy's house only a few minutes before Shipman's arrival. Although it is theoretically possible that she could have begun to suffer the effects of a heart attack within that short time, such an event is highly unlikely. Moreover, that is not what Shipman said had happened.
If Shipman did find Mrs Dudley suffering a coronary thrombosis, he did not react appropriately. He should have summoned an ambulance. If morphine was necessary for the relief of severe pain, it should have been given gradually and the dose should have been recorded. If and when the patient went into cardiac arrest, he should have tried resuscitation. Of course, it is possible that Mrs Dudley had a heart attack and Shipman failed to do what he should have done. However, it is clear from other cases of which I have read, that Shipman knew perfectly well what to do in the event of a heart attack. That he chose not to do what any reasonable doctor would have done indicates to me that there was no heart attack and that the morphine or, more likely, diamorphine was given not for the relief of pain but with intent to kill.
Mrs Dudley's appearance in death was not typical of a patient who had just suffered a coronary thrombosis. It was, however, entirely typical of many of Shipman's victims who had been given a lethal injection of opiate.
From this evidence, I am driven, without hesitation, to the sure conclusion that Shipman killed Mrs Dudley.

name: William Earnshaw
title: Mr
place_of_death: his daughter's house, 58 Ferney Lee Road, Todmorden
conclusion:
It is clear on the evidence that Mr Earnshaw had been approaching death over a period of some days and had been well cared for by his family. His death was not sudden or unexpected. Although Dr Grenville considers that Shipman's completion of the MCCD was inadequate and although the family is puzzled by the reference to bronchitis, the certificate itself does not give rise to any suspicion that Shipman was responsible for the death.
When Shipman visited in Dr Dacre's stead, his reported conduct towards Mr Earnshaw and Mrs Shaw was unprofessional and inhumane. However, there is no direct evidence that he gave Mr Earnshaw an injection. There is evidence that he had the opportunity to do so. We do not know whether he did or, if he did, what the drug was or how much was given. It is possible that Shipman injected Mr Earnshaw with opiate or some sort of sedative drug. A small dose of either would have been appropriate, as Mr Shaw was unsettled and distressed. Mrs Shaw says that her father was no longer restless or delirious after Shipman's visit. If Shipman considered it appropriate to administer any drug, he should have told Mrs Shaw what he was going to do and why.
Mrs Earnshaw is not now sure whether Shipman's visit occurred on the day of the death or on the preceding day. I have the impression that the death occurred on the day of the visit but not very shortly after it. If so, it is unlikely that Shipman caused or hastened Mr Earnshaw's death. If Shipman had given a lethal injection of opiate, Mr Earnshaw would have died within an hour. If, as I think likely, he survived for more than an hour after Shipman's visit, he had not been killed directly by an injection of opiate but his death might have been slightly hastened by the effect of an injection of an appropriate amount of opiate, given for perfectly proper reasons.
If Mr Earnshaw lived until the following day, his death was not caused or contributed to be an injection of opiate. However, it is possible that Shipman had contributed to Mr Earnshaw's death by giving him an excessive dose of some sort of sedative drug, such as Largactil, which could have had the effect of sending him into a very deep sleep for many hours. During such a sleep, Mr Earnshaw would have been vulnerable to bronchopneumonia and his death might have been hastened on that account. However, these are only possibilities and it is far more likely, on the evidence available, that any drug which Shipman gave served only to relieve Mr Earnshaw's distress.
My conclusion is that I think it is unlikely that Shipman caused or even accelerated Mr Earnshaw's death. It is understandable that members of his family have been distressed, as they have been, by the discovery that Shipman is a serial killer and used opiate drugs to kill. Their concerns have been heightened by the recollection of his callous attitude during the visit. Their distress and worry have been increased by the attention of the press. Although I cannot absolutely rule out the possibility that Shipman accelerated Mr Earnshaw's death, I can say that I think it is unlikely that he did and, if he did, it could only have been by a very short period. I hope that this decision will help to set the family's minds at rest.

name: Phyllis Farrell
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 52 King George Road, Hyde
conclusion: Unlike Professor Baker, the Inquiry has had the benefit of witness evidence, which shows that this death must have been due to natural causes. Whether the cause of death was in truth heart attack, as Shipman stated, or some other natural cause, we shall never know. However, the family has never expressed any concern about this death and I am sure their confidence was entirely justified.

name: Rose Garlick
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 31 Taylor Gardens, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of highly suspicious features in this case. The first and most obvious is that Mrs Garlick was found dead within a very short time of Shipman's departure. Indeed, if Shipman's note of the time of his visit is correct at 10.30 am, and it is known that the ambulance was called at 10.54am, the time span is very short indeed. This is a highly suspicious factor.
Mrs Garlick was feeling lethargic in the days leading up to her death and had back and hip pain during the night of 21st March. However, she had a conversation with a neighbour between 8am and 9am and, shortly afterwards, with her daughter. Neither was concerned by her condition. The quite detailed description of her condition, which Mrs Garlick gave to her daughter, did not include any reference to chest pain or sickness and sounds more like a problem of pain in the hips and back than a heart attack. In my view, it is more likely that Mrs Garlick was suffering from back and hip pain of musculo-skeletal origin than that she had recently had a heart attack. In any event, a post-mortem examination was necessary to establish the true cause of death.
On Shipman's account, Mrs Garlick described symptoms indicative of a heart attack and he diagnosed her as having suffered a heart attack that morning. However, experience has taught me that Shipman's records relating to a patient's death must always be treated with suspicion. These are typical of those frequently made to explain and conceal a killing. The note describes a condition much worse than that perceived by Mrs Doyle and Mrs Davidson and paints a picture of a woman quite seriously ill and requiring medical attention, but refusing the advice offered. This is a common feature of cases in which Shipman has killed. When the patient is found dead a while later, Shipman has his explanation ready. In this case, in an attempt to add weight to this account, Shipman offered to show Mrs Davidson the handwritten note made following his earlier visit. This is an odd thing to do, unless he felt the need to justify his actions. Also, Shipman's claim that back pain is a classic sign of a heart attack, which it is not, sounds like an attempt to bolster his diagnosis.
Shipman's claim that Mrs Garlick had refused hospital admission is particularly implausible in this case. If an elderly patient who had just suffered a heart attack were refusing admission to hospital, the doctor would suggest speaking to a relative there and then. He would not leave him or her unattended even for an hour. That Shipman was a personal friend of Mrs Davidson makes his failure to suggest an immediate discussion about the future quite incredible. Even if Shipman had left Mrs Garlick alone, as he claims, I would have expected her to telephone her daughter as soon as he had gone. The fact that she did not points to an inability to do so, probably because she was already dead.
Shipman's false entries on Form B appear to me to be designed to create the impression that Mrs Garlick was still alive when she was found by Mrs Wright, when in truth she was not.
Shipman recorded that he intended to revisit at noon. This would have been the opportunity for him to 'discover' that Mrs Garlick had died, had Mrs Wright not intervened.
The fact that Mrs Garlick was found to have vomited is consistent with the administration of a high dose of morphine or diamorphine, as it is also consistent with death following a heart attack. Mrs Garlick's position lying on the bed is more consistent with death by opiate overdose than with death by heart attack.
Overall, this death bears many of the typical hallmarks of cases in which Shipman killed. I am satisfied so as to be sure that Shipman killed Mrs Garlick.

name: Josephine Hall
title: Mrs
conclusion:
This case arouses suspicion because Mrs Hall died soon after a visit by Shipman. No one saw her alive or spoke to her after his departure. Having said that, Mrs Hall did have a medical history of high blood pressure and must therefore have been at some increased risk of suffering a stroke.
Shipman's note of his first visit on the day of the death provides a plausible account of a developing stroke. Mrs Hall had complained to her daughter of a headache. Dr Aneez Esmail, medical advisor to the Inquiry, has advised that a headache is not usually a sign of a cerebrovascular accident although it can be an indication of a ruptured aneurysm. However, the other symptoms, weakness, tingling and poor gait, are typical signs of a stroke. Experience has shown that Shipman frequently fabricated medical records in order to create a plausible cause of a sudden death. Accordingly, all notes relating to a death must be viewed with suspicion. Shipman would usually select a cause of death that would be feasible in the light of the past medical history. Here, Mrs Hall's high blood pressure made a death by cerebrovascular accident a real possibility.
There are a number of aspects of this record which make me suspect that it is false. First, I think it highly likely that if Mrs Hall had developed weakness on one side or tingling in the arm, she would have telephoned her daughter to tell her. Second, I think it most unlikely that she would have stopped taking her tablets without even mentioning this to her daughter. Third, in the light of Dr Esmail's opinion on this case, I consider that the course of action Shipman claims to have adopted would have been so obviously wrong as to be very unlikely. As Dr Esmail says, no doctor would leave a patient alone if he suspected that he or she might be having a stroke. The stroke could develop over a few hours and the patient could become unconscious. If possible, Shipman should have made arrangements for someone to sit with Mrs Hall. If this was not possible, he should have arranged for the district nurse to call or, at the very least, he should have said he would call back later that day. In this case, it is highly likely that Mrs Allen or one of the granddaughters would have come to sit with her. In any event, it is inconceivable that Mrs Hall would not have telephoned either her daughter or one of her granddaughters immediately after the visit if Shipman had said that she needed either hospital admission or a domiciliary visit from a consultant. The reason she did not do so must be because she was already dead. On close examination, this entry in the medical records and the circumstances surrounding the visit do not make sense. In my view, the entry is probably a fabrication designed to provide an explanation for Mrs Hall's sudden death from morphine poisoning.
The position of Mrs Hall's arm half in and half out of the cardigan sleeve, and the discolouration of her arm observed later, are not conclusive evidence that Shipman gave Mrs Hall an injection although they lend some support to that suggestion.
Shipman's estimate of the time of death found in the second entry for the day is something of a mystery. There is no direct evidence of the time of Shipman's visit. Generally, Shipman would seek to suggest a time of death well after his departure from the house. He would, I believe, take this precaution in case someone had noticed the time of his visit. However, it would seem likely that Mrs Cheetham noticed the barking of Mrs Hall's dog soon after Shipman's departure. That would indicate that the visit and the death had occurred in the mid-afternoon. It is strange that Shipman should suggest that the death had occurred at 2pm if that were before the time of his visit. It is possible that he visited her quite early, soon after noon, and that the dog was very patient. Whatever the explanation for Shipman's quite elaborate and wholly unscientific attempt to suggest a time of death, it makes no difference to my overall view of this case.
In all the circumstances, I am driven to the conclusion that Mrs Hall's death was not a natural one. I am sure that Shipman killed her.

name: Alice Mary Jones
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 67 Garden Street, Hyde
conclusion:
There are several suspicious features surrounding this death. The first and most obvious is that the death was discovered very shortly after Shipman had visited. Mrs Jones was not obviously unwell when Mrs Allen spoke to her on the telephone that morning, yet she was found dead within a short time after Shipman's visit. It would be a coincidence if Mrs Jones died a natural death shortly after his departure. 'Coincidences' of this kind seemed to occur frequently in Shipman's professional life. My view is that they were not coincidences at all. The temporal connection between Shipman's visit and Mrs Jones' death gives rise to a high degree of suspicion that Mrs Jones was dead when Shipman left her. The fact that the front door was not locked when Mrs Allen arrived confirms my suspicions. It appears to me that the probable reason for the unlocked door was that Mrs Jones was unable to see Shipman out and lock it after him.
Little is known about Mrs Jones' medical history. Mrs Allen was unaware that her sister-in-law was suffering any illness in the days leading up to her death. She says that had Mrs Jones been unwell, she would have mentioned her illness. However, it does appear that Shipman visited Mrs Jones twice in the week before her death and I infer that Mrs Jones must have had some medical problem, which Mrs Allen has forgotten about. Having said that, I do not think this could have been a serious or life-threatening illness. If it had been, I think Mrs Allen would have remembered it. Shipman said on Form B that he had attended Mrs Jones for three days during her last illness. As he claimed that she died of cerebrovascular accident, he seems to be suggesting a stroke, which developed over a period of three days. However, that is not consistent with either Mrs Allen's recollection or Shipman's assertion that no one had nursed Mrs Jones during her last illness. It is possible that Mrs Jones could have had one stroke three days before her death and another on the day of the death, but I think Mrs Allen would have remembered if Mrs Jones had had a stroke a few days before her death. In any event, if she had had a stroke, which did not warrant admission to hospital or nursing care at home, some one would have had to look after her and Mrs Allen would have been aware of the situation. I conclude that the picture Shipman sought to present does not ring true and that the likelihood is that Mrs Jones had a minor illness, which Shipman turned into an opportunity to kill her. He then invented the history of stroke to explain the death.
Mrs Jones' position and appearance after death was not typical of that usually seen following a sudden death from cerebrovascular accident, as Dr John Grenville has explained in his generic evidence. However, her position was typical of that of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by a lethal intravenous injection of opiate. That she should have had a torch in one hand and a magnifying glass in the other is not typical of a Shipman killing. However, it is hard to imagine that Mrs Jones could have had a sudden fatal stroke and yet have kept her torch and magnifying glass in her hands. It seems to me that the most likely explanation for these unusual features is that Shipman put these items in position when Mrs Jones had had her injection and was lapsing into unconsciousness.
This case carries Shipman's hallmark. Despite the loss of the medical records, I feel able to say that I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Jones, almost certainly by giving a lethal injection of strong opiate.

name: Alice Kennedy
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 34 Ogden Court, Frank Street, Hyde
conclusion:
Mrs Kennedy's death was discovered soon after Shipman had visited. No one saw her alive or spoke to her after Shipman had left. That in itself is a cause for suspicion. Mrs Kennedy was very elderly and it must be accepted that old people can and do die sudden and unexpected deaths. But that she should do so in the short window of time after Shipman left and before Mrs Higgins returned would be something of a coincidence.
If Mrs Kennedy had been taken ill after Shipman's departure, she could very easily have summoned the warden by pulling on her alarm cord. That she did not do this indicates to me that she was probably not aware of any illness. This supports the suggestion that Shipman was with her as she died.
Often, in cases where Shipman killed a patient, it is found that he has fabricated, in the medical records, a florid account of an illness the signs of which were observed by him shortly before the death. Here, he has not done so. He recorded minor signs of congestive heart failure, namely swollen ankles without raised jugular venous pressure. He recorded a complaint of
'odd chest pain'
radiating into the arm at times, which sounds as if it might be a sign of some form of heart trouble. Yet, at the end of the visit, he appears to have thought so little of these signs and symptoms that he did not plan to review Mrs Kennedy for three months. I find the low key nature of this note puzzling.
Less puzzling is Shipman's rather strange suggestion to Mrs Higgins that her mother was not entirely well and an eye should be kept on her, but that there was no need to go round straight away. This, when considered in conjunction with the contents of Form B, is highly suspicious. Where Shipman has killed, he frequently sought to increase the time interval between his visit and the time of discovery of the death, so that he could estimate the time of death at a significant period after his visit. Here, he suggests that the death occurred at 5.30pm and claims that he had seen Mrs Kennedy alive three hours earlier. He was suggesting that his visit took place at about 2.30pm. He might well have been seen arriving or leaving the premises and it would be dangerous to be too inaccurate on Form B about the time of his visit. If he had killed Mrs Kennedy at some time around 3pm, shortly before he telephoned Mrs Higgins, he would not wish the body to be found too quickly as someone might notice that the death had been discovered only just after his departure. I suspect that that is why he made the rather strange telephone call to Mrs Higgins, in which he suggested that there was no need for her to hurry round. In the event, she went to her mother's home at about 5.15pm and Shipman did not attend until 6.30pm. He took advantage of the delay by suggesting a time of death which was a little later than the time of discovery of the body. In that way he made it look as though the death had occurred well after his departure.
Shipman certified old age as the cause of death, although Mrs Higgins' evidence is that her mother was well that day and his own handwritten note suggests that he thought that Mrs Kennedy was sufficiently well that she did not need to be reviewed by him for three months. In my view, Shipman put old age on the MCCD because the medical history did not reveal any other plausible explanation for the death. He certified congestive heart failure as contributing to the death, even though there was no elevation in the jugular venous pressure when he saw her that afternoon. He recorded an odd chest pain radiating to the left side. It seems there that he might have had in mind a possible heart attack, but he did not include any reference to that possibility on the MCCD. The inclusion of congestive heart failure on the MCCD simply does not make sense and gives me the impression that either Shipman could not, or could not be bothered to, think of anything plausible to put on the certificate.
On the basis of his own notes, this was a sudden death of which the cause was unknown. Shipman should not have signed the MCCD and the case should have been referred to the coroner. I have accepted that it is theoretically possible that Mrs Kennedy died a sudden and natural death that afternoon. But if she did and if Shipman was not involved, it is hard to see why he did not refer the case to the coroner.
These factors all point to the conclusion that Shipman called at Mrs Kennedy's house on the afternoon of 9th
January 1995 and administered a lethal injection of diamorphine. I believe that he decided to go to her flat with the express purpose of killing her. The documents reveal no request for a visit nor any legitimate reason why he would have wished to visit her. Indeed, on looking back to the previous visit on 8th
November 1994, which appears in the record as a wholly improbable discussion about rehousing, I feel bound to suspect that he may well have intended to kill her on that occasion but for some reason his plan was foiled. In any event, I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Kennedy.

name: Dorothy Long
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 10 Woodfield Avenue, Hyde
conclusion:
In my view, it is highly likely that Shipman killed Mrs Long on the afternoon of Friday, 13th
March.
Mrs Long showed no sign of illness in the days and weeks before she died. Her death was sudden and quite unexpected by all who knew her. Although she had a history of raised blood pressure, this was well controlled by medication. If this was a natural death, Shipman could not possibly have known its cause. There was no proper basis on which he could have concluded that it was due to a cerebrovascular accident. He should have referred the case to the coroner, with a view to a post-mortem examination.
There is no direct evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Long on 13th
, 14th
or 15th
March 1998. However, there is evidence from which I can infer that he probably did. He certainly had the time to do so but that is not significantly probative. He made an entry in the medical records in the late afternoon of 13th
March, for which the only rational explanation I can think of is that he knew that Mrs Long was dead and wished to create a false entry in her records to give the impression that he had seen her on 5th
March. Shipman's usual motive in claiming to have seen a deceased patient alive within 14 days before the death was to avoid contact with the coroner. This fabricated entry and the assumed wish to avoid contact with the coroner is not of itself probative of guilt, as Shipman sometimes told such lies in cases where he had not killed the patient. I think sometimes he wished to avoid the trouble of a referral and possibly wished to spare the deceased's family the additional distress. However, Shipman also told this type of lie in many cases where he had killed his patient and this lie is certainly consistent with a guilty desire to avoid a referral to the coroner.
Quite apart from Shipman's false claim that he had seen Mrs Long alive on 5th
March, his entries on Form B are a tissue of lies. First, Shipman claimed that he knew the time of Mrs Long's death. If this was a natural death and the body was found on Sunday morning, there is no way in which Shipman could have known or deduced that Mrs Long died at 8pm on Friday, 13th
March. In my view, he must have decided to put that time because it suited him for some reason. In other cases where he has done this, and there are many of them, I have almost always concluded that he has picked a time so as to create the impression that the patient died a considerable time after his own visit. If Shipman visited Mrs Long on the Friday afternoon, he would not know whether or not he had been observed. It would help him to avoid any suspicion if he could establish that the death occurred some hours later.
Shipman also falsely claimed that he had been treating Mrs Long in connection with her last illness for nine days. Even on the face of the false record he himself made, this can be seen to be untrue. On 5th
March, eight days before the death, Shipman does not claim that Mrs Long had any illness, only that he advised her to keep taking her tablets.
The most blatant and obvious lie appears where Shipman stated on Form B that the paramedics were present at the moment of death. This is bizarre, as the body was not found for almost two days after the death, on Shipman's own assessment of the time of death. This demonstrates Shipman's apparent confidence that no one would check the truth, or even consistency, of his answers. Shipman's claim that the paramedics and neighbours had provided information from which he could diagnose the cause of death or describe its mode and duration is plainly false.
A further cause for suspicion that Shipman killed Mrs Long arises from the position of her dentures. I have come across a number of cases in which a deceased patient has been found with dentures removed and one case where they had disappeared altogether. I do not fully understand the significance of this, although Dr Grenville may well have been right when he suggested that Shipman might have had a bad experience, when a patient's dentures became dislodged and possibly stuck in the throat as the patient became unconscious. Dr Grenville suggested that Shipman might have thought it prudent to remove dentures to avoid such an event. Whether or not that is right, I do think that where a patient is found dead without his or her dentures, that amounts to evidence that Shipman has been there.
As I have said, I think it is highly likely that Shipman killed Mrs Long. I stop short of saying that I am sure, because of two factors. It is possible that Ms Monte was right when she said that she saw Mrs Long alive on Saturday, 14th
March. Shipman would have been far less likely to visit her on a Saturday afternoon than a Friday. Second, I acknowledge that Mrs Long's position in death was not typical of that of most of Shipman's victims. Her position gives rise to a possibility that her death was natural. That said, I think it far more likely that Shipman killed her.

name: Elizabeth Ellen Mellor
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 27 Sidley Place, Hyde
conclusion:
There can be no doubt in this case that Shipman unlawfully killed Mrs Mellor. The finding of morphine in the body tissues is powerful evidence. There is no apparent explanation for it within the medical records. Shipman admitted that he had visited Mrs Mellor shortly before her death, but described her state of health in such terms as would provide no explanation for the administration of morphine. The manner of her death was entirely typical of many cases in which Shipman killed by means of lethal injection, probably administered in the form of diamorphine, to which he had ready access. I believe he must have killed her on his second visit that day.
The medical records are also of interest. On the day of the death, it appears that Shipman took blood samples. I have little doubt that he used a supposed need to take a blood sample as an excuse to introduce a needle into one of Mrs Mellor's veins to inject her with diamorphine. I note also that, in the computerised records, he suggested that Mrs Mellor had complained of transient ischaemic attacks. There is no reference to these in the handwritten records. I have little doubt that Shipman fabricated this computerised entry in order to create the impression that Mrs Mellor was at increased risk of suffering a stroke.

name: Violet Nicholls
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
Mrs Nicholls had been very confused for several months before her death. Her condition deteriorated in the days leading up to her death. Her death was neither sudden nor unexpected. The picture revealed by the daily diary would justify giving the cause of death as senility, which at the time was used interchangeably with old age.
Apart from Shipman's entry on the MCCD counterfoil, there is no evidence that Shipman saw Mrs Nicholls on the day of her death. It is possible that he saw her on 12th
July even though neither his visits book nor the daily diary has recorded the visit. I think it is more likely that he made an error when completing the MCCD. He was often careless in completing death and cremation certificates.
If Shipman did see Mrs Nicholls on the day of her death, it is possible that he visited her shortly before she died and gave her an excessive dose of an opiate which hastened her death. I think that this is very unlikely because the Charnley House staff usually recorded a doctor's visits and, also, Shipman usually made his visits between late morning and mid-afternoon. A lethal injection of an opiate given during that time would have resulted in death well before 7pm.
There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman over-sedated Mrs Nicholls in the days before her death. She appears to have been conscious until not long before her death. Also, there is no reference to injections in the daily diary.
I conclude that it is very likely that Mrs Nicholls died a natural death.

name: Margaret Ousey
title: Miss
place_of_death: her home, 22 Well Meadow, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Miss Ousey died a natural death.
There is compelling evidence that Miss Ousey was critically ill in the days leading up to her death and that her condition had not improved after two courses of antibiotics. The records indicate that the doctor who attended on 2nd
October, who was Shipman, gave an injection of amoxicillin. This would not have caused Miss Ousey's death and would have been appropriate treatment for her very serious infection.
Shipman's usual method of killing his patients was to give a lethal injection of the opiate, diamorphine. In Miss Ousey's case, there could have been no justification for giving any opiate, as Miss Ousey was not in pain. It is extremely unlikely that Shipman would have given an inappropriate drug in the presence of a district nurse. In any event, Miss Ousey lived for about 12 hours after the injection. As Dr Grenville has explained in his generic evidence, if a lethal dose of opiate is given, death will occur within an hour.
It is understandable that Mr Ousey should feel concern about the circumstances of his daughter's death, bearing in mind the publicity surrounding Shipman's activities. I hope that this investigation and decision will put his mind completely at rest.

name: Alice Prestwich
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 12 Ogden Court, Frank Street, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
There are highly suspicious features surrounding this death.
First, the death occurred in Shipman's presence, supposedly of a heart attack. Mrs Prestwich had asked for a visit by Shipman because she had pains in her knees, not because she was suffering from anything that sounded like a cardiac problem. Although it is not possible, in the absence of the medical records, to say with certainty that Mrs Prestwich did not have any heart disease, her son was not aware of any. Moreover, Mrs Simpson's records do not suggest any recent heart problems. They suggest an underlying problem connected with eyes, an attack of vertigo in early September, and a gastric upset in late September. During October, Mrs Prestwich had been well. That Mrs Prestwich should suffer a heart attack at the very moment when Shipman came to visit her on account of her knees is stretching credibility beyond its limits. Other doctors find that patients do not die suddenly in their presence. With Shipman, this seemed to happen frequently.
According to the information supplied by Shipman in Form B, he attended Mrs Prestwich for the last half hour of her life. If she did suffer a coronary thrombosis, one would have expected him to try to revive her and to have summoned assistance, first by pulling the emergency cord, and then by asking someone to call an ambulance. That none of these steps was taken suggests that Mrs Prestwich did not, in fact, suffer a fatal coronary thrombosis.
Mrs Prestwich was found seated in her chair, looking peaceful. Her appearance in death was not consistent with the appearance of one who had died of coronary thrombosis. Her appearance was, however, entirely typical of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of diamorphine.
This death bears many of the hallmarks of cases in which Shipman killed. I am quite sure that Shipman was responsible for Mrs Prestwich's death. There is every reason to think that Shipman killed her in his usual way, by giving a lethal injection of diamorphine.

name: Betty Royston
title: Mrs
conclusion:
There are a number of suspicious circumstances surrounding this case.
Shipman was asked to visit Mrs Royston because her son was concerned about her ability to look after herself. He was not called because she had suddenly developed acute symptoms. Although she had suffered a stroke in 1992 and must have been at some risk of another, it would be a considerable coincidence had she suddenly developed symptoms of a further stroke during or shortly before Shipman's visit.
I am satisfied that Shipman visited Mrs Royston between 1pm and 4pm on 4th
February. There is no evidence that anyone saw her alive or spoke to her after that time. In a building such as Ogden Court, it is highly likely that someone would have seen her if she had set foot outside her front door. It is also highly likely that that person would have mentioned this sighting to Mrs Simpson on learning of Mrs Royston's death. Although it is not possible to say with certainty that no one saw her alive or spoke to her after Shipman's visit, it is highly unlikely that anyone did. I am confident that Shipman's claim that a neighbour saw her at 7pm was a deliberate lie. He had no source of information that would not have also been available to Mrs Simpson. I am also satisfied that he told that lie so as to give the impression that he was not the last person to see Mrs Royston alive. In my view, he was the last person to see her alive.
Shipman telephoned Mr Royston after his visit. He did not tell him that his mother had shown clinical signs of having suffered a stroke. It is virtually inconceivable that a competent doctor would have failed to mention his findings and his diagnosis to a relative to whom he was speaking, and that he would have left a patient in that condition unattended. It appears to me that Shipman's note of his consultation on 4th
February was a fabrication, designed to lend plausibility to the cause of death that he was later to certify.
Mrs Royston's spectacles and cardigan had been removed and placed on the sofa, although she usually wore both. She might well have removed both before having a blood sample taken, but, if she had been alive for long after that process, one would have expected her to roll down her sleeve and put her cardigan and spectacles back on. This is a suspicious factor.
Mr Royston thought that the body had been laid out tidily on the floor. People do not usually die 'tidily' in a natural death. However, if Shipman killed her, he could easily have straightened Mrs Royston's body.
It does not appear that Mrs Royston attempted to use the intercom or one of the emergency cords. Dr Grenville says that patients who suffer even a massive stroke of the kind that can kill suddenly usually have enough time to make some effort to summon help. If Mrs Royston died as the result of a lethal injection, she would not have attempted to summon help.
So far, everything points to an unlawful killing. The only piece of evidence that might cast doubt on the conclusion that Shipman had killed Mrs Royston is that patches of vomit were observed in the room where she was found. As Dr Grenville has said, patients who are suffering a stroke or heart attack often vomit. However, Dr Grenville has also explained (in giving evidence in the case of Mrs Mary Coutts) that morphine or diamorphine can cause a patient to be sick. The presence of vomit on the body or close to it is not inconsistent with death by lethal injection of diamorphine, Shipman's known method of killing. Here, the vomit was found not far from the body. As the body was found on the floor and appeared to have been 'arranged', I cannot deduce where Mrs Royston was when she was injected. It follows that, although the position of the vomit is slightly puzzling, I do not think it raises any real doubt in my mind that this was an unlawful killing. It is possible that the explanation is that part of the injection entered Mrs Royston's body subcutaneously and took longer to act than it would have done if all the injection had gone straight into a vein. In that event, she might have moved about the room and been sick before collapsing to the floor, where Shipman arranged her body.
The evidence pointing to Shipman's involvement in this death is compelling. My conclusion is that Shipman killed Mrs Royston by giving an injection of strong opiate during the afternoon of 4th
February 1997. I feel able to say that I am sure of that conclusion.

name: Kenneth Ernest Smith
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 15 Garden Street, Newton, Hyde
conclusion:
Mr Smith was in normal health between Shipman's visit on 9th
December and the day of his death. He appeared well when Mrs Elsie Cheetham saw him only a few hours before his death.
The death was discovered a short time after Shipman had visited on 17th
December. No one saw Mr Smith alive or spoke to him after Shipman's departure. Although Shipman admitted on the MCCD and Form B that he had visited on the day of Mr Smith's death, he did not tell the family.
It appears to me highly unlikely that Mr Smith died from congestive heart failure. There is no history of any heart disease in his medical records until 9th
December 1996, eight days before his death. The records then suggest quite a severe state of heart failure of which the family was unaware. The entry in the records for that day does not ring true, for the reasons I have outlined above. Additionally, it appears that there never was a prescription for Lasix. I believe this record was a fabrication.
In my view, the record for the day of the death was also fabricated. If Mr Smith was as ill as the record suggests, it is unlikely that he would have eaten his usual lunch. If Mr Smith was as ill as Shipman suggested and was unwilling to go to hospital, Shipman would not have left him in that condition without making some provision for his care. Faced with the situation Shipman claimed existed, the doctor would have sought permission to contact a relative who might persuade the patient to change his mind or at least come round to care for him. Shipman did none of those things but simply walked away, claiming to have decided that he would arrange a domiciliary visit. This record does not ring true.
Shipman's claim on the MCCD that Mr Smith had ischaemic heart disease for 12 to 18 months before his death is not borne out by the records. Also, the claim that he attended Mr Smith for six to nine months during his 'last illness' is false. As Mr Smith is supposed to have died from heart failure, Shipman is implying that the last illness was at least connected with the heart. Yet there was no history of heart disease.
I have said that I believe the medical record entry for 9th
December was fabricated. It was undoubtedly made on 9th
December. The inference I am bound to draw is that Shipman was laying the ground for an opportunity to kill Mr Smith and to pass it off as death from heart failure. The entry for the day of the death and the false entries on the MCCD and in Form B were designed to provide support for the claimed cause of death.
There is no basis for any suggestion that Mr Smith might have died a sudden death from some cause other than heart failure. Nothing in his medical records suggests that he was at an increased risk of any of the conditions that might lead to sudden death.
Mr Smith's appearance in death and the circumstances surrounding it were not typical of death from heart failure and were entirely typical of a death caused by Shipman by the administration of diamorphine.
I am sure that Shipman killed Mr Smith, almost certainly by his usual method of injecting diamorphine. Mr Smith had survived his brother by less than four months.

name: Lily Newby Taylor
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 83 Brabyns Road, Hyde
conclusion:
The evidence in this case points strongly towards the conclusion that Shipman killed Mrs Taylor.
It must be recognised that a sudden death is always a possibility for someone of Mrs Taylor's age. However, Mrs Taylor was in remarkably good health for her age. She had not had occasion to consult Shipman for six months before her death. Even then, it was only for sleeping tablets. During recent months, she had coped with her severely disabled husband. The night before her death, she had entertained friends and, although she had seemed tired, she was in good spirits. On the morning of the day of her death, Mrs Friday found her to be her usual self. Shipman arrived at about lunchtime. Mrs Taylor was never seen alive again. Those facts alone strongly suggest that Shipman killed Mrs Taylor.
There are other factors that point to the same conclusion.
Shipman lied on Form B. He said that a neighbour had seen Mrs Taylor alive after he had left. The purpose of that lie is obvious. He also sought to suggest that the death had taken place at 3.30pm which was actually the approximate time at which the body was found. If Mrs Taylor died naturally in Shipman's absence, he could not possibly have known the time of her death. Yet, by suggesting a time, he was able to create the impression that her death took place a substantial time after his visit.
Shipman concealed from Professor Taylor that he had seen Mrs Taylor on the morning of her death. He appears to have passed the death off to Professor Taylor as being due to a heart attack. No doubt, had Professor Taylor learned that Shipman had seen his mother so short a time before the death, he would have wished to ask questions about his mother's state of health at that time.
Shipman made no attempt to explain the death in Mrs Taylor's medical records. Indeed, he made no record at all in Mr or Mrs Taylor's notes until after he had been recalled to the house following discovery of the death. When he did make an entry, it offered no explanation for the death. If asked about this death, by another doctor or the medical referee, he would have found it extremely difficult to explain. The cause of death, 'old age', was obviously inappropriate for a woman who had, that morning, been walking about and doing her chores. The reference to Parkinsonism as a contributory cause of death is grossly misleading as, even assuming the diagnosis was correct, the condition was so mild as to make no possible contribution to the death. There was no identifiable last illness and no available explanation for this death. The case should certainly have been referred to the coroner. Shipman seems to have conveyed the impression to Professor Taylor that he had done him a good turn by avoiding a referral. I am quite sure that Shipman must have been very anxious to avoid the possibility of referral.
Taking all these factors together, I am left in no doubt that Shipman killed Mrs Taylor.

name: Frederick Vickers
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 41 Bennett Street, Hyde
conclusion:
Despite the absence of any direct evidence concerning the day of Mr Vickers' death, it does seem clear that he was seriously ill with heart disease. The chest problems which Mrs Grace remembers may well have been respiratory problems secondary to his heart disease. It does not appear that his death was unexpected when it came. His long-standing heart condition no doubt left him at increased risk of an acute cardiac death, which is what Shipman certified as having been the primary cause of his death.
Unfortunately, however, the absence of direct evidence makes it impossible to say with confidence whether Shipman did or did not play any sinister part in Mr Vickers' death. The fact that he certified that he saw Mr Vickers alive on the day of his death and saw the body after death gives rise to a degree of suspicion, as so many of Shipman's victims died during a routine visit. That Mr Vickers was known to be in poor health does not mean that Shipman would not have killed him. Shipman killed many patients who were in poor health and some who were close to death.
There are several possibilities. It is quite possible that Shipman was called out to see Mr Vickers because he was suffering from an acute cardiac episode, that Mr Vickers had died by the time Shipman arrived and that Shipman decided to certify the cause of death, saying that he had seen Mr Vickers alive that day so as to avoid the perceived inconvenience of referring the death to the coroner. Another possibility is that Shipman was called out in the morning because Mr Vickers had deteriorated and his wife had become concerned; or perhaps he was in discomfort or distress and Shipman came out to give him some medication which would make him more comfortable. Shipman might then have left and Mr Vickers might have died some time later. Shipman could have returned to confirm the death and certify the cause. Those circumstances might or might not give rise to suspicion that Shipman had given Mr Vickers something which had hastened his death. Yet another possibility is that Shipman was called out to see Mr Vickers, on account of some sort of deterioration in his health, and that Mr Vickers died in his presence. In those circumstances, the death would have to be regarded as suspicious.
Unfortunately these issues cannot be resolved and I regret that I am unable to reach a decision. I cannot say whether Shipman did or did not kill Mr Vickers, but I am suspicious that he did.

name: Mary Emma Andrew
title: Miss
place_of_death: her home, 8 Mona Street, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to congestive heart failure, in turn caused by ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
Miss Andrew had suffered from heart disease for some time before her death and she must have been at risk of a cardiac death. She was suffering from pain in the back during the evening of the previous day and it was severe enough for her to describe it as
'very painful'
when she telephoned the surgery. However, all the available evidence suggests that she was not seriously ill when Shipman called on her. She was not in obvious pain and she did not mention pain to either of her friends. It appears to me possible, but unlikely, that Miss Andrew was suffering from angina or might have had a coronary thrombosis.
Shipman's account of his consultation with Miss Andrew cannot be taken at face value, as he is known to have made false records in many cases in order to conceal his unlawful activities. His note, if true, might support the assertion that Miss Andrew had had a heart attack. However, if Miss Andrew had displayed the signs described, one would have expected Shipman to call an ambulance, as she needed hospital treatment. Instead, he claims to have administered 10mg of morphine. He does not say that Miss Andrew was in severe pain. Having given the morphine, Shipman claims to have left the house and, within a very short time, Miss Andrew was dead. In my view, the claimed administration of 10mg of morphine is highly suspicious. Shipman usually carried diamorphine, not morphine. Moreover, at this time, he usually carried it in 30mg ampoules. I think it is highly likely that he administered either all or a substantial part of a 30mg ampoule of diamorphine to Miss Andrew. Such a dose would result in death within a very short time.
Shipman's note does not mention that he ever left the premises and returned to find Miss Andrew dead. There is no evidence to confirm that he did. It seems to me more likely that, knowing of Mrs Page's close friendship with Miss Andrew, he telephoned Mrs Page from Miss Andrew's house to ask her to speak to him before going to Miss Andrew's house. Then, on leaving the house, he met and spoke to Mrs Page's daughter. In my view, his claim to Mr Andrew that he had gone in search of a neighbour to keep an eye on Miss Andrew was probably a fabrication, designed to make it appear that Shipman was not present at the moment of death.
Miss Andrew died during Shipman's visit, a highly suspicious feature in itself. She was found sitting peacefully in her chair, fully clothed. Her appearance in death was not consistent with the appearance of a person who has died of a coronary thrombosis. It was, however, entirely typical of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of diamorphine.
Taking these factors into account, it appears to me that, despite Miss Andrew's vulnerability to a sudden cardiac death, the overwhelming likelihood is that she was killed by a lethal injection of diamorphine administered by Shipman. I am sure that this is what happened.

name: Joseph Bardsley
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 42 Hough Lane, Newton, Hyde
conclusion:
The circumstances of Mr Bardsley's death are highly suspicious. Mr Bardsley was in good health at lunchtime and was dead by 3pm. Whilst it must be accepted that elderly people can and do sometimes die suddenly, without any significant prior illness, where such a death occurs, no reasonable and honest doctor will be prepared to certify a cause of death. The death will be referred to the coroner with a view to post-mortem examination to establish the cause of death. If Shipman had not killed Mr Bardsley, it is hard to see why he would have sought to avoid what would have been a routine referral to the coroner. But if he had killed Mr Bardsley, and wished to avoid referral to the coroner, he would have to advance a feasible cause of death. As Dr Grenville has explained, it was not acceptable, in a case such as this, for the death to be certified as due to old age, because Mr Bardsley had not suffered a gradual decline. However, it seems likely to me that Shipman had to choose old age because he knew there was nothing in Mr Bardsley's medical history that could provide a plausible explanation for his sudden death.
If Mr Bardsley's death was natural, the most likely cause would be a heart attack or a stroke. In either event, Mr Bardsley would almost certainly have had sufficient time to pull the emergency cord or call for assistance over the intercom. Moreover, as Dr Grenville explained, his appearance in death, sitting peacefully in his chair, as if watching the television, is not typical of a death from either of these causes. It is, however, what would be expected following a death from morphine poisoning.
Shipman's claim to Mrs Laithwaite was that he was passing by and decided to obtain a blood sample from Mr Bardsley. I have already observed that this was a most unusual procedure to undertake on a Sunday afternoon. Shipman then suggested to Mrs Laithwaite that he had not entered the bungalow until he did so with her. He had seen Mr Bardsley through the window and had been unable to attract his attention, ostensibly because he was already dead. However, no reliance can be placed on Shipman's account of events. He has shown himself to be an inveterate liar. If it were feasible for him to have gained entry to the bungalow and to have killed Mr Bardsley, then it would be my view that that is what must have happened. Mrs Laithwaite said it would have been possible for Shipman to approach the bungalow without being noticed. There is no reason to suppose that Mr Bardsley would not have let Shipman in, had he knocked at the door. I have little doubt that Shipman would have been able to persuade Mr Bardsley that it was in his best interests to allow him either to give him an injection or to let him take a blood sample. He could then have given an injection of diamorphine, which would have resulted in a rapid and peaceful death.
In my judgement, the only sensible inference that can be drawn from the circumstances of this case is that Shipman killed Mr Bardsley. I am sure that that is what occurred.

name: Ann Cooper
title: Miss
place_of_death: her home, 68 Old Road, Hyde
conclusion:
The circumstances of Miss Cooper's death are highly suspicious. The death was discovered very shortly after Shipman's visit. Miss Cooper was plainly quite well when he arrived; she was doing her washing. Although the evidence is hearsay, it appears that Miss Cooper did not move about after Shipman's visit. Ms Taylor became concerned and went to look through the window. She saw Miss Cooper on the bed. I think she must then have telephoned the surgery and Dr Moysey must have come out and have declared Miss Cooper dead. Although it is possible that Miss Cooper was alive when Shipman left and then died a short time later, this seems most unlikely. It would be a most remarkable coincidence. The sequence of events gives rise to grave suspicion that Shipman killed Miss Cooper during his visit.
It appears to me that Form B is thoroughly misleading. First, if Shipman were not present at the death, he would have had no way of knowing the time of Miss Cooper's death. It is theoretically possible that Dr Moysey was present at the death but this is so unlikely that I discount it. Had that been so, I am sure Shipman would have said so on Form B and Mrs Nield would have been told. I think that Shipman's claim to know the time of death was an attempt to create the impression that the death occurred some time after his own visit. Second, Shipman's claim that he had attended Miss Cooper for three months during her last illness was plainly an attempt to create the impression that Miss Cooper's death was not sudden and unexpected, which in fact it was. I think the entries on Form B were devised to create a plausible account of the death.
I have come to the conclusion that Shipman must have killed Miss Cooper. The case bears his hallmark. I accept that, at 93, Miss Cooper was at risk of having a sudden fatal stroke but it would be a remarkable coincidence that she should have such a stroke so soon after Shipman's visit. I feel able to say that I am sure of this conclusion.

name: Ronnie Devenport
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 116 Chartist House, Hyde
conclusion:
This case is not straightforward. Mr Devenport was at an increased risk of sudden death due to heart attack. If Shipman's records are genuine, that risk had greatly increased within the last day or two of his life, as Mr Devenport's angina was less well controlled than formerly. So, a sudden death due to heart attack was at least a possibility and might have been a real risk.
Usually in a Shipman killing, there is a close temporal relationship between Shipman's visit and the death or the discovery of it. Here, that close association cannot be clearly established. Mr Devenport was last seen alive at about 12.30pm on 25th
May and was not found dead until about midday on 26th
May. Mr Devenport was not socially active and there is no report of any attempt to contact him between those times. How Shipman arrived at his estimate of a time of death between 10pm to 1am is not known. In any event, Dr Grenville thinks the estimate is unreliable. If Mr Devenport was found wearing nightclothes, it would suggest that he died either during the late evening of 25th
May or quite early in the morning of 26th
May. The time of Shipman's visit on 25th
May is not known. It could have been at about 1pm or between 2.30pm and 4pm or at about 6.30pm. At any of those times, one would normally expect Mr Devenport to be wearing day clothes, although it is possible that he might have changed into nightwear as early as 6.30pm. He was, in any event, somewhat eccentric in habits of dressing, although there is no evidence that his eccentricity extended to wearing nightclothes during the day. Consideration of these aspects of the evidence tends to suggest that Mr Devenport probably died at a time when Shipman would not have been visiting him. However, there are so many uncertainties that it is entirely possible that Mr Devenport died while Shipman was visiting. It is entirely possible that Mr Devenport was wearing a T-shirt and shorts rather than pyjamas and that these were day clothes which others were not accustomed to seeing him in.
That is the evidence that tends to suggest that Shipman did not kill Mr Devenport. It is far from conclusive.
Considering the evidence that suggests that Shipman did kill Mr Devenport, I consider, first, Dr Grenville's suspicions, which I share, about some of the most recent entries in Mr Devenport's medical records. I am particularly suspicious of the ECG taken on 18th
May, which Shipman appears to have instructed Sister Morgan to enter in the records as showing ischaemic heart disease. I accept Dr Grenville's evidence that it does not. It seems to me that Shipman was seeking to create the impression that Mr Devenport was more seriously at risk of heart attack than in fact he was.
Second, I am suspicious of Shipman's decision to visit Mr Devenport at home on 25th
May, only a day after he had seen him in the surgery. If Mr Devenport's condition was truly serious on 24th
May he should have been admitted to hospital there and then. Mr Devenport was not one who would have refused admission. If his condition was not serious on 24th
May it is hard to see why it would be necessary for Shipman to visit him the next day. The notes of neither visit record any physical signs, as one might expect them to do, if there was any concern about worsening angina. Both notes record
'chats'
about referral. There is no detail at all and no explanation as to why two chats were necessary. Some detail creeps in when Shipman came to complete Form B and even more detail was provided when the medical referee spoke to him. Indeed it rather appears that the story is developing with time. Shipman's use of the expression
'tluk'
(to let us know), tends to arouse suspicion in my mind, as it is a record he often made when leaving a patient whom he had killed. I have a strong suspicion that, on 24th
May, Shipman decided to kill Mr Devenport the next day and went to his flat for that purpose.
Third, I am suspicious of Shipman's claim that he could estimate the time of death as having occurred between 10pm and 1am. Dr Grenville says that no estimate is possible. Shipman frequently pretended that he could estimate the time of death and did so in an attempt to create the impression that the death had occurred several hours after his last visit.
Finally, I consider Mr Devenport's peaceful appearance sitting in a chair. Dr Grenville has said in his generic evidence that it is unusual to find the victim of a fatal heart attack sitting peacefully in a chair. More usually the victim is found collapsed on the floor. Usually he or she will have realised that something very serious is happening and will have got up in an attempt to summon help.
