On the other hand, Mr Devenport's peaceful appearance is entirely typical of that of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of opiate.
Mr Devenport was very vulnerable to Shipman. I now recognise that Shipman had little sympathy with those of his patients whom he thought were not genuinely ill. He had little patience with those of his patients who had psychiatric illness. Examples are Mrs Bianka Pomfret, Miss Joan Harding and Mrs Ivy Lomas. These were all patients who were very frequent visitors to his surgery and whose physical illness was not serious. There is reason to think that he became tired of attending to them. I suspect that Shipman had had enough of Mr Devenport and decided to kill him.
Although the evidence in this case falls far short of that which would be required to convict Shipman of Mr Devenport's murder, I have come to the conclusion that Shipman probably killed Mr Devenport.

name: Bethel Anne Evans
title: Miss
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
Miss Evans was clearly unwell during the days before her death. She seems to have been in considerable pain. The cause of her pain does not appear to have been established. She does not seem to have had any pain-relieving medication and there is no record in the daily diary that any doctor attended her after Dr Bennett's visit on 22nd
December. It is possible that Shipman visited on other occasions, for example on 29th
December, and that the visit was not recorded in either his visits book or the daily diary. Miss Evans' family seems to have been unaware of the seriousness of her condition until 2nd
January. However, Mr Richard Boden visited that evening and recalls that Miss Evans seemed close to death. She was 92 years of age. Against that background, her death cannot be described as sudden or unexpected.
Suspicion arises from the fact that a doctor was called to Charnley House shortly before Miss Evans died and appears to have been present at the moment of death. Shipman was later to certify that he had seen Miss Evans alive on the day of her death. I think it is likely that it was Shipman who attended at the home late at night on 3rd
January. However, the matter is not free of doubt. I note that the words
'Charnley House'
appear in Shipman's visits book for the day of Miss Evans' death. That would suggest that he intended to visit the home on his rounds, during the day. Yet, there is no reference in the daily diary to Shipman or any other doctor attending on that day until 11.15pm. I find this puzzling, as Shipman did not usually note emergency visits in the visits book; he seems to have used it as an aide-memoire for his daily rounds. I conclude that it is possible that Shipman visited Charnley House during the day on 3rd
January. If so, his visit has not been noted in the daily diary. If he did, it is possible that the doctor who came at night was another Donneybrook doctor, who happened to be on out of hours duty. However, I think it more likely that the doctor who came late at night was Shipman.
Although Ms Kilgariff does not remember summoning a doctor that night, she must have done and I infer that she did so either because Miss Evans was in severe pain or because Ms Kilgariff thought that she was close to death. The former is more likely, as the staff of Charnley House were accustomed to keeping watch over patients who were close to death and did not usually call out a doctor on that account alone.
The doctor is recorded as attending at 11.15pm and certified death at 11.30pm. According to the daily diary, the doctor, probably Shipman, was at the home for 15 minutes before certifying death. He might well have been left alone with Miss Evans. It follows that Shipman might well have had an opportunity to give Miss Evans an injection. If he gave her an intravenous injection of a lethal dose of an opiate, she would have died within about five to ten minutes. Mrs Stansfield, the matron at Charnley House, said (in connection with the case of Mrs Leah Johnston) that doctors who visited the home would 'administer a drop of morphine to residents if they were in pain'. It is quite possible that Shipman gave such an injection.
A second cause for suspicion arises out of the cause of death that Shipman certified. Although there is some evidence that Miss Evans had become confused, she does not seem to have suffered the gradual decline towards death which would make it appropriate for the doctor to certify that the death was due to senility. That Miss Evans' final illness appeared to begin with a painful condition of the urinary tract, and that her pain continued until death, would suggest that her death was not due to a gradual deterioration and the failure of several vital organs. I suspect that Shipman attributed the death to senility either out of laziness or because he knew that the real cause was morphine poisoning.
Although there is real suspicion that Shipman was present at Miss Evans' death and might well have had an opportunity to hasten her death, I do not think that I could say that it is likely that he did or that he did not. In those circumstances, I regret to say that I am unable to reach any positive conclusion about the circumstances of this death.

name: Hilda Fitton
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 5 Burkitt Street, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis, due to ischaemic heart disease and hypertension
conclusion:
I recognise that Mrs Fitton was at an increased risk of sudden death by coronary thrombosis because of her previous cardiac history. Such incidents can occur without prior warning, so the fact that Mrs Fitton appeared to be in reasonably good health shortly before her death does not show that she could not have had a heart attack on 6th
July.
Having said that, there are several highly suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. The first and most obvious is that the death was discovered not long after a visit by Shipman. There is no evidence that anyone saw Mrs Fitton alive or spoke to her after Shipman's visit on the day of her death. It is possible that someone did and the evidence has not emerged but that is unlikely as people tend to talk about when they have last seen a person who has died suddenly. The temporal association between Shipman's visit and the death gives rise to real suspicion. Even accepting that Mrs Fitton was at risk of a heart attack, it is a coincidence that it should supposedly happen shortly after Shipman's visit.
My suspicions are increased, as I cannot think of any good reason why Shipman would have visited Mrs Fitton that day. He had seen Mrs Fitton at the surgery the previous day. It appears likely that she had a chest infection but it was not of such severity as to require any treatment. Mrs Fitton's condition does not appear to have justified a visit on the following day. Although it is theoretically possible that Mrs Fitton could have telephoned the surgery asking for a visit in the early morning, that is extremely unlikely, as Mrs Gee (who had stayed the night) would have known if Mrs Fitton was unwell in the morning. I suspect that Mrs Gee's consultation with Shipman, on the morning of 6th
July, acted as a prompt for Shipman's visit to Mrs Fitton. He might well have made the connection. The two might even have spoken about Mrs Fitton. I think he made an unsolicited visit. I regard the fact that Shipman made a visit with no obvious purpose as highly suspicious.
Having made a visit for no good reason, it would be a wholly remarkable coincidence if Mrs Fitton were to have reported chest pains and other signs of a coronary thrombosis in the night. That entry can be seen to be quite false. Mrs Gee would have known if her sister had had such a bad night. Mrs Fitton was up and dressed when Mrs Gee left the house. This entry in the records is quite typical of many I have seen in cases where Shipman has killed a patient. The suggestion that a patient, in this case Mrs Fitton, had refused to go to hospital is a common feature of cases in which Shipman killed. It is incredible in this case. Mrs Fitton had been willing to go to hospital only a few weeks before and had made an excellent recovery while there. Another common feature of cases in which Shipman killed is the expression 'TLUK'. That usually gives rise to suspicion as it does here. If Mrs Fitton really had been suffering from chest pains and breathlessness and if Shipman really did think she had had another coronary thrombosis and if she really had refused to go to hospital, he could not have left her without treatment or care. At the very least, he would have had to ensure that she received attention from a relative. I am quite sure that this note was fabricated in an attempt to provide a plausible explanation for Mrs Fitton's death when it was discovered.
When Mrs Fitton's body was discovered, she was neatly laid out and had a peaceful expression. This is inconsistent with her having suffered a coronary thrombosis but it is entirely consistent with her having been injected with a lethal dose of morphine or diamorphine.
Notwithstanding the fact that Mrs Fitton was at risk of having a heart attack, I am quite satisfied that Shipman killed her when he made an unsolicited visit on 6th
July.

name: Millicent Garside
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, Flat 30 St John's Drive, Godley, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to congestive heart failure and ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
There are a number of highly suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. First and most obvious, the death was discovered about an hour after Shipman had visited Mrs Garside and had been alone with her. No one saw Mrs Garside alive or spoke to her after that visit. That in itself is a highly suspicious feature.
Mrs Garside was at a significantly increased risk of suffering a heart attack. If, however, one sets aside the handwritten note made by Shipman himself on the day of Mrs Garside's death, there is no good evidence that she was exhibiting the signs or symptoms of a heart attack or severe congestive heart failure either on the day of her death or on the previous day. Indeed, there is positive evidence to the contrary. It would appear that Mrs Garside was breathless but, when calmed down, she was otherwise well. That her breathlessness settled when she was calm suggests that it was due to asthma and anxiety rather than congestive heart failure or heart attack. For that reason alone, I suspect that Shipman's entry in the medical record for the day of the death was not a genuine account of the history and findings. A further reason for suspecting that Shipman's entry is not genuine is that I find it almost inconceivable that Mrs Garside could have suffered a bad attack of chest pain in the night and not have mentioned it to her son or daughter-in-law. I am also slightly suspicious of Shipman's claim that Mrs Garside said that she wanted to stay at home rather than be admitted to hospital. This is a feature of so many cases in which Shipman killed that it raises suspicion, even though I know that some elderly people do resist the idea of hospital admission. Shipman's account is a clear description of a heart attack associated with congestive heart failure. However, it does not ring true. If Mrs Garside were in the condition he described, he should have tried to persuade her to go to hospital. If she refused, he should have contacted a relative first to make an attempt to persuade her to change her mind and, if she resolutely refused, so that she could be cared for. To inform a relative would be the very least any sensible doctor would do. Shipman says that Mrs Garside was confused about the history of recent events. It would be imperative that her son should be told of the situation so that she could be adequately cared for. In short, this medical record does not make sense and I am sure that it is false.
I note that Shipman's record includes a reference to an intravenous injection. It is quite possible that Shipman gave an intravenous injection, which might well have left a mark, and he would wish to explain that. The question remains whether the injection was of Lasix, as he claimed, or a strong opiate.
Shipman told a number of lies on Form B, which give rise to grave suspicion. First and most obvious, he falsely claimed that Mr Garside was present at the death. He would know that it would not be possible to give a reliable diagnosis that the death was due to a coronary thrombosis unless someone had witnessed the final event. In addition, Shipman often claimed that someone was present at the death when the true situation was that the body was found soon after he himself had visited. He did this to create the impression that someone had seen the patient alive after his own departure.
Second, he claimed to know the time of death and said it had occurred at about 4pm. He also said that this was two hours after his own visit. According to his medical note, his own visit was at 3pm. If Mrs Garside had died a natural death at some time after his departure, as he claimed, there is no way in which he could have known whether it was a minute after his departure or a minute before the body was found. By claiming to know the time of death, Shipman was creating the misleading impression that he could say that the death occurred a considerable time after his own visit.
I attach no weight to the evidence that Shipman is said to have mentioned an injection of warfarin and to have claimed that Mrs Garside had only 20 per cent remaining lung capacity. Those remarks, if made, are not probative of guilt.
Mrs Garside's position and appearance in death were not typical of those seen following a heart attack or indeed any of the common causes of sudden natural death. They were, however, entirely typical of those seen in many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of opiate.
Mrs Garside was at considerable risk of suffering a sudden cardiac death and I cannot rule out the possibility that her death was natural. However, the close temporal association between Shipman's visit and the discovery of her death persuades me that it is overwhelmingly likely that he killed her. I feel able to say that I am sure of my conclusion.

name: Joan Milray Harding
title: Miss
place_of_death: Shipman's surgery at 21 Market Street, Hyde
conclusion:
The circumstances of this death are suspicious because it occurred on surgery premises and behind closed doors. Such evidence as is available shows that a death in a general practitioner's surgery is very unusual. On the rare occasions when such a death does occur, following a sudden collapse, there is an emergency, an ambulance is called and strenuous and concerted attempts are made to save the patient. This was not the case here.
The level of suspicion increases, as Miss Harding had no history of heart disease of any kind. A sudden death from coronary thrombosis was possible but very unlikely. On any view, this was a case that cried out for referral to the coroner and a post-mortem examination.
Did Miss Harding have a coronary thrombosis or not? If she did not, there does not seem to be any other plausible reason why she might have died a sudden natural death, and the overwhelming inference must be that Shipman killed her. Even if she did have a heart attack, it may be that Shipman gave her an injection of diamorphine that ensured her death. The third possibility is that Miss Harding died of natural causes. If she did, she must either have had a sudden massive heart attack in the consultation room, or the minor symptoms, from which she might have been suffering as she came into Hyde, suddenly became more serious in the consulting room, resulting in collapse, cardiac arrest and death.
The evidence of Mrs Chapman, that Miss Harding looked pale and ill and might not have been able to walk unaided, would, if accurate, be evidence of signs consistent with (but not diagnostic of) the occurrence of an attack of angina or the onset of a heart attack. The pain in the back, of which Mrs Bolton said Miss Harding complained during the journey into Hyde, might be explained as having a cardiac origin. However, there are many other potential explanations for Miss Harding's pallor and pain. One is that it was connected with the complaint of biliousness from the previous day, another is that it was related to her arthritic neck. As Miss Harding had no history of heart disease, other explanations seem more likely. Dr Grenville says that the upper back pain of which Mrs Bolton says Miss Harding complained is not typical of a heart attack. Dizziness might be associated with a silent heart attack but this dizziness had lasted on and off for two weeks. It seems to me that Miss Harding's symptoms of back pain and paleness are likely to have been due to a cause other than cardiac problems. Some cardiac episode is a possibility although I regard it as unlikely. Although there are conflicts between the evidence of Mrs Chapman and Mrs Bolton, I am satisfied that that would be my conclusion however I resolved those conflicts.
The suggestion that Miss Harding might have suddenly suffered a massive heart attack in the consulting room, after coming to the surgery for unrelated problems, seems to me so fanciful that I reject it.
I turn therefore to consider the unlikely possibility that Miss Harding did have pain of cardiac origin as she arrived at the surgery. If she did, what happened and how did it develop? Is there a plausible account of development into a full-blown fatal heart attack?
Shipman's note of the consultation must be examined with care and some suspicion, as he frequently fabricated records to pass off a killing as a natural death. However, for the moment, for the purposes of analysis, I shall assume that the note is genuine. If Miss Harding was having some sort of cardiac episode as she came into the surgery, Shipman's response should have been to recognise that she was ill and to call an ambulance immediately. He does not appear to have done so. According to his note, he let her speak about her elbow, then her back, her indigestion and her dizziness. Then he took her blood pressure, tested her pulse and noticed that her colour was grey. All that appears to have occurred before he noticed that her lips were blue. He then listened to her heart sounds and noted ectopic beats. Then, having diagnosed a heart attack, and having wondered when it might have occurred, he summoned an ambulance. Then he recorded that Miss Harding collapsed, and noted the time, with apparent precision, as 11.20am. I note that the ambulance records show that an ambulance was summoned at 11.31am.
I find it almost incredible that a patient who was supposed to be suffering cardiac pain was able to go through a history of elbow pain, mid-thoracic pain, indigestion and two weeks of dizziness, without the doctor noticing that she looked ill and her face or lips were grey or blue. I think this note makes sense up to the stage where Shipman noted that the patient felt unwell, but thereafter I find it highly suspicious.
I continue with the history, as it must have occurred if Shipman's account is true. After the collapse, he went to fetch Nurse Morgan and made an apparent attempt to resuscitate Miss Harding. Was this genuine? I accept that Nurse Morgan believed that it was. I doubt that it was, as Shipman did not make use of drugs and equipment that would have been available in the surgery. He decided to stop before the ambulance had arrived and did not carry out a thorough examination to ascertain that Miss Harding was dead. Dr Grenville has explained that, when someone is in cardiac arrest, it is very difficult to tell whether he or she is dead. Careful examination is necessary, including listening to the heart sounds with the stethoscope and examination of the eyes. Shipman did neither of those things. Of course, if he knew Miss Harding was already dead or inevitably dying from a large dose of diamorphine, there would be no point in him examining her carefully for signs of life. A perfunctory examination is one of the hallmarks of cases in which Shipman killed. Had this been a genuine attempt to resuscitate, Shipman would have continued the efforts until the ambulance arrived, when a defibrillator could have been used. If it were not a genuine attempt and if Shipman knew throughout that Miss Harding was dying of morphine poisoning, he would wish to call a halt to the efforts and cancel the ambulance before it arrived. I incline to the view that the resuscitation attempt was a sham.
Considering all these factors, I conclude that Shipman's note of the consultation cannot be accepted as genuine. I am satisfied that Miss Harding did not have a coronary thrombosis or suffer cardiac arrest at any time that day.
I conclude that Shipman listened to Miss Harding's problems, which would have comprised the elbow and back pain she had mentioned to Mrs Bolton and probably the biliousness of which she had complained to Mrs Spoors. She may well also have mentioned feeling light-headed. I think it likely that Shipman then decided to kill Miss Harding, asked her to lie on the examination couch and gave her a diamorphine injection. When she was unconscious, he asked a receptionist to summon an ambulance, called for Nurse Morgan and went through a charade of resuscitation. Inevitably the 'resuscitation' failed and, after an appropriate interval, he called it off and cancelled the ambulance. He then created a medical record, giving a plausible account of a heart attack.
I am sure that Shipman unlawfully killed Miss Harding.

name: Robert Edward Jones
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 26 Princess Street, Hyde
certified_cause: cerebrovascular accident due to cerebral arteriosclerosis
conclusion:
It appears to me that Mr Jones must have died a natural death.
Mr Jones had suffered a stroke some time before his death. It is also possible that Mr Jones' loss of memory might have been the result of a number of small strokes, sometimes called transient ischaemic attacks. He must have been at risk of suffering another stroke. His death cannot be regarded as wholly unexpected.
There is no evidence that Shipman saw Mr Jones alive on the day of his death. There is good evidence that Mr Jones suffered a collapse while having lunch, in the presence of his wife. I think it is likely that Mrs Jones thought her husband must have had a heart attack and this is why Mrs Bancroft has thought for many years that that was the cause of her father's death. In fact, the collapse as described might well have been due to a stroke and, bearing in mind the past history, it seems likely that that is what must have happened.
When Professor Baker said that he thought the circumstances of the death were moderately suspicious, he relied only on the cremation documents and did not have the statement of Mrs Bancroft, describing the circumstances of the death. The only possible cause for suspicion is that Shipman's claim that he had seen Mr Jones alive on 30th
March might have been false. However, even if it was, I do not entertain any real suspicion that he was involved in causing Mr Jones' death. Shipman seemed to be under the impression that the registrar would refuse to accept his certification of the cause of death unless he had seen the patient within 14 days before death. He quite often made a false claim of this kind in cases where he had certainly not caused the death. I think he wanted to avoid the risk of a coroner's referral and post-mortem examination, with its attendant delay and distress for the family. Standing alone, that probable falsehood does not give cause for concern.
I hope this decision will allay any anxiety Mrs Bancroft might have felt about her father's death.

name: James Joseph King
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 32 Ogden Court, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of suspicious features surrounding this death.
First and most obviously, the death was discovered very shortly after a visit by Shipman. Mr King was dizzy but otherwise well when his daughter left him at about 1pm. At that time Shipman had not yet visited. We know that he did visit. No one saw Mr King alive or spoke to him after Shipman's visit. It is highly likely that he was already dead when Mrs Griffiths tried to telephone him at about 2pm. Thus there is a very close temporal association between the death and Shipman's visit.
The witness evidence indicates that, on the day of his death, Mr King was experiencing dizziness and was finding it difficult to walk. In Dr Grenville's view, the most likely cause of Mr King's complaint was vestibulitis. This is not a condition likely to lead to a sudden death.
Shipman's note of his visit does not make medical sense. He suggests that there is a history of a TIA but records no signs or symptoms on which that diagnosis could be based. He does not record any current symptoms or complaints, despite the fact that less than an hour earlier Mr King was unable to walk unsupported. This note does not provide credible support for the certified cause of death.
Shipman told a number of lies on Form B. He said that he had attended Mr King during his last illness for a period of 24 hours. That was untrue. He did not attend him until shortly before his death. Shipman said that death occurred at 2pm. That might well be true. However, Shipman claimed that he had last seen Mr King about three hours before the death. That was certainly a lie, as Shipman had not visited when Mrs Griffiths left at about 1pm. In my view, that lie was designed to create the impression that a substantial interval had elapsed between the visit and the death. It is almost certainly untrue that Shipman made a complete external examination of the body. However, I attach little significance to that as Shipman rarely seems to have examined any body properly and, in any event, the paramedics had already confirmed that Mr King was dead. Shipman's assertion that Mrs Griffiths nursed her father in his last illness is clearly false and was designed to give the impression that the death was not unexpected. Shipman's assertion that Mrs Griffiths was present at the death is also quite false and he must have known it. This lie was, in my view, designed to create the impression that the death was not unexpected and did not occur while Shipman was alone with the patient. Mrs Griffiths could not have given Shipman any information from which he could have inferred the mode or duration of Mr King's death. Form B is a pack of lies designed to create the impression of a natural death.
As Dr Grenville has explained, if this death was natural, Shipman could not possibly have known its cause. He virtually admitted to Mrs Griffiths that he did not know what to put on the MCCD, as a natural cause. He should have referred the death to the coroner.
Mr King's appearance in death was entirely consistent with the appearance of many of Shipman's victims who died by lethal injection of diamorphine and was not typical of death by cerebrovascular accident.
Taking all these factors together, I am quite sure that Shipman killed Mr King. I have no doubt that Mr King was still feeling dizzy when Shipman arrived and that Shipman said he would give him an injection for the relief of those symptoms. That injection must have been a lethal dose of opiate, almost certainly diamorphine.

name: Carrie Leigh
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 26 Joel Lane, Gee Cross, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease due to hypertension
conclusion:
Mrs Leigh's death was very sudden. She had been well for some time before her death and her only recent complaints had been related to non-fatal conditions. In particular, she had not complained of chest pain or breathlessness on exertion. This, coupled with her appearance in death, shows, as Dr Grenville observed, that a heart attack was probably not the cause of her sudden death. That is so, even though Mrs Leigh might well have died of a heart attack at any time.
There is no direct evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Leigh on the day of her death. However, there is evidence from which I could infer that he probably did. This is the evidence that he appears to have something to hide in respect of Mrs Leigh's death. He told a number of lies on the MCCD and Form B, which I detail below.
First, I have come to the conclusion that Shipman almost certainly lied when he said that he had last seen Mrs Leigh alive on 11th
July, five days before her death. I do not think he did see her, first, because there is no confirmation in any surgery record of either a surgery appointment or a home visit and, second, Shipman's note of the supposed consultation does not make sense. It is not about any medical condition or social problem or any form of routine monitoring. I think it is highly likely that Shipman has fabricated a record of a consultation in order to give the impression that he had seen Mrs Leigh within 14 days before her death and also to give the impression that she had some form of illness which required a referral. In fact she did not. She had no 'last illness' at all and Shipman could not properly and should not have signed her MCCD. If Shipman had admitted that he had not seen Mrs Leigh since 31st
May, the last properly recorded and confirmed consultation before her death, the registrar would probably have referred the death to the coroner. Shipman sometimes falsely claimed to have seen a patient within 14 days before death in cases where it is clear he had not killed the patient. It appears he might have done so in order to save the family the added worry of a post-mortem examination. This does not appear likely in this case. Shipman might have had other, more sinister motives. He told this lie on many occasions where he had killed the patient. The effect would be to reduce the risk that the death might be referred to the coroner.
Dr Grenville says that, if he had read Form B, in his capacity as a doctor about to sign Form C or as a medical referee considering whether or not to authorise cremation, he would have gathered the impression that Shipman had been treating Mrs Leigh for ischaemic heart disease for the past six months. That, he says, is the implication behind Shipman's statement. I am satisfied that that was deliberately misleading. If Shipman had admitted that Mrs Leigh had not suffered any 'last illness', the death would have been referred to the coroner. There would then have been a danger that the pathologist would not have found anything to explain the death and this might have resulted in toxicological tests on body tissues.
Shipman also stated that the death occurred at about 3.30pm, when he could not possibly have known what time Mrs Leigh died, unless he was with her at the time. If he had nothing to hide, one would have expected him to say that he could not tell at what time she had died and to give the bracket of times between which the death must have occurred. In my view, Shipman probably wished to specify a time of death which was almost certainly well after the true time. If anyone had seen him visiting Mrs Leigh in the early afternoon, it would then appear that she had been alive for some time after his visit.
Shipman's statements on the certification and cremation documents give rise to a strong suspicion that he had something to hide in respect of Mrs Leigh's death.
Drawing these factors together, I have come to the conclusion that Shipman probably killed Mrs Leigh in the early afternoon of 16th
July 1996. The evidence is not sufficiently clear for me to say that I am sure of that conclusion but I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities.

name: Emily Morgan
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 8 Mansfield Road, Hyde
conclusion:
Mrs Morgan was not in the best of health and it may be that she had not long to live. However, I have come to the conclusion that her death was not natural.
Shipman's account of events and explanation for the death, as appearing in the medical records and Form B, are not consistent with the observations of witnesses.
First, Shipman claims that Mrs Morgan was showing signs of a stroke on 11th
May. However, her daughter who put her to bed that night was unaware of any such signs. Second, Shipman claims that, when he arrived on the afternoon of 12th
May, Mrs Morgan was showing even clearer signs of a stroke. Yet Mrs Hillson, who had been with her until a few minutes before he arrived, was unaware of any such signs. I do not believe Mrs Morgan showed the signs Shipman claimed to have observed. Third, Shipman claims to have advised that admission to hospital was necessary and that Mrs Morgan refused. Yet he failed to take the most obvious steps to persuade her, such as suggesting that he should speak to the warden or to her daughter. If he really thought she had a developing stroke, it would have been quite disgraceful for him not to make some arrangements for her care, for example by speaking to the warden. Fourth, a developing stroke does not result in a sudden death, over a period of minutes. As Dr Grenville has explained, death from a developing stroke usually takes place over a period of two to three days. I am quite satisfied that Mrs Morgan's last illness and death did not occur as Shipman claimed.
It is possible, although unlikely, that Mrs Morgan might have died suddenly from some other natural cause. However, her death occurred within the very short period between the departure of Mrs Hillson and the arrival of Mrs Waters. For virtually the whole of that period, Shipman was alone with Mrs Morgan. It is stretching coincidence too far to suggest that Mrs Morgan might have died naturally within the few minutes between Shipman's departure and Mrs Waters' arrival. It seems clear that Mrs Morgan died while Shipman was alone with her and he walked out and left someone to find her body. No honest doctor would do that. No doubt, Shipman thought it would be some time before the body was found and the death would not be too closely associated with his visit. In the event, Mrs Waters' discovery of the body, while he was still sitting outside in his car, provided an extremely close association.
Shipman had the opportunity to give a lethal injection while he was alone with Mrs Morgan. Her appearance in death was very similar to the appearance of many of Shipman's victims, who are known to have been killed by diamorphine injection. It was not typical of a person who had suffered a sudden death as the result of heart attack or stroke.
For those reasons, and because I regard it as extremely unlikely that Mrs Morgan could have died naturally in the few minutes after Shipman left her house, I feel driven to say that I am sure he killed her.

name: Lily Nichols
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion: I am quite satisfied that Mrs Nichols died a natural death. The daily diary records a gradual decline and the death was neither sudden nor unexpected. It appears that it was appropriate for Shipman to certify the cause of death as old age. There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman saw Mrs Nichols in the period before her death and had probably not seen her for six days. Mrs Nichols' name probably appears in Shipman's visits book for the day of the death because he had been asked to attend the home to certify the cause of death. I am sure Mrs Bridge was right to have no suspicions about Shipman's role in her mother's death.

name: Marjorie Parker
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 5 Werneth Avenue, Gee Cross, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to congestive heart failure and hypertension
conclusion:
Mrs Parker suffered from extremely severe ischaemic heart disease and was at high risk of a further heart attack at any time. Shipman was called to see her on the day of her death because she was unwell. His first note of 27th
April records that she was complaining of central chest pain. However, Shipman did not judge her symptoms sufficiently serious to warrant hospital admission.
Shipman was called back to see Mrs Parker shortly before she died. The second entry in the visits book suggests that her condition was serious because she had reportedly collapsed on the floor and this evidence is corroborated by what Mrs Smith told Mr James Parker. Mr Parker states that his wife suffered a 'kind of seizure', in that she started to shake. This could be associated with heart failure or angina or anxiety. Shipman made no entry at all in the records to describe Mrs Parker's condition when he arrived. That is a matter of some concern, as I have found many cases in which Shipman has killed his patient, he had made an inadequate record of the patient's condition before death. However, he was a poor note taker generally and I do not attach great weight to his failure to make a proper note of Mrs Parker's symptoms or the results of his examination. Whilst the evidence is far from certain, it appears to me that it is possible that Mrs Parker had had, or was having, a heart attack and, if so, it is likely that she had cardiac pain.
I think it likely that she was in pain and was very anxious when Shipman arrived. I infer that an injection of opiate was appropriate, provided the dose was suitable and the drug was administered slowly.
We do not know what dose was given of what drug. Shipman made no record. This is a serious matter, particularly if the drug given was a controlled drug such as morphine or diamorphine. Not only did Shipman fail to make a record of the treatment, he does not appear to have told Mr Parker what he was doing or why. Both of these factors give rise to suspicion that he was doing something illicit.
There are two other factors which excite suspicion. First, Shipman obtained a 30mg ampoule of diamorphine in Mrs Parker's name that day. A dose of that size would have been lethal for Mrs Parker. We do not know whether Shipman collected it before or after her death. At his trial, Shipman said that, at this time in 1993, he had fallen into the 'bad habit' of prescribing 30mg ampoules of diamorphine, although he agreed that this was far too much to give a patient as a single dose for the relief of acute pain. He claimed that he used to give only part of the ampoule and would throw away the rest. This explanation is not easy to accept when 5mg and 10mg ampoules are readily available. The series of events and transactions by which Shipman obtained diamorphine between February and May 1993 does not prove that Shipman used a 30mg ampoule of diamorphine to kill Mrs Parker, but it raises a strong suspicion that he did.
The second additional cause for suspicion is that Shipman completed the MCCD at the house immediately after the death. Unless Shipman had decided to kill Mrs Parker that afternoon, it is hard to see why he had the book of certificates with him. He did not usually carry it with him on his rounds. Usually, the relatives of patients who had died had to go to the surgery the next day to collect the MCCD. There is no reason to think that Shipman had the MCCD book with him for another patient, who had just died or was terminally ill. Although another patient died later that day, in Charlotte House Residential Home, it appears that patient died in the late afternoon or early evening.
These suspicious features must be seen in the context of Mrs Parker's undoubted illness and Shipman's very poor standard of note taking. A feature which tends to suggest that Shipman did not give a frankly lethal dose of diamorphine is that it appears that Mrs Parker was still alive 20 minutes after the injection was given. If Shipman gave 30mg of diamorphine all at once, one would have expected Mrs Parker to die rather sooner than that. However, it may be that, as Mrs Parker was in pain before the injection, the dose was barely lethal and took a longer than usual time to take effect. In any event, it appears that she became unconscious immediately and did not recover consciousness. I find it suspicious that Shipman seems to have been prepared to wait as long as 20 minutes after giving the injection. Usually, if a doctor gives an injection to relieve pain, he will wait until the patient has settled and will then leave. Here, I suspect that Shipman was waiting until Mrs Parker died. He would not have waited unless he expected her to die.
Taking all these factors into account, I have come to the conclusion that Shipman probably gave Mrs Parker an inappropriately large dose of diamorphine, intending that she would die that day. It may be that she would have died that day in any event. I think Shipman's actions were probably designed to ensure that she did. The evidence falls some way short of that which would enable me to say that I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Parker. However, I find that he probably did.

name: Eileen Robinson
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 47 Marlborough Road, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
This death is highly suspicious. Shipman is known to have visited Mrs Robinson on 22nd
December, for the purpose of taking a blood sample. No one is known to have seen her alive or spoken to her after that visit. I recognise, of course, that it is possible that someone did see her or speak to her and that the police and the Inquiry have failed to locate that person, but I think that is unlikely.
Mrs Robinson had raised blood pressure, which put her at a significantly increased risk of suffering a stroke. It also put her at a slightly increased risk of suffering a heart attack. However, until 22nd
December, there was no suggestion that she had any cardiac signs or symptoms. Anyone looking at her records on 21st
December would not have thought that she was at any real risk of having a heart attack.
I am deeply suspicious of Shipman's note of 22nd
December. There is no doubt that he visited her on that day for the purpose of taking blood samples. He did so and sent them to the laboratory for analysis; the results came back on 24th
December. I observe that his manuscript note did not refer to the blood samples. I can see that, given Mrs Robinson's history of raised blood pressure, Shipman would naturally take the opportunity of taking a reading while visiting. If the result was high, as he claimed, he might well wish to adjust the medication. The note then suggests that, when he asked if she had any chest pain, Mrs Robinson told him that she did not, only indigestion, thereby implying or admitting that she did have some symptoms of pain or discomfort in her chest. Shipman then suggested that she might have angina. He found no positive signs of any cardiac problem but he claims to have advised Mrs Robinson to take things easy and to contact him if she had chest pain. The effect of this is to suggest to the reader that, in fact, Mrs Robinson had a heart condition.
This entry is typical of many I have seen in cases where Shipman has killed a patient. In this type of case, he begins a consultation by noting the matter for which the appointment or visit has been made. He then goes on to deal with another matter, which apparently gives rise to some concern and which subsequently turns out to be related to the cause of the death which follows shortly. In other cases, I have found that these 'hybrid' entries, part true, part false, are highly suspicious. I suspect that the latter half of this record is false and was designed to put a question mark over Mrs Robinson's cardiac health. I think it unlikely that she had been suffering from any chest pain, whether or not she attributed it to indigestion. If she had had chest pain, it is likely she would have mentioned it to her daughters or consulted Shipman about it voluntarily.
I suspect that Shipman took a blood sample from Mrs Robinson on 22nd
December and then, under the guise of taking another sample, injected her with diamorphine.
Shipman told a lie when he arrived at Mr McCrosson's house in the early afternoon of 23rd
December. He claimed that he was concerned because Mrs Robinson had missed an appointment. She had not. In my view, it is far more likely that Shipman was concerned that he had not been called out to certify Mrs Robinson's death, although he knew she had been dead for about 24 hours. I think he would have become anxious and would wish to create an excuse for 'discovering' the body. I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Robinson.
I find it remarkable and highly suspicious that Shipman should have been prepared to decide that an ambulance was not necessary after seeing Mrs Robinson's body through the window. Unless he had been present at her death, he could not possibly have known that she was dead. To call an ambulance would have been the most obvious preparation for dealing with an emergency if she were alive.
The account written down by the police of what Shipman said to the emergency services operator is not consistent with the note which Shipman made, apparently on 22nd
December. In the note he suggested obliquely that Mrs Robinson might have a heart problem. To the police he said that she was 'very poorly' the day before. One must ask, if she had been 'very poorly', why had he not admitted her to hospital or at the very least alerted her daughters to her condition?
Mrs Robinson's position and appearance in death, lying on her front with her legs straight out, are not what one would expect if she had suffered a heart attack and fallen from her chair. Mr McCrosson now has the impression that the body had been straightened out.
In Form B, Shipman sought to suggest that the death had occurred in the night. That would have the effect of putting it probably about 10-12 hours after his own visit on 22nd
December. He could not have known when the death occurred (unless he had been present). He could not have made any sensible estimate from body temperature, although on some occasions he claimed to do so. He could only have said that the death was not recent when the body was found, as rigor mortis was present and there was discoloration on the legs. In any event, if the death occurred at midnight, it is surprising that Mrs Robinson was sitting downstairs, dressed in day clothes and with the curtains open. If one wants to make an estimate of the time of death, it would seem necessary to take such factors into account. In my view, Shipman said that the death occurred at midnight in order to distance himself from the death.
Finally, if Shipman really had had a consultation with Mrs Robinson, which had proceeded on the lines of the note he made in the records, he could not possibly have certified honestly that her death a few hours later was due to a heart attack. He would have had no idea of what had caused her death. The case would have been a sudden and unexpected death of which the cause was not known. The death should have been referred to the coroner. Shipman did not refer it.
Taking all these factors into account, I am left in no doubt that Shipman must have killed Mrs Robinson, almost certainly by giving her an injection of diamorphine, under the guise of taking a blood sample.

name: John Stone
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 297 Dukinfield Road, Hyde
certified_cause: congestive heart failure due to hypertension
conclusion:
There are several highly suspicious features to Mr Stone's death.
The first and most obvious is the temporal association between Shipman's visit and the death. Shipman claimed to have found Mr Stone dead in his chair at about 3.30pm. I infer that from the time of Shipman's receptionist's telephone call to Mr Ronald Stone. Mr Stone had been well enough to telephone his son about his milk supplies just over half an hour before. It would be something of a coincidence if Mr Stone had died a sudden but natural death within that short period of time. That in itself is highly suspicious.
If, as Mr Ronald Stone recalls, Shipman told him that he had been present at the moment of death, the inconsistency between that account and what Shipman told the coroner would give rise to further suspicion. However, I think it likely that Mr Ronald Stone's recollection is at fault on this issue, as his wife seems to have been under the clear impression that Shipman found Mr Stone dead when he arrived at the house. Mrs Stone wanted to know how Shipman had gained access to the house, if Mr Stone had not let him in. Shipman's claim that the door had been left open for him seems rather improbable and is a further ground for suspicion.
The medical evidence does not support a death by natural causes. There is no corroboration of Shipman's diagnosis that Mr Stone suffered from congestive heart failure. Whilst it must be accepted that Mr Stone was suffering from renal failure, this condition does not lead to sudden death. Death follows a gradual decline. The course of events was not consistent with a death from congestive heart failure. Mr Stone was quite well in the hours before his death and spoke to his son less than an hour before his death.
Shipman was obliged to refer this case to the coroner because Mr Stone had recently undergone surgery. However, the way in which the referral was made seems to me to have been designed to ensure that the coroner did not send the body for a post-mortem examination. Shipman appears to have assured the coroner that this would not be necessary. I think Shipman wished to avoid a post-mortem examination.
The purpose of Shipman's visit was to take a blood sample. From my experience of other cases, I have come to realise that Shipman quite often used the occasion of taking a blood sample as an opportunity to give a lethal injection. Many patients do not watch the doctor while a blood sample is being drawn and some would not realise the difference between the administration of an injection and the taking of a blood sample even if they watched. Taking a blood sample gave Shipman an opportunity to introduce a needle into the patient's vein. I think that is what happened here.
When these factors are considered together, I am sure that Shipman killed Mr Stone, by administering a lethal injection of opiate under the guise of taking a blood sample.

name: Dorothy Tucker
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 102A Armadale Road, Dukinfield
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
This is a difficult case to decide, mainly because of the lack of any medical records. I have the impression from the witnesses that Mrs Tucker was in poor health and I must assume that she was at some risk of suffering sudden death either from a heart attack or as the result of a pulmonary embolus following a deep vein thrombosis.
There is some doubt about when Shipman last visited Mrs Tucker. According to the MCCD counterfoil, he last saw her on 6th
January, the day before her death. However, Shipman often lied about the times and dates of his visits, so that cannot be relied on as accurate. He might well have visited her on 7th
January and not have entered it in any record. If he did visit her on 7th
but did not enter the visit in his visits book, one must ask whether there might be a sinister reason for that failure.
There is some evidence from Mrs Lynch that on the morning of 7th
January, the curtains remained closed and the milk stayed on the step with the result that she became concerned and raised the alarm. As it is reasonably clear that the alarm was raised in the late afternoon or early evening, I discount her evidence as probably mistaken.
Mrs Bennett has consistently said that Mrs Tucker told her that Shipman had already been to visit, and had given her an injection, when the two women spoke to discuss Mrs Tucker's shopping needs. She puts that conversation at about 2pm. The impression I gain is that Mrs Tucker was saying that Shipman had only just left. If Shipman had given her an intramuscular injection of a strong opiate, it is possible that she would have been able to speak to Mrs Bennett on the telephone and that Mrs Bennett would not have realised that there was anything seriously wrong with Mrs Tucker. This would fit with Mrs Tucker's declared intention to have a rest. It would also account for the fact that Mrs Tucker's dog was locked in the kitchen. The dog might well have been put there during a consultation with the doctor. Mrs Tucker might not have let him out before she felt drowsy and sat on the settee. Although Shipman usually gave diamorphine injections intravenously when killing his patients, it is a real possibility that he might have acted differently with Mrs Tucker. Due to her obesity it might have been very difficult for him to find a vein. He might either have chosen to give an intramuscular injection or the needle may have slipped out of the vein, causing the drug to enter Mrs Tucker's system subcutaneously. If either hypothesis were correct, it would mean that Shipman left his patient alive, knowing that she would soon die. From my experience of other cases, it appears that he did not usually do that. He preferred to wait in the house until he was sure that the patient was dead. With an intravenous injection that would only be a matter of minutes. With an intramuscular or subcutaneous injection he would have had to wait much longer. There would be a risk that the patient might be found or might summon help and might survive. The risk to Shipman would be very great. However, on this occasion, Shipman would have known that he would be on duty all weekend, so the risk of another doctor being summoned to deal with Mrs Tucker was minimal. There would be some risk that an ambulance might be called, but it may be that he decided to take that risk.
It must also be said that although Mrs Tucker was only 51, she was in many respects a typical Shipman victim. Shipman preyed mainly on women who lived alone and were in poor health. Mrs Tucker, although only 51, was in very poor physical condition.
Mrs Tucker's appearance in death is not unlike that of many of Shipman's victims. She seemed to have fallen asleep and did not appear to have been in pain. As Dr John Grenville has said in his generic evidence, patients who die after a heart attack usually have time to make a move towards seeking help. Although Mrs Tucker's mobility was poor, she was able to get out of her chair or settee. One would expect that if she had begun to suffer the pain that usually accompanies a coronary thrombosis, she would have made some attempt to reach the telephone. Similarly, a pulmonary embolus is usually painful and a similar reaction might be expected.
All the witnesses who attended Mrs Tucker's flat after the death noticed that the room was very hot. This suggests that Shipman might have turned up the fire. This is an odd feature of several Shipman killings. A high ambient temperature would accelerate the onset of rigor mortis. It would also have the effect of slowing the rate at which the body temperature falls after death. The result of leaving a body in a warm room would be to make it difficult or even impossible for a pathologist to make a reliable estimate of the time of death. There is a suspicion that Shipman would wish to achieve that end if he was concerned about his own role in the death. I do not attach much weight to this factor but it gives rise to slight suspicion.
After much hesitation, I have come to the conclusion that it is likely that Shipman killed Mrs Tucker. The evidence falls a long way short of that which would make me sure that he had killed her, but I think he probably did.

name: Amy Whitehead
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 122 Haughton Green Road, Denton
conclusion:
This death is highly suspicious, if only because it took place while Shipman was alone with his patient. This is something that occurs only rarely in the experience of other doctors. If Shipman is to be believed, a natural death in the presence of the doctor is commonplace.
Although Mrs Whitehead was at a very high risk of suffering a heart attack, the evidence as to her condition on the day before her death points to her being fit and well but for gastrointestinal upset. It is clear that the reason she asked Shipman to visit was on account of that and not because of anything such as chest pain, which might indicate the onset of a heart attack. Common sense would suggest that it would be a great coincidence if a patient who has requested a visit for one condition should suddenly develop an unrelated life-threatening condition while the doctor is on his way to visit. I think it highly likely that Mrs Whitehead was suffering only from a stomach upset and did not complain of any symptoms relating to her heart.
Shipman claims that, when he arrived, Mrs Whitehead was in heart failure to such an extent that he wondered how she had managed to let him in. Yet, his medical note of the consultation suggests that she first told him about her bowel trouble. This is a feature I have observed in some other cases where Shipman has claimed that the patient was obviously ill and yet has recorded discussions about relatively minor and less urgent problems. I am suspicious of Shipman's claim that Mrs Whitehead was obviously ill when he arrived.
Shipman told Mrs Mary Whitehead that he had given her mother-in-law an injection. In the records he said that this was 10mg morphine sulphate. That would be reasonable treatment for someone suffering severe pain from a heart attack. He could not lawfully have been carrying this drug and there is no evidence that he obtained it unlawfully. When she saw the body it was obvious to Mrs Mary Whitehead that Shipman had given an injection. The arms were bruised. It rather sounds to me as though Shipman had some difficulty in finding a vein and caused bruising of the arms. As he knew this would be visible, he has pre-empted the questions which would be asked by volunteering that he has given an injection and specifying one that was acceptable treatment. However, as Shipman was not known to carry morphine sulphate but was known to carry diamorphine, one must suspect that this injection was in fact diamorphine. It is known that Shipman obtained 30mg diamorphine that day in Mrs Whitehead's name. We do not know whether he obtained that before he went to her house or later in the day. In either event, there must be a grave suspicion that he either obtained this amount in advance to use on her or he has obtained it afterwards to replenish his stocks.
Later, Shipman was at pains to explain his decision not to attempt resuscitation. He must have known that the decision could not have been justified on the basis of the facts as known to him. He sought to involve Dr Goldthorp, implying to the family that Dr Goldthorp knew that Mrs Whitehead was suffering from cancer and would have faced a painful death.
Mrs Whitehead's appearance in death was not typical of that found in patients who have suffered a heart attack. It was, however, very similar to the appearance of many of Shipman's victims who are known to have died as the result of diamorphine poisoning.
In my view, there are so many suspicious features surrounding this case that I have been driven to the conclusion that Shipman killed Mrs Whitehead. Like the coroner, I am sure that he did so.

name: Dora Elizabeth Ashton
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Shipman's surgery, 21 Market Street, Hyde
certified_cause: cerebral embolus due to atrial fibrillation and ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
Mrs Ashton was at risk of suffering a sudden death from cerebrovascular accident. Such deaths can occur without much prior warning. However, it seems to me to be unlikely that Mrs Ashton would have walked to the surgery and chatted normally to Mrs Chapman if she had been in the throes of developing an embolus that was about to kill her. If she did, it was a remarkable coincidence that she just managed to reach Shipman's consulting room before it struck. Of course remarkable coincidences do occur. If such an event were to occur once in the professional lifetime of a doctor, I would have no great difficulty in accepting it as a genuine coincidence. But several of Shipman's patients have died suddenly, of a stroke or heart attack, in his consulting or examination rooms after having walked in without apparent difficulty. Such a coincidence stretches credibility beyond its limits. In at least one of those cases, that of Mrs Ivy Lomas, it has been proved beyond doubt that Shipman took the opportunity to inject his patient with diamorphine in the privacy of the consulting room. He plainly had the chance to do the same to Mrs Ashton.
Shipman's record of the consultation during which the death occurred cannot be taken at face value. He is known to have fabricated entries in his patients' records in order to give plausibility to the cause of death he had selected to explain a killing. In this case, no reliance can be placed on the claims that Mrs Ashton had an upgoing plantar reflex, racing pulse and very irregular heartbeat. Nor can it be accepted that she had signs of heart failure. Such signs are not consistent with her healthy appearance and ability to walk into Hyde.
Shipman's behaviour at the time of Mrs Ashton's death was highly suspicious. He told Mrs Chapman that Mrs Ashton had refused to go to hospital, although there is no reference to this in the notes. The notes imply that Mrs Ashton suffered a second stroke and lapsed into unconsciousness in his presence. He then left her alone and asked Mrs Chapman to summon Mr Ashton and to tell Mrs Ashton that her son was coming. Meanwhile he went to chat to someone. When told of the death he was not surprised, let alone shocked. He did not even conduct an adequate examination to diagnose death. He must have known already that she was dead.
Mrs Ashton's position on the examination couch is not typical of that found after a sudden death from stroke. It is, however, entirely typical of the appearance of many of Shipman's victims.
Whatever may have been Mrs Ashton's susceptibility to stroke, embolic or otherwise, the facts of the case point irresistibly to Shipman's involvement in her death. I am satisfied so as to be sure that Shipman killed her.

name: Ethel Bennett
title: Miss
place_of_death: her home, 6 Cunliffe Street, Hyde
conclusion:
This death is highly suspicious. The evidence shows that, on the day of her death, Miss Bennett was not in good health; she was suffering from a cough and wheezy chest. However, she was well enough to chat to Mr Terence Bennett, cook and eat lunch and wash up the dishes. She did not appear to have been suffering from a severe infection such as might cause her death in the near future. Shipman visited her at some time between noon and 2.30pm. In my view, he probably interrupted Miss Bennett washing up. He had the opportunity to give her an injection. She was never seen alive after the visit and I am satisfied that she was not heard to be moving about. The fact that she did not put the chain on the door when he left is a strong indication that she was unable to do so, because she was already dead or at least unconscious.
Shipman's claim that Miss Bennett was very poorly when he saw her is almost certainly false. She would not have deteriorated so suddenly after her nephew's departure. The story that a patient had refused admission to hospital was one of Shipman's recurrent themes. Had Miss Bennett really been very ill and had she really refused to go to hospital, he would have telephoned a relative to try to exert pressure on her. As it was, he left her alone and, some time later, told Mrs Cropper that she was ill but would not go to hospital. It is clear to me that by the time of Shipman's visit to Mrs Cropper, Miss Bennett was already dead.
The contents of Form B are, in my view, plainly false. There is an internal inconsistency within the document. In one place Shipman says he last saw Miss Bennett six hours before her death (which on his timings would be 10am) and in another he says he saw her at 1pm, only three hours before the supposed time of death. It would be most unusual for Shipman to visit as early as 10am. A much more likely time is 1pm, although he could have been at Miss Bennett's home rather later than that. Shipman falsely claimed that a neighbour had heard Miss Bennett moving about after his departure. This falsehood was plainly designed to create the impression that Miss Bennett was alive when he left and that the death had taken place some hours after his departure.
Miss Bennett's appearance in death was not consistent with a death from bronchopneumonia but was entirely typical of the appearance of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of opiate.
I cannot make any positive finding about the property which the family says was missing from Miss Bennett's home. There is a suspicion that Shipman might have stolen it but no more.
This death has Shipman's hallmark on it. I am quite sure that Shipman killed Miss Bennett. He must have administered a lethal injection, almost certainly of diamorphine.

name: Mary Coutts
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 26 Marler Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I think it likely that Shipman was at Mrs Coutts' flat from about 1.40pm until about 2.10-2.15pm. As Mrs Coutts was found dead only a few minutes after his departure, the level of suspicion that he caused her death is very high.
For all the reasons given by Dr Grenville, I do not accept that Mrs Coutts died of bronchopneumonia. Save in very unusual circumstances, that condition develops over a period of days. Mrs Coutts was not obviously ill until the morning of the day of her death. If she were so close to death from bronchopneumonia when Shipman was at the house, she would not have been able to get up and dress herself a few hours earlier. Nor is it plausible that Shipman would have left her alone in the house without any arrangements for her care.
Shipman's account to the family that Mrs Coutts had refused to go to hospital does not ring true. I do not think Mrs Coutts would have refused to go to hospital if Shipman had advised her that she was seriously ill and in need of admission. It is one thing to tell a friend that one does not want to go to hospital and quite another to refuse to do so in the face of medical advice.
I am also confident that Shipman has falsified the time of his attendance when completing Form B, so as to make it appear that the death occurred over an hour after his departure.
So far, everything points towards Shipman having killed Mrs Coutts. However, there are two features of this death that are not typical of cases in which Shipman has killed. First, there is clear evidence that Mrs Coutts was not sitting in the relaxed position in which so many of Shipman's victims were found. She was turned to one side, giving the impression that she might have been trying to reach for the telephone. Dr Grenville has observed that this position is consistent with a death by natural causes and is not typical of the appearance following cases in which Shipman has killed. However, he also made the point that the appearance is not necessarily inconsistent with a diamorphine death. Some patients do not like to watch an injection and turn their bodies away from the doctor during the procedure. He also suggested that it is possible that Mrs Coutts may have felt a wave of nausea as she was given the injection and may have turned away from Shipman for that reason.
The second atypical feature arises from the evidence (if it is correct) that Mrs Atherton saw Mrs Coutts walk across the room back to her chair just after Shipman had left. She had the impression that Mrs Coutts had seen him out and then walked back to her chair. Dr Grenville said that Mrs Coutts would not have been able to do this if she had been given a large dose of diamorphine intravenously. However, if the dose had been given intramuscularly, or, if the needle had accidentally come out of the vein during the procedure so that the diamorphine had entered subcutaneously, it would have taken longer for the drug to take effect. If Shipman had decided to leave, Mrs Coutts might have been able to show him out and walk back to her chair, possibly feeling dizzy and wishing to reach the telephone. She could then have lost consciousness and died. However, it was Shipman's usual practice to wait until a patient to whom he had given diamorphine had died. To do otherwise would be very risky. If for any reason the patient was found and resuscitated vigorously, he or she might survive to tell the tale. If Shipman had given Mrs Coutts an injection of diamorphine, it would be unusual for him to leave her alive. However, it is possible that he did so, confident that it would not be long before she lapsed into unconsciousness.
There is another possible factual finding. Mrs Atherton might be wrong when she says that she saw Mrs Coutts walking across the room just at the time Shipman was leaving. Mrs Mary Clarke is sure that Mrs Atherton told her that Shipman had come out of the flat and gone back in, carrying his black box. She could be right and Mrs Atherton could have forgotten that part of the incident. It could have been at that stage that Mrs Coutts showed Shipman out and returned to her chair. That would have been before he had given her an injection.
I have come to the conclusion that Shipman was responsible for Mrs Coutts' death. The death was discovered so soon after Shipman's departure that it would have been a quite remarkable coincidence for a natural death to occur within the five to ten minutes that had elapsed between his departure and Mr Fox's arrival.
The problems in this case arise, not in deciding whether Shipman killed Mrs Coutts, but exactly how he did it. There are two possibilities, either of which is feasible. He might have given her an intravenous injection of opiate, in which case she would have died quickly, and would not have been able to see him out and return to her chair. On the other hand, he might have given an intramuscular or subcutaneous injection, in which case Mrs Coutts would have been able to show Shipman out and return to her chair, as Mrs Atherton suggests. I have no doubt that Mrs Atherton is an honest witness doing her best to assist the Inquiry, but I cannot be sure that every detail of her evidence is accurate. I do not know which is the true explanation. But I am sure that Shipman did kill Mrs Coutts.

name: Miriam Davies
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 10 Clarence Street, Hyde
conclusion: I am quite sure that Mrs Davies died from natural causes and there is no reason to suspect that Shipman was in any way involved. His visits book discloses no visit to Mrs Davies on the day of her death. I have included this case in my Report because it illustrates the type of concern felt by the residents of Hyde as the result of Shipman's criminal conduct. Mr Davies was understandably concerned about his grandmother's death, as she was found dead in circumstances similar to those of the deaths of many of Shipman's victims. I hope his concern has now been allayed.

name: Agnes Edge
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
It would appear from the daily diary that from the time of her admission, Mrs Edge was suffering from confusion, a state of mind that may well have been attributable to cerebroatherosclerosis. Moreover, her condition seems to have deteriorated in the days leading up to her death. The record indicates that her daughter was very concerned about her and her relatives asked that a priest should visit her. I infer from these aspects of the evidence that Mrs Edge's death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
There is no satisfactory evidence that Shipman saw Mrs Edge alive after 16th
March. There is some slight suspicion that he did so, raised by the entry in his visits book and the alteration he made on the MCCD counterfoil.
It is likely that Shipman last saw Mrs Edge alive on 16th
March as he claimed on the MCCD counterfoil and as indicated by the daily diary. I do not think he can have given a lumbar puncture. Dr Esmail says that such procedures are usually carried out in sterile conditions in hospital. The object of a lumbar puncture is to take a sample of spinal fluid for the purpose of analysis. I can only think that the person who made the record has misdescribed what Shipman did. It may be that he gave Mrs Edge a spinal injection, possibly of local anaesthetic, in the hope that it would give her relief from the pain of her bedsores. It may be that the note seeks to describe an injection into the buttock. Whatever the treatment was, it seems that Mrs Edge remained unsettled. I have also considered the possibility that Shipman administered an injection of something other than Valium on that day. It is possible that he administered an opiate. Even if he did, I can rule out the possibility that this injection caused or hastened Mrs Edge's death. She did not fall into a deep or prolonged sleep and lived for four days after the injection. By then, its effect would long since have worn off.
I cannot rule out the possibility that Shipman saw Mrs Edge alive on 20th
March. If he did and the Charnley House staff did not note his visit, it is possible that he did something to hasten her end. However, it is clear that Mrs Edge was very close to death by the morning of 20th
March. It seems to me likely that Mrs Edge died of the natural causes certified by Shipman.

name: Thomas Fowden
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 40 Mona Street, Hyde
certified_cause: left ventricular failure due to chronic obstructive airways disease
conclusion:
There are some suspicious features surrounding this death, although the circumstances are not wholly typical of cases in which Shipman killed.
I do not know how Mr Fowden came to be in the condition in which Mrs Ralphs found him. It is possible that her visit coincided with a severe acute exacerbation of his respiratory problems or an acute attack of left ventricular failure. However, his condition does not sound typical of what one would expect in such circumstances. Mrs Ralphs does not say that Mr Fowden was gasping for breath. Rather, she gives the impression that he was about to expire quite gently. It is also possible that Mr Fowden was in the condition in which he was found because Shipman had been at the house a short time earlier and had done something to him. I suspect that that was so for several reasons. First, on Form B Shipman said that he had seen Mr Fowden two hours before the death. That is not necessarily accurate, as Shipman often fabricated entries on Form B. However, it is unlikely that Shipman would have admitted that he had seen Mr Fowden earlier if he had not. Second, I note that Mr Edwin Fowden recalls that Shipman said he had given his uncle an injection. Mrs Ralphs does not mention this and certainly does not seem to have witnessed the administration of an injection. This suggests that the injection was given before her arrival. Third, Shipman seems to have responded with exceptional promptness to Mrs Ralphs' request for help, even taking into account that Mona Street is only a short distance from the surgery. It is quite possible that Shipman did not attend in response to her request but had returned to the house expecting to 'discover' his patient either dead or dying. It would be entirely typical of Shipman's method that he should administer a lethal injection and then leave the patient to die, while he went away for a few minutes, in search of a neighbour whom he would bring back to be present at the moment of death. Alternatively, he sometimes left the patient dead and went about his business, returning an hour or so later to 'discover' the body. Either is possible here. It seems likely that Shipman had been at Mr Fowden's house quite recently. Whether he returned in response to a request or of his own volition, he cannot have been far away.
Shipman's conduct that day is highly suspect. If he had visited Mr Fowden and found him so unwell that he needed an injection of some kind and in such condition that his subsequent death was not a surprise, one might have expected him to do something more for Mr Fowden. He might have telephoned for an ambulance. He might have telephoned Mr Edwin Fowden. He might have gone in search of the home help. What he would not have done is leave Mr Fowden alone for anything approaching two hours, as he appears to suggest on Form B.
One question which arises is why Shipman would have called on Mr Fowden that day, supposedly two hours before his death. Mr Fowden's name is not in the visits book, which suggests that there was no request that morning for a routine or non-urgent visit. It is possible that someone requested an urgent visit, which would not usually be noted in the visits book, but if that had happened, one would have expected that person to have remained on the scene or at least to have identified himself or herself to Mr Edwin Fowden after the death. The remaining possibility is that Shipman decided to make an unsolicited visit. His visits book shows that he had only one visit booked for that day and there is a real possibility that he decided of his own volition to call on Mr Fowden. That would not of itself give rise to any suspicion. Mr Fowden was 81 and it would be good practice to call on him from time to time. However, for a patient to die suddenly during such a visit would be highly suspicious.
The question also arises as to what sort of injection Shipman gave Mr Fowden. If Mr Fowden had been in left ventricular failure, it might have been appropriate for Shipman to give an injection of a strong diuretic, which would relieve the pressure on the heart. However, Mrs Ralph's description is not typical of a person dying of left ventricular failure. It is more suggestive of one dying of gradual respiratory depression. The suspicion must arise that Shipman gave an injection of opiate or some other drug which had the effect of depressing Mr Fowden's respiration. Shipman's usual method of killing was to give an intravenous injection of a lethal dose of opiate, usually diamorphine, which causes unconsciousness and death within a few minutes. In a few cases, I believe he gave an intramuscular injection of a lethal dose of opiate. This would usually take between half an hour to an hour to kill, although it might act more quickly in a patient with poor respiratory function such as Mr Fowden. There are other possibilities, such as a very large dose of Largactil, which might also have the effect of depressing respiration and might well kill a patient with poor respiratory function. It is possible that Shipman gave an intravenous injection of opiate and left Mr Fowden for a few minutes, during which time Mrs Ralphs arrived and found him shortly before he lapsed into unconsciousness. It is also possible that Shipman gave an intramuscular injection of opiate or some other sedative and went away for a longer period, during which time Mrs Ralphs arrived to find Mr Fowden still conscious but unable to speak.
My conclusion is that I think it likely that Shipman killed Mr Fowden, but in the absence of any medical records and any reliable evidence of Shipman's movements on the day of the death, I do not feel able to rule out the possibility that this was a natural death.

name: John Sheard Greenhalgh
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 23 Cheetham Fold Road, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of very suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. The first and most obvious is that the death was discovered not long after a visit from Shipman.
