No one spoke to Mr Greenhalgh or saw him alive after Shipman's visit. That in itself is a highly suspicious circumstance. I suspect that this was a completely unsolicited visit. There is no record of a visit request in the surgery records and I have already said that I think it unlikely that Mr Greenhalgh would have made such a call himself and more likely that he would have asked Mr Cropper to do it for him. It is entirely possible that Shipman had heard that Mr Greenhalgh had gone back on his agreement to move into sheltered accommodation and decided to speak to him about that.
Although Mr Greenhalgh suffered from a number of disabilities, none of these was of a life-threatening nature. There is nothing in the medical records to suggest that Mr Greenhalgh was at an increased risk of dying a sudden death. Shipman did not suggest that Mr Greenhalgh's death was sudden; he certified that it was due to old age. In his generic evidence, Dr John Grenville explained that it is not appropriate to certify that a death was due to old age unless the patient has deteriorated gradually over a period of time and has reached a moribund state. Usually the patient will have been bedridden and in need of nursing care. In those circumstances, it may be difficult for the doctor to specify exactly what organ failure led to the death and it is appropriate to put 'old age'. Mr Greenhalgh did not fall into this category. He was not bedridden. He had been looking after himself with help from his care worker and the meals on wheels service. As Shipman said on Form B, no one nursed him in his 'last illness'. In fact, there was no last illness. Mr Cropper saw him twice daily and knows that he had not deteriorated significantly in the past weeks. Shipman quite often certified a death as due to old age when he had killed a patient and the medical history did not reveal a plausible explanation for the death. His last victim, Mrs Kathleen Grundy, was one such case. I regard an unwarranted certification of old age as the cause of death as a suspicious feature.
Shipman told some deliberate lies on Form B. I have already mentioned his false claim that he attended Mr Greenhalgh for three months during his last illness. He also claimed to know that the death had occurred at about 8pm. There was no rational basis on which he could say that. There were good, common-sense reasons why he could properly say that the death had occurred on 27th
rather than 28th
February. Mr Greenhalgh had obviously not been to bed on the night before his body was found. But there was nothing which would have enabled Shipman to say that the death occurred at 8pm as opposed to 2pm, which was the time of his visit. It seems to me that Shipman was seeking to distance the death from the time of his visit and there was no basis for him to do so. Shipman also painted the picture of a man who had fallen asleep while watching television and had died in his sleep. The evidence is that the television was not on. It is likely that the television would not have been on during a doctor's visit. On Form B, Shipman has sought to paint a false picture of a man who had been ill for three months, whose death was therefore not unexpected, and who died in his sleep.
I have considered the possibility that Mr Greenhalgh might have died quite suddenly from some natural cause. Given his age, this must be a real possibility. However, the medical records do not reveal any likely cause. Shipman has made a rather pathetic attempt to suggest that Mr Greenhalgh had suffered a right-sided stroke about five days before his death. We know that that is not true, as Mr Cropper would have noticed if his speech was slurred and he had weakness on one side. This false entry in the records is another suspicious factor in itself. It indicates that Shipman was trying to create a plausible cause of death. However, it seems very unlikely that Mr Greenhalgh died of a stroke. If a stroke, which had begun five days earlier, was going to prove fatal, it would have developed before 27th
February and the signs would have been obvious to all. I think it highly unlikely that Mr Greenhalgh died of a stroke or any other of the common causes of sudden death. His position and appearance in death were not typical of such deaths. They were, on the other hand, entirely typical of the appearance of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by a lethal injection of an opiate.
Taking all these factors into account, I have come to the conclusion that the overwhelming probability is that Shipman killed Mr Greenhalgh. I am satisfied so as to be sure of this conclusion. Shipman's method was almost certainly to inject him with a lethal dose of diamorphine.

name: David Jones
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 27 Rufford Avenue, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
Mr Jones had a history of ischaemic heart disease, unstable angina, sub-endocardial myocardial infarction, chronic obstructive airways disease and hiatus hernia. He had been a frequent patient at hospital on account of his chest pain. This history suggests that Mr Jones was at high risk of suffering a death from cardiac causes, although correspondence from the hospital suggests that he was well on 21st
December. His death was sudden but by no means inexplicable.
However, there are some circumstances surrounding this death which raise a suspicion that Shipman might have been involved. The first is the suddenness of the death. Mr Jones was out and about on 21st
December and was found dead the next morning, wearing his day clothes. It seems at least possible, even likely, that he died on 21st
December. In such circumstances, most doctors would refer the death to the coroner with a view to post-mortem examination. Shipman did not.
Another factor which arouses some suspicion is that Shipman claimed on Form B that he was able to tell at what time the death had occurred. In his generic evidence, Dr John Grenville has explained that it is not possible to estimate the time of a death without taking an internal body temperature, usually in the rectum. Even then, the task of estimation is a difficult operation and is usually only attempted by a pathologist. Pathologists do not usually claim to be able to make an exact estimate, as Shipman often did and appears to have done in this case. Whenever I see that Shipman made a precise estimate of the time of death, I suspect that he might have an ulterior motive. I have come across many cases in which he has killed a patient and has claimed to be able to estimate the time of death precisely. He had always estimated it some hours after his last visit. In other words, he has distanced himself from the death. In the present case, he had estimated the time of death at midnight and the death has been registered as having occurred on 22nd
December. Shipman could not possibly have known when the death occurred. All he could honestly have said was that it had occurred at some time between whenever Mr Jones had last been seen, which was probably when Mrs Knipe saw him going out, and the time when his body had been found. I suspect that Shipman wanted to create the impression that the death occurred at midnight because he could not have visited at that time. If he had visited, the latest time would probably have been about 6.30pm and he would not know whether or not he had been seen.
As I have said, there is no eyewitness evidence to show that Shipman visited Mr Jones on 21st
December. Moreover, the layout of Rufford Avenue, which I have seen for myself, is such that a visitor who came by car in the hours of daylight would probably be noticed. The houses are set round an oval grassy area and there are usually very few cars parked on the road. I can well understand why Mrs Aughton thinks she would have noticed if Shipman had visited. Having said that, it would not be at all surprising if Shipman were able to visit in the hours of darkness without being noticed. On 21st
December it would have been dark by 4pm.
In Form B of the cremation certificate and on the MCCD counterfoil, Shipman claimed that he had last seen Mr Jones alive on 12th
or 14th
December. As 12th
December was a Sunday, that seems unlikely unless Mr Jones called Shipman out in an emergency. There is no evidence that he did. For Tuesday, 14th
December, there is an entry in the medical records but it does not appear to suggest a personal consultation. The appointments sheets and visits books do not suggest that Shipman actually saw Mr Jones. I recognise that Shipman was often cavalier in respect of his duties of certification and frequently claimed to have seen a patient when he had not, even when there is no suspicion that he might have killed the patient. This kind of white lie does not raise a high degree of suspicion. However, it is possible that Shipman wished to create the impression that he had seen Mr Jones within 14 days so as to avoid the possibility that the registrar might refer the death to the coroner. It is possible that he fabricated an entry in the medical records and initially created one for 12th
December. When he realised that this was a Sunday, he might have changed it to 14th
December.
There is an entry in the computerised records which suggests a visit on 20th
December, but it gives no detail at all. This is puzzling, because if Shipman had seen Mr Jones on 20th
December, one would have expected him to enter that date on the MCCD counterfoil and Form B rather than 14th
December. Mr Jones' name does not appear in Shipman's visits book for 20th
December and I suspect that there was no such visit. Unfortunately, it is not possible to check when that entry was made, as there was no audit trail facility on the computer in 1993. I suspect that this entry might have been made after Mr Jones' death as part of a cover-up. If someone had seen Shipman at the house on 21st
December, he might have been able to show that that person was wrong and had really seen him on 20th
December.
These suspicions do not in themselves amount to very much. However, it appears to me that Mr Jones would have been a suitable and likely victim for Shipman. Shipman disapproved of patients who would not accept advice. He sometimes killed patients who he thought were a nuisance and required a great deal of his attention. In my view, he also disapproved of the use of public resources on patients who would not take care of themselves. I think Mr Jones would have excited Shipman's disapproval on all three grounds.
These suspicions do not amount to enough for me to say that I think Shipman probably killed Mr Jones. Mr Jones might well have died a natural death. However, there are such grounds for suspicion that I am not prepared to say that he probably did. I feel unable to reach any positive conclusion.

name: Florence Lewis
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 41 Mansfield Road, Hyde
conclusion:
The circumstances of this death are very highly suspicious. I am quite satisfied that the man in the red 'people carrier' seen by Mr Graham outside Mrs Lewis' house in the early afternoon of 10th
November was Shipman. When he arrived, she was working in her garden. Mrs Lewis was found dead the next morning. No one saw her or spoke to her after Shipman's visit. That factor is highly suspicious in itself.
Mrs Lewis' death was wholly unexpected. She had been in reasonably good health. Her raised blood pressure, atheroma of the carotid arteries and past history of transient ischaemic attacks put her at an increased risk of suffering a cerebrovascular accident. A sudden death from that cause was, therefore, possible. Other factors point away from this being a death due to a massive stroke. Mrs Lewis' appearance in death was not typical of that seen following a massive fatal stroke. It was entirely typical of that seen in many of Shipman's victims. It would have been an extraordinary coincidence that a sudden death from natural causes should have taken place so soon after Shipman's visit.
Shipman made false entries on the MCCD and on Form B. First, and most important, he concealed the fact that he had seen Mrs Lewis on the day of her death. He also failed to make any note of that visit in the medical records. I can only conclude that this was a dishonest concealment. He also sought to suggest that Mrs Lewis had been found by her son late in the evening of 10th
November. He does not say that she was found dead. As he suggested that the death had occurred in the late evening, it seems that he might have been seeking to suggest that the son was present at the death. However, he does not state that in specific terms. He does give the impression that the son and paramedics were able to tell him something about the cause and mode of death. That is wholly misleading.
Shipman claimed to be able to certify the cause of death at a time when he had not apparently seen the body. If this was a natural death, it was sudden and unexpected and its cause could not have been adequately established without a post-mortem examination. Shipman's failure to refer this death to the coroner is suspicious.
Taking all these matters into account, I am left in no doubt at all that Shipman killed Mrs Lewis during his visit on the afternoon of 10th
November. The mode of killing was almost certainly his usual method, a lethal injection of diamorphine.

name: Martha Marley
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 10 Mona Street, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of suspicious circumstances surrounding this death.
Mrs Marley was badly disabled by osteoarthritis and suffered from chronic obstructive airways disease. She had also been diagnosed by Shipman as having congestive heart failure but the diagnosis was based on rather slender evidence. If the diagnosis was correct, the condition was kept under very good control. There is nothing in her medical history to suggest that she was particularly at risk of sudden death by the two most common causes, heart attack or stroke. This does not mean that she cannot have died a sudden death, only that such an event was less likely for her than for others with risk factors. Her chronic obstructive airways disease was extremely stable. Her medical records show that she very rarely needed a doctor. This death was sudden and unexpected.
Shipman certified that Mrs Marley's death was due to old age. This was quite inappropriate. Mrs Marley was living a relatively independent life, with some support from her family. She was not confined to bed. She was mentally quite alert. She had not suffered the gradual decline which would make it appropriate for the doctor to certify death as due to old age. It must be a rare case in which a patient dies of old age alone at home and without ever having needed nursing care. Usually the patient will have been confined to bed for some time, will have required a high level of care and will be attended at the time of death by members of the family or other carers. Shipman admitted on Form B that Mrs Marley had not had nursing care. However, he sought to create the impression that she had declined gradually over a period of a year by claiming that he had attended her during that time in connection with her last illness, which he implied was old age. This was quite misleading.
I ask myself why Shipman chose to certify this death as due to old age in circumstances when he must have well known that it was not appropriate. It is possible that Mrs Marley had died a sudden natural death, in which case Shipman could have had little idea of the cause. Mrs Marley's medical history did not provide an explanation for any sudden death. There was no history of hypertension, heart disease or venous problems, such as might give rise to an embolism. The only way to find out the real cause would have been by referral to the coroner and post-mortem examination. Instead, Shipman decided not to refer the death but to certify the cause as old age. If he had certified the cause as heart attack or stroke, he might well have thought it necessary to fabricate some entries in the medical records to provide a background for his diagnosis. He had done that on a number of occasions. Instead, he chose old age. He seems to have felt that no great alteration of the medical history was necessary and all that was required was a claim on Form B that he had been attending Mrs Marley for 12 months in connection with her last illness.
I ask myself why any doctor would stoop to or even bother to make a misleading entry on an official form just for the sake of avoiding a referral to the coroner. If the death were natural, why would Shipman seek to avoid referral to the coroner? He often did make false entries in order to avoid referral in cases where there is no suspicion that he caused the death. The common form of false entry was to claim, as he did here, that he had seen the patient within 14 days of the death when he had not. He seemed to think that unless he could say this he would not be qualified to certify the cause of death. Why did he want to avoid referral to the coroner? I think in some cases he wished to spare the family the delay and emotional distress involved. But in this case, where a referral was clearly needed, Shipman did not seek to find out whether the family would be distressed at the thought of a post-mortem examination. He planted in their minds the idea that it would be better not to have a post-mortem examination. I conclude that Shipman's motive in seeking to avoid a post-mortem examination was connected with himself and not with the family. It is possible that he did not want to be bothered with the procedures involved. However, it is also possible that the death was not natural and he feared detection by toxicology if the initial autopsy did not provide an acceptable explanation for the death. Knowing, as I now know, that by March 1998 Shipman had already killed a great number of his patients, I think it far more likely that Shipman wished to avoid referral because he was guilty than because he could not be bothered with the procedures involved.
Mrs Marley's position and appearance in death were not typical of those seen following a sudden natural death from any of the common causes. Usually where a person dies of a heart attack or stroke, they have the time and opportunity to get up in an attempt to seek help. Mrs Marley appeared to have gone to sleep and showed no sign of an agonal event. Shipman emphasised her peaceful appearance in his description on Form B. This peaceful appearance is entirely typical of that of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by a lethal injection of opiate.
Further suspicion arises from Shipman's claim that he was able to estimate the time of death as 5.30pm. He would not have been able to do this. All he could properly have said was that Mrs Marley was known to have been alive at 9am when she spoke to her daughter and was probably dead at 6pm when she failed to answer the telephone. If there were no rigor mortis he would have been able to say that the death was more likely to have occurred in the afternoon than in the morning. Instead, he gave a precise time of death. I have found many cases in which Shipman has done this and I have formed the view that he usually did it in order to create the impression that the death occurred a considerable time after he had last been with the patient. He was distancing himself from the death. In this case, there is no evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Marley on the day of her death. If he did and if he killed her, he would not know whether or not he had been seen arriving at or leaving the house. At 5.30pm, he would have been in his surgery seeing patients. That Shipman should bother to pretend that he knew the time of death raises my level of suspicion.
If there were any evidence that Shipman had visited Mrs Marley on the day of her death, I would say that this was a typical Shipman killing. There is no such evidence. Nor is there any obvious prompt for a visit. Moreover, whilst it is well known that Shipman used to call in unannounced to see many patients and that such visits would not be routinely recorded in his visits book, I do not think he often called in on Mrs Marley. Thus, if Shipman did visit her that day, the reason is obscure. I am satisfied that Shipman had the time to visit her and that a visit would not have been inconvenient. I also think that a visit would not necessarily have been observed by the neighbours, particularly as it is quite possible Shipman did not take his car or did not leave it in Mona Street.
I must consider the time at which Shipman could have killed Mrs Marley. As I think Mrs Marley was already dead at 6pm when Mrs Siddelley telephoned her, Shipman must have visited her before 4pm, if he visited her at all. When Mrs Siddelley found the body at about 6.45pm, she formed the impression that the body was warm. That was about three hours after Shipman could have been there. The fire was on in the room but it would be surprising if the body still felt warm three hours after death. Mrs Siddelley's evidence that the body felt warm to the touch suggests that Shipman was not involved. I do not place great reliance on this evidence as it appears to me to be based largely on impression.
Taking all these factors into account, I conclude that Shipman probably killed Mrs Marley. The evidence of his falsehoods on Form B is readily explicable on the basis of guilt and is inconsistent with innocence. I stop short of saying that I am sure of that conclusion. There is no evidence that Shipman had access to Mrs Marley. I have inferred that he probably did. I also infer that he probably killed her by his usual method, an intravenous injection of opiate. I have borne in mind my knowledge that by March 1998, Shipman was and had for some years been an habitual killer.

name: Bertha Parr
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 3 Booth Street, Hyde
conclusion:
There are some suspicious features surrounding this death. First, Shipman certified an unacceptable cause of death. Second, he appears to have lied when claiming that he had last seen Mrs Parr alive on 31st
October. Both these factors raise the suspicion that he was anxious to prevent this case from being referred to the coroner for post-mortem examination. However, such factors, taken by themselves, may be explained by a desire on Shipman's part to avoid the trouble of referring the case to the coroner. The Inquiry has now seen several cases where Shipman entered false details in cremation documents, but played no sinister part in the deaths in question.
On cremation Form B, Shipman claimed to have treated Mrs Parr during her last illness when he had not done so. This must have been a lie, as Mrs Parr had had no illness and Shipman had been unable to suggest any condition or illness from which Mrs Parr had died.
When Mrs Parr's body was found on 12th
November, Shipman claimed to be able to estimate that the death had occurred in the mid-afternoon of the previous day. In his generic evidence, Dr Grenville explained that it would not have been possible for Shipman to estimate the time of death from the information which was, on the face of it, available to him. Estimation of the time of death from body temperature is a difficult process and lies within the province of an expert pathologist. A rectal temperature must be taken. Shipman often pretended to be able to estimate the time of death. Whenever I see that Shipman has done that, as he has done here, I suspect that he might have done so in order to distance the death from the time of his own visit. In this case, Shipman has suggested on Form B that the death took place in the mid-afternoon of 11th
November. Yet Mrs Haslip claims to have seen Mrs Parr alive between 4pm and 5pm. If Mrs Haslip is right, the only time that Shipman could have visited Mrs Parr and killed her would have been in the early evening on his way home from work. If he had done that, he would not have wished to suggest that Mrs Parr had died in the mid-afternoon. He would have been more likely to suggest that she had died late in the evening. It seems unlikely that Mrs Parr did die in the evening. Her curtains were open. On 11th
November, most people would close their curtains at about 4.30 to 5pm. It is possible that when Mrs Parr returned from her visit to Mrs Haslip, she felt ill and died before having the chance to close the curtains. This would suggest that the death was natural. However, it is also possible that Mrs Haslip is mistaken about the day on which Mrs Parr visited her. If Mrs Parr was not in fact seen between 4pm and 5pm on 11th
November, it would be entirely possible that Shipman had visited and killed her in the late morning or early afternoon and had then sought to give the impression that she had died some hours after his visit.
Mrs Parr's position in death was consistent with sudden death from natural causes such as a heart attack, stroke, pulmonary embolus or ruptured aortic aneurysm and was not typical of the position in which Shipman's victims were found. However, it is possible that she could have slumped into this position following a lethal injection.
Mrs Parr was at a higher risk than normal of a sudden death because of her diabetes and hypertension. A natural death would not have been wholly unexpected. There is no positive evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Parr on 11th
November. These factors would suggest that the death was natural, although of an unascertained cause. However, Shipman told a number of lies on the certification documents and showed a distinct reluctance to allow this sudden death to be referred to the coroner. It is not fanciful to suggest that he might have visited Mrs Parr and killed her on 11th
November. I feel unable to reach a positive conclusion on this case and suspect that Shipman may be responsible for the death.

name: Ernest Rudol
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 11 Forrest Road, Haughton Green, Denton
conclusion:
There are a number of highly suspicious features to this death. The first and most obvious is that the death was discovered not long after a visit by Shipman, at which he had been alone with Mr Rudol. No one saw Mr Rudol alive or spoke to him after Shipman's visit. That factor, in itself, is sufficient to give rise to strong suspicion.
Mr Rudol was not in the best of health at the time of his death and must have been at a significantly increased risk of suffering a stroke. He had a fall on 26th
June, the day before his appointment at the renal clinic. However, he was very thoroughly examined by the doctor at the clinic and was not found to be showing any signs of a stroke at that time. I think it highly unlikely that the clinic doctor would have missed signs of a stroke if they had been present.
On the morning of the day of his death, Mr Rudol was upset and telephoned his daughter-in-law. At some time that morning, someone telephoned the surgery to request a visit. This might have been Mr Rudol or it could have been Mrs Darragh, Mrs Rudol or the district nurse. In any event, the message was that Mr Rudol had had a fall two days earlier and was shaky. There was no sense of urgency about this and nothing that clearly suggested that Mr Rudol had had a stroke. I think it highly unlikely that Mr Rudol was showing any signs of a stroke that morning, as, if he had been, I think at least one of his visitors would have observed something seriously amiss.
Shipman must have visited either in the late morning or early afternoon. In the medical records and on the MCCD and Form B, he has sought to suggest that, when he arrived, he found that Mr Rudol had had a stroke and concluded that this had begun two days earlier. I think that this suggestion was misleading and probably a deliberate lie. Mr Rudol had not had a stroke when his son saw him in the evening two days before his death. Nor was he showing any signs of a stroke in the early morning of 29th June. It is possible that Mr Rudol had suffered a stroke after the last of his visitors had left and before Shipman arrived, but this would be something of a coincidence. In any event, that is not what Shipman has sought to suggest. I think it highly likely that Mr Rudol was showing no signs of a stroke at all. Had he been weak on one side, as Shipman claims, it is inconceivable that he could responsibly leave Mr Rudol completely unattended. In my view, Shipman has created a false history of a stroke. He has also sought to suggest that Mr Rudol's son was in a position to provide information relevant to the cause or mode of death. This is misleading, as Mr Rudol's son knew nothing of the circumstances of the death.
In his generic evidence, Dr Grenville explained that, where a patient suffers an occlusive stroke, the type of stroke that causes weakness on one side of the body, the patient does not usually die. If the stroke does prove fatal, death usually occurs following a gradual deterioration in the patient's level of consciousness. The changes usually occur over a period of several days but certainly at least over a number of hours. It would be most unusual for a patient to die suddenly of an occlusive stroke. A brain stem haemorrhage can cause sudden death but it would be most unusual for a patient to have two different types of stroke at about the same time. This is a further reason for suspecting Shipman's claim that this death was due to a stroke.
Mr Rudol's appearance in death was wholly typical of many of Shipman's patients who had been killed by lethal injection of diamorphine.
I have come to the conclusion that the only sensible inference I can draw from the evidence is that Shipman killed Mr Rudol. I think it likely that, when he heard that Mr Rudol had had a fall, Shipman seized on that as an opportunity to kill Mr Rudol and to pass off his death as being due to a stroke. I am sure of this conclusion.

name: Edith Scott
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 155 Dowson Road, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of suspicious features surrounding this death.
Mrs Scott was 85 years old. The picture I have from the evidence is that she had been fit and independent until her attack of shingles in early 1995, but that from then onwards she became rather frail. She had no history of heart trouble. It is possible for a woman of 85 to die suddenly of a heart attack even without having exhibited any signs of heart disease. However, the fact that she should die of such an attack on a day when Shipman has visited her at home (not apparently in response to an urgent request to attend) arouses a significant degree of suspicion. If Mrs Scott had telephoned the surgery to request a visit, the usual practice would have been for the staff to record the reason for her request. If the request had been urgent, it would have been most unusual for the staff not to record the reasons. No reason is recorded. There is a real possibility that Shipman had seen Mrs Scott in the road when he was on his way to visit his other patient nearby. They might have spoken to each other; she might have said that she was not feeling well and he might have promised to visit her later that afternoon. To a large extent these suggestions are supposition, but they are feasible and are not untypical of Shipman's conduct in other cases.
The only evidence that Mrs Scott suffered a heart attack on 13th
April comes from Shipman's own note. I am bound to treat that note with some suspicion, as there are many cases in which Shipman has made false or exaggerated entries in the records of patients he has killed. I find the suggestion that Mrs Scott was suffering from chest pain on that day to be implausible. There is evidence from Mrs Clarke that Mrs Scott was looking pale and feeling tired that day, but I think that Mrs Scott would have said that she had chest pain if that had been so. Moreover, I am confident that she would have telephoned her daughter and probably her niece if she had been suffering chest pain. I also find it implausible that Mrs Scott would have refused to go to hospital if Shipman had so advised, at least without speaking to her daughter. Shipman's entry in the records, suggesting that Mrs Scott had had a heart attack but had refused hospital admission and had died shortly afterwards, is typical of several cases in which I have found that he has killed the patient. In many respects, the circumstances of this death are entirely typical of cases in which Shipman killed.
The evidence of Mrs Clarke is puzzling. Mrs Clarke suggests that Mrs Scott had been to the surgery that morning under her own steam. That is possible, although it appears that, if she had, she had not seen Shipman. I am satisfied that Shipman visited Mrs Scott that day, although I have no means of knowing at what time. It is possible that Mrs Clarke is mistaken about the events of that day. After all, she was not asked to recall the details until more than three years later. If she were mistaken about meeting Mrs Scott outside the house, but correct in her recollection that Mrs Scott had said that she had already seen the doctor, her account would point to Shipman having visited before 1pm. That would mean that Mrs Scott was seen alive after Shipman had gone. If Mrs Clarke was correct about meeting her outside, but mistaken in recalling that Mrs Scott had said that she had already seen Shipman that day, her account would be consistent with a visit by Shipman after Mrs Clarke had left. He would then have had the opportunity to administer a lethal injection and leave Mrs Scott dead, to be found later that afternoon by Mrs Clarke and Mr Adams. In my view, the most likely explanation is that Mrs Scott had seen and spoken to Shipman while she was out that morning but had not yet had a consultation with him.
Mrs Scott's peaceful appearance is not typical of a death following a heart attack. Her appearance in death is very similar indeed to that of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by diamorphine injection. That Mrs Scott appears to have vomited shortly before death is consistent with death from heart attack or death from diamorphine injection. That a cup and saucer had been knocked over on the floor is consistent with death by heart attack or death by diamorphine.
There are some probable inaccuracies on Form B. In particular, Shipman suggested that he had last seen Mrs Scott alive at about 9am. Given what is known of Shipman's usual practice, and the appointments sheet for that day, it seems highly likely that he was in the surgery from 8.45am until about 11am. He would then usually do some paperwork before setting out on his rounds. It is possible that he could have visited Mrs Scott very early in the morning before surgery. If he did, there is no reason to suppose that he killed her, as Mrs Clarke says she saw Mrs Scott alive at about 1pm. If Shipman did not visit until after 1pm, which would be his usual visiting time, it would appear that he has made a false entry on Form B, which has had the effect of distancing him from Mrs Scott's death.
Finally, this was a sudden and unexpected death in the case of a lady with no history of heart disease. Shipman should have referred it to the coroner. The fact that he did not arouses some suspicion. However, it must be acknowledged that Shipman's attitude to the requirements of the law relating to the registration of deaths was cavalier, even in cases in which he cannot be suspected of criminal involvement. I cannot attach great weight to his failure to report this death to the coroner.
Taken together, these points are sufficient to persuade me that Shipman probably killed Mrs Scott by a lethal injection of diamorphine. However, there remains a possibility that she died a natural death and I cannot dismiss that as fanciful. For that reason, I cannot be sure of my conclusion. I find that Shipman was probably responsible for Mrs Scott's death.

name: Margaret Townsend
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 13 Busheyfield Close, Newton, Hyde
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to carcinoma of the stomach
conclusion:
It is not possible to reach a clear conclusion about Mrs Townsend's state of health in the weeks and days leading up to her death. It is possible that she had cancer of the pancreas but this was never demonstrated. As most other common causes of pain had been excluded and as pancreatic cancer cannot be cured, it was reasonable to treat Mrs Townsend symptomatically.
Whatever the cause of Mrs Townsend's problems, it seems likely that she did complain of pain in the days leading up to her death. It also seems likely that Shipman prescribed dihydrocodeine on or about 7th
December, that he saw her on 10th
December and prescribed morphine tablets, and that the duty doctor was called out that evening. What cannot be known is the extent to which those complaints were of pathological pain or, if so, what was their cause. It does seem likely that there was a psychosomatic element in Mrs Townsend's pain. This is suggested by the 'miraculous' improvement on Tagamet. Her previous doctor thought her pain was partly or wholly psychosomatic. It is, therefore, hard to gauge the extent of the organic component of her pain.
It is not only the cause and level of Mrs Townsend's pain that is uncertain. It is also unclear to what extent she was disabled in the days before she died. The picture painted by the family is that she was effectively confined to bed for four days before she died. They ascribe this to the tablets that Shipman had given, and Dr Grenville confirms that the prescription of strong opiates may explain why Mrs Townsend apparently became rapidly weak and tired. Alternatively, of course, it could be that Mrs Townsend had been rendered weak by illness and pain and that her drowsy condition was due to the effect of the opiates which she genuinely needed.
What is plain is that Shipman visited Mrs Townsend on the day of her death and that she died in his presence. His medical note suggests that her blood pressure was very low and that she was very weak when he found her. This represents a dramatic change from her condition when seen by the duty doctor the previous evening. Such a rapid change arouses some suspicion. The medical notes which Shipman made at or shortly after a death cannot be accepted as genuine unless confirmed by independent evidence. I have seen many cases where he has fabricated an entry to provide a feasible explanation for a death which he has himself caused. I must approach that entry with extreme caution.
The family says that Shipman admitted giving Mrs Townsend an injection to make her more comfortable. In none of their witness statements has any member of the family suggested that it struck them as strange that there was a need to make Mrs Townsend comfortable. The inference must be that they believed that she was or had been in discomfort, and, even if they had not been with her that morning, this is something that they would have had the opportunity to confirm with Mr Townsend. It was not until Shipman's
modus operandi
was well known that Mr Orson expressed his concerns to the police. I cannot be sure that the Orsons' recollection about what Shipman said at the time is accurate. Their recollection in other respects has been found to be unreliable.
Although there are many uncertainties in this case, the fact remains that Mrs Townsend died in Shipman's presence. Shipman certified the death as being due to cancer of the stomach when this diagnosis had been excluded. The diagnosis of pancreatic cancer had never been confirmed. There is a possibility that Mrs Townsend had pancreatic cancer, but the full and careful note made by the duty doctor does not convey the impression of a woman in the terminal stages of a cancer. Nor for that matter does it appear that the duty doctor thought that Mrs Townsend was close to death from any other cause. As Dr Grenville said, it is possible that Mrs Townsend died as the result of any one of a number of natural causes but, if she did, it was a remarkable coincidence that she should have done so in Shipman's presence.
Taking all the evidence into account, I have come to the conclusion that Shipman probably killed Mrs Townsend. I cannot be sure of this conclusion, as there are a number of uncertainties in the evidence, but I do think it is far more likely that he killed her than that she died of carcinomatosis or any other natural cause.

name: Maureen Alice Ward
title: Miss
conclusion:
Although this was a cremation case, with no direct evidence of morphine poisoning, it was a very clear case of murder:
This was a sudden death discovered very shortly after Shipman had had access to Miss Ward alone and the opportunity to inject diamorphine.
The cause of death was not plausible given the past medical history. Miss Ward was not terminally ill. Even with heavily altered records, Shipman's explanation for the death did not make medical sense.
Shipman gave a false account of events on Form B where his entries were plainly designed to distance him from the death.
Miss Ward's appearance was not what one would expect if Miss Ward had had a sudden collapse. On the other hand her appearance was consistent with her having been given an injection of diamorphine.

name: Irene Aitken
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 19 Burkitt Street, Hyde
conclusion:
There are several suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. The first and most obvious is that it took place in Shipman's presence. Dr John Grenville, in his generic evidence, has advised that it is extremely unusual for a patient to die during a routine visit of a general practitioner, where the patient is not terminally ill and the doctor has not been called out in an emergency, following the onset of acute symptoms indicating, for example, a heart attack or stroke. Mrs Aitken was not suffering from a terminal illness. Nor did Mrs Aitken need to see a doctor on account of any symptoms. Shipman was not called out to her at all that day. He made a wholly unsolicited visit. It would be too much of a coincidence that Mrs Aitken should have begun to suffer a stroke shortly before Shipman happened to visit, so that he was in time to see her die. This single factor is enough to persuade me that Shipman probably killed Mrs Aitken.
Mrs Aitken had a history of strokes and was certainly at risk of suffering another, possibly fatal, episode. A fatal stroke can occur without any warning. However, Shipman did not claim that Mrs Aitken had had a sudden fatal stroke. He claimed that her stroke had begun about two hours before death and progressed to death, following a period in a coma. However, the timing of other events do not fit with Shipman's claims. Mrs Aitken was observed by a number of people to have been well on the day of her death. Mrs Freeman last saw her at about midday and although she was weak following her spell in hospital, she was mentally alert and did not complain of any specific illness. Shipman claimed that he was with Mrs Freeman for about half an hour before Mrs Aitken's death, which he said occurred at 3.30pm. Mrs Freeman believes that the death occurred between 1pm and 1.30pm. Mrs Aitken thought that she received news of the death just after lunchtime. The first of the long telephone calls took place at 2.04pm. I think it highly likely that this telephone call was made to break the news of the death to a friend or member of the family. On Shipman's account, Mrs Aitken would have been lying alive but comatose in her house. I am satisfied that Shipman has pretended that the death occurred later than it did, probably because either Mrs Freeman or Mr Aitken and Mrs Mary Aitken told him when they had last seen Mrs Aitken alive and well.
Shipman's conduct that day does not accord with what any reasonable and competent general practitioner would have done if he had found his patient suffering from a stroke. In his generic evidence to the Inquiry, Dr Grenville said that where a stroke due to subarachnoid haemorrhage is suspected, the patient should be admitted to hospital for possible neurosurgical intervention. As to an occlusive or haemorrhagic stroke, Dr Grenville said that the decision to admit a patient to hospital depends on the severity of the stroke and the wishes of the patient or those close to her. As Shipman claimed that Mrs Aitken was in a state of collapse, she would not have been able to give any instructions as to whether she wished to be admitted to hospital. It would, in any event be very difficult to diagnose a cerebrovascular accident in a patient in a state of collapse. However, it must be accepted that if Shipman had found Mrs Aitken collapsed, it would be reasonable to assume she had probably had another stroke. In any event, Shipman should not have done nothing for half an hour. He should either have summoned an ambulance or have tried to contact a friend or relative. There is no evidence that he did either.
On Form B, Shipman claimed that Mrs Freeman was present at the moment of death. It is possible that she was, in that Mrs Aitken might still have been just alive when Mrs Freeman arrived. However, Shipman's statement on Form B is clearly misleading as it gives the impression that Mrs Freeman was present during the process of death and was able to give Shipman relevant information about the mode of death. I am quite sure that Shipman wished to create the impression that he was not alone with Mrs Aitken throughout her death, as was in fact the case.
Mrs Aitken's position and appearance in death were not typical of those seen following a death due to a stroke. On the other hand, they are entirely typical of the position and appearance of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of opiate.
This case has Shipman's hallmark on it. All the evidence suggests that Shipman killed Mrs Aitken. I am sure that he did, almost certainly by administering a lethal injection of opiate, under the guise of taking a blood sample or giving some therapeutic treatment.

name: John Baddeley
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, Flat 6 Rowan Court, Stockport Road, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
I am satisfied that Mr Baddeley died a natural death.
Mr Baddeley had a history of cerebrovascular accidents and on the day of his death seems to have suffered a final stroke. It would be entirely proper practice for Shipman to give a sedative injection to his patient if, as Mr Wood remembers, he was becoming agitated and distressed. Shipman should have noted the injection in the medical records. He was a poor record keeper however, and the fact that he did not note the injection does not, of itself, give rise to any suspicion that the injection was not given for proper therapeutic reasons. I do not believe that the injection he gave contained an overdose of opiate or sedative. It was also appropriate for Shipman to arrange for a district nurse to catheterise Mr Baddeley, as he apparently did.
The only criticism that could be made of Shipman's conduct is his callous attitude towards a family in distressing circumstances, awaiting the death of a loved one.

name: Hilda Mary Couzens
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 10 Knott Lane, Hyde
certified_cause: myocardial infarction due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
Mrs Couzens was a very elderly woman with a history of heart disease and a fairly recent history of coronary insufficiency. She was therefore at considerable risk of dying suddenly from a heart attack.
Shipman said on cremation Form B that he visited her at 1.40pm on 24th
February. That is entirely possible. It seems unlikely that he would have said he had visited her that day if he had not. He made no entry at all in her medical records. He should have done. He asked Mrs Chapman to arrange a domiciliary visit the following day, as (so he said) he was concerned about Mrs Couzens and by the fact that she had refused to be admitted to hospital. This aspect of Shipman's conduct gives rise to strong suspicion. Mrs Couzens had not requested a visit as a matter of urgency or on account of anything that sounded like a cardiac episode. At 1pm she was well, had had her hair washed and set and was enjoying a cooked lunch. In my view it is unlikely that there was anything seriously wrong with her when Shipman arrived. Yet she was never seen alive again. It seems to me highly likely that Shipman killed her, using one of his recently acquired 30mg ampoules of diamorphine and, on arrival back at the surgery, set in train an arrangement which would provide him with some corroboration for his explanation for the death which would soon be discovered.
I have learned to suspect Shipman's claims that his patient has been unwilling to be admitted to hospital. Although I accept that many old people are unwilling, one would usually expect that there would be some discussion with a member of the patient's family before the refusal was accepted. If the patient were ill enough to require admission, one would expect that the patient would need care if he or she were to stay at home. Yet Shipman left without making any such arrangements for Mrs Couzens. Shipman's actions and account, to the extent that it was given, do not make sense.
Mrs Couzens had an alarm pinned to her dress. Dr John Grenville has explained in his generic evidence that patients suffering from a heart attack seldom die without realising that something unusual, even catastrophic, is happening to them. Usually, the patient will get up and make some attempt to seek help, as for example by moving towards the telephone. Mrs Couzens did not activate her personal alarm. That must be because either her death occurred so quickly that she was unable to do so or perhaps she did not realise that she needed help. Dr Grenville's view is that there would usually be time to activate such an alarm in the case of a heart attack. It seems to me, therefore, that it is more likely that Mrs Couzens did not use her alarm because she did not appreciate any need to. She would not have pressed her alarm if her family doctor were with her, giving her an injection or possibly pretending to take a blood sample. As Dr Grenville has also said in his generic evidence, patients who have had a heart attack are not usually found sitting peacefully in an armchair. On the other hand, Mrs Couzens' position and appearance are entirely typical of many of Shipman's diamorphine victims. Patients who have died after a heart attack are often found collapsed on the floor.
There is a startling similarity between Shipman's handling of the cases of Mrs Couzens and Mrs Heginbotham. He gave almost identical instructions to Mrs Chapman, to make arrangements for each woman to receive a domiciliary visit the following day. In each case he would have been able to say to relatives, or to the Form C doctor or medical referee, that he had been sufficiently concerned about the patient's condition to have recommended admission to hospital and, when the patient had refused, he had arranged a visit. This would demonstrate that in neither case was the death unexpected.
Taking these factors into account, I have come to the conclusion that Shipman must have killed Mrs Couzens. He probably visited her at about 1.40pm as he said on Form B. He probably used one of the ampoules he had obtained two days before. Despite the confusing evidence in connection with Mr Dawson's supposed visit, which I have had to put from my mind completely, I am in the end sure that Shipman killed Mrs Couzens.

name: Eric Davies
title: Mr
place_of_death: Hyde Nursing Home
certified_cause: glioma of the parietal lobe, which is a tumour of the brain
conclusion:
It is likely that Mr Davies died a natural death from the cause certified by Shipman. It is clear from the witness evidence and from the medical records that Mr Davies had a brain tumour and had reached the terminal stage of his illness.
There is evidence that Shipman gave an injection during the evening of 7th
September. As Shipman said he would give morphine, he probably did so, although it was more usual for him to carry diamorphine than morphine. If he gave either of those drugs, it is clear that he did not give a lethal dose. Mr Davies lived for about a further 12 hours after the injection. There is no evidence that Shipman had access to Mr Davies after his visit during the evening of 7th
September. He could not have given a further injection. Because I do not know what dose was given, I cannot rule out the possibility that Shipman gave a larger dose than was appropriate for the relief of distress, which might have depressed Mr Davies' respiratory drive and indirectly shortened his life by a small margin. However, as Shipman warned the family, the giving of an opiate does carry this risk. The doctor should weigh the risk against the benefit and estimate the appropriate dose as well as he can. It is quite possible that an appropriate dose might shorten life.
If the injection had been of some drug other than morphine or diamorphine (such as Largactil), it is theoretically possible that Shipman gave a larger dose than was appropriate. If he did, this could have shortened Mr Davies' life by a small margin, as over-sedation can render the elderly or terminally ill more vulnerable to bronchopneumonia, a common mechanism of death. However, I regard this possibility as remote, as Shipman said that he intended to give an opiate.
I wish to make two observations about this case. First, if as seems likely, Shipman openly gave an injection of morphine or possibly diamorphine on the evening of 7th
September, it is remarkable that he did not record this in Mr Davies' medical notes. Second, the prescription for diamorphine made out in Mr Davies' name on 23rd
July 1994 cannot possibly have been intended for him. The quantities are so large they would only be suitable for use in a syringe driver, which would be provided for a person in the terminal stages of a painful cancer. The diamorphine must have been kept by Shipman for his own purposes.

name: Hannah Everall
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 16 Commercial Street, Hyde
conclusion:
In the absence of the records, it is not possible to form a clear view as to the exact nature of Mrs Everall's medical condition. However, it is clear that she was very unwell in the period before her death. It would appear that her final illness had begun by about 26th
October, when Mr Brian Everall thought his mother looked unwell. In any event, it is clear that her condition deteriorated during the ensuing days. I have the impression that her pain was severe and this led to immobility. She might have developed a chest infection and this could have led to bronchopneumonia. On the other hand, it is possible that she had a stroke but that the family has forgotten about it. Bronchopneumonia is a common complication in elderly stroke patients and a frequent mechanism of death. The period of about 36 hours of unconsciousness would be entirely consistent with death following a developing stroke, with or without added bronchopneumonia. Whatever the cause, it appears that the death was not sudden or unexpected.
It appears that Shipman visited Mrs Everall on at least three occasions during her last illness and there is evidence that on at least one occasion, possibly more, he administered an injection which he said was designed to make Mrs Everall more comfortable. If she was in pain, as her son, Mr Brian Everall, says she was, this would have been an entirely proper thing to do. It is possible that Shipman gave Mrs Everall an opiate drug or he might have given a sedative drug such as Largactil. There is no reason to suppose that he gave a lethal dose of opiate. If he had done so, Mrs Everall would have been dead within an hour of the injection. The evidence suggests that she lived for about 36 hours after the last injection. Even if the family has confused the events of the Friday and Saturday, it would appear that she lived for about 12 hours after the lunchtime injection. I think it is unlikely that Shipman gave another injection in the afternoon or at 6pm as suggested by Mr Paul Ramsbottom. Even if he did and even if that injection were given on the Saturday and not on the Friday, it cannot have been a lethal injection of opiate. Mrs Everall lived for about six hours after the time when she might last have been injected.
If the injection or injections were of a sedative or of non-lethal amounts of opiate, it is possible that the dose or doses resulted in Mrs Everall being put into a deep sleep sooner than was appropriate. A patient who is deeply unconscious is more vulnerable to bronchopneumonia, which is, as I have said, a common mechanism of death in elderly patients. In this way, Mrs Everall's death might have been hastened by a small margin. However, if the dose was honestly intended to relieve pain or discomfort, it would not have been unlawful to give it, even if the effect was to hasten Mrs Everall's death.
It appears to me highly likely that Mrs Everall's death was natural. I cannot absolutely rule out the possibility that Shipman gave an inappropriately large dose of sedative or opiate which rendered her unconscious sooner than was desirable and might have hastened her death by a small margin. However, there is no evidence that he did so.

name: Edwin Foulkes
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, Westwood Farm, Mottram Road, Hyde
conclusion:
There are some puzzling and suspicious features to this case. Mr Foulkes was clearly quite unwell when his daughter called the doctor out early in the morning of New Year's Day. Dr Grenville suggests that the symptoms sound not unlike those of left ventricular failure, although he would have expected Mr Foulkes to be very short of breath. Without the medical records, it is not possible to form a reliable view about Mr Foulkes' underlying condition. Shipman's explanation to Mrs McKeown fits with left ventricular failure and if that is what Mr Foulkes had, it would have been appropriate for Shipman to give a diuretic. Usually, if the patient is very ill and facing death, the injection should be given intravenously as the drug would then act more quickly. Shipman gave an injection in the thigh. It is possible that he was unable to find a vein. Sometimes this can be difficult in very old people. Shipman then left immediately. Dr Grenville regards this as poor treatment. He says that Shipman should either have admitted Mr Foulkes to hospital or, if that was thought not appropriate, he should have stayed with Mr Foulkes to see whether the diuretic provided any relief. I would have thought that the decision whether or not to admit Mr Foulkes should have been taken after consultation with his daughter. Shipman's poor treatment of Mr Foulkes, followed so quickly by Mr Foulkes' death, give rise to the suspicion that Shipman made no real effort to treat Mr Foulkes but left him to die. It rather sounds as though he had formed the view that it was time for Mr Foulkes to die. Where those suspicions arise, it is inevitable that I should suspect that Shipman might have taken a positive step to hasten the death rather than merely leaving Mr Foulkes to die.
It is possible that Shipman's conduct was wholly proper. It may be that he gave Mr Foulkes an intramuscular injection of diuretic, designed to relieve the strain on his heart. Although this was not the treatment of choice, it might have been the best available. It is possible that admission to hospital was discussed and that Mrs McKeown has forgotten. Shipman might have been under great pressure to reach another patient as a matter of urgency. It is possible that Shipman gave substandard treatment and effectively left Mr Foulkes to die. On the other hand, it is also possible that Shipman did not give a diuretic at all but gave a dose of opiate with the intention of hastening Mr Foulkes' death. I think it is, perhaps, unlikely that he would have given a dose of opiate to the patient of another doctor, as that other doctor would be involved in the death certification process and, if he or she were puzzled by the death, it might be referred to the coroner.
I regret to say that I do not feel able to reach a positive decision about this case. I am, however, suspicious about it.

name: Rebecca Gray
title: Mrs
certified_cause: left ventricular failure due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
It seems highly likely that Mrs Gray died as the result of natural causes.
Mrs Gray's medical records suggest that she suffered from congestive heart disease and was not perhaps as meticulous in taking her medication as she should have been. Although Shipman claimed to have a system to monitor patients with heart problems, it does not appear that he had seen Mrs Gray for about six months before her death. The witness evidence suggests that Mrs Gray had become very frail towards the end of her life. The post-mortem report shows that she had quite severe heart disease. Although Mrs Gray's death seemed very sudden, I do not think it was unexpected from a medical point of view.
There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman visited Mrs Gray on the day of her death. It appears that he had not seen her for about six months. I cannot rule out the possibility that Shipman called on Mrs Gray on 5th
May.
Mrs Gray's mode of death was not typical of a death following a lethal injection of opiate, which was Shipman's preferred method of killing. Following such an injection, given intravenously, the patient's respiration is depressed and he or she falls into a very deep sleep and dies within a few minutes. Mrs Gray appears to have been unconscious for at least two hours, possibly longer, and her breathing was heavy and loud.
The presence of venepuncture marks on Mrs Gray's arm gives rise to the suspicion that she had been given an injection of some sort not long before her death. It seems to me most likely that these marks were made in the course of some procedure carried out at the hospital in an attempt to revive Mrs Gray.
Although I cannot absolutely rule out the possibility that Shipman was involved in Mrs Gray's death, it seems highly likely that he was not and that her death was entirely natural.

name: Elsie Harrop
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 32 Frank Street, Hyde
conclusion:
Mrs Harrop's body was discovered very soon after Shipman had paid her a visit and had been alone with her. No one saw her alive or spoke to her after his departure. That in itself is a highly suspicious factor.
According to the family, the only symptom of which Mrs Harrop complained in the days before her death was vertigo. The family does not describe signs of a developing stroke. Unfortunately, because the medical records have not survived, it is not possible to discover whether Mrs Harrop was suffering from high blood pressure and if so, to what extent. Mrs Harrop might have been at an increased risk of suffering a stroke. Whatever the underlying risks, it would not be at all likely that Mrs Harrop would die suddenly from a stroke, as suggested by Shipman. It is highly unlikely that she would have been well at 1pm, when Mrs Beryl Harrop left, suffering from mild stroke symptoms soon afterwards when Shipman visited, and dead by 4pm. As Dr John Grenville explained in his generic evidence, the expected course of events after the onset of a mild stroke would be recovery. If the stroke were to develop, there would be a gradual deterioration over a period of two to three days. It is possible that Mrs Harrop could have died suddenly from a catastrophic brain haemorrhage or heart attack, although her appearance in death was not consistent with death from those causes. Any doctor, acting honestly, would have regarded Mrs Harrop's death as sudden and unexplained and would have declined to certify the cause of death. There would then have been a referral to the coroner. Shipman avoided this and declared that a post-mortem examination was not necessary.
On Form B, Shipman appears to have made a number of false or misleading statements. In particular he sought to suggest that Mrs Harrop had died at 2pm. She might have done, but if he was not there, he could not have known the time of death. Dr Grenville has said in his generic evidence that the assessment of time of death is a difficult and complex process, even when undertaken by an experienced pathologist. At the very least, an internal body temperature must be taken. Shipman did not do this. It appears that Shipman was seeking to establish that a period of two hours elapsed between his visit and the death.
Mrs Harrop's appearance in death was not typical of a stroke victim. There was no evidence of any agonal event. Mrs Harrop's appearance was entirely typical of the appearance of many of Shipman's victims who are known to have been given a lethal injection of diamorphine.
Taking all these factors into account, I am driven to the conclusion that Shipman killed Mrs Harrop. Notwithstanding the absence of the medical records, I am sure of this.

name: Ronald Jameson
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 57 Grosvenor Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite sure that this was a natural death. All the evidence suggests that Mr Jameson died of a heart attack at which Shipman was not present.
I can well understand why Professor Baker felt moderately suspicious about this death. The medical records are extremely scanty. However, Professor Baker did not have available to him the witness evidence describing the circumstances of Mr Jameson's death. He would not have known that Mr Jameson had a history of chest discomfort and pins and needles. He was unaware that the emergency doctor was called out in the late evening of 21st
February because Mr Jameson felt unwell. It was Dr Rogers who attended, not Shipman. Nor did Professor Baker know that Mrs Jameson and Mrs Platt were in the house with Mr Jameson when he collapsed, and remained throughout the efforts to save him. Now that Mrs Platt's account is available, all suspicions are laid to rest.

name: Ellen Kelly
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
It appears from the witness evidence that Mrs Kelly had enjoyed good health until shortly before her death. It seems that she had become immobile and unable to look after herself. There does not seem to have been any medical history which would increase Mrs Kelly's risk of suffering a heart attack. However, this cannot be checked from her medical records. In any event, a woman of 82 is at some risk of sudden death from a heart attack even without any previous history or warning signs.
On the morning of 9th
December, the evidence strongly suggests that Mrs Kelly suddenly became ill while waiting for her family to collect her from Charnley House. It seems quite likely that this sudden deterioration was due to a heart attack, although other explanations are quite possible. Mrs Stansfield realised that the situation was serious and believes that Mrs Kelly died as she was being put to bed. It appears that someone immediately telephoned the family and Shipman. There is no witness who remembers seeing Shipman at the home that morning. Mrs Stansfield believes that Shipman was not even summoned until after Mrs Kelly had died and she does not think that he saw her alive.
There is no clear evidence to suggest that Shipman saw Mrs Kelly alive. If he did, she must have been on the verge of death. The possibility that Shipman visited Charnley House and was responsible for the sudden deterioration which occurred while she was sitting in the lounge should be raised only so that it might be dismissed. Mrs Kelly was not Shipman's patient and he was not due to see her or any other resident that morning. It is implausible to suggest that he might have entered the house and, without reference to the staff on duty, given Mrs Kelly an injection while she was sitting in a room to which many other people had access.
Most of the evidence suggests that Mrs Kelly died a natural death. However, I am puzzled by Shipman's claim that he saw her before she died. I think the probable explanation for this is that Shipman wanted to complete the MCCD himself and did not want to refer the case to the coroner. He would not be qualified to sign the MCCD unless he had attended Mrs Kelly during her last illness. In fact it seems highly likely that he had not attended Mrs Kelly during her last illness (which had only lasted a few minutes) and was almost certainly not qualified to complete the MCCD. He should have referred the case to the coroner. It may be that he pretended to have seen Mrs Kelly alive so that he could claim to be qualified to sign the MCCD. Why he did not want to refer the case to the coroner I cannot say. In cases where I suspect that he has killed the patient, I can see why he would not wish to have the coroner involved. Where there is no real suspicion that he has killed the patient, it is hard to see why he should wish to avoid this. In some cases, I think perhaps he wanted to save the family the distress and delay which referral can cause. Here, the family wanted a post-mortem examination. It may be that Shipman simply could not be bothered to refer the case.
This aspect of the case makes me hold back from saying that I am sure that Mrs Kelly died a natural death. I think she probably did, as all the remaining evidence suggests that her death was sudden but natural. The circumstances at Charnley House were such as to make it highly unlikely that Shipman could have done anything to Mrs Kelly to cause her sudden collapse and death.

name: May Lowe
title: Miss
conclusion:
There are a number of suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. First, there is good evidence that Shipman visited Miss Lowe at home on the day of her death, although Shipman himself has sought to create the impression that he did not. The good evidence of a home visit on 27th
March is that he himself made entries on the computer at 3.32pm to the effect that he had seen her at home that day and that she had given a history of an incident in the street which sounded like a stroke. The following Tuesday, he made further entries on the computer which seem to suggest that, on 27th
March, he had had a telephone conversation with Miss Lowe and had seen her in the surgery. It is, I suppose, possible that these entries related to a visit by Mrs Andrew who came to collect the MCCD. However, if they are intended to relate to contact with Miss Lowe on 27th
March, neither incident seems plausible. Miss Lowe had not been in good health and was very unlikely to have been able to go to the surgery. In any event, her name does not appear on the appointments sheet. It is possible, although unlikely, that she spoke to Shipman on the telephone. She certainly did not do so from her own home. It is possible that she did so from another telephone. If so, it must follow that she was out in the street that day and could possibly have had an episode about which she wanted to speak to or see her doctor.
Considering all these factors, I am quite satisfied that Shipman did visit Miss Lowe at home on 27th
March and made entries on the computer on his return to the surgery. He must have visited her at some time between midday and 3.15pm. Why he visited is not clear. It is possible that Miss Lowe telephoned from somewhere other than her home. It is possible that someone else telephoned on her behalf and it is quite possible that Shipman made an unsolicited call. I suspect the latter as Mrs Andrew's recollection of her conversation on 1st
April is that Shipman only admitted to having been 'in the area', as he certainly was. At that time, he was, I think, seeking to conceal the fact that he had seen Miss Lowe on the day of her death.
That Shipman should have visited Miss Lowe on the day of her death, and that her death should have been discovered shortly afterwards, gives rise to grave suspicion that Shipman was involved in the death. There is no evidence that anyone saw Miss Lowe alive or spoke to her after his visit. He subsequently sought (not very competently) to conceal the fact that he had visited that day. These factors are enough in themselves to lead me to the conclusion that Shipman probably killed Miss Lowe.
However, there are other factors to be considered.
How likely is it that Miss Lowe died of a stroke? She was unwell during January and it was thought that she had influenza. Her illness continued into February and in the middle of that month she had a fall. In the computerised records, Shipman diagnosed a cerebrovascular accident, but there were no recorded signs or symptoms to justify that diagnosis. It is possible that he was right but I am suspicious that Shipman was, at this early stage, laying the ground for Miss Lowe's sudden death.
On Shipman's account, as taken from Form B, he last saw Miss Lowe alive at 12.30pm on the day of her death. According to the note he made just after 3.30pm, she reported a transient ischaemic attack in the street. Shipman's comment
'tluk'
, meaning 'to let us know', is a familiar refrain in suspicious cases. There is nothing in the note to suggest that Miss Lowe was seriously ill. If she had been, he ought to have arranged for her admission or at least have contacted a relative. He did neither. If she was not seriously ill, her death a few hours later would have been very sudden and unexpected. Yet, he did not refer the death to the coroner. Dr Grenville says that it would have been reasonable to certify the death as due to a stroke if Miss Lowe really did describe a stroke that day. We have only Shipman's word for it that she did. If she did, it is strange that no one knew of this and mentioned it to Mrs Andrew after the death. Not even Shipman mentioned it to her when she saw him on 1st
April.
I am suspicious of Shipman's claim on Form B that the death had occurred at 6.30pm. Shipman often claimed that he could estimate the time of death with some accuracy. He often used this spurious information to distance himself and his visit from the supposed time of death. Here, he claims to have visited at 12.30pm. He might well have done. He would not wish to give too inaccurate a time, as he would not know whether or not he had been observed. But he could have had no idea of the true time of death. It may be that Mrs Andrew told him that her aunt felt warm when she was found. She might well have done, as the body had been kept quite warm. It is an odd feature of a number of cases in which Shipman has killed that the gas fire is found to be on high when the body is discovered. This gives rise to a suspicion that Shipman has turned it on or turned it up. I do not fully understand why he would do this. It might be to slow down the rate at which the body cools. It might be to speed the rate at which rigor mortis sets in. It might be to confuse any pathologist who tried to estimate the time of death. It might even be that Shipman thought that it would speed up the rate at which any opiate drug would be metabolised after death. I do not know. However, it is a common thread and it gives rise to suspicion.
That the back door of Miss Lowe's house should be unlocked causes me to suspect that Shipman used that door as his departure route.
Miss Lowe was found on the kitchen floor. Her position and appearance in death are not wholly typical of Shipman's victims, many of whom were found sitting in a chair, after being given a lethal injection of opiate. Miss Lowe's position and appearance were consistent with a natural death. However, they were not inconsistent with a death following an injection of opiate. It would have been quite possible for Shipman to inject her while she was sitting on an upright chair, which did not offer much support, and that he allowed her to fall to the floor.
My conclusion is that Shipman killed Miss Lowe. There is no significant piece of evidence which suggests that this was a natural death. I feel able to say that I am sure of this conclusion.

name: Samuel Mills
title: Mr
conclusion:
The circumstances of this death give rise to grave suspicion. There is no independent evidence that Mr Mills was close to death before Shipman arrived at his flat. When Eldercare received the message that Mr Mills was very ill, Shipman was with him. I am satisfied that it was Shipman who contacted Eldercare, just before 10.30am. Shipman must have told Eldercare that Mr Mills was dying. That was the message conveyed to Mrs Jones. It appears that the process of dying began while Shipman was present and this, in itself, gives rise to grave suspicion that he was responsible for the death. Other general practitioners find that deaths occur in their presence very rarely indeed. Death frequently occurred in Shipman's presence.
Mr Mills had a terminal illness but, as Dr Grenville has explained, he did not appear to have reached the final phase. His death on that morning was sudden and unexpected. Although a natural death cannot be positively ruled out, it seems very unlikely that Mr Mills died on that day as the result of cancer. It is also possible that he could have died naturally from some other cause of sudden death, such as heart attack or stroke, but there is no particular reason to suppose that he did.
The timing of events warrants consideration. I infer that Shipman was with Mr Mills at 10.29am when the message was received by Eldercare. At that time, Shipman said that Mr Mills was dying. If Shipman did kill Mr Mills, by lethal injection, it would seem more likely that he would have administered it before calling Eldercare than afterwards. Yet Mr Mills was still alive when Mrs Jones arrived at about 10.40am. He died about ten minutes later, that is more than 20 minutes after one would have expected the injection to be given. Dr Grenville has explained that an intravenous injection of a lethal dose of opiate will cause death within about five minutes of administration. I think it is unlikely that Mr Mills was given a lethal dose by the intravenous route. However, as Dr Grenville explained, it can sometimes be difficult to find a vein in an elderly or emaciated patient. It is therefore quite possible that Shipman decided to give an intramuscular injection or that he tried to give an intravenous injection but that this went wrong and the drug entered the body subcutaneously. In either event, it is entirely possible that it would have taken about 20-30 minutes for Mr Mills to die.
When Mrs Jones arrived, Shipman was not in sight. I do wonder what had been going on. If Shipman really had found Mr Mills seriously ill, it is extraordinary that he should leave him alone. He claimed that he could have saved Mr Mills. By doing what, one wonders? If Mr Mills were dying of carcinomatosis, there would be no question of 'saving' him. If he had had a heart attack, it might well have been possible to 'save' him by an emergency admission to hospital. I strongly suspect that the claim that Shipman could have saved Mr Mills was completely untrue and part of the display of power and knowledge that he often liked to show.
The medical records arouse suspicion. There is no adequate note of the consultation immediately preceding the death.
Taking these factors into account, I have been driven to the conclusion that Shipman killed Mr Mills, almost certainly by administering a lethal injection of diamorphine. I think it likely that Shipman found Mr Mills feeling unwell and low in spirits. He decided to kill him. He gave him an injection and called Eldercare to tell them that Mr Mills was dying.
