Then, for some reason, he left Mr Mills alone for a few minutes, during which time Mrs Jones arrived. Together they waited for the death, which Shipman knew was inevitable. Although it is theoretically possible that Mr Mills died a natural death that day, Shipman's presence at the death is so suspicious a factor that I am satisfied so as to be sure that he was responsible for the death.

name: Phyllis Oxley
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 25 Chestnut Avenue, Todmorden
conclusion:
Notwithstanding Mr Oxley's understandable concerns about some aspects of Shipman's behaviour, it is unlikely that Shipman caused Mrs Oxley's death. Mrs Oxley was clearly in the terminal phase of cancer and was, quite properly, given opiate drugs for pain relief. In those days, such drugs were usually injected by a doctor, possibly several times a day. Nowadays, patients would be provided with a syringe driver, which would give them a continuous supply of analgesic drug. On the last day of Mrs Oxley's life, Shipman gave her at least two and probably three injections of opiate. The last injection seems to have been given before 10pm. Mrs Oxley lived for about three hours after that injection. As Dr Grenville has explained in his generic evidence, if a lethal dose of opiate is given intravenously, the patient will die within a few minutes. If the dose is given intramuscularly, the patient will die within about an hour. That Mrs Oxley lived for three hours after her final injection shows that she did not die as a direct result of a lethal injection.
Dr Grenville also explained that a smaller excessive dose given to a debilitated patient could have the effect of depressing respiration, with the result that the patient might die some hours later, possibly from bronchopneumonia. The opiate would then be a contributory cause of death although not the immediate cause. Because he was later proved to be a serial killer, I cannot rule out the possibility that Shipman deliberately gave Mrs Oxley such a dose of morphine, which contributed to her death in this way. I regard this, however, as unlikely, in all the circumstances.
Dr Grenville has told the Inquiry that it can be difficult for a doctor to assess the correct amount of opiate to give for pain relief when the patient has been taking opiates for some time but the pain is breaking through. The doctor will wish to give enough to relieve the pain but the dose can have the effect of shortening the patient's life, although probably only to a small extent. Provided the dose is assessed in good faith as being for the patient's benefit, the administration would be lawful. It is possible that Shipman did shorten Mrs Oxley's life by a small margin by giving a dose of opiate, which was assessed in good faith.
My conclusion is that Mrs Oxley probably died a natural death.

name: Rosetta Pedley
title: Mrs
place_of_death: between 10am
conclusion:
There is very little evidence as to the circumstances of Mrs Pedley's death. The available witnesses had not seen her in the weeks leading up to her death. Her body was not discovered for some days after she had died. Very little is known about Mrs Pedley's state of health. Her medical records have not survived. The witnesses say that she appeared fit and well. The only condition referred to in the police reports is arthritis.
The cause of Mrs Pedley's death was not satisfactorily ascertained at the post-mortem examination.
There is some hearsay evidence that Mrs Pedley last consulted Shipman in the week before she died. She was well enough to attend the surgery and was told that she had influenza and should stay at home and keep warm. There is no clear evidence that Shipman visited her at home after that consultation although it would have been typical of him to do so. If he had visited her and killed her, it would have been entirely typical of other cases in which he had killed, that the deceased person should be found seated in an armchair, in front of a fire. According to the Report of Sudden Death, Shipman saw Mrs Pedley at home but the report does not say when.
Shipman's visits book suggests that he was on holiday from Friday, 29th
May but it appears that he probably spent at least part of his holiday at home. There is some indication that Mrs Pedley was seen alive at 5pm on 29th
May. It therefore seems unlikely, although not impossible, that Shipman visited Mrs Pedley between 5pm on 29th
May and the time when her death was discovered. I also observe that, in 1981, Shipman was not a frequent killer. If Shipman had killed Mrs Pedley, it would be atypical of him to give up control of events and to allow the fact of death to be certified by another doctor who would almost certainly refer the death to the coroner with a view to a post-mortem examination.
Although the circumstances of this death are far from clear and it is possible that Shipman visited and killed Mrs Pedley, I have come to the conclusion that it is likely that Mrs Pedley died a natural death.

name: Tom Balfour Russell
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 18 Harrison Street, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
There are several suspicious features surrounding this death.
Mr Russell was found dead probably a little over four hours after Shipman had visited him. If Mrs Hesford's evidence is accurate, it appears that Shipman was the last person to see or speak to Mr Russell before his death. That, in itself, is a highly suspicious factor.
Although Mr Russell faced an increased risk of suffering a sudden cardiac death and had recently suffered an exacerbation of his congestive heart failure, there is evidence that, on the day of his death, he was in a reasonably good state. That does not mean that he could not die suddenly from heart failure. It is not clear why Shipman was called out on the morning of Mr Russell's death. It is unlikely that Nurse Gilchrist was very worried about his condition because she would probably have noted her concern if she had been. Mrs Hesford's recollection is that Mr Russell seemed well. If there was no real cause for concern and if Mr Russell seemed well on the morning of the day he died, it is quite possible that Shipman's medical note of his visit is not authentic. As Mrs Ann Russell noted that Mr Russell's feet and ankles were not swollen after death, it seems likely that the medical note describing severe ankle oedema and other signs of congestive heart failure is false. If Mr Russell was as ill as the note suggests, one might have expected Shipman to arrange, or at least suggest, re-admission to hospital. If it is false, the only real reason why Shipman would have made it up, is that he knew that he had killed Mr Russell and that he wanted to bolster the evidence in favour of a death resulting from natural causes.
Shipman's claim that he was able to state the time of death with accuracy was spurious. When that spurious claim is taken together with the claim (which is almost certainly false) that Mr Russell was seen alive at 3pm, one sees that Shipman has put forward a false account designed to distance himself from the death and to create the impression that he could not have been involved in it.
I have come to the conclusion that Shipman must have killed Mr Russell. It seems to me that the medical record for the day gives a false account of Mr Russell's condition. Although Mr Russell was suffering from congestive heart failure, and a sudden death from an exacerbation of that condition was possible, I am satisfied that Mr Russell did not suffer such an exacerbation on that day. Shipman's lies on Form B indicate that he wished to distance himself from involvement in the death. I am sure that Shipman killed him by administering a lethal injection of opiate.

name: Elizabeth Teresa Sigley
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 49 Stockport Road, Gee Cross, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to right ventricular hypertrophy due to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
conclusion:
There are some suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. Although Mrs Sigley was in poor health in late 1995, she was not thought to be terminally ill and was not expected to die when she did. She had no history of heart disease. I do, of course, accept that it is possible that she died of a heart attack without any prior warning. However, her death was sudden and unexpected.
If this was a natural death and if Shipman had not seen Mrs Sigley since 6th
December, as he claimed, he could not possibly have known the cause of her sudden death. The death should have been referred to the coroner, with a view to post-mortem examination. This should not have been a matter of choice for Miss Sigley. Shipman should have decided to refer and should have explained the reasons to Miss Sigley. That he appeared to offer Miss Sigley the opportunity to have a post-mortem examination, would appear to suggest that he was not seeking to avoid a referral. I suspect that he was anxious to avoid a post-mortem examination but wished to create the impression that it was Miss Sigley who had decided not to have one.
The cause of death which Shipman certified was probably not the true cause of death. Not only was there no indication in the medical records that Mrs Sigley suffered from heart disease such as would increase the risk that she would have a heart attack, there was no real evidence that she had right ventricular failure. Moreover, her position and appearance in death were not typical of what is seen following a heart attack.
In short, there are good reasons to suspect that Mrs Sigley's death was not natural.
There is no direct evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Sigley on 14th
December. He certainly had the opportunity to do so in the sense that he had time to visit her and would have been near to her home during the day. It is also likely that Shipman had Mrs Sigley in mind that day, as she or her daughter had telephoned the surgery to request the provision of a portable oxygen dispenser. It is quite possible that that telephone call acted as a prompt for a visit, which Shipman did not enter in his visits book and subsequently decided to conceal.
Why Mrs Sigley was found sitting in a chair that she did not like, some distance from her oxygen supply, is something of a mystery. It could be that she had let the doctor in and had sat there at his suggestion. However, I do not think I can attach much importance to that factor. However, I do regard it as significant that Mrs Sigley's appearance in death was not only untypical of that seen following death from a heart attack but was wholly typical of that of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of morphine or diamorphine.
Although the evidence falls some way short of that which would make me sure that Shipman killed Mrs Sigley, there are sufficient causes for suspicion to persuade me that Shipman probably visited her that day and killed her by giving an injection of opiate. Very little opiate would be needed to kill Mrs Sigley. Dr Chopra had advised that she must avoid any respiratory depressant, because her respiratory function was already quite severely compromised.

name: Walter Tingle
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 4 Walker Close, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to systemic arteriosclerosis
conclusion:
The circumstances of Mr Tingle's death give rise to an irresistible inference that Shipman must have killed him. Mrs Roscoe's account, the essentials of which were recorded contemporaneously, shows that Mr Tingle died very shortly after Shipman had given him an injection. Mrs Roscoe does not say that Mr Tingle was in great pain, such as might indicate that he was having a heart attack or was in need of a pain-relieving injection. Shipman did not record the administration of any drug. These circumstances alone give rise to grave suspicion.
It seems to me unlikely that Mr Tingle had a heart attack on the day of his death. He must have been at some risk of such an event, if only on account of his age and gender, but there is nothing in the medical records to suggest that he was at a significantly increased risk over and above that which was inherent in his age and gender. More to the point, such description as we have of Mr Tingle that morning is not suggestive of a heart attack. He told the driver that he did not feel well enough to go to the day centre. The driver called the doctor. I do not have the impression that the driver thought Mr Tingle was obviously in a serious condition. When Mrs Roscoe saw him, she thought he looked pale or grey and unwell but did not think he was sweating. She does not suggest that he appeared to be in pain. Shipman's entry in the medical records is woefully inadequate on any view, but he proffers no description of signs or symptoms to substantiate his apparent diagnosis of coronary thrombosis.
In support of the claimed diagnosis of heart attack, I note that Shipman instructed Mrs Roscoe to call an ambulance. That would be an appropriate course. However, it is entirely possible that Shipman did that so as to appear to be doing the right thing. He also told her to cancel it as soon as Mr Tingle had died. Second, if Mr Tingle were suffering a heart attack and were in severe pain, it would be appropriate to administer a small dose of opiate. Of course, details of that administration should have been recorded in the medical notes and were not. We have no idea how much of which drug Shipman gave, but the fact that no record was made and that Mr Tingle died within about two minutes makes it highly likely that the dose was lethal and was designed to kill rather than to relieve pain. There is no evidence that Mr Tingle was suffering such pain as would have warranted a pain-relieving injection.
Shipman knew that Mr Tingle was depressed by his physical condition. Even if he did not hear Mr Tingle's statement to that effect on the day of his death, he would have been aware from the entry for 13th
July 1988 that he had expressed a wish to die. I think it quite likely that Mr Tingle told Shipman that day that he had had enough and wanted to die. I think it likely that Shipman was prepared to ensure that he did.
In all the circumstances, the overwhelming probability is that Mr Tingle was unlawfully killed by Shipman. That the killing took place in the presence of a third party does not deter me from drawing the necessary inferences. I have come across other cases in which Shipman has killed in the presence of a third party, sometimes even an experienced carer. The evidence in this case is such that I feel able to say that I am sure that this was an unlawful killing.

name: Joseph Frank Wilcockson
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 62 Dow Street, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
There are very suspicious circumstances surrounding Mr Wilcockson's death. Shipman admitted that he visited Mr Wilcockson during the morning of his death and, on the evidence, no one saw Mr Wilcockson alive or spoke to him after Shipman's visit. This in itself gives rise to grave suspicion that Shipman was implicated in the death.
It is not possible for me to form any view as to whether Mr Wilcockson was at serious risk of a sudden death from heart attack. As there are no surgery records, it is not possible to tell whether there were any clinical signs of heart disease. Miss Wilcockson says that she had never known her grandfather to have an angina attack. Nor is it possible to tell how well his blood pressure was controlled. I recognise that, at the age of 85, and with some reported history of angina and raised blood pressure, Mr Wilcockson probably faced an increased risk of sudden cardiac death.
The lack of medical records for the day of death is less serious, as so little reliance can be placed on any record made by Shipman of circumstances surrounding a death. However, it is unfortunate that it has not been possible to check whether or not Mr Wilcockson requested a visit on 6th
November. If there were a request for a visit it would probably have given some indication of what symptoms Mr Wilcockson was experiencing at the time. It might have given some indication of urgency. Shipman did not volunteer to the family the reason for his morning visit. Indeed, he seems to have made no more than a passing reference to it. If he had visited in response to a request, particularly an urgent request, I would have expected him to tell the family about it and I am sure Miss Wilcockson would have remembered the detail. In fact, Miss Wilcockson says that Shipman told her that her grandfather had been quite well when he had called and said that he was surprised at the death. Also, when Shipman was called out by the district nurse, I would have expected him to tell her that he had been called out to Mr Wilcockson that morning, if such had been the case. Looking at the evidence overall, I incline to the view that Shipman made an unsolicited visit and did not tell anyone why he had called. I regard that as suspicious.
Mr Wilcockson's bandage had been partially removed from his ulcerated leg. On seeing this, the family thought that he must have been preparing for the nurse's visit when he had a heart attack and died. However, there is another plausible explanation. It is quite possible that, when Shipman arrived, he asked Mr Wilcockson how he was. The answer would probably have been that he was not too bad except for his leg, which was very painful. Shipman might well have suggested that he should look at the ulcer and that he would give an injection to relieve the pain. Shipman might well have removed the bandage, looked at the ulcer and then replaced the bandage loosely. He could then have given a substantial dose of diamorphine, sufficient to kill Mr Wilcockson. Mr Wilcockson's appearance in death was entirely typical of that seen in so many of Shipman's victims who have been killed by diamorphine injection. It was not typical of that seen following a sudden cardiac death.
Form B contains a series of lies and half-truths typical of cases in which Shipman has killed. By stating that he was in attendance two hours before the death, Shipman appears to be trying to create the impression that he was sufficiently well informed to state the cause of death with confidence. By fixing his time of arrival earlier than it probably was, I think Shipman was seeking to distance himself from the death.
Taking all these factors into account, I have been driven to the conclusion that Shipman killed Mr Wilcockson. Despite the lack of medical and surgery records, which would usually make certainty impossible, I do feel confident that my conclusion must be right. I consider the possibility that this was a natural death so unlikely that I can properly discount it, notwithstanding Mr Wilcockson's advanced age. I am sure that Shipman killed Mr Wilcockson.

name: Winifred Arrowsmith
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 44 Chartist House, Hyde
conclusion:
In the absence of medical records, I cannot form a view about the seriousness of Mrs Arrowsmith's heart condition. As there are no cremation forms, I do not have Shipman's own account of the circumstances of the death. As Mrs Unsworth cannot remember the death, I have no account of Mrs Arrowsmith's appearance in death. I only know that she was said to have been found in her chair.
I accept as accurate the evidence of Mrs Maureen Arrowsmith and Mr Lomax that Mrs Arrowsmith appeared to be in her normal state of health on the day before her death. Normal health might not have been very good health and a sudden death was quite possible. I accept that on the day of her death, she was up and dressed, had made her bed and had prepared and eaten a hot lunch. She had washed up afterwards. I infer that Mrs Arrowsmith was still alive and still capable of walking about at 12.30pm or even 1pm. I accept that Shipman telephoned the Lomax house between 1.30pm and 2pm. It follows that Shipman's visit and Mrs Arrowsmith's death both occurred within a very short period, which I estimate at no more than an hour. Of course it is quite possible that Mrs Arrowsmith died a natural death in the short time between eating her lunch and Shipman's arrival. However, it would be an extreme coincidence if Mrs Arrowsmith were to have died a natural death within so short a time before Shipman's visit.
It would have been perfectly possible for Shipman to call on Mrs Arrowsmith at about 1pm. The door might have been left on the latch and he might have been able to walk in. She might have let him in. Even if Mrs Arrowsmith had no particular complaints, Shipman did not find it difficult to make an excuse to give an injection or, more likely, to take a blood sample. He could then have given her a lethal dose of diamorphine, by intravenous injection, which would have caused her to die within a few minutes. He could then have let himself out, locking the door behind him and have gone down to Mrs Unsworth to tell her that there was no reply at Mrs Arrowsmith's flat. He was to use a similar device on other occasions, in particular in the case of Miss Maureen Ward, of whose murder he was convicted. Mrs Unsworth would then accompany him, use her pass key and the body would be 'discovered'.
Knowing what I know of Shipman's later practices, I believe that this death was not natural but was the result of a lethal injection by Shipman. I am sure of that conclusion.

name: Elizabeth Mary Baddeley
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, Flat 6 Rowan Court, Stockport Road, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of suspicious features surrounding this death.
Mrs Baddeley was in good health on the day of her death and her medical history provides no possible explanation for her sudden death. Old age was not an appropriate cause of death for a woman who had been out and about only an hour or so before her death and who had washed her car a few hours earlier. This was a case where any honest doctor should have referred the death to the coroner for post-mortem examination. That Shipman did not do so arouses suspicion as to his involvement. However, I must remind myself that I have come across other cases in which Shipman has certified the cause of a death, which ought to have been referred to the coroner, but where he could not have killed the patient. Accordingly, Shipman's apparent desire to avoid a post-mortem examination is suggestive but not probative of guilty involvement.
The position in which Mrs Baddeley was found was more suggestive of a death due to opiate poisoning than of one due to heart attack or stroke. Dr Grenville has said that it is usual in cases of heart attack or stroke to find the patient collapsed in circumstances which imply an attempt to call for help. The explanation is that, when a stroke or heart attack begins, the patient usually realises that something is seriously wrong and tries to take action. It cannot be said that Mrs Baddeley's position in her chair and peaceful appearance are probative of an unlawful killing by Shipman, but they are suggestive of it.
Shipman told a number of lies on the MCCD and on cremation Form B. First, he claimed that he had seen Mrs Baddeley alive on 12th
November. The medical records and the appointments sheets indicate that he last saw her alive on 14th
October. That would have been more than 14 days before the death. Although it is not necessary for a doctor to have seen a patient within 14 days of the death in order to qualify him or her to certify the cause (it is sufficient if he or she has attended the patient during the last illness and has seen the body after death), many registrars and doctors are under the impression that the doctor cannot certify the cause of death unless he or she has seen the patient within 14 days before the death. Shipman seems to have been under that impression and frequently made false entries suggesting that he had seen the patient within that time limit. He often did this in cases where he had killed the patient and the inference I have drawn is that he would wish to avoid the risk of referral to the coroner. However, sometimes he would make a false entry even where he had not killed the patient. I assume that in such cases he wished to avoid the trouble and potential delay caused by a coroner's referral. Thus, this particular false entry is not significantly probative.
There are, however, other more significant lies. Most important is Shipman's claim on Form B that Mrs Wood was present at the moment of death and was able to provide relevant information about the circumstances of the death. Shipman implies that he knows the time of death, presumably from what he has been told by Mrs Wood. He implies that Mrs Wood has described the mode of death. She was not present. She was not even the daughter who discovered the death. This is an important lie, especially in the context of death supposedly from old age, which is by definition not sudden and where one would expect the patient's family to be in attendance. This lie seems to give the impression that the death was not sudden or unexpected and took place in the presence of a close relative. I cannot see any point in Shipman telling that lie, unless he wished to avoid his medical colleagues asking questions about the cause and circumstances of the death.
Shipman's untruthful claim that he had attended Mrs Baddeley for four years during her last illness is also significant. He is seeking to create the impression that Mrs Baddeley had been declining over a long period. Nothing could have been further from the truth. I can think of no innocent reason for his telling that lie.
Thus, although there is no single factor pointing decisively towards guilt, the features mentioned above are strongly suggestive of it.
On the other side of the scales, there are factors suggestive of natural death and Shipman's innocence.
There is no evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Baddeley on the day of her death or that he intended to see her on that day. That does not mean that he could not have done so. Stockport Road is a very busy thoroughfare and it would not be surprising if he had come and gone without being noticed or remembered. He certainly had time to visit Mrs Baddeley that day. If he did visit her, the visit was unsolicited. Had she been expecting a visit, she would have told her family or Mrs Todd because she would have had to make sure she was back from her outing before 2.30pm. If the visit was unsolicited, it is hard to see anything that might have triggered it. In some cases investigated by the Inquiry, Shipman seems to have taken the opportunity to visit and kill his patient after that patient had come to his attention for some innocuous reason, perhaps because of a request for an acute prescription. There is here no evidence that Mrs Baddeley came to Shipman's attention in any way in the days preceding her death. Of course, that does not mean that she did not come to his attention. He might have seen her out in her car that day.
How Shipman came to give 3pm as the time of death is not clear. He could not have estimated it from body temperature, as he sometimes claimed to do. It seems to me that he probably heard the family discussing Mrs Baddeley's habits and the fact that she would not usually sit in the dark with the curtains open as evening fell. However, the family would not have known at what time Mrs Baddeley returned home in the afternoon. It is possible that Shipman knew the time of death because he was there. If he did visit Mrs Baddeley, it must have been between about 2.30pm and 3.30pm. His usual practice after a killing would be to state a time of death some hours after his visit and the death. In that way he would distance himself from the death. Here he does not seem to have done that and I think this factor points, albeit not strongly, towards innocence.
In my view, the fact that a bottle of pills was found on the table next to Mrs Baddeley is neutral and supports equally the proposition that Mrs Baddeley put out her pills in the course of a visit by Shipman and the alternative proposition that she felt unwell in the minutes leading up to her death and decided to take a tablet.
There is no reliable evidence that Shipman stole from patients he visited or murdered. There is much suspicion that he did but no item of jewellery found on Shipman's premises was ever identified as belonging to one of his deceased patients. In my view, where property is missing, it is not safe to infer that it was taken by Shipman.
Taking these various factors into account, it seems to me that the weight of the evidence points to this being an unnatural death. I bear in mind that, in late 1997, Shipman was killing patients very frequently. At this time, his murderous conduct had reached a crescendo. My conclusion is that Shipman probably killed Mrs Baddeley.

name: Frank Crompton
title: Mr
conclusion:
There are some suspicious features of this death but the evidence that Shipman killed Mr Crompton is not at all clear.
I consider first the question of when Mr Crompton died. It seems to me, from the circumstantial evidence of the date of the shopping receipt and the
TV Times
, that he almost certainly died in the afternoon of 24th
March. There is no evidence that Shipman visited Mr Crompton on that day. However, that does not mean that he did not do so as there is evidence to suggest that Shipman was in the habit of visiting Mr Crompton unannounced and that details of his visits would not necessarily be recorded in the practice visits book. It is quite possible that Shipman's attention was drawn to Mr Crompton by the arrival of his blood test results. I have come across cases where Shipman has used the arrival of test results as an excuse to visit and take further blood tests, probably on the pretext that the first set of results had not been technically satisfactory. He would then use that opportunity to give a lethal injection.
Shipman does not suggest that Mr Crompton died as the result of his cancer. All the evidence shows that the treatment he had undergone for that had been successful and he was at the time symptom-free. Shipman lied to Ms Crompton when he said that the cancer was becoming rampant.
It is possible that Mr Crompton died of a heart attack. Although it appears that Mr Crompton's angina had not been troublesome, he could have had a heart attack at any time. However, Mr Crompton's appearance when found was not consistent with death by coronary thrombosis. He was seated and looked peaceful and had not collapsed, as Shipman certified. His appearance in death was typical of that of many of Shipman's victims who had been injected with diamorphine.
This was an unexpected death of which the cause was not known and should have been referred to the coroner. Shipman was prepared to certify the cause of death when he could not possibly have known what it was.
Shipman's entries on the MCCD, Form B and medical records are riddled with inconsistencies. There are two different dates of death on the face of the Lloyd George envelope. Yet another date is given on the MCCD and Form B. There is an inconsistency between the MCCD and Form B as to the date when Shipman examined the body. I know that Shipman was cavalier in the way he completed official forms, even in cases in which he was not involved in the death. Accordingly I do not attach any significance to those inconsistencies.
I am, however, very suspicious of several other entries on Form B. First, Shipman could not possibly have stated honestly that the death occurred at 6pm on 26th
March. Nor could that time have been intended as a reference to the time at which the body was found. The body was found some time after 8pm. This entry concealed the fact that no one who had provided information knew when Mr Crompton died. When that entry is read in conjunction with Shipman's claim that he had last seen Mr Crompton alive three days before his death, the suspicion is aroused that Shipman was trying to distance himself from the death. He was giving the impression that he knew the time of death and was asserting that it was three days since he had seen Mr Crompton. I am also suspicious of Shipman's statement that he had attended Mr Crompton for one year during his last illness. He implies that Mr Crompton had been suffering from ischaemic heart disease for a year. Although it was not misleading to say that Mr Crompton had angina, and angina is related to ischaemic heart disease, it was misleading to suggest that anything had changed a year before, so as to enable Shipman to mark the commencement of a last illness. The effect is to give the impression that the heart disease was serious and that the death was not therefore unexpected. The truth is that the death was wholly unexpected. Even more sinister is Shipman's claim that the mode of death was collapse and that others had provided information to that effect. That must be a lie, as the people named would, if asked, have described Mr Crompton's position and appearance in death as one which did not suggest collapse. It seems to me that Shipman was deliberately presenting a picture consistent with a heart attack when he must have known that the true picture was not consistent with a death from that cause.
I know from examination of other cases that Shipman sometimes told lies on Form B in order to avoid the need for a referral to the coroner. He did this often in cases where he had killed the patient but, on occasions, he also did it in cases where I am quite satisfied that he was not involved in the death. I do not know his motive for making false entries on those occasions. It might have been to save the family the delay and distress occasioned by a post-mortem examination. In this case, I have asked myself whether these false entries were simply designed to avoid referral to the coroner or whether they were designed to provide a comprehensive and plausible account of the death so as to conceal an act of homicide. I suspect the latter.
I do not attach any significance to the fact that Shipman used Mr Crompton's name to obtain large quantities of diamorphine in the weeks before this death. It is obvious that Shipman had a good stock of the drug at that time, but then I think he usually did.
I have come to the conclusion that Shipman probably killed Mr Crompton. The factor which influences me most is that I think it unlikely that this was a death from a heart attack. Mr Crompton's appearance in death was not such as would usually be found following a heart attack. Although a death from a heart attack was possible, there is no other aspect of the evidence to suggest that this was the cause. All the other features of the case are either neutral or else give rise to some suspicion that Shipman was involved. There is nothing which points clearly against his involvement. The evidence falls far short of that which would be required to convict Shipman of murder. Nonetheless, I have concluded that he probably caused Mr Crompton's death by administering a lethal injection of diamorphine.

name: Joseph Drummond
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 10 Ashley Street, Newton, Hyde
conclusion:
There is no evidence that Shipman visited Mr Drummond on the day of his death. Nor is there any evidence that Shipman was in the habit of visiting Mr Drummond at home. There is no suggestion that Mr Drummond was suffering an acute exacerbation of his chronic condition, which might have caused him to request a visit.
If Shipman had killed Mr Drummond, it would be surprising that he did not take the opportunity to certify the cause of death when he was called out to certify the fact of death. That was his typical course of action after killing a patient. He might well have claimed that he had seen Mr Drummond shortly before his death so as to avert the possibility of questions from the registrar.
Finally, the medical records reveal that Mr Drummond suffered from poor health. In Professor Whitwell's opinion, the circumstances of the death and the previous medical history are consistent with the certified cause of death, although firm corroborative pathological evidence is lacking.
In my judgement, it is overwhelmingly likely that Mr Drummond died of the natural causes certified by the coroner.

name: Joseph Vincent Everall
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 16 Commercial Street, Hyde
conclusion:
There are several suspicious circumstances surrounding Mr Everall's death.
Although it appears that Mr Everall suffered from cancer, the evidence does not suggest that he had yet reached the terminal stage. Indeed, Shipman does not suggest that Mr Everall died of cancer. I have the impression that Mr Everall had been able to go to church and possibly even to walk into Hyde to shop until his most recent surgery. Shipman's visits book does not suggest that Mr Everall was receiving regular visits from Shipman as one would normally expect with a patient in the terminal stage of illness. Nurse Clegg only saw him to bath him and to dress his post-operative wounds. She did not provide terminal nursing care. Thus it appears that, despite his illness, Mr Everall was in reasonable health. His family regarded his death as sudden.
Shipman certified the cause of death to be cerebroarteriosclerosis. This is hardening and narrowing of the cerebral arteries. It is a risk factor, which predisposes the patient to a cerebrovascular accident, which might be fatal. Shipman did not say that Mr Everall died of a stroke but certified that death was due to the underlying condition which might give rise to a stroke. There is no evidence that Mr Everall had cerebroarteriosclerosis. A patient who has that condition to a severe degree might well suffer signs of dementia or have a history of transient ischaemic attacks or strokes. Mr Everall's family does not mention any such signs, symptoms or history. The family's description of his activities would not suggest that Mr Everall was suffering from cerebroarteriosclerosis to the extent that he might die as a result. In the absence of the medical records, it is not possible to form a reliable view about Mr Everall's risk factors for suffering a fatal stroke. I suspect that Mr Everall might have died of some cause quite unrelated to cerebroarteriosclerosis.
The immediate circumstances surrounding the death are not suggestive of a stroke. Mrs Ramsbottom had the impression that her father had only just died when she found him at about 2pm on 17th
December. It would appear likely that he had been able to get up that morning and dress himself. The family says that he would not usually go back to bed to rest during the day. If he had had a stroke one would have expected him to subside gradually into unconsciousness and die over a considerable period. A rapid death is possible but uncommon. Dr John Grenville says in his generic evidence that patients who are alone when a stroke occurs usually make some effort to seek help before they collapse. Mr Everall was found lying peacefully on his bed. This is a position in which many of Shipman's patients were found after being killed by means of a lethal injection of opiate.
There is no direct evidence to show that Shipman visited Mr Everall on the day of his death. However, the entry for that day in the visits book suggests that he probably did. Although I recognise that it is possible that this entry was made in the afternoon when Mr Everall's death had been discovered, in my view that is unlikely. Shipman usually compiled the list of names in the book before leaving the surgery to go on his rounds in the late morning. He often did not enter emergency requests in the book. The book was used more as an aide-memoire for visits which had been requested or which he had decided to make. I consider that it is likely that Shipman had put Mr Everall's name in the visits book as a reminder to himself that Mr Everall was due a visit. He had recently been discharged from hospital. Shipman had seen him exactly a week earlier.
These factors give rise to real suspicion that Shipman caused Mr Everall's death. Mr Everall was in many respects a typical Shipman victim. He lived alone and was in poor health. It is likely that he would have required a great deal of medical and nursing support in the coming months if he had remained alive. Shipman might well have taken the view that Mr Everall's quality of life would never again be good. His philosophy seems to have been that he did not believe that such patients should be 'kept going'. Taking all these factors into account, I have come to the conclusion that it is likely that Shipman killed Mr Everall.

name: Hilda Fish
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Laurel Bank, a residential home for the elderly, Knott Lane, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
The numerous inaccuracies in Form B completed by Shipman naturally excite some suspicion and concern. In many cases where it is known that Shipman has killed a patient, false entries are found on Form B and sometimes on the MCCD. However, in this case, there is no reason to think that Shipman was in any way involved in the death. This case demonstrates that Shipman displayed a cavalier disregard to his duty to provide accurate and truthful information when completing the statutory documentation.
The clear contemporaneous evidence from Laurel Bank, and the equally clear witness evidence obtained from the staff, confirm that Mrs Fish died of natural causes. Those who knew her can be reassured.

name: Minnie Doris Irene Galpin
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 6 Meadowfield Court, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of highly suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. First, and most obvious, is the temporal association between the death and Shipman's visit. Although the time of Shipman's visit is not known, it probably occurred between 1.15pm and 3.45pm. There is no evidence that anyone spoke to Mrs Galpin or saw her alive after Shipman's visit. Although some hours passed between the probable time of Shipman's departure and Mrs Verrall's discovery of the body, it would be something of a coincidence if Mrs Galpin had died naturally in that intervening period. If this were to have occurred with any doctor other than Shipman, I would accept it as a coincidence. After all, natural deaths can and do occur suddenly at any time. However, if Shipman is to be believed, natural deaths very frequently occurred within a short time of his visits. The frequent repetition of such an event cannot be accepted as coincidence. I regard the temporal connection between this death and Shipman's visit as highly suspicious.
There are other causes for suspicion. Mrs Galpin's medical records did not reveal any history from which it would appear that she was at increased risk of suffering a fatal heart attack. That does not mean that she could not have done, but there was no particular reason to expect it. Shipman would have had difficulty in justifying his certification of the cause of death as being due to coronary thrombosis, as he could not or did not wish to claim that he had been present at the death. It appears to me that Shipman has fabricated the computerised record of his visit on the day of the death to create a basis on which he would, if asked, be able to explain the death. I think it is extremely unlikely that Mrs Galpin mentioned any chest pains to Shipman on 12th
March. Had she done so, I would have expected the fact to be recorded in the handwritten records. I would also have expected either Shipman or Mrs Galpin to contact one of her relatives.
If this were a natural death, no reasonable and honest doctor could have certified its cause on the basis of the information supposedly available to Shipman, even supposing there had been a complaint of vague chest pains on the day of the death. This was a sudden and unexpected death for which the cause was not known and should have been referred to the coroner. It appears to me that Shipman seized on Mr Verrall's proffered explanation for the death, based on the family's surmise, and created a little evidence which would support the suggested cause.
Mrs Galpin's appearance in death was not typical of that seen following a death from a coronary thrombosis but was wholly typical of that seen in many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by a lethal dose of strong opiate. I share Dr Grenville's suspicion that Shipman had prescribed MST for Mrs Galpin so that, if her body were subjected to toxicological testing which revealed the presence of morphine, there would be a ready explanation for it.
Taking these factors into account, I am driven to the conclusion that Shipman killed Mrs Galpin, almost certainly in his usual way, by administering a lethal injection of diamorphine. I am sure of this conclusion.

name: Mary Keating
title: Miss
place_of_death: The Sycamores, a residential home for the elderly, Victoria Street, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that this was a natural death.
Miss Keating's gradual decline is well documented in The Sycamores nursing records. It is clear from the note of Dr Wan's visit that he recognised that she was very unwell and it appears that he discussed with her family whether it would be in her best interests to be taken into hospital or to stay at the home. It must have been recognised by all that Miss Keating had not long to live. Her death on 28th
April was neither sudden nor unexpected.
There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman saw Miss Keating alive after 22nd
April. All the documents confirm a visit on that day and none suggests any later visit. I do not think there is any reason to suspect that Shipman had access to Miss Keating in the period before her death.

name: Joseph Leigh
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 50 King George Road, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of highly suspicious circumstances surrounding this death.
Mr Leigh was clearly unwell in the weeks before his death. However, on Shipman's account, as recorded in the Lloyd George notes and Form B of the cremation forms, Mr Leigh suffered a drastic deterioration in his condition on the day of his death. Shipman had decided to visit Mr Leigh that day. Shipman had not been summoned on account of any perceived deterioration or emergency. It is something of a coincidence that Mr Leigh should deteriorate suddenly at the time of Shipman's visit.
I am deeply suspicious of Shipman's note of his consultation with Mr Leigh on 16th
December. Only two days earlier, the jugular venous pressure had not been raised. The heart sounds had been normal and there had been no basal crepitations. The sudden change is too much to believe, especially as Mrs Naughton does not appear to have been aware of any sudden crisis. The note is implausible in other respects. It is incredible that Shipman would provide no treatment at all for a patient who had suddenly deteriorated in this way. I think Shipman's note has been fabricated to provide a plausible explanation for Mr Leigh's death. The only part that rings true is Shipman's claim that Mr Leigh refused to go to hospital. I think Shipman was probably aware of Mr Leigh's strong views on that subject and made the point to add verisimilitude to an otherwise wholly unconvincing story.
Dr Grenville has considered the possibility that Shipman might really have found Mr Leigh in a parlous state and might have given him a small dose of opiate in a genuine 'last ditch' attempt to bring his heart failure under control. If the attempt had failed, Mr Leigh would probably have died very quickly. This cannot have happened. Not only would any doctor who had done that be most anxious to record and explain what he had done (which Shipman did not), no doctor would just walk away, leave the relatives to find the body and not even tell them later what had happened. The idea is unthinkable. I reject this suggestion as bordering on fanciful.
My suspicions that Shipman killed Mr Leigh are heightened by the report of the conversation between Shipman and Mrs Naughton at some time shortly before the death, possibly on the day of the death, possibly a little earlier. Mrs Naughton was finding her duties in caring for her uncle to be very burdensome and I have little doubt that she wanted him to be taken into residential care. Shipman assured her that the problem would soon be resolved. It sounds as though what he had in mind as a solution was not residential care but death. This response would be wholly in keeping with his philosophy that he did not believe in prolonging the lives of elderly people in poor health. However, I shall not attach much weight to this aspect of the case. The evidence is hearsay and the meaning of his remark might have been distorted. That said, one interpretation of what Shipman said is that he was intending to end Mr Leigh's life.
I note and accept Dr Grenville's point that Mr Leigh's appearance in death was not typical of a death from congestive heart failure but was entirely typical of the appearance of many of Shipman's victims. I note also that the position of the chair, at right angles to the table, is exactly what one would expect to see if a doctor had wished to take a blood sample or give an injection and had sat the patient by the table, so that the arm could rest on the table during the procedure.
I have come to the conclusion that Shipman killed Mr Leigh. Although I recognise that Mr Leigh was unwell and it is theoretically possible that he died a natural death, the temporal association between the death and Shipman's presence drives me to the sure conclusion that this cannot have been a natural death. I think Mrs Naughton must have left Shipman alone with Mr Leigh and he took the opportunity to give him an injection of opiate, which caused his death.

name: Pamela Grace Mottram
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home at 6 Ward Street, Hyde
conclusion:
There is no reliable evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Mottram over the weekend of 20th
-21st
July. It is possible that he visited her but there is no reason to think that he did.
If Shipman had killed Mrs Mottram, it would have been courting a considerable risk for him to refer her death to the coroner with the suggestion that she might have committed suicide. Such a suggestion would mean that there was bound to be a post-mortem examination with toxicological tests. If a lethal quantity of opiate were to be found he might be able to pass it off as the result of a self-administered overdose, but he would have risked bringing suspicion on himself. If he had killed Mrs Mottram, it would be more usual for him to claim that he could certify a cause of death and, if necessary, to fabricate entries in the medical records which would support his diagnosis.
The only way in which I can imagine that Shipman could have killed Mrs Mottram would be by giving her an intramuscular injection of opiate of an amount which was not sufficient to kill her but was sufficient to reduce her level of consciousness for a substantial period. After the injection Mrs Mottram would have felt drowsy and might have lain on the floor with a cushion to make herself comfortable. She might then have vomited, inhaled the vomit and developed bronchopneumonia. To give a dose of opiate which was insufficient to kill would be atypical of Shipman, although he did do this by mistake, I think on one or two occasions. To give an intramuscular injection would always be risky, as the patient might be found and revived. Shipman was usually careful to ensure the death of any patient he decided to kill. By 1996 he had considerable experience of killing by injecting opiates and I think it unlikely he would have given an inadequate dose by mistake.
Taking these factors into account, it seems to me unlikely that Shipman played any part in Mrs Mottram's death. If, as I accept, the immediate cause of death was bronchopneumonia, it seems likely that the underlying cause was a cerebrovascular accident. Mrs Mottram had been diagnosed as suffering such an episode in the past and must therefore have been at risk of a further stroke at any time.

name: Samuel Oldham
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 65 Mottram Old Road, Hyde
conclusion:
Mr Oldham was suffering from advanced cancer of the bowel. He was clearly very unwell and had not long to live. Towards the end of his life, he was in considerable pain and was taking analgesic drugs. Although it appears that those drugs were initially taken orally, it is likely that towards the end he also needed injections for breakthrough pain. These were probably of an opiate such as morphine or diamorphine and would probably have been given intramuscularly.
Mr Lynn Oldham recalls that Shipman visited his father on the morning of the day of his death. Some doubt is cast on the accuracy of his recollection not only by the accounts given by his wife and Mrs Shore, but also by what is written in Shipman's visits book for the day of the death and the MCCD counterfoil. Mr Lynn Oldham himself concedes that his memory of events is unclear.
Even if Mr Lynn Oldham's recollection is correct and even if Shipman administered an injection of opiate that morning, it seems highly unlikely that the injection could have caused or hastened Mr Oldham's death. If Mr Lynn Oldham is right, a period of at least two hours passed between Shipman's visit and Mr Oldham's death. Professor Henry McQuay and Dr John Grenville have given joint generic evidence to the Inquiry as to the timing and effect of opiates. If a lethal injection of opiate is administered intravenously, death follows within minutes. If administered intramuscularly, a lethal injection of opiate will cause death within about an hour. That Mr Oldham lived for two hours after Shipman's departure appears to rule out the possibility that Shipman gave a lethal injection. If Shipman did give Mr Oldham an injection that morning, it would appear that it was given for the purpose of relieving pain and was not designed to shorten life.
Mr Lynn Oldham's concern arose because he recalls that Shipman seemed to think he could predict the time of death with some accuracy. In view of the recollections of other members of the family, it seems unlikely that any such conversation took place between Shipman and Mr Oldham on the morning of 2nd
March. It is difficult for witnesses to remember events occurring so long ago.
It seems to me that the overwhelming likelihood is that Mr Oldham died a natural death, due to his advanced cancer.

name: Ethel May Proud
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 144 Lodge Lane, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that this was a natural death. There is no evidence that Shipman saw Mrs Proud shortly before her death. His only involvement in her death was to visit after the death to pronounce life extinct. To the extent that Form 751 suggests that Shipman was present at the death, it is misleading.
The evidence of Professor Whitwell shows that the cause of death was either ischaemic heart disease or bronchopneumonia.

name: Konrad Peter Ovcar-Robinson
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home
conclusion:
There is no doubt that Mr Ovcar-Robinson was terminally ill. His condition deteriorated in the days leading up to his death, particularly on the night of 24th
November. When Shipman arrived at the house, Mr Ovcar-Robinson's breathing was noisy and he almost certainly had some form of pneumonia or bronchopneumonia. If he was in pain or distressed, or if Shipman genuinely believed that his pain might return with a recovery of consciousness, Shipman would be justified in giving him an opiate drug.
Shipman's intention in administering that opiate can be determined by reference to the dose administered and what he said to the family. It appears to me, from the reported conversations, that he probably intended to ensure that Mr Ovcar-Robinson would die that afternoon. In order to achieve that end, he would need quite a large dose of diamorphine, although Mr Ovcar-Robinson was already in a very debilitated state. In his evidence to the Inquiry, Professor Henry McQuay said that 30mg of intravenous diamorphine is likely to prove fatal to a fit adult not previously exposed to strong opioid drugs. He said that 20mg could prove fatal to an elderly, unfit and opioid naïve person. I think that 20mg would certainly have been enough to kill Mr Ovcar-Robinson. It is possible that even 10mg might have done, if he was sufficiently debilitated. However, I think it likely that Shipman would have wished to record a justifiable dose, even though he might well have given considerably more.
I am by no means convinced that the dose was necessarily limited to 10mg of diamorphine. At this time in 1995, Shipman had in his possession a large quantity of diamorphine, mainly in 100mg ampoules. He had almost certainly obtained ten ampoules of 100mg diamorphine on 23rd
September 1995, following the death of Mr Peter Neal, who had had the use of a syringe driver for pain relief in the last few days of his life. It is not impossible that Shipman also had some 10mg ampoules in November 1995, but I think his main stock was in 100mg ampoules. He might also have had some 30mg ampoules. One of Mr Ovcar-Robinson's sisters recalls seeing Shipman take an ampoule from his pocket. It is not impossible that he gave Mr Ovcar-Robinson precisely 10mg but I regard it as more likely that he administered a larger dose than that. I also think it quite likely that the dose was not a whole ampoule and was not therefore precisely measured. I think it likely that the dose was administered intramuscularly, rather than intravenously. Death followed within about 30 to 60 minutes after the injection was given. As Professor McQuay said, that is entirely typical of the effect of a lethal dose given intramuscularly.
My conclusion is that it is likely that Shipman deliberately and unlawfully hastened Mr Ovcar-Robinson's death. I cannot say that I am certain of that conclusion, as it is possible that the dose was of only 10mg and was given lawfully, with the intention only of relieving pain or distress.

name: Lena Norah Slater
title: Miss
place_of_death: her home, 10 Newton Hall Court, Hyde
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to carcinoma of the breast
conclusion:
At the time of her death, Miss Slater was extremely unwell. She had been suffering from cancer for many months but, a month before her death, she had refused further chemotherapy treatment. The cancer had spread and Miss Slater clearly knew that she would not live for much longer. It is theoretically possible that Miss Slater died a natural death on 2nd
May.
Set against the background of her recent activities, however, Miss Slater's death was very sudden. She had been shopping on 30th
April and had voted on 1st
May. She had been coping in her own home and the district nurse was not visiting frequently. It does not appear to me that Miss Slater had reached the terminal stage of her illness. For that reason, the suddenness of her death, and its temporal association with a visit from Shipman, gives rise to deep suspicion that the death was not natural.
The question arises as to whether Shipman killed Miss Slater during his first visit to the house. I cannot say with certainty that no one spoke to or saw Miss Slater alive after Shipman's first visit. It is possible, but unlikely, that Miss Slater spoke to Mrs Brelsford after that visit. It is also possible that Miss Slater was seen by a neighbour at about 3pm, although there is no confirmation that such a person existed. However, if Shipman's own note of the time of his visit on the visit request form is accurate and he saw Miss Slater at 1.45pm, he might well have been the last person to communicate with her. Only the mysterious neighbour might have seen her, but she might have been an invention of Shipman's. These considerations raise the index of suspicion that Shipman might have killed Miss Slater at his first visit.
That Shipman should make a second visit in order to give himself an opportunity to 'discover' the body would be entirely typical of his conduct in other cases where he has killed a patient. The accounts that Shipman gave to Mrs Taylor and Mr Slater as to the reason for his first visit, his departure and his second visit were inconsistent with each other. That may prove nothing, as one or both of the witnesses might be mistaken in their recollection. However, it seems to me that Shipman's stories are essentially implausible. If Miss Slater was in need of terminal care or even temporary care, there is no sensible reason why Shipman could not have picked up the telephone there and then to see how it could be arranged. We cannot be certain whether Shipman actually made enquiries with either St Ann's Hospice or The Sycamores. However, he certainly did not report the outcome of his enquiries to Mrs Taylor or Mr Slater. In my judgement, it is highly likely that the accounts were fabricated.
The computerised medical records created at 4.47pm and 4.48pm, after the discovery of the body, are misleading and give rise to suspicion. If the first entry were genuine, one would have expected Shipman to record his conversation with Miss Slater on his return to the surgery. If he had made any arrangements for admission to an institution, one would expect them to be recorded. However, he made no entry at all until after the death had been 'discovered'. Then he made two entries which gave the impression that they had been made on separate occasions but which had in fact been made at one sitting. He gave the impression that the first had been made while Miss Slater was still alive. In fact she was already dead.
Shipman's reference to a neighbour in the second computerised entry gives rise to suspicion. He suggests that a neighbour spoke to Miss Slater at 3pm, which would be well after Shipman's first visit. This neighbour is not identified. On the visit request form, Shipman says that a Mary McGowan found Miss Slater dead. Efforts to trace her have failed. The evidence suggests that it was Shipman himself who 'found' Miss Slater's body. If a Mary McGowan had been involved, one might have expected Mrs Taylor or Mr Slater to be aware of her. They are not. In my view, these entries are a deliberate attempt by Shipman to create the impression that he was not the last person to see or speak to Miss Slater before her death, when in fact he knew that he was. He has also tried to give the impression that it was not he who found the body. I have found that, in other cases, Shipman has made such false entries, usually on Form B but occasionally in medical records.
This is a difficult case in that it is clear that Miss Slater had not long to live and it is theoretically possible that she died a natural death. However, the case has many of the hallmarks of a Shipman killing and I am sure that Shipman killed Miss Slater by administering an injection of strong opiate, probably diamorphine.

name: Alice Thomas
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 26 Sidley Place, Hyde
conclusion:
There are several reasons to suspect that Shipman might have killed Mrs Thomas.
Mrs Thomas' medical records have not been recovered and so little is known about her medical condition prior to death. However, the fact that she had suffered a number of strokes in the past would put her at increased risk of further stroke. Mr Thomas has also said that his mother's face was 'extremely distorted', a feature that would point towards her having suffered a stroke. Mrs Randall described Mrs Thomas' face as 'drooping' on one side, which might also indicate that she had had a stroke. However, the rest of the evidence suggests that Shipman unlawfully killed Mrs Thomas.
The most suspicious feature is that Shipman was present at the moment of Mrs Thomas' death. She told her son, the day before she died, that she was expecting Shipman to attend for a check-up. His visit was, therefore, routine and not in response to an emergency such as the onset of new symptoms which might suggest an illness which carried a risk of sudden and unexpected death. Had there been such an emergency, this would almost certainly have been mentioned at the time by Shipman or Mrs Ridgeway or both.
In his generic evidence to the Inquiry, Dr John Grenville said that it would be most unusual for a patient to die during a routine visit. Such an event might happen once in a doctor's professional lifetime. Shipman claimed to have been present at the deaths of a number of his patients and this cannot be explained by coincidence. That Mrs Thomas died during a routine visit by Shipman is a highly suspicious factor in its own right.
On Form B, Shipman said that he saw Mrs Thomas 40 minutes before she died. However, when read in conjunction with his other answers, it is clear that he meant that he arrived at her house about 40 minutes before the death. It appears that he diagnosed a right-sided stroke and that she then entered a progressive coma, which lasted for about 20 minutes, before she died at 11.55am. If events really had occurred in this way, not only would it have been an enormous coincidence that Shipman happened to arrive at the crucial time, but also Shipman would have behaved very differently. If a doctor had found Mrs Thomas showing signs of having a developing stroke, he would certainly have tried to contact her relatives or a neighbour. Several of Mrs Thomas' relatives lived in the area. Most doctors in that position would probably have summoned an ambulance as well. Shipman did neither. Mrs Randall thought that this was strange at the time and she is right.
I am also suspicious about Shipman's claim that this right-sided stroke led so quickly to Mrs Thomas' death. The type of stroke which causes a weakness on one side of the body is usually an occlusive stoke occurring in the upper part of the brain. Such strokes are not usually fatal and most patients recover with varying degrees of residual disability. However, such a stroke can progress, in which case the patient will usually suffer a gradual loss of consciousness leading to death. The process usually lasts about two to three days. The type of stroke that can lead to sudden death is usually a haemorrhagic stroke in the brain stem, which does not produce weakness on one side of the body.
Shipman's action in leaving a note and the MCCD with Mrs Ridgeway is rather an unusual procedure for a doctor to follow after a death. This note would have served to prevent the involvement of other agencies such as the police and the ambulance service, with the attendant likelihood that the death would be referred to the coroner. It seems likely to me that Shipman left the note and certificate because he wished to avoid a referral to the coroner.
I think it is likely that Shipman killed Mrs Thomas. The weight of the evidence suggests that he did. However, I must give weight to the observations of Mr Thomas and Mrs Randall who noted that Mrs Thomas' face was distorted or drooping at one side. There are two possible explanations for this. One is that Mrs Thomas' face had been 'distorted' by her earlier strokes and once the muscles were relaxed in death this appearance was more noticeable than it was when she was alive and awake. Another possible explanation is that Shipman found Mrs Thomas in the early stages of a further stroke. Rather than calling a relative and then waiting to see whether or not the stroke developed, he decided to ensure that the stroke would be fatal.
My conclusion is that Shipman probably killed Mrs Thomas, by giving her a lethal injection of opiate. I stop short of saying that I am sure of that conclusion because it is possible that Mrs Thomas died of a right-sided stroke.

name: Mary Winterbottom
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 181 Grange Road South, Hyde
conclusion:
There are some suspicious features surrounding this death. First, it appears that Shipman was present at the moment of death. That in itself arouses grave suspicion, as other doctors find that patients very rarely die during the course of a routine visit. This visit seems to have been little more than that. It was certainly not an emergency visit.
It is possible that this was a natural death from coronary thrombosis. It is clear that Mrs Winterbottom did have angina and, in the absence of the medical records, I cannot assess the severity of her heart disease. She may well have had ischaemic heart disease for 15 years as Shipman claimed although, if she did, it does not seem to have affected her activities until quite shortly before her death. People with angina or ischaemic heart disease can and do die sudden deaths. So a sudden cardiac death is a real possibility in this case.
If this was a natural death, the hand of coincidence played an extraordinary role. If it occurred in the manner claimed by Shipman, Mrs Winterbottom succumbed just at the moment when he walked through the door. Such an event could happen, although it is very unlikely. If Shipman is to be believed, in this and other cases, deaths quite frequently occurred just at the time of his visit. I cannot but be deeply sceptical of his claim that Mrs Winterbottom was having a heart attack just as he arrived.
I also doubt that Shipman attempted resuscitation. Effective resuscitation must be carried out on a hard surface. A soft bed would not be satisfactory. The clothing did not appear to be disturbed. Although the dentures could have been removed to facilitate resuscitation, Shipman might have removed them to create the impression he had tried to revive Mrs Winterbottom. But her otherwise tidy appearance belies any serious attempt.
Another factor of some concern is that Shipman claimed that Mrs Winterbottom would simply have lain down and gone to sleep. Such a mode of death would not be typical of death by coronary thrombosis. Usually, a fatal heart attack is a very painful event, although occasionally it is not. However, I do not attach much weight to this factor, as Shipman might have offered this explanation, knowing it to be untrue, but wishing to reassure an anxious relative.
The appearance of the body, lying neatly on the bed, fully clothed, is not typical of a patient who has suffered a heart attack. Usually such a patient is found collapsed on the floor having made an effort to seek help. On the other hand, Mrs Winterbottom's position and appearance is typical of the deaths of many of Shipman's victims from morphine poisoning.
Taking these factors into account, it seems overwhelmingly likely that Shipman killed Mrs Winterbottom by giving her an injection, almost certainly of diamorphine. I say that even in the absence of Mrs Winterbottom's medical records, which, if available, whould have enabled me to assess more accurately the seriousness of her heart condition. Shipman's account of events is wholly implausible. I am sure Shipman unlawfully killed Mrs Winterbottom.

name: Brenda Ashworth
title: Miss
conclusion:
There are several suspicious circumstances surrounding this death.
First, it appears that Shipman was the last person to see Miss Ashworth alive. That in itself is a factor which always arouses strong suspicion. It is not clear from Shipman's records whether he visited Miss Ashworth once or twice on 16th
June and it is not clear at what time or times he visited. It appears that Miss Ashworth did not request a visit until about lunchtime. She had not done so when Miss Yates brought her shopping. Shipman might have visited in the afternoon before his afternoon surgery began. In the computerised records, he said that she had pneumonia and that he would review her again that day. He gave her no treatment. It is possible that he returned in the evening on his way home. In any event, there is no evidence that anyone other than Shipman saw Miss Ashworth alive or spoke to her after Miss Yates' departure.
It is not known at what time Miss Ashworth died. Shipman sought to suggest that she had died at about 8am, after being in a coma for
'several hours'
. How he was supposed to know either of these things is not clear. As no one except Shipman had seen Miss Ashworth since lunchtime on 16th
June, the claim that she had been in a coma for several hours was, at best, supposition. In any event, there was no basis on which he could have made an honest assessment of the time of death. I find it suspicious that he should wish to pretend that he knew what time she had died. I suspect that he was seeking to create a substantial period of time between his last visit and the supposed time of death. I suspect that she died in the afternoon or early evening of 16th
June.
Even if she had died at 8am on 17th
June, it does not appear likely to me that Miss Ashworth could have died of bronchopneumonia and certainly not of three to four days' duration, as Shipman claimed on the MCCD. There can be no doubt that Miss Ashworth had a chest infection, which by 15th June was bad enough to cause her to ask Shipman for an antibiotic. When Miss Yates last saw Miss Ashworth, she appeared to be 'a bit poorly with some chest problems'. Miss Yates did not think that Miss Ashworth's condition was serious. She had asked Miss Yates to bring her a sandwich. Dr Grenville told the Inquiry that bronchopneumonia does not usually cause a very sudden death. The illness usually develops over a period of several days, during which the patient deteriorates gradually. He says that, if a patient were going to die of pneumonia, it would be evident to someone who had seen the patient the day before death that they were seriously unwell. Thus, Miss Ashworth's appearance, as witnessed by Miss Yates, and her wish to have some food brought in are inconsistent with a death from bronchopneumonia the next day. Miss Ashworth was not sufficiently ill at lunchtime on 16th
June for it to be likely that she would die from bronchopneumonia at 8am the next day.
I also find it suspicious that Miss Ashworth was found sitting upright in her chair, wearing her day clothes. If her illness had come on gradually, as would be the case with bronchopneumonia, she would almost certainly have gone to bed, where she would be warm and comfortable. Shipman seems to be suggesting that Miss Ashworth must have sat fully dressed in her chair for some hours while she became ill and that she then fell into a coma and eventually died. That does not make sense. On the other hand, Miss Ashworth's appearance in death was entirely consistent with death by a fatal dose of diamorphine. Dr Ashworth, her distant relative, noticed her unusual appearance.
The computerised notes and the Lloyd George cards are inconsistent. The computerised records reveal a diagnosis of pneumonia and influenza, but the handwritten records give a diagnosis of a chest infection and a possible coronary thrombosis. If Miss Ashworth was suffering from pneumonia, she should not have been left alone. She should have been admitted to hospital. If she had refused, the fact should have been noted and arrangements should have been made for some care or supervision at home, probably by the district nurse. Whenever Shipman's records suggest that his actions were not those of a reasonably sensible, competent doctor, I suspect that they do not present a true picture of events. I suspect that in this case.
Shipman's conduct in returning to the scene to 'discover' the body is entirely typical of many cases in which he killed. Shipman would often leave the body of a patient to be found by neighbours or relatives, but if the body was not found within a reasonable time he would return and 'find' it himself. Why he did this is not clear. It may have been in order to avoid the risk that another doctor would be summoned, the police involved and the case referred to the coroner before he had the chance to say that he would certify the cause of death. In this case, it appears that he went to 'find' the body before going home for the weekend.
The several factors that I have mentioned all point to the conclusion that Shipman killed Miss Ashworth. He was the last person to see her alive. The medical records are suspicious. Shipman told lies on cremation Form B. Death from bronchopneumonia does not fit the known facts. Her appearance in death was typical of Shipman's victims. Miss Ashworth probably was at an increased risk of suffering a cardiac death. It is possible that she died of a heart attack or stroke. However, it would be something of a coincidence if Miss Ashworth succumbed to a sudden death between two visits by Shipman.
The overwhelming likelihood in this case is that Shipman killed Miss Ashworth, almost certainly by a lethal injection of diamorphine. I believe I can safely discount the possibility of a natural death. My conclusion is that I am sure that he killed her.

name: May Brookes
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 49 Cross Street, Hyde
conclusion:
Mrs Brookes' medical records have not been recovered and very little is known about her medical condition prior to death. Although she did suffer from hypertension she led a fit and active life. Despite the lack of medical evidence, there is still good evidence that Shipman unlawfully killed Mrs Brookes.
The most suspicious feature is the fact that Shipman was present at the moment of death, particularly as Mrs Brookes was not suffering from a terminal illness and Shipman had not been called out as an emergency. As Dr Grenville has commented, there are a number of cases where Shipman has been present at the death of a patient who, not having suffered from a terminal illness, has died suddenly at home. That this should occur in any individual case is a remarkable coincidence. That this occurred on so many occasions cannot be explained by coincidence. This is a highly suspicious feature in its own right.
Mrs Brookes was fit and well when seen by her grandson on the morning of her death and by Mrs Wood immediately before Shipman's visit. She made no complaint of ill health to Mrs Wood and said that Shipman was due to visit her in connection with her hip. Yet on Shipman's account, he found her collapsed on the floor. She was said to be alive but
'dying'
and he therefore lifted her into a chair. Beyond the obvious point that this would be an extraordinary coincidence, a number of further points arise. Where a patient is not suffering from a terminal illness or some obvious serious injury, it is not possible to determine whether a patient is dying. Dr Grenville has commented that there would be no reason for Shipman to lift Mrs Brookes into a chair. In any event Mrs Brookes' appearance was inconsistent with her having collapsed and thereafter being lifted into a chair. Her glasses were straight and her clothing was not ruffled. Further, due to Mrs Brookes' weight, it would be extremely difficult, if not impossible for Shipman to have lifted Mrs Brookes into a chair. I conclude that Shipman lied about having found Mrs Brookes collapsed on the floor.
Had Shipman really found Mrs Brookes in a collapsed state then he should have summoned an ambulance in order for her to receive emergency treatment in hospital. Where a patient is semi-conscious or unconscious, it would be very difficult to diagnose a cerebrovascular accident. For example, the patient could be in a state of hypo or hyperglycaemia. Further, as it would not have been possible for Shipman to diagnose the fact that Mrs Brookes was
'dying'
, he would not have been able to predict future events or that calling an ambulance would be futile. A patient who is unconscious may well regain consciousness and, in any event, survive for some time.
