Shipman recorded on Form B that Mr Ridings was present with him at the moment of death. According to the accounts of both Mrs Bentley and Mr Reed, when Shipman first spoke to Mr Ridings he said that Mrs Brookes was dead. I believe that Shipman lied in completing Form B.
Taken as a whole the evidence satisfies me that Shipman unlawfully killed Mrs Brookes and I am sure that he did so.
It is not possible to determine from the medical records whether Mrs Brookes did in fact require a blood test. If she did, then, considering her good health, she would have been able to attend at the surgery in order for the sample to be taken. Therefore, it would appear likely that the killing of Mrs Brookes was premeditated, and the offer to attend at her home in order to take a blood sample was a pretext and an excuse on Shipman's part to introduce a needle.

name: Ann Coulthard
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 9 Southside, Hyde
conclusion:
There seems little doubt that Mrs Coulthard had a stroke soon after her return from holiday. It is possible she had had a minor stroke while away. It is not possible to trace the course of her illness, as her medical records have long since been destroyed. However, it is clear that her health deteriorated gradually over about four weeks and it became clear that she had not long to live.
I found the evidence of Mr Ian Coulthard and his wife to be reliable, despite the passage of 20 years. I accept that in the last few days of her life, Mrs Coulthard was restless and in some pain. The reasons for that cannot now be ascertained. It appears highly likely that Shipman first gave Mrs Coulthard an intramuscular injection within a few days of her death, possibly on the day before. That seems to have made her very drowsy. She did not die, so that injection cannot have been lethal. We do not know what it was. It might have been an opiate; it might have been a sedative.
It seems likely that Shipman came again the following morning and might have given another injection. If he did, it was probably of some form of opiate or sedative. That would be appropriate if Mrs Coulthard was restless and seemed to be in pain. Whatever the injection was, the dosage was not lethal. When Mrs Gash was sitting with her that day, Mrs Coulthard was very sleepy and appeared to be sedated. By late afternoon, Mrs Coulthard was restless again and seemed to be in pain. Shipman gave another intramuscular injection. That might well have been an opiate and might well have been a lethal dose. I say that because, approximately an hour later, Mrs Coulthard died. Professor Henry McQuay and Dr Grenville agree that an opiate given intramuscularly provides maximal effect about 30 minutes to an hour after administration. If the dose is lethal, death will follow within about an hour. It is possible that Mrs Coulthard's last injection was of a different nature from the earlier injections or was of a greatly increased dose and was intended to end Mrs Coulthard's life. However, the injection might have been a sedative or an opiate in a quantity which was not lethal and the death might have been natural. It is not possible to say.
A further possibility is that Shipman might have given Mrs Coulthard quite large doses of a sedative over a period of two to three days with the intention of keeping her asleep. This might have been a reasonable thing to do, if it was the only way to keep her comfortable. However, if kept asleep for a long period, Mrs Coulthard would be vulnerable to bronchopneumonia, a common mechanism of death in elderly people who have suffered strokes. If Shipman did this, it would not be possible to say whether he did it because he genuinely considered it to be the only way of keeping Mrs Coulthard comfortable or whether he used it as an indirect way of hastening her death.
I regret that I cannot reach a positive decision in this case. There are grounds to suspect that Shipman might have hastened Mrs Coulthard's death.

name: Fred Davies
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 21 Lumn Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mr Davies died a natural death. He was clearly in the terminal stage of lung cancer and his death was expected. His pain was such that it was appropriate for Shipman to give him regular injections of an opiate drug. Exactly what was being used is not known.
It is not known how long elapsed after Shipman's last visit before Mr Davies died. Shipman usually carried out his visits between about midday and 3.30pm. Mr Davies died after 5pm, probably at about 6pm. In any event, the death must have been at least two hours after the last injection and was probably more like four hours later. Professor Henry McQuay and Dr John Grenville have given joint generic evidence to the Inquiry as to the timing and effect of opiates. If a lethal injection of opiates were administered intravenously, then death would follow within minutes. If administered intramuscularly, a lethal injection of opiate would cause death within about an hour. As Mr Davies lived for at least two hours after the time of the last possible injection, I can say with confidence that he cannot have been given a lethal dose.

name: Harold Freeman
title: Mr
place_of_death: The Sycamores, a residential home for the elderly, Victoria Street, Hyde
conclusion:
I regret that I am unable to reach a conclusion about Mr Freeman's death. I agree with Dr Grenville that Shipman's medical note suggests that Mr Freeman's chest infection had responded to treatment and was no longer a cause for concern on 19th
February. However, Shipman's notes cannot be trusted and it is quite possible that the chest infection remained serious. Certainly the staff who requested the visit on 19th
February thought that his breathing was bad and his colour
'shocking'
.
There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman had access to Mr Freeman in the period immediately before his death. The medical records, visits book and Form B all suggest that Shipman last saw Mr Freeman during the day on 19th
February, at least 12 hours before the death and probably more like 15 to 16 hours.
There is a real possibility that during his daytime visit on 19th
February, Shipman decided to ensure that Mr Freeman's chest infection should lead to death. He could have done that by giving an injection, possibly of opiate or possibly of a sedative. If this happened, it is clear that Shipman did not give a lethal dose of opiate, as Mr Freeman lived for about 15 to 16 hours afterwards. However, he could have given a dose which made Mr Freeman deeply unconscious. While unconscious, Mr Freeman would be very vulnerable to the development of bronchopneumonia. His chest infection could have deteriorated and have resulted in death within the 15 to 16 hours between Shipman's visit and death. That is a real possibility.
On the other hand, as Dr Grenville says, Mr Freeman was at risk of suffering a sudden cardiac death. It is also possible that the chest infection took hold and led to death without any intervention by Shipman.
I do not think that the fact that Shipman prescribed 30mg of diamorphine in Mr Freeman's name indicates that Shipman gave Mr Freeman that type of drug. He could have done, as I have said. However, prescribing diamorphine in the name of a deceased patient was one of Shipman's methods of obtaining the drug for his own purposes and a method which he used regularly in 1993.
I regret that I cannot reach a positive conclusion. There are grounds to suspect that Shipman killed Mr Freeman but I cannot say more than that.

name: Christine Hancock
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 12 Thistley Fields, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
This death is highly suspicious because Shipman was alone with Mrs Hancock in the brief interval of time, probably of the order of half an hour, between the telephone call to Mrs White (at which time Mrs Hancock had not had a stroke) and the arrival of Mr White at her house, by which time she was unconscious. If Mrs Hancock did indeed suffer a massive stroke in that short interval, the coincidence is remarkable.
The fact is that Shipman was alone with her in that brief interval and had the opportunity to administer a lethal diamorphine injection. As Dr John Grenville said in his generic evidence, following such an injection, the patient would lapse into sleep which would become deeper, respiration would slow and the patient would die.
Mrs Hancock was feeling ill on the morning of her death and asked Shipman to visit. However, although the visits book entry says that she was
'VERY ILL'
, she cannot have given the impression to the surgery staff member that her condition was serious. If she had given such an impression, the staff member would have advised her to call an ambulance or would have called an ambulance from the surgery. That was the practice. In any event, if Mrs Hancock had been seriously ill, the tenor of her conversation with Mrs White would have been different. It seems to me more likely that Mrs Hancock was suffering from a worse than usual episode of the symptoms attributable to her multiple sclerosis, symptoms with which she would be familiar.
Dr Grenville has said that multiple sclerosis is not a cause of sudden death and patients with that condition are no more likely to die of stroke than others. There was nothing in Mrs Hancock's medical history to indicate that she was at an increased risk of stroke.
Mrs Hancock's position and appearance in death are not typical of what is usually seen following a death from a sudden fatal stroke. That Mrs Hancock was observed sitting peacefully in her chair, with her hands folded on her lap is, however, entirely consistent with, and typical of, death by morphine or diamorphine injection.
In my view, it is highly unlikely that Mrs Hancock had a stroke.
Taking these factors into account and bearing in mind the startling coincidence relied on by Shipman, that Mrs Hancock is supposed to have had a fatal stroke at the very time he visited, I am driven to the sure conclusion that he killed her.

name: Norah Johnson
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 27 Rydal Avenue, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite sure that Mrs Johnson died a natural death.
It seems highly likely that Shipman visited Mrs Johnson on 5th
July, rather than 7th
July. Even if he did visit on 7th
July, two people saw Mrs Johnson alive afterwards. During the afternoon, her daughter stayed with her until about 3pm. During the evening, Ms Wood stayed until about 10pm. When Ms Wood left, Mrs Johnson applied her security chain, which was still in place the next morning. It is hard to see how anyone could have been into Mrs Johnson's flat during the night.
Although the death was unexpected and a shock to Mrs Adshead, Mrs Johnson had been suffering from a persistent episode of bronchitis. It is not possible to discover, so many years later, whether Mrs Johnson had also been suffering from congestive heart disease. Whatever the precise cause of the death, there is no reason whatever to think that Shipman, or any other person, had any hand in it.

name: John Louden Livesey
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 130 Dowson Road, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
There are several highly suspicious circumstances surrounding this death.
Although Shipman did not admit that he had visited Mr Livesey on the day of his death, I strongly suspect that he did. If he did and if no one spoke to or saw Mr Livesey alive after the visit, the temporal connection between the visit and the death would, of itself, be a highly suspicious circumstance. If Shipman visited and later sought to conceal his visit, the level of suspicion would rise further.
The following factors have persuaded me that Shipman did visit Mr Livesey on the day of his death. First, at about midday on 25th
July, Mr Livesey told his son-in-law that he was expecting Shipman but that he had not yet arrived. It appears that Shipman had promised to let Mr Livesey have his test results that day. We know that he did not use the surgery telephone to contact Mr Livesey. Second, when Mr Livesey-Carter arrived at the house at about 4pm, he found the front door unlocked and the key in the lock on the inside. That would indicate that someone had called at the house, that Mr Livesey had let the person in and that he or she had left the house but was not shown out by Mr Livesey. Although it is theoretically possible that some other person could have called, rather than Shipman, Shipman was expected and no other person has told Mr and Mrs Livesey-Carter that they visited shortly before the death. In any event, an unlocked door is a common feature in several cases in which Shipman killed. Third, it would be something of a coincidence if Shipman happened to make a detailed backdated entry in the medical records shortly before 2pm if nothing had happened to trigger that action. Just after 1pm, it was probably he who entered the previous day's blood test results in the records. Just before 2pm, he made the backdated entry. This strongly suggests to me that Shipman had had further contact with Mr Livesey in the meantime. Finally, I mention that I do not place any weight on the evidence of what Shipman told the paramedics as Mr Livesey-Carter is not sure whether Shipman told them he had seen Mr Livesey that day or 'recently'.
That Mr Livesey should have died quite suddenly of kidney failure on 25th
July is medically most improbable. On the previous day, he went to the surgery complaining of pain in his stomach. Shipman took a blood sample and diagnosed a duodenal ulcer. These is nothing in the note made on that day to suggest that Mr Livesey had kidney failure, or was seriously ill, or at risk of dying a sudden death. At no time did Shipman test Mr Livesey's kidney function. Dr Grenville says it is inconceivable that someone should die suddenly of kidney failure shortly after having worked on accounts at a computer. Also, it is hard to see on what possible basis Shipman could supposedly have come to the conclusion that Mr Livesey died of renal failure some 24 hours after he had last seen him. Even the backdated note made on 25th
July would not have helped him. How Shipman was supposed to have known that the mode of death was a coma of a few minutes' duration is not clear. In any event, this would not be a typical mode of death where the cause was renal failure. Shipman's claim that Mr Livesey died of renal failure is nonsense. Unless Shipman killed Mr Livesey, he could not possibly have known why he had died and the death should have been referred to the coroner. There was an additional reason why this death should have been referred. Mr Livesey had been exposed to asbestos in the past and the possibility that his death was related to that should have been investigated.
The backdated entry made on 25th
July is highly suspicious. It purports to relate to a consultation in the surgery, at which time Mr Livesey must have been well enough to drive into Hyde. It is hard to see any innocent reason why Shipman would have made this backdated entry when he had already made his clinical entries concerning the consultation of 24th
July. In many respects the backdated entry is typical of notes which I have seen in cases where Shipman has killed his patient. In these cases, Shipman has fabricated a note in order to provide an explanation for the death. However, in the present case, the fabricated note does not tally with the cause of death which Shipman was later to certify. It appears to me that Shipman probably intended to kill Mr Livesey and to certify the cause of death as left ventricular failure. He could then have relied on the fabricated note. For some reason, which I cannot fathom, Shipman decided to put the death down to renal failure. That there is nothing in Shipman's note suggestive of renal failure and nothing to suggest that Mr Livesey was seriously ill demonstrates that the attempt at falsification was poor, but does not dilute its sinister connotation.
The circumstances in the house suggest that Mr Livesey was working at his computer when he was disturbed. He unlocked his door. He did not drink his cup of tea. He did not switch off his computer. He then died on his sofa, still wearing his slippers and glasses. He did not re-lock the door. Mr Livesey's peaceful appearance in death was wholly consistent with death by lethal injection of diamorphine. That appearance, combined with the evidence as to how he spent his last few hours, is wholly inconsistent with death due to renal failure. Mr Livesey's appearance in death was not typical of any of the common causes of death, such as stroke or heart attack, from which Mr Livesey could possibly have died a sudden death.
There is an odd feature of the case, which relates to Form B. Shipman said that the death occurred at about 1.30pm. How he thought he could estimate the time with any accuracy, when seeing the body some time after 4pm, I cannot imagine. He often pretended that he could estimate the time of death by body temperature, which Dr Grenville says is not possible, at least without taking an internal body temperature. Usually Shipman stated a time of death several hours after his own last visit. He would distance himself from the death. Here, he has given a time of death which was probably round about or only a little later than the time of his own last visit, if, as I believe, he made a visit on 25th
July. It is also odd that he should have claimed, falsely, that Mr Livesey's son (by which he probably meant son-in-law) had telephoned Mr Livesey at 1pm, presumably thereby establishing that he was still alive at that time. If Shipman visited at about 12.30pm, these entries would make sense from Shipman's viewpoint. If he had been entering the house, or his car had been seen outside, he would be distancing himself from the death in the usual way, albeit by a narrow margin. However, if he had wanted to distance himself from the death more effectively, one might have expected him to estimate the time of death much later in the afternoon. It appears to me that Shipman was either very confused that day or was possibly becoming careless in covering his tracks.
Taken together, the circumstances of this case persuade me that Mr Livesey was unlawfully killed by Shipman. His method was probably the usual one, an intravenous injection of strong opiate. Despite the slightly unusual features of the case, I feel sure of this conclusion.

name: John Bennett Molesdale
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 22 Old Road, Newton, Hyde
conclusion:
There are several highly suspicious features surrounding this death.
The most suspicious feature is the temporal link between the death and the final visit from Shipman. Shipman visited at about lunchtime on the day of the death. Mrs Brelsford recalls him saying that his visit was at 1.30pm. Shipman certified the time of death to be 2pm, half an hour after his visit. The body was discovered less than an hour after his visit. No one saw Mr Molesdale alive or spoke to him after Shipman's visit.
Shipman did not visit Mr Molesdale to attend to a pressing medical concern. The visit had not been requested and is recorded in the Lloyd George notes as a
'Routine visit'
. Whilst an unsolicited visit by a doctor to an elderly patient would not normally give rise to suspicion, in Shipman's case it does, especially where the patient is found dead very soon afterwards. In this case, the death was wholly unexpected, as Mr Molesdale had no recent history of illness and was seen to be in normal health at about 11.30am on the day of his death.
That Mr Molesdale's condition might deteriorate so rapidly and that he should die, within half an hour of a routine visit, due to old age, is wholly implausible. In his generic evidence given to the Inquiry, Dr John Grenville explained that to certify a death as being due to old age:
'is an appropriate thing to put where an elderly patient has been suffering for some time with generalised degenerative disease involving several organs, the elderly patient has been ill for a significant period of time, usually weeks or months, with multiple organ failure and the death is fully expected. It may be difficult in those circumstances to determine exactly which organ it was that ultimately failed and brought about the death'
.
Old age is plainly inappropriate in a case where there has been no such general degenerative disease.
This death ought certainly to have been referred to the coroner. It was a sudden and unexpected death. Its cause was unknown. Old age was wholly inappropriate as a cause of death. There is no suggestion or indication that Mr Molesdale could have died from a sudden cardiac or cerebrovascular condition.
When Shipman returned to the house he did not examine Mr Molesdale before declaring that he was dead. He only touched his neck. In his generic evidence to the Inquiry, Dr Grenville described the steps that should be taken by a doctor to establish the fact of death. The first is to check for a pulse in the wrist and then the neck, for about 30 seconds in each location. Following this, he should observe the chest wall for respiratory movements, again for 30 seconds or more. Then he should listen to the chest with a stethoscope for both heart and respiratory sounds, again for a period of 30 seconds or longer. If those tests are negative, a torch should be shone into each eye to check the pupillary reaction and the interior of each eye should be examined with an ophthalmoscope. Finally, best practice would be to then apply a painful stimulus and to see whether this created a response. Of the six steps identified by Dr Grenville, Shipman partially carried out only one and in a perfunctory way. This point should not be overstated, as Shipman has been observed not to follow these steps in deaths that are clearly natural. However, Shipman could only have known with certainty that Mr Molesdale was dead if he had seen him die during his earlier visit. The inference is that, on the second visit, he well knew that Mr Molesdale was dead.
The lies and misleading statements made on Form B give rise to some suspicion. It appears to me that Shipman wished to create the impression that he saw Mr Molesdale regularly and to avoid giving the impression that he personally had seen the patient only a very short time before his death.
Mr Molesdale's appearance in death is entirely typical of the appearance of many of Shipman's victims who have been killed by the administration of a lethal injection of diamorphine.
Taking all these factors into account, I am driven to the conclusion that Mr Molesdale was killed by Shipman. I am sure of that conclusion. The overwhelming likelihood is that the death was caused by an injection of strong opiate, probably diamorphine. I cannot reach a positive conclusion that Shipman stole Mr Molesdale's wallet and pension but I strongly suspect that he did.

name: Agnes Oldham
title: Mrs
place_of_death: The Sycamores, a residential home for the elderly, Victoria Street, Hyde
conclusion:
In my view, it is likely that Mrs Oldham died a natural death.
The recollections of the staff are not consistent with each other, or with the medical records. It is clear that Mrs Oldham declined gradually and I do not think that her death on 18th
November was either sudden or unexpected. However, that does not necessarily mean that the death was natural. Shipman visited Mrs Oldham on the day of the death. It appears that he was probably at the home in the late morning or early afternoon, a few hours before Mrs Oldham died. That the death did not follow within an hour of the visit means that I can rule out the possibility that Shipman gave Mrs Oldham a lethal injection of opiate. If he had, she would have died rather sooner than she did. That leaves open the possibility that Shipman gave Mrs Oldham a non-lethal dose of opiate or a substantial dose of some other sedative-type drug, such as Largactil, which might have had the effect of hastening the death of a patient as frail as Mrs Oldham. If he did, it would not be possible to say whether he did so because he genuinely believed that the drug was necessary to keep Mrs Oldham comfortable or whether he deliberately gave such a dose as would hasten the end.
There is no evidence that Shipman did give Mrs Oldham any drug which could have hastened her death. There is a possibility that he might have done. In my view, it is far more likely that Mrs Oldham died a natural death.

name: Leah Pickering
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 28 Wellington Road, Todmorden
conclusion:
This death was investigated only because Shipman certified the cause of death. There has never been any reason to suspect that he was involved in causing the death.
There is no evidence that Shipman had access to Mrs Pickering in the hours before her death. Shipman claimed that he saw Mrs Pickering alive on 25th
July, although Mrs Standring does not think he did. Whether he did or not, there is no reason to suppose that any treatment he might have given on that day had any connection with her subsequent death.
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Pickering died a natural death.

name: Jane Frances Rostron
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 5A Hamel Street, Hyde
conclusion:
There are several suspicious features surrounding this death. The strongest evidence that Shipman killed Mrs Rostron is the temporal link between his visit and her death. He visited at about noon, no one saw her alive thereafter and he certified on Form B that she died at 2pm. That, in itself, is a factor which gives rise to grave suspicion that Shipman was responsible for the death.
Mrs Rostron probably suffered from some degree of hypertension and there is a real possibility that she was at risk of suffering a stroke. Although she had eaten breakfast on the morning of her death, she was certainly unwell and had requested a visit from Shipman. She had not dressed that morning, which tends to confirm that she was unwell. Mrs Harper recalls that Shipman told her that, when he visited that day, Mrs Rostron had suffered a slight stroke in her left arm. It sounds as though he was describing an occlusive stroke affecting the left side of the body. It is entirely possible that Mrs Rostron had had or was having a stroke that morning, although her illness could have been something entirely different. However, the question is not so much whether she had a stroke as whether or not she died of a stroke. As Dr John Grenville has explained in his generic evidence, the occlusive strokes that cause one-sided weakness originate in the upper part of the brain and do not usually result in sudden death. Usually the outcome is survival, with or without permanent damage. If the stroke is to be fatal, death will occur following a substantial period of gradual deterioration, usually lasting something of the order of two to three days. The type of stroke that can cause sudden death occurs in the brain stem and does not give rise to one-sided weakness. Dr Grenville says that it is extremely unlikely that a patient would suffer two different types of stroke within a few hours. In my view, Mrs Rostron died too quickly for her death to be plausibly attributable to the development of a left-sided stroke earlier in the day. She might well have had a stroke but I think it unlikely that she died as the result of it.
Shipman claimed that Mrs Rostron refused to be admitted to hospital. Shipman quite often said this of patients who he had recently killed. In some cases, he would also blame the death on the patient's refusal to be admitted. Those features in the present case give rise to some suspicion. Although Mrs Harper found it credible that her mother would refuse to go to hospital, Shipman did not claim to have made any attempt to contact a relative who might persuade her to do so. More important is the question of why Shipman did not make any attempt to arrange for Mrs Rostron to be looked after. If Mrs Rostron had indeed suffered a stroke, it might not have been imperative for her to be admitted to hospital. But it was absolutely necessary that she should not be left alone. Her stroke might have developed and her condition worsened. Had Shipman attempted to contact Mrs Harper, from midday he would have found her at home. Alternatively, Shipman could have sought the assistance of Mrs Stamp, the neighbour who had telephoned the surgery on Mrs Rostron's behalf that morning.
Instead of arranging care, Shipman simply issued a prescription. The range of medication available for the treatment of a stroke is limited. If Mrs Rostron's blood pressure was dangerously high, then it might have been appropriate to prescribe medication to reduce her blood pressure. However, if that were the case, then again Shipman should have contacted a relative or neighbour to collect the medication urgently and not simply have left the prescription on the sideboard. It seems likely that the prescription was part of the device used by Shipman to substantiate symptoms compatible with the certified cause of death. It is likely that the same device was used in the medical records for that day, although these are not available now.
Shipman recorded an intention to revisit Mrs Rostron the next day. As I have already observed, he was not working the following day. Although it is possible that Shipman might have intended that one of his partners should visit Mrs Rostron the next day, it is at least equally likely that he made the entry knowing that a visit would not be necessary.
Mrs Rostron's peaceful appearance in death is consistent with the appearance of many of Shipman's victims who are known to have been killed by the administration of a lethal injection of diamorphine.
Shipman did not perform any examination of Mrs Rostron's body. In his generic evidence, Dr Grenville outlined six steps that should be taken to establish the fact of death. Shipman apparently did not perform any of these steps and is described by Mrs Harper as simply having 'glanced' at her mother before confirming the fact of death. Although it is known that Shipman did not examine deceased patients thoroughly even in cases where the death was not suspicious (and thus no great reliance should therefore be placed on the point), one explanation for Shipman being able to announce the fact of death without examining the body would be that he had killed Mrs Rostron during his earlier visit.
Taking the evidence as a whole, I am driven to the conclusion that Shipman killed Mrs Rostron. This case has Shipman's hallmark on it. Notwithstanding the absence of the medical records, I feel able to be sure of my conclusion.

name: Joseph Shaw
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 14 Talbot Road, Newton, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of highly suspicious factors surrounding this death.
The first and most obvious is that Mr Shaw's death was discovered very shortly after a visit by Shipman. No one saw him alive or spoke to him after Shipman's visit on 3rd
March. This in itself is a highly suspicious factor.
Mr Shaw's general health was not good towards the end of his life. His mobility was restricted and he had a tendency to fall. He suffered occasional chest infections and I think it likely that his motor neurone disease made his cough reflexes weak. The fall three weeks before his death gave rise to an increased risk of a chest infection, which might develop into pneumonia. Having said that, the evidence does not support the suggestion that Mr Shaw developed a chest infection during a period of four to five days before the death. Mrs Hirst noted nothing wrong with his breathing on the evening of 1st
March. Nor is there any independent evidence that Mr Shaw had a severe chest infection as late as 12.30pm on the day of the death.
The circumstances in which Shipman came to visit Mr Shaw on 3rd
March are not clear. It is possible that Mr Shaw telephoned the surgery to request a visit, although if he did I would have expected to find an entry in the visits book. If he did so, it must have been because he was feeling unwell or had some concern about his health. It is possible he asked for a prescription of amoxicillin, which he had had before for chest infections. It is possible the staff suggested that the doctor would visit. Had he given the impression to the staff that he was seriously ill, they would, following usual practice, have advised him to call an ambulance or called one from the surgery. It is also possible that Shipman visited of his own volition, making a routine call on an elderly patient who had had a fall three weeks earlier. The fact that Mr Shaw was expecting Shipman leads me to conclude that it was more likely than not that Mr Shaw had requested a visit that day. I think it likely that he was feeling under the weather, possibly with the beginnings of a chest infection. However, I am satisfied that at 12.30pm he was not showing obvious signs of illness.
Shipman's record of the visit on 3rd
March raises some suspicion. It is very similar to many I have seen in cases in which I am sure Shipman has killed. Shipman presents a picture of a condition that requires hospital treatment but says that the patient was unwilling to go. I accept of course that elderly people are sometimes reluctant to go into hospital. In this case, Shipman does not appear to have made any real attempt at persuasion and there is no suggestion in the note that a relative should be contacted. As Dr Grenville has explained, no conscientious doctor would leave a sick and elderly patient alone, without even making any arrangements for the urgent delivery of medication.
The death and cremation certificates give rise to grave suspicion. On the MCCD, a document that might be seen by the relatives, Shipman recorded the interval between the onset of bronchopneumonia and death as 12-24 hours. On Form B, a document that would not be seen by the relatives but would be subjected to scrutiny by other doctors, he said he had attended Mr Shaw during his last illness for four to five days. Not only is that latter entry a lie, but it is a lie with a purpose. On Form B, Shipman is presenting a more plausible progression of a case of bronchopneumonia, less likely to arouse the suspicion of a confirming doctor and the medical referee than the very short period suggested on the MCCD.
Shipman claimed to know that the death occurred at 4pm. He could not have known this with any precision. He suggested that he had visited at about noon. That is possible. I cannot be sure of the accuracy of Mrs Schofield's recollection of the time she left Mr Shaw's, although I accept that she is probably right because she was following her usual routine. What does strike me as sinister is the positive statement of the time of death, which seeks to put a period of four hours between Shipman's visit and Mr Shaw's death. I think the statement of the time of death is a deliberate attempt by Shipman to distance himself from the death.
Although bronchopneumonia can develop quite suddenly and proceed rapidly to death in a debilitated patient, it does not appear to me that Mr Shaw was a candidate for so rapid a death. He was not debilitated. He was up and dressed on the day of his death. Shipman claimed that Mr Shaw was in a coma for
'hours'
before death. How he was supposed to know this is not clear. He claims to know it of his own knowledge. If he did, he must have seen him in a coma at the time of his visit. But Shipman suggests in the medical records that Mr Shaw was awake and talking. In any event, it would be unthinkable for a doctor to leave a patient alone in a house if he were lying in a coma. So, the statement that Mr Shaw was in a coma for
'hours'
is a lie. In my view, it is a lie designed to create a plausible picture of a man dying of bronchopneumonia.
The position in which Mr Shaw was found, sitting peacefully in a chair, was inconsistent with a death from bronchopneumonia but entirely typical of the appearance of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by the administration of a diamorphine injection.
Taking these factors into account, I have come to the conclusion that Shipman killed Mr Shaw. Although Mr Shaw was at risk of death from some form of pneumonia, he died so quickly after Shipman's visit that I am driven to the conclusion that this cannot have been a natural death. I am satisfied so as to be sure of this.

name: Maria Thornton
title: Miss
place_of_death: her home, 369 Stockport Road, Gee Cross, Hyde
certified_cause: cerebrovascular accident due to arteriosclerosis and that she died on 28th July 1994
conclusion:
There are many suspicious features surrounding this death. The death was discovered soon after a visit by Shipman. There is no evidence that anyone saw Miss Thornton alive or spoke to her after Shipman's visit on 27th
July. That in itself is highly suspicious.
Bearing in mind Mrs Johnson's evidence that Miss Thornton was sweeping her garden on the afternoon of 27th
July, I think it extremely unlikely that she had had a stroke. I think it far more likely that she had fallen on Friday, 22nd
July and had hurt her leg. I think she probably decided to call Shipman because she had had a number of dizzy spells in the previous months and the medication had not prevented a recurrence. I am fortified in that view by the fact that Mrs Lamb was quite unaware that her aunt was ill in the days before her death. I think Miss Thornton would have told her niece if she knew she had suffered a stroke. Her niece was coming to stay in a few days' time.
Dr Grenville suggests that, if Shipman's accounts were genuine and Miss Thornton had suffered a stroke, the history given indicates a gradually developing stroke. It is likely that such a stroke would be occlusive and therefore unlikely to cause sudden death. As set out above, Dr Grenville noted that, where a stroke causes sudden death, it is usually a brain stem haemorrhagic stroke. In Dr Grenville's opinion, the position in which Miss Thornton was found was inconsistent even with that type of stroke.
Shipman's note in relation to the visit on Saturday, 23rd
July, records a history of Miss Thornton having fallen two weeks prior to the visit. It then goes immediately into a description of the signs and symptoms of a stroke. There is no independent evidence that Miss Thornton ever showed any such signs or spoke of such symptoms. For the reasons I explained above, I suspect that this entry was a late fabrication. The reason for fabricating such a note is likely to be because Shipman had to provide an explanation for a death that he had caused.
I am persuaded that Miss Thornton did not have a stroke at all and her death must have had some other cause. Given what we know of Shipman's unlawful activities, the most obvious alternative cause is that he killed her. He certainly had the opportunity. He made false entries on Form B, designed to give the impression that the death occurred in the evening and not in the afternoon when he had visited. Miss Thornton's appearance in death was entirely typical of that of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of diamorphine.
Taking all these factors into account, I have come to the conclusion that Shipman must have killed Miss Thornton. I find that, when he visited her on 23rd
July, she had fallen and injured her leg. She did not display signs of a stroke. He made an entry on the computer but did not make a handwritten note. On 27th
July, he visited Miss Thornton and gave her an injection of strong opiate, almost certainly diamorphine, and left her dead, sitting at the kitchen table. He was not called out to examine her body until the following day. He then made a series of written notes in her medical records. He made entries in Form B which were designed to suggest that Miss Thornton had died some hours after his visit. I am satisfied so as to be sure of the conclusion that Shipman killed Miss Thornton.

name: Mona Ashton White
title: Miss
place_of_death: her home, 18 Thorpe Hall Grove, Newton, Hyde
conclusion:
This death occurred during the brief period of a visit by Shipman, very shortly after Miss White was seen by witnesses to be in apparently normal health. That, in itself, is a factor which gives rise to grave suspicion.
According to Shipman's account, as derived from Form B, he arrived at 12.30pm. When he arrived, Miss White was suffering a heart attack and was lapsing into a coma. She lay in a coma for half an hour, during which time a home help arrived. Miss White died at about 1pm. I accept, of course, that people can and do have heart attacks and die very suddenly. However, for that to happen as the doctor arrives is a remarkable coincidence, especially when the patient was reasonably well shortly before, as Miss White was, according to both her home helps.
Quite apart from that coincidence, Shipman's conduct that day is not consistent with what would be expected of a doctor who found a 63 year old patient suffering a heart attack. The first thing a reasonable doctor would have done would be to call an ambulance. The patient would have required urgent treatment in hospital. No doctor would have known that the thrombosis was inevitably going to be fatal. If the patient were in severe pain, it would be reasonable to give her a small dose of opiate. If she went into cardiac arrest, the doctor should have attempted resuscitation until the paramedics arrived. It appears that Shipman did not call for an ambulance or attempt resuscitation. It appears that he gave Miss White an injection of something to relieve the pain and left her. When Mrs Shawcross arrived at the house at about 12.40pm, Miss White was alone and apparently dead. Mrs Shawcross went to find Mrs Foley, and when they returned together, Shipman had come back. He immediately told them that Miss White was dead. The telephone call was then made to Mrs Forder in which, on Shipman's instruction, Miss White was described as 'slipping away', in other words not yet dead. I am satisfied that was not true. When Mrs Forder arrived about ten minutes later, Shipman told her that Miss White had only just died. I am satisfied that that was not true. She had probably been dead for about half an hour.
On Form B, Shipman falsely claimed that a home help had been present at the moment of death. If, as Shipman appears to have suggested, Miss White died after the two home helps had returned, then both were present at the death. If she died before the two returned, then neither was present at the death, as it could not be said that Mrs Shawcross was present at the death when she went in alone and found Miss White. Shipman's false claim that another person beside himself was present at the death was the kind of lie that he was wont to tell. There are many cases in which he has sought to suggest that another person was present at the death when in truth he was there alone. I am satisfied that the contents of Form B were designed to present a plausible account of the death, which would not arouse suspicions. In my view, when Shipman gave Miss White an injection, it is far more likely that it was intended to bring about her death than it was to ease her pain.
Miss White's appearance after death, sitting upright in her chair, was not typical of a death from coronary thrombosis but was entirely typical of death by morphine injection.
Despite the absence of medical records, I am sure that Shipman killed Miss White.

name: Lily Acton
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 34b Harbour Farm Road, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
Very little is known about the circumstances of Mrs Acton's death. It is not even known whether she died on 24th
December, as stated on her death certificate, or in the evening of 23rd
December.
In the absence of any medical records it is not possible to discover whether she was suffering from ischaemic heart disease. Although it appeared to Mr Critchlow that his great-aunt was in reasonable health for her age, it is likely that, at 91, she was at some risk of suffering a heart attack. It would appear that, on 23rd
December, there were special reasons for concern about Mrs Acton's health. What they were is not clear.
Shipman probably saw Mrs Acton on 23rd
December. The purpose of the visit is not known. However, it appears from Mrs Curry's evidence that Mrs Acton was alive and walking about after Shipman's visit that day. In his generic evidence to the Inquiry, Professor Henry McQuay has explained that a lethal dose of opiate administered intravenously will kill within a few minutes and if given intramuscularly will kill within about an hour. Within a short time of such an injection the patient would feel drowsy and possibly sick and anyone watching would realise that something was seriously wrong. Although Mrs Acton appeared angry and agitated on 23rd
December, her condition did not indicate that she had been given an opiate. The time of Mrs Curry's visit to Mrs Acton is not known but it is unlikely to have been within a short time of Shipman's visit. It is possible, but seems highly unlikely, that Shipman administered a lethal dose of opiate during his visit on 23rd
December.
In any event, as the security chain on the front door was found to be in place on 24th
December, Mrs Acton must have been in a position to apply the chain either after she had entered the flat for the last time or, alternatively, after seeing her last visitor to the door. If that visitor was Shipman, he could not have given her a lethal dose of opiate intravenously. That leaves open the possibility that he administered a lethal dose of opiate intramuscularly. However, in all the circumstances, that appears very unlikely.
The position in which Mrs Acton was found is consistent with her having suffered a fatal heart attack. In his generic evidence, Dr John Grenville said that a patient suffering a fatal heart attack usually has a short time in which he or she realises that something terrible is happening and often tries to seek help. Mrs Acton may have wished to attract attention by going outside. Mr Critchlow says that her position was consistent with an attempt to reach the door.
Although I cannot absolutely rule out the possibility that Shipman gave Mrs Acton an intramuscular injection of a lethal dose of opiate shortly before she spoke to Mrs Curry on 23rd
December, I think that Mrs Acton probably died a natural death.

name: Nellie Bennett
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home
conclusion:
There are several suspicious factors surrounding this death.
Mrs Bennett appeared well to her daughter during a shopping trip on 24th
June. She attended for lunch at Yew Tree House as usual on 25th
June, at which time she also appeared well. She must have telephoned the surgery at some time that day because she felt dizzy. Shipman admitted having visited Mrs Bennett during the afternoon of 25th
June. There is no evidence that Mrs Bennett was seen alive after this time save for Shipman's assertion that this was the case. Although Shipman recorded on Form B that a neighbour saw Mrs Bennett at 6pm on 25th
June, the neighbour has not been traced.
The evidence that the newspaper was found behind the door and the facts that Mrs Bennett was wearing day clothes, the curtains were open and there was no reply to Mrs Spencer's telephone call on the evening of 25th
June, all point to the conclusion that Mrs Bennett died during the afternoon of that day, between her return from lunch and the delivery of the newspaper at about 4pm. I find that that was so. It follows that Mrs Bennett's death occurred at, or very close to, the time of Shipman's visit. That in itself is a highly suspicious factor. Although it is theoretically possible that Mrs Bennett could have had a sudden massive stroke in the interval between Shipman's departure and the arrival of the newspaper, that is essentially unlikely and stretches coincidence beyond its limits.
Shipman's statement on Form B about breakfast being ready and his assertion, which had no scientific basis, that death had occurred at about 8am on 26th
June are inconsistent with the evidence of Mr Hargreaves. In my view, this was an attempt by Shipman to distance the death from the time of his visit and to obscure the fact that he was the last person to see Mrs Bennett alive.
There is a discrepancy between the blood pressure reading recorded, as altered, in the Lloyd George notes, and the computerised notes. It also appears that Shipman might have added
'48 hours'
to his handwritten note. It appears to me that Shipman has revisited the handwritten note and has made two alterations. He has increased the diastolic blood pressure reading, thereby making Mrs Bennett's blood pressure seem worse, and has stated that the dizziness has lasted for two days. The suggestion that Mrs Bennett experienced symptoms from the afternoon of 23rd
June is certainly at odds with the evidence of Mrs Spencer who states that her mother appeared fit and well during their shopping trip on 24th
June. Although I cannot be sure that Shipman made these alterations, I find that he probably did.
The death, if naturally occurring, should have been referred to the coroner with a view to a post-mortem examination being carried out. Professor Baker says that the blood pressure reading as stated was
'an inadequate reason for giving CVA as the cause of death'
. Even on Shipman's own note (with the alterations I believe he made), there is no way in which he could have known that she died of a stroke and no way in which he could have known that the mode of death was collapse of seconds' duration. If, which is unlikely, the symptoms recorded by Shipman in the Lloyd George notes had suggested to him that Mrs Bennett was suffering or was likely to suffer a stroke, then he should have contacted her relatives and not left her alone at home.
The position in which Mrs Bennett was found was inconsistent with her having suffered a stroke, but consistent with a lethal dose of opiates having been administered. In his generic statement to the Inquiry, Dr John Grenville stated as follows:
'Even in a person suffering a brain stem haemorrhage or subarachnoid haemorrhage I would not expect to find the deceased patient sitting upright in a chair looking peaceful and as if asleep. There is likely to be a period of at least a few seconds to possibly a minute or two after the destruction of vital areas of the brain when there is still sufficient oxygenated blood in the body for muscular activity to be possible. I would expect the patient to attempt to rise to seek help or to lie down. It might be possible for a patient who is deeply asleep and who suffers a brain stem haemorrhage to be found looking as if they remain asleep'
.
All these factors point to the same conclusion, namely that Shipman killed Mrs Bennett by lethal injection during his visit on the afternoon of 25th
June. I am satisfied so as to be sure that that is so.

name: John Charlton
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 14 Ogden Court, Frank Street, Hyde
conclusion:
There are some highly suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. The first and most obvious is that the death took place in the course of a short visit by Shipman. There is no evidence that Mr Charlton was thought to be seriously ill that day or that Shipman was called out as a matter of emergency. The evidence suggests that he was asked to visit on account of an episode of urinary incontinence which occurred the day before. On the morning of the day of his death, Mrs Simpson had not thought it appropriate to record any concern about Mr Charlton. His condition seems to have been included in the general statement that everyone was
'reasonably well'
. Against that background, the fact that Mr Charlton should die suddenly during Shipman's visit gives rise to grave suspicion.
I accept of course that Mr Charlton probably had a history of congestive heart failure, which would account for his breathlessness and his general illness in the week or so before he died. It follows that I accept that it is possible that Mr Charlton could have died a natural death without much warning.
Shipman's conduct at the time of Mr Charlton's death is highly suspicious. If Mr Charlton was so ill that Shipman formed the view that he must be admitted to hospital, Shipman would have pulled the alarm cord and asked Mrs Simpson to call an ambulance. Instead he chose to walk down to Mrs Simpson's office, leaving Mr Charlton alone. No doctor acting in the genuine interests of his patient would have chosen to do that. I suspect that Shipman had no intention of admitting Mr Charlton to hospital. He then asked Mrs Simpson to go up to the flat. She went immediately and Mr Charlton was already dead. The inference that he was already dead when Shipman left him is very readily drawn.
I suspect that Shipman's statement on Form B, that no one was present at the moment of death, was an attempt to distance himself from the death. By involving Mrs Simpson as he did, he sought to involve another person in the death and its discovery. These are devices that Shipman used in the cases of patients whom he undoubtedly murdered, amongst them another resident at Ogden Court, Mrs Maureen Ward. Another such case was that of Mrs Gladys Saunders, who died on 17th
June 1996 at Ogden Court. In that case Shipman involved Mrs Simpson in the discovery of the death, in much the same way as he did in the present case.
Mr Charlton was found lying on the bed, which he no longer used, in a position in which he found it difficult to breathe. It seems to me that he lay on the bed so that Shipman could examine his abdomen in connection with the urinary incontinence. It might well be that Shipman then suggested that he required a blood sample, to check kidney function. For that he would have introduced a needle into one of Mr Charlton's veins. It would have then been very simple for Shipman to administer a lethal injection of opiate.
Mr Charlton's appearance in death was not consistent with the appearance of someone who had died of cardiac failure. His appearance was, however, entirely typical of someone who had been killed by lethal injection of diamorphine.
Taking these factors into account, I have come to the conclusion that Shipman killed Mr Charlton. Notwithstanding the lack of medical records and my inability to establish how serious Mr Charlton's heart failure was in the days before his death, I feel sure of that conclusion.

name: Edgar Dobb
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 6 Halton Street, Hyde
conclusion:
It seems to me that Mr Dobb died of natural causes. He was clearly very unwell and his death was fully expected. Although there are no medical records, the description of his condition given by Mrs Glithero is compatible with a death from congestive heart failure, the cause of death certified by Shipman.
As Mr Dobb's name appears in Shipman's visits book for 7th
February 1980, the day of the death, it seems likely that Shipman visited the house. Shipman used this book as an aide-memoire when making his scheduled visits and did not necessarily enter all visits he made later in the day when called out as an emergency. I infer therefore that it is quite likely that Shipman visited Mr Dobb in the late morning of the day of the death. He probably also came out later in the day to certify the fact of death. It is possible that he also came out in the late afternoon while Mr Dobb was still alive, but there is no evidence that he was at the house in the period immediately before the death and I am sure that he played no sinister part in Mr Dobb's death.

name: Arthur Floyd
title: Mr
place_of_death: The Sycamores, a residential home for the elderly, Welch Road, Hyde
conclusion:
There are no real causes for suspicion in connection with this death. Mr Floyd was very old and must have been at considerable risk of sudden death. There is no evidence that Shipman saw Mr Floyd in the hours leading up to his death. It appears that Mr Floyd died during the night, when Shipman would be most unlikely to visit unless specifically requested. If Mr Floyd had been ill in the night and Shipman had been called, I would have expected the staff to tell his niece the following day.
Although it seems that it was inappropriate to certify that Mr Floyd's death was due to senility, this factor does not of itself give rise to any suspicion that Shipman might have been involved in the death. Shipman did not take his duties of certification very seriously and his entries were frequently inaccurate. I would think that he gave senility as the cause of death because Mr Floyd was very old and he did not really know the true cause.
The overwhelming likelihood in this case is that Mr Floyd died a completely natural death.

name: Marion Gaskell
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Tameside General Hospital
conclusion: There are no grounds to suspect that Shipman was in any way connected with Mrs Gaskell or her death. She was not his patient. She died in Tameside General Hospital following surgery. There was an inquest at which the coroner accepted Dr Rutherford's opinion as to the cause of death. I am sure that Mrs Gaskell died a natural death.

name: Mary Emma Hamer
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Donneybrook House (the surgery premises of the Donneybrook practice of which Shipman was then a member), Clarendon Street, Hyde
conclusion:
This death is highly suspicious. The first and most obvious cause for suspicion is that this sudden death occurred in Shipman's presence. This in itself excites a high degree of suspicion. Other doctors say that it is very rare indeed for a sudden death to occur while they are there. With Shipman, such an event occurred quite frequently.
Mrs Hamer's medical records have not been found, but the evidence suggests that she was a healthy and active lady who was not in need of a home visit. In addition, Mrs Lee told the Inquiry that Mrs Hamer did not look unwell when she entered the surgery. It appears to me that Mrs Hamer was not having a heart attack when she walked into Shipman's consulting room. If she had been, she would have looked ill and I am sure Mrs Lee would have noticed. If she did indeed suffer a heart attack, it must have occurred in the few minutes after she went into Shipman's room. Although that is theoretically possible, it is highly unlikely.
Shipman told Mrs Lee that he had asked Mrs Hamer to undress in the examination room and that he wished to see other patients in the meantime. Mrs Lee says he left Mrs Hamer for about 30 minutes and saw two or three more patients. If Shipman's version of events to Mrs Lee is correct, it would mean that Mrs Hamer entered the examination room, climbed onto the examination couch without removing any clothing, folded her hands in her lap and suffered a fatal heart attack. When that attack commenced, she remained lying on the couch and did nothing to alert Shipman to her plight. Such a scenario is wholly unbelievable.
Shipman's account of events, as given to Mrs Stafford, is quite inconsistent with Mrs Lee's recollections. If what Shipman told Mrs Stafford was true, and Mrs Hamer appeared to be having a heart attack in his room, one would not have expected him to see other patients whilst this was going on. He would have an emergency on his hands. If Mrs Hamer was in such pain as to need morphine, Shipman should not have left her alone. His claims that he contacted the hospital and called an ambulance are not supported by Mrs Lee. It is inconceivable that, if he had done either of those things, Mrs Lee would not have known. I am quite sure that Shipman's account to Mrs Stafford was untrue.
Mrs Hamer's appearance in death was not typical of that usually seen in a death following a coronary thrombosis. It was, however, very similar to that of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection.
I am quite sure that Shipman killed Mrs Hamer. In my view, it is highly likely that he took her into the examination room and asked her to lie on the bed. The overwhelming likelihood is that he then administered to her a fatal injection of an opiate, on the pretext of either taking blood or administering some necessary medication. He then left her in the examination room and returned to his consulting room where he proceeded to see other patients for about half an hour. After he had finished his morning surgery, he pretended to Mrs Lee that he had suddenly 'discovered' Mrs Hamer to be dead.

name: Leah Johnston
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
It seems likely that Mrs Johnston had a history of heart disease and that she suffered a heart attack in the late afternoon of 10th
November 1979. The description of her condition, as recorded in the daily diary, shows that she was cold, clammy and in pain. She was sweating profusely and had a very slow and irregular pulse. Shipman, for I believe it was he who attended, diagnosed a heart attack. It is not known what medication he prescribed. If Mrs Johnston were still in pain when he attended, it would have been in order for him to give a small injection of morphine or diamorphine to relieve the pain. There is no evidence that he did so on that occasion. It may be that the pain had subsided by the time he arrived. Having suffered this heart attack, Mrs Johnston would certainly have been at risk of suffering a further episode.
There is conflicting evidence as to the time of Mrs Johnston's death on 11th
November. Mr Johnston's recollection of the Town Hall clock striking 11 o'clock is certainly vivid, but he did not repeat that account in his statement. The daily diary records the time of death as 2pm. I think it is likely that the death took place at about 2pm. In my experience, the staff at Charnley House were usually careful to note the time of a death. If the death had occurred at about 11am, it would have been recorded by Mrs Stansfield in the morning report. Mr Pickford recalls that the death occurred at some time in the afternoon.
There is no evidence of the time at which Shipman visited on 11th
November and gave an injection. We do not know in what condition Mrs Johnston was when he arrived. There is no note in the daily diary to show that she was in pain or to suggest that she had suffered another heart attack. She could have done but it may be that she was just unwell as the result of the previous day's attack. Nor do we know what drug Shipman injected. Mrs Stansfield suggests that the doctors would sometimes give 'a drop of morphine' to patients who were in pain or distress but says she does not know what Shipman gave Mrs Johnston.
It appears that, at some time after the injection was given, Mrs Johnston fell asleep and never awoke. It is certainly possible that she died within an hour of receiving the injection. It is possible that she died rather more quickly than that. I note that the diary does not say that Shipman was sent for after the death and it appears to me quite possible that he had not left the building by the time the death had occurred. It is possible, therefore, that Mrs Johnston died shortly after Shipman had given her an injection.
This case gives rise to some suspicion that Shipman might have killed Mrs Johnston. However, I am unable to reach a decision, even on the balance of probabilities, about the circumstances of this death. There are too many uncertainties. It is possible that Shipman gave an excessive dose of opiate to Mrs Johnston and killed her. On the other hand, it is quite possible that he gave an appropriate dose of something, such as an opiate or a sedative, and that Mrs Johnston died of natural causes. There is a further possibility, which is that he gave a dose of opiate or sedative which was not sufficient to kill Mrs Johnston, but was larger than was appropriate for therapeutic purposes and was intended to ensure that she did not wake up again before her death.

name: Elsie King
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs King's death was natural.
First, the Charnley House daily diary records a gradual deterioration. Her death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
Second, there is no evidence that Shipman saw Mrs King for several days before her death. From the daily diary it would seem that the last time he could have seen her was on 20th
July. The visits book confirms a visit to Charnley House on that day but not to see Mrs King. That Shipman inaccurately claimed that he had last seen Mrs King alive on 25th
July, does not of itself give rise to suspicion that he was involved in her death. He was very careless in the way in which he completed death and cremation certificates and often made mistakes. Sometimes he made deliberately false claims that he had seen a patient within 14 days before the death in cases where he had not killed the patient. He might have done that on this occasion. It is quite possible that he had not seen Mrs King since 13th
July, which would be more than 14 days before the death. Shipman was always anxious to say that he had seen the patient within 14 days of the death, even in cases where it was not necessary for him to make that claim in order to qualify him to certify the cause of death.

name: Wilfred Leigh
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 54 Chapel Street, Hyde
certified_cause: respiratory failure due to chronic bronchitis
conclusion:
There is very little evidence on which to base this decision.
It is clear from the evidence that Mr Leigh was very ill shortly before his death. The last time Mrs Fuggle saw him, she expected him to die at any time. He clearly required nursing care.
Although Mrs Fuggle's account of the day of the death is secondhand, it is broadly consistent with Shipman's entries on Form B. On Form B, Shipman said that he visited about an hour before the death. Mrs Fuggle told both the police and the Inquiry that her mother told her that Shipman gave her uncle an injection on the day of his death. I think that is probably true. Moreover, since all the evidence touching on the reason for the injection suggests that it was given for pain, it is quite likely to have been an injection of opiate. We do not know whether the injection was given intravenously or intramuscularly. Mr Leigh did not die immediately after the injection but it does appear that he died within the hour. As Mr Leigh's respiratory function was already severely impaired, a relatively modest dose of diamorphine might well have hastened Mr Leigh's end. If the injection was given by the intramuscular route, it is possible that the injection contributed to or hastened the death. As Dr Grenville has explained, an intramuscular injection of opiate will be at maximal effect within between 30 minutes and an hour. It is therefore quite possible that the injection given by Shipman caused or contributed to the death.
Having said that, it is not possible to determine what Shipman intended when he gave the injection. Supposing that the injection was of an opiate, we do not know how much was given. We do not know whether Mr Leigh's pain or distress was such as to justify the giving of an injection of opiate, despite the risks that such a course would entail. It is possible that Shipman gave an injection for proper therapeutic reasons for the relief of pain and distress, but recognising that the drug might also have the effect of hastening death. It must be admitted that there is also a possibility that Shipman, recognising that Mr Leigh was in distress and did not have long to live, decided to give him a dose which he knew would hasten the end. As Shipman was prepared to kill patients who were not close to death, it is unlikely that he would shrink from hastening Mr Leigh's end by a few hours or a day or two.
I am unable to reach a positive conclusion about Mr Leigh's death, although I am suspicious about it.

name: Selina Mackenzie
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 35 Perrin Street, Hyde
conclusion:
There are several highly suspicious circumstances surrounding this death.
The first and most obvious is that Mrs Mackenzie was found dead very shortly after a visit by Shipman. No one spoke to her or saw her alive after his visit. That in itself excites great suspicion. It would be a very substantial coincidence if Mrs Mackenzie had died a natural death in the short period between Shipman's departure and the arrival of her afternoon carer. It appears that the time span was very short. Shipman was seen at the house by a neighbour at about 3pm and the carer arrived at about 3.45pm. Although these times cannot be relied on as accurate, they give an idea of the time span involved. If Shipman had found Mrs Mackenzie to be showing any signs of a stroke when he saw her at about 3pm, it would be mandatory for him to contact someone to ensure that she was not left alone. No competent doctor would leave an elderly patient alone in such circumstances.
Mrs Mackenzie had had at least two strokes in the past, as well as some so-called mini-strokes. I must and do assume that she was at considerable risk of having another stroke. Although it appears that her past strokes had been of the occlusive type (which do not usually cause sudden death but give rise to loss of speech and limb movement), it is possible that she could have had a sudden fatal brain stem stroke. However, the chances of that sudden stroke happening within the short period after Shipman's departure and the carer's arrival are minimal.
It is theoretically possible that Mrs Mackenzie could have died a sudden natural death from some cause other than a stroke. For example she could have had a heart attack. However, the chances of such a sudden fatal event occurring so shortly after Shipman's departure are also minimal.
Mrs Mackenzie's position and appearance were not typical of what is usually seen when a patient has had a sudden fatal stroke or heart attack. They were, however, entirely typical of those seen in many of Shipman's victims whom he had killed using a lethal injection of opiate.
I am quite satisfied that Shipman killed Mrs Mackenzie. Shipman's visit that day was never intended to be more than a routine check before she went away for Christmas. It seems to me quite clear that Shipman planned that visit as an opportunity to kill Mrs Mackenzie.

name: Elizabeth Pearce
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 34 Byrom Street, Todmorden
conclusion:
The circumstances of this death are lost in the mists of time. Nobody who was present at the death or who knew anything of the immediate circumstances is available to give evidence. The medical records have not survived. Although the grandchildren do not remember that their grandmother was ill in the weeks and months before her death, it is quite possible that she was and that they were either not aware of her illness or have forgotten about it. It is quite possible that the real reason why Mrs Pearce moved to Todmorden to live with her daughter was because she was ill. It is possible that she had suffered a stroke and that the grandchildren do not now remember it. Mrs Pearce was 84 years old and, simply by reason of her age, was at some risk of dying quite suddenly either from a stroke or from a heart attack.
On the other hand, if the grandchildren's recollection is right and Mrs Pearce was in good health, this seems to have been a sudden and unexpected death, although as I have said, by reason of her age, a sudden death could not have been a wholly unexpected event. Shipman's presence at the house on the day of the death might give rise to a suspicion that he had played some part in it. However, we have no idea whether he was there shortly before the death or several hours before. The entries on Form B do not make the position clear. That of itself might be thought suspicious. However, it must be remembered that Mrs Pearce was not living alone. She was at all times under the care and, one would expect, the watchful eye of her daughter. The opportunities for Shipman to do something unlawful would be much less than if Mrs Pearce were living alone.
Dr Stella Brown completed most of the Forms C for the doctors practising at the Abraham Ormerod Medical Centre. She appears to have undertaken her duties conscientiously, in that it seems that she spoke to Mrs Smythe and her sister, Mrs Dobby, about the circumstances of the death. We have no way of knowing what questions were asked or what answers were given. However, we do know that there would have been an opportunity for Mrs Smythe and Mrs Dobby to express their concerns to Dr Brown, if they had any.
There is no evidence that Shipman played any part in bringing about Mrs Pearce's death. However, he saw her on the day of her death and it is quite possible that he had an opportunity to give her an injection that caused or hastened her death. He was later to become a serial killer and his most common victims were elderly women in poor health. There is no positive evidence that he killed Mrs Pearce, but he could have done. In these circumstances, I do not feel able to reach a decision about the circumstances of the death. I am, however, suspicious about it.

name: Jack Leslie Shelmerdine
title: Mr
place_of_death: Tameside General Hospital
conclusion:
This case does not fit the pattern of what was later to become Shipman's habitual and preferred method of killing his victims. Over many years, Shipman administered substantial doses of morphine or diamorphine, which had the effect of suppressing respiration and causing death within about an hour at most.
However, the circumstances of this case do give rise to concern and suspicion that Shipman may have intentionally caused Mr Shelmerdine's death.
It is clear that in the late evening of Monday, 26th
November, Mr Shelmerdine was very poorly. He had chronic bronchitis and it appears that at this time he had particular difficulty in breathing. He may have been in panic and some distress. Shipman suggested, and this seems quite likely to be true, that Mr Shelmerdine was suffering from left ventricular failure. There is no doubt that Shipman gave an injection. As Shipman himself said that he gave morphine, there is every reason to believe that he had given morphine or diamorphine. It is apparent from the circumstances that Shipman must have brought the drug with him in his medical bag.
Because Shipman had been convicted of criminal offences in connection with controlled drugs in 1976, he had declared his intention not to keep a personal controlled drugs register. His possession of an opiate that evening did not accord with the regulations. I infer that it is likely that Shipman had obtained that drug illicitly, probably by prescribing more than was needed for one of his patients who was dying of cancer. Shipman had attended two such patients within recent months. By obtaining drugs in this way, Shipman would not be able to prescribe the drug of choice and would have used whatever he had available. On an occasion such as this, he might have had a morphine product or diamorphine. I have come across many cases in which Shipman has claimed to have given a modest dose of morphine for therapeutic reasons, but where I have concluded that he had in fact given a larger dose than he admitted. On some occasions, because I have been able to identify the source of supply, I have been able to say with confidence that he actually gave diamorphine when he claimed to give morphine.
It is clear from Dr Grenville's evidence that any doctor must know that to give an opiate to a patient with impaired respiratory function carries real risks. A modest dose of opiate may be justified for a patient who is in left ventricular failure, but if that is combined with chronic bronchitis, extreme caution is required. Yet Shipman gave a dose of morphine which was considerably larger than Dr Grenville says would be usual in such circumstances. It does not appear that he titrated the dose against Mr Shelmerdine's response. Had he done so, I would have expected it to be given intravenously and I would have expected that Shipman would have explained the process in his quite detailed letter in response to the complaint. In all the many sets of medical records I have examined, I have never found one in which Shipman claimed to have given a titrated dose.
It seems to me that what Shipman did was extremely dangerous for Mr Shelmerdine. Even if the dose was of 10mg morphine, that would have been large enough to make him sleep very deeply for several hours. Dr Grenville is very critical of Shipman's drug selection, of the dose he gave and of the route by which he gave it. With a history of chronic respiratory disease and recent chest infection, a sub-lethal dose of opioid medication would undoubtedly render the patient vulnerable to fatal bronchopneumonia by the indirect mechanism of suppressing the body's natural protective reflexes. In giving morphine, Shipman might have intended to achieve that end. If Shipman gave a larger dose of opiate than he later admitted, the risk to Mr Shelmerdine would have been even greater and it is quite possible that Shipman hoped and intended that Mr Shelmerdine would die that night as the direct result of the drug he had injected. Shipman had prepared the family for the worst by telling Mr Shelmerdine junior that his father was very, very ill.
I recognise that Shipman might have given an excessive dose of morphine in ignorance of the danger to which he was exposing him. That he was prepared to tell the Regional Health Authority that he had given Mr Shelmerdine 10mg morphine, would tend to suggest that he thought there was no harm in it. However, I do not think that can be the explanation for Shipman's actions. I say so for several reasons. First, Shipman had had a special interest in pethidine in the mid-1970s. By 1979, he had, I am satisfied, used strong opiates to kill several patients. I think he was very interested indeed in opiates and would have made it his business to be well informed on the subject. I think he well knew that opiates present a particular risk for patients with poor respiratory function. I think it is possible that he felt driven to admit that he had given morphine and in a not insubstantial dose, because by the time he wrote his letter of explanation, he might not have known whether or not there had been a post-mortem examination. If morphine were discovered, he would have to explain its presence. Second, Shipman gave this dose at home, late at night, and left Mr Shelmerdine in the care of his family. He would have known that Mr Shelmerdine would not have been closely monitored during the night and there would be little prospect of intervention if his respiration became severely depressed.
My conclusion is that it is likely that Shipman gave a dose of at least 10mg morphine, possibly more, with the intention and expectation that Mr Shelmerdine would die while unsupervised during the night of 26th
November. I think he would have known that even if the dose did not have that effect, it would increase the likelihood that he would die the following day. I think it likely that Shipman caused Mr Shelmerdine's death. However, I cannot say whether Mr Shelmerdine would have survived for much longer. It does appear that he was very seriously ill.

name: Mary Tuff
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 44 Cambourne Road, Hattersley, Hyde
conclusion:
There are some features of this case which excite suspicion.
Shipman certified that the death was due to congestive heart failure, although there was nothing in Mrs Tuff's medical records to suggest that she had ever suffered from that condition.
