He also claimed that she had been suffering from her last illness for six days, when the records show that, during that time, she had had a viral illness and sore throat. It is true that Mrs Tuff had an enlarged heart as a result of chronic obstructive airways disease, but this enlargement was not causing any clinical symptoms. Mrs Tuff's death was sudden and unexpected and Shipman was not in a position confidently to certify the cause of death. He should have referred the case to the coroner. These factors give rise to suspicion that he was involved in the death.
Shipman claimed on Form B that he was able to estimate the time of death from the body temperature. He often made such claims and they were completely bogus. Dr John Grenville says that it is very difficult to estimate the time of death from body temperature. It is a task for an experienced pathologist. In any event, it is necessary to take the body temperature internally, usually in the rectum. Shipman did not do that. In many cases where he has killed a patient, Shipman claimed to estimate the time of death and gave a time some hours after his last known visit. His motive in such cases is clear. He was seeking to distance himself from the death. His claim to know the time of death raises some suspicion. In this case, there is no evidence that he visited Mrs Tuff in the hours before her death was discovered. It is possible that he visited her late at night or very early in the morning, although this seems unlikely. If he had not visited her, his only motive for pretending that he could estimate the time of her death was that he was showing off.
Despite these grounds for suspicion, however, the other circumstances suggest that Mrs Tuff died from natural causes. First, on the day before she died, although she seemed to have recovered from her recent infection, she became unwell again and specifically complained of chest pain. This pain could have been the precursor to a fatal heart attack some hours later. However, there is no record of any history of ischaemic heart disease or congestive heart failure. Second, the position in which she was found was consistent with her having suffered a heart attack and having made an attempt to reach the telephone when she realised that something was seriously wrong.
There are one or two unexplained features of the evidence. It appears that a neighbour noticed that a light was on during the night. It is possible that Mrs Tuff felt ill in the night and put the light on. It is possible that she died in the middle of the night. The other matter is that it appears that Mrs Tuff had had something to eat after her daughter left her at 10.30pm on the Sunday. Mrs Page thought that the bowl in the sink was evidence of her mother's early breakfast. It might equally well have been a late supper. Neither of those factors is particularly suggestive of a late visit by Shipman.
It is possible that the request for a visit on Sunday evening reached Shipman who had set off to visit before the request was cancelled. It is possible that he arrived late at night, when Mrs Tuff had had some supper and changed into her nightclothes. He might then have given her a lethal injection of opiate and waited until she collapsed. If he had done so, he might well have wished to pretend that he could estimate that she died at 6am.
The evidence in this case is such that I do not feel able to reach any positive conclusion as to whether Mrs Tuff died of natural causes or was killed by Shipman.

name: Marjorie Hope Waller
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 4 Kew Avenue, Hyde
conclusion:
I do not accept that Mrs Waller had bronchopneumonia on 18th
April. If she had, she would not have eaten a healthy meal the evening before. If she had, it would have been obvious to Mrs Thompson that morning that her friend was seriously ill. I accept Mrs Thompson's evidence that Mrs Waller sounded brighter and said that she was feeling better. I am satisfied that Mrs Waller had only a fairly mild respiratory tract infection. It follows that Shipman's first entry in Mrs Waller's records for the day of the death was fabricated.
I also feel able to reject as fanciful the possibility that Mrs Waller died suddenly of a heart condition or stroke in the short period after Shipman had visited and before Mr Jones arrived. She had no medical history that would predispose her to such an event. Also, for the death to occur in that short window of opportunity would be a most remarkable coincidence.
Shipman's account of the death, as inferred from the medical records and the content of Form B, does not make sense for the reasons I have set out above. He recorded no signs and symptoms to support his diagnosis of severe illness. He did not behave as any reasonable doctor would have behaved if faced with a severely ill patient refusing to go to hospital. I observe that for Shipman to say that a patient had refused hospital admission was a typical feature of the murder cases.
Shipman fabricated several entries on Form B. Most important is the implication that someone had picked up the prescription he had given her. This was plainly designed to make it appear that someone else had seen Mrs Waller alive since his visit to her at about 1pm. He also stated that the death had occurred later than it really did, no doubt to add plausibility to this suggestion and to distance himself from the death. His assertion that he had attended Mrs Waller for seven days during her last illness is inconsistent with the contents of the medical records, which give no indication that Mrs Waller was suffering from a 'last illness' until the day of her death.
If Mrs Waller was alive and walking about the house when Shipman left, the unlocked doors would be a mystery. I accept the evidence of her friends that she was very conscious of security and would have locked the door behind Shipman if she had been able to show him out. Of course, if she was already dead, as I believe she was, Shipman would have had to let himself out and would have been unable to lock the Chubb-type locks which secured both the inner and outer doors.
I have come to the conclusion that there is only one explanation which will fit all the facts of this case. That is that Shipman killed Mrs Waller by giving her a lethal injection of diamorphine or other strong opiate. I am sure that he did so.

name: Albert Arrandale
title: Mr
certified_cause: carcinomatosis peritonei due to carcinoma of the sigmoid colon
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mr Arrandale died a natural death. He was clearly very unwell and had been advised that he had not long to live. He was in considerable pain and was taking morphine tablets, but these did not control his pain completely. It was therefore appropriate for Shipman to give Mr Arrandale an injection on the afternoon of 11th
May. That was almost certainly morphine or diamorphine. It relieved his pain for a time and he was able to sleep. However, as he awoke from that sleep, the injection cannot have directly caused his death. Professor Henry McQuay and Dr John Grenville have given the Inquiry information about the timing and effect of opiates. If a lethal injection of opiate is administered intravenously, death follows within minutes. If administered intramuscularly, a fatal injection of opiate will cause death within about an hour. Mr Arrandale was still alive shortly before 10pm, when his nephew left the house on 11th
May, about eight hours after Shipman had administered the injection. There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman visited Mr Arrandale after his nephew had left him in bed that evening and no possibility that he gave another injection late that night. When his nephew left, Mr Arrandale was very unwell and seems to have sensed that he was about to die. It appears that he died without leaving his bed.
According to Mr John Arrandale, Shipman claimed that he was able to pinpoint the time of Mr Arrandale's death and said it had occurred at 10pm. Dr Grenville has explained that it would not be possible for Shipman to make an accurate assessment. However, Shipman quite often pretended that he could do this, possibly out of conceit. In any event, having declared that Mr Arrandale died at 10pm on 11th
May, he stated on the MCCD counterfoil that he had died on 12th
May. As no one really knows at what time Mr Arrandale died, his death was properly registered as having occurred on 12th
May, the day when the death was discovered.

name: Charlotte Bennison
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 19 Rowbotham Street, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
There are several suspicious features surrounding this death. It is known that Shipman visited Mrs Bennison on the day of her death and, so far as is known, no one saw her alive or spoke to her after that visit. There is a remote possibility that someone did see her alive or speak to her and that that person did not communicate with the family after the death. I regard that possibility as so remote that I can dismiss it. I am also quite satisfied that, when Shipman said on Form B that Mr Williamson had seen Mrs Bennison alive at 4.30pm, he was lying. His claim that the death occurred at about 5.30pm is also plainly false. He wanted to make it appear that Mrs Bennison had died several hours after his visit and had been seen alive in the mean time. These factors create a very high degree of suspicion that Shipman killed Mrs Bennison.
As Dr Grenville has said, the medical evidence supporting a death due to cerebrovascular accident is extremely poor. There were no factors creating a risk of a stroke. Blood pressure was well within normal limits; indeed it was good for a woman of Mrs Bennison's age. Shipman's conduct towards Mrs Bennison was inappropriate for a stroke victim. As Dr Grenville has said, the timing of the onset of a supposed stroke, of the occlusive type, and the subsequent quite sudden death are not compatible. It is theoretically possible that Mrs Bennison could have died a natural death, but it seems to me to be highly unlikely. In any event, it is stretching the bounds of coincidence beyond its limits to think that a natural death should occur so shortly after Shipman's visit.
The note made by Shipman of his consultation on the day of the death gives rise to suspicion. It includes reference to some, although not all, of the concerns that Mrs Bennison had mentioned to her family. But it then went on to deal with problems or signs that no member of the family was aware that Mrs Bennison had. This is a very common feature in cases in which Shipman killed. He would often make a note which was partly genuine and would then add on a reference to a problem which was subsequently to be used to explain the sudden death, which followed shortly after. I think that is what he has done here. I do not think Mrs Bennison had had a stroke that day. I think it far more likely that she had vomiting with diarrhoea (indicating a problem in the gut) rather than vomiting without diarrhoea. If she had had a stroke, I think she would have said something about its symptoms to Mrs Annie Williamson, when asking her to arrange for Mrs Kay to telephone the surgery. I think Mr Bent would have noticed something amiss at lunchtime. I believe that this entry in the medical records is largely false and was designed to provide Shipman with an explanation for Mrs Bennison's death. Shipman might well have asked a member of his staff to contact Social Services in connection with Mrs Bennison's future care. If he did, no doubt any arrangement made would soon be cancelled.
Mrs Bennison's appearance in death was entirely typical of that of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of diamorphine.
Taking these factors into account, I am entirely satisfied that Shipman killed Mrs Bennison. There is no reason to think that he used any method other than his usual one, diamorphine injection.

name: John Crompton
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 37 Gloucester Road, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
This is one of many deaths where a patient was found dead shortly after a visit from Shipman. No one saw Mr Crompton alive or spoke to him after Shipman's visit. That in itself is a highly suspicious factor.
Mr Crompton appeared to be well in the days leading up to his death. He did not request a visit from Shipman on 21st
March 1995. If he had wanted to see Shipman, Mrs Taylor would have known about it. It is apparent from the visits book that Shipman had made his own decision to visit. I would not automatically regard an unsolicited visit as sinister as many doctors pay unannounced visits to their very elderly patients. However, it appears that Shipman had planned this visit. According to Mrs Taylor, it was the first time he had paid an unsolicited visit to Mr Crompton. The fact that Mr Crompton was found dead so soon after the visit raises the suspicion in my mind that Shipman might have gone round specifically for the purpose of killing Mr Crompton.
I am also suspicious of Shipman's claim that Mr Crompton complained of chest pain that day. First, if he had had chest pain, he would have told Mrs Taylor about it. Second, if there had been a complaint of chest pain which Shipman suspected might be angina, he would surely have prescribed GTN, as Professor Baker has suggested. If the GTN relieved the pain, Shipman would know that the pain was due to angina. If it did not, the pain would have been due to some other cause. To tell a man of 87 to let the doctor know if his pain recurs is not the action of a reasonable doctor. Whenever Shipman is found to have acted in a way which was not what a reasonable doctor would have done, the suspicion arises that events did not occur as Shipman has claimed. The handwritten entry for 21st
March 1995, which is so strikingly similar to the entry for 10th
October 1994, does not contain any reference to chest pain, angina or contacting the surgery if necessary. I think the medical records are a hotchpotch of untruths.
There are other suspicious features. It is remarkable that Shipman should not tell Mrs Taylor that he had seen Mr Crompton at lunchtime on the day of his death, as I am satisfied that he did. Such concealment is deeply sinister, as are the lies Shipman told on Form B, which, as I have said, seem to me to be designed to give the impression that Mrs Taylor was with her father while he had a heart attack and died.
The locked back door is not consistent with a natural death. It is hard to see why Mr Crompton would have locked his back door, which he always left unlocked. On the other hand, if Shipman had killed Mr Crompton, he could have locked the back door and left by the front door, thereby leaving the house secure and creating the impression that Mr Crompton was alive when he left the house.
Mr Crompton's position and appearance in death were a little different from those of many of Shipman's known victims but were not in my view inconsistent with death following the administration of a lethal injection of diamorphine.
Taking the evidence as a whole, I have come to the conclusion that Shipman must have killed Mr Crompton. Although I recognise the possibility that this very elderly man could have died naturally from a heart attack or a stroke during the afternoon, the lies told and the deception practised by Shipman have driven me to the conclusion that this cannot have been a natural death. I am satisfied so as to be sure that Shipman killed him.

name: Alice Dixon
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Dixon died a natural death.
It is clear from the Charnley House diary that Mrs Dixon's condition declined following the fracture of her femur. Her immobility rendered her vulnerable to bronchopneumonia, a very common cause of death in elderly, immobile patients. It is clear from the diary that the death was expected.
There is no evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Dixon after 24th
February. That day was a Friday. It is very unlikely that Shipman would have visited her again over the weekend, unless called out. It would appear that Dr Bills was the Donneybrook doctor on duty that weekend, as it was he who came out to certify the fact of death.
It appears to me that the overwhelming likelihood is that Mrs Dixon died of bronchopneumonia and that Shipman played no sinister part in her death.

name: Moira Ashton Fox
title: Miss
place_of_death: her home, 104 Chartist House, Mount Street, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of suspicious features about this death. First, the death was discovered by Shipman. He claimed that he had visited Miss Fox at her request, although his own visits book suggests that he had decided in advance that he would visit her to take blood samples. This inconsistency alone gives rise to some suspicion. Shipman's account seems inherently unlikely. Miss Fox lived in sheltered accommodation. The warden, Mrs Unsworth, called round every morning to check on the welfare of her residents. If Miss Fox had been ill that morning, she would have told Mrs Unsworth. Probably Mrs Unsworth would have telephoned Shipman. If Miss Fox had begun to feel ill after Mrs Unsworth's visit, I would have expected her to summon the warden by pulling her emergency cord. It appears that she had not done so. I think it likely that Shipman called on Miss Fox of his own volition and not at her request. For him to find her dead, with the door open, when he arrived on what was probably an unsolicited visit, is highly unlikely and his claim that this is what happened gives rise to grave suspicion.
In the absence of the medical records, it is not possible to form a view of Miss Fox's health in the days, weeks and months before her death. The impression created by the witnesses, however, is that Miss Fox appeared to be in quite good health and tended to exaggerate her symptoms. There is no indication that she suffered from a heart condition and it seems that if she had done, she would certainly have told Mrs Ellison, and in all likelihood Mr Unsworth, of it. Mr Unsworth was shocked by her sudden death.
Mr Unsworth describes a series of events which were to become part of the familiar pattern of cases in which Shipman killed. On many occasions in the later years of Shipman's career, he was to discover the body of a patient. In those cases I have concluded that he had killed the patient and had pretended that he had found the body. Sometimes he would visit, kill the patient, leave the premises and return later to discover the body. Sometimes he would arrive, kill the patient and go immediately to find a neighbour or warden to whom he would say that the patient had been dead when he arrived. This case is of the second type. Shipman's extraordinary conduct in asking Mr Unsworth's opinion as to whether Miss Fox was dead is not a common feature of many Shipman killings, but it does nothing to allay my suspicion that he had just killed her.
In the present case, Shipman claimed that the door had been open. There are other cases in which he has made such a claim. Often that claim was implausible. On other occasions, he has claimed that he was unable to gain entry and has gone to find a warden, asking him or her to return with him with a key to the patient's flat. On entry they would find the patient dead. In the present case, Shipman's account is designed to give the impression that Miss Fox had begun to have a heart attack and had gone in search of help. She had opened the door and collapsed behind it. In my view, it would be far more likely that Miss Fox would have summoned the warden by pulling her cord than that she would open her door. In any event, if Shipman had indeed found the body behind the door, the first thing he would have done would have been to summon the warden by pulling the emergency cord. I regard Shipman's account as implausible.
Mr Unsworth noticed that the body seemed to have been laid out and neither the bed nor Miss Fox's clothing were in any way disturbed, as one might expect them to be if Shipman had lifted her single-handed and put her on the bed. This tidy appearance is consistent with Miss Fox having lain on the bed for examination or for the taking of a blood sample. If she had been injected intravenously with a lethal dose of opiate, she would have died where she was. If Shipman told her that he had come to take a blood sample, it would have given him the opportunity to introduce a needle into one of Miss Fox's veins.
This case has the hallmarks of a case in which Shipman killed and it seems to me to be overwhelmingly likely that Shipman killed Miss Fox by injecting her with opiate. Notwithstanding the absence of the medical records and cremation documents, I feel sure of this conclusion.

name: Florence Heywood
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Godley Court, Hyde Nursing Home, Grange Road South, Hyde
conclusion:
This is not an easy case. It is most unfortunate that the nursing records are not available. However, I am satisfied that a proper search has been made and that it is likely that these were routinely destroyed before Shipman's crimes came to light.
The first question to arise is what the time of death was. As the nursing home report and the family recollection suggest that the death occurred at about 9pm, I think that is more likely to be accurate than Shipman's entry on Form B.
I find Shipman's other entries on Form B suspicious. Shipman suggests that Mrs Heywood was in a coma for about two hours before she died. Dr Grenville says that is unlikely if she was indeed suffering from left ventricular failure. Shipman claims that he saw Mrs Heywood at about 9pm, at which time she was alive, and then either stayed for an hour or returned to see her again at about 10pm. That conflicts with the evidence of the nursing home staff and members of the family, all of whom say that Mrs Heywood was dead by 9pm. It also conflicts with the members of the family who say that they saw Shipman leaving the nursing home as they were arriving, which they think was at about 9pm or soon after. I think it is unlikely but not impossible that Shipman should stay an hour at Mrs Heywood's bedside. I also think it is unlikely but not impossible that he should return to her bedside at 10pm. I am also suspicious of his claim that he returned to examine the body at 11.30pm. I note that none of this activity is recorded in Mrs Heywood's medical notes. In short I find his account of his movements as described in Form B to be highly unlikely and therefore probably wrong. The question arises whether Shipman's account was inaccurate because he was careless or deliberately untruthful.
I know from other cases involving Hyde Nursing Home that it was the usual practice of the staff to warn relatives as soon as they realised that a resident was critically ill. I infer that the staff did not know that Mrs Heywood was very ill until about 8.30pm. I think it likely that they then telephoned Shipman and the family. It is entirely possible that the nature of Mrs Heywood's sudden illness was acute ventricular failure. If so, it is possible that Shipman arrived before the family, found Mrs Heywood in extremis and gave an injection of a strong diuretic and a small dose of an opiate, which did not prevent her from dying by 9pm. It is also possible that when he arrived he gave not a diuretic but a lethal dose of opiate which ensured that Ms Heywood died immediately, that is at about 9pm. He then left and did not return that night. Whichever of those two possibilities is correct, Mrs Heywood died at about 9pm. I can see that for Shipman to suggest that the death occurred two hours after he left might help to deflect any suggestion that his treatment had caused the death. However, I cannot see how Shipman's rather elaborate and improbable account of his movements would have helped him to conceal his guilt. I have come across a number of cases where Shipman's entries on Form B have been manifestly inaccurate in cases where he has not killed a patient and have concluded that the inaccuracies arose out of carelessness. Although I am not certain of this, on balance I think it is more likely that Shipman's account on Form B was inaccurate due to carelessness rather than deliberately untrue.
I cannot accept the accounts of the various members of the family as wholly reliable. I accept that they are doing their best to recollect events that took place some years ago. However, I fear that their recollections have been affected by the discussions which have taken place between them and their exposure to the newspaper and television coverage of Shipman's crimes. Their memories all focus sharply on the claim that Mrs Foster told them that Shipman had given Mrs Heywood an injection. They recall almost nothing about what she told them about the circumstances of the death. Indeed they suggest that she told them very little. I have seen Mrs Foster and I accept her evidence. I do not think she would have given the bare information that Shipman had given an injection without explaining why the doctor had been called, what the doctor had said and done and what she understood had been the cause of death. It may well be that Mrs Foster told them a history, which included the information that Shipman had given an injection. If she did, I am sure she must have put that information in context. Unfortunately, the family has no recollection of the discussion as a whole. As Mrs Foster cannot remember the event and as the nursing notes are not available, I am left without any information as to the true circumstances of Mrs Heywood's death. I do, however, accept that Mrs Foster was not concerned about the death and did not suspect that Shipman might have done anything wrong.
I think it is highly likely that Mrs Heywood was very ill before Shipman arrived on 10th
November 1994. That is why he was called out and why the family was summoned. Her condition was of sudden onset and I think it likely that she was in cardiac failure. Shipman certified that the cause of her death was left ventricular failure. I think that this makes it quite likely that Shipman administered an injection because the range of appropriate treatments for left ventricular failure includes the intravenous administration of a strong diuretic and, if required, a small dose of opiate. I reach that conclusion despite my reservations as to the accuracy of the family's evidence.
I am satisfied that Mrs Foster was not surprised by Mrs Heywood's death and cannot remember it. It is quite possible that Shipman gave a lethal dose of opiate and lied about the injection he gave, and that Mrs Foster was not surprised by the death because of the severity of the episode that had caused her to summon Shipman in the first place.
I regret that I am unable to say whether Mrs Heywood was probably killed by Shipman or probably died of natural causes. I am, however, suspicious about the death because it occurred during or shortly following Shipman's visit.

name: Richard Johnson
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 28 Woodbrooke Avenue, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mr Johnson died a natural death.
His physical and mental decline is well described by Mrs Mackenzie. His death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
It appears that Shipman probably attended in the morning of 3rd
May. He claimed to have seen Mr Johnson alive on that day and the entry in his visits book supports this. According to the statements of Dr Roberts and Dr Napier, Shipman was usually off duty on Thursday afternoons. That is probably why another doctor attended after the death.
There is no evidence that Shipman gave Mr Johnson an injection that morning. The evidence suggests that he prescribed some form of medication, which I infer was to be taken orally. The medication was supplied by a pharmacist who would have written the dosage on the container and would have raised a query if it had seemed inappropriate. Moreover, it was put into the hands of the district nurse who would surely not have given it without speaking to the doctor if she had thought that the dose was dangerously large. Assuming that Mr Johnson was given some of the medication, there is no evidence that it had any noticeable effect on him. Some time elapsed before his breathing went quiet.
Mrs Mackenzie's concern arises from the remarks made by the district nurse on seeing the medication which Shipman had prescribed for her father. Her impression was that the nurse thought that the medication might be expected to hasten his death. However, it is quite possible that the nurse was only expressing her opinion as to Mr Johnson's life expectancy, which differed from the doctor's opinion.

name: Jane Ellen Lord
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 961 Rochdale Road, Walsden, Todmorden
certified_cause: left ventricular failure due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
Mrs Lord was of advanced years and, in the days before her death, she was sufficiently tired and unwell to stay in bed. She requested a visit from the doctor. We know from the generic evidence of Dr John Grenville that the certified cause of death, left ventricular failure, can be of sudden onset. The usual symptoms would be extreme tiredness and lack of energy. The patient might also be breathless but that might not be apparent if she was resting in bed. Thus, there is consistency between Mr Kershaw's observations and the certified cause of death.
There is a conflict between what Mr Kershaw told the police and what he told the Inquiry. The hearsay account contained within Mr Kershaw's Inquiry statement must be treated with caution, especially as it relates to events more than a quarter of a century ago. If Shipman did in fact visit Mrs Lord during the morning of the day of her death, then the possibility that he administered a lethal injection of opiates must be considered. However, from the course of events described, it seems highly unlikely that any opiates were given. Professor Henry McQuay and Dr Grenville have given joint generic evidence to the Inquiry as to the effects of the administration of opiates and the timing of those effects. If a lethal injection of opiates were administered intravenously, then death would follow within minutes. If administered intramuscularly, a fatal injection of opiates would have a maximal effect within 30 to 60 minutes, during which time the patient would lapse into unconsciousness and die. In the immediate post-injection period, an onlooker might not see anything strange but, within 15 to 30 minutes, it would be clear that something was seriously wrong. From the history now given of the day of Mrs Lord's death, it is clear that she had not received a lethal dose of opiate from Shipman as, some time after he left, Mrs Lord ate her lunch and it was some time after that when she suddenly died.
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Lord died a natural death.

name: Deborah Middleton
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 4 Manor Road, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of highly suspicious circumstances surrounding this death.
It is possible that Mrs Middleton was suffering from a chest infection on 7th
January and also that she felt very tired. Extreme tiredness could be a symptom of heart failure; however, I do not think her symptoms could have been very serious that morning. Had they been, her daughter would not have gone to work, leaving her alone. Had Mrs Middleton felt ill during the day, I think it likely that she would have telephoned either her daughter or granddaughter. As it was, it appears that she went about her usual daily duties, which included making preparations for the arrival of her great-grandchildren after school. There is no evidence to suggest that Mrs Middleton had anything seriously wrong with her in the early afternoon when those preparations would have been made.
On Form B, Shipman admitted that he had seen Mrs Middleton on the afternoon of her death. No one saw her or spoke to her after his visit. That in itself is a highly suspicious feature. For a woman who was not apparently ill to die suddenly at about the time of Shipman's visit would be a real coincidence.
The timings provided by Shipman on Form B are hopelessly inconsistent. Shipman said that death had occurred at 5pm, having crossed out his first entry. Shipman claimed to have seen Mrs Middleton alive two hours before her death, again having overwritten his first attempt. He went on to say that Mrs Middleton was found at
'14.20'
by her granddaughter, 40 minutes before he admitted last having seen her alive, and that she was dead by 3pm when the ambulance crew arrived. At the very least, this inconsistency shows extreme carelessness by Shipman. When I see signs of Shipman making alterations to the timings on Form B, I suspect that he has been trying to work out how best to distance his own visit from the time of the death. Here he seeks to put about two hours between his visit and the time of death. However, the witness evidence suggests that the time of death was well before 5pm, as Shipman first suggested on Form B. Mrs Slaney says that she found Mrs Middleton dead at about 4.30pm and she would have no way of knowing how long Mrs Middleton had been lying dead. What Shipman was thinking of when he said later on Form B that the time of death was 3pm I cannot say. It appears to me that he was either confused or simply very careless.
There is an obvious lie on Form B, where Shipman alleged that Mrs Slaney was present at the moment of death. I am satisfied that she was not. In my view, Shipman told that lie in order to dispel the idea that he might have been present and to create the impression that a member of the family was there, as would be usual if Mrs Middleton's death had been expected.
Mrs Middleton's appearance in death was wholly inconsistent with death due to cardiac failure but was wholly consistent with the appearance of many of Shipman's victims who had died by lethal injection of diamorphine.
My conclusion is that Shipman must have killed Mrs Middleton, almost certainly by lethal injection of diamorphine. Notwithstanding the absence of the medical records, I feel sure of this conclusion.

name: Annie Alexandra Powers
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
There can be no doubt that Mrs Powers was at high risk of suffering a sudden death due to heart attack or stroke. Dr Grenville has said that the events described by Mrs Meadows are consistent with a natural death by heart attack or possibly a stroke.
However, I have some concerns about the circumstances of this death. First, Mrs Brimble went home when her shift finished at 1pm. I do not think she would have done so had she been worried about her aunt. I do not think she thought Mrs Powers was about to die and it follows that I do not think Mrs Meadows or Mrs Spencer thought she was about to die. I think it likely that either Mrs Spencer or Mrs Meadows told Mrs Brimble that she should go home as her aunt would be all right. When Mrs Brimble left, Shipman had not yet arrived.
Second, I do not think that Mrs Kaye was summoned to attend the home until very shortly before the death. I think it likely that she was not summoned until after Shipman had arrived and had said that Mrs Powers had not long to live. That is consistent with my view that the staff did not think that Mrs Powers was critically ill until Shipman arrived. If they had thought so, they would have summoned Mrs Kaye sooner.
Third, I am concerned that Mrs Meadows did not write a complete and accurate note of the death. She did not record that Shipman was present and she described the death as peaceful, when her own recollection was that it was painful and lasted over an hour. However, I am satisfied that she did not seek to conceal Shipman's presence at the death. She told Mrs Kaye that he had been there. I cannot think why she should wish to write a bland description of the death in the daily diary. I could well understand that she would not wish to cause distress to relatives but they would not see what had been written in the daily diary. However, I accept that it was her practice to describe all deaths as peaceful.
Fourth, I remain concerned that I have not received a clear account of Mrs Powers' death. The best account I have is from Mrs Meadows. She says that Mrs Powers was in pain both before and after Shipman arrived. If Mrs Powers was experiencing pain, I would have expected Shipman to give her an injection of opiate to relieve the pain. That would be entirely proper treatment, provided that the dose was small and was given slowly so as to avoid the risk of overdose. There is no evidence that this was done. It is possible that an injection was administered and that for some reason the staff members were not willing to tell me. I had an uneasy feeling that neither Mrs Meadows nor Mrs Spencer was being wholly frank.
On account of these concerns, it seems to me that it is possible that before Shipman arrived, it was not inevitable that Mrs Powers would die that day but that Shipman ensured that she did. The evidence is not sufficiently clear for me to reach any positive conclusion. I suspect, however, that Shipman might have killed Mrs Powers.

name: Dorothy Rowarth
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 30 Farm Lane, Hyde
conclusion:
It appears highly likely that Mrs Rowarth died very shortly after an opiate injection given by Shipman. I say that because both Mr Rowarth and Miss Rowarth say that Shipman gave an injection at the last visit and Shipman himself said that the death occurred within five minutes of him last seeing Mrs Rowarth alive. As the death occurred so soon after the injection, I infer that it is likely that there was a causal connection between the injection and the death. It does not follow that Shipman deliberately gave a lethal dose of opiate. He might have made a genuine assessment of Mrs Rowarth's needs and given the injection in good faith; it could be that the hastening of the death was the unintended effect of a dose intended only to relieve pain. With any other doctor, I would assume that that was the case. However, I know that Shipman frequently used diamorphine to kill healthy patients and I have also found that he sometimes gave an excessive amount with a view to hastening the death of a terminally ill patient.
In those circumstances, I think it most likely that Shipman deliberately gave an excessive dose of opiate. My conclusion is that Shipman probably hastened Mrs Rowarth's death. However, I stress that her death was imminent and he cannot have shortened her life by very long.

name: Harry Stafford
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 51 Rock Street, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
There are several highly suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. The first and most obvious is that Mr Stafford died in Shipman's presence. Mr Stafford had almost certainly called Shipman out because he was suffering from a cold. There is no evidence that Shipman was called out because Mr Stafford was suffering from chest pain. At about 9.30am, almost certainly after he had asked Shipman to visit, Mr Stafford told his daughter-in-law that he had a bad cold. If he had had chest pain, I think he would have told her. In his generic evidence, Dr John Grenville has said that it is most unusual for a patient to die in the presence of his general practitioner during the course of a visit not arranged as an emergency. With Shipman this happened quite frequently and the event gives rise to a strong suspicion that Shipman has caused the death.
The history recorded by Shipman in the Lloyd George notes describes a patient suffering from acute heart failure. If this were a genuine note, it would mean that Mr Stafford had suffered a sudden and catastrophic deterioration in the short period between speaking to Mrs Stafford and Shipman's arrival, which appears to have been at about 10.30am. In my view, it is highly likely that Shipman's note of the consultation is fabricated.
I am further persuaded to that view by consideration of the note itself. It appears that, when Shipman commenced his clinical examination, Mr Stafford was able to give a history and to submit to examination of his pulse, chest and blood pressure. From the observations recorded, one would expect a reasonable doctor to realise that his patient was seriously ill, and the usual and proper response would be to summon an ambulance. Shipman did not do so even when Mr Stafford collapsed. Nor did he attempt resuscitation. Those are not the actions of a reasonable doctor acting honestly in the best interests of his or her patient.
Shipman claimed, although this cannot be verified, that he gave appropriate treatment in the form of intravenous Cyclimorph and Lasix. However, when Shipman was arrested in 1998, he claimed that he did not routinely carry controlled drugs in his bag. He claimed that he had never done so since his conviction for pethidine abuse in the 1970s. However, it is now known that he did carry diamorphine and used it to kill his patients. That Shipman should claim to have injected an unspecified amount of Cyclimorph into a patient who died soon afterwards is highly suspicious.
Mr Stafford's position and appearance in death are not typical of what is to be expected after a death from left ventricular failure or coronary thrombosis. However, his appearance was entirely typical of that of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of opiate.
Shipman told a lie on cremation Form B, when he said that Mrs McEvilly was present at the moment of death. She was not, as he himself admitted to her when he apologised for not telling her immediately that Mr Stafford had died. In my view, this entry on Form B was designed to create the impression that others were involved at the time of the fatal episode, when the truth is that Shipman was alone with Mr Stafford throughout.
Everything points to the conclusion that Shipman must have killed Mr Stafford. I am sure that he did so, almost certainly by injecting him with a lethal dose of diamorphine.

name: Frances Elizabeth Turner
title: Miss
place_of_death: her home, 36 Peveril Terrace, Hyde
conclusion:
Very little is known about the circumstances surrounding Miss Turner's death. However, there are several reasons to suspect that Shipman killed her. The first is that she appears to have died in his presence. In his generic evidence, Dr John Grenville advised that it is most unusual for a patient to die during a routine visit of a general practitioner, where the patient is not terminally ill and the doctor is not responding to an emergency call following the onset of acute symptoms indicating, for example, a heart attack. He has said that this might be expected to occur once in a general practitioner's professional lifetime. Shipman was present at the deaths of a number of his patients who died at home and this repeated 'coincidence' gives rise to grave suspicion. So far as is known, Miss Turner was not suffering from a terminal illness. It is likely that she called Shipman out on the day of her death, as her name appears in his visits book. However, it does not appear that the request was a matter of urgency. Shipman put her in fifth position on his list. If Miss Turner had told the receptionist of symptoms which sounded like a heart attack or stroke, I would have expected Shipman to give her priority or for the surgery staff to have arranged for an ambulance to attend. In any event, Shipman himself did not suggest that Miss Turner died as the result of some sudden event such as a stroke or heart attack. In my view, the fact that Miss Turner died during what was probably a routine visit by Shipman is a highly suspicious factor.
Shipman claims that Miss Turner died of old age. In his generic evidence, Dr Grenville has explained that it is only appropriate to give old age as the cause of death where the elderly patient has deteriorated gradually over a significant period of time until he or she has reached a moribund state. The patient will almost always have become bedridden and will have required nursing care. The death will have been expected. In such circumstances, it might be difficult for the doctor to determine the specific cause of death and it is then appropriate to certify the cause as old age. On Form B, Shipman recorded that Miss Turner had not received nursing care during her last illness. That is clearly inconsistent with the gradual deterioration described by Dr Grenville. There are a number of patients killed by Shipman (among them Shipman's last victim, Mrs Kathleen Grundy), where Shipman has certified that the death was due to old age when it was clearly inappropriate. In those cases, it appears to me that Shipman has put 'old age' because the medical records revealed no plausible explanation for the death. The fact that Shipman certified this death as being due to old age when Miss Turner had not required nursing is a highly suspicious factor.
I am also slightly suspicious about the inconsistencies between Shipman's various accounts of when he last saw Miss Turner alive. However, as he has admitted that he was present at the death, it seems likely that those inconsistencies are more likely explained as due to muddle and incompetence than as a deliberate attempt to mislead.
There are two major grounds for suspicion here. Despite Miss Turner's advanced years, her frail state of health and the absence of her medical records, what is known of this death shows features which are so typical of cases in which Shipman killed that I have come to the conclusion that he probably killed her. It is likely that he did this in his usual way, by administering a lethal injection of opiate.

name: Harry Waller
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 4 Kew Avenue, Hyde
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to carcinoma of the left main bronchus
conclusion:
It is clear to me that Mr Waller's death was due to natural causes, as certified by Shipman.
Mr Waller was terminally ill and, according to Dr Grenville, the treatment provided by Shipman was within the bounds of reasonable practice. I think it highly unlikely that a syringe driver was used. Such equipment is obvious and, if Mr Waller's son was staying in the house, I think it is almost inconceivable that he would not have been aware that his father was being treated in that way. In any event, syringe drivers were not in common use in community medicine in the 1980s.
It appears to me that Shipman's last visit probably occurred about 15 to 18 hours before Mr Waller died. Even if Shipman paid a second visit during the evening of 24th
October, Mr Waller survived for at least six to eight hours afterwards. The possibility that Shipman administered a lethal dose of opiate to Mr Waller can be excluded. We know from the joint report provided by Professor McQuay and Dr Grenville that, even if an opiate were to be injected intramuscularly, the maximal effect would occur within 30 to 60 minutes. Therefore if a lethal injection were to be administered, death would be expected to occur within one hour. It can safely be inferred that Shipman did not give Mr Waller a lethal injection of opiate.
Mr Waller's son has also expressed concern that his father might have been sedated more heavily and sooner than he should have been. Dr Grenville has explained, both in his generic evidence and in his report in this case, that it is not always easy to assess the best quantity of medication to give a terminally ill patient. He says that some doctors will err towards ensuring that the patient has as little as possible. Others will give larger amounts, so as to ensure that the patient is not in pain, even though this might mean that the patient is unconscious sooner than might otherwise be the case. Neither of these approaches is right or wrong. Both are acceptable practice, provided that the doctor makes a genuine attempt to give the dose that he or she thinks is best for the patient. It appears that, on 22nd
October, Shipman administered an intramuscular injection into Mr Waller's buttock, after explaining that the injection would send Mr Waller to sleep. We do not know what the injection was; it could have been an opiate or it could have been a sedative. That injection does indeed seem to have sent Mr Waller to sleep and it appears that he was not conscious for long periods after that time. Patients who are heavily sedated are at increased risk of developing bronchopneumonia, a common mechanism of death in the terminally ill. It is theoretically possible that Mr Waller's death was hastened slightly by the decision to sedate him as early as 22nd
October. However, as Shipman appears to have discussed this course of action with Mrs Waller, it seems highly likely that Shipman gave the advice that he did in good faith, believing it to be the best way of keeping Mr Waller comfortable and not intending it to be an indirect way of hastening his death.
I can understand why Mr Waller's son has felt some concern about his father's death now that it is known that Shipman has killed many of his patients by giving excessive doses of diamorphine. In some of those cases, the patient has been terminally ill and Shipman has given a lethal dose intended to hasten the death. In such cases, the death will have taken place within about an hour of the final injection. In this case there is no reason to fear that Mr Waller was given a lethal dose. He lived for at least six hours after the final injection, probably rather longer. I hope the concerns of Mr Waller's son have now been laid to rest.

name: Ellen Ashton
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Hazeldene, a residential home for the elderly, Beaufort Close, Hattersley, Hyde
certified_cause: bronchopneumonia due to congestive heart failure
conclusion:
I think it is highly likely that Mrs Ashton died from natural causes, almost certainly of the cause certified by Shipman.
From the history recounted by Mr Sowter, it would appear that Mrs Ashton developed a chest infection, which developed into bronchopneumonia. She became very poorly and obviously could not manage in her own home. Following her admission to Hazeldene, she appears to have declined steadily towards death. This is typical of the course of bronchopneumonia, as described by Dr John Grenville in his generic evidence to the Inquiry. Her death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
There is no reason to suspect that Shipman did anything to cause or hasten Mrs Ashton's death. It appears that the last time he saw her was probably during the morning or at lunchtime on the day before she died. Mr Sowter visited after the doctor had been that day and, although Mrs Ashton was unwell during his two hour visit, she was obviously conscious. I therefore rule out the possibility that Shipman administered any type of drug that might have hastened Mrs Ashton's death during that visit. No mention was made to Mr Sowter of a further intended visit from the doctor. However, it is possible that Shipman saw her later that day or on the morning of 10th
August and for that reason I cannot absolutely rule out the possibility that he was involved in her death. It would be most surprising if Shipman had killed a new resident in a residential home, with whose staff he cannot have been very familiar, only months after his arrival in Hyde.

name: Elizabeth Battersby
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 12 Norbury Avenue, Hyde
conclusion:
It appears very likely that Mrs Battersby did suffer a DVT in early December. She was at risk of so doing and Sister Morgan's evidence tends to confirm that this occurred on the Day of Death. It does appear that Shipman advised Mrs Battersby to go into hospital, although he does not seem to have taken all reasonable steps to persuade her to do so. Nor did he protect himself from future criticism by making a full and careful note. Nor does he appear to have given the treatment she needed, which was heparin or at the very least a large dose of warfarin. After her death, I would have expected Shipman to write a full explanation of events, whether or not Mrs Battersby's death had been natural. In the circumstances, she was at risk of a sudden death from pulmonary embolism.
It appears likely that the following sequence of events occurred on the day of the death. Shipman may have visited Mrs Battersby some time before 3pm; in relation to this first possible visit he made a record some time later, saying that he had taken a blood sample, which might or might not have been true. Mrs Battersby mentioned this visit to Mr Gardner when she spoke to him around 1 to 1.30pm. Shipman certainly then went to Mrs Battersby's house at some time after 3pm. Whether she was alive or dead when he arrived is not clear but she was certainly dead or dying when he then went to Mr Vejki's house. Shipman then made one telephone call to the surgery and aborted another to Mrs Gardner's mobile telephone. He then probably went across to Mr Vejki again, told him of the death and left him a key to Mrs Battersby's house. He then returned to the surgery and made two entries on the computerised records. The first he fabricated to suggest that Mrs Battersby's blood test result showed a prothrombin time of 1.45. The second recorded that he had found her dead at 3.30pm of a pulmonary embolus.
The temporal association between Shipman's two visits and Mrs Battersby's death is enough in itself to make me think that Shipman probably killed her, even though I cannot say whether he did it during his first visit or his second. There are other factors within the evidence which point to the same conclusion.
The fabrication of the blood sample result is a highly suspicious factor. It could have had two possible uses for Shipman. First, it might have provided Shipman with an excuse to give Mrs Battersby an injection or a second injection, if he had in fact given her one in the morning. Second, it would provide Shipman with corroboration of his claim that Mrs Battersby was at grave risk of a pulmonary embolism, as it would appear that her blood had not been adequately thinned by the anti-coagulant she had taken at that stage.
The prescription of morphine tablets (unusual treatment for a DVT) would, even if not taken, provide an explanation for the presence of morphine in the body in the unlikely event that it should be forensically examined.
Mrs Battersby's appearance in death was entirely typical of that of many of Shipman's victims who had been injected with a strong opiate.
My conclusion is that, notwithstanding the uncertainties as to the time of the killing, I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Battersby. I also suspect that he stole money from her purse but do not feel able to reach a positive conclusion on that point.

name: Eileen Theresa Cox
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 11 Hunters Court, Dukinfield, Cheshire
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
In the absence of medical records, it is difficult to be sure about Mrs Cox's health in the weeks and months before her death. However, I did feel that, in Mrs Davies, I had an unusually reliable source of information. My impression is that Mrs Cox was in quite good general health for her age, but tended to exaggerate any symptoms she had noticed. I accept that her main medical problem was recurrent bronchitis. That Mrs Cox had a spray and tablets for use in angina attacks implies that she had had some signs or symptoms to warrant them being prescribed. However, I am sure that, if chest pain had been a regular occurrence, Mrs Davies would certainly have known of it and would have remembered it.
I accept as accurate Mrs Davies' recollection of the events of the morning of Christmas Eve. I found the details she was able to recall entirely convincing. I accept that she was well able to detect that her mother was not really suffering from a severe bout of bronchitis, but was exaggerating her symptoms of what may well have been the start of a cold. I am quite sure that, if Mrs Cox had been suffering from chest pain, she would have told her daughter. I am sure that she did not.
It is known that Shipman visited Mrs Cox that morning. He says it was at about noon and he could be right about that. What is clear, however, is that no one saw Mrs Cox alive or spoke to her after his visit. That is a highly suspicious factor. It appears to me that Mrs Davies tried to telephone her mother very shortly after Shipman's visit, by which time she was already dead. Knowing what is now known of Shipman's habits and method of killing, it is just too much of a coincidence to suggest that Mrs Cox might have died a natural death within so short a time after Shipman's departure.
Mrs Cox's appearance in death was not consistent with a death following a heart attack. First, her demeanour struck everyone as very peaceful. That is not usual following a heart attack. Second, the way in which Mrs Cox was tucked up in bed is not consistent with her having undergone an 'agonal event'. Quite apart from her personal preferences for having the bedcovers kept loose, it sounds to me as though she could not have tucked herself in and would not have stayed tucked in during a heart attack. On the other hand, her position in bed and her peaceful appearance are entirely consistent with what would be expected if Shipman had visited her, injected her with a strong opiate, and tucked her up before leaving.
The timings given on Form B appear to me to be an attempt by Shipman to distance his visit from the time of death. He might well have given an accurate time for his visit. Noon was the time when Mrs Cox said she was expecting him. But, if Mrs Davies' recollection is reasonably accurate, and I think it is, the time of death was demonstrably earlier than 2pm.
Shipman's claim on Form B that Mrs Cox complained of chest pain at noon and was known to suffer from angina, was intended to provide an explanation for what was otherwise a wholly unexpected death. I do not think that claim was true. But, in any event, as Dr Grenville has said, if it were true, Shipman's conduct in leaving her alone without contacting her daughter would have revealed a quite unacceptable standard of care. In several later cases, I have seen examples of Shipman using this device, of suggesting that the patient was quite seriously ill when last seen but doing nothing about it. Later, the claim of prior illness is used to explain the following death.
There is no evidence available to the Inquiry about Shipman's access to diamorphine or other strong opiate drugs in the 1980s. The drugs registers are no longer available. However, Shipman obtained pethidine and some morphine illegally in the 1970s and he obtained huge quantities of diamorphine by similar methods in the 1990s. Plainly he knew how to obtain such drugs illegally in the 1980s. I infer that he did so.
In summary, this death is entirely typical of many deaths that were to occur in the later years, in which I am quite sure that Shipman has killed his patient. His 'hallmark' is on this case. Despite the absence of medical records and despite the lapse of time since this death, I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Cox, almost certainly by injecting her with a lethal dose of strong opiate.

name: Christopher Denham
title: Mr
place_of_death: Bowlacre, a residential home for the elderly, Stockport Road, Hyde
conclusion:
Mr Denham was very elderly and quite unwell in the period leading up to his death. The evidence suggests that his death was neither sudden nor at all unexpected. Mrs Mellor was able to sit with her father until his death.
Although there is no witness evidence that Shipman visited Mr Denham on the day of his death, the MCCD counterfoil and the visits book suggest that he did so. If Mrs Duggan is right in thinking that her grandfather died in the afternoon or early evening, it is likely that Shipman had visited that day while Mr Denham was alive. There is a possibility therefore that Shipman might have given Mr Denham a drug that hastened his end. However, I think this is unlikely as Mrs Mellor was with her father throughout the day until his death.
Although I cannot absolutely rule out the possibility that Shipman hastened Mr Denham's death, I think it highly likely that his death was due to natural causes.

name: Mary Elizabeth Firman
title: Miss
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am sure that Miss Firman died of natural causes. Her death was clearly expected by those who were looking after her, who contacted her nephew shortly before she died, almost certainly to inform him of her deteriorating condition.
Although Miss Firman's name appears in Shipman's visits book for the day of her death, it seems unlikely that he saw her alive on that day. Miss Firman died at 9.30am. Shipman had several patients to see on that day. It seems likely that he was called out to certify the fact or cause of her death, particularly since he signed the MCCD counterfoil on the day of the death.
There is no positive evidence to suggest that Shipman saw Miss Firman after the visit on 27th
February 1981.

name: Nora Grundy
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Bowlacre, a residential home for the elderly, Stockport Road, Hyde
conclusion:
The evidence suggests that, by the evening of 10th
October, Mrs Grundy was very unwell. Although Mr Grundy was shocked by his mother's death, he had not seen her for three or four days. From Mr Dyson's description of her condition on the evening of 10th
October, I do not think it could be said that her death during that night was either sudden or unexpected.
There is no evidence that Shipman saw Mrs Grundy on the day of her death or in the days leading up to her death. Mr Grundy was told that his mother had died in the night. That must have been some hours after Mr Dyson had visited. If the staff had requested a visit from a doctor during the evening or night, it is likely that it would have been Dr Napier or a doctor sent by the deputising service who would have visited and not Shipman. In the circumstances it appears extremely unlikely that Shipman had any contact with Mrs Grundy in the hours leading up to her death. I therefore rule out the possibility that Shipman unlawfully killed Mrs Grundy by administering to her a lethal dose of opiates.
When Mr Dyson last saw Mrs Grundy, in the early evening of 10th
October, she was unwell but conscious and I therefore rule out the possibility that Shipman might have over-sedated Mrs Grundy to the extent that it might have contributed to her death.
In my view, it is overwhelmingly likely that Mrs Grundy died of natural causes.

name: Olive Heginbotham
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 1 Fawley Avenue, Hyde
certified_cause: congestive heart failure due to ischaemic heart disease and hypertension
conclusion:
From the circumstances surrounding the death, it seems highly likely to me that Mrs Heginbotham died during the hours of daylight on 24th
February. The overwhelming likelihood is that, if she had been alive as darkness fell, Mrs Heginbotham would have switched on the lights and closed the curtains. Even if she had left her curtains open, she would have put the lights on.
Shipman visited Mrs Heginbotham on 24th
February. There is no evidence that anyone saw or spoke to Mrs Heginbotham after Shipman's visit. In many cases, this factor carries great probative force. However, it does not in this case, as Mrs Heginbotham did not often go out. Nor did she often receive visitors, and her family did not telephone her every day. So the fact that she was not seen alive that afternoon does not prove that she was already dead. Having said that, whether Shipman visited her between noon and 2pm or between 3pm and 4pm, it would appear that she was probably dead within a couple of hours of his visit, at the most; this is evidenced by the fact that her curtains were open and the lights were off. It is something of a coincidence that she should die so soon after his visit.
Mrs Heginbotham had been suffering from quite severe cardiac failure. This seemed to have been brought under control with appropriate medication but was liable to recur. When her son visited her on the Saturday before her death, he did not notice anything unusual about her state of health. Mrs Heginbotham did not ask for a visit on 24th
February. Shipman visited of his own volition, apparently to follow up his previous attendance. Mrs Heginbotham was aged 86 and a sudden death from cardiac failure or heart attack was a real possibility.
When Shipman visited Mrs Heginbotham on 24th
February, he claims to have found that her condition had deteriorated since his last visit. His note does not suggest that he advised admission to hospital, rather that that question should be addressed the following day. However, he appears to have told Mrs Chapman that Mrs Heginbotham had refused to be admitted. I do appreciate that elderly people sometimes do refuse to go into hospital. However, when Shipman claims that a patient has refused admission, it raises suspicion because he is known to have made this claim in a number of cases where he had killed the patient. He often used this device as a means of explaining the death that soon followed. In practice, if an elderly patient were refusing admission, contrary to Shipman's advice, one would expect him to suggest a discussion with a relative or to make some arrangements for the patient's care. In this case, Shipman did not attempt to discuss the need for admission with a relative; nor did he make arrangements for Mrs Heginbotham's care. In my view, this gives rise to suspicion that his note of 24th
February is not genuine, but was designed to provide an explanation for Mrs Heginbotham's death, which he himself caused.
Shipman's entries on Form B are clearly designed to create the impression that Mrs Heginbotham died in the early hours of the morning. He could not have known when she died, unless he was with her. If he were not involved in her death, one would have expected him to give a bracket between the time she was last seen alive and the time when her body was found. As it is, Shipman has attempted to give a spurious authority to his estimate of the time of death. In my view, he has done this in order to distance the death from the time of his own visit.
Mrs Heginbotham's appearance in death, sitting peacefully in her chair, with her playing cards and a cup of tea at her side, is entirely typical of the appearance of many of Shipman' s victims who had died of diamorphine poisoning.
Shipman asked Mrs Chapman to arrange a domiciliary visit for Mrs Heginbotham. At the same time, he asked for such a visit for Mrs Couzens. He had visited both that day, probably within a short time of each other. He told Mrs Chapman that both had refused admission to hospital. Neither lived long enough to receive the domiciliary visit arranged. It would be a remarkable coincidence if two women died natural deaths within a short time of a visit by Shipman at which each refused admission to hospital and each was recommended a domiciliary visit.
It must be borne in mind that, during this period, Shipman was in the habit of prescribing single 30mg ampoules of diamorphine for patients who were either already dead or who did not have any requirement for the drug. A 30mg ampoule of diamorphine is a lethal dose. On 22nd
February, Shipman had obtained two ampoules. On 26th
February, he obtained two more, one of them in Mrs Heginbotham's name. There must be a real suspicion that, in obtaining diamorphine in Mrs Heginbotham's name, he was replacing the ampoule that he had used to kill her. As Dr Grenville said, if Mrs Heginbotham was in heart failure on 24th
February, it might have been appropriate to give her a very small dose of diamorphine to relieve distress. There could be no possible justification for giving anything like 30mg, which would have been a lethal dose for her. However, there is no record that the drug was given for therapeutic reasons.
Taking these factors into account and notwithstanding Mrs Heginbotham's poor state of health and her high risk of suffering a sudden cardiac death, I think it is highly likely that Shipman killed Mrs Heginbotham during his visit in the early afternoon of 24th
February 1993. Because of Mrs Heginbotham's underlying medical condition, I cannot rule out the possibility that this was a natural death.

name: Mary Ellen Jordan
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 11 Godley Hill Road, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to aortic stenosis with ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
Mrs Jordan had some history of heart trouble. Mrs Nadin has not mentioned that Mrs Jordan had ever suffered from cancer. However, she had noticed that Mrs Jordan's condition had deteriorated during the last month or two of her life. Her appetite was poor and she could not climb the stairs. The fact that the bed was moved downstairs the day before she died, suggests that there had been a further deterioration in Mrs Jordan's condition in the days leading up to her death. Given her history, Mrs Jordan was certainly at an increased risk of having a heart attack.
According to what Mrs Nadin was told by the hairdresser, a doctor was called to the house during the evening of 30th
August. Mrs Jordan must have been quite poorly for the hairdresser to call the doctor out as an emergency. Since it was Shipman who certified the cause of death, saying that he had seen Mrs Jordan alive that day, that doctor must have been Shipman. The hairdresser said that the doctor gave Mrs Jordan an injection. Mrs Jordan died shortly afterwards.
The circumstances as described by Mrs Nadin give rise to real suspicion that Shipman might have killed Mrs Jordan. However, there is a possibility that Mrs Jordan was having a heart attack when Shipman arrived and that she died a natural death. There is also a possibility that Mrs Jordan was having a heart attack and that Shipman gave her an injection which ensured that she died, thereby depriving her of the chance of recovery. Which is the more likely?
If Mrs Jordan was having a heart attack, one could understand why Shipman might have given her an injection, possibly of a small amount of opiate to relieve her pain and distress. One might expect that he would call an ambulance and have her admitted to hospital, but that does not seem to have been suggested. If she were having a heart attack, it would be very strange and quite unacceptable if he left her in the care of a hairdresser, who would be unable to stay with her. Mrs Nadin has the impression that the doctor had already left the house before the hairdresser set off to fetch Mrs Nadin. It is possible that she is mistaken about that and that he sent the hairdresser off to find Mrs Nadin, giving the impression that he would stay until her return. I think this is unlikely, as the hairdresser would have been very surprised to find that Shipman was not at the house when she returned and Mrs Nadin might have remembered that. In short, I do not think that Shipman behaved as any sensible competent doctor would have behaved when called to a patient suffering a heart attack. I infer that if Mrs Jordan was having a heart attack, Shipman did not take proper steps to treat her for it.
If on the other hand, Mrs Jordan was not having a heart attack and was not apparently very ill, it might have been perfectly acceptable for Shipman to leave, knowing that some arrangements were to be made for Mrs Jordan's supervision. But if she were not seriously ill, I feel bound to wonder what injection did Shipman give? It is possible but very unlikely that Mrs Jordan was in pain as the result of a cancer about which Mrs Nadin was unaware and which did not cause the death. If Mrs Jordan had not been having a heart attack, I ask myself, how could Shipman have certified the cause of her subsequent death? He would not have known the cause.
I find myself unable to decide whether or not Mrs Jordan was having a heart attack when Shipman arrived. However, I do feel able to conclude that if she was, then he did not treat her as he would have done if he had wanted her to survive. He would have called an ambulance; he would not have allowed her to be left alone. I think it likely that the injection was of an inappropriate dose of opiate and was designed to kill. If Shipman gave Mrs Jordan a lethal dose of opiate, he would know that it would make no difference to her whether she were left alone or accompanied. If the injection were given intravenously, Mrs Jordan would have been dead within a few minutes. If it had been given intramuscularly, she would have been asleep within 15 to 30 minutes and dead within 30 minutes to an hour.
I have not found this case easy, as the evidence is uncertain on some important issues. However, taking the evidence as a whole, I have come to the conclusion that it is likely that Shipman killed Mrs Jordan.

name: Eva Lyons
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 16 Keswick Close, Todmorden
conclusion:
It is not possible to reach a firm conclusion as to Mrs Lyons' state of health immediately before her death. Mrs Bartlett does not really know how her mother was at that time. However, if Mr Lyons had the impression that Shipman had 'helped' his wife to die, and was not alarmed or distressed by that possibility, it seems reasonable to infer that he believed that his wife's prognosis was hopeless and that she was suffering considerable pain or distress. I think Mrs Lyons was probably in the terminal stage of her illness and was in either pain or distress or both. It seems likely that Mr Lyons called Shipman out late that night because his wife was suffering.
If she were, it would be appropriate for Shipman to administer an opiate to relieve that pain and distress. It would be his duty to make the best assessment he could of the amount needed to relieve the pain and distress. He would know that the amount needed could have the effect of depressing Mrs Lyons' respiration and might hasten her death. Provided that he assessed the dose in good faith, believing that the amount was necessary for the relief of pain, his actions would be appropriate and lawful. If, however, he assessed the dose intending that it would hasten Mrs Lyons' death, his actions would be unlawful, even though he might have felt it was appropriate to end Mrs Lyons' suffering.
There is good evidence that Shipman gave Mrs Lyons an intravenous injection shortly before her death. It is possible that the injection was of pethidine, but it is also possible that it was of a stronger opiate such as morphine or diamorphine. It would be normal practice for a doctor to have a supply of such drugs in his bag for use in emergencies and at this time Shipman would have been entitled to carry such drugs with him. A very large dose of pethidine would be required to cause death. However, it would have been quite possible for Shipman to give an excessive dose of morphine or diamorphine, which would cause death. If a lethal dose were given, death would follow within five to ten minutes. There is evidence that death followed quite shortly after the injection and that Mr Lyons and Shipman talked during that time. We do not know how large a dose was given, but that the interval was so short, gives rise to a strong suspicion that the dose was a lethal one.
We now know that, in later years, Shipman was to become a serial murderer. We also know that he used intravenous injections of opiate as his preferred method of killing.
I have come to the conclusion that it is likely that Shipman deliberately gave Mrs Lyons an excessive dose of an opiate, with the result that he hastened her death. I think she was probably in severe pain. I also think it likely that death was imminent and her life was not shortened by very much.

name: Samuel Mellor
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 27 Sidley Place, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to chronic obstructive airways disease due to emphysema
conclusion:
There is clear independent evidence that Mr Mellor suffered severe long-standing chronic obstructive airways disease. It appears that he deteriorated gradually towards death. His death was not sudden or unexpected.
There is no evidence that Shipman administered an injection to Mr Mellor in the hours leading up to his death.
Shipman's only questionable action is that he advised that the oxygen supply should be removed. Dr Grenville says that this did not significantly hasten the death. It has been submitted on behalf of the family that, notwithstanding the opinion of Dr Grenville, Mr Mellor was unlawfully killed by Shipman.
I cannot accept the submission that Shipman unlawfully killed Mr Mellor by terminating the oxygen supply. In order to reach a conclusion that Shipman unlawfully caused a death, there are two essential findings: first, that there was an unlawful act and, second, that that unlawful act caused (or materially contributed to) the death. Even if the act of removing the oxygen supply were unlawful, which is doubtful, I cannot find that Shipman's action caused or materially contributed to the death. The only evidence on this issue comes from Dr Grenville. He says that Shipman's decision to remove the oxygen supply did not cause Mr Mellor's death. On behalf of the family, it is submitted that the removal of the supply 'inevitably contributed' to the death. In the face of Dr Grenville's evidence that the removal of the supply did not cause the death, I cannot infer that it must have done. In those circumstances, the only possible conclusion open to me is that this was not an unlawful killing.
It would be sterile to debate the issue of whether Shipman's action in removing the oxygen mask was unlawful. Dr Grenville says that it was inappropriate because the oxygen supply made Mr Mellor comfortable. That, of course, I accept and I can understand that this evidence might have caused some distress to the family. However, not all inappropriate actions are unlawful. There is no evidence that Shipman's action was obviously dangerous or that it was intended to harm the patient.
My conclusion is that I am quite satisfied that Mr Mellor died a natural death. The grounds for Professor Baker's suspicions have been addressed by the further evidence available to the Inquiry, which was not available to him.

name: Annie Parkes
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
It is now twenty years since Mrs Parkes' death. Although her daughter now recalls that the death was sudden and unexpected, I think her memory of her mother's condition during the last day or two of her life must be at fault. I cannot reconcile Mrs Bailey's account of her mother's condition during the afternoon of 4th
June with that in the daily diary, which records that she had a very bad chest that morning and was prescribed penicillin. That evening, the staff noted the first sign of a pressure sore. That is usually an indication that the patient has been confined to bed or to a chair for some time and is in a debilitated condition. I think Mrs Bailey's recollection must be slightly at fault. I accept that Mrs Parkes' final illness was short and her death quite sudden, but I think it was not quite as sudden or inexplicable as Mrs Bailey now remembers.
There is no evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Parkes at a time when he might have done anything which could have directly caused her death. It appears likely that he visited quite early on the morning of 5th
