June. I say that because Mrs Bailey herself was at the home from about 8.45am until 1pm and Shipman did not visit during that time. Yet his visit was recorded by Mrs Stansfield, who wrote the report at the end of the morning shift. She has told the Inquiry that her shift ended at 1pm and that she usually wrote the report at that time. Although it is possible that Shipman visited Mrs Parkes between 1pm and 2pm while Mrs Bailey was away, this seems unlikely.
Even if Shipman did visit between 1pm and 2pm, there is no reason to think that he gave Mrs Parkes a lethal dose of an opiate. Mrs Parkes appeared to Mrs Bailey to be in much the same condition when she returned at about 2pm as when she had left at 1pm. She was still unconscious and her breathing was variable, as one might expect in an elderly woman who was close to death as the result of a chest infection. If Shipman had given Mrs Parkes a dose of opiate between 1pm and 2pm, it is highly likely that she would have died quite soon afterwards, as her respiratory function was already severely compromised. As it was, she did not die until about 3.15pm.
I cannot rule out the possibility that Shipman administered a sub-lethal dose of opiates or a large dose of a sedative when he visited Mrs Parkes on the morning of the day of her death. I think it likely that Mrs Parkes was suffering from a severe chest infection, possibly bronchopneumonia, which had developed over the course of about 36 hours before her death. By the morning of 5th
June, her respiratory function would have already been severely compromised. The likelihood of her dying from bronchopneumonia, a common mechanism of death in elderly people, would, therefore, have been increased had she been heavily sedated. If Shipman did administer a sedative, it would not be possible to say whether he had done it with the intention of keeping Mrs Parkes comfortable or whether he used it as an indirect way of hastening her death.
I think it very likely that Mrs Parkes died as a result of natural causes, although the cause of death might more appropriately have been certified as bronchopneumonia, or some other chest condition, as opposed to senility.

name: Jose Kathleen Diana Richards
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 32 Meadowfield Court, Flowery Field, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to left ventricular failure
conclusion:
There are several suspicious features surrounding this death. First and most obvious, this death occurred in Shipman's presence. Mrs Richards had not asked him to visit and there is no evidence that the warden had asked him to attend as an emergency. Mrs Richards had seemed to be in normal health when she spoke to Mrs Holland at about 12.20pm. If Shipman is to be believed, she just happened to have a fatal heart attack at about the time he just happened to arrive. Such coincidences do not occur. Dr John Grenville is of the view that it is extremely rare for a patient to die during a routine visit by a general practitioner. Now that it is known that many of Shipman's patients died in his presence, this factor alone is enough to convince me that Shipman probably killed Mrs Richards.
However, there are other factors which point to the same conclusion.
I am suspicious of the entry in the medical records which purports to have been made at some time in July, but before the day of the death. I cannot properly decipher the date. The main thrust of the entry seems to relate to symptoms of congestive heart failure, yet Shipman prescribed pethidine. I am always suspicious where Shipman appears to have prescribed an opiate drug in circumstances where it seems inappropriate. I suspect that he might have done so in order to ensure that there would be some morphine in the patient's body after death. If there were to be a post-mortem examination with toxicological tests and if morphine were found, he would have a ready explanation. When that entry was made and to what extent it was genuine, I cannot say, but I suspect that it might have been fabricated to lend support to Shipman's claim that Mrs Richards had congestive heart failure which might lead to left ventricular failure and heart attack.
The entry in the medical records for the day of the death excites great suspicion. Shipman's records can never be taken at face value, as it is known that he often fabricated records of patients he had killed. However, this one is suspicious even on its face. Shipman diagnoses a heart attack but does not record any sign or symptoms which could justify the diagnosis. He does not even claim that the patient is in pain. Yet, he decided to give 10mg diamorphine, which is the equivalent of 20mg morphine. That is a substantial dose for a fit and healthy person. However, for a woman of 72, with a known history of chronic obstructive airways disease, it could well prove fatal. I have considered the possibility that Shipman might have killed Mrs Richards by mere negligence in giving her an excessive dose of opiate with the best of intentions. However, I discount that notion as, if Shipman had realised he had made a mistake and had given too much diamorphine, he could and should have given an antidote. Shipman should not have been carrying diamorphine in his medical bag, as he did not keep a controlled drugs register. However, it is known that he often did carry opiate drugs and used them unlawfully. I suspect that Shipman actually gave more than 10mg diamorphine and intended that it should kill Mrs Richards.
The medical note is also remarkable in that it shows that Shipman did not attempt to summon an ambulance or even the warden, who might at least have been able to offer some comfort. If and when Mrs Richards went into cardiac arrest, as presumably Shipman would contend she did, he made no attempt at resuscitation. That is remarkable as Mrs Richards was only 72 and did not have a long history of heart disease. Whenever I find that Shipman's account of events shows that he failed to take steps which any reasonable doctor would have taken, I suspect that events did not happen as Shipman claimed.
Mrs Richards' position and appearance in death were not at all typical of those usually seen following a death from heart attack or left ventricular failure. They were, however, entirely typical of those seen in many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of opiate. I note that Mrs Richards' dentures had been removed. I have come across a number of cases in which Shipman removed the patient's dentures. I do not know why he did this but it is possible that he wished to avoid the risk that the dentures might lodge in the patient's throat as they lapsed into unconsciousness.
I am quite sure that Shipman killed Mrs Richards. This case has his hallmark on it. The circumstances show the extent to which he was confident and relaxed while killing a patient. He made himself a cup of tea while waiting for the next of kin to arrive.

name: Grace Sumner
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Tameside General Hospital
certified_cause: myocardial infarction due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
I am quite sure that Mrs Sumner died a natural death following a heart attack. In 1995, she had a history which was highly suggestive of angina and ischaemic heart disease, although the diagnosis was not proved. I am sure that in 1996 she was at an increased risk of sudden death from heart disease.
There is no evidence that Mrs Sumner saw Shipman on the day of her death. The fact that Mrs Sumner was able to go shopping after visiting the surgery, return home, make lunch and spend the afternoon going about her usual tasks, indicates that she cannot have been given any lethal or sub-lethal injection that morning at the surgery. The effect of an overdose of opiate or sedative is to make the victim fall asleep quite soon after its administration.
The symptoms described by Mr Sumner are those typical of the onset of a myocardial infarction and the diagnosis was confirmed by ECG.
Mrs Sumner's remarks to her children about the fact that she had been given an injection that day or that morning should not give rise to any cause for concern. It seems that at the time, the family thought that Mrs Sumner was referring either to her tetanus injection that morning or to an injection she had been given since her arrival at the hospital. I think it is only since they have realised the possible significance of an injection given by Shipman that they have been concerned that Shipman might have played some part in their mother's death. It is also possible, as Dr Grenville has suggested, that Mrs Sumner was a little confused that evening, as she had just been given some morphine to ease her pain. It is possible that she did not explain herself very clearly. It is also possible that Mrs Sumner herself, not truly appreciating the nature of her illness, linked its sudden onset with the injection she had had earlier that morning. It is clear, however, from the medical evidence that no such link exists in this case.
The family has raised concern over the fact that Mrs Sumner's medical records were found at Shipman's home. At an early stage in the investigations, the Inquiry legal team shared that concern, as there can be no doubt that Shipman's possession of medical records of deceased patients was highly unorthodox. However, the team examined those cases in which the only reason the death had come to the attention of the police was that the records had been found at Shipman's house. That exercise revealed that many of the deaths were wholly unconnected with Shipman, having occurred, for example, after a stay in hospital or for reasons that were conclusively established by post-mortem examination. It was clear, from that examination, that there was no overall pattern to Shipman's retention of records. The Inquiry team's initial suspicion, that there might be something sinister about the deaths of patients whose records were found at his home, was not confirmed.
I hope the investigation of Mrs Sumner's death and this decision will have served to put the minds of her family at rest.

name: Mary Taylor
title: Miss
place_of_death: her home, 26 St John's Drive, Hyde
conclusion:
Little is known about Miss Taylor's health in the period before her death. It appears that she had become frail and forgetful but she was still living alone, with the assistance of her home help and home care aide. The evidence does not suggest that her health had declined to the point where she had become confined to bed or was dependent on nursing care. To that extent, her death must be regarded as unexpected and this does not appear to be the kind of case where it is appropriate to certify the cause of death as senility or old age.
If there were any evidence that Shipman had made contact with Miss Taylor, I would say that there was some slight suspicion that he might have killed her. However, the evidence is remarkably clear considering that this death took place nearly 20 years ago. The available documentary evidence suggests that Shipman had not seen Miss Taylor for about three weeks before her death. More significantly, there is evidence that she put the security chain across the door when she said goodbye to Mrs Prosser on the evening of 27th
November. The next morning, the security chain was still in place and Miss Taylor was dead in her bedroom. That would suggest that no one had had access to the house during that period. It is possible that Miss Taylor had admitted other visitors after Mrs Prosser's departure but, if she did, she must have been able to put the chain on the door after they left. It is possible that Miss Taylor felt ill and managed to find a way to summon a doctor. If she had done so, it is unlikely that it would have been Shipman, as he was not on duty that evening. It seems extremely unlikely that Shipman could have visited Miss Taylor after Mrs Prosser's departure.
I am quite satisfied that Shipman was not involved in Miss Taylor's death. The exact cause of her death is unknown but I am sure that it was a natural one.

name: James Wood
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 27 Rydal Avenue, Hyde
conclusion:
There are several highly suspicious factors relating to this death. First and most obvious, the death was discovered very shortly after a visit by Shipman. No one saw Mr Wood alive after Shipman's visit. That in itself is a highly suspicious factor. If Mr Wood did indeed die a natural death that afternoon, as Shipman would have us believe, it is a remarkable coincidence that he should do so very shortly after Shipman's departure.
On Form B, Shipman sought to suggest that the death occurred at 4pm and that this was two to three hours after his own visit. It is clear that this must have been an attempt by Shipman to distance himself from the death. If Mr Wood really did die a natural death some time during the afternoon, Shipman could not possibly have known at what time it had occurred. Dr John Grenville has explained that it is not possible in such circumstances to estimate the time of death accurately, although Shipman often pretended that he could do so. If Mrs Wood's recollection is right and Mr Wood's body was cold when she arrived at about 4pm, it would seem that the death could not have taken place as recently as 4pm. If Mrs Wood's recollection is right when she says that she did not leave her father-in-law until about 2pm, it can be seen that Shipman has tried to advance the time of his visit, which he suggests was between 1pm and 2pm. Here again, he must have been trying to distance himself from the death. These factors suggest that Shipman left Mr Wood dead, probably some time between 2pm and 3pm.
There is some evidence that Mr Wood had been unwell in the week or two before his death and had required Shipman's attention on several occasions. Mrs Wood's recollection was that he was almost better and had eaten a good lunch on the day of his death. Shipman's own entry on Form B suggests that Mr Wood was well when Shipman visited. It is of course always possible for an elderly person to die suddenly without any forewarning and without any previous medical history that could explain the death. When that occurs, an honest doctor will refer the case to the coroner for a post-mortem examination. He will not pass the death off as being due to old age. Dr Grenville has described the circumstances in which it is appropriate for a doctor to certify a death as due to old age. This will be where the elderly person has been ill for a significant period of time (usually weeks or months) and has become frail and weak. Death will be fully expected. In these circumstances it can be difficult to determine exactly which specific organ failure has caused the death and a diagnosis of old age is acceptable. A patient in such circumstances would necessarily have been receiving a high level of care from nurses, relatives or friends before death. If a frail elderly patient with multiple organ failure had not been receiving a high level of nursing care, the question would arise as to whether neglect had contributed to the death and it would be mandatory to report the death to the coroner. Mr Wood did not fall into this category of patient and the fact that Shipman certified the death as due to old age increases my suspicion that he killed Mr Wood.
Mr Wood's position and appearance in death were not typical of those usually seen in patients who have died following a heart attack or stroke or other common form of sudden death. On the other hand, they were entirely typical of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of opiate.
This case has the hallmark of a case in which Shipman killed. I am quite satisfied that Shipman killed Mr Wood during his visit on the afternoon of 23rd
December. It is highly likely that Shipman gave Mr Wood an injection of opiate either under the pretext of taking a blood sample or of giving him an injection which would be some form of appropriate treatment.

name: Norman Adshead
title: Mr
place_of_death: Bowlacre, a residential home for the elderly, Stockport Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mr Adshead died as the result of natural causes.
The evidence shows that Mr Adshead's health deteriorated gradually before his death and he was in a coma when his daughter visited on 4th
December. His death during the following night was neither sudden nor unexpected.
There is no evidence that Shipman had access to Mr Adshead shortly before his death. It appears that Shipman was probably not working for several days before the death and it seems most unlikely that he would have visited Bowlacre late at night, especially while on holiday.

name: Lily Bardsley
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 145 Ashton Road, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of suspicious features surrounding Mrs Bardsley's death.
The death occurred in Shipman's presence. Shipman had not been summoned because Mrs Bardsley was showing any sign of having a stroke. On the contrary, she had appeared well enough to be sent home from hospital following treatment for her fall. He was only asked to visit to check on her general welfare. If Shipman is right, Mrs Bardsley suffered a stroke in the short period that elapsed after Mr and Mrs Braddock departed and before Shipman arrived. If that happened, which is theoretically possible, it was a remarkable coincidence of the sort that seemed to occur very frequently in Shipman's professional life. I find it hard to accept that a coincidence of that kind occurred in this case.
Shipman told Mrs Braddock that he had not had time to call an ambulance, yet on Form B he stated that he attended Mrs Bardsley during her last illness for a period of half an hour and that her collapse lasted 10-15 minutes. This is more than enough time in which to call an ambulance. Further, Shipman told Mrs Braddock that he put Mrs Bardsley on her bed and she died before he could telephone for an ambulance, which implies that Mrs Bardsley died within seconds of being placed onto her bed. Shipman has not been consistent in his accounts and it is reasonable to infer that he has lied about this death.
In his generic evidence Dr Grenville has explained that an occlusive stroke of the kind which causes weakness down one side and slurring of speech does not usually cause a sudden death. Usually the patient recovers, although not necessarily completely. If the stroke develops, it does so gradually. The patient deteriorates gradually over a period of two to three days before death. The type of stroke which can cause a sudden death affects the brain stem and does not produce the kind of signs described by Shipman. In any event, as Dr Grenville has explained, it is highly unlikely that a patient would have strokes in two different parts of the brain within so short a time. A far more likely explanation for this very sudden death was that Shipman gave Mrs Bardsley a lethal dose of a strong opiate, probably diamorphine.
The overwhelming likelihood in this case is that Mrs Bardsley was killed by a lethal injection of diamorphine administered by Shipman. Although at the age of 88, it is possible that Mrs Bardsley could have died suddenly either from a stroke or from a heart attack, I am satisfied so as to be sure that her death was not natural.

name: Sydney Hoskins Copeland
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 68 Grosvenor Crescent, Hyde
conclusion:
In my view, notwithstanding the coroner's permission, Shipman was not in a proper position to issue the MCCD because he had not seen Mr Copeland since 24th
November, two months before the death, and then not in connection with any last illness. However, having said that, I remain quite satisfied that Mr Copeland died a natural death. The family was right not to feel any concern about Shipman's involvement, which was limited to attendance at the house after the death.

name: Ethel Dolan
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Dolan died from natural causes, properly described by Shipman on the MCCD as old age. It is clear from the Charnley House daily diary that Mrs Dolan had deteriorated gradually and had been confined to bed for some time before her death. It is reassuring to know that she was seen by Dr Moysey only a day before she died and that he agreed that nothing could be done for her.
There is no evidence that Shipman saw Mrs Dolan in the day or so before her death. There is, therefore, no reason to suspect that he did anything which could have caused or hastened her death.
It would seem that Shipman showed his usual disregard for the need for truth and accuracy when filling out the MCCD and the Form B. He entered the wrong date of death on the MCCD counterfoil and it is extremely unlikely that he last saw Mrs Dolan on 16th
April, as he claimed. It is probable that he made this latter false statement simply in order to avoid the time and trouble involved in referring the death to the coroner. Even had he done so, it is most likely that the coroner would have given authority for Shipman to certify the death in any event, because Dr Moysey had seen Mrs Dolan very recently and Shipman was aware of her general condition. The inaccuracies on the certificates do not give rise to any suspicion that Shipman was involved in the death.

name: Hannah Frith
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 2 Stansfield Road, Hyde
certified_cause: congestive cardiac failure due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
Shipman was not Mrs Frith's doctor and there is no evidence to suggest that he was in any way involved in her death. It may be that Mr and Mrs Frith thought that he might have been the doctor who spoke to Mrs Vivien Frith because that doctor was rather abrupt, as Shipman sometimes was. However, I can think of no reason why Shipman might have been at Mrs Frith's flat that morning. In any event, it seems most unlikely that Shipman would visit a woman who was not a patient of his, kill her and then allow the death to be referred to the coroner. He was busy in his surgery around the time when the death was discovered and when someone who identified himself as a doctor spoke to Mrs Frith.
The certified cause of death, following post-mortem examination, is consistent with Mrs Frith being found in a collapsed state on the floor and is the likely true cause of death.
All the evidence suggests that this was a natural death and I am quite satisfied that it was.

name: Mary Alice Garratt
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
certified_cause: ischaemic heart disease due to coronary atherosclerosis
conclusion:
It is clear from the Charnley House diaries that Mrs Garratt was very unwell in the days before her death. As her medical records have not survived, it is not possible to discover her medical history or the opinions of Shipman and Dr Matin as to the nature of the illness which afflicted her in late April 1979. In any event, it appears that Mrs Garratt's death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
It seems likely that Shipman was puzzled by the last illness, as it was he who referred the death to the coroner with a view to post-mortem examination. Shipman must have known that Mrs Garratt had heart disease, as he had been treating her for it, as appears from the coroner's papers. I have the impression that Shipman must have thought that the heart disease was probably not the cause of death, as he apparently said that he had no idea why Mrs Garratt had died.
The only cause for suspicion in this case arises out of the fact that Shipman saw Mrs Garratt on the day that she died. The time of the visit is unknown. In the coroner's papers, the visit was said to have taken place in the morning, which implies some time before noon. The Charnley House diary implies that it was at some time before 1pm. There remains a possibility that Shipman could have given an injection of opiate which hastened Mrs Garratt's death, although it seems very unlikely that he would have done so and then have referred the case to the coroner.
My conclusion is that Mrs Garratt almost certainly died of natural causes, probably of the cause certified by the coroner, although the post-mortem examination evidence was not conclusive.

name: Marion Elizabeth Higham
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 57 Joel Lane, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
There are some highly suspicious circumstances surrounding this death.
Mrs Higham enjoyed excellent health despite her advancing years. Consideration of her medical records reveals no evidence of any chronic illness which might cause sudden death, or evidence of any factors which would have put her at higher than usual risk of suffering a stroke or heart attack or a sudden death from any other cause. I accept of course that all elderly people are, on account of their age alone, at an increased risk of suffering a heart attack or stroke. However, it seems to me that this death was sudden and wholly unexpected.
In his generic evidence, Dr John Grenville has said that it is quite unacceptable for a doctor to certify that a death was due to 'natural causes'. If the doctor cannot provide a more specific cause, it must be because he does not know the cause and the death should be referred to the coroner with a view to post mortem-examination. It may be thought that 'natural causes' should be an acceptable cause of death for a person of Mrs Higham's age, being analogous to 'old age', which in some circumstances is acceptable. In Mrs Higham's case, old age would not have been acceptable as a cause of death because, although she was 84, Mrs Higham was fit and active shortly before her death.
If Mrs Higham's death was natural, as Shipman claimed, he could not possibly have known why she had died. Even according to the records he made (which I have found were fabricated), there was nothing wrong with her on 9th
July. I have said that I do not think he saw her then. Even if I were wrong about that, she was not suffering from anything which could be subsequently described as a 'last illness'. This death should have been referred to the coroner. That it was not, and that Shipman proposed 'natural causes' as the cause of death, makes me suspect that the death was not natural and that Shipman wished to avoid a post-mortem examination. I acknowledge that I have come across cases where Shipman has clearly not killed the patient yet has avoided referring the death to the coroner. It follows that Shipman's apparent wish to avoid referral in this case is not of itself probative of guilt. It does, however, raise suspicion that he might have killed Mrs Higham.
I have already indicated that I think it likely that Shipman had not seen Mrs Higham on 9th
July, as he claimed on the MCCD and Form B, and as the medical records appear to confirm. Shipman often pretended that he had seen a patient within 14 days of the death when he had not. It may be that he was under the impression that he would not be qualified to sign the MCCD unless he had seen the patient within that time. In fact, the only requirements are that he should have been in medical attendance during the last illness and that he should either have seen the patient alive within 14 days before death or seen the body after death. In the present case, it would appear that Shipman felt the need to say that he had seen Mrs Higham within 14 days either because that was necessary or because he might have to explain to someone what the last illness was. In any event, I think it likely that he had not seen Mrs Higham on 9th
July, and his claim that he had done so was related to his wish to complete the MCCD himself and avoid referral to the coroner. That Shipman's desire to avoid a referral to the coroner led him to fabricate medical records increases my suspicion that he was afraid of the results of a post-mortem examination.
Mrs Higham's position and appearance in death are not typical of what is usually seen where a patient has died suddenly from stroke or heart attack or other common cause of sudden death. In his generic evidence, Dr Grenville explained that such patients are usually found collapsed in circumstances which suggest that they have tried to summon help. On the other hand, the position in which Mrs Higham was found is entirely consistent with her having succumbed to a lethal injection of diamorphine and is typical of the appearance of many of Shipman's victims.
There is no evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Higham on the day of her death. He could have done, in that he had the time and opportunity to do so. There is a small indication that he might have done: unusually, the front door was ajar when Mr Smith arrived.
There is another feature of the evidence which gives rise to some suspicion that Shipman killed Mrs Higham. On Form B, he claimed that he knew the time of the death. He put it at 2.30pm. If this was a natural death which occurred when Mrs Higham was alone, there is no way in which he could have known when she died. He should have stated that the death had occurred some time between the time when she had last been seen (which on enquiry would have been when she left Werneth House) and the time when her body was found, which was at about 3.45pm. I cannot think of any honest reason why Shipman would wish to pretend that he knew the time of death when he did not. I have come across many cases when Shipman has stated a specific time of death in order to distance himself and his visit from the time of death. Suppose, for example, that Shipman had seen Mrs Higham walking home from Werneth House at about 1pm. By that time, he would have been out on his rounds and quite possibly in the area of Joel Lane. Suppose that he visited her soon after that time and killed her. He would not know whether he had been seen arriving at or leaving the house. It would be in his interest to create the impression that Mrs Higham had died some time after he left. I know this is speculation but it is not fanciful and it accords with what I have found to be his practice in many other cases.
Taking these factors together, I have come to the conclusion that Shipman probably did kill Mrs Higham. The evidence falls some way short of that which would make me sure that he had done so. However, I think he probably did.

name: Beatrice Jeffries
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Godley Court, Hyde Nursing Home, Grange Road South, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Jeffries died of natural causes, although the precise cause of her death is not clear. She had suffered from a number of serious medical conditions. She was very frail when she was admitted to Hyde Nursing Home and was not expected to live long. She deteriorated quite quickly. Her death on 4th
December was neither sudden nor unexpected.
It is not clear precisely why Mrs Jeffries was prescribed strong pain-relieving drugs in the last two weeks of her life. It may be that she was in pain or distress. In any event, her daughter does not appear to have had any concerns about her medication.
All the evidence suggests that Shipman last saw Mrs Jeffries on 2nd
December, probably about 36 hours before her death. There is no evidence that he saw her again after that recorded visit and it is highly unlikely that he would have been called out to see her in the very early morning of 4th
December. It is therefore very unlikely that Shipman had the opportunity to give Mrs Jeffries any diamorphine on 4th
December. It is most unlikely that he caused or hastened her death.
I am sure that Mrs Tinning was right not to have been worried or suspicious about the circumstances of her mother's death.

name: Robert Henry Lingard
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 2 Eagle Street, Todmorden
conclusion:
There can be no doubt that Mr Lingard was very ill in the period before his death and his death was expected to follow soon, though not perhaps that day. Shipman visited at some time on the day of the death. We have no evidence of the time that he visited or what, if any, treatment he gave. If Mr Lingard was suffering chest pain, it is possible that Shipman gave him an injection of some kind of sedative or analgesic to ease his pain and distress. As his breathing was poor, even a small amount of any drug that was also a respiratory depressant could have had the effect of hastening Mr Lingard's death. The difficulty is that there is no evidence as to the time of Shipman's visit or as to the nature of any treatment provided.
I regret the evidence is not sufficiently clear for me to say whether Mr Lingard died a natural death or whether his death was hastened by Shipman. I do not doubt that death was imminent. Usually, one would not entertain any suspicion about the actions of a doctor who attended a seriously ill patient on the day of the death. However, Shipman was later to become a serial killer. The contents of Form B, which show that Shipman was present before and immediately after the death, give rise to the suspicion that Shipman might have injected Mr Lingard with a drug supposedly to ease his breathing, but in fact designed to depress his respiration so that he would die.

name: Mary Middleton
title: Mrs
conclusion:
Mrs Middleton's health had deteriorated following the death of her husband in 1978. Although it does not appear that she consulted Shipman very frequently, the records suggest that she was probably at increased risk of sudden death either from a heart attack or a stroke.
The circumstances in which Mrs Middleton was found strongly suggest that she collapsed and died while preparing for bed in the evening of 2nd
May. She was in her nightclothes and had made her bedtime drink. It is possible, but very unlikely, that she was visited by Shipman at that time. He was not on out of hours duty. Her collapse on the kitchen floor is suggestive of a sudden natural death, from either a heart attack or stroke.
The Inquiry has made extensive efforts to ascertain whether there is any evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Middleton on 2nd
May 1991. These enquiries have proved negative. Thus, there is no evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Middleton shortly before her death.
Some of Shipman's entries on the MCCD counterfoil and Form B appear to be inaccurate and probably dishonest. These factors would usually give rise to suspicion that he had something to hide and was seeking to create a plausible explanation for a death which he himself had caused. In particular, there seems to be no evidence to suggest a final illness of four weeks' duration. The date on which Shipman last saw Mrs Middleton alive was more likely to have been 29th
April than 21st
April although the incorrect entries seem more likely to have been the result of carelessness than deceit. I think Shipman's estimate of the time of death was probably reasonable but owes more to common sense inference from the domestic circumstances of the death than any scientific deduction from the body temperature. I do not think Shipman could possibly have been in a position to certify the cause of death with an appropriate degree of certainty. In my view, this death should certainly have been referred to the coroner.
I can understand why Professor Baker regarded the death as highly suspicious. There are flaws on Form B and the medical records do not adequately support the cause of death. However, Professor Baker was not aware of the circumstances in which Mrs Middleton's body was found. Those circumstances, witnessed by her son, persuade me that this was probably a natural death. I cannot say that I am certain that the death was natural. It is possible that Shipman might have visited Mrs Middleton and killed her but this seems extremely unlikely.
My conclusion is that this was very probably a natural death.

name: Marion Platt
title: Mrs
place_of_death: The Sycamores, a residential home for the elderly, Victoria Street, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Platt died as the result of natural causes.
Mrs Platt had not enjoyed good health for some years before her death. She had been disabled by a severe stroke many years before. Then, in her late seventies, she developed bowel cancer. This was already far advanced at the time of diagnosis. The prognosis was poor. It appears that Mrs Platt's condition deteriorated suddenly a few hours before her death. A deputising doctor was called out. The precise nature of the deterioration is not clear, as the doctor's note is rather vague. However, as Dr Grenville has observed, given her underlying condition, her death at that time was not surprising.
There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman had access to Mrs Platt during the period immediately before her death. It appears that he saw her on 22nd
December, probably around the middle of the day when he usually carried out his routine visits. Shipman did not attend during the night at the request of the staff and there is no reason to suspect that he might have been at the home again until after the death.

name: Mary Alice Smith
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her third floor flat at Chartist House
conclusion:
There are some highly suspicious circumstances surrounding this death.
Although I recognise that Mrs Smith was very unwell and suffering from a terminal illness, I am satisfied, from a consideration of all the evidence, that she had not yet reached the terminal phase of her diagnosed illness, lung cancer. In making that assessment, I have given no weight to the recollection of Mrs Woodhouse as to what Mrs Smith was able to do on 17th
May. I rely on the other evidence, including Mrs Smith's presence at the wedding on 12th
May and the recollection of Mrs Unsworth. Death from lung cancer on 17th
May 1994 was therefore unlikely, although not impossible. Although a sudden death from another cause cannot be ruled out, I think it is unlikely that Mrs Smith died of bronchopneumonia or a heart attack. Death from bronchopneumonia is usually preceded by at least several hours of obvious illness, which does not seem to have occurred in this case. Death by heart attack does not usually leave the victim sitting peacefully in a chair. I conclude therefore that this death at this time is not adequately explained.
When did Mrs Smith die? She was found on the morning of Wednesday, 18th
May but no one had tried to contact her after her brother had left at about 5pm the previous afternoon. Mrs Smith could have died at any time after 5pm on 17th
May. As she was found in the living room and was still wearing the same day clothes as she had worn throughout the Tuesday, it seems likely that she died (or at least deteriorated to the point where she could no longer move) before bedtime on the Tuesday.
We know that Shipman claims to have visited on the Tuesday and I have concluded that he probably did. Mrs Woodhouse says that he came on the Monday but not on the Tuesday. I have already said that I think she is mistaken. She may have confused the days, although she is now convinced that she has not. I think that Shipman would know that, when visiting a patient at Chartist House, there was always a real possibility that he would be noticed. I think he would not wish to create obvious disparities between his actions and his records, unless absolutely necessary. As Shipman had not planned to visit Mrs Smith that day, I think it likely that he called in on her while visiting Mr Ronnie Devenport. I think it likely that he visited in the middle of the day and talked to Mrs Smith about admission to a hospice. I am satisfied that there must have been some discussion about this with Mrs Smith, as otherwise Mrs Woodhouse would not have been aware of the proposal. I think Shipman might have promised to call back later in the day to tell Mrs Smith when she was to be collected. On the other hand, there might have been no discussion about that. It is possible that the discussion about a hospice might have been in more general terms than Mrs Woodhouse now recalls. It is quite likely that in the course of the conversation Shipman would have learned what the current arrangements were for Mrs Smith's care. He would then have known that she was managing on her own at night but usually had company during the day. It may well be that by this time Shipman was planning to kill Mrs Smith and wished to plant in the minds of her family the realisation that she had not long to live. Discussion about a hospice would have that effect. At some stage during that day, Shipman obtained a very large quantity of diamorphine in Mrs Smith's name. She did not need it and I am quite sure that he used her illness as a pretext for obtaining a large amount for his own purposes. However, later in the day he would certainly have been in a position to use some of it on her. Although there is no positive evidence of this, I think it quite likely that, after obtaining his supplies, he returned to Mrs Smith's flat in the early evening and gave her a lethal injection. In case he had been seen, which would always be possible in Chartist House, he made an entry in the records to suggest that Mrs Smith was deteriorating rapidly. This would enable him to demonstrate that her death was not as sudden as it might appear to others. This reconstruction fits all the known circumstances.
This account also fits in with the false claim Shipman made on Form B that he was able to estimate the time of death from the body temperature. He would wish to create the impression that the death had occurred some considerable time after his second visit.
I am suspicious about Shipman's second handwritten note made on 17th
May. If that were a genuine note, it would be most surprising that Shipman did not make any arrangements for Mrs Smith's care. I suspect that this note was not genuine but was designed to explain the otherwise unexpected death, which he knew would soon be discovered.
There are enough suspicious factors in this case to draw me to the conclusion that Shipman killed Mrs Smith. The evidence is not sufficiently clear for me to say that I am sure of this conclusion. However, I think it much more likely that he killed her than that she died of natural causes. I also suspect that Shipman might have taken Mrs Smith's pearls and some money from her purse but the evidence is not sufficiently clear for me to reach any firm conclusion on that issue.

name: Margaret Anne Waldron
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 2 Woodend Lane, Gee Cross, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis caused by ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
There are a number of suspicious features surrounding this death.
The death was extremely sudden. Mrs Waldron had had back pain and sciatica in the days before her death, but there was no sign of any systemic illness. Although high cholesterol levels indicate some risk of developing ischaemic heart disease, there is no evidence whatever that Mrs Waldron had ever shown any signs or symptoms of that condition. Although it is possible that she suffered a sudden and wholly unexpected coronary thrombosis resulting in sudden death, such events are comparatively rare. Most heart attacks are presaged by some warning signs or symptoms and most people survive their first heart attack. Although Mrs Waldron could have died of a heart attack that day, her death from that cause was not at all likely. Nor is there any evidence that she was at risk of dying from any of the other common causes of sudden death. In particular, her blood pressure was normal. Although Dr Grenville says that the position in which Mrs Waldron was found was consistent with a natural death, he has also said that it is not positively inconsistent with death from lethal diamorphine injection. I conclude that, although a natural death was possible, it was unlikely.
Although there is no direct evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Waldron that day, there is some evidence from which it could be inferred that he might have done. First, there is the suggestion that Mrs Waldron seems to have been disturbed while doing her manicure. It would seem that she had been sitting in the lounge area, on one of the settees. Something appears to have occurred to cause her to go into the dining area and to close the curtain. A visit from the doctor is a likely explanation.
Shipman certainly had sufficient time to visit Mrs Waldron that afternoon. The family was anxious to impress upon me that Shipman appeared at the house extremely quickly after he was summoned and that there was no sign of his car in the street outside. Parking is very limited. They suspect that he had visited Mrs Waldron, killed her and left the house, remaining in the area until the body was found, when he could return and handle the formalities. I do not think that is likely. It is entirely feasible that Shipman could have arrived within ten minutes of being summoned even if he had returned to the surgery. He would be unlikely to remain in the area, if he knew Mrs Waldron was dead, as he would have no idea when the body would be found and he would have to be at Market Street by 4pm for afternoon surgery.
The false entries on the MCCD and cremation certificates give rise to real suspicion, as do the lies told by Shipman about Mrs Waldron's pre-existing heart disease and the supposed ECG trace. Shipman was seeking to present a plausible explanation for the death, when none was available. His suggestion in the medical records and on Form B, that Mrs Waldron was still alive when found by Mr Wardley and when the paramedics arrived, is highly suspicious. In my view, these statements are very unlikely to be based on a misunderstanding and are much more likely to be deliberately misleading. I think Shipman was trying to suggest to medical colleagues that Mrs Waldron had not been alone when she died and that responsible paramedics had given a description of the event, which had enabled him to give a reliable diagnosis of the cause of death.
Although there is no direct evidence of Shipman's presence at Mrs Waldron's house at the relevant time, the suspicious circumstances outlined above are such that I am satisfied that Shipman killed Mrs Waldron. The evidence falls short of that which would make me sure of my conclusion but I think it probable that Shipman killed her, probably by injecting her with diamorphine.

name: Clara Ethel Aveyard
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
Mrs Aveyard had difficulty in breathing on 10th
April. On 11th
April, Shipman diagnosed
'bronchial pneumonia'
. Mrs Aveyard could not eat that day and took only fluids. She was put to bed at lunchtime. Her relatives were informed of her condition. It was the practice of the staff to inform relatives if a resident's condition gave cause for serious concern. Mrs Aveyard's death on 12th
April could not be regarded as sudden or unexpected.
There is no positive evidence that Shipman saw Mrs Aveyard alive on the morning of 12th
April. Such evidence as there is suggests that he did not, but that evidence is far from conclusive. Whenever it is possible that Shipman had access to a patient shortly before the death, I feel bound to consider whether he might have been involved in the death.
In this case, there is some cause for suspicion because we know that Shipman was at Charnley House during the morning of 12th
April 1980 and it is possible that he arrived before Mrs Aveyard died. Mrs Lanceley does not specifically recall the events surrounding Mrs Aveyard's death and has sought to assist the Inquiry by drawing inferences from the daily diaries. Although she is of the view that Shipman could not have attended before Mrs Aveyard died and so could not have been in a position to kill her, I cannot dismiss the possibility that he did so.
So long as that remains a possibility, the Inquiry cannot be sure that Shipman played no part in the death. It is likely, however, that Mrs Aveyard died of natural causes and not as the result of an unlawful act on Shipman's part.

name: Geoffrey Bogle
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 12 Lord Derby Road, Hyde
conclusion:
Mr Bogle was at high risk of suffering a heart attack and sudden death. The fact that he was reasonably well on the day of his death does not mean that he could not have suffered a sudden cardiac death. He was in reasonable spirits when Mrs Aldred left him at about 1.30pm. He died either during or very shortly after Shipman's visit. No one saw him alive or spoke to him after Shipman's visit. Shipman had the opportunity to kill Mr Bogle. That the death should have been discovered so soon after the visit is a highly suspicious factor.
Shipman's note of the home visit indicates that, at that time, Mr Bogle's heart gave no cause for concern. There was no complaint of chest pain and there were no other signs of a pending coronary thrombosis. Shipman often made such entries when he had in fact killed his patient and left the premises. When the body was found, he would say that the patient had been well when he left but must have had a heart attack or stroke since then.
Mr Bogle's appearance in death was entirely consistent with a death from an overdose of diamorphine and was not typical of a death caused by coronary thrombosis.
Shipman attributed Mr Bogle's death to myocardial infarction, without having the benefit of any account of the events that had led to the death. In Dr Grenville's view, Shipman should at least have reported this death to the coroner with a view to asking the coroner to allow him to sign the MCCD, based on his supposition as to the cause of death. The coroner might then have directed a post-mortem examination. In this case, as in many, it appears that Shipman wished to avoid any form of referral to the coroner.
Taken together, these points satisfy me that Shipman killed Mr Bogle by giving a lethal injection of diamorphine. There is a theoretical possibility that Mr Bogle had a sudden fatal heart attack very shortly after Shipman's departure, but I regard that as so unlikely that I feel able to say that I am sure of my conclusion that Shipman killed him.

name: Alice Carrington
title: Mrs
certified_cause: congestive heart failure due to hypertension
conclusion: In any event, I am quite satisfied that there is no cause for concern. Mr Carrington has stated categorically that for several days prior to her death, his wife had not been seen by Shipman. I am quite sure that she died from natural causes.

name: Alice Drinkwater
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Norbury House, a residential home for the elderly, Great Norbury Street, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Drinkwater died as the result of natural causes.
Mrs Drinkwater was plainly very unwell in the weeks before her death and her condition was deteriorating. It seems to have been recognised that she had not long to live and Mrs Pugh was summoned to the home. It does not appear that the death was either sudden or unexpected.
Although she was not Shipman's patient, he saw Mrs Drinkwater on 3rd
July 1992. There is no evidence that Shipman saw her alive again. Mrs Pugh was present at the home at the time of the death and did not see Shipman or any other doctor. It was not Shipman who attended the home to certify the fact of Mrs Drinkwater's death. Thus, it is extremely improbable that Shipman was in Norbury House on the day of the death.
It is unclear how Shipman came to certify the cause of Mrs Drinkwater's death, although it may well be that her registered general practitioner, Dr Smith, was not available to do so, perhaps because he was on holiday. Since Shipman had recently seen Mrs Drinkwater during her last illness, there was no reason why he could not legitimately certify the cause of death, although he unfortunately displayed his habitual disregard for the need for accuracy in completing the cremation forms when he said that he was her ordinary medical attendant.

name: John France
title: Mr
place_of_death: Hyde Nursing Home, Grange Road South, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mr France died of natural causes as certified by Shipman.
Mr France was clearly very unwell and there is independent evidence in a letter from Mr Cooper Wilson that his life expectancy was very limited.
It was on Mr Cooper Wilson's suggestion that Shipman prescribed Oramorph, an opiate analgesic, to Mr France in the days before he died. The letter from Mr Cooper Wilson highlighted the need for
'narcotic pain relief'
and in my view it was appropriate for Shipman to prescribe Oramorph. It appears likely that the nursing staff administered the drug, so there was no need for Shipman to attend regularly.
There is no evidence that Shipman had access to Mr France in the hours before his death. Mrs Morris' impression that someone had told her that Shipman visited her father the day before the death was probably a misunderstanding. I think it likely that a member of staff told her that Shipman had visited and had prescribed morphine; then during the night before his death, Mr France had suffered back pain and morphine had been given. The evidence suggests that the last time Shipman saw Mr France was at least two or probably three days before he died. There is no reason to suspect that Shipman gained access to Mr France and killed him on the morning of 25th
August.

name: Donald Anthony Grundy
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 17 Spring Avenue, Hyde
certified_cause: circulatory failure due to hypertension due to chronic obstructive airways disease
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mr Grundy died a natural death. He was clearly very ill and his death was expected. On 7th
September, Shipman gave an injection which was probably some form of opiate. However, it was plainly not a lethal dose as Mr Grundy lived for well over 12 hours afterwards. It is clear that this injection was given for a proper therapeutic reason, the relief of pain and distress. It appears to have had a wholly beneficial effect and enhanced the quality of the last few hours of Mr Grundy's life.
Professor Henry McQuay and Dr John Grenville have given joint generic evidence to the Inquiry as to the timing of the effect of opiates. If a lethal injection of opiate is administered intravenously, death can be expected to follow within minutes. Even if administered intramuscularly, a lethal injection of opiate will cause death within about an hour. Mr Grundy remained conscious for some hours after the injection was administered. The possibility that this injection in any way hastened Mr Grundy's death can be discounted.

name: Sarah Ann Hill
title: Mrs
place_of_death: the home of her daughter, Mrs Joan Rooney
conclusion:
It is clear to me that this must have been a natural death.
It is established that Shipman visited Mrs Hill on the day of her death. He left at about 2.30pm. Mrs Hill's condition between that time and her death about four hours later is quite inconsistent with Shipman having given her an injection of diamorphine. In his evidence to the Inquiry, Professor Henry McQuay said that 30mg diamorphine would be likely to prove fatal within about five minutes if given intravenously over a period of one minute to a fit adult, not previously exposed to strong opioid drugs. A dose of about 20mg could well prove fatal within a similarly short time in the elderly, unfit and opioid naïve people. He also told the Inquiry that any dose of diamorphine over 5mg would make the victim aware that something had happened to them. They would feel strange and drowsy and, if they tried to move about, would probably feel nauseated and would vomit. In Professor McQuay's opinion, those who saw such a person would be aware that something was wrong. If Shipman had administered a lethal dose of morphine or diamorphine intramuscularly to Mrs Hill, the actual effects of the drug would have been the same. Although in the immediate post-injection period an onlooker might not observe anything strange, within about 15 minutes, and certainly within 30 minutes, it would be clear that something was seriously wrong. The opiate would reach maximal effect within an hour and death would occur within that period. Mrs Hill's demeanour after Shipman's visit excludes the possibility that Shipman administered a lethal dose of opiate. Dr Grenville cannot think of any other drug which could have been administered in the early afternoon, have allowed Mrs Hill to speak to her son-in-law and daughter as she did and then have caused death at about 6pm to 6.30pm.
Due to the paucity of information provided by the post-mortem report, there remains some uncertainty over the true cause of death. There is no evidence, however, that the death was due to unlawful activity on the part of Shipman. I can well understand why Mr and Mrs Rooney were concerned about Mrs Hill's death when they heard of Shipman's convictions for killing 15 female patients. I hope that the evidence given at the brief hearing and the contents of this decision will serve to put their minds at rest. I am sure that Shipman did not kill Mrs Hill.

name: Ivy Jones
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Tameside General Hospital, Ashton-under-Lyne
conclusion:
Mrs Jones did not enjoy good health and her medical history combined with the evidence from the post-mortem examination suggests that she was vulnerable to a sudden cardiac death. There is only limited information about Mrs Jones' condition in the period immediately before her death. However, the possibility that Shipman deliberately killed Mrs Jones can be ruled out. First, Mrs Jones was still conscious for over two hours after Shipman had departed. If he had given her an overdose of opiate, she would have been unconscious within a short time. In fact, she was conscious while in the care of the paramedics and even until her arrival at hospital. Second, it would be quite atypical of Shipman to call an ambulance and despatch a patient to hospital if he had given a lethal drug. It would be more usual of him to keep the patient at home, wait until the death occurred and sign the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death.
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Jones died as the result of natural causes.

name: Florence Leach
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
certified_cause: left ventricular failure due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
It seems to me clear that Mrs Leach died of natural causes but what the cause was is not known.
Mrs Leach's health deteriorated in the days before her death. The deterioration seems to have been related to the development of a swelling in the neck and the production of blood either from the lungs or throat. The nature of the swelling was not understood by the treating doctor and it would appear that Mrs Leach continued to deteriorate despite the administration of antibiotics, first taken orally and then, when Mrs Leach could no longer swallow, by injection. Her death on 30th
May was neither sudden nor unexpected. However, in the light of the recent history, it is not surprising that Shipman would wish to discover the nature of the unidentified pathology.
It may be that the pathologist who carried out the post-mortem examination was unaware of the recent history of Mrs Leach's deterioration or her treatment. He did not note any abnormal findings in the region of the neck. It is not clear how detailed an examination he made. He found a sufficient degree of atheroma in the cardiac vessels to explain the death. Many people have similar degrees of change but do not die of them. The pathologist did not find, or did not note, any signs which would suggest that the death had in fact been due to those atheromatous changes. His conclusion that death was due to left ventricular failure related to ischaemic heart disease might or might not have been correct.
Whatever the cause of death, there is no evidence to suggest that Shipman caused or hastened it. The mere fact that Shipman referred the death to the coroner would indicate that he had nothing to hide. The evidence suggests that he had not seen Mrs Leach for several days before her death. There is no positive evidence to suggest that he was at the home immediately before the death. It is possible that he was and that he remained on the premises until the death had occurred.
Taking the evidence as a whole, it seems highly likely that Mrs Leach died a natural death. I cannot rule out the possibility that Shipman was involved but it is very unlikely.

name: Mary Ann Mansfield
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, The Hare and Hounds Hotel, Werneth Low Road, Hyde
certified_cause: respiratory failure due to chronic bronchitis
conclusion:
Mrs Mansfield was clearly unwell the evening before she died. From the description given by Mrs Oldham, it sounds as though she was suffering from congestive heart failure. It appears that Dr Smith thought she was in need of a diuretic. It would appear that Mrs Mansfield might not have been taking the tablets which Shipman had prescribed and might have been taking an antibiotic given to her by a friend. It is entirely possible that Mrs Mansfield's health deteriorated and that she died a natural death during the evening of 23rd
June.
There are, however, other possibilities. The events of 23rd
June are something of a mystery. Mrs Oldham says that Shipman prescribed tablets for her mother without seeing her, which seems strange and inappropriate, particularly as Mrs Mansfield was reported to be rather more unwell than usual. Yet Shipman's visits book suggests that he did visit Mrs Mansfield, or at least intended to. On the MCCD counterfoil, he claimed that he had visited her that day. It is possible that Shipman visited Mrs Mansfield while neither Mrs Oldham nor her sister Mrs Nuttall was present. Mr Mansfield was alone with his wife between about 3pm and 7pm. Mrs Nuttall arrived at about 7pm. Even if Shipman did visit that afternoon or early evening, I am satisfied that he cannot have given Mrs Mansfield a lethal injection of opiate. If he visited that day, it must have been before 7pm. If he had given a lethal injection, Mrs Mansfield would not have lived until 8.30pm. A lethal injection of opiate can thus be ruled out.
There is a further possibility, which is that Shipman prescribed an inappropriate drug in the morning or gave inappropriate medication in the afternoon when he visited, if he did. I have come across one or two cases where I have suspected that Shipman gave either an opiate or some other form of sedative to a patient whose respiratory function was already severely compromised. Such a drug would cause further depression of respiratory function and might well hasten death. Only a small dose of such a drug would be needed to produce that effect. There are occasions when a doctor might properly give such a drug to a patient who is in pain or distress, but the consequences of so doing should usually be discussed with relatives first.
It will never be possible to discover what drugs Mrs Mansfield was given on the day of her death. If follows that I am unable to reach a positive conclusion about the cause of her death.

name: Ada Marjorie Preston
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 183 Grange Road South, Hyde
certified_cause: cardiac failure due to ischaemic heart disease and mitral stenosis
conclusion:
It appears from the evidence that Mrs Preston was suffering from a terminal illness, although its precise nature cannot be ascertained in the absence of the medical records. Bearing in mind Mrs Preston's lifelong history of cardiac problems, it seems highly likely that she was suffering from heart failure.
There is no evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Preston within a few hours before her death. There is conflicting evidence as to whether he visited on the evening before the death. Mr Preston says he did. The visits book suggests that he did not and that he had not seen Mrs Preston since 5th
October. However, Shipman's visits book cannot be assumed to be a complete record. The entry on the MCCD counterfoil tends to corroborate the visits book, but the visits book could be the source of inaccurate information provided on the MCCD counterfoil. On the other hand, I cannot be sure that Mr Preston's recollection is right. After so long, it would not be surprising if he were mistaken. I cannot make any definite finding as to whether Shipman visited on the evening before the death.
If Shipman did visit Mrs Preston on the evening before her death and if he gave Mrs Preston an injection, as Mr Preston recalls, that injection cannot have been of a lethal dose of opiate and cannot have killed Mrs Preston. Mrs Preston did not die until about 9.30am the next day, about 12 hours after the visit, if it took place. Dr John Grenville and Professor Henry McQuay have given evidence to the Inquiry about the timing and effect of large doses of opiate. If a lethal dose of opiate is given intravenously, it will cause death within a few minutes. If given intramuscularly, a lethal dose will cause death within about an hour. If a patient is alive for 12 hours after a suspected injection of opiate or sedative, it can confidently be stated that that injection has not directly caused the death.
If Shipman did visit Mrs Preston during the last two days of her life and if he did give her injections, as Mr Preston recalls, it is quite likely that these were of a diuretic, which could be expected to relieve Mrs Preston's symptoms. It is also possible that Shipman might have given a small dose of opiate to settle Mrs Preston if she was in distress. This would be an appropriate and perfectly proper thing to do and would not have caused or hastened Mrs Preston's death.
I am quite sure that Mrs Preston died a natural death and hope that this decision will put Mr Preston's mind at rest.

name: Ernest Colin Ralphs
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 25 Baron Road, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
In my view, there is no reason to suspect that Mr Ralphs' death was unnatural. There is clear evidence that the death occurred in the middle of the night and there is no evidence that Shipman had had recent access to Mr Ralphs. It appears that Mr Ralphs must have collapsed when he got out of bed in the night. He had been quite ill for some time and his death from cardiac causes cannot have been unexpected.
Postscript
On 20th
May 1993, a prescription for Ernest Ralphs, signed by Shipman, was presented at the Co-op Pharmacy in Market Street, Hyde. It was for a single 30mg ampoule of diamorphine. There is no record that this was ever administered to Mr Ralphs. At the time, he was an inpatient at Tameside General Hospital, having recently suffered a severe heart attack. I have no doubt whatever that Shipman obtained this ampoule of diamorphine for his own purposes, using Mr Ralphs' name.

name: Jane Elizabeth Shelmerdine
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 9 Napier Street, Gee Cross, Hyde
certified_cause: left ventricular failure due to congestive heart failure
conclusion:
There are a number of suspicious features surrounding this death.
The first and most obvious is that the death occurred either during or very shortly after a visit by Shipman. On the morning of her death, Mrs Shelmerdine was well enough to do some washing and make and eat a good lunch. She was speaking to her daughter when Shipman arrived. No one saw Mrs Shelmerdine alive or spoke to her after Shipman's visit. From that fact alone, a grave suspicion arises that Shipman killed her during his first visit.
Shipman's diagnosis of left ventricular failure due to congestive heart disease is very much open to question. Dr John Grenville has observed that Shipman was in the habit of diagnosing congestive heart failure even when there was very little by way of signs or symptoms. Dr Grenville has sometimes felt that the diagnosis could not be justified. In this case, there are multiple entries in the records, but no account of the signs or symptoms on which the diagnosis was based. If the medication prescribed is an indication of the severity of the condition, it must be concluded that the congestive heart failure was not severe. If Mrs Shelmerdine was developing increasingly severe congestive heart disease, one would have expected the doctor in Nottingham to have diagnosed it. He did not. There are other good reasons to doubt Shipman's diagnosis of left ventricular failure. First, if Mrs Shelmerdine had had that condition, she would not have been able to do the washing, hang it out, make her lunch and eat it. Miss Shelmerdine would have realised that her mother was ill if she had been suffering from that condition. Finally, she would not have been found sitting peacefully as though asleep. Dr Grenville says that death from left ventricular failure is a distressing process. The patient almost always has lung secretions round the mouth. Mrs Shelmerdine's appearance in death was inconsistent with a death due to left ventricular failure but was entirely typical of that of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection, almost certainly of diamorphine.
Shipman's claim that Mrs Shelmerdine rejected his advice that she should be admitted to hospital is not plausible. Shipman has frequently claimed that patients with life-threatening conditions have refused admission to hospital. Although there is no doubt that some elderly people do refuse admission, Mrs Shelmerdine's family does not believe she would have done. In any event, it seems highly unlikely that she would have refused without discussing the issue with either her son or daughter, both of whom were close to her. I regard this as a very suspicious feature.
On the MCCD, Shipman said that the interval between the onset of left ventricular failure and death was more than 12 hours. That is quite inconsistent with the evidence of what Mrs Shelmerdine was able to do on the morning of her death. In my view, it is almost certainly a lie, told by Shipman in an attempt to give a plausible account of a death from heart failure.
Taking these factors into account, I have been convinced that Shipman must have killed Mrs Shelmerdine. I am satisfied so as to be sure of this.

name: Mary Ann Tempest
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 16 Major Street, Todmorden
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
Although very little is known of the nature of Mrs Tempest's last illness, it is clear that she was very ill and required nursing care. Her death appears to have been expected.
There is no reason to suspect that Shipman visited Mrs Tempest on the day of her death or to doubt that he last saw her on 29th
August 1975, as recorded on Form B. From the fact that Shipman did not see Mrs Tempest (who seems to have been his patient) for three days before her death and did not examine her body for a further three days after the death, it would appear likely that Shipman had taken a week's holiday and that Dr Grieve was covering his patients in his absence.
In those circumstances, I am quite sure that Mrs Tempest's death was due to natural causes.

name: Vera Whittingslow
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 110 Dowson Road, Hyde
conclusion:
There are several highly suspicious factors in the circumstances surrounding this death.
Mrs Whittingslow was clearly unwell at the time of her death and, in particular, suffered from high blood pressure. However, the hypertension was well controlled by medication and during the days before she died, Mrs Whittingslow appeared well. She died during a visit from Shipman. This is a highly suspicious factor in itself. Other doctors say that this is a very rare occurrence in their experience. Many of Shipman's patients died in his presence. Where that has happened, it is necessary to examine his conduct with extreme care and scepticism.
It is possible that Mrs Whittingslow's blood pressure was raised to the extent recorded by Shipman in the Lloyd George notes and, if so, it may have been reasonable for Shipman to ask Mr Whittingslow to collect the medication required to reduce her blood pressure. However, taking the circumstances of this case as a whole, it is far more likely that Shipman fabricated the blood pressure reading and sent Mr Whittingslow to the chemist in order to be left alone with Mrs Whittingslow and also to create the impression that a medical emergency existed. While Mr Whittingslow was away, Shipman had an opportunity to administer an injection of diamorphine.
When Mr Whittingslow returned from the chemist, Shipman said that he had taken a blood sample for the purposes of analysing the cause of the high blood pressure. Such tests exist and it is possible that Shipman took a blood sample. However, it is more likely that Shipman did not take a sample but said that he had done so to provide an explanation for the mark on Mrs Whittingslow's hand where he had injected her. I have come across other cases where Shipman has explained a mark in this way.
When Mr Whittingslow said to Shipman that he thought his wife had died, Shipman placed two fingers on her neck and said that she was dying. If it is possible to tell that a patient is dying by feeling a pulse (which is doubtful), any doctor who believed that to be the situation should not walk away and do nothing. He should consider whether the patient should be taken to hospital as an emergency. I accept that there are circumstances in which such action is not in the patient's best interest but such a decision should not be taken without discussion if a relative is present. When Shipman returned to the bedroom, he did not carry out a full external examination, as he was later to claim. He only felt for a pulse in the neck. Dr Grenville states that it is not possible to diagnose death in such a way. The suspicion arises that Shipman already knew Mrs Whittingslow was dead because he had killed her.
I have said that I think Shipman made a false entry in the medical records when he said that Mrs Whittingslow had had multiple cerebrovascular accidents during the last few days. In my view, this false entry was designed to make her condition appear more parlous than it was. This entry would have allayed any concerns expressed by the doctor signing Form C or by the medical referee.
Shipman's account of events is wholly implausible. It would have been the most extraordinary coincidence if Mrs Whittingslow, having been her normal self on the day of her death, suddenly presented with extremely high blood pressure as soon as Shipman arrived, settled down and had a cup of tea whilst her husband went to pick up a prescription, then lapsed into a coma, seconds before her husband returned from the chemist, and died half an hour later. That implausibility, and the other factors to which I have referred, have driven me to the sure conclusion that Shipman killed Mrs Whittingslow by injecting her with a strong opiate, almost certainly diamorphine, of which he was known to have illicit supplies.

name: Sarah Adkinson
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 16 Strines Court, Hyde
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to carcinoma of the stomach
conclusion:
I am satisfied that Mrs Adkinson died of natural causes, almost certainly as certified by Shipman.
Although the medical records are not available, the history described by Mrs Ottridge is entirely consistent with the onset of cancer of the stomach, which later spread to other organs and led quite quickly to death. The visits book suggests that Shipman saw Mrs Adkinson three times in the week before her death. We do not know what treatment she was receiving from him, but it is likely that she was receiving some medication for pain relief. However, as Shipman was not apparently visiting daily and as Mrs Adkinson was not confined to bed, it seems unlikely that she was receiving regular injections of a strong opiate.
Although her name does not appear in his visits book for 1st
August, from the witness evidence it seems likely that Shipman visited Mrs Adkinson that morning. We do not know at what time he visited, except that it was before Mrs Porter arrived. He might have been called out by the neighbour who spoke to Mrs Porter, possibly because Mrs Adkinson was in severe pain. He might well have given her an additional dose of pain-relieving medication. This might have been morphine or diamorphine. It is quite possible that he did this, even though Mrs Adkinson did not mention it to her nieces. However, the important feature of the evidence is that Shipman did not see Mrs Adkinson for at least ten hours before the death and probably rather more. I say that because it appears that Shipman visited on the morning of 1st
August (which I take to be before noon) and Mrs Adkinson was still alive when her nieces went to sleep, which I take to be at about 10pm. That being so, I can say with confidence that any injection which Shipman might have given Mrs Adkinson on the morning of 1st
August cannot have directly caused her death. The fact that she was conscious after his departure and made no mention of any injection, makes me sure that she was not given any injection that might even have contributed to her death.

name: Vera Brocklehurst
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 1 Queensway, Dukinfield
certified_cause: congestive heart failure due to hypertension
conclusion:
There are a number of highly suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. The first and most obvious is that the death was discovered not long after Shipman had visited Mrs Brocklehurst. He had been alone with her. There is no evidence that anyone had seen her alive or spoken to her after his visit. That factor arouses a high degree of suspicion, which is further heightened by Shipman's entry on Form B of the cremation certificate, where he sought to create the impression that someone had seen and spoken to Mrs Brocklehurst after his departure. I am satisfied that that entry was false and was fabricated in an attempt to demonstrate that he could not have killed Mrs Brocklehurst.
Mrs Brocklehurst's death was sudden and wholly unexpected. The picture painted by all the witnesses is that she was well in the weeks before her death and, in particular, was well on the day of her death while awaiting Shipman's routine visit. The medical records show that she suffered from high blood pressure, which would put her at some increased risk of stroke and heart attack. She might also have had angina, although the evidence of this is not clear. The
'odd chest pain'
,
recorded by Shipman on 31st March, might well have been a fabrication. If she had angina, she would have been at an increased risk of heart attack. The evidence that she suffered from congestive heart failure is unconvincing and must be treated with some suspicion, as the recorded signs are by no means diagnostic of that condition. In any event, it does not appear to me that the medical history as recorded would lead to any expectation that Mrs Brocklehurst might die suddenly.
There could certainly be no expectation that she might die of congestive heart failure. As Dr Grenville has explained in his generic evidence, congestive heart failure is a chronic condition although it can also present as an acute episode, in which case it is usually referred to as left ventricular failure. In the MCCD, Shipman implies that Mrs Brocklehurst died of the chronic condition. That is possible but the signs and symptoms must be much worse than were apparent in this case before the patient will die. Further, a patient dying in an acute episode experiences a very frightening and unpleasant death in which he or she is gasping for breath. Usually lung secretions are found around the mouth.
