Mrs Brocklehurst's peaceful appearance in death is quite inconsistent with such a death. I conclude that it is very unlikely that Mrs Brocklehurst died from congestive heart failure. Mrs Brocklehurst's peaceful appearance in death was entirely typical of the appearance of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by the intravenous administration of a lethal dose of diamorphine.
Shipman claimed that Mrs Brocklehurst had died at 6pm. In my view, that claim is plainly spurious. Shipman could have had no genuine basis for making that estimate. As Dr Grenville has explained, it would not have been possible for him to make a sensible estimate of the time of her death. Shipman often claimed that he could estimate the time of death accurately and then proceeded to give a time of death which would have the effect of distancing him from the death. I am sure that is what he has sought to do in this case.
This was a sudden and unexpected death. There was nothing in the medical records which could have enabled an honest doctor to certify the cause of death. The case should have been referred to the coroner with a view to post-mortem examination. In cases where Shipman had killed a patient, he usually avoided such a referral.
The close temporal association between Shipman's visit and the death leads me to the conclusion that he probably killed Mrs Brocklehurst. The other considerations I have mentioned, which all point to the same conclusion, make me sure that that is what happened. I note that Shipman took blood during the final visit. That would have given him the opportunity to introduce a needle into one of Mrs Brocklehurst's veins. I have no doubt that he then used a needle to inject her with diamorphine.

name: James Clough
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 3 Lanegate, Hyde
certified_cause: carcinomatosis with adenocarcinoma of the colon as a contributory condition
conclusion:
Although at one stage the police were under the impression that Shipman had given Mr Clough an injection shortly before his death, it seems, on the totality of the evidence, that this was most unlikely. Mrs Janet Clough is adamant that she was present throughout both visits and no medication was given that day. I have spoken to Dr Aneez Esmail, medical advisor to the Inquiry, and he has advised me that it is entirely feasible that Mr Clough's pain could have been adequately controlled by oral methadone, without the need for any additional or stronger opiate. In any event, even if Shipman had given an injection, it cannot have been a lethal dose, as Mr Clough lived for another eight or nine hours after Shipman's 5pm visit. I am quite satisfied that Mr Clough died from natural causes. It appears that Shipman's care was exemplary.
I feel a sense of real regret that a family which has suffered a bereavement and which was wholly satisfied with the treatment and assistance which Shipman gave, should have been troubled by the need for this investigation. The police acted quite properly in seeking to investigate Mr Clough's death, in the light of Professor Baker's suspicion over this death. I can understand why Professor Baker felt some concern over the death. I fear that this train of events was an unfortunate consequence of the need to investigate all deaths where some suspicion had arisen.

name: Fanny Dawson
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 64 Cheetham Fold Road, Hyde
certified_cause: respiratory failure due to chronic bronchitis
conclusion:
In this case there is cause to suspect that Shipman might have hastened Mrs Dawson's death. There can be no doubt that Mrs Dawson was very ill indeed and had not long to live. The recollections of the various family members differ slightly but the evidence suggests that there was some concern that Mrs Dawson was in distress. It seems to have been agreed that Shipman would give her something to ease her distress. Whether that suggestion came first from Shipman or from the family, does not greatly matter. It seems clear that Shipman gave an injection into the thigh and that Mrs Dawson died not long afterwards.
It is quite possible that Mrs Dawson would have died when she did notwithstanding the injection. It is also possible that Shipman injected a drug knowing and intending that it would hasten Mrs Dawson's death. It seems likely that Mrs Dawson died within about an hour of the injection, when an opiate injected intramuscularly would have reached maximal effect. It is also quite possible that he gave an injection intending only to relieve Mrs Dawson's distress. We do not know what drug was given or how much. If the drug were an opiate, very little would be required to kill Mrs Dawson, as her respiratory function was already severely compromised. Any form of sedative would be likely to have the effect of depressing respiratory function further. It is possible that Shipman gave a very small dose of opiate, intending that it would ease Mrs Dawson's distress rather than shorten her life, but recognising that it might also have that latter effect. Such an action would not have been unlawful. A doctor, faced with a patient in distress on account of respiratory failure, faces a dilemma. He or she knows that whatever is given to relieve the distress might have the effect of shortening life.
There are several possibilities. I cannot resolve these, as it will never be possible to discover what drug Shipman gave or how much of it. All I can say is that there is a suspicion in my mind that Shipman might have deliberately given a dose that was certain to hasten Mrs Dawson's end. I am sure that her death was imminent and that, if Shipman did shorten her life, he did not do so by a long period.

name: Winifred Freeman
title: Mrs
place_of_death: The Sycamores, a residential home for the elderly, Welch Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Freeman died as a result of natural causes.
Mrs Freeman suffered from a number of medical complaints. She had angina and had suffered a stroke. The deterioration in her condition shortly before her death is independently confirmed by Dr Matin's letter written after his domiciliary visit five days before the death. He said that Mrs Freeman was in need of nursing care. It is clear that Mrs Freeman's death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
Although Shipman claimed on the MCCD counterfoil that he had last seen Mrs Freeman alive on 12th
March and on Form B that he had last seen her on 13th
March, it appears from the visits book that he last saw her on 10th
March. These discrepancies do not matter, as there is no evidence whatsoever that Shipman saw Mrs Freeman in the period immediately before her death. Although the precise time of death is not clear, it is apparent that she died during the night, at a time when it would be most unlikely that Shipman would have visited her. Her death was confirmed by a deputising doctor. I therefore rule out the possibility that Shipman killed Mrs Freeman by administering a lethal dose of opiates which directly caused her death. I have considered whether it is possible that Shipman over-sedated Mrs Freeman in the days leading to her death and thereby indirectly hastened her death. There is no evidence to suggest that he visited Mrs Freeman in the three days before she died and, given the deterioration in her condition as independently verified by Dr Matin, I think that it is most unlikely that Shipman was involved in hastening her death.

name: Clifford Gess
title: Mr
place_of_death: 15 Rufford Avenue, Hyde, the home of his friend, Mrs Edith Griffiths
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mr Gess died a natural death.
It is clear that he was extremely ill and was known to have a terminal illness. He had become very weak and his breathing had deteriorated. It was apparent to all that his death was imminent.
The recollections of Mr John Griffiths and Mrs Jean Griffiths differ as to the exact course of events on 2nd
August, the day of Mr Gess' death. It is common ground that Shipman visited that day. Mr John Griffiths remembers that Shipman gave Mr Gess an injection at around lunchtime and predicted that he would not live out the day. Mrs Jean Griffiths remembers that Shipman visited in the late afternoon, but before 4pm. I think it is highly likely that Shipman gave some form of opiate, and such medication would be entirely appropriate for the relief of pain, provided that the dose was intended to relieve pain and not to hasten the death. It is clear that the dose was not excessive, as Mr Gess lived for about seven to eight hours after its administration. Dr John Grenville has said that a lethal injection of opiate given intramuscularly will kill within about an hour. A dose which is excessive but not lethal might so depress the respiratory function that it would contribute to the death. However, if the patient lived beyond about four hours after the injection, it can safely be said that the injected drug had not caused or contributed to the death. In any event, as Dr Grenville has explained, it can be very difficult for a doctor to assess the appropriate amount of opiate to give a terminally ill patient. It is quite possible that in giving a dose sufficient to relieve pain, the doctor might unintentionally hasten the death.

name: Jesse Hampson
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 11 Walker Close, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mr Hampson died a natural death from the cause certified by Shipman. The course of events described by Mr Jack Hampson is entirely typical of a developing stroke, which culminated in death. Mr Jack Hampson was with his father throughout his illness and was present when Shipman visited. Shipman's final visit took place at least three hours before the death, possibly more. There can be no cause to suspect that Shipman was wrongfully involved in this death. He appears to have attended only to keep an eye on his patient and to give support to Mr Jack Hampson.
I can understand why Professor Baker regarded this death as moderately suspicious, when he had examined Form B. Shipman there said that he had seen Mr Hampson alive three hours before death. In isolation, this gives rise to a degree of suspicion. The Inquiry has the benefit of a witness statement from Mr Jack Hampson and it is clear that he was present throughout his father's last days and at the moment of his death, as recorded by Shipman on Form B.
Having considered the description of events provided by Mr Jack Hampson, I am entirely satisfied that Mr Hampson died a natural death.

name: Laura Frances Linn
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 5 Acorn Avenue, Gee Cross, Hyde
certified_cause: left ventricular failure due to ischaemic heart disease due to hypertension
conclusion:
There can be no doubt that Mrs Linn was very unwell and at grave risk of suffering a sudden cardiac death. Her death was not unexpected. The little we know about her condition on the morning of the day of her death suggests that she was experiencing breathlessness prior to Shipman's arrival. This is consistent with the onset of an acute episode of left ventricular failure and the fact that Mr George Linn wanted to call an ambulance and actually called the surgery a second or third time at about 10.44am, would suggest that he was very anxious about his wife's condition.
It seems to me, however, to be more than a coincidence that Mrs Linn survived until Shipman arrived but succumbed very shortly after his arrival. During that period, Shipman did not summon an ambulance. Even though it does appear that Mrs Linn did not want an ambulance to be called, I think it more likely that she expressed that wish before Shipman arrived rather than afterwards. I suspect that Shipman did not want to call an ambulance and had decided that the most appropriate course was to end her life as swiftly as possible. It is theoretically possible that he discussed the issue of resuscitation and hospital admission sensitively and appropriately with the Linns. I have difficulty in accepting that he did because I think that any advice he gave was probably distorted by his own perception of what was best for Mrs Linn. By February 1998, Shipman had unlawfully killed a very large number of patients, many in the preceding 12 months. Dr Banks' recollection is that the Lloyd George notes recorded that an injection of frusemide had been administered and I think it likely that he did indeed see that record. I believe, however, that Shipman did not give an injection of frusemide at all. I believe that he gave an injection of morphine or diamorphine and I believe that he did so not primarily to relieve Mrs Linn's pain but in order to hasten her death. If an injection of frusemide were to have been given, it would be surprising if death followed as quickly as it apparently did. If diamorphine were given, death would follow rapidly, as it apparently did. The totality of the evidence from several sources causes me to accept that an injection was given, contrary to what is suggested by the evidence of Mrs Rook.
Mrs Linn would have been a typical Shipman victim in many respects. She was in poor health and it would have been entirely in keeping with his philosophy if Shipman had decided that it was time to let Mrs Linn go.
I have come to the conclusion that it is probable that Shipman injected Mrs Linn with diamorphine, under the pretence of giving frusemide. It is quite possible that Mrs Linn would have died on that day or shortly afterwards in any event. However, I think that Shipman probably decided that she was to die that day and ensured that result by giving her diamorphine.

name: Wilbert Mitchell
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, Pasture Side Farm, Walsden, Todmorden
conclusion:
As Mr Mitchell's medical records have not been recovered, little is known about his state of health except that he suffered from angina. Although he was clearly active until his death, Mr Mitchell must have been at an increased risk of sudden death from heart failure or heart attack. He was also at an increased risk due to his advanced age. However, he was well on the day before his death and seems, on the day of his death, to have been able to get up, dress himself, make and eat breakfast, and eat the lunch left for him. A sudden death was unexpected but not improbable.
It seems unlikely that Mr Mitchell would have called a doctor out that day except in a real emergency. It is possible that he felt very ill, possibly due to chest pain, and telephoned the surgery. As this was Easter Tuesday, one would expect the doctors to be back at work and dealing with their own patients. If so, one would expect that Dr Lewin would have visited her own patient. However, it is possible that some doctors were taking an extra day's holiday and that Shipman was on duty. It is possible that he went out to Mr Mitchell during the afternoon. He seems to have been on duty later that day, although the call after discovery of the death was probably made after normal surgery hours. If Shipman had been to the farm earlier in the day, he seems to have concealed that fact from the family, which would be a cause for suspicion. I think his hostile conversation with Mr Knowles suggests that Shipman had not seen Mr Mitchell that day and had in fact never seen him. What Shipman put on the MCCD, I do not know. It is quite possible that he spoke to Dr Lewin and agreed with her what should be put. He was relatively new to the practice and I think it unlikely that he would have signed the MCCD for one of Dr Lewin's patients without speaking to her about it. However, I cannot absolutely rule out the possibility that he did see Mr Mitchell that afternoon, concealed that fact from the family, and completed the MCCD, indicating when he had seen Mr Mitchell alive.
There is another slightly suspicious feature about the death. Mr Mitchell was found sitting in his chair looking very peaceful. Although he did not appear to be asleep, he did not, according to Mr Knowles' recollection, appear to have been in pain or distress. Dr John Grenville says that patients who die of acute left ventricular failure die a distressing death and are usually found with lung secretions on the face. Of course, Mr Mitchell might have had such secretions and the family has forgotten.
Shipman certified that the cause of Mr Mitchell's death was heart failure. In his first generic report to the Inquiry, Dr Grenville uses the phrases 'ventricular failure' and 'heart failure' interchangeably. According to Dr Grenville, heart failure may be acute or chronic. If the family's recollection is right, it would seem that Mr Mitchell did not have chronic heart failure. Acute left ventricular failure is associated with myocardial infarction. Mr Mitchell suffered from angina, which is a sign of ischaemic heart disease. One can therefore postulate a correlation between the history of angina and the stated cause of death. However, if Dr Lewin had found Mr Mitchell in his usual health the previous Thursday, as the family seems to think she did, I would have thought that this death ought probably to have been referred to the coroner.
There are some slightly puzzling features about this death and I unfortunately find myself in the position where I can reach no positive conclusion about it.

name: Reginald Potts
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 242 Clarendon Road, Hyde
conclusion: The evidence in this case is very limited and the Inquiry has been unable to find any witness who can assist. That Shipman states that he saw Mr Potts alive on the day of his death inevitably raises some suspicion of his involvement. I note that the death certificate states that Mr Potts had carcinomatosis. It is likely that he was very ill for some time before his death. In those circumstances it would not be at all surprising that Shipman should have visited him on the day of his death. It is entirely possible that Shipman's visit was wholly innocent. However, the possibility exists that Shipman visited shortly before Mr Potts' death in circumstances in which he could have had the opportunity to give Mr Potts an injection which hastened his death. Without evidence from a witness with knowledge of the circumstances of the death, it is not possible for me to reach any conclusion as to the cause of death or whether Shipman was improperly involved.

name: Alice Richardson
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 8A Hamel Street, Newton, Hyde
certified_cause: heart failure due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Richardson died of natural causes. She had a chronic heart condition and was acutely unwell in the days leading up to her death. The treatment given by Shipman on the day before death seems to have been appropriate.
There is no evidence of Shipman administering an injection to Mrs Richardson in the hours before her death. Shipman had not seen her for well over 24 hours and he was not alone with her at the last consultation. Death occurred in the presence of at least two members of the family. There is no evidence that Shipman was involved in the death.
I can understand why Professor Baker was suspicious about this death. The medical notes are extremely scanty. However, he did not have the benefit of the witness statements that have enabled me to lay all suspicion to rest.

name: Monica Rene Sparkes
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 15 Rock Gardens, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
There are several highly suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. First and most obvious, Shipman was the last person to see Mrs Sparkes alive. He also discovered her dead body. There was no reply to a telephone call soon after he had spoken to Mrs Holt, at which time he was still at Mrs Sparkes' house. This telephone call was made at a time when, if Shipman is to be believed, Mrs Sparkes had recently lain down on her bed to rest. There is a close temporal association between Shipman's presence at the house and Mrs Sparkes' failure to answer Mrs Cope's telephone call. This suggests that Mrs Sparkes was probably dead when Shipman left the house.
Shipman's claim that Mrs Sparkes died as the result of a stroke seems quite improbable. As Dr Grenville said, she did not suffer from high blood pressure. She had called Shipman out that morning in connection with the latest in a series of falls, which had always, in the past, been attributed to vertigo resulting from her accident. It is therefore extremely unlikely that Mrs Sparkes should have developed a stroke in the interval between telephoning Shipman and his arrival. There is no evidence in the medical records of any examination upon which Shipman could properly have based his diagnosis of stroke.
This case has Shipman's hallmark on it. I have come across many cases in which he has returned to the home of a victim later in the day and has pretended to discover the dead body. It is in other respects typical of cases in which Shipman killed his patient.
My conclusion is that Shipman killed Mrs Sparkes, almost certainly by injecting her with a lethal dose of opiate. Although there is a theoretical possibility that she could have suffered a sudden fatal stroke or heart attack in the short period between Shipman's departure and return, I think this possibility can be safely discounted. It would be too great a coincidence. I am able to say that I am sure that this was an unlawful killing.

name: Sarah Tideswell
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion: I am quite satisfied that Mrs Tideswell died of natural causes. It is clear that she was very unwell in the few weeks before her death. It would appear that she was declining gradually towards death. There is no evidence that Shipman gave her any treatment in the few days before she died or that he saw her alive on the day of the death.

name: Sarah Jane Williamson
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 2 Thorsby Avenue, Hyde
conclusion:
In the absence of medical records it is not possible to discover Mrs Williamson's state of health at the time of her death. She was 82 and overweight so she would certainly have been at risk of suffering a heart attack. However, Shipman was not visiting her regularly and her brother was not aware that she had ever had cardiac problems. It is quite possible that Mrs Williamson had a cardiac episode on the afternoon of Sunday, 15th
October and that this was why the warden called out Shipman.
Suspicion arises that Shipman might have killed Mrs Williamson from examination of his conduct that afternoon. It appears from Form B that Shipman was with Mrs Williamson for about half an hour before her death. That would have been quite long enough for him to have summoned an ambulance and removed Mrs Williamson to hospital, which most doctors would think was the appropriate place for her to be if she were suffering from severe chest pain or having a heart attack. At some stage, Mrs Williamson must have gone into cardiac arrest. Yet Shipman did not attempt any form of resuscitation. For that he would have had to put her onto a hard surface, probably the floor. He did not; he left her in her chair. We do not know whether Shipman gave Mrs Williamson any medication. It might well have been appropriate for him to give a very small dose of an opiate drug, if Mrs Williamson was in severe pain. He certainly had the opportunity to give her any drug he had with him.
In many cases, the fact that the death takes place in Shipman's presence gives rise to a very high degree of suspicion. Dr John Grenville has said that it is extremely rare for a patient to die suddenly during a doctor's visit unless the patient is known to be suffering from a terminal illness or the doctor has been called out as an emergency on account of symptoms indicating a serious episode such as a heart attack or stroke. In this case, there was an emergency request. We do not know what the symptoms were but it is possible they were indicative of a heart attack. The mere fact that this death took place in Shipman's presence does not therefore raise a high degree of suspicion. What does arouse suspicion is that Shipman does not appear to have done what most reasonable doctors would have done in the circumstances. It is possible that Shipman might have made the decision to do nothing and to let nature take whatever course it would. I accept that there are some doctors who would regard that as appropriate. There is also a possibility that he decided to ensure that Mrs Williamson would not recover from her heart attack by giving her an excessive dose of opiate, which he always carried with him.
Mrs Williamson's position and appearance in death were not only inconsistent with any attempt at resuscitation, they were not typical of those usually seen following a death from heart attack. Mrs Williamson looked too comfortable. It is possible that Shipman decided not to do anything to attempt to prolong life, but gave a small dose of opiate to relieve the pain and then settled Mrs Williamson into a comfortable position. That might explain her appearance. However, my suspicion on this score remains, as her position and appearance were entirely typical of those seen in many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of opiate. If Shipman gave an injection of opiate (which I think he must have done to produce Mrs Williamson's peaceful and comfortable appearance), I think it is more likely that he gave a large dose, thereby ensuring death, than a small one, which might leave Mrs Williamson alive. My reason for so saying is that it would be entirely typical of his conduct.
The evidence in this case is far from clear. If, as is quite likely, Mrs Williamson had a heart attack that afternoon, Shipman certainly did not do what most doctors would have done in an attempt to prolong her life. There are real grounds to suspect that he killed her, by ensuring that she would not survive the heart attack. It would be entirely consistent with Shipman's philosophy that Mrs Williamson should not survive a heart attack. He did not believe in 'keeping elderly people going'. By 1989, Shipman had killed a large number of patients, mainly elderly and unwell. He was by this time an habitual killer. For that reason, I think it significantly more likely that he took a positive step to ensure that Mrs Williamson died (and died quickly) than that he merely gave palliative care and waited to see the outcome. My conclusion is that Shipman probably killed Mrs Williamson by giving her a lethal dose of opiate.

name: Rose Ann Adshead
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 2 Lawton Street, Hyde
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to adenocarcinoma of the rectum
conclusion:
The circumstances of the death are clearly established. Mrs Adshead was extremely ill and was suffering a great deal of pain. She cannot have had long to live. Shipman came at the request of the family and it is clear that she needed pain relief. Although no one was present in the bedroom besides Shipman and Mrs Adshead, I infer that he must have given her a strong pain-relieving drug. That is what both she and her family wanted. After Shipman's visit, Mrs Adshead slept until she died an hour later. It is possible that her death was entirely natural and its timing was unaffected by the treatment Shipman had given.
However, it is also possible that Shipman's treatment hastened Mrs Adshead's death. It is not known what drug Shipman gave, how large a dose he gave or how he administered it. The likelihood is that he gave an intramuscular injection of an opiate, probably morphine or diamorphine. That would be an entirely proper thing to do provided that the dose was genuinely intended to relieve pain rather than shorten life. Dr John Grenville has explained that it can be very difficult for a doctor to estimate the appropriate dose of opiate so as to achieve pain relief without shortening life. This can be especially difficult if the patient has been taking increasing amounts of the drug and has become accustomed to it. It is not known whether the injection Shipman gave an hour before the death was the first injection Mrs Adshead had had or whether she had been receiving opiate injections for some time. Dr Grenville has also said that sometimes when a doctor estimates what dose to give, he or she realises that in order to control the patient's pain, it may be necessary to give a dose which has the side effect of depressing respiration and shortening the patient's life. Provided that the doctor makes a genuine attempt to estimate a therapeutic dose, his actions are not unlawful, even though the death is hastened.
That Mrs Adshead should have died about an hour after the injection was given, causes me to suspect that the dose was not intended merely to relieve pain but was, instead, intended to end Mrs Adshead's life. That may have been what she wanted, but if Shipman deliberately gave a lethal dose, it would have been unlawful. My suspicions are aroused because Professor Henry McQuay and Dr Grenville have explained to the Inquiry that an opiate given intramuscularly will reach its maximal effect within about 30 minutes to an hour after administration. If the dose is a lethal one, death will follow within about an hour of administration. The dose might not have been lethal and it might just have been coincidence that Mrs Adshead died an hour later, but the coincidence would be quite considerable. If the dose was not lethal and Mrs Adshead had died naturally, it would be unlikely that she would just happen to die an hour after the drug was given. My suspicions are heightened by the evidence that Shipman forecast that Mrs Adshead would die in about an hour. That suggests that Shipman had administered a lethal dose and knew that Mrs Adshead would be dead within the hour.
Although I recognise that Mrs Adshead might have died when she did from natural causes or as the result of a dose of opiate genuinely assessed as being that which was necessary to control her pain, I have come to the conclusion that it is likely that Shipman made a conscious decision to give her a lethal dose and ensure that life ended within the hour. If he did that, as I think he probably did, that was unlawful. It is, however, almost certain that the effect of his unlawful intervention was to hasten Mrs Adshead's death by only a very short time.

name: Nancy Anne Brassington
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 12 Laburnum Avenue, Hyde
conclusion:
This death is highly suspicious.
Mrs Brassington was clearly unwell and appears to have been suffering from cancer. It is likely that she had not long to live and it may well be that her quality of life would not have been good during her remaining days. Having said that, she was certainly not in the terminal phase of her cancer and, indeed, Shipman does not suggest that she died as the direct result of that condition.
There is some evidence that Mrs Brassington had had a stroke some time before her death. Her stepdaughter does not mention this, but Mrs A does. I shall assume that Mrs A is right in her recollection and that would mean that Mrs Brassington was at risk of suffering a further stroke.
The circumstance which suggests compellingly that Shipman killed Mrs Brassington is that her death was discovered within a few minutes of his departure. Mrs Brassington did not see Shipman out, as she usually would with any visitor. The overwhelming inference is that she died while he was with her. For Mrs Brassington to have suffered a fatal cerebrovascular accident within a minute of two of Shipman's departure is so unlikely that the possibility can be safely discounted. The inference that Mrs Brassington was dead when Shipman left is supported by Shipman's attitude on his return. If the receptionist's message had been relayed to him accurately, he should have thought that Mrs Brassington had collapsed. Yet he displayed no sense of urgency. I can only infer that he knew there was no urgency, as Mrs Brassington was already dead.
Mrs Brassington's peaceful appearance in death was not typical of that seen in a death due to cerebrovascular accident but was wholly consistent with a death by lethal injection of opiate.
Shipman's answers on Form B are frank, in that he admitted that the death must have occurred within a very short time of his visit to Mrs Brassington. Presumably he knew that Mrs A had seen him come and go. However, the course of events he describes is so improbable that it is surprising that more penetrating questions were not asked. On any view, this was a sudden and unexpected death for which the cause could not have been known. It should have been referred to the coroner.
Mrs Brassington was a typical Shipman victim. She was a widow, living alone and she was in poor health. Shipman was known to have expressed the view that he did not like 'keeping his patients going'. He seems to have thought that he knew when the right time had come for someone to die. His conduct on this occasion when he suggested to Mr and Mrs A that, if Mrs Brassington had lived, she would have suffered much pain, is consistent with his philosophy.
Despite the absence of the medical records, I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Brassington, almost certainly by administering a fatal intravenous dose of diamorphine.

name: Margaret Ann Conway
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 21 Mary Street, Dukinfield
conclusion:
The circumstances of this death are highly suspicious.
Shipman visited Mrs Conway for a routine check on her progress some time during the early afternoon of 15th
February. She was found dead at about 4.15pm. No one saw Mrs Conway alive after Shipman's visit. The evidence suggests that no one spoke to her either, although Shipman has tried to create the impression that Mrs Conway spoke to one of her daughters after he had left. I am satisfied that she did not speak to any of her daughters that afternoon after his visit. I have seen many cases in which Shipman has killed a patient and has made a false entry on Form B designed to create the impression that the patient was alive some time after his departure. I believe this is another example of that ruse.
Mrs Conway had had a stroke in 1983 and must have been at risk of another. There is no evidence that her health had deteriorated shortly before her death. However, I accept that a stroke can occur without warning. Having said that, it would seem to be something of a coincidence if Mrs Conway had suffered a fatal stroke in the short period which elapsed after Shipman's visit and her daughter's arrival. Although some strokes are immediately fatal, most are not fatal at all and, in those that are fatal, death usually follows some hours or even days after the onset.
I regard the close temporal association between Shipman's visit and the death as a highly suspicious factor and his attempt to create the impression that Mrs Conway was alive after his visit increases my suspicion.
There are other factors which increase my suspicion. Shipman's note is suspicious. He had never previously left a note when he had seen Mrs Conway alone. I think he was seeking to establish that Mrs Conway was alive and well when he left her. I think the various timings that Shipman gave on Form B and the alterations he made are also suspicious. On the first page of Form B, he says that the time of death was about 3.30pm and that he had last seen her alive at 1.30pm. On the second page, he said that he had seen her at 2.30pm, although he initially said
'seen 13.30'
. If Mrs Whittle's recollection of Shipman's note is accurate, he there wrote that he had seen Mrs Conway at about 3pm. Because it is possible that Mrs Whittle is mistaken about the time written on the note, I shall leave that out of account and consider only what can be seen on Form B. It appears to me that Shipman has changed his mind about the timings and has altered the timings on the second page but has forgotten to alter those on the first page. If Shipman really had left Mrs Conway alive and well at either 1.30pm or 2.30pm and if she really had had a sudden fatal stroke after his departure, he could not possibly have known when it had occurred. It could have occurred immediately after he left or only a few moments before Mrs Whittle arrived. Shipman often pretended to know the time of a patient's death when he could not have done. Usually he did this in order to distance the death from the time of his own visit. Here he began by suggesting a separation of two hours between the visit and the death. Then he changed his mind and suggested an interval of only an hour. I suspect that he must have done this because he knew he had left a note saying what time he had been at the house. To some extent this is speculation. However, what is significant is that Shipman was obviously concerned to 'get his story right'.
Mrs Conway's position and appearance in death were not typical of those of a person who has suffered a fatal stroke. Usually a patient having a stroke is aware that something terrible is happening and gets up in an attempt to seek help. More usually, such patients are found collapsed on the floor. On the other hand, Mrs Conway's position and appearance in death were wholly typical of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of diamorphine.
Finally, if Shipman's account were true and if Mrs Conway really had been found dead only an hour or two after he had left her well, he could not possibly have known the cause of her death and he would have been obliged to refer the case to the coroner. That he chose not to do so is typical of his conduct in many cases in which he had killed the patient. It is true that he sometimes chose not to refer deaths for which he was not responsible. Accordingly I do not attach much weight to this factor.
Taking all the evidence into account, I have reached the conclusion that Shipman must have killed Mrs Conway. Notwithstanding the passage of time and the loss of the medical records, I feel sure of that conclusion.

name: Bessie Delaney
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charlotte House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to a squamous cell carcinoma of the uterus
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Delaney died of natural causes as certified by Shipman. Her squamous cell carcinoma was diagnosed at hospital. No treatment was offered. It was to be expected that Mrs Delaney would deteriorate gradually towards death. Her death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
There is clear evidence that Shipman saw Mrs Delaney on 23rd
May and no evidence that he saw her again. A duty doctor certified the fact of her death in the early hours of 25th
May and it appears that Shipman did not learn of the death until 7.30am. There is no reason to suspect that Shipman played any part in Mrs Delaney's death.

name: Annie Grimshaw
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Pole Bank Hall, a residential home for the elderly, Stockport Road, Hyde
certified_cause: cerebrovascular accident due to cerebral arteriosclerosis
conclusion:
I am satisfied that Mrs Grimshaw died as the result of natural causes, as certified by Shipman.
Mr Grimshaw recalls that his mother had a severe stroke several weeks before her death, after which she was confined to bed. When he saw her a few hours before her death she was virtually comatose and he realised that she was dying. It appears that her death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
Shipman claimed that he last saw Mrs Grimshaw alive on the day before her death. Her name is in the visits book for that day. That would suggest that he probably visited her in the morning after surgery, which usually finished at about 10am on a Saturday. It is theoretically possible that he visited her again in the evening after Mr and Mrs Grimshaw had left, either of his own volition or at the request of the staff of Pole Bank Hall. It is theoretically possible that he killed her during that visit. However, it is highly unlikely that Shipman would have visited Mrs Grimshaw late on a Saturday evening. Indeed, he would not usually visit a patient at that time, save in an emergency. The theoretical possibility that he did so can be safely ignored.

name: Barry Higgins
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 20 Barleycroft Road, Hyde
conclusion:
Mr Higgins was known to be suffering from lung cancer and was extremely unwell in the period before his death. A death from that cause was to be expected.
I can well understand why Professor Baker expressed some suspicion about this case after considering the medical records. He only had access to the handwritten records and Shipman had not made any entry after 8th
February 1991. A much fuller (although probably still incomplete) picture is gathered from the computerised records.
It seems likely that Shipman would have visited Mr Higgins every few days. The last visit recorded in the visits book was on 1st
May, although this is not recorded in the medical records. It is possible that this was not Shipman's last visit to Mr Higgins, even though he said that it was. However, there is no evidence at all that Shipman visited Mr Higgins in the period shortly before his death. For that reason there is, in my view, no cause for suspicion in this case. I think it is almost certain that Mr Higgins died a natural death. I stop short of saying that I am certain that the death was natural only because it has not been possible to interview Mrs Higgins, to check the accuracy of Mrs Thomasson's impression that Shipman had not been present before the death. Mrs Thomasson should have no cause for concern.

name: Elsie Lewis
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Lewis died a natural death. It is clear from the daily diary that her condition had declined gradually to the stage where her death was expected.
There is no evidence that Shipman had access to her in the hours before her death. The evidence suggests that he last saw her alive on 13th
July.
There is no cause to suspect that Shipman was involved in Mrs Lewis' death.

name: Maud Matley
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
certified_cause: congestive heart failure due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Matley died a natural death. It appears from the Charnley House diary that she became increasingly ill over the last two days of her life. Although the symptoms described in the diary would suggest that she had a chest infection, it is possible that she was suffering from congestive heart failure. Either of those conditions could have resulted in her death.
The evidence suggests that Shipman last saw Mrs Matley alive on 7th
August. The diary does not record that he gave her an injection or treatment of any kind. It is, therefore, likely that he did not. However, even if he had given an injection of an opiate and Mrs Stansfield had failed to record the fact, there would be no reason to suspect that it caused Mrs Matley's death. Shipman usually visited Charnley House around lunchtime. If he visited at lunchtime on 7th
August, Mrs Matley lived for about 15 hours after the visit. Even if his visit was later than usual, she seems to have lived for at least 12 hours afterwards. It is theoretically possible that Shipman could have gained access to Mrs Matley and given her a lethal injection in the middle of the night. In my view, this possibility can be discounted. The doors of Charnley House were locked at night.
A further theoretical possibility is that Shipman might have sedated Mrs Matley on 7th
August. Over-sedation can cause increased vulnerability to bronchopneumonia, a common mechanism of death in the elderly. I do not think Shipman sedated Mrs Matley. Not only is there no record of any injection in the daily diary, the evidence suggests that Mrs Matley was not unconscious during the evening of 7th
August.
I hope that this decision will have served to reassure Mrs Wilson and her family that Shipman did not play any unlawful part in Mrs Matley's death.

name: Edith Pitman
title: Miss
place_of_death: Charlotte House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
There is very little evidence as to the circumstances surrounding Miss Pitman's death. We do, however, know that her death was not unexpected and appeared to her brother to be explicable.
The evidence suggests that Shipman had not seen Miss Pitman for nearly a week before her death. It is possible that he saw her later than that but there is no positive reason to suspect that he did. The fact that Miss Pitman's name appears in Shipman's visits book suggests that she might have died quite late on Thursday, 18th
May. If so, Shipman's note in his visits book for the following day probably indicates that he had been asked to certify the cause of death and possibly to complete cremation Form B. If a visit had been requested during the evening of 18th
May, either Dr Bills or the deputising service would have answered the call.
As there is no witness evidence of the circumstances of the death, I cannot say with complete confidence that Shipman was not involved in the death. However, it seems likely that the death was due to natural causes.

name: Edith Roberts
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 14 Pudsey Road, Cornholme, Todmorden
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
There are a number of strange and potentially suspicious circumstances surrounding this death.
First, the family says that the death was sudden and unexpected. Mrs Roberts was in good health. Yet Shipman reported on Form B that Mrs Roberts was known to be in poor health and that the death was expected. In the absence of any medical records, I cannot resolve this conflict. I have no doubt that Mrs Mycock and Mrs Ross are doing their best to recollect events, but the death occurred over 26 years ago and it is extremely difficult to remember events accurately after such a period. If Mrs Mycock and Mrs Ross had been able to refresh their memories from medical records, it may be that they would have remembered that, towards the end, Mrs Roberts had not been in such good health as they now recall.
Second, there are other strange entries on Form B. Shipman must have had an account from Mrs Mycock about when Mrs Roberts was last known to be alive. That is the usual basis on which a doctor assesses the bracket of time within which the death occurred. Here, it seems likely that Shipman was told that Mrs Roberts was alive at about 9.30pm and appears to have had time to prepare herself for bed. She was found at about midday on 21st
March and her body was then cold. I can well understand why he would have estimated 10pm as the earliest possible time of death. Why he should have crossed out 22.00 hours and substituted 1am is hard to imagine, unless he had some involvement in the death late that evening and wanted to put some distance in time between his visit and the death. Nor can I think why he should innocently have estimated the latest time of death as 6am. It would not have been possible to be sure that death occurred before that from the condition of the body. A further oddity is that, although he could not state the time of death with precision, he claimed to be able to say that he saw the body 12 hours after death. The inconsistency is obvious.
The sitting position and peaceful appearance of Mrs Roberts in death are not typical of those seen in a death from heart attack. As Dr John Grenville has said in his generic evidence, patients who begin to suffer the crushing pain that generally accompanies a coronary thrombosis usually make some attempt to call help. Often they are found collapsed on the floor. Usually there is some sign of an agonal event. Mrs Roberts did not have a telephone in her bedroom; it was in the living room downstairs. It does not appear that she made any attempt to move towards the telephone. Dr Grenville says that it is possible for death from heart attack to occur while the patient is deeply asleep. That could be the explanation for Mrs Roberts' appearance and position, although most people put their book down, put the light out and lie down before going to sleep. Her appearance is entirely typical of many of Shipman's victims killed by opiate injection.
If Mrs Mycock is right when she recalls that Mrs Roberts was well at 9.30pm, one could postulate that she was taken ill some time later and telephoned for a doctor. It is possible that Shipman might have been on duty and might have attended at her house. If so, she must have been well enough to let him in. If she did so, it is possible he could have given her a lethal injection. If he had given it intravenously, Mrs Roberts would not have been able to let him out of the house and lock the door after him. It is possible that he could have let himself out, locked the door behind him and taken the key away. If, however, he gave her an intramuscular injection of a lethal dose of opiate, it is possible that she would have been able to accompany him downstairs, let him out, lock the door and return to bed and pick up her book before lapsing into unconsciousness and death. My knowledge of Shipman's subsequent habits teaches me that to give an intramuscular injection was not his preferred method of killing. He preferred the faster acting intravenous route. However, these were early days and I cannot rule out the possibility that Shipman killed Mrs Roberts by giving her an intramuscular injection of opiate. If he did, I can understand why he would wish to give the impression on Form B that the death had occurred later than 10pm. He would have wished to distance the time of death from his own visit, which he might fear had been observed.
I do not think I can reach any positive conclusion about this death. I accept that Mrs Roberts was alive at 9.30pm. There is no evidence that Shipman visited her at all after that time. It would be most unlikely that he would have done so unless requested. If Mrs Roberts was sufficiently ill to call the doctor out late at night, or in the early hours of the morning, she must have been quite worried about herself. Yet she must also have been well enough to go downstairs to make the call and to let Shipman in. She must also have been insufficiently worried to telephone her niece or sister at an inconvenient time. These considerations tend to suggest to me that Shipman was not called out and did not visit. Yet, as I have indicated, there are some features of the case which arouse my deep suspicion that he might have been involved. I am afraid that I am unable to say whether it is probable that Shipman killed Mrs Roberts or whether it is probable that she died a natural death. I regret that this decision will not have served to put the minds of Mrs Roberts' relatives at rest. Whilst I suspect that Mrs Roberts was killed by Shipman, I do not find myself able to say that she probably was.

name: Alice Smith
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 39 Tower Street, Hyde
certified_cause: congestive heart failure, due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
There are some causes for suspicion in this case. The most obvious is that the death was discovered quite shortly after Shipman had visited Mrs Smith. If it could be said with confidence that no one had spoken to Mrs Smith or seen her alive after that visit, I would say that Shipman had probably killed her, unless there was some other evidence which pointed against that conclusion. Here, there is some evidence that Mrs Douglas saw Mrs Smith at about 1pm. She has no recollection of that. Shipman's claim that he visited at noon should be treated with circumspection, as he quite often gave false information about his movements in order to distance himself from a death. Here, there is no firm basis on which I could say that Shipman must have been lying about the time of his visit and no clear basis on which I could say that I am satisfied that Mrs Douglas did not see Mrs Smith at 1pm.
The medical evidence is neutral. Mrs Smith had sufficient ischaemic heart disease to account for a cardiac death, but there was no clear sign that her death had in fact been caused by a heart condition. It could quite well have been caused by a lethal injection.
Mrs Smith's position in death, collapsed on the floor, is not typical of the usual appearance of Shipman's victims, most of whom were found sitting on a chair or sofa or lying on a bed. Such positions would not be typical of a sudden cardiac death. On the other hand, Mrs Smith's position is quite consistent with a sudden cardiac death. This factor is not conclusive. A number of patients that I am satisfied Shipman killed have been found on the floor.
In general, when Shipman had killed a patient, he usually managed to avoid a referral to the coroner. He did this by ensuring that he would be called to the death when it was discovered. In this case, the death was not discovered until just after 6pm and he was not on duty that evening. The police were called and the case was referred to the coroner before Shipman was able to take control of matters. I have come across very few cases in which Shipman has killed a patient where he allowed events to go beyond his control. He would often make a return visit to the deceased's house to 'discover' the body himself. He would then 'find' the body, inform the relatives and give an assurance that he would be able to certify the cause of death and that a post-mortem examination would not be necessary. In such cases, the police and paramedics were not usually called. Even if they were, they would see no obvious sign of foul play and they would be under no obligation to take further action. Mrs Smith's death is not typical of cases in which Shipman killed in that he made no attempt to prevent a referral to the coroner. However, these were early days in Shipman's career as a murderer and it is quite possible that he had not yet perfected his technique of retaining control.
It is possible that Shipman was the last person to see Mrs Smith alive and it is also possible that he killed her. But there is nothing that points clearly to that conclusion. The medical evidence is neutral. Mrs Smith's position in death points more to a natural death than to a killing. The general circumstances are not typical of cases in which Shipman killed, in that the sudden death was handled by the police and referred to the coroner. Although I cannot state this conclusion with any great confidence, I think it is likely that Mrs Smith died a natural death.

name: Caroline Mary Taylor
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite sure that Mrs Taylor died of natural causes, although whether her death could properly have been attributed to old age seems rather doubtful. It does not appear from the daily diary that she had undergone any prolonged physical decline. Her final illness appears to have been quite brief. However, that does not mean to say that the death was not natural.
There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman saw Mrs Taylor at all in the weeks before her death. Rather, it appears that he claimed that he had done, so that he would appear qualified to certify the cause of her death. Shipman was often cavalier as regards his duties in respect of death certification and the fact that he told a lie on the MCCD counterfoil and probably on the certificate itself does not raise any suspicion that he might have killed Mrs Taylor.

name: Percy Ward
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 6 Hollins Avenue, Hyde
conclusion:
Mr Ward was clearly very unwell in the days leading up to his death. On the morning of his death, he had great difficulty in breathing and was very restless. He was confined to bed and was receiving nursing care from the district nurse. The evidence is that Shipman came and administered an injection of some kind. As the medical records are not available, there is no possibility of knowing what was given. If Mr Ward was struggling to breathe and was very restless, he may have been distressed and it may, therefore, have been appropriate to give some sort of sedative or euphoric drug such as an opiate. That he appeared to relax after the injection would suggest that some such drug was given. The question then arises as to whether Shipman gave the injection primarily to relieve distress or in order to hasten Mr Ward's death.
There is real cause to suspect that Shipman might have given a dose of drug which was intended to kill. It appears that Mr Ward died within an hour of the injection, possibly even sooner. If a lethal dose of opiate had been given intramuscularly, death would have followed within about an hour. However, that does not show that the dose was a lethal one, as it is possible that Mr Ward died naturally an hour after the injection. A further cause for suspicion arises from Shipman's words after giving the injection. He appeared to know that Mr Ward would not live long. That might indicate that he knew that Mr Ward would die soon because he had just received a lethal injection. On the other hand, these words might have no more significance than the doctor's observation that the patient had not long to live.
Some of the information contained on Form B is inconsistent with the recollection of the witnesses. In particular, Shipman recorded that he last saw Mr Ward alive approximately six hours before his death, which would have been at about 7.30am. I think it unlikely that Shipman visited as early as that in the day. It is possible that Shipman was seeking to distance himself from the death. Shipman claimed that the mode of death was a coma lasting 12 hours. This is not consistent with the evidence of Mr Ward's daughter who said that he was able to speak to her on the morning of 4th
January. It is also not consistent with the need to administer a drug to relieve pain or distress. It would, however, be a plausible mode of death for someone dying of senility. It appears possible that Shipman was painting a picture of a death due to senility.
These factors give rise to a real suspicion that Shipman deliberately hastened Mr Ward's death. If circumstances such as these arose in connection with any other doctor, I would have little difficulty in concluding that the doctor had probably not intended to hasten the death. However, I know that by 1983 Shipman had killed a number of patients, some of whom were terminally or seriously ill. It would be typical conduct for Shipman to give an overdose of something, possibly an opiate, possibly a very large dose of Largactil, in order to hasten the patient's end. Taking this additional factor into account, I have come to the conclusion that Shipman probably hastened Mr Ward's death and that the death was not entirely due to natural causes.

name: Elizabeth Ashworth
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 38 Peel Street, Hyde
conclusion:
As a heavy smoker, Mrs Ashworth was at increased risk of cerebrovascular accident. It also appears that she was taken ill while working in her garden on the day of her death. It is possible that she had suffered a stroke that afternoon, from which she died naturally a few hours later. However, when Mr and Mrs Driver arrived, Mrs Ashworth did not appear to be seriously ill.
There are reasons to suspect that the death might have been caused by Shipman. The death occurred not long after a visit by Shipman during which he gave Mrs Ashworth an injection. It would not be usual to treat a stroke patient with any injected drug. The usual treatment is to watch and wait. I think it highly unlikely that Shipman gave Mrs Ashworth a steroid drug to reduce brain swelling. He would not have had it with him in his bag. Accordingly, I strongly suspect that the drug was an opiate. I am also suspicious because Shipman seemed to anticipate that Mrs Ashworth would die, rather than survive. Most stroke patients survive and recover to a variable extent. I strongly suspect that Shipman gave an injection which ensured that Mrs Ashworth would die. There is a possibility that he gave an injection for genuine therapeutic reasons but I regard that as most unlikely.
There is some uncertainty about the time of Mrs Ashworth's death. Mrs Driver thinks that Shipman returned to the house about two hours after he had given the injection, although I think she is not sure of how long had elapsed. I am puzzled by her evidence that it was not until Shipman returned that she and her husband realised that Mrs Ashworth had died. It seems quite possible that she had been dead for some time and they had not noticed. Shipman's question, 'Is she still here?', suggests that he expected Mrs Ashworth to be dead.
That Mrs Ashworth remained sitting in her chair suggests that she had not had a stroke. Dr Esmail says that a stroke patient would tend to slump or fall unless very well supported. On the other hand, many of Shipman's victims were found sitting peacefully in a chair.
Although there are some unexplained features of the evidence in this case, I have come to the conclusion that it is likely that Shipman killed Mrs Ashworth with a lethal injection of opiate.

name: Charles Edward Brocklehurst
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 6 Park Avenue, Hyde
conclusion:
There are highly suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. The first and most obvious is that the death took place in Shipman's presence and while he was alone with the patient. That in itself is a cause for suspicion because Shipman was not called out as an emergency that morning. The family had the impression that Mr Brocklehurst was suffering an exacerbation of his breathing problems and did not think that his condition was in any way critical. However, I note that whoever telephoned the surgery said that Mr Brocklehurst had been poorly all week and that his breathing was bad. I note that Mr Anthony Brocklehurst was anxious to return from shopping as soon as he could. It is possible that the family has failed to recall the seriousness of Mr Brocklehurst's illness.
The central issue in this case is whether or not Mr Brocklehurst's condition at the time of Shipman's arrival was as Shipman claimed. If it was, it was entirely possible that Mr Brocklehurst would die within the next few minutes. If it was not, then it was a remarkable and highly suspicious coincidence that his condition should have deteriorated suddenly and that he should have died within the short compass of Shipman's visit.
I cannot place any reliance on Shipman's records. I have seen many cases in which Shipman has fabricated a description of a patient's condition in order to explain the death that he himself has caused. It is entirely possible that Shipman killed Mr Brocklehurst and fabricated the account in order to explain the sudden death and the presence of morphine in the body, in the event that it might be detected. Such conduct would be typical of him.
One of the features of this case, which strikes me as suspicious, is that Shipman apparently had his book of MCCDs with him. This is a substantial book and a general practitioner does not usually carry it about with him. There was no reason within the medical history or the message received at the surgery for Shipman to suspect that Mr Brocklehurst would have died before he arrived or would die while he was there. I suspect that he decided in advance of the visit that Mr Brocklehurst would die.
There are some slightly suspicious features within Shipman's account contained in the records and Form B. First, he claimed that Anthony, Christine and Paul Brocklehurst were present at the moment of death, when they all think that they arrived after the death. Second, Shipman said that he had seen Mr Brocklehurst a week before his death, implying that Mr Brocklehurst had needed medical attention at that time. If Shipman did see Mr Brocklehurst on about 24th
December, he did not record the fact in the medical notes. The family says that Mr Brocklehurst was well over Christmas.
Dr Grenville's suspicions were particularly aroused by the apparent sudden change in Mr Brocklehurst's condition within the very short time that Mr Paul Brocklehurst was away from his grandfather's side. I agree with Dr Grenville's view but I do not feel able to be certain of the accuracy of Mr Paul Brocklehurst's recollection. I think it is possible that Mr Paul Brocklehurst went back home to see if his parents had returned because he was becoming increasingly concerned about his grandfather's health. That is not to say that I think he had reached the very serious stage described by Shipman. I think Mr Paul Brocklehurst would have remembered if his grandfather had been in a state of collapse or near unconsciousness when he left.
It is not possible to resolve the issue as to Mr Brocklehurst's state with certainty. Mr Brocklehurst's general health was poor and it is possible that he could have deteriorated to the condition described by Shipman. However, taking into account all the factors I have mentioned, I have come to the conclusion that Shipman gave Mr Brocklehurst a lethal injection. I am sure that he killed Mr Brocklehurst by giving him a larger dose of opiate than he admitted in the medical note and one which he knew would be fatal.

name: Irene Chapman
title: Mrs
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis, with smoking as another significant condition contributing to the death
conclusion:
There are some extremely suspicious features surrounding this death, several of which are typical of a case in which Shipman killed. First, Shipman quite often visited the patient twice on the day of death. He would kill the patient during the first visit and then return later to 'discover' the body. A second typical feature is Shipman's claim that the patient had been advised to accept admission to hospital but had refused. When Shipman returned to 'see if the patient had changed her mind', she was found dead. The death was readily explicable, as Shipman had already noted that the patient was ill enough to require hospital admission.
On this day, Mrs Chapman was certainly not well. She requested a visit as she was suffering chest pain and was not able to travel to the surgery. It appears that Shipman visited soon after 9.30am and that no one saw Mrs Chapman alive or spoke to her after that visit. That is a highly suspicious factor. However, it must be accepted that, as a lifelong heavy smoker, Mrs Chapman was at risk of suffering heart disease and of dying a sudden cardiac death. It would not be surprising if Mrs Chapman did experience the symptoms that Shipman described in the medical record. However, I doubt the genuineness of the records Shipman made of the first visit. In particular, I suspect that the actual blood pressure reading was 160/100 and not 130/70. It appears that Shipman was anxious to make the point that Mrs Chapman's blood pressure was much lower than normal. The only reference he had for normality was a reading taken in 1987, but he implies that that is to be treated as her usual level. The sudden reduction, which he purports to have found on the day of the death, would, if genuine, be indicative of a heart attack. However, I do not think there was any such reduction. I think Shipman was seeking to paint a picture of a heart attack with atrial fibrillation. As he felt the need to fabricate medical signs, I am led to suspect that Mrs Chapman had not had a heart attack.
Even more telling are the lies that Shipman told on Form B. A common feature of Form B in cases where Shipman has killed is a claim that someone else has been present at the moment of death. Shipman seeks to create the impression that he was not alone with the patient at the time of death. Here, he has pretended that his wife was present at the moment of death. Mrs Shipman was quite clear in her evidence. She was not present at the moment of death. Mrs Chapman was already dead when she entered the house. That was why she went in. Painful though it was for Mrs Shipman to admit that fact, which carried the necessary implication that her husband had lied on Form B, she did not seek to offer any explanation. There could not have been any satisfactory explanation. Mrs Shipman could not have been in a position to give Shipman any information about the cause or mode of death. I am satisfied that Shipman lied on Form B. It is hard to think of any reason why he would tell lies involving his wife, unless he felt the need to do so in order to allay any possible suspicion about the circumstances of this death. It is inconceivable that he would have told such lies, if this death had been natural.
Mrs Chapman's position and appearance in death were not typical of what is usually seen after a heart attack. As Dr Grenville has said, a patient who begins to suffer the crushing pain usually associated with a coronary thrombosis generally tries to summon help. The patient is not usually found sitting in a chair, but is more commonly found collapsed on the floor. Nor does the patient usually look entirely peaceful. Mrs Chapman's position and appearance were entirely typical of those of many of Shipman's victims killed by a lethal injection of strong opiate.
Taking these factors together, I have no doubt that Shipman killed Mrs Chapman during his first visit to her house between 9.30am and 10am. His claim that Mrs Chapman was breathing her last when he arrived soon after 1pm was pure pretence.

name: Elaine Dutton
title: Mrs
conclusion:
It appears to me to be highly likely that Mrs Dutton died as the result of natural causes, as certified by Shipman.
It is clear from the evaluation sheets that Mrs Dutton had suffered at least one, if not two, further strokes in the days before her death. Her condition deteriorated. She was weak and tired. The staff realised that she would not live long and advised Mr John Dutton to come to the home. The death on 11th
April was neither sudden nor unexpected.
The evidence shows that Shipman saw Mrs Dutton quite shortly before she died. The evaluation sheet suggests that he was there half an hour before the death; on Form B, Shipman said that he was there an hour before. It is theoretically possible that, during that visit, Shipman gave Mrs Dutton a drug which hastened her death. However, this seems unlikely, first because Mr John Dutton was at the home and was probably present during the consultation, and second, Ms Berry believes that she would have been present. If she was, and if any injection had been given, I do not think she would have written
'no treatment'
.
There remains a possibility, no more, that Shipman did see Mrs Dutton alone that afternoon and took the opportunity to give her a drug which caused her to die rather sooner than she otherwise would have done. I cannot rule that out.

name: Edith Goddard
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
It seems clear that Mrs Goddard's health had deteriorated during the days before her death to the extent that, when she died, her death was not unexpected.
There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman visited Mrs Goddard in the hours before her death. Her name appears in his visits book on the day of the death but it seems likely that this entry would reflect a request that he should visit the home to certify the death.
In all the circumstances I see no reason to suspect that Shipman was in any way involved in Mrs Goddard's death. I am quite satisfied that she died of natural causes.

name: Winifred Healey
title: Mrs
certified_cause: congestive heart failure due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
Although Mrs Healey's death was sudden and unexpected and although the cause of her death has not been adequately established, it does not seem to me that there is any reliable evidence to show that it was caused by Shipman.
There is no evidence that Shipman went to Mrs Healey's flat on the day of her death. No one saw him there. He did not claim to have been there. There is no record of an intention to visit in the surgery records. These matters are not conclusive, of course. A visit is still a possibility.
Mrs Healey's body was found locked inside her flat. The snick on the Yale lock was on and the key would not open the door. Although it is thought that Mrs Healey did not usually put the snick on during the day, it appears that she must have done on this occasion. If one postulates that Shipman had visited her and had given her a lethal injection of opiate, he must have left her at a time when she was able to accompany him to the door, lock it and go to her bed before lapsing into unconsciousness and death. As Professor Henry McQuay and Dr Grenville have explained, a lethal dose of opiate, given intravenously, would act so quickly that such movements would not be possible. If Shipman had given an intravenous injection, which was his usual and apparently preferred method of killing, he would not have been able to leave the house with the snick of the Yale in the locked position. If Shipman had given Mrs Healey a lethal injection intramuscularly, she would have been able to remain upright and mobile for a few minutes. It is therefore physically possible that she could have let him out, locked herself in and gone to bed. If he did not do that, it would appear that her death must have been natural. I am satisfied that there was no other means by which Shipman could have let himself out of the house, leaving Mrs Healey locked inside. There was no practicable means of egress besides the front door. I was told that there was a patio door but that this was never used. It would seem likely that the police officer would have tried the patio door to see if that was open before climbing in through a window. Although it is possible that Shipman gave Mrs Healey an intramuscular injection, that was not his usual method of operation.
Mrs Healey appears to have been in good health on the morning of the day of her death. However, her medical history was such that she was at an increased risk of a sudden death from a heart attack. Although her congestive heart disease had been well controlled by medication, it seems to me that, at her age, a sudden cardiac death could not be described as wholly unexpected.
The evidence about Mrs Healey's appearance in death is conflicting. Dr Grenville has said that no clear conclusions can be drawn from the medical evidence. Nor can any inferences be drawn from the MCCD. Although Dr Grenville has said that Shipman should not have certified the cause of death, as he had insufficient information to reach a diagnosis, I cannot draw a clear inference that he must have wished to avoid a referral to the coroner so as to avoid detection of an unlawful act. He might have certified the death on inadequate material to save the family the distress of a post-mortem examination.
Bearing in mind these various factors, it seems to me that the death was probably natural. I cannot say with certainty that the cause was a natural one; nor can I say what the natural cause probably was. However, I think it unlikely that Shipman played any part in the death.

name: Olive Lees
title: Miss
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Miss Lees died a natural death. She had been in poor health for some time and the Charnley House daily diary records her gradual decline. Her death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
There is no evidence that Shipman had access to Miss Lees on the day of her death. He was almost certainly not on duty. His last visit to Miss Lees was probably on 14th
March, three days before the death.
There is no cause to suspect an unnatural death.

name: Miriam Rose Emily Mycock
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
Very little is known about Mrs Mycock's health or even why she moved into Charnley House. The reason for the concern as to her condition on 2nd
April, the day before she died, is not clear. Nor have I any idea why Mrs Mycock was moaning in the night of 2nd
to 3rd
April. If she had chest pain (such as might be the precursor of a heart attack) one might expect the staff to telephone Shipman early in the morning. It is not clear from the entry whether or not they did.
There seem to be several possibilities. One is that Mrs Mycock died a natural death at 9.20am and that Shipman came some time later to certify the cause of death. Another is that Shipman was summoned very early, called on his way to the surgery, at, say, about 8.30am, found Mrs Mycock to be in pain and gave her an injection of opiate. She then died at 9.20am. If he gave her an injection of opiate, I would not be able to say whether or not the injection had caused or hastened her death. My experience of the Charnley House diaries leads me to believe that, on occasions, they did not contain a complete account of all that had happened. That is not to say that members of staff were knowingly concealing relevant matters. It seems entirely possible to me that the member of staff making the morning shift report would not think it important to record if Shipman visited twice.
For the reasons I have outlined, I find myself unable to decide whether Mrs Mycock died of natural causes or as the result of an unlawful act by Shipman.

name: Laura Victoria Parkin
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Parkin died a natural death. Her gradual deterioration is clearly recorded in the Charnley House daily diary. She had been confined to bed for some time and her death was neither sudden nor unexpected to the staff.
There is no evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Parkin on the day of her death. He visited her on 31st
July and prescribed Temgesic, an opioid analgesic, to relieve her pain. He seems to have recognised that she was close to death. There is no evidence that Mrs Parkin was unconscious after Shipman's visit, so there is no reason to suspect that he might have given her an excessive amount of sedation. There is no reason to suspect that Shipman did anything to hasten Mrs Parkin's death.

name: Jane Isabella Rowland
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 8 Laneside Street, Todmorden
certified_cause: congestive heart failure (CHF) due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
There is evidence that Shipman administered an injection to Mrs Rowland shortly before she died. He did so quite openly. In the absence of the medical records, it is not possible to know what the injection was or how large the dose. We do not even know whether Shipman recorded giving the injection. As he is reported to have said that the injection was intended to make Mrs Rowland more comfortable, it is not unreasonable to suppose that the injection might have been of opiate. It is quite possible that Shipman issued and collected a prescription for pethidine in Mrs Rowland's name on the day of her death. As he was at this time probably addicted to pethidine, he might well have done so as a means of obtaining supplies for himself, whether or not he intended to use any of it on Mrs Rowland.
I note that Dr Brown completed Form C of the cremation certificate. It is said that she was very thorough when completing Forms C. It appears that she consulted three of Mrs Rowland's relatives.
