Although one would like to think that relatives who had an opportunity to express a concern to a doctor would do so, I am far from convinced that these relatives would necessarily have mentioned their concerns about Shipman giving an injection. They well knew that Mrs Rowland was very poorly and had not long to live. They probably felt a sense of relief that the agony was over. They would not have wished to delay the funeral. They might have hesitated to say anything because they would not have been on very certain ground in making the allegation. I can well understand why they would not have mentioned any concerns they had about the effect of an injection.
There are too many unknown factors in this case for me to be able to reach a decision. First, the nature of Mrs Rowland's illness is in some doubt. The family thought she had pneumonia; Shipman certified that the death was due to CHF. Second, we do not know what Shipman injected. Nor do we have any reliable estimate of how long elapsed after Shipman gave the injection and before Mrs Rowland died. The best estimate we have is a couple of hours, but that is what has been reported to Mrs Pickles by those present, who are now dead. She is recalling events that occurred more than a quarter of a century ago.
On the one hand, it is quite possible that Mrs Rowland was in acute distress as a result of CHF or pleuritic pain due to pneumonia. Shipman could quite properly have given her a small dose of opiate. She might then have gained some relief but died quite naturally two hours later. On the other hand, it is possible that Shipman decided to hasten her end and gave her an excessive dose of opiate, intramuscularly, after which Mrs Rowland would have lapsed into unconsciousness and died, almost certainly within an hour. That would have been an unlawful act by Shipman. If that happened, it appears that he would have hastened her end by only a short period. There are other possibilities. Shipman might have given a dose of opiate which was genuinely intended to relieve Mrs Rowland's distress but which actually had the effect of depressing her respiration and shortening her life. That would not have been unlawful. It can be very difficult for a doctor to assess the right amount of opiate to give a terminally ill patient.
If these events had been reported of any doctor other than Shipman, I would have no hesitation in saying that the death was almost certainly natural. Mrs Rowland had been ill for some time and was being nursed downstairs. However, I cannot ignore the fact that Shipman became a serial killer and that his favoured method of killing was to inject opiates. He was at this time abusing pethidine by injecting himself. On or about 12th
February 1975, he had obtained ten 30mg ampoules of morphine sulphate. It would not be surprising if he was prepared to hasten the end of a terminally ill patient. I note that this was a Saturday and Shipman was on duty. He would have been on duty over the whole weekend, including during the night. It is possible that he wished to bring Mrs Rowland's life to an end so that he would not be called out during the night. To suggest such a thing of any other doctor would be unthinkable but, as we know that Shipman was later prepared to kill perfectly healthy patients, it is not fanciful to suggest that he might hasten a patient's end for his own convenience.
For these reasons, I am unable to say whether or not Shipman hastened Mrs Rowland's death. There are grounds to suspect that he might have done but the uncertainties are such that I cannot say whether it is likely that he did. If he did, I am sure that her life would have been shortened by only a small margin.

name: Cicely Sharples
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 11 Swindells Street, Newton, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of very suspicious circumstances surrounding this death.
First, Mrs Sharples was found dead quite soon after a visit from Shipman. The evidence suggests that, apart from Shipman, the last people to see Mrs Sharples alive on the day of her death were Mr Ashworth and the meals on wheels lady. No one appears to have seen or spoken to Mrs Sharples after Shipman's visit. The temporal association between Shipman's visit and the death gives rise to suspicion. My suspicion is increased because there does not seem to have been any indication that Mrs Sharples was in any way unwell that day. When Mr Ashworth saw her she was well. It is reported that, when the meals on wheels lady left, Mrs Sharples was eating her lunch. She appears to have finished it and tidied the kitchen. Shipman's visit was not at Mrs Sharples' request; it was a revisit, which he chose to make. Of course, elderly people can and do sometimes die suddenly without previous signs of serious illness. Mrs Sharples had had one stroke and she must have been at some risk of suffering another. Nonetheless, it would be something of a coincidence if she had a fatal stroke soon after Shipman's visit. I regard the circumstances as very suspicious.
I suspect that Shipman's medical notes are not genuine. The first one indicates that the signs of congestive heart failure that Shipman had noted a week earlier were settling. He found nothing to concern him and decided to visit Mrs Sharples in four weeks' time. That note seems to be complete in itself. The second note presents a very different picture. Mrs Sharples is said to have been very sick. She was complaining that she still had a headache. Neither of those complaints appeared in the previous note and the people who had seen her that day were unaware of sickness or headache. There is a discussion about the need for Mrs Sharples to go into residential care. If Shipman made a visit and found Mrs Sharples in good health, as he claimed in his first note, I cannot imagine why he would then have returned. His second note is quite inconsistent with the first. Then he has made a third note recording the death. I suspect that Shipman made the first note during or just after a visit in the early afternoon. I think he killed Mrs Sharples during that visit but made a note to suggest that she was well when he left her. I do not think he then returned while she was still alive. I suspect that he made the second note at some later time with the intention of providing some support for his diagnosis for the cause of death. It may well be that he had forgotten that he had already made one entry relating to that visit. The two were on separate cards.
As Dr Grenville says, if this were a natural death which had occurred while Mrs Sharples was alone, Shipman could not possibly have known the cause of her death. He ought to have referred the case to the coroner. That he did not gives rise to some suspicion.
There are a number of entries on Form B which increase my suspicion. First, Shipman claimed that he knew the time of death. He did not and there is no way in which he could properly have assessed it. I have found many cases in which Shipman has killed a patient in which he has pretended to know the time of death. He has stated a time considerably after his own visit. His motive must have been to distance his visit from the death. I think he has done that in this case.
Second, he sought to create the impression that the ambulance crew were present at the death and had been in a position to give him information from which he was able to diagnose the cause of death and describe the mode of death. Shipman often did this when he wanted to give the impression that he could not have been the last person to see the patient alive and to suggest that his diagnosis of the cause of death was based on information supplied by responsible people.
Although the position in which Mrs Sharples was found could be consistent with a sudden death from natural causes, the other attendant circumstances render it far more likely that her position in death resulted from her having been injected with a fatal dose of a strong opiate whilst sitting at the kitchen table.
I have come to the conclusion that Shipman killed Mrs Sharples. I think he probably found her in the front room and for some reason helped her to walk through to the kitchen, leaving her walking frame behind. Otherwise, I do not see how she came to be in the kitchen without her frame. I think he then told her either that he wanted to take a blood sample or to give her an injection. While she was sitting on her stool, I think he gave her a lethal injection of opiate. I think she fell to the floor as she became unconscious. I feel able to say that I am sure of this conclusion.

name: Edna Mary Taylor
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charlotte House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
certified_cause: cardiac arrest due to congestive heart failure
conclusion:
The evidence suggests that Mrs Taylor collapsed in the late afternoon of 27th
April and died before either an ambulance or a doctor could attend. It is recorded that following her collapse she was having difficulty in breathing. This would be consistent with either a heart attack or an episode of acute left ventricular failure. Either event could have resulted in death.
There is strong evidence to suggest that Shipman was not at Charlotte House on the day of Mrs Taylor's death until after the death had occurred.
I am satisfied that this was a natural death and that Shipman was not unlawfully involved.

name: George Lawton Wagstaff
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 2 Gerrards Gardens, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
I can well understand why Professor Baker regarded this death as moderately suspicious on the basis of his examination of the medical records. They are extremely scanty and contain no account of the death. Form B is not satisfactory either. First, it is doubtful whether Shipman saw Mr Wagstaff on 22nd
July, as he claimed to have done. Also, it appears likely from Mr Peter Wagstaff's account, that his mother found her husband only a few moments before she telephoned him at 7am. When he arrived at the house, his father was already dead and felt cold. Thus, it is not clear on what basis Shipman has concluded that the death occurred at about 5am or how he could describe the mode of death, other than by assuming that Mr Wagstaff had collapsed and died within minutes. It was probably misleading for Shipman to say that Mrs Wagstaff was present at the moment of death, as she was probably asleep in bed. However, these probable inaccuracies do not affect the main issue, which is whether Mr Wagstaff died a natural death. On that issue, I am quite satisfied that he did. Mr Wagstaff was known to be suffering from angina and was therefore at risk of a sudden cardiac death. There is no evidence that Shipman had access to him in the hours before his death. The probable inaccuracies in Form B demonstrate Shipman's cavalier attitude to his duties in respect of death certification.

name: Joseph Andrew
title: Mr
place_of_death: Hyde Nursing Home, Grange Road South, Hyde
conclusion:
Mr Andrew's medical history of transient ischaemic attacks and increasing confusion was entirely typical of the effect of cerebroarteriosclerosis, in which the oxygen supply to the brain becomes inadequate. He declined gradually and it would appear that his death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
Mr Andrew almost certainly died at about 1am on 17th
November 1991. Shipman thought he had died about 12 hours later. Shipman stated on the MCCD counterfoil that he last saw Mr Andrew alive on 16th
November 1991, and on Form B of the cremation certificate he said that he had last seen him alive 24 hours before death. He clearly meant to suggest that he had seen Mr Andrew at about lunchtime on 16th
November. Shipman used to work on Saturday mornings and it is quite possible that he saw Mr Andrew on the 16th
, but failed to make any entry in the medical records. Shipman was not a careful note taker. It is also possible that Shipman saw Mr Andrew for the last time on Friday, 15th
November, as recorded in the medical records, and made a mistake when completing the MCCD and Form B of the cremation certificate. In any event, there is no evidence at all to suggest that Shipman saw Mr Andrew in the period immediately preceding the death. I therefore rule out the possibility that Shipman unlawfully killed Mr Andrew by administering to him a lethal dose of opiates.
The theoretical possibility remains that Shipman might have given Mr Andrew quite large doses of a sedative over a period of two to three days before his death with the intention of keeping him asleep. This might have been a reasonable thing to do, if it was the only way to keep him comfortable. However, if kept asleep for a long period, Mr Andrew would be vulnerable to bronchopneumonia, a common mechanism of death in elderly people. If Shipman did this, it would not be possible to say whether he had done it because he genuinely considered it to be the only way of keeping Mr Andrew comfortable or whether he used it as an indirect way of hastening his death.
Although there remains this theoretical possibility, there is no evidence that Shipman did keep Mr Andrew heavily sedated. I note that none of the drugs prescribed for Mr Andrew on 10th
November was a sedative.
Taking the evidence as a whole, I am quite satisfied that Mr Andrew died as a result of natural causes.

name: Charles Henry Barlow
title: Mr
conclusion:
Mr Barlow was not well at the time of his death but he did not appear to be close to death. He was not seen to be in severe respiratory distress. He was not as weak or obviously ill as would be expected if he were about to die of bronchopneumonia. There is no evidence that he died of a heart attack or stroke. Although the post-mortem findings were suggestive of bronchopneumonia, the diagnosis was not proved by histology. When the surrounding factors are taken into account, I am driven to the conclusion that the death was probably not due to bronchopneumonia. There is no other obvious natural cause and on the medical evidence there is a real possibility that this death was due to diamorphine overdose.
Mr Barlow died during a visit by Shipman. That factor always gives rise to very grave suspicion that Shipman has killed the patient. Other doctors find that patients very rarely die during their visits. With Shipman this happened frequently.
There are some features of this case that are typical of cases in which Shipman killed. After the death, Shipman made a note in which he did not record any complaints or signs observed on examination. The note contained no description of the transition from life to death and no explanation for the death. In this case, it contains a diagnosis unsupported by evidence and later proven to be wrong. The note did not contain any reference to the administration of a drug although Mr Barry Barlow says that Shipman told him that he had given his father an injection, ostensibly to help his breathing. In short, the note is not what one would expect if a patient had died suddenly from natural causes during a consultation.
Another feature typical of cases in which Shipman killed is that he involved a neighbour. One wonders why Shipman went over to fetch Mr Newton if the consultation with Mr Barlow had been only a chat about admission to hospital. If an ambulance were to be called it is possible Shipman might have wanted Mr Newton to collect Mr Barlow's personal requirements for a hospital stay. It is possible that Mr Barlow had refused admission and Shipman wanted someone to persuade him. It is also possible that Shipman wanted Mr Newton to be present in the house so that he could say that someone else was present at the death. Shipman would also be free to leave the house before the arrival of relatives.
Another typical feature of a Shipman killing is that the electric fire was turned up high and Shipman restrained Mr Newton from turning it down. Shipman's motive in keeping bodies warm is not entirely clear. In some cases I have thought that he may have wished to make it difficult for a pathologist to establish the time of death. In this case, there was no doubt about the time of death or Shipman's presence at it. It is possible that Shipman thought that morphine might metabolise more rapidly if the body were kept warm. Whatever his belief or his motive, this is a suspicious factor as the electric or gas fire has been found left on high in a significant number of cases in which Shipman killed.
If this is a Shipman killing, there is an unusual feature in that Mr Newton believes that Mr Barlow was still alive when he and Shipman returned to Mr Barlow's house. It is possible that Mr Newton is mistaken about this and did not actually hear Mr Barlow's voice. He could not see Mr Barlow properly and it is possible that Shipman pretended that Mr Barlow was still alive and kept Mr Newton back so that he could not see that he was already dead. If Shipman had spoken to Mr Barlow, Mr Newton might have had the impression that Mr Barlow responded when in fact he did not. It is also possible that Mr Barlow was on the verge of unconsciousness as Mr Newton and Shipman arrived and that he died a few minutes later. However, if Shipman had given an intravenous injection of a lethal dose of opiate, which was his usual method of killing, he must have gone to fetch Mr Newton immediately and Mr Newton must have returned with him within a very short space of time. A further possibility is that Shipman gave Mr Barlow a lethal injection but that part of the dose failed to enter the vein directly and entered the body subcutaneously. It can be difficult to inject a very old thin person intravenously. If that had happened, Mr Barlow's death would have been somewhat delayed. This might account for Mr Barlow saying that he did not feel well and Shipman replying that he was going to die anyway.
If this was a case in which Shipman killed, there was another unusual feature. Shipman must have known that Mr Barlow had undergone an operation recently and that if he died, his death would have to be referred to the coroner. One might think that Shipman would be taking a big risk if he killed him. But it appears that this was not so. Mr Barlow was obviously not in good health. It would be highly likely that a feasible explanation for the death would be found, as it was. It is not usual for specimens of tissue to be sent for toxicological examination and the risk of detection would be very slight. Even if a test had been ordered and had produced a positive result for morphine, it would not have been too difficult to explain its presence in a patient who had recently undergone operative treatment.
Although at first sight there are features of this case which suggest that Shipman might not have killed Mr Barlow, on further examination they do not appear significant. The fact remains that Mr Barlow was not thought to be on the verge of death when Mr Newton saw him at lunchtime. He died about two hours later in Shipman's presence. I am quite satisfied that Shipman had been with Mr Barlow for some time before Mr Newton was brought in. It seems to me that Shipman killed Mr Barlow, almost certainly by his preferred method of giving him a lethal dose of diamorphine. After giving the injection, I think he went over to fetch Mr Newton so that if he could say that someone else had been present at the death. He would also be able to leave the body in Mr Newton's care while he went about his duties.
I am sure that Shipman unlawfully killed Mr Barlow.

name: Beatrice Helen Clee
title: Miss
conclusion:
There are several suspicious features surrounding this death.
According to the witness evidence and Shipman's entries on Form B of the cremation certificate, there was a visit by Shipman very shortly before the death was discovered. No one saw Miss Clee alive after the visit. If the information in Mrs Clee's letter is accurate (and she wrote it very shortly after the death), Shipman told her that Miss Clee had died at about midday, which was the very time, according to his entry on Form B, that he had visited her. This very close temporal association between the visit and the death excites a high degree of suspicion. Even if Mrs Clee's recollection on this point is wrong, there is still a close temporal association between the visit and Miss Clee's death.
It is not known whether Miss Clee was unwell on the morning of the day she died. It is possible that she was unwell and asked Shipman to visit. On the other hand, it is entirely possible that Shipman's visit was a routine matter, connected with her ulcerated legs. Of the two it seems more likely to me that Shipman made a routine visit to examine Miss Clee's legs. I say that because his medical note begins with a reference to her legs. It then goes on to describe the conditions which he later relied upon as an explanation for her death. I have seen that pattern within the notes of many patients whom Shipman has killed.
Miss Clee's medical condition was not such as to place her at an increased risk of suffering a fatal coronary thrombosis. It is difficult to accept the truth of Shipman's clinical note and his diagnosis of angina, when it represents the only reference to heart problems for many years and the only recorded reference to angina in Miss Clee's life, apart from when she was first referred to the cardiologist in 1976. In my view, Shipman probably fabricated this record in order to explain the death.
Shipman has asserted that he attended Miss Clee during her last illness for a period of 12 hours. He certified the death to have occurred at 1pm, which would mean that he saw her on the day of her death at about 1am. This seems highly unlikely. It is probably a mistake rather than a lie, as I cannot see any purpose in Shipman claiming to have seen Miss Clee at that time.
It is a strange feature of many cases in which Shipman has killed that the victim is found sitting by a gas fire in a room that seems unusually warm. This occurred on enough occasions to make it appear likely that Shipman used to either put the fire on himself or turn it up. Dr Esmail has explained that rigor mortis sets in more rapidly in a warm environment than in a cold one. Also, a body resting in a warm atmosphere would lose heat more slowly than one in a cold room. Shipman often pretended that he could estimate the time of death from body temperature and often referred to body temperature when estimating the time of death on Forms B. He did not do so in this case, possibly because the body was discovered so soon after the death. I think it likely that he turned up the gas fire in Miss Clee's living room in order to make it difficult for a pathologist to make a reliable estimate of the time of death, in the event that his own statement of the time was challenged.
Miss Clee's appearance in death, seated peacefully in her chair, is not typical of that usually seen after a cardiac death or any of the causes of sudden death mentioned by Dr Esmail. It is, however, entirely typical of that seen in many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by a lethal injection of diamorphine.
Taking all the evidence into account, I feel driven to conclude that Shipman caused Miss Clee's death. In my view, the overwhelming likelihood is that Miss Clee died from a lethal injection of diamorphine.

name: Nellie Gee
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 32D Harbour Farm Road, Hyde
certified_cause: congestive heart failure due to bronchopneumonia and ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
It is likely that Mrs Gee died a natural death. It is clear that she was seriously ill on 4th
April and it was obvious to Mrs Kinsella that her mother had not long to live. Her death on 6th
April was neither sudden nor unexpected.
Shipman last saw Mrs Gee about 15 hours before her death. Before that visit Mrs Gee had been agitated and distressed. Shipman gave her an injection which he said would give relief. It is not known what the injection was, but whatever it was it produced the desired effect. It might have been an opiate or something like Largactil. Whatever it was, I do not think it could have directly caused Mrs Gee's death. A lethal dose of opiate given intramuscularly, as this injection was given, would cause death within an hour. A non-lethal but inappropriately large dose of opiate or a sedative such as Largactil would not kill outright but might depress the respiratory function and, in a patient who was already ill, might indirectly hasten the death. This is a possibility in Mrs Gee's case but I think it very likely that her death was natural.

name: Clara Hackney
title: Mrs
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to carcinoma of the stomach
conclusion:
Although it is clear that Mrs Hackney was suffering from terminal cancer and had not long to live, there are good reasons to suspect that her death was hastened by Shipman's intervention.
It would appear from the contemporaneous records that Mrs Hackney was not in pain and had not been receiving pain-relieving drugs. Probably pain was not to be expected from this type of cancer. Nor had Mrs Hackney been confined to bed for long. On the day before her death, she told the nurse that she was very tired and was sleeping more. On the day of her death, she said that she was staying in bed for most of the time. It was only for the last day or two that the district nurses had started to visit daily. It appears that Mrs Hackney might have had a night sitter for the first time on the night before her death. The general impression I have is not one of a woman whose death was imminent. That also seems to have been the impression of Mrs Alma Collins, her sister. I accept of course that cancer patients can deteriorate very quickly and die suddenly. There is evidence that Mrs Hackney had deteriorated on 14th
April and seems to have sent for her sister. It seems to me that it is medically possible that she died a natural death on that day.
The main cause for suspicion is that the death took place in Shipman's presence and followed immediately after a period of a few minutes in which Mrs Collins left Shipman alone with Mrs Hackney, at his request. In these few minutes, Shipman had the opportunity to give Mrs Hackney a lethal dose of opiate. If he gave it intravenously, as was his usual method of killing, Mrs Hackney would die within a few minutes. It seems to me that it would be an enormous coincidence if Mrs Hackney died naturally shortly after Shipman arrived and very shortly indeed after Mrs Collins had been asked to leave the room.
It seems to me that it is likely that Shipman injected Mrs Hackney and hastened her death. I think the timing of her death is too great a coincidence to admit of any other explanation. It may well be that he injected her with some of the diamorphine he had obtained in her name the day before. Certainly, the fact that he obtained that drug indicates he had on his mind that day both Mrs Hackney and diamorphine, which she did not need, at any rate in the large quantities he obtained.
This case bears a considerable resemblance to the case of Mr Harold Bramwell who died in Shipman's presence very shortly after Shipman had asked the relatives to leave the room.
The overwhelming probability is that Shipman gave Mrs Hackney a lethal dose of diamorphine which hastened her death. Despite Mrs Hackney's serious ill health, I do not think there is room for doubt about this. I am sure that Mrs Hackney's relatives appreciate that she had not long to live.

name: Thomas Alfred Longmate
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 9 Gresham Street, Denton
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis and that multiple sclerosis had contributed to the death
conclusion:
The evidence suggests that Mr Longmate was unwell on 6th
September and that the district nurse called Shipman out in an emergency. Although Mrs Forrester does not mention that her father complained of chest pain, she does say that he was sweating profusely and it is quite possible that he had suffered a heart attack.
The fact that Shipman was present at the moment of death excites a degree of suspicion that he might have caused the death. It is not known whether Shipman attempted to treat Mr Longmate in any way. If Mr Longmate were in pain or distress, it might have been appropriate for Shipman to give a small dose of a pain-relieving drug, such as diamorphine. If that were to be done, the injection should be given slowly and the process should be stopped as soon as the pain was relieved. If too much were given or if the dose were to be given too quickly, it might cause respiratory depression and death. It is not known whether the district nurse was present during the consultation. If she was, it might seem unlikely that Shipman would have attempted anything unlawful. If she was not present, it is entirely possible that he might have given an inappropriately large dose, with fatal consequences. I stress that there is no evidence that Shipman did this, but the possibility cannot be ruled out.
I regret to say that I am unable to decide whether Mr Longmate died a natural death or whether Shipman did something to cause or hasten the death.

name: Sarah Hannah Marsland
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, Flat 30 Ashton House, Victoria Street, Hyde
conclusion:
Very little information is available to me in respect of this death. Although this case has been considered without an oral hearing, I have had the advantage of hearing Mrs Saxton give evidence in connection with the death of Mrs Irene Chapman, who was killed by Shipman in 1998. I regard her as an honest witness. However, the accounts she and Mrs Antrobus have provided are what they can remember of what they were told over 20 years ago. Since that time, much has been written about Shipman's activities and there will no doubt have been much discussion of Shipman within the extended family. If the facts were as they now relate, I find it strange that Mrs Saxton, in particular, did not feel or express any concern about her grandmother's death during the three years between September 1998 and August 2001. As a result, I must approach the accounts with caution. That is not to suggest that I think the witnesses are not telling the truth. My concern is that their memories might have been affected by what they have learned of Shipman over the last three years.
Having said that, Mrs Saxton gives so graphic an account of the scene Mrs Chapman described that I am inclined to accept it. I accept that Shipman did make unsolicited visits to elderly patients and I have no reason to doubt Mrs Antrobus' word that he called on Mrs Marsland from time to time. I am satisfied from the contents of the MCCD counterfoil that Shipman saw Mrs Marsland on the day of her death, and the entries are certainly consistent with the evidence that he was present at the moment of death. If Shipman had been called out because Mrs Marsland was seriously ill, it would not be entirely surprising if she died in his presence. If she died during an unsolicited visit, this would arouse a very high degree of suspicion. It would be a remarkable coincidence.
Little is known about Mrs Marsland's state of health. Mrs Saxton says that she enjoyed good health. However, she was 86. It is the experience of the Inquiry that where a death occurred a long time ago, witnesses can and often do innocently paint a rosier picture of a relative's health than that which appears from hospital or other contemporaneous notes and records, where available. However, there is some support for the witnesses' claim that their grandmother was well. I note that on, the MCCD counterfoil, Shipman did not suggest that Mrs Marsland had any chronic heart condition which had given rise to the coronary thrombosis. I cannot rule out the possibility that Mrs Marsland had underlying cardiac disease. She was, on account of her age alone, at some risk of having a sudden fatal heart attack. However, that the risk should strike at the very moment when Shipman was visiting would be a very great coincidence. In so saying, I rely on the generic evidence of Dr John Grenville, who said that, for a doctor to be present at the death of a patient at home, where that patient was not suffering from a terminal illness or called out as an emergency, is a very rare event which might occur perhaps once in a doctor's professional career.
If Shipman had killed Mrs Marsland just before Mrs Chapman arrived, I find it strange that he should have volunteered the information that he had just called on her to see if she was 'all right'. It seems to me more likely that he would say that he had come because Mrs Marsland was ill. If he had made an unsolicited call, someone might think it was rather a coincidence that Mrs Marsland had died while he was there. This might suggest that he had not killed her and that the death, at that moment, was a genuine coincidence. I think that is unlikely and it is far more likely that Mrs Saxton's memory is at fault in this respect. It is also possible that such matters did not worry Shipman.
Shipman apparently claimed to have attempted to 'bring Mrs Marsland round', by which he probably meant that he had attempted to resuscitate her. If he said that, it must have been untrue. According to the evidence of Dr Grenville, cardiopulmonary resuscitation is most effectively carried out with the assistance of another person. As Mrs Marsland lived in warden-controlled accommodation and had an emergency cord within her flat, it is likely that assistance was readily available. Shipman does not appear to have called for the warden. To give effective resuscitation, the patient must be laid on a firm flat surface. Usually the floor is the only suitable place. If Shipman had tried to resuscitate Mrs Marsland, I would have expected that he would have put her on the floor and would probably have left her there if and when he gave up his attempts.
There are some features of this death which bear the hallmark of a case in which Shipman killed. The mere fact that the death took place in Shipman's presence following what was probably an unsolicited visit, is enough to persuade me that he probably killed Mrs Marsland. Because of the hearsay nature of the evidence and the absence of medical and surgery records, I cannot be sure of this conclusion. However, I find that Shipman probably killed Mrs Marsland.

name: Frances Potts
title: Mrs
place_of_death: The Sycamores, a residential home for the elderly, Victoria Street, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Potts' death was due to natural causes. It appears that she had had several strokes and her condition had finally deteriorated over a period of at least ten days. When the end came, her death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman saw Mrs Potts during the last two days of her life and no reason to suspect that he did anything which could have caused or hastened her death.

name: Audrey Reade
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Tameside General Hospital
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Reade died from natural causes.
It is clear that Shipman did not administer a lethal dose of opiates to Mrs Reade. There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman came into contact with Mrs Reade after her attendance at the surgery on 23rd August 1994. Even if Mrs Reade had come into contact with Shipman immediately before setting off on her journey on 3rd October 1994, the fact that she was capable of changing buses and travelling to Mossley before she collapsed shows that she had not been given a lethal or sub-lethal dose of opiates.
There is clear evidence, in the form a brain scan carried out at the hospital, that Mrs Reade died as the result of a brain haemorrhage. Mr Dyson and Mrs Bickerdike say that Mrs Reade's death was very sudden and unexpected. They are concerned that Shipman might have been able to bring about that event by some method other than the mode of killing that was uncovered at his trial. However, Dr Esmail has said that he cannot think of any way in which Shipman could have induced a delayed brain haemorrhage. It must be accepted that apparently healthy people can and do die quite unexpectedly.
My conclusion is that it is clear that Shipman did not play any part in Mrs Reade's death. I hope this decision will serve to allay the anxieties of her relatives.

name: Winifred Amy Tuffin
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
certified_cause: left ventricular failure due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Tuffin died a natural death. She was clearly unwell in the days before her death, although the nature of her illness was not understood. Professor Whitwell's opinion is that the underlying heart disease with coronary arteriosclerosis and slight enlargement of the heart, together with pyelonephritis, would be sufficient to account for death in association with a degree of heart failure. I consider that the evidence is sufficient to explain the death satisfactorily.
There is no evidence that Shipman saw Mrs Tuffin in the few hours before her death. There is no reason to suspect that he played any part in her death.

name: Henrietta Walker
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 14 Orchard Street, Hyde
conclusion:
There are several very suspicious features of this death. First and most obvious, the death was discovered very shortly after a visit by Shipman. No one saw Mrs Walker alive after Shipman's departure. If, as Shipman suggests, Mrs Walker died a natural death very shortly after he left, it would be something of a coincidence. In Shipman's professional life, this kind of 'coincidence' happened very frequently. In real life, such repeated coincidences do not occur and the temporal connection between Shipman's visit and the death is enough to lead me to the conclusion that Shipman probably killed Mrs Walker.
On Shipman's timings, as set out in the official documents, he visited at about 1.30pm while Mrs Walker was still alive and again at about 3.30pm, to certify the death. These timings do not accord with Mrs Lees' recollection but, as her memory is hazy on some details, I do not think I should find that Shipman's timings are wrong. However, on the MCCD, Shipman claimed that Mrs Walker had begun to suffer a stroke four hours before her death, which would have been at about 10.30am. That can be seen to be untrue, as when Mr Lees spoke to a receptionist at the surgery, he did not describe any sign or symptoms indicative of a stroke. A person suffering a right-sided stroke would have weakness in the right arm and leg and would probably have slurring of speech. Mr and Mrs Lees would have noticed such signs and Mr Lees would have reported them.
Dr Grenville has said in his generic evidence that an occlusive stroke (of the kind which causes weakness on one side) does not usually lead rapidly to death. Most patients survive such a stroke, with or without remaining disabilities, and those who do not, generally deteriorate gradually towards death over a period of two to three days. The circumstances prevailing here are not typical of death resulting from an occlusive stroke. It is possible that Mrs Walker died of a brain stem haemorrhage, which can cause sudden death but, if she did, Shipman cannot have diagnosed a right-sided stroke at the time of his visit. The claim that Mrs Walker died of a stroke does not ring true. My view is that Mrs Walker did not die of a stroke at all but as the result of an injection of opiate, probably diamorphine.
As Dr Grenville observed, any doctor who had a patient with signs of a stroke would not leave her alone. Whenever I find that Shipman has behaved in a way that no reasonable and competent doctor would behave, I suspect that events have not taken place as he claims. A claim that a sick patient has refused to go to hospital is a recurring theme in many cases in which Shipman killed.
This case has Shipman's hallmark on it. All the evidence either suggests that Shipman killed Mrs Walker or is consistent with the theory that he did. Although I recognise that it is possible that Mrs Walker died of a massive stroke in the brief interval between Shipman's departure and Mr Lees' return, I think that such an event would be so great a coincidence that I feel able to say that I am sure that Shipman caused Mrs Walker's death.

name: James Ashworth
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 38 Peel Street, Hyde
conclusion: Due to the lack of any evidence of the circumstances of Mr Ashworth's death, I am unable to reach a conclusion as to whether or not the death was due to natural causes.

name: Alice Black
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, Flat 32, Plain Pitt Street, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease and hypertension
conclusion:
There are several suspicious features surrounding this death.
Mrs Black had enjoyed good health and was active at the time of her death. From her medical history it appears that she was at only a slightly increased risk of heart attack. The only evidence of ill health in the period before the death comes from Miss Burgess who thought Mrs Black looked unwell at lunchtime and was sufficiently concerned to wish to speak to her in the afternoon. Save for that small indicator, Mrs Black's death was sudden and unexplained. As such, it should have been reported to the coroner. When Shipman avoided reporting a death to the coroner, in circumstances where a report should have been made, my suspicion is aroused. However, I do recognise that Shipman sometimes failed to report deaths that should have been reported even where it is clear that he had not caused the death. Accordingly, this factor is of limited probative force. However, if Mrs Black's death was from natural causes, it is not known to a satisfactory degree of certainty what the cause was. There is no basis on which it could properly be said that the cause was a heart attack.
Shipman's claim that Mrs Black had had ischaemic heart disease for two years is not borne out by the medical records. Nor was he justified in suggesting that ischaemic heart disease could have provided a working diagnosis to explain her death. If, as he claimed, Shipman had not seen Mrs Black since her appointment in the surgery on 17th
December, he would not have known that she was feeling unwell on the morning of 18th
December and had mentioned symptoms which might have been suggestive of angina. I regard it as very suspicious that Shipman should attribute the death to a coronary heart attack without any proper basis for doing so. Shipman also claimed that he had attended Mrs Black for four weeks during her last illness. Her recent attendances at the surgery had been in connection with her cough and routine blood tests. There was no last illness and this entry on Form B is a significant lie.
The position in which Mrs Black was found and her appearance in death was more consistent with an opiate death than with death from coronary thrombosis or death from any of the common causes of sudden death. Her appearance was typical of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of diamorphine.
The evidence that Shipman told Miss Black that her mother had refused to take medication for her angina is implausible and is reminiscent of his claim in several cases of unlawful killing where he has claimed that the patient had refused to be admitted to hospital.
Shipman certified that the death occurred in the early hours of the morning of 19th
December, when all the evidence suggests that it occurred on 18th
December, probably in the early afternoon. This could well be an attempt by Shipman to distance the death from the time of a visit, if in fact he did visit Mrs Black that afternoon. On the other hand, it could be that Shipman gave as the time of death the time when the deputising doctor pronounced Mrs Black dead because he had no other information on which to base his estimate. I think the former is more likely. As I have said, Shipman usually gave an estimate of the time of the death even though, if the death were natural, he would have had no idea of when it had occurred. I suspect that on this occasion the time at which the deputising doctor confirmed the death provided Shipman with a time of death a long time after his visit and that this suited his purposes.
There are some factors which suggest that Shipman was not responsible for this death. First, there is no evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Black on the day of her death. He was not seen in the vicinity, although he probably did visit a patient in Rutland Street, only a short distance away. If Shipman killed Mrs Black, he must have visited her between 1.30pm, when her grandson telephoned her, and 3pm when she failed to respond to Mrs Burgess' telephone call. There is no doubt that he could have done so. He was probably out on his rounds from that time and he had only three essential visits listed in his book. Although the evidence suggests that he had never before made an unexpected call on Mrs Black, it is well known that he often did call on patients, especially the elderly, if he happened to be in the area. There is no reason to think that Mrs Black was expecting a visit that day. However, it is possible that Mrs Black was in Shipman's mind because he had seen her in the surgery the day before. All that I can say is that an unsolicited visit was a real possibility.
Second, there is some evidence that Mrs Black's door was locked with a mortise key from the inside. If it was, the only reasonable inference is that Mrs Black locked herself in. If she did, and if Shipman had given her a lethal dose of opiate a short time previously, the injection must have been given in such a way that Mrs Black remained mobile for long enough to see Shipman out and lock the door behind him. That is possible, as an intramuscular or sub-cutaneous injection of a lethal dose of opiate would not take effect for about 15 minutes and would not reach maximal effect until about 30 minutes to an hour after administration. In his Report for the Inquiry, Professor Henry McQuay said:
'With an intramuscular dose, because of the slower absorption, it is possible that there would be a period of time between injection and the time of maximal effect of the injection during which the victim could walk and talk. As the effect of the drug began to be felt the victim would feel nauseated and could vomit, particularly if they were trying to move about. In the immediate post-injection period an onlooker might not see anything strange, but by 15 minutes, and certainly by 30 minutes, it would be clear that something strange was happening'
.
However, Shipman did not usually kill by intramuscular or subcutaneous injection. Usually he gave an intravenous injection, which takes effect very rapidly, thus enabling him to stay with the patient until he was sure he or she was dead. To leave a patient alive and mobile would be to run a grave risk of detection. If the patient began to feel ill and called for help before lapsing into unconsciousness, there would be a real risk that help would arrive in time to save the patient and allow him or her to tell the tale.
The evidence that the front door was locked on the mortise is not wholly reliable. Mr Henshaw was doing his best to describe what happened by reference to what he would usually do in such circumstances and also what actually happened on this occasion. Almost 12 months passed between the incident in question and the time when he was asked to make his police statement about it. In 1997 he was on call quite frequently and he says in terms that he had had access to many properties previously and on six occasions had found dead bodies. In those circumstances, there is a very real possibility that he is mistaken in his impression that the mortise was locked. If the door was secured only on the Yale lock, Shipman could have visited, given an intravenous injection and let himself out, leaving Mrs Black sitting in her chair.
A small factor that might suggest that the death was natural is Miss Black's report of the possible presence of vomit in the bath. If correct, this might suggest that Mrs Black had had a heart attack. It would also be consistent with her having been given an intramuscular injection of opiate, after which she was able to move about and felt sick. However, it is not consistent with the theory that she had an intravenous injection of opiate. She would not have had time to move to the bathroom before losing consciousness. It is quite possible that she had been sick for reasons totally unconnected with Shipman's attendance.
It is reported that some items were missing from the flat after the death. I note that the windows were wide open, which was unusual for December. Although there is suspicion that Shipman stole property from patients he had killed, the evidence is not strong enough for me ever to be able to infer that he was present and had killed from the mere fact that property was missing.
I have not found this an easy case to decide. There are pointers in both directions. I think the weight of the evidence suggests that Shipman probably killed Mrs Black. I am fortified in that view by the knowledge that, at this time, Shipman was killing a large number of patients. The evidence falls some way short of that which would make me sure that he killed Mrs Black but my conclusion is that he probably did.

name: Fanny Clarke
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 10 Darwin Street, Newton, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
There is strong evidence that Mrs Clarke suffered from ischaemic heart disease and was at risk of further myocardial infarction or heart attack. The evidence suggests that, on the day of her death, Shipman was called to see Mrs Clarke because she was complaining of chest pain. It is, in my view, probable that Mrs Clarke had suffered a heart attack when she called Healthcall.
The position in which Mrs Clarke was found, as to which the evidence is conflicting, does not suggest that she died as the result of an injection of opiate. No one suggests that she looked as though she was asleep.
On the other hand, the fact that Shipman was present at the moment of death excites a considerable degree of suspicion. According to the information supplied by Shipman on Form B, he attended Mrs Clarke for a period of 15 minutes before she died. His note indicates that he attempted resuscitation during this period, but Mrs Clarke's position when she was found was inconsistent with any attempt at resuscitation having been made. In any event, if a resuscitation attempt were to be made, it would be usual to summon an ambulance, as the prospects of success would be greatly enhanced by the skilled efforts of the paramedics, who would also have a defibrillator, not otherwise available to Shipman. Shipman claimed that the mode of death was coma of 20 minutes' duration. This implies that Mrs Clarke was already in a coma when Shipman arrived. In such circumstances Shipman should have contacted the ambulance service immediately. There is no suggestion that he did so. Dr John Grenville has told the Inquiry, in his generic report that:
'During the last 15 years at least, virtually all ambulance services have been able to dispatch a trained paramedic with a defibrillator to a patient whom they are told is in cardiac arrest. It follows that a doctor performing CPR
(
cardiopulmonary resuscitation
)
on a patient in the community should ensure that an ambulance is called with the least possible delay'
.
I think it is highly likely that Shipman did not attempt resuscitation and did not call an ambulance. In other words, he made no real attempt to prevent Mrs Clarke from dying. He might also have ensured her death by administering an injection of opiate but his failure to resuscitate her or call an ambulance is not probative of that. His failure to do those things is equally consistent with a decision to let Mrs Clarke die of the heart attack she had suffered. Such a decision would be entirely consistent with his general philosophy that he did not believe in prolonging life in the elderly.
There is evidence that Mrs Clarke's arm was hanging over the side of the bed. Although there is some confusion in the evidence as to whether this was her left or right arm, this evidence is consistent with her having received an injection from Shipman. If the cause of Mrs Clarke's pain was that she was suffering a heart attack, an injection of diamorphine might have been appropriate. Mr Stephen Clarke suggests that his grandmother had attempted to pull the emergency cord and this too is possible.
There is almost always cause for suspicion in connection with a death which occurred in Shipman's presence. However, in this case, the immediate background to his visit was an independently verified emergency call. Thus, it would not be particularly surprising if Mrs Clarke had died in his presence. However, Shipman does not appear to have made appropriate attempts to help or treat Mrs Clarke. He might simply have decided to let her die or he might have seized the opportunity to ensure her death by injecting her with an excessive amount of opiate. I find I am unable to reach any positive conclusion about this case, although I am suspicious about it.

name: Edith Graham
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 61 Werneth Road, Woodley, Stockport
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to carcinoma of the left breast
conclusion: I regret to say that there is insufficient evidence for me to reach any decision. Shipman certified that Mrs Graham had carcinomatosis. She may well have done but there is no evidence that she had reached the point of natural death. Shipman says that he did not see Mrs Graham alive on the day of her death but saw her body that day, after death. That might be true, but it is also possible that Shipman saw Mrs Graham alive, killed her and certified the death during the same visit. I cannot say whether this death was due to an unlawful act on the part of Shipman or whether it was a natural death.

name: Dorothy Doretta Hopkins
title: Miss
place_of_death: her home, 18 Darwin Street, Hyde
conclusion:
The evidence suggests that Shipman visited Miss Hopkins at about 10.30pm on the eve of her death. He cannot have killed her then, as she was alive the following morning.
The evidence in support of a visit late on the Saturday evening is very strong. First, there are the contemporaneous records made by Mrs Lyons on 9th
August which suggest that she asked for the doctor to visit Miss Hopkins and that he had not yet visited by 9.30pm. Second, there is the evidence of Mrs Wilde, who called on Miss Hopkins at about 9.30am on Sunday, 10th
August and took her prescription to the pharmacy. That prescription must have been written the previous evening. Third, there is the record made by Miss Kelly, the warden who attended after the death, which suggests that she was told that the doctor had visited the night before the death. Fourth, there is the Healthcall documentation which records that at 9.59pm Shipman was asked to visit Miss Hopkins. Fifth, there is Shipman's own record of the visit and his claim, entered in the duty doctor diary, which suggests that he visited Miss Hopkins at 10.30pm.
There is very little evidence that Shipman visited Miss Hopkins on 10th
August. It is clear that a return visit was a real possibility following the visit late the previous evening. However, that is not evidence of a visit. The witness evidence is conflicting and vague. There is the hearsay account of what Lottie supposedly told Mrs Haywood. That suggests that Shipman visited at about 10am, after which Miss Hopkins was alive but not entirely well and was looking forward to a sleep. She is said to have handed her keys to Lottie and asked her to return later. It is not clear when this conversation is supposed to have taken place. There is the account of what Lottie supposedly told Mr Bridge, which was that she had seen Shipman leaving Miss Hopkins' flat, but it is not clear whether this visit had taken place in the evening of 9th
or the morning of 10th
August. There is the evidence of Mrs Wilde, who last saw Miss Hopkins around noon, at which time she was in her nightdress but was able to answer the door and appeared to be not particularly unwell. She did not tell Mrs Wilde that Shipman had been that morning or was expected later that day. Shipman himself made no record relating to a visit on 10th
August. There is therefore no direct evidence to show that Shipman visited Miss Hopkins at a time when he might have killed her.
However, there remain causes to suspect that Shipman might have visited Miss Hopkins and have killed her. If he did so, it must have been at some time after Mrs Wilde's second visit. This would mean that Mrs Haywood's account of what Lottie told her was not accurate. I do not regard the reported accounts of what Lottie said to Mrs Haywood or Mr Bridge as particularly reliable. The maker of the hearsay statements is dead. It is entirely possible that Mrs Haywood and Mr Bridge are confused about what they were told.
There are four separate reasons why I suspect that Shipman might have killed Miss Hopkins. The first reason is because I suspect that Shipman's medical record is not genuine. The contents of the medical record cannot be accepted as a genuine record unless supported by other evidence. Shipman often fabricated medical records to provide a plausible explanation for a death he had caused. This entry was not made until the early morning of Monday, 11th
August, the day after the death. Although I accept that the record is genuine in that Shipman did visit in the late evening of Saturday, 9th
August, I am by no means satisfied that the record was a true account of what he found. I say that for the following reasons. First, the medical record, taken in conjunction with the duty doctor diary, suggests that Shipman visited at 10.30pm on 9th
August and found that Miss Hopkins had signs of a stroke. This is not consistent with the observations of Mrs Lyons, who had first seen Miss Hopkins at about 6.30pm, found her to be feeling sick and dizzy, called for the doctor to visit, did not record any signs of a stroke and found that she was feeling better by 9.30pm. It would be surprising, although not impossible, if Miss Hopkins had developed the signs and symptoms of a stroke some hours after the warden service contacted Healthcall requesting that a doctor visit her on account of sickness. Second, Shipman said on Form B and on the MCCD that the stroke of which Miss Hopkins was supposed to have died began three hours before her death, that is at about 11am on 10th
August, whereas according to the medical record it had already begun at 10.30pm. Third, I am suspicious of the claim that Miss Hopkins' blood pressure was raised. Shipman claimed on the MCCD that Miss Hopkins had had hypertension for ten years but the medical records do not confirm this. Fourth, I am suspicious of his claim that she had been falling to the right. If that were true, I would have expected Mrs Lyons to mention it in at least one of her records of 9th
August and for this information to be passed on to Healthcall. Moreover, if Miss Hopkins had a developing stroke, I would have expected Mrs Wilde to observe some signs of it on the morning of 10th
August. It appears that she did not. Fifth, if Miss Hopkins really was showing signs of a stroke, I do not think a competent doctor, acting honestly in the interests of his patient, would leave her alone overnight without ensuring that a relative or friend was aware of the situation and could keep an eye on her. Sixth, Shipman's note that Miss Hopkins was to let him know if her condition were to alter, is typical of notes I have seen in many cases in which Shipman has killed his patient. In general, he used this device to make it appear that the patient had been quite ill when last seen by him so that the subsequent death was explicable, but not so ill as to require admission to hospital or the summoning of a relative. Considering these factors, I think it likely that this computerised entry is false. I think it unlikely that Miss Hopkins showed any signs of a stroke on 9th
August or, for that matter, on 10th
August.
The second reason why I suspect that Shipman might have killed Miss Hopkins is because the contents of the certificates are suspicious. I have already mentioned that there is an inconsistency between Shipman's claim on the MCCD that the stroke began three hours before death and his medical note, which suggests that it had begun the previous evening. There are several suspicious features on Form B. First, Shipman claims to know at what time Miss Hopkins died, although he also said that no one was present with her at the death. He could not possibly have known. If this had been a natural death occurring in the absence of any witness, Shipman could only have given the bracket within which the death must have occurred. Shipman often pretended to know the time of a death when he wanted to distance the time of his visit from the death. He frequently placed the death several hours after his own last visit and, especially in the later years when his devices became more elaborate, he often claimed that someone had seen the patient alive since his last visit. Here, I suspect that he has done both. If we postulate that Shipman visited Miss Hopkins at, say, between noon and 1pm and killed her, he would wish to distance the death from his visit. He might not know whether his visit had been observed. Here he said that the death occurred at 2pm. He also claimed that someone had seen Miss Hopkins alive at 2pm, an inconsistency which seems to demonstrate a degree of carelessness on his part, whether guilty of killing Miss Hopkins or not. There is no evidence available to the Inquiry to suggest that a neighbour saw Miss Hopkins alive at 2pm. It is possible that Shipman is right and that Lottie had seen Miss Hopkins alive at that time and had told Shipman so. However, the making of a false entry of this nature would be entirely typical of Shipman's practice in the late 1990s. Second, on Form B Shipman claimed that he had last seen Miss Hopkins alive about 24 hours before death, which would suggest that he had seen her in the early afternoon of 9th
August. There is no other evidence to support that and it is inconsistent with his own medical note. Third, I am also suspicious of Shipman's claim that Miss Hopkins had been in a coma for two to three hours before her death. There is no way in which he could have known that and no one who could have given him that information. It is not something which a doctor could infer from the circumstances. In any event, that entry is inconsistent with the entry below it, where Shipman says that Miss Hopkins was seen by a neighbour at 2pm. That implies that the neighbour saw her in a coma but went away and did not find her dead until three hours later. That seems rather unlikely. There is also an inconsistency between the time at which Shipman said in his medical record that the body had been found and the time stated on Form B.
In short, the certificates present a confused and inconsistent picture of the timing of events. I accept that these inconsistencies might be explained by mere carelessness on Shipman's part. However, they are also consistent with a desire to present a picture of the circumstances which will not cast suspicion on him. If he had visited and killed Miss Hopkins at, say, between noon and 1pm, he would wish to create the impression that she had died some time later and had been seen alive by another after his visit. If he were seeking to present the picture of a stroke death, he might well wish to suggest a period of coma. I suspect that his desire to create the desired impressions led him into making inconsistent statements.
The third reason why I suspect that Shipman might have killed Miss Hopkins is that I am also slightly suspicious about the position in which Miss Hopkins was found. It appears that she was lying propped up on her pillows with the covers brought up over her chest. It seems rather unlikely that she could have gone to bed, then had a stroke and fallen into a coma and died and yet have remained so neatly arranged in bed. Yet her position and appearance in bed were very much what one might expect if she had been given an injection of strong opiate and had died in Shipman's presence. However, it is possible that she fell into a deep sleep on the afternoon of 10th
August and suffered a sudden heart attack or haemorrhagic stroke while asleep.
The fourth reason is that it would not be at all surprising if Shipman had killed Miss Hopkins. I take into account that, in 1997, Shipman was killing patients at a very high rate. This death has some of Shipman's hallmarks.
This is not an easy case to decide. In favour of a natural death, there is evidence that Miss Hopkins was unwell, although those who saw her did not have the impression that she was seriously ill. It is possible that she died a natural death during the afternoon of 10th
August. There is no direct evidence of a visit by Shipman after Mrs Wilde's departure, although an unsolicited second visit would not have been atypical of him. In favour of Shipman's unlawful involvement, there is the creation of a false medical record and a series of conflicting and, I think, self-serving entries on the MCCD and Form B. After some hesitation, I have come to the conclusion that it is likely that Shipman killed Miss Hopkins.

name: Gertrude McLoughlin
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 30 Sidley Place, Hyde
conclusion:
In the absence of the medical records it is not possible to discover the nature of the last illness, which seems to have begun, as Mr McLoughlin recalls, about two weeks before the death. According to the visits book, Shipman visited Mrs McLoughlin with increasing frequency from 30th April and was at her home on 8th
and 9th
May.
It is not possible to form a clear picture of the events preceding Mrs McLoughlin's death as the two witnesses have rather different recollections. However, there is nothing in the statement of either witness to suggest that the visits book is inaccurate.
There is no evidence that Shipman gave Mrs McLoughlin any specific treatment during any of his visits and certainly no evidence that he administered any injections. Even if he had given an injection on Wednesday, 9th
May, as Mr McLoughlin suggests, that injection could not have contained a lethal dose of opiate and could not have caused Mrs McLoughlin's death in the early hours of Thursday morning. Professor Henry McQuay and Dr John Grenville have given joint generic evidence to the Inquiry as to the timing and effect of opiates. If a lethal injection of opiate is administered intravenously, death will follow within minutes. If administered intramuscularly, a lethal dose will cause death within about an hour. That Mrs McLoughlin lived for at least 12 hours after Shipman's last visit shows that Shipman did not directly cause her death by giving a lethal dose of opiate.
I have considered also the possibility that Shipman might have over-sedated Mrs McLoughlin during the last few days of her life. Over-sedation can render an elderly patient more vulnerable to the development of bronchopneumonia, a common mechanism of death in the elderly. However, there is no evidence that Mrs McLoughlin was unconscious in the last few days. On the contrary, Mr McLoughlin says that he expected his mother to recover and he can recall nothing out of the ordinary when he saw her on the evening before she died. I rule out the possibility of over-sedation.
I am quite satisfied that Mrs McLoughlin died a natural death.

name: Vara Penney
title: Miss
place_of_death: her home, 8 Rowbotham Street, Hyde
conclusion:
It seems likely that Miss Penney died of natural causes, probably some form of cancer.
The history of gradual deterioration and increasing weakness is entirely typical of the progression of many forms of cancer. During the last two weeks of her life she was very weak, often comatose and could hardly communicate. Her death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
There is some cause for concern in this case because Shipman claimed that he had last seen Miss Penney alive on the day of the death. Miss Penney's friend does not remember him visiting that day, but she might have forgotten. If he did visit, it seems to me unlikely that the visit could have been at or shortly before the death; Miss Penney's friend would have remembered that.
My conclusion is that Miss Penney almost certainly died of natural causes.

name: Kate Maud Sellors
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, Flat 6 Ashton House, Victoria Street, Hyde
conclusion:
As Dr Grenville has said, it is possible that Mrs Sellors died of a stroke during the afternoon of 4th
May. However, there are a number of highly suspicious factors surrounding her death.
Mrs Sellors was discovered to be dead shortly after a visit from Shipman. This visit probably took place at about 2pm. Shipman was the last person to see her alive. This in itself is a highly suspicious factor.
Shipman said to Mrs Marshall that he had visited Mrs Sellors at around 8am. He could have done, although it seems unlikely. There is no reason to think that Mrs Dick would have visited Mrs Sellors earlier than her usual time of 8.30am. If Shipman had already been to see Mrs Sellors, it is highly unlikely that she would have asked Mrs Dick to telephone the surgery without telling her that Shipman had been there within the last half hour. We know that Mrs Dick telephoned the surgery, which did not open until about 8.30am. We know that her message was recorded by a receptionist in the usual way. Until about 8am, Shipman's calls would usually be transferred to the deputising service, Healthcall, who would contact Shipman to see whether he wished a duty doctor to attend or to deal with the matter himself. Only if Mrs Dick had telephoned very early could a message have reached Shipman before he arrived at the surgery. It is possible that Mrs Dick had visited Mrs Sellors very early and had then telephoned the surgery and a message had reached Shipman before he left home. So he could have visited Mrs Sellors at 8am as he claimed. However, this is very unlikely, first because I think Mrs Dick would have remembered that unusual course of events and second because I would not then have expected to find the message requesting a visit recorded in the visits book by a member of staff. I am almost certain his claim to have visited at 8am is a lie.
Experience shows that Shipman's medical records can never be relied on as an honest or accurate account of events. These notes contain familiar suspicious features. It appears to me that in making entries on the computer Shipman has tried to create the impression that he visited twice on 4th
May while Mrs Sellors was still alive. Shipman does not state this expressly but he seeks to give the impression that, on a first occasion, he diagnosed a minor haemorrhagic stroke and advised Mrs Sellors that she should be admitted to hospital; he implies that she was not keen on the idea. This is a regular feature of Shipman's explanations of the circumstances surrounding his patients' deaths. In this series of notes, Shipman implies that he visited Mrs Sellors later in the day, to see what she had decided and, because she would not go to hospital, he decided to arrange a domiciliary visit by a consultant. This again is a common feature of cases in which Shipman has killed. The patient always dies before the consultant is contacted. The notes do not make good medical sense. As Dr Grenville has observed, it is not possible to distinguish between a haemorrhagic and an occlusive stroke on clinical grounds. Nor is there any sensible reason to call a consultant if the patient declines to go into hospital. If Mrs Sellors had really refused to go to hospital, it would have made sense if Shipman had sought to make arrangements for her care at home. I think these notes are fabricated.
Shipman admitted having administered an injection. He might have made this admission because he was aware that he had left Mrs Sellors' sleeve rolled up. As far as Dr Grenville is aware, there is no injection that might appropriately be administered to a patient suffering a stroke in the circumstances described by Shipman. On the other hand, Shipman's method of unlawfully killing his patients was to administer a lethal dose of opiates by injection.
Shipman's response to the news of the death is suspicious. He said he had expected Mrs Sellors to die. In his generic evidence to the Inquiry, Dr Grenville stated that of patients suffering a cerebrovascular accident approximately one third would be expected to die within a month, another third would survive but with disability and may die later of the complications and the final third would make a reasonable recovery. In the computerised medical records Shipman described the cerebrovascular accident as minor in nature. Therefore, even if Mrs Sellors' presentation was as recorded in the medical notes, far from there being an expectation of death, death would have come as a surprise. Of course, Shipman would not have been surprised at the news of the death if he already knew she was dead.
Taking these matters into account, I have come to the conclusion that Shipman killed Mrs Sellors. I do not think that he visited her at 8am. I think he visited her at about 2pm. She might well have suffered a minor stroke. I think it likely that he gave her an injection, not to 'bring her round' but to kill her. It is likely that the injection was diamorphine, which we know he often had with him. I think he made a false set of entries on the computer after the event. Although there is a theoretical possibility that Mrs Sellors suffered a fatal stroke, I feel able to say that I am sure that Shipman killed her.

name: Florence Taylor
title: Miss
place_of_death: her home, 8 Walker Close, Hyde
conclusion:
It is difficult to be sure about Miss Taylor's state of health in the absence of her medical records but her age, combined with her history of raised blood pressure, put her at increased risk of sudden death and made her vulnerable to a relatively rapid death resulting from bronchopneumonia. There is clear evidence that on 26th
June, she was laid up in bed with a chest infection. Her perception was that she was a 'poorly lady'. If there were no suggestion of a subsequent visit by Shipman, I would have no reason to suspect that her death resulted from anything other than the natural progression of a severe chest infection and bronchopneumonia.
Whilst none of the documents produced by Shipman suggest that he did visit Miss Taylor on the day of her death or on the previous day, Mrs Stubbs remembers being told that he did visit. Although she cannot be sure, the impression she formed when she spoke to her mother on the morning of Miss Taylor's death was that Shipman had visited at some time early that morning rather than on the previous evening.
Mrs Stubbs remembers that her mother told her that Miss Taylor was given an injection to help with her breathing. I think that the doctor referred to was Shipman, although it may be that he called later than Mrs Stubbs remembers. Whilst it might have been legitimate for Shipman to give some sort of injection to assist with Miss Taylor's breathing, I would be extremely suspicious that the injection in question had been of morphine or diamorphine if the death occurred shortly afterwards. I say that, not only because of what I know about Shipman's general method of killing, but also because had Miss Taylor died as a result of heart problems, induced by an injection of aminophylline or salbutamol, she would have died as the injection was being given or immediately afterwards, which is clearly not the case.
I am, therefore, suspicious about the close connection in time between the visit that Mrs Stubbs remembers and Miss Taylor's death. I think it unlikely that Shipman gave a lethal intravenous dose of morphine or diamorphine when he saw Miss Taylor because this would have resulted in death within a small number of minutes and that is not the impression that Mrs Stubbs was given by her mother. On the other hand, it is possible that Shipman gave a lethal intramuscular injection in which case the death might not take place until one hour after the administration of the injection. Even if Shipman had visited the previous evening, if the effect of any injection given during the course of that visit was to heavily sedate Miss Taylor, in effect to put her into a coma, then it could be that the effect of such sedation was to hasten her death by rendering her more vulnerable to the onset or progression of fatal bronchopneumonia.
I gain little comfort from what Shipman wrote on the MCCD counterfoil and on Form B of the cremation forms, which are, as I have pointed out, inconsistent. Although he does not suggest that he saw Miss Taylor on the day of her death, he does admit on the cremation forms that he last saw her alive 18 hours before her death and this is precisely the duration of the coma which he said represented the mode of her death. I am inclined to accept Mrs Stubbs' evidence that her great-aunt was conscious and alert the previous evening, evidence which is inconsistent with Shipman's assertion about the coma.
The circumstances of this case do not allow me to reach a positive conclusion that Shipman unlawfully killed Miss Taylor but I am, unfortunately, suspicious that he did.

name: Muriel Margaret Ward
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 41 Ogden Court, Frank Street, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
Mrs Ward had some history of heart disease and was probably at an increased risk of heart attack. However, the circumstances of her death make it extremely unlikely that this was the cause of her death.
The most obviously suspicious feature is that the death was discovered within a very short time of Shipman's first visit to Mrs Ward. Working back from the time at which Miss Ward alerted Eldercare (2.37pm), it would appear likely that she arrived back from the shops at about 2.30 to 2.35pm. She had only been to do some shopping at Kwik Save and she thought she had not been out for more than a few minutes according to Mrs Simpson. More likely, she would have been out for about half an hour. On Form B, Shipman suggested that the death occurred at 2.30pm and that he had been with Mrs Ward 15 minutes earlier. It appears to me that Shipman probably arrived at or shortly after 2pm. Thus, Mrs Ward was alive and well when Shipman arrived and Miss Ward left to go shopping. According to Shipman, Mrs Ward was well when he left at 2.15pm. Fifteen minutes later, she was dead. It is of course physically possible to suffer a fatal heart attack within that short time span. If the doctor involved were not Shipman, one would say that it was strange and remarkable that Mrs Ward should die just after the doctor had left, but one would not say it was wholly unbelievable. However, with Shipman, a known serial killer, such a coincidence is beyond belief. That evidence alone persuades me that Shipman must have killed Mrs Ward. However, there are other aspects of the evidence that point to the same conclusion.
If events had taken place as Shipman suggested, he would not have had any real idea of why Mrs Ward had died, shortly after his departure.
