As Dr Grenville said, Mrs Ward was certainly as much at risk of dying of cardiac arrhythmia or pulmonary embolism as coronary thrombosis. No one had seen Mrs Ward in her death throes so as to provide Shipman with information from which he could infer that she had had a heart attack. This death should have been referred to the coroner. However, Shipman would not wish that to happen as, if the post-mortem examination had not revealed a plausible cause of death, the coroner might have commissioned toxicological tests.
Mrs Ward was found sitting in her chair, looking peaceful. Her appearance in death was not consistent with the appearance of one who had died of a coronary thrombosis. It was, however, entirely typical of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of diamorphine.
I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Ward, as he was later to kill her daughter, almost certainly by a lethal injection of diamorphine.

name: Arthur Bent
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 15 Meadowfield Court, Hyde
conclusion:
By the time of his death, Mr Bent was very frail. He was known to suffer from cardiac arrhythmia. His son wondered from week to week whether he would see his father alive again. Mr Bent's death cannot be described as unexpected.
There is no evidence that Shipman had access to Mr Bent on the day of his death. He could have had access without inconvenience to himself, but there is no evidence that he did. So far, there is no reason to suppose that Shipman was in any way involved in this death.
There are, however, some suspicious features. It is slightly strange that Mr Bent's front door was ajar. This is a feature which is not uncommon in Shipman killings and usually gives rise to some suspicion. However, there is another possible explanation in this case. The meals on wheels staff might have left the door ajar. As the door had a Yale lock, if Shipman had been there, it would have been more typical of him to close it behind him as he left.
A rather more suspicious feature is Mr Bent's appearance in death, which is typical of a Shipman victim. However, the point does not carry much weight, as Dr Grenville says that it is possible to die of a fatal arrhythmia while asleep, in which case the appearance in death would not be inconsistent with a natural death.
Another feature, which raises some suspicion in my mind, is Shipman's claim that he knew the time of Mr Bent's death. He said he had died at about 8pm. There is no way in which Shipman could possibly have known the time of death. Shipman often claimed that he could estimate the time of death so as to create the impression that the death had occurred a considerable time after he had visited the patient. Often he pretended that he could tell the time of death from body temperature, which can only be done if an internal temperature is taken and is, even then, a difficult process. Here Shipman simply stated the time of death. He had no basis for doing so.
There are some other puzzling features to this death. First, Shipman seems to have been anxious to avoid a referral to the coroner. I am quite satisfied that he lied on Form B and the MCCD when he claimed that he had last seen Mr Bent alive on 10th
May. I think he fabricated an entry in the medical records to suggest that he had seen him alive on 12th
May. I do not think he had seen Mr Bent since 6th
December 1994. I think he well knew that he was not qualified to sign the MCCD, even though he had seen the body after death, and I think he knew he ought to refer the death to the coroner. He virtually admitted as much to Mr Michael Bent. That he sought to avoid referral to the coroner does not necessarily imply guilt. Shipman might have wished to save the family the upset of a post-mortem examination. Certainly, Mr Michael Bent was keen to avoid one. Alternatively, Shipman might simply have wanted to avoid the time and trouble of a referral to the coroner.
Second, Shipman certified an inappropriate cause of death. He must have known that Mr Bent had not deteriorated to the extent where such a cause was warranted. But he seems also to have been confident that neither the registrar nor the medical referee would query old age as a cause of death in a man of 90. The odd thing is that, if Shipman had bothered to read Mr Bent's medical records, he could have found a perfectly plausible cause of death, a fatal cardiac arrhythmia due to ischaemic heart disease.
There are reasons to believe that Mr Bent died a natural death. There are other reasons why I suspect that Shipman killed Mr Bent but I do not feel able to make a positive decision either way.

name: Edith Calverley
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 19 Mansfield Road, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
Mrs Calverley was not in good health at the time of her death. She apparently had a history of ischaemic heart disease and would have been at a significantly increased risk of suffering a sudden cardiac death. Her sudden death was unexpected to her family but cannot be regarded as improbable.
Shipman visited Mrs Calverley on the last day of her life. Why he visited is not known. However, there is nothing in the evidence to suggest that the visit was called for as an emergency. If anything, it seems likely to have been a routine matter.
Mrs Calverley's death was discovered early in the morning on the day after a visit by Shipman. It seems likely that he was the last person to see or speak to her before her death, although this cannot be positively asserted. Mrs Winson's recollection of the events of the previous day is far from perfect. However, I think it likely that when Mrs Winson returned to see her mother on the Monday afternoon, as I think she did, Shipman had probably not yet visited Mrs Calverley. If he had already visited, I think Mrs Calverley would have told her daughter that he had and Mrs Winson would not have forgotten about it. If Shipman were the last person to see Mrs Calverley alive, my suspicions would be aroused.
That Mrs Calverley's doors were unlocked in the early morning would suggest that she had almost certainly died before changing into her nightclothes and retiring to bed the night before.
Shipman's note in the medical record for 16th
August appears incomplete. That may be because the remaining part of the note, written on a new card or separate piece of paper, has been lost. However, the note as it stands suggests that Mrs Calverley told Shipman that she had had a sudden onset of pain in the neck and chest a day earlier and had had pain on and off. Although Mrs Calverley suffered from ischaemic heart disease, it does not appear that she often complained of chest pain. I would have thought that, if Mrs Calverley had had chest pain the day before or that morning, she would have told her daughter about it. I am very suspicious of Shipman's claim that Mrs Calverley complained to him of chest pain. I suspect that he has fabricated a note to provide a plausible explanation for her death. He has done this in a large number of cases in which he has killed his patient.
If Mrs Calverley did complain of chest and neck pain and if Shipman had really thought she was having or had had a coronary thrombosis, one would have expected him to do something about it. He might have admitted her to hospital. At the very least, he should have alerted her daughter. It is possible that there was originally more to the medical note than is now available. I cannot be certain that he did not have any treatment plan for Mrs Calverley. However, I am sure that he did not contact her daughter. On his supposed account, he saw Mrs Calverley at about noon and left her alone. No sensible doctor would have done that with an elderly woman suffering a suspected heart attack. I suspect that he came later than he admitted and left Mrs Calverley alone because she was already dead.
Shipman told two important lies on Form B. First, he said that he had been treating Mrs Calverley for three weeks during her last illness. This suggests that she had been suffering from ischaemic heart disease for three weeks before her death. She had not. For two of those weeks she had been on holiday in North Wales. There is not a shred of evidence that he had seen her at all in that three week period. The medical records show that he had not seen her since early July.
Shipman's second lie was to pretend that he could estimate the time of Mrs Calverley's death from her body temperature. It is not possible to make any reliable estimate of the time of death unless an internal body temperature is taken, usually within the rectum. Shipman did not do that. Even if that had been done, it is highly unlikely that Shipman had the expertise to make a reliable estimate. In his generic evidence, Dr John Grenville says that this is a matter for a skilled pathologist. Shipman often claimed that he could estimate the time of death and used this as a means of creating the impression that the death had occurred a considerable time after he had been with the patient. I think that is what he has done here. He has pretended that the death occurred at about midnight in order to distance the death from his visit the previous afternoon.
The position in which Mrs Calverley was found does not suggest that she died of a coronary thrombosis. Dr Grenville says that most patients who have a fatal heart attack are found collapsed in circumstances which suggest that they have been trying to seek help. If Mrs Calverley had wanted to call for help, she could have pulled on one of her emergency cords. The evidence suggests that she did not. Her appearance in death was, however, similar to that of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by a lethal injection of opiate.
Taking all these factors into account, I conclude that Shipman probably killed Mrs Calverley. I stop short of saying that I am sure of this conclusion. Mrs Calverley was at some risk of a sudden cardiac death. I cannot be certain that she was not seen alive after Shipman's visit on 16th
August. The missing part of the medical record, if there was more, might contain relevant information. Notwithstanding those uncertainties in the evidence, I think that Shipman probably killed Mrs Calverley.

name: Violet Garlick
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Pole Bank Hall residential care home, Stockport Road, Hyde
conclusion:
Mrs Garlick had been in poor health for some years and her condition had gradually deteriorated. When her son visited her on the evening of 7th
April, she appears to have been unconscious and he realised that she would not live long. Her death during the ensuing night was neither sudden nor unexpected.
Without the medical records or any nursing records from Pole Bank Hall, it is not possible for me to say which doctor visited Mrs Garlick on 7th
April. It might have been Shipman, although when completing the MCCD counterfoil he did not say he had seen Mrs Garlick on 7th
April but said that he last saw her alive on 5th
April. However, Shipman was often careless in the way he completed MCCDs and cremation certificates.
It is quite possible that it was Shipman who visited Mrs Garlick in the late afternoon of 7th
April. Even if he did, he cannot have given her a lethal injection of an opiate because Mrs Garlick was alive when her son left the home at about 10.30pm. A lethal injection of opiate given in the late afternoon would have caused her death long before 10.30pm.
Mr Garlick thinks that a member of staff said that the doctor who had visited earlier would call back later that night. If that doctor were Shipman, there might be a possibility that he came back to the home and gained access to Mrs Garlick. I think that is most unlikely. I think perhaps there was a misunderstanding about the second visit, as it seems most unlikely that a doctor would undertake to return late at night. In any event, Dr Carroll, who was on duty that night, handed over to the deputising service at 8.30pm. It seems to me most likely that the doctor who visited said he would call back the following day rather than that evening. It would be most unusual for Shipman to return late at night, particularly to a home where night staff were available to care for the patient. I feel able to rule out the possibility that Shipman killed Mrs Garlick by administering a lethal dose of opiate late at night.
If Shipman did visit Mrs Garlick on 7th
April, it is possible that he administered an injection of a sedative, for example Largactil, which had the effect of putting Mrs Garlick to sleep. This would have been a reasonable thing to do if it was the only way to keep her comfortable. However, if the dose was very large and if Mrs Garlick was kept asleep for a long time, this would have increased her vulnerability to bronchopneumonia, a common mechanism of death in elderly people who have suffered strokes. If Shipman did this, it would not be possible to say whether he genuinely considered it to be the only way of keeping Mrs Garlick comfortable or whether he used it as an indirect way of hastening her death.
My conclusion is that it is highly likely that Mrs Garlick died a natural death. I cannot absolutely rule out the possibility that Shipman deliberately gave her a large dose of sedative in the late afternoon of 7th
April, which could have had the effect of hastening her death. However, there is no evidence that he did.

name: John Hilton
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 13 Queens Drive, Gee Cross, Hyde
certified_cause: congestive heart failure due to hypertension and diabetes mellitus
conclusion:
It is clear that Mr Hilton had gangrene in his right foot and leg and that he was doomed to die very soon unless he had his leg amputated. However, it appears that the consultant surgeon did not expect him to die as the result of gangrene as early as 4th
November. Shipman does not suggest that gangrene was the direct cause of death.
Mr Hilton had many other underlying conditions, any one of which could have been fatal. Only the day before his death, he had a hypoglycaemic attack. He could have had another, which could have been fatal, but it appears that he did not. According to Shipman, the death was due to congestive heart failure. Yet there is no indication in the medical records that Mr Hilton's underlying heart failure was reaching a critical stage. There is no description of the process of death in the medical records. This causes me (as it caused Professor Baker) to suspect that the death might not have been natural. Congestive heart failure was one of the causes of death most frequently relied on by Shipman when he had killed a patient.
Mr Hilton was, in some respects, typical of Shipman's victims. True, he was not an elderly woman, living alone. However, he was in very poor health, had been receiving a very high level of medical and nursing care and was about to undergo an operation which would probably prolong his life but which would result in the prolongation of the high level of care. I think it likely that Shipman took the view that Mr Hilton's quality of life would never be good. I have come across a number of cases where Shipman killed patients whose quality of life he knew was poor or who were causing difficulties for their carer or were expensive to the National Health Service. Mr Hilton fell into that category.
There is no clear evidence that Shipman was at Mr Hilton's house on the morning of 4th
November while he was still alive. The visits book suggests that Shipman was aware that he was needed urgently at Mr Hilton's house. There is no urgency after death. There is other evidence to suggest that Shipman did not attend at the house that morning, while Mr Hilton was alive. Shipman himself said in the computerised medical records, on the MCCD and on Form B that he had last seen Mr Hilton alive on 3rd
November. I do not attach great weight to anything Shipman says unless corroborated by others, as he frequently told lies in medical records and certification documents. There is no convincing corroboration of his claim. Mrs Wigley did not see him when she arrived at the Hiltons' house on 4th
November. That proves nothing. Shipman could have been there earlier and have given Mr Hilton a lethal injection. He was held in such high regard by Mrs Hilton that he could easily have given her a plausible account of his intentions.
I regret to say that I do not feel able to reach a positive conclusion in this case. A natural death was entirely possible and would not have been wholly unexpected. On the other hand, there are real causes for concern and suspicion that Shipman might have caused the death.

name: Edith Leech
title: Mrs
place_of_death: The Sycamores, a residential home for the elderly, Victoria Street, Hyde
conclusion:
I regret to say that it is not possible for me to say Mrs Leech died as a result of natural causes or alternatively as a result of an unlawful act on the part of Shipman. She was clearly unwell and unable to look after herself. Despite that, the witnesses who saw her in the days before she died remember that she appeared well and say her death was unexpected and came as a shock.
There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman played any part in Mrs Leech's death. The only possible grounds for suspicion are, first, that Mrs Leech's death seemed sudden and unexpected and, second, that although Shipman claimed that he last saw Mrs Leech alive almost two weeks before her death, his visits book suggests that he visited The Sycamores on the day of her death.

name: Christina McCulloch Mackie
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Pole Bank Residential Care Home (Pole Bank Hall) in Hyde
conclusion:
It seems very likely that Mrs Mackie died of natural causes.
There is very little evidence of Mrs Mackie's health in the weeks before her death. It would appear that Mrs Mackie became senile and deteriorated gradually. She was said to have been in a coma for ten days before her death. If that is right, as her son confirms that it is, her death cannot have been sudden or unexpected.
The only information about Shipman's access to Mrs Mackie comes from Shipman's visits book for 1985 and his entries on the MCCD counterfoil and Form B. All these documents suggest that Shipman last saw Mrs Mackie alive two days before her death.
I cannot absolutely rule out the possibility that Shipman visited Mrs Mackie on the day of her death and injected her with a lethal substance. However, there is no reason to suppose that he did. As I have said, it seems highly likely that Mrs Mackie died a natural death.

name: Annie Rowbottom
title: Miss
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Miss Rowbottom died of natural causes. The daily diary charts the course of a gradual decline. Her death was neither sudden nor unexpected. It does not appear that Shipman saw her for some days before she died. Although her name appears in Shipman's visits book for the day of her death, the likelihood is that this entry was made after the death.
There is an inconsistency between the date Shipman gave on the certificates as the last occasion when he saw Miss Rowbottom alive and the entries in the visits book and daily diary. However, Shipman was often careless in completing death and cremation forms and I do not think the discrepancies give rise to suspicion that he was involved in this death.

name: Ernest Shawcross
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 47 Lyne View, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mr Shawcross died a natural death.
The nature of the treatment given by Shipman during his visit on the morning of 11th
March is unclear. It is recorded in the two reports prepared by the police that Shipman gave Mr Shawcross at least one injection. The recollection of both Mr Kenneth Shawcross and Mrs Hudson, however, is that they were told that Shipman gave him tablets. That does not exclude the possibility that Shipman gave both an injection and tablets. If Shipman did give an injection, it cannot have caused Mr Shawcross' death. If it had been a large dose of opiate, Mr Shawcross would have fallen asleep soon afterwards and would have died within the hour. As it was, he remained awake for some hours after Shipman's first visit.
Professor Henry McQuay and Dr John Grenville have given joint generic evidence to the Inquiry as to the timing and effect of opiates. If a lethal injection of opiates is given intravenously, death follows within minutes. If given intramuscularly, a lethal injection would cause death within about an hour. According to the reports prepared by the police at the time, Shipman visited Mr Shawcross at about 11am, and Mr Shawcross died more than four hours later at 3.20pm.
There is a possibility that Shipman misdiagnosed Mr Shawcross' condition. He seems to have thought that Mr Shawcross had congestive heart failure. This might explain why he did not arrange for Mr Shawcross to be admitted to hospital and why he seemed surprised at the death. I have the impression that his surprise was genuine and think he might have made an honest mistake about Mr Shawcross' condition. I think he probably gave an injection designed to relieve congestive heart failure, which Mr Shawcross did not have. It is not now possible to discover what treatment he gave or why. However, resolution of this issue does not affect the ultimate issue as to whether Shipman unlawfully killed Mr Shawcross.
There seems no doubt as to the cause of death. The physical findings and the witness evidence are consistent with death due to gastro-intestinal haemorrhage.

name: May Warren
title: Mrs
certified_cause: left ventricular failure due to ischaemic and hypertensive heart disease
conclusion:
In my view, it is highly likely that Mrs Warren died as the result of natural causes. Very little indeed is known about her medical history, but it is clear that she had a severe degree of ischaemic heart disease. It would appear that this gave rise to only minor symptoms of discomfort, which Mrs Warren attributed to indigestion. It seems likely that she might have used a proprietary indigestion remedy. It appears that on the evening of 21st
July, her symptoms were rather more severe and she told Mrs Chatburn that she had chest pain. Although Mrs Chatburn advised her to call the doctor, I think it is very unlikely that she would have done so. Her daughter says that she was wary of doctors and it appears that she had not seen a doctor for eight years. I think, therefore, it is unlikely that she would have called the doctor out either late on the Saturday night or early on Sunday morning. I think it is more likely that she took a dose of indigestion medicine and left the glass by the sink. I think that at some stage, her symptoms became suddenly worse and she must have opened the back door to get some fresh air. Dr Grenville says that this is a common reaction in patients suffering from acute ventricular failure. I think she must then have collapsed onto her chair, slumped over the table and died. Whether this happened in the late evening shortly before she went to bed, or shortly after she got up in the morning, I do not think we will ever know.
It is theoretically possible that Mrs Warren telephoned for a doctor, either late on Saturday evening or early on Sunday morning, and that Shipman visited her. If he did, it is possible that he killed her. However, in all the circumstances, I regard that as extremely unlikely.
The fact that a visit by Shipman cannot be ruled out makes it impossible to conclude that her death was due to natural causes. If he did attend, there is a possibility that he could have killed her with a lethal injection of diamorphine. The major findings at post-mortem examination, however, reveal that Mrs Warren had severe underlying natural heart disease and the heart showed evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy. These findings could explain the death but in the absence of evidence of acute pathology, cannot be said definitively to do so.

name: Lily Broadbent
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 27 Welbeck Road, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. First and most obvious, Mrs Broadbent was found dead very soon after a visit from Shipman. Although she was unwell on the day of her death, Mrs Broadbent did not appear to Mrs Rawson to be seriously ill. In Form B, Shipman sought to suggest that Mrs Broadbent had died a sudden natural death about two hours after he left. People aged 75 sometimes do suffer fatal heart attacks without any prior warning. If this were the only case where a patient of Shipman had apparently suffered a heart attack or stroke shortly after he had visited, I would accept without hesitation that the temporal connection was pure coincidence. I would even accept it if it had happened two or three times. But Shipman would have us believe that this type of coincidence happened very frequently. I cannot accept that and I regard this kind of temporal connection as a highly suspicious factor.
There are other causes for suspicion. In Form B, Shipman sought to present a picture of a woman who had been suffering from cardiac symptoms since 10am, whom he visited at about 2pm (possibly for the second time, the first having been at 10am) and found suffering from a coronary thrombosis, atrial fibrillation and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. Had Mrs Broadbent been suffering from symptoms of that kind in the morning, I would have expected the surgery staff to treat her request for a visit as an emergency and either to arrange for Shipman to attend quickly or to telephone for an ambulance. I would also have expected Mrs Broadbent to look ill and Mrs Rawson to be concerned about her. Even if the seriousness of the situation had not been appreciated until Shipman's arrival, I would then have expected him to advise Mrs Broadbent to go into hospital. Of course, if we had the medical records, we might see that he claimed to have advised admission but that Mrs Broadbent had refused. A very large number of Shipman's patients refused to accept his advice to go into hospital if Shipman is to be believed. This is a recurring theme in the records of patients he has killed. However, if Shipman had advised admission and if Mrs Broadbent had refused, no reasonable doctor would have left her alone in the condition Shipman claims she was in. Any reasonable doctor would have made arrangements for Mrs Broadbent's care and treatment at home. Whenever I find that Shipman's account indicates that he must have acted in a wholly unreasonable way, I suspect that events did not occur as he claims. This factor increases my suspicion that Mrs Broadbent did not die of a heart attack but died at Shipman's hand.
A further factor which excites suspicion is the gas fire. When Mrs Rawson discovered the body, the gas fire was on a higher setting that usual. Suspicion arises that Shipman turned it up. A very hot room, with the fire full on, has been a feature of several Shipman killings. Dr Aneez Esmail, medical advisor to the Inquiry, has explained that a high ambient temperature would accelerate the onset of rigor mortis and would slow the rate at which the body temperature falls after death. The result of leaving the body in a warm room would be to make it difficult or even impossible for a pathologist to make a reliable estimate of the time of death. I cannot think of any reason why Shipman would wish to achieve that end unless he was concerned about his own role in the death. For that reason I regard the gas fire as a suspicious factor.
If Mrs Rawson's recollection of the timing of events is correct, Shipman appears to have made false entries on Form B. He suggested that his visit was at 2pm and the death at 4pm. Mrs Rawson says she had found the body by about 1.45pm. However, it is possible that her recollection of times is at fault and I do not place reliance on this point. Even so, Shipman's claim that he knew the time of death to be 4pm gives rise to suspicion. If he was not present at the death, he could have not have made a reliable estimate of the time. His pretence at an estimate appears to me to be an attempt to distance himself from the death.
Finally, Mrs Broadbent's position and appearance in death are not typical of those seen in a death following a heart attack. They are, however, entirely typical of those seen in many of Shipman's victims, who had been killed by lethal injection of diamorphine.
My conclusion is that the overwhelming likelihood is that Shipman killed Mrs Broadbent. Despite the absence of medical records, I feel able to say that I am sure of that conclusion.

name: Genevieve Challoner
title: Mrs
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Challoner died of natural causes and that Shipman played no part in her death whatsoever.
When Mr Clough last saw his mother alive she was unwell and suffering from a cold. Mrs Northrop also says that Mrs Challoner appeared unwell in the days before she died. She smoked and suffered from angina and, although her death may have been unexpected, it must be recognised that she was at considerably increased risk of suffering a heart attack.
The account offered by Mrs Flanagan concerning Mrs Challoner's contact with Shipman is not only implausible and contrary to all other evidence in this case, it is quite bizarre. I cannot accept that there is a word of truth in it.
There is no evidence to support Mrs Flanagan's assertion that Mrs Challoner transferred to Shipman's register and there is positive evidence that she remained a patient of Dr Clark. I do not accept that Mrs Challoner ever had any contact with Shipman.

name: Annie Elizabeth Golds
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 28 Woodbrooke Avenue, Hyde
certified_cause: congestive heart failure due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
It appears to me that Mrs Golds must have died from natural causes, probably associated with her heart condition. The information in the medical records is not sufficient for me to form a clear picture of Mrs Golds' medical history. However, she was being monitored for congestive heart failure. It seems likely that she had ischaemic heart disease and suffered a sudden cardiac episode on the morning of 28th
May. Her collapse on the kitchen floor is consistent with such an episode.
It seems very unlikely that Shipman would have visited Mrs Golds on the morning of 28th
May. He was not on out of hours duty either that day or the day before. In any event, Mrs Golds was not on the telephone so it is hard to see how she could have summoned a doctor without one of her neighbours (probably Mrs Winson) being aware of the fact.
There is some room for concern because Shipman recorded on Form B that he had last seen Mrs Golds alive 13 days before her death, whereas there is no reference to a consultation on 15th
May in the medical records, nor does Mrs Golds' name appear in the visits book for this date. It is clear from many cases investigated by the Inquiry, however, that Shipman was far from meticulous in the way he carried out his duties of certification and this single factor cannot found real suspicion that he caused the death. He may have suggested this recent contact in order to avoid the trouble of a referral to the coroner.
My conclusion is that I am sure that Mrs Golds died a natural death.

name: Ada Matley Hilton
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 31 St John's Drive, Godley, Hyde
certified_cause: cardiac arrest due to cardiac arrhythmia and ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
There are several suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. First and most obvious, Mrs Hilton was found dead very shortly after a visit by Shipman. Shipman would have us believe that she died a sudden but natural death about an hour after he left. Mrs Hilton had not asked for Shipman to visit that day on account of any illness. He was paying a routine visit of his own volition. Mrs Hilton was well at about midday and ate a good lunch. Although I accept that she was very frail and also was at an increased risk of a cardiac death, it would seem to me to a quite remarkable coincidence if she died naturally soon after he left. I could accept that such a coincidence might happen very occasionally but with Shipman it seems to have happened quite frequently. I do not accept that such frequent coincidences happen and I regard the temporal connection between Shipman's visit and the death as highly suspicious.
In the medical records Shipman claimed that Mrs Hilton had cardiac problems when he saw her. After the death, he told Ms Grimshaw that he had asked Mrs Hilton to go into hospital for treatment of her heart problems. He implied that she had refused. There is no reference to the advice or the refusal. Nor is there any record of the treatment he arranged or the care to be provided. There are two causes for suspicion arising from this aspect of the evidence. First, it is a common feature of many cases in which Shipman killed that he would claim that he had found a patient unwell, had advised admission to hospital but the patient had refused. The patient had then died, shortly afterwards, of the condition for which he or she had (as Shipman would suggest) effectively refused treatment. That Shipman made the suggestion here is a cause for suspicion. However, I am also suspicious in any case where I find that Shipman's note reflects a course of action which no reasonable and competent doctor would follow. No reasonable and competent doctor would leave a woman of 88 years of age alone in the house if she were in need of hospital treatment or care. If there were no relative or neighbour who could provide care, he would have to make arrangements with the district nursing service and possibly Social Services. That would not have been necessary in this case, as Mrs Godley lived nearby. That Shipman left without making arrangements for Mrs Hilton's care leads me to the conclusion that she did not need care as she was already dead.
On Form B, Shipman claimed to know the time of death. Unless he was present at the death, there would be no way in which he could know or assess when Mrs Hilton had died. Shipman very frequently claimed to know the time of death, which he always stated was an appreciable time after his own visit. Usually (although not always), I think he was fairly accurate when stating the time of his own visit. Occasionally he would say it was a little earlier than it had been. But his claim to know the time of death was very often an attempt to create the impression that a substantial time had elapsed between his visit and the death. I think he did that in this case.
Finally, the circumstances in which Mrs Hilton's body were found and her peaceful appearance in death were not typical of death by cardiac arrest, but wholly consistent with death by lethal injection of diamorphine.
The overwhelming likelihood in this case is that Shipman killed Mrs Hilton, almost certainly by lethal injection of diamorphine. Notwithstanding her great age, her frail condition and her past history of heart problems, I am able to say that I feel sure of this conclusion.

name: Harry Lomas
title: Mr
place_of_death: Hyde Nursing Home
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mr Lomas died as the result of natural causes, as certified by Shipman.
Mr Lomas was known to be suffering from inoperable cancer at the time of his admission to Hyde Nursing Home on 4th
August 1997. Although he appears to have deteriorated very rapidly, his death could not be described as sudden or unexpected.
The records suggest that Shipman saw Mr Lomas on only one occasion, 5th
August. There is no reason to suppose that Shipman saw Mr Lomas in the hours preceding his death. Indeed it would be most unusual if he had done so, as he would have had to come to the nursing home in the very early morning. I think it is safe to discount that possibility completely.
Shipman claimed to have seen Mr Lomas on 8th
August 1997. There is no note of a visit on that day in the medical records or indeed the medical intervention records. I think it most unlikely that Shipman visited. Shipman was often very careless about his duties in respect of death registration and cremation certification. I think he did not see Mr Lomas on 8th
August. However, the fact that he told a lie or made a mistake on Form B does not imply that he played any sinister part in Mr Lomas' death.

name: William James McLaren
title: Mr
place_of_death: Bowlacre, a residential home for the elderly, Elson Drive, Stockport Road, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
The evidence suggests that Mr McLaren's health had deteriorated gradually during his time at Bowlacre and, when it occurred, his death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
Mr Alexander McLaren was told that his father had died during the night of 27th
to 28th
April. Although he was not informed about the death until the middle of the morning, there is no reason to suspect that the information he was given about the time of death was untrue. He was given an explanation for the delay in making contact and he seems to have accepted the explanation as genuine at the time. As the death was said to have occurred on 28th
April, I infer that the death took place some time between midnight and about 6am.
It seems likely that Shipman visited on 27th
April. His usual visiting hours were between about 11.30am and 3.30pm. It seems likely therefore that Shipman last saw Mr McLaren at least eight hours before he died and probably rather longer than that. As Mr McLaren was conscious when his son visited that evening, I can say with confidence that Shipman had not that day given Mr McLaren any drug which caused his death. There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman visited Mr McLaren during the night in which he died. Indeed, it would be most unusual for Shipman to turn out in the night unless there was a real emergency.
I am quite satisfied that Mr McLaren died of natural causes.

name: Stanley Riley
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 25 Vale Avenue, Hyde
certified_cause: right cerebrovascular accident due to hypertension
conclusion: I am quite satisfied that Mr Riley died as the result of natural causes, as certified by Shipman. Mrs Clement has a clear recollection of her father's medical condition and remembers what her mother told her of the circumstances surrounding his death. There is no reason to suspect that Shipman was in any way responsible for Mr Riley's death.

name: Winifred Isabel Smith
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 14 Longfield Way, Todmorden
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to carcinoma of the right breast
conclusion:
Mrs Smith was suffering from advanced cancer of the breast, which had spread to other parts of her body. From the description given, it appears that she was in the terminal phase of her illness.
Although Shipman admitted having prescribed and administered pethidine to Mrs Smith, the family was aware of this and the administration of an opiate would have been entirely appropriate for the relief of pain, given the advanced state of Mrs Smith's cancer.
Although there is no evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Smith shortly before her death, there is no evidence that he did not. For that reason, I am unable to reach any positive conclusion as to Shipman's involvement in this death. If Shipman did give Mrs Smith a lethal dose of opiate, it would appear that her life was shortened by only a small margin.

name: Kenneth Wharmby Woodhead
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 1 Sawyer Brow, Hyde
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to adenocarcinoma of the lung
conclusion:
Mr Woodhead was terminally ill with lung cancer. By 14th
December, he was not expected to live long. The deputising doctor who attended during the night seems to have formed the impression that the death was imminent. It is very likely that, even without any intervention from Shipman, Mr Woodhead would have died over the course of the next few days. However, it appears that neither Mrs Woodhead nor Mrs Hibbs expected him to die on 14th
December. Mrs Woodhead asked for the help of a night nurse so that she would not be too tired to cope on 15th
December. Shipman arranged this. During the afternoon, Mr Woodhead was able to converse. When Shipman came in the early evening and told Mrs Woodhead that her husband would die in the next 48 hours, she was very shocked that he would die so soon. Even Shipman did not appear to think that he would die within the next half hour. To that extent, the death was sudden and unexpected. I accept, of course, that accurate predictions of the time of death are not possible.
The death was discovered within half an hour of Shipman's departure. It appears that Shipman left the house just before 7pm and that the death was discovered at about 7.20pm. It is possible that Mr Woodhead died very soon after Shipman's departure, solely as the result of the natural progression of his disease. However, this would be something of a coincidence, particularly bearing in mind that his death had not appeared to be imminent. There is a real possibility that Shipman gave Mr Woodhead a large dose of diamorphine to supplement the dose being given by the syringe driver.
The suspicion arising from these factors is increased by the lies that Shipman told on the cremation form. Specifically, he seems to have attempted to distance himself from the death in terms of time by suggesting, wholly contrary to the recollection of Mrs Hibbs, that six hours had passed between his last visit and Mr Woodhead's death. Having said that, there would be no obvious sinister reason why he should suggest that death occurred at 5.45pm rather than some time after 7pm, when I am satisfied that it did occur. It is possible that he gave that time in error. I think it likely that Shipman lied in saying that Mr Woodhead had been in a coma for
'Hours'
before his death. He was not in a coma when Mrs Hibbs left in the afternoon. That she and Mrs Woodhead seemed to think that they were going to have Mr Woodhead with them for another two days (after being given the news that he had only about 48 hours to live), suggests to me that their expectation was that he would continue to be able to converse with them for a little longer. I think it is fairly clear that Shipman also lied in saying that Mrs Woodhead was present at the moment of death. It appears that she went into the room and found Mr Woodhead already dead.
My conclusion is that, when he visited in the early evening of 14th
December, Shipman probably gave Mr Woodhead a large dose of diamorphine which hastened his death. There is no evidence that Mr Woodhead's pain was breaking through, despite the diamorphine he was receiving through the syringe driver. I think it likely that Shipman gave Mr Woodhead an injection of 100mg of diamorphine, using one of the ampoules from the previously unopened box. He then took the rest of that box away. The nurses noticed that a box of ampoules had gone. I could not possibly say that I am sure of my conclusion in this case, as Mr Woodhead could have died naturally on that day. I must also stress that he would inevitably have died within a very short time.

name: Violet May Bird
title: Mrs
certified_cause: cardiac arrest due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
There are a number of highly suspicious circumstances surrounding this death.
The death occurred during the course of a visit by Shipman and this factor alone excites a high degree of suspicion. Whilst it appears that Mrs Bird was experiencing dizzy sensations on the day of her death and might even have had chest pain, it is highly coincidental that she should die within a short time of Shipman's arrival. However, if Mrs Bingham's recollection is correct, and I think it is, it seems unlikely that Mrs Bird was suffering chest pain during Shipman's visit, in which case his record of the visit must be inaccurate.
Shipman claims that he gave a 10mg injection of diamorphine, presumably to relieve Mrs Bird's chest pain. I do not think she was suffering from severe chest pain. However, if she were, it would be appropriate for Shipman to have given her a very small dose of opiate. Only the minimum amount necessary to relieve the pain should be given and the injection should be stopped as soon as the desired effect is achieved. Usually this would be a dose of the order of 5mg. A dose of 10mg would be a very large amount to give in such circumstances and might be dangerously large. However, there is every reason to suspect that Shipman gave Mrs Bird a much larger dose of diamorphine than 10mg. At this time in 1993, Shipman had been in the habit of obtaining 30mg ampoules of diamorphine from the Norwest Co-op Pharmacy by illicit means. There is no evidence that he legitimately carried 5mg or 10mg ampoules for emergency use, as many doctors do. I think it likely that Shipman gave a dose of diamorphine which was sufficient to kill Mrs Bird.
Shipman's pattern of behaviour in calling for a neighbour is typical of his modus operandi. It would appear that he sought to involve Mrs Bingham so that it would not be he alone who discovered the body of Mrs Bird. Although it was unusual for him to call an ambulance and to make some attempt at resuscitation, this was almost certainly a sham on his part. There would be no danger of Mrs Bird being revived and the paramedics would simply examine her for signs of life and pronounce her dead. I think, on this occasion, Shipman thought that calling an ambulance and giving the kiss of life would make it appear that this was a sudden death from a heart attack.
Taking these factors together, I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Bird. I think it highly likely that he gave her a large dose of diamorphine, almost certainly under the pretence of giving her something to help her dizziness.

name: Alfred Cheetham
title: Mr
certified_cause: respiratory failure due to chronic obstructive airways disease due to cor pulmonale
conclusion:
The medical records show that Mr Cheetham suffered from a severe respiratory disorder for which he received regular treatment and of which there was an acute exacerbation in the period just before he died. In those circumstances, it would not have been surprising had Mr Cheetham died in his sleep, as the result of respiratory failure.
Mrs Cheetham is concerned that Shipman visited on the day before the death and gave Mr Cheetham some tablets, which he took that evening before going to bed. It is not known what those tablets were. If Mrs Cheetham's recollection is right, it would appear that Shipman had acted in a most unorthodox manner in giving his patient tablets from his bag without recording the fact in the medical notes. However, the tablets could have been quite harmless. On the other hand, they could have been an opiate, such as morphine or Diconal. Such a drug would have caused respiratory depression and this could have had a severe effect on Mr Cheetham, whose respiratory function was already severely compromised. A dose of opiate that would be harmless to most people might have had a fatal effect on Mr Cheetham. Even a sedative such as temazepam might well be dangerous for someone like him. Mr Cheetham might have taken the tablets, which would not have had any immediate effect, and then have fallen into a deep sleep. His respiration might then have become depressed and have ceased altogether.
I must bear in mind that Mrs Cheetham accepts that her memory of these events is no longer good. My concern about this death arises because Shipman stated on the MCCD counterfoil and in Form B that he visited Mr Cheetham on 20th
March but did not make an entry in the medical records. I recognise that it is quite possible that Shipman did not visit on 20th
March; indeed in one respect it seems unlikely that he would, as Mr Cheetham was due to attend the hospital that day. My concern is heightened by Shipman's entry in Form B, where he states that the death occurred, quite suddenly, at 9am. If Mrs Cheetham is right when she says she found her husband dead when she awoke, Shipman's entry is misleading. One would have expected him to say that Mr Cheetham died during the night. If Shipman had provided tablets the day before, it could be that he wanted to create the impression that Mr Cheetham died quite a long time after taking them.
If Shipman did give Mr Cheetham two tablets of an opiate drug, intending to hasten his death, it would be an unusual method for him to choose. Shipman usually killed by giving an intravenous injection of opiate, which caused death almost immediately. I have concluded that he might, on occasion, have given an intramuscular injection of opiate to hasten the death of terminally ill patients.
There is no clear explanation for the profuse bleeding which Mrs Cheetham recalls that she found after the death. It seems likely that Mrs Cheetham is confused about this aspect of her husband's death.
Owing to the uncertainties surrounding this case, I do not feel able to reach any conclusion as to whether Mr Cheetham's death was due to natural causes or whether it might possibly have been caused by some intervention by Shipman.

name: David Alan Harrison
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 40 Talbot Road, Hyde
conclusion:
There are several suspicious circumstances surrounding this death.
The first and most obvious cause for suspicion is that the death occurred when Shipman was present. Dr Grenville has said that it is most unusual for a patient to die during a visit by a general practitioner unless the patient is terminally ill or the doctor has been called out in an emergency where there is a report that the patient is suffering symptoms indicating a life threatening condition such as a heart attack or stroke. Mr Harrison was not known to be terminally ill. Nor had his visit request, made at 12.10pm, been expressed to be an emergency. Nor was it treated as such by the surgery staff or by Shipman. Shipman did not visit until 2.30pm, on his own account. He had only one other visit that day and a relatively light surgery list. If this had been an emergency, he could have been there much sooner. According to Shipman's accounts, taken from Form B and the MCCD, Mr Harrison began to have his heart attack at some time between 1.30pm and 2.30pm, that is well over an hour after he had telephoned the surgery. He then died at 3.30pm, after Shipman had supposedly been with him for an hour. While it could not be said to be an impossible course of events, it does seem to be something of a coincidence that Mr Harrison should suddenly collapse and die during Shipman's visit. I find that suspicious.
My suspicions are also aroused by Shipman's apparent conduct in respect of the ambulance. If Shipman arrived at about 2.30pm and found Mr Harrison in the condition described in the first handwritten note for 3rd
January, it is very strange that Shipman did not call the ambulance until 3.38pm. On his own account, he seems to have waited until Mr Harrison was in cardiac arrest.
I am also doubtful of the authenticity of Shipman's medical note. I have found many cases in which Shipman has fabricated a medical note to provide a plausible explanation for the death which Shipman himself had caused. Here, Shipman presents a picture of a man who has had chest pain (extending into the neck and left arm and highly suggestive of angina) for seven days. The picture presented by the visits request form is that he had had chest pain for a few days but not at present. It appears that the pain had not been of such severity that Mr Harrison had called out the doctor before. I bear in mind that some patients might hesitate to call out a doctor over the New Year holiday but the previous day, Thursday, 2nd
January, was a normal working day. I doubt if many patients would hesitate to call the doctor out if suffering from severe chest pains. I suspect that the account given by Shipman in the medical records paints a rather more serious picture than was the position. However, I would not attach great weight to this factor were it not for Shipman's failure to call an ambulance promptly. That factor, combined with the serious picture presented in the note, makes me highly suspicious.
Shipman claimed that he had given Mr Harrison cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Yet, he does not appear to have laid Mr Harrison on a firm surface. Probably the only available firm surface would have been the floor. It would be surprising if Shipman had put Mr Harrison on the floor, attempted resuscitation and having failed lifted him single-handedly back onto the bed. I suspect that no such attempt was made.
Mr Harrison was clearly unwell in the weeks and months before his death. However, it had never been clearly demonstrated that he suffered from ischaemic heart disease or any other cardiac condition. Yet Shipman asserted that he had been suffering from ischaemic heart disease for a year before his death. That assertion was not borne out by the hospital investigations. If Mr Harrison really had died a sudden natural death during the afternoon of 3rd
January, Shipman should have referred the case to the coroner with a view to post-mortem examination.
Shipman falsely stated on Form B that the ambulance personnel were present at the moment of death and had provided information from which Shipman had been able to diagnose the cause of death and describe the mode of death. Shipman often claimed that others were present at the moment of death, when the truth was that he had been alone with the patient. In this case, it is not known whether or not Mr Harrison's parents were present at the death. Mr Harrison's sister says that her parents did not usually stay with their son when the doctor called to see him. They were elderly and confused.
Mr Harrison's appearance in death was not typical of a death from coronary thrombosis but was very similar to that of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of opiate.
I have come to the conclusion that Shipman killed Mr Harrison. Mr Harrison was in poor health and it is theoretically possible that he died a natural death while Shipman was in the house, remarkable though the coincidence would have been. However, Shipman's account of events as set out in Form B, the MCCD and the medical record is so implausible that I am left in no doubt that he was responsible for Mr Harrison's death.

name: Hannah Moss
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
On the basis of the information available, it would seem likely that Mrs Moss suffered from ischaemic heart disease. Her daughter recalls that she had slight angina. The daily diary refers to an angina attack. She had the type of medication usually prescribed for angina. There is also some evidence from which it can be inferred that Mrs Moss' angina had worsened shortly before her death. It appears that Mrs Moss was very unwell on the night before her death and was a bad colour in the morning. The symptoms described during the night do not sound typical of a cardiac problem but it is entirely possible that they were, or were at least a mixture of bowel and cardiac problems. The daily diary does not describe a painful event, such as a heart attack. It says that Mrs Moss passed peacefully away. I have learned to be sceptical of such entries as it appears that the staff always used to write words of that kind in the diary, whatever the mode of death had been. It is entirely possible that Mrs Moss had had a heart attack and the staff would still describe her end as peaceful.
That Mrs Moss is recorded as having died at 9.30am makes it unlikely that Shipman was involved in any sinister way in her death. He was working that day and in all likelihood had a list of patients to see in the surgery before he went out on his visits. By the time Mrs Moss' name was entered in his visits book, three other visit requests had already been made.
Although I cannot rule out the possibility that Shipman went to Charnley House on the morning of 15th
March and injected Mrs Moss with a lethal substance, it seems to me to be highly unlikely that he did. In summary, the likelihood is that Mrs Moss died of natural causes and that Shipman is not in any way implicated in her death.

name: Joe Ainscow Stansfield
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 84 Halifax Road, Todmorden
conclusion:
It is clear that Mr Stansfield was extremely unwell in the weeks leading up to his death. It appears to me that he had reached the terminal stage of his illness.
The main indicator of suspicion in this case is the fact that Shipman last visited Mr Stansfield on the day of his death and that he recorded having seen Mr Stansfield immediately after death. Professor Baker inferred from these two facts that it was likely that Shipman was present at the moment of death. I agree that that inference is possible, although Shipman had expressly said that only Mrs Stansfield was present at the death. Such further evidence as is now available makes it appear unlikely that Shipman was present at the death. Mrs Stansfield did not mention the doctor's presence at the death in circumstances where she might have been expected to mention it had he been there. I conclude that it is unlikely that Shipman was present at the death.
However, that does not dispose entirely of all possible causes for suspicion. It would have been quite possible for Shipman to give Mr Stansfield an intramuscular injection of an excessive dose of opiate or sedative and to go away, leaving him to lapse into unconsciousness and death during the following hours. However, it does not appear likely that this occurred. It appears that the imminence of the death was appreciated by Mr Suthers by about 11.30am; that is, over two hours before it occurred. Either the imminence of the death must have been obvious to him as a layman or he had been advised by Shipman that the death was likely to occur that day. If the latter, we know approximately when Shipman was there. Professor Henry McQuay and Dr Grenville have said that if a lethal dose of opiate is given intramuscularly, death will usually follow within the hour. Given that Mr Stansfield's respiratory function was already severely compromised, one would expect him to die quite quickly if given an opiate.
There remains the possibility that Shipman gave an injection of opiate, with the intention of relieving Mr Stansfield's distress, but recognising that the consequence might be the hastening of death. Provided this is done in the best interests of the patient, it is not unlawful.
Mrs Stansfield's description of her husband, staring at the top of the wardrobe, does not seem to me to be consistent with a death from an overdose of opiate or sedative. If he had been given an opiate or sedative, I would have thought Mr Stansfield would have fallen asleep some time before he died.
While I cannot absolutely rule out the possibility that Shipman hastened Mr Stansfield's death, it seems to me to be highly likely that the death was due to natural causes as set out on the death certificate.

name: Albert Redvers Williams
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 76 Industrial Street, Todmorden
conclusion:
The evidence from the police suggests strongly that Mr Williams' health was poor in the weeks before he died. The evidence of the pathologist, Dr Edwards, supports this. Although Mr Ormerod does not remember this, it seems likely that Mr Williams was suffering severe breathing problems in the period before he died.
The post-mortem report and the opinion of Professor Whitwell show that the findings were sufficient to account for a natural death. However, as toxicological tests were not carried out, the post-mortem findings do not exclude the possibility that Mr Williams' death was hastened by the giving of an inappropriate drug, either in tablet form or injectable form, or in both forms.
There is some evidence that Shipman did give Mr Williams some tablets that morning. We do not know what they were. If they were an opiate, they would be dangerous to Mr Williams, whose respiratory function was already compromised. He may also have given an injection when Mrs Williams was absent from the room.
If the doctor who had attended Mr Williams had not been Shipman, I would say without hesitation that it was highly likely that this was a completely natural death. However, it appears that Shipman did attend shortly before the death. We know that Shipman became a serial murderer. His method of killing was by the administration of opiates. We know that, at this time, he was abusing pethidine himself. It is quite possible that his judgement at this time was impaired. For those reasons, I feel unable to reach any conclusion about Shipman's rôle in this death. There is no positive evidence that he hastened the death but it is possible that he did and I am suspicious about it.

name: Nellie Bardsley
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 32 Rufford Avenue, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. First, the death occurred in Shipman's presence. As Dr Grenville has explained in his generic evidence, it is extremely unusual for a patient to die in the presence of the general practitioner unless the patient is suffering from a terminal illness or the doctor has been called out as an emergency in response to a report of symptoms of, for example, a stroke or heart attack. Mrs Bardsley was not suffering from a terminal illness. Nor do I think she gave the impression to the surgery staff that her request for a visit was an emergency. Had she done so, I think the staff would have arranged for Shipman to attend immediately or, if that were not possible, they would have called an ambulance. As it was, it appears that Shipman attended during the period in which he would carry out his routine visits. I think this was a non-urgent visit and, for Mrs Bardsley to die while Shipman was there, gives rise to a high degree of suspicion that he caused her death.
I acknowledge that Mrs Bardsley was at risk of suffering a further heart attack. If she had had an episode of palpitations in early December, the risk would have been high. I accept therefore that it is entirely possible that Mrs Bardsley was suffering some cardiac symptoms on 29th
December. I do not think she was having a major heart attack, as I think she would have told her daughter or would at least have alerted the warden. If her symptoms had increased significantly during the morning, I think she would have telephoned her daughter again. I bear in mind that it is also quite possible that Mrs Bardsley's reason for calling the doctor was nothing to do with her heart. However, I think it likely that it was, as she seemed to be concerned that Shipman might want her to go to hospital. Experience has taught me that Shipman's patients were most vulnerable to him when they were suffering from a potentially life-threatening condition. The subsequent death would then be readily explained.
My suspicions are heightened in this case by Shipman's supposed conduct on arrival at Mrs Bardsley's bungalow, as recorded in his note. For the reasons I outlined above, Shipman's account of events does not ring true. Whenever I find that Shipman has acted in a way in which no reasonably competent doctor would act, I suspect that events did not take place as Shipman has claimed.
Shipman claimed to have administered 10mg morphine to Mrs Bardsley, which would be appropriate treatment for the relief of the severe pain experienced during a heart attack, provided that the administration were stopped as soon as the pain had been adequately relieved. However, suspicion arises that Shipman did not give 10mg morphine as he claimed. If Shipman were to give any opiate as an emergency during a home visit, he must have taken it from his own bag rather than obtaining it by prescription in the patient's name. It is usual practice for most doctors to carry small amounts of an opiate for use in an emergency. However, Shipman told the police in interview after his arrest that he did not carry controlled drugs in his bag or keep a controlled drugs register because of his convictions for drug abuse in the 1970s. It is known that this is not true and that on many occasions he was carrying enough opiates to kill a patient. The evidence available to the Inquiry suggests that when he obtained opiates by unlawful means, he obtained diamorphine rather than morphine. The suspicion therefore arises that he used diamorphine rather than morphine on this occasion. If his note is inaccurate as to the drug given, it may well be inaccurate as to the amount as well. I have come across several cases in which Shipman claimed to have given 10mg morphine after which the patient has died. In all those cases, and in this case, I suspect that he gave diamorphine rather than morphine and that he gave more than the recorded amount. It is noteworthy that he makes no mention of the presence of a neighbour.
Mrs Bardsley's appearance in death was not typical of that seen in a patient who has suffered a heart attack and acute left ventricular failure. It was typical of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of opiate. However, as on Shipman's account Mrs Bardsley had received a small dose of morphine to relieve her pain, I can accept that she might have looked peaceful even if she had had a heart attack with left ventricular failure. Accordingly, I do not attach any weight to the evidence of Mrs Bardsley's appearance in death, although I repeat that I treat the note itself with great caution.
Shipman claimed on Form B of the cremation certificate that Mrs Hindley, the warden at Rufford Avenue, was present at the moment of death. As she has since died, it is not possible to find out whether or not she was. Mrs Chapman claimed that Shipman told her he had summoned the warden after he had cancelled the ambulance. If that is right, it is significant for two reasons. First, Shipman should have summoned the warden to assist in cardiopulmonary resuscitation, which is more effectively carried out by two people. Second, his claim on Form B would be false. I have found a large number of cases in which Shipman has killed where he has sought to give the impression on Form B that he was not alone at the death, when the truth is that he was alone with the patient until after the patient had died. In this case, due to the uncertainty surrounding the time of the warden's arrival, I attach less weight than I otherwise might to the possibly false entry on Form B.
My conclusion is that Shipman killed Mrs Bardsley. I think he gave her a much stronger dose of opiate than he recorded in the notes, intending that she should die. I am sure of that conclusion. I dismiss the theoretical possibility that Mrs Bardsley died naturally of a heart attack in his presence.

name: Marion Carradice
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 4 Kensington Street, Hyde
conclusion:
Although I have not had the advantage of hearing Mrs Rhodes and Mrs Piper in person, I have no hesitation in saying that I find Mrs Piper's account of events to be the more reliable. Not only were her two accounts consistent with each other, they were also consistent with the brief account which Mrs Mitchell gave to the police. Mrs Rhodes' two accounts are inconsistent with each other and are extremely vague in some important particulars. I shall base my conclusions on the account of Mrs Piper.
It appears to me that Shipman must have arrived at Mrs Carradice's house not long after Mrs Piper had left her sitting on the sofa downstairs. I think it likely that Mrs Carradice was still downstairs when Shipman arrived and that Shipman took her upstairs, possibly to facilitate his examination. I think it unlikely that Mrs Carradice, who had been sitting on her sofa, fully dressed, for about two hours, would have decided to go upstairs in the few minutes before Shipman arrived. When next seen by any of her neighbours (the first being Mrs Mitchell), Mrs Carradice was dead. Shipman had been alone with her for no more than ten to fifteen minutes and had then fetched Mrs Mitchell, who had fetched Mrs Piper. These circumstances excite a high degree of suspicion, as it would be quite remarkable if Mrs Carradice had died naturally during such a short time.
There is some evidence that Mrs Carradice suffered from hypertension and was therefore vulnerable to a stroke. There is also evidence to suggest that she might possibly have had a stroke on the morning of 14th
August. On the other hand, the history of a fall on account of dizziness is quite non-specific. Had she had a stroke, one would have expected her to show some signs of weakness of the limbs or slurring of the speech, which Mrs Piper would have noticed.
The evidence suggests that it was Mrs Carradice herself who telephoned for the doctor. The procedure at the surgery would be for the receptionist to note a request for a visit, usually including a brief note of the nature of the problem. The message would be conveyed to Shipman, who would note the name and address in his own visits book but not usually the nature of the problem. In this case, the entry in Shipman's visits book comprises the name and address and the fact that Mrs Carradice had died of a cerebrovascular accident. The references to the fact that Mrs Carradice had suffered a stroke and died must have been entered after the visit. I think it is unlikely that Mrs Carradice suggested to the receptionist that she had suffered a stroke. First, had she done so, the receptionist would probably have asked Shipman to visit as a matter of urgency or would have suggested that an ambulance should be called. Second, the evidence suggests that Mrs Carradice was not unduly worried about herself when Mrs Piper returned at about midday. She was still sitting on the sofa. From the evidence of Mrs Piper, it seems likely that Mrs Carradice told the receptionist that she had had a fall and was feeling dizzy and unwell. In my view, it is possible but very unlikely that Mrs Carradice had a stroke that morning.
While Shipman was with Mrs Carradice in the back bedroom, either he or she removed her dentures. That is a feature that arouses some suspicion. In several cases in which Shipman has killed his patient, the patient has been found with their dentures removed. Dr John Grenville has suggested that Shipman might have had an alarming experience when killing a patient, when the dentures had perhaps slipped out of position as the patient became unconscious and had lodged in the throat. Dr Grenville suggests that perhaps Shipman felt it prudent to remove the dentures to prevent this.
I think that when Mrs Carradice had died, Shipman went to find a neighbour who could help him find the telephone number of the next of kin. That is a further reason why I am sure Mrs Rhodes is mistaken in her account. He would not have done that if Mrs Rhodes had been in the house and was able to give him the telephone number. I think Mrs Mitchell found the address book for him and he made the call while she went to fetch Mrs Piper. When Mrs Mitchell and Mrs Piper arrived together, Shipman was on the telephone and Mrs Rhodes was nowhere to be seen. I think she arrived a while later. She has clearer recollections of such matters as the dentures. I think it likely that she did indeed put Mrs Carradice's dentures back in.
The real question is what happened during the short period in which Shipman was alone with Mrs Carradice. It seems to me that there are really only two possibilities. Either Mrs Carradice died of a stroke that had begun earlier that morning or else Shipman killed her in his usual way, by giving her an intravenous injection of a lethal dose of opiate.
The witness evidence suggests that Mrs Carradice could have had a cerebrovascular accident that morning. That is not to say that she died of it. In his generic evidence, Dr Grenville has said that it is possible for a patient to die very suddenly of a stroke, usually caused by a haemorrhage within the brain stem. However, an occlusive stroke usually develops over a period of time. The initial signs may be very similar to those described by Mrs Carradice, a fall followed by dizziness and a feeling of malaise. Then as it develops, there is usually weakness on one side and other neurological signs such as slurring of the speech. The patient may stabilise and recover or at least improve but, if not, he or she will then suffer a gradual loss of consciousness over a period of hours or even a day or two, and death will usually take place two to three days after the initial stroke. It appears to me that Mrs Carradice did not have a massive stroke of the kind that causes sudden death. She was able to talk to Mrs Piper at least two hours after her fall. Yet she died within a very short time of Shipman's arrival. I think this is highly suspicious and I believe it is likely that Shipman was responsible for her death. It is possible that she had a stroke that morning but I do not think she died from it.
There are a number of features typical of cases in which Shipman killed. In particular, Shipman often called upon a neighbour to come to the house within a very short time of the death. Only very rarely did he call a neighbour in time to be present at the death, although he often claimed in the cremation documents that the neighbour was present at the moment of death. Here, he fetched Mrs Mitchell too late to be present, although I think he tried to suggest that she had been present when he completed Form B. He did not identify the neighbour whom he claimed was present.
My conclusion is that Shipman probably killed Mrs Carradice.

name: Ellen Higson
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 1 Marler Road, Hyde
conclusion:
There are some very suspicious features surrounding this death. It is clear from Form B that the death occurred while Shipman was present. That always arouses suspicion. In his generic evidence to the Inquiry, Dr Grenville said that it is an enormous coincidence for a doctor to be present at the death of a patient at home, where the patient is not suffering from a terminal illness and the doctor is not responding to an emergency call following the onset of acute symptoms, indicating, for example, a heart attack or stroke. Dr Grenville says that this type of unusual occurrence might occur once in a general practitioner's professional lifetime. Shipman was present at the deaths of a number of his patients who died at home. Such events cannot be coincidence. Mrs Higson was not suffering from a terminal illness and there is no indication that she was suffering from acute symptoms that might indicate a heart attack or stroke. Indeed, Shipman claimed that her death was caused by renal failure as opposed to any type of sudden death. Therefore, that Shipman should be present at the moment of death is a highly suspicious feature in its own right.
It would appear that, for some time before her death, Mrs Higson had required domestic help. It is known that she had arthritis, rheumatism, glaucoma and a thyroid problem. It seems likely that she might have been anaemic. The visits book suggests that she was receiving regular visits from Shipman throughout January and that she also received at least one visit from the district nurse. I infer from this that Mrs Higson was rather more seriously unwell than the family now recollects. Without the medical records it is impossible to assess the seriousness of her condition. It is inconceivable, however, that Mrs Higson could have been critically ill. Her family had not been told and there does not appear to have been any suggestion of admission to hospital. Mrs Holt would have told the family if she had been worried about Mrs Higson. It seems to me highly unlikely therefore that Mrs Higson could have reached the terminal stages of renal failure. As Dr Grenville has said, such a patient would have required nursing in bed and would not be found sitting upright in her chair. I think it highly unlikely that Mrs Higson died of renal failure.
It is theoretically possible that Mrs Higson died suddenly from a heart attack or stroke or some other cause of sudden death. However, that can be discounted, as Shipman would not have relied on renal failure as a cause of death if Mrs Higson had indeed suffered a heart attack or stroke in his presence.
It appears that Mrs Holt was holding Mrs Higson's hand as she was dying. It might seem unlikely for Shipman to administer a lethal injection in the presence of a witness but the Inquiry has discovered cases where Shipman has killed even in the presence of an experienced nurse or carer. One such case is Mrs Eileen Daphne Crompton, who was killed by Shipman at Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly on 2nd
January 1997, in the presence of an experienced care worker, who was completely taken in by his explanation for what occurred. It would seem that Shipman's powers of persuasion were such that he was able to explain his actions in an innocent way. In any event, it is quite possible that Mrs Holt was not present when Shipman examined Mrs Higson and gave her an injection and only allowed Mrs Holt to return when Mrs Higson was close to death.
The position in which Mrs Higson was found is inconsistent with her having died of renal failure but it is consistent with her having died from an injection of opiate.
Taking these factors into account, I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Higson by administering a lethal dose of strong opiate. It is theoretically possible that Shipman was called because Mrs Higson was suddenly taken very ill and that she died a natural death in his presence, but taking the evidence as a whole I confidently dismiss that possibility.

name: Esther Lowe
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
certified_cause: respiratory failure due to carcinomatosis of unknown origin
conclusion:
There is no evidence of the nature of Mrs Lowe's illness at the time of her admission to Charnley House. However, it is clear from the daily diary that she was in very poor health. The night before her death she was very confused. On the morning of 22nd
July, she was said to be
'very poorly'
. It would appear that her death that day was neither sudden nor unexpected.
There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman visited Mrs Lowe on the day of her death. Although it was Shipman's practice to carry out routine visits on Saturday mornings, he did not usually do so on Saturday afternoons. It appears that Dr Napier was probably the Donneybrook doctor on out of hours duty that weekend. It is therefore extremely unlikely that Shipman would have visited Mrs Lowe on the afternoon of 22nd
July.
In these circumstances, I feel able to say that I am sure that Mrs Lowe's death was due to natural causes.

name: Margaret Metcalfe
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Metcalfe died of natural causes. The Charnley House daily diary records a gradual deterioration, which is entirely consistent with a death due to multiple organ failure for which old age or senility is an appropriate cause of death.
There is no evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Metcalfe in the hours before she died. It would have been surprising had he done so, as she died at 7am. Had he been called out to see her as an emergency, it is very likely that this would have been recorded in the Charnley House diary.

name: Alice Rawling
title: Mrs
