place_of_death: Pole Bank Hall, a residential home for the elderly, Stockport Road, Hyde
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to carcinoma of the stomach
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Rawling died a natural death.
The witness evidence suggests that Mrs Rawling's health deteriorated in the weeks leading up to her death. Mrs Haynes recalls that Mrs Rawling began to experience stomach pain in about June 1988. Dr Grenville said that if Mrs Rawling was in severe pain it would have been appropriate to give her diamorphine, even though this might well have contributed to her death. The evidence suggests that Mrs Rawling did, at times, complain of excruciating pain and it appears that Shipman's decision to treat her with opiate pain relief was justified. She had become bed bound and, according to the evidence of Mrs Oakes, had been barely conscious, or was possibly in a coma, for a few days before her death. Although the diagnosis of cancer was never confirmed and the medical records contain only sparse information, the general picture is consistent with a gradual decline towards death resulting from a painful condition. Mrs Rawling's death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
None of the witnesses who worked at the home recalls Shipman visiting Mrs Rawling on the day of her death and Mrs Oakes told the police that Shipman did not visit that day. However, the documentary evidence suggests that he did visit on that day. He usually went on his rounds between about noon and 3.30pm. I think it is likely that he visited during this period, as he claimed on Form B. It is not in the least surprising that the staff do not remember this routine visit.
If Shipman did visit Mrs Rawling on the afternoon of her death, he did not administer a lethal dose of an opiate to her. The evidence of Mr Alan Broadbent is that his aunt was alive and breathing when he visited her at about 7pm. If Shipman had visited Mrs Rawling earlier that day and injected her with a fatal dose of a strong opiate, she would have died within minutes if the injection were given intravenously or within an hour at most if administered intramuscularly. It is unlikely that Shipman visited again during the evening. Had he been present at or about the time of the death, it is likely that the staff would have remembered.

name: Lilian Shaw
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 922 Burnley Road, Portsmouth, Todmorden
conclusion: I am quite sure that Mrs Shaw died a natural death, the cause of which was established at post-mortem examination. The circumstances give rise to no suspicion that Shipman did anything which caused or contributed to the death.

name: Jack Wills
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 16 Woodhouse Grove, Todmorden
conclusion:
I have no doubt that Mr Wills died from natural causes.
The death was investigated only because Shipman had certified the cause of death. There is no reason to suspect Shipman's involvement in the death and he was not involved in Mr Wills' treatment at any time.

name: Vera Bramwell
title: Miss
place_of_death: her home, 23 Rufford Avenue, Hyde
conclusion:
Little is known about Miss Bramwell's state of health in the weeks leading up to her death, but there is no note in the visits book of any visits by Shipman. In the absence of the medical records, I cannot discover whether Miss Bramwell had any history of heart disease, which might indicate that she was at particular risk of coronary thrombosis. However, as Shipman did not say that the coronary thrombosis, which caused the death, was due to any underlying condition, I infer that it is unlikely that there was any clear evidence of heart trouble in Miss Bramwell's medical records. Having said that, at her age Miss Bramwell could quite easily have had a fatal heart attack even though there was no previous history of heart trouble.
The reason why Miss Bramwell asked the warden to contact Shipman on the day of her death is not known but it can be inferred that she felt ill. However, I think it unlikely that her condition was critical. Had the warden been seriously concerned, I think it likely that she would have called an ambulance or at least telephoned Miss Bramwell's brother. The evidence does not suggest that Miss Bramwell mentioned symptoms that might indicate the onset of cardiac problems. The request for a visit was made in the morning. The fact that Shipman did not come until the afternoon suggests that the warden did not indicate that there was any urgency. According to what Shipman told the warden, Miss Bramwell must have had a fatal heart attack between the warden's departure and Shipman's arrival. That is believable. However, on Form B, Shipman makes it plain that he was present while the heart attack occurred. In his generic evidence to the Inquiry, Dr John Grenville said that it is a very rare occurrence for a general practitioner to be present at the moment of a patient's death where the patient is not suffering from a terminal illness and the doctor has not been called out in response to an emergency such as a sudden heart attack or stroke. Dr Grenville has said that a doctor might expect a death in his or her presence to occur once in a professional lifetime. Shipman was present at the deaths of a number of patients who died at home. In this case, he would have us believe that Miss Bramwell suffered a fatal heart attack just at the time of his visit. As Dr Grenville said, such a coincidence might happen once, but I cannot accept that it could happen again and again, as Shipman claims. That Miss Bramwell died in Shipman's presence is a highly suspicious feature.
On Form B, Shipman claimed that the warden was present at the moment of death. The warden said that Shipman had told her that he had found Miss Bramwell dead. She did not say that she was present at the moment of death. Of course I must be careful before relying on hearsay evidence, particularly in a case such as this where the witnesses might have been subconsciously influenced by accounts of Shipman's methods reported in the media. However, I note that Mrs Ardern gave her account to the police long before she knew what Shipman had written on Form B. For that reason, I think her account is probably accurate. Shipman claimed in a number of cases that some other person, such as a warden, was present at the moment of death, where the witness evidence suggests that they were not. If Shipman had killed Miss Bramwell, then he would have a motive to lie about the presence of others at the moment of death because their presence would allay any suspicions that medical colleagues might otherwise have when examining Form B.
Shipman claimed on Form B that he had attended Miss Bramwell during the last 40 minutes of her life. There is no suggestion that he telephoned for an ambulance or summoned the warden to assist with cardiopulmonary resuscitation (which is best performed by two people) even though there was an emergency cord in the house. It is clear that Shipman did not even attempt resuscitation alone, as this could not have been carried out while Miss Bramwell was sitting in her chair. Wherever Shipman appears to have behaved in a way that would not be acceptable to most reasonable and competent doctors, I suspect that events did not occur as he claimed. However, I do not attach a great deal of weight to this factor as I recognise that, at least in 1985, some doctors would have thought it inappropriate to attempt resuscitation on a woman of 79.
Although a detailed description of the position in which Miss Bramwell was found is not available, the evidence is that she was found sitting in a chair. In his generic evidence to the Inquiry, Dr Grenville has said that such a position is not typical of a patient who has suffered a fatal heart attack, but is consistent with the appearance of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by the administration of a lethal dose of diamorphine.
This case has many of the hallmarks of a Shipman killing. Taking all the evidence into account, I am sure that Shipman killed Miss Bramwell.

name: Albert Cheetham
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 11 Brooks Avenue, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. First, the death was supposedly discovered by Shipman. As far as is known, Shipman had been the last person to see Mr Cheetham alive or to speak to him. This course of events, one visit followed by another at which the patient is found dead, is typical of a Shipman killing and gives rise to strong suspicion. I have already said that there are good reasons to suspect that Shipman's account of how he came to visit Mr Cheetham on both 1st
and 2nd
April might not be true. That Shipman should be concerned to explain that he had found the front door open on 2nd
April and seek to explain why it might be that the door had been left open, only adds to my suspicion, especially as his explanation does not make sense. If Shipman were postulating that Mr Cheetham had died in the early evening, he would not have been expecting the doctor that day and would not have left the door open for him. That the door was open on the morning of 2nd
April suggests to me that Mr Cheetham had not been able to lock it on 1st
April because he was already dead. If it was his practice to leave the door open for a visitor, he might well be expected to lock the door after the last expected visitor of the day. It is of course possible that Mr Cheetham was alive and well when Shipman left on 1st
April and died before he had locked the door. However, the circumstances would be explained if Mr Cheetham were already dead when the doctor departed. He would then be unable to lock the door. In short, the circumstances of this death lead me to the conclusion that Shipman probably killed Mr Cheetham during his visit on 1st
April, that Shipman was unable to lock the door from inside when he left and was able to gain access the next morning when he went to 'discover' the body.
Whilst the absence of any medical records makes it impossible to be sure about Mr Cheetham's state of health, the witness evidence is consistent and strongly suggests that he enjoyed extremely good health for his age. If Shipman had indeed found Mr Cheetham to be 'nervy' on 1st
April and dead in his chair on 2nd
April, he could not possibly have known the cause of the death. The case ought to have been referred to the coroner. I regard that as a suspicious factor, although I am aware that Shipman often failed to refer a death to the coroner when there was no suggestion that he could have killed the patient.
Shipman said on Form B that Mr Cheetham died in the evening of 2nd
March. That was obviously a mistake and it appears that he meant to say that he died in the evening of 1st
April. He implies that Mr Cheetham had suffered a stroke about 24 hours before his death. That would be in the evening of 31st
March. There is no eyewitness evidence to prove that was untrue. However, one might have thought that Mr Cheetham would have alerted a neighbour, possibly the Hopwoods, if he had been ill that evening or the following morning. Shipman claims that he saw Mr Cheetham about 12 hours before his death. That would be in the morning of 1st
April. It is unthinkable that a doctor, who found an elderly patient suffering from a stroke, would leave the patient completely unattended and make no arrangements for his or her care. Shipman claims on Form B that Mr Cheetham was in a coma for some hours before his death but there is no possible basis on which he could have known that. I am quite sure that Mr Cheetham had not had a stroke. First, Shipman's entries on Form B do not make sense. Second, Shipman's suggestion of a stroke, followed by a visit, followed by a coma, is not consistent with what Mr Neville Cheetham understood from Shipman when he spoke to him after his father's death. Shipman told him that he had called in to see his father on the eve of his death simply because he was in the area at the time. He arranged to see him the following day either because he was feeling 'nervy' or to give a repeat prescription, or both. There was no suggestion, however, at that time of any stroke. Third, it would be an extraordinary coincidence if Shipman had visited Mr Cheetham because he was passing on the very day that Mr Cheetham had suffered a stroke.
These considerations, taken together, lead me to the conclusion that Shipman must have killed Mr Cheetham. Notwithstanding the absence of the medical records, I feel sure of that conclusion.

name: Ada Heywood
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 27 Green Street, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Heywood died a natural death. Although the information about the circumstances of the death is not as clear as I would wish, there is no reason to think that Shipman saw Mrs Heywood shortly before her death. Nor does it appear that she was 'found dead' as the report of death to the coroner suggested. It appears that her brother was probably with her throughout the final episode.
The findings on post-mortem examination demonstrated severe ischaemic heart disease as well as pathology consistent with left ventricular failure. The little information we have as to the circumstances leading up to Mrs Heywood's death is consistent with the certified causes of death. The evidence tends to suggest that Shipman was called to the house when Mrs Heywood was taken ill but did not arrive until after her death.

name: William Henry Leech
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 13 Plain Pitt Street, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mr Leech died of natural causes, although I doubt that the cause of his death could properly be described as senility. Shipman was often careless in the way in which he completed official forms in connection with death registration.
It appears that Mr Leech suffered a sudden medical episode on the morning of 18th
February. Mrs Foy says that he was definitely alive when she telephoned for Shipman, but it appears that he had died by the time Shipman arrived. It rather sounds as though he had a sudden fatal heart attack, or possibly a massive haemorrhagic stroke.
It is clear from Mrs Foy's evidence that Shipman did not do anything to Mr Leech which might have caused his death. There is no reason to suspect that Shipman was unlawfully involved in Mr Leech's death.

name: George Henry Mottram
title: Mr
place_of_death: Laurel Bank, a residential home for the elderly, Knott Lane, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mr Mottram died of natural causes and that Shipman played no part in his death. There is no evidence that Shipman had access to Mr Mottram in the hours before his death.
I very much doubt if Mr Mottram's death should have been attributed to old age. He does not appear to have declined gradually. He was not confined to bed but was walking about the home only the day before he died. It sounds to me as though Mr Mottram died as the result of an acute chest infection. He had been ill for a few days and then seemed to recover. He deteriorated suddenly during the night before his death. That morning he had a fever and was coughing blood. I have the impression that Shipman put old age on the MCCD because Mr Mottram was old and no one would query the true cause or manner of his death.
I do not think Shipman saw Mr Mottram on 16th
or 17th
February, as he claimed. I have come across many cases in which there is no suspicion that Shipman caused the death, but in which he is quite cavalier about what he put on the MCCD and cremation forms. I think he did not care what he put, so long as it did not cause him any trouble.

name: Elsie Royles
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 6 Hough Lane, Hyde
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to carcinoma of the breast
conclusion:
It is clear that Mrs Royles was suffering from cancer and probably did not have long to live. It may be that even on the day when Mrs Mina Royles helped to bathe her, she was already close to death. However, that is by no means certain. Both Mr and Mrs Royles recall that on the day when Mrs Royles had had a bath, Shipman visited and she passed into a coma from which she did not emerge. That gives rise to some suspicion that Shipman might have given Mrs Royles a large dose of an opiate or sedative drug. However, if their recollection is right and Mrs Royles did lapse into a coma and if she did so as the result of a drug given by Shipman, it does not appear that Shipman can have given her a lethal dose of whatever drug it was. A lethal dose of opiate would have killed Mrs Royles within the hour. It appears that she lived for at least 12 hours (and probably rather more) after any injection which could have been given on that day.
There is no clear evidence as to how long elapsed between the visit on the day of the bath and the death. It may be that Mrs Royles lay in bed, in a comatose state, for more than a day. It is possible that Shipman might have visited on the day after the bath and might have given Mrs Royles more medication. However, if Mrs Mina Royles is right in her recollection that her mother-in-law's death was discovered in the early morning, it seems unlikely that any drug which Shipman might have given her in the course of a daytime visit could have led directly to her death. Although it is not impossible that Shipman might have come out during the late evening or in the night, it is much more likely that he would have visited during the day.
If the death did not occur during the night, but during the day, it is quite possible that it occurred during a visit by Shipman. On the MCCD counterfoil, Shipman claimed that he had seen Mrs Royles alive on the day of the death. He also claimed to have seen the body after death, on the same day. Those circumstances make me suspect that the death might have occurred during a visit by Shipman. If it did, I would have real suspicion that Shipman might have caused it. If he did, the most likely way was by giving an injection of a lethal dose of opiate.
It is also possible that, a day or so before her death, Shipman gave Mrs Royles an overdose of a sedative which effectively 'put her to sleep' and hastened her death by rendering her more vulnerable to bronchopneumonia. If he had done that with the intention to shorten her life, that would be unlawful. However, I must bear in mind that it is quite possible that Shipman gave Mrs Royles only the drugs that he genuinely believed were necessary if she was to be kept comfortable.
There are too many uncertainties in this case. I regret that I cannot reach any decision. I am, however, suspicious about it.

name: Lily Shore
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
In my view it is overwhelmingly likely that Mrs Shore died as a result of natural causes.
Her condition, as recorded in the Charnley House diary, clearly deteriorated in the days leading up to her death. She was eating very little. When Mrs Quinn saw Mrs Shore in the week before her death she thought that she was suffering from influenza. The description of Mrs Shore's condition and the findings on post-mortem examination are consistent with death having been caused by suppurative bronchitis and bronchopneumonia.
Shipman visited Mrs Shore on 24th
February. As the visit is recorded in the morning report, I infer that he was there before 1pm. There is no record that he gave any treatment, in particular any injection. In any event, Mrs Shore appears to have been conscious some time after his departure, so he cannot have given her a lethal dose of strong opiate. Nor can he have given her an overdose of sedative. There is no record that Shipman visited again later in the day. However, the diary does not identify the doctor who pronounced life extinct following Mrs Shore's death at about 9.40pm. It is theoretically possible that Shipman returned to the home, gave Mrs Shore an injection which ended her life and pronounced her dead. However, I think it is most unlikely that Shipman would have done that at this stage in his career. He had only recently started work in Hyde. He had been obliged to tell the other Donneybrook doctors about his convictions for drug offences in early 1976. I think it is unlikely that at that time he would have risked killing a patient in a residential home. He would not then have been well known and trusted by the staff as he later became. Further, although he might have been alone with the patient for a short time, there would always be a risk that a care worker might enter the room.
My conclusion is that Mrs Shore died a natural death.

name: Margaret Wilmore
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 21 Mount Pleasant Street, Portsmouth, Todmorden
conclusion:
I have no doubt that Mrs Wilmore's death was natural. There is no evidence that Shipman attended Mrs Wilmore while she was still alive. It is clear that his only involvement was to attend after the death and to confirm the fact of death.
It appears to me that Ms Janice Bailey's recollection of attendance by two doctors is mistaken. Even if a second doctor had attended on 26th
September, and even if that doctor had been Shipman, and even if he had given Mrs Wilmore an injection, there is no reason to think that the injection caused or contributed to Mrs Wilmore's death. Mrs Wilmore was still alive in the early morning of 27th
September. She died suddenly in circumstances which suggest strongly that she had a heart attack. This was confirmed later by post-mortem examination.

name: Charles Geoffrey Brassington
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 12 Laburnum Avenue, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
The medical records reveal a history of a previous myocardial infarction and frequent angina attacks. It is clear that Mr Brassington was at high risk of suffering another, possibly fatal, heart attack.
The evidence suggests that Mrs Brassington was present at the moment of death and never entertained any suspicion that her husband's death was other than natural. The family has never expressed any concern that Shipman might have been involved in the death.
There is no evidence that Shipman visited Mr Brassington in the days leading up to his death. Indeed, the evidence suggests that the last doctor to see Mr Brassington alive was Dr Bills and not Shipman.
I am quite satisfied that Mr Brassington died a natural death.

name: Wilfred Chappell
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 51 Newton Hall Road, Hyde
conclusion:
There are a number of suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. First and most obvious, Mr Chappell's death was discovered very shortly after Shipman had visited him. No one had spoken to Mr Chappell or seen him alive after Shipman's visit. That in itself is a highly suspicious factor.
Very little is known about Mr Chappell's health. His medical records are not available and he did not tell Mr and Mrs Wilkinson a great deal about himself. It seems to me that I must assume that Mr Chappell did suffer to some extent from chronic obstructive airways disease. As Dr John Grenville has said in his generic evidence to the Inquiry, this expression covers a variety of different conditions but usually includes chronic bronchitis. It may well include emphysema and asthma. As Mr Chappell used an inhaler, it seems reasonable to infer that he had some asthma. Mr Chappell's feeling of tiredness and malaise of which he told the Wilkinsons on Saturday, 28th
January, was probably an exacerbation of his chronic disease. However, it does not appear that this was a serious exacerbation because Mr and Mrs Wilkinson were not worried about him and Shipman does not seem to have thought that his forthcoming visit was a matter of urgency. Moreover, when Shipman attended on the day of the death, he does not appear to have thought it necessary to admit Mr Chappell to hospital or to communicate with any relative to express concern about Mr Chappell's health. A death from chronic obstructive airways disease usually follows quite a long period of gradual deterioration during which the patient has increasing difficulty in breathing. Frequently, the patient becomes dependent on oxygen from a cylinder. Usually, the patient is bedridden before the death. Mr Chappell did not die in this way. It is possible that he might have died from a sudden, severe attack of asthma. However, such an attack would be extremely distressing and frightening. Mr Chappell's peaceful appearance following death and his apparent failure to reach for the telephone suggests that he did not die as a result of a sudden asthma attack. His death is very difficult to explain. In any event, it would appear that, if Shipman is right and Mr Chappell died suddenly about an hour after his departure, it was a quite remarkable coincidence. I find the circumstances of this death highly suspicious.
Mr Chappell's position and appearance in death were not what would be expected after death from any of the most common causes of sudden death, such as stroke or heart attack. They were, however, entirely typical of the position and appearance of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by a lethal injection of opiate.
All the available evidence suggests that Shipman killed Mr Chappell. My conclusion is that I am sure that he did so. I think he gave him a lethal injection of diamorphine.

name: Frank Halliday
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 21 Saxon Avenue, Dukinfield
conclusion:
There are a number of suspicious circumstances surrounding this death. This was a sudden and unexpected death, which occurred in Shipman's presence. I say that it was sudden and unexpected for several reasons. First, Shipman's visits book does not suggest that Mr Halliday had been ill in the days before his death. This was Shipman's first visit for over two months. Second, if Mr Halliday had been unwell for some time, to the extent that his health was giving cause for concern, Mrs Hefferan would not have been in Scotland. She would have been looking after her brother in Hyde. I am satisfied from Shipman's medical note and from Form B, that Mrs Hefferan was not in Hyde at the time of the death. If she had been present, Shipman would not have telephoned Scotland. If she had been present at the death, Shipman would have said so. He was always anxious to say that others had been present at a death. He often said others were present when they were not. I have never come across a case in which Shipman has omitted to mention as present someone who was in fact there. Although Shipman's medical note suggests that Mr Halliday had been ill for two days when Shipman saw him on 30th
March, no reliance can be placed on that note. Shipman often fabricated medical notes so as to provide an explanation for a death he had caused. Shipman's notes do not suggest that the death was due to respiratory failure. He certified that the cause was coronary thrombosis, a common cause of sudden death and one which Shipman frequently relied on when he had killed a patient. If the death had followed the kind of gradual decline or a chest infection which are the usual precursors of death from respiratory failure, I would have expected Shipman to certify respiratory failure as the cause. The long-term medical history was such as would have led to the expectation of a death from respiratory failure. There was no clear history of heart disease such as would have led to the expectation of a cardiac death, although it is true that, as a heavy smoker, Mr Halliday must have been at some increased risk of heart attack. For those reasons, I deduce that Mr Halliday's final illness was very short, so short that Mrs Hefferan did not reach Hyde before the death.
The death occurred in Shipman's presence. That, in itself, is a factor which arouses real suspicion that Shipman caused the death. Dr John Grenville says that it is extremely unusual for a patient to die in the course of a home visit by a general practitioner, unless the patient was terminally ill or the doctor had been called out as an emergency on account of acute symptoms of a serious nature, such as might indicate a heart attack or stroke. This visit took place in the early afternoon, at a time when Shipman would usually be making his routine calls. It is possible that he was called out on account of acute and serious symptoms. However, I think this is very unlikely, as Mr Halliday's name appears in the list of Shipman's visits for that day without any indication that there had been an urgent request. If the request was not made as a matter of urgency, it was an extraordinary coincidence that Mr Halliday should have died during the visit. This kind of coincidence does not occur in the experience of other doctors. Shipman would have us believe that it happened frequently with him. I regard any death which occurred during a visit by Shipman as highly suspicious.
The note Shipman made of the consultation during which Mr Halliday died arouses further suspicion. It creates the impression that Mr Halliday was suffering from a heart attack. Shipman claims to have called an ambulance and to have cancelled it before arrival because Mr Halliday had already died. This is a pattern I have seen in many Shipman killings. In other cases, where it has been possible to verify that claim, it has almost always been found that Shipman had not called an ambulance. This death occurred so long ago that the ambulance records have long since been destroyed. However, I note that Shipman claimed on Form B that he had been with Mr Halliday for an hour before his death and that the death was preceded by a coma of 30 minutes. I find it hard to believe that the ambulance, if called, would not have arrived in that time. In any event, unconsciousness for a period of 30 minutes between a coronary thrombosis and death would be most unusual. The usual course of events, if the heart attack is to prove fatal, is for the patient to go into cardiac arrest and die within a few minutes. The attending doctor should call an ambulance as an emergency and then carry out cardiopulmonary resuscitation procedures until the paramedics arrive. Shipman did not do this. His medical note and Form B entries do not make good medical sense. I do not think Shipman ever called an ambulance. I regard this as a highly suspicious feature.
The medical note also refers to the presence of a neighbour at the death. That, too, is a feature which appears in many cases in which Shipman killed his patient. He liked to create the impression that he had not been alone with his patient throughout the death. In this case, I cannot say whether or not a neighbour was present, but Shipman's claims give rise to some suspicion.
Shipman claimed that he had administered 10mg morphine to Mr Halliday. A very small dose of morphine might be appropriate treatment if Mr Halliday were suffering extreme pain or distress during a heart attack or an attack of acute ventricular failure. However, such an injection must be given slowly and with great care, observing the effect on the patient, and the injection should be stopped as soon as the desired effect is achieved. For Mr Halliday, 10mg would have been a dangerously large dose, as his respiratory function was already compromised. Such a dose might, of itself, have caused Mr Halliday's death. However, the question arises as to whether Shipman gave more than 10mg. In any case where it is seen that Shipman's use of opiates is followed by death, great suspicion arises. Shipman did not have a controlled drugs register and should not have had opiates in his medical bag. It is known that, on many occasions, he had a sufficient quantity with him to kill his patient.
My conclusion is that Shipman killed Mr Halliday by administering to him a lethal injection of opiates. I am sure of this conclusion. I think that Mr Halliday had probably been in reasonable health in the days before his death. He probably felt unwell on the morning of 30th
March and either telephoned the surgery to ask for a visit or asked his neighbour to do so. When Shipman arrived, he found that Mrs Hefferan was not there, which was unusual, and took the opportunity to kill him.

name: Charles MacConnell
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 130 Foxholes Road, Hyde
conclusion:
It is not possible for me to say whether Mr MacConnell died as a result of natural causes or as a result of an unlawful act on Shipman's part.
Mr MacConnell was terminally ill. He was housebound for the last month of his life and spent the last few days of his life either sitting in a chair or lying in bed. He was suffering from advanced cancer, probably of the stomach and lung. He also had a tumour in his neck. His family had been summoned and it is clear that his death was expected.
It was almost certainly Shipman who came to see Mr MacConnell, after Mrs Pendlebury had left the house at 6pm on 24th
May, because he recorded on the MCCD counterfoil that he had seen Mr MacConnell alive on that day. It appears that he administered some form of medication. Bearing in mind the advanced stage of Mr MacConnell's cancer, he would almost certainly have been justified in giving an injection of morphine or diamorphine for the relief of pain or distress. Although there is no direct evidence to suggest that Shipman did administer an injection of opiate, the evidence that he told Mrs MacConnell that her husband would now sleep is entirely consistent with him having done so. Alternatively, he might have given some other type of drug, such as Largactil.
In his evidence to the Inquiry, Professor Henry McQuay said that death would follow within a few minutes following a lethal intravenous injection of diamorphine. It is clear from the history that Shipman did not kill Mr MacConnell with a lethal intravenous injection of an opiate. He would have been dead by the time Mrs Pendlebury spoke to her mother on her arrival home. A lethal dose of opiate given intramuscularly would have caused death within about an hour. The period of time that elapsed between Shipman's visit and the death is unclear. It is Mrs Pendlebury's recollection that the doctor had called before 8.30pm but she is unable to say at what time her father died. It is possible that Mr MacConnell died within an hour of Shipman having administered some medication. If he did, it is possible that Shipman deliberately gave an excessive dose, intending it to hasten Mr MacConnell's end. It is also possible that rather more than an hour elapsed between the injection (if there was one) and the death, in which case, Shipman could not have directly caused the death.
A further possibility is that Shipman gave an injection of opiate which was not sufficient directly to cause Mr MacConnell's death. He might possibly have given a sedative such as Largactil. Either might have caused Mr MacConnell to go to sleep. Either type of drug might have been justified, if given in a suitable dose. However, for a patient such as Mr MacConnell, there are particular problems. Where a patient is suffering from breathing difficulties, only a modest dose of opiate or sedative may be sufficient to cause death. The doctor may face a difficult task in deciding whether to give the drug. He or she may realise that the drug will hasten death but, on the other hand, the doctor may think that something must be given to ease the patient's distress. Because Shipman killed so many patients, I am bound to suspect that he might have given an unjustifiable amount of opiate with the intention of shortening Mr MacConnell's life. However, it can be no more than suspicion.
In the light of all these uncertainties, I cannot reach any positive decision. I can say that, if Shipman did administer an excessive dose of any drug, I do not think he can have shortened Mr MacConnell's life by very long.

name: Mildred Robinson
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 2 Mona Street, Hyde
conclusion:
The evidence in respect of Mrs Robinson's health is unclear. On balance, it seems likely that she had some respiratory problems associated with her smoking. I think it unlikely that Shipman would have mentioned chronic bronchitis as a contributory cause of death if there was no factual basis for it. There is nothing, however, to suggest that anyone expected her to die when she did. Shipman had not visited her at home for about six weeks before her death. This suggests that she was not known to be in poor health at the time of her death. There is no evidence that Mrs Robinson was known to be suffering from a heart condition. I bear in mind, however, that, at the age of 84, she must have been at some risk of dying of a heart attack.
Something caused Shipman to visit Mrs Robinson while she was alive on the day of the death. That much can be safely inferred from the MCCD. As her name appears in the visits book, I think it unlikely that Shipman just decided to pay her an unsolicited visit. I think the most likely explanation lies within Mrs Page's recollection of what Mrs Taylor told her soon after the death, namely that she had called on Mrs Robinson early that morning and had found her to be unwell. (I think Mrs Robinson had probably stayed in bed.) I think Mrs Taylor called in at the surgery to request a visit. (Mrs Taylor worked near to the Donneybrook Surgery.) I think that Mrs Taylor was not unduly worried, as the proposed visit does not seem to have been given any priority in Shipman's visiting list. It appears likely that Shipman visited in the late morning. I think the evidence that he was seen leaving Mrs Robinson's house is unreliable. I think that Mrs Robinson died during Shipman's visit.
Whether or not Shipman had killed Mrs Robinson, he would need to contact someone who knew her and who could contact her relatives. I think it is likely that he asked one of the receptionists to go to Mrs Taylor's shop and ask her to return home. That is why Mrs Taylor recalls being asked to go home and cannot remember who it was who spoke to her. It is quite likely that she was not told at that stage that Mrs Robinson had died, which is why she has a recollection of being told that Mrs Robinson was very ill. I think Mrs Taylor is probably mistaken in her recollection that she received this call in the afternoon. I think it more likely that it was at around lunchtime. When she arrived at Mrs Robinson's home, it is likely that Shipman was still there and I think it highly likely that Mrs Robinson was already dead. I am satisfied that she was still in bed, although Mrs Taylor has no recollection of this. What Shipman said to her, I am not sure. It is possible that he told her that he had found Mrs Robinson dead in bed (which would account for Ms Knowles' recollection that Mrs Robinson had been found dead in bed). Alternatively, it is possible that Shipman told Mrs Taylor that he had just given her an injection and that she would 'not be long'. Perhaps the latter is more likely as otherwise Shipman would not have admitted that he had seen Mrs Robinson alive on the day of her death. A real possibility is that he combined the two and told Mrs Taylor that he had arrived to find Mrs Robinson breathing her last. This would be typical conduct for Shipman. Whatever he said, I think that Mrs Taylor contacted Ms Knowles, who came to the house, and it was probably she who telephoned Mr Hartley. Meanwhile, Shipman had departed leaving the MCCD on the sideboard.
That seems to me to be the most likely course of events. I have considered the possibility that Mrs Taylor found Mrs Robinson dead in bed when she went round in the morning and called Shipman out to see the body. However, that would not account for Shipman's admission on the MCCD that he had seen Mrs Robinson alive on the day of her death.
The course of events which I have outlined gives rise to a very strong suspicion that Shipman killed Mrs Robinson. I think it likely that Mrs Robinson was unwell on the morning of 26th
June and stayed in bed. Mrs Taylor asked Shipman to visit but not as a matter of emergency. That Mrs Robinson should die before Shipman arrived, is possible but unlikely. If that had happened, Shipman would not have said that he saw her alive on that day. For Mrs Robinson to die during his visit gives rise to a very grave suspicion that he killed her. It would be an enormous coincidence if she had suffered a fatal heart attack during a routine visit.
Unfortunately, there are no cremation documents and we do not have Shipman's contribution to the evidence of what happened that day.
Mrs Robinson was said to look peaceful, as though she had fallen asleep. That expression is not typical of a person who has suffered a fatal heart attack. However, I do not attach any weight to this factor, as it is possible (although, in my view, unlikely) that Shipman arrived to find Mrs Robinson suffering the chest pain of a heart attack and gave her a small injection of a drug to ease her pain.
My conclusion is that Shipman probably killed Mrs Robinson. Because of the passage of time, the failing recollection of the witnesses and the lack of medical records and cremation documents, I cannot be sure of that conclusion.

name: Albert Edward Saunders
title: Mr
place_of_death: Hyde Nursing Home, Grange Road South, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mr Saunders died of natural causes as certified by Shipman.
Mr Saunders had had a stroke and was in poor health towards the end of his life. He appeared to develop influenza or a chest infection and then deteriorated. The description of his condition given by the witnesses is consistent with that of bronchopneumonia. The death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
There is no evidence that Shipman had access to Mr Saunders in the hours before his death. It appears that his last visit was on 8th
January. Although there is a theoretical possibility that Shipman could have entered Hyde Nursing Home unnoticed on the morning of 9th
January, there is no reason to suspect that he did or that, if he did, he did anything which caused or hastened Mr Saunders' death, such as administering a lethal dose of strong opiate. Ms Greer's description of his death is not typical of a death due to opiate poisoning. Nor is there any evidence to suggest that Shipman over-sedated Mr Saunders in a manner which might have increased his vulnerability to bronchopneumonia.
There is no reason to suspect that Shipman was unlawfully involved in Mr Saunders' death.

name: Joseph Beech
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 5 Bryce Street, Hyde
conclusion:
The medical evidence suggests that Mr Beech died a natural death. He was very unwell in the months leading up to his death. He was very weak, had taken to his bed and was unable to attend the day hospital. Mr Beech's daughter was concerned about his deterioration the day before he died.
There would be no cause for concern about Shipman's role in this death were it not for the possibility that he visited Mr Beech shortly before his death on 12th
April. This possibility cannot be ruled out. The family is unable to say when Shipman last visited Mr Beech. The fact that a financial claim was made in respect of a visit on 12th
April, suggests that Shipman did visit Mr Beech whilst he was still alive. However, it is possible that the financial claim was made in error, perhaps due to an administrative mix-up, and related to the visit that Shipman made after the discovery that Mr Beech had died. The claim may even have been an opportunistic and dishonest attempt on the part of Shipman to gain remuneration for a visit during the night, which did not in fact take place.
If a request for a visit was made during the late evening of 11th
April or early morning of the 12th
, it is difficult to see how Shipman was contacted. According to Mrs Shipman, calls made during the night were dealt with by Healthcall, who have no record of a request for a visit before the telephone call made by the neighbour at 7.59am. It certainly would have been an unusual time for Shipman to make an unsolicited visit, even though Mr Beech's daughter had been in contact with the surgery on 11th
April and, in requesting a domiciliary visit, had presumably expressed concern as to his condition.
The understanding that Mrs Beech found her husband dead at 5am suggests that he was alive when she went to bed the night before. If Shipman had visited during the night, one might have expected the family to be aware of that. As I cannot rule out the possibility of a visit in the night, I cannot absolutely rule out the possibility of Shipman having administered an injection of opiate.
My conclusion is that it is likely that Mr Beech died a natural death, but I cannot rule out the possibility that Shipman visited shortly before the death and did something to hasten Mr Beech's end.

name: Michael Connors
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 16 Shade Street, Todmorden
conclusion:
Shipman last saw Mr Connors on the Friday, three days before he died. This was in consultation at the surgery. It appears that Shipman took a blood sample, which was consistent with his attempts to diagnose and treat Mr Connors' liver complaint. Although Mr Connors felt ill and retired to bed on his return home on the Friday afternoon, the fact that he lived for over two days after leaving the surgery rules out any possibility that Shipman caused his death by the administration of a lethal dose of opiate. Professor Henry McQuay and Dr John Grenville, in their joint generic evidence, have explained that, if a lethal dose of opiate were administered intravenously, it would take effect within a few minutes. If given intramuscularly, it would take effect within an hour.
Mr Connors' movements between leaving the surgery and returning home on the Friday afternoon are not known. Nor is it known how he came to lose the £65 he had been saving.
The real concern in this case is not that Shipman might have deliberately killed Mr Connors by injecting him with a lethal dose of opiate, but that he might have precipitated his death by prescribing morphine-based tablets inappropriately. If Mr Connors' sleepiness or near coma during the last two days of his life was due to the tablets Shipman had prescribed, and if Mr Connors developed bronchopneumonia while lying in bed, there might be a causal connection between Shipman's decision to prescribe morphine-based tablets and Mr Connors' death. I do not think I can reach any firm conclusion on that because, for one thing, we do not know for certain that the tablets were morphine-based. Nor do I think I can properly reach any decision about whether or not Shipman might have deliberately prescribed medication which was harmful to Mr Connors.
I am afraid I cannot reach a positive conclusion about this case. The fact that Mr Connors was emaciated, had a large necrotic bronchial tumour and a grossly enlarged spleen suggests strongly that he was very poorly for a week before he died.

name: Peter Higginbottom
title: Mr
place_of_death: Tameside General Hospital
conclusion: I am quite sure that Mr Higginbottom died of natural causes. The evidence shows that he was already unresponsive when Shipman's attendance was requested. Shipman's only contribution was to arrange for the patient to be admitted to hospital.

name: Kathleen McDonald
title: Miss
place_of_death: her home, 26 Carter Place, Hyde
conclusion:
The evidence of Mr Seddon suggests that his aunt enjoyed good health. The visits book reveals two visits by Shipman in the weeks leading up to her death, although the reasons for those visits are not known. They were not close together in time and it seems unlikely that Miss McDonald's state of health was such that her death was thought to be imminent. If anything, it appears that her death was sudden and unexpected.
There are real grounds for suspicion that Shipman might have been unlawfully involved in this death. Mrs Virgin told Mr Seddon that Shipman was present at the death and that he had been 'just passing'. It is not clear what was meant by 'just passing'. It is possible that Miss McDonald was suddenly taken ill and Shipman was summoned and was able to reach the flat very quickly because he was close by. On the other hand, it would be entirely typical of Shipman to make an unscheduled visit to a patient, kill him or her, and then tell relatives or neighbours that he had just called in, as he was passing, and had found the patient to be very ill and close to death. That Shipman was due to visit a patient who lived close by makes it rather more likely that he would make an unsolicited call on 22nd
February. If Shipman made an unsolicited call and Miss McDonald happened to die in the course of it, I would regard this death as extremely suspicious. A sudden fatal stroke is a rare event and the chances of such an event occurring by coincidence during a doctor's visit are very slight. Shipman claimed that such events occurred quite regularly but, as Dr Grenville says, it is extremely rare in the experience of other general practitioners.
My suspicions are heightened by the evidence that Miss McDonald was lying on her bed with her boots removed. Had she collapsed from a massive fatal stroke, she would not have had time or the chance to remove her boots. It would be unlikely that Shipman would remove them for her if he came to her aid. It is far more likely that she removed them before getting onto the bed, possibly at Shipman's request for the purpose of allowing him to take a blood sample or give an injection.
I am concerned, too, that this case was not referred to the coroner. If Shipman had not seen Miss McDonald since 5th
February, it is hard to see how he could have been justified in certifying the cause of death as a stroke.
Even though the evidence is very limited, such evidence as is available is so resonant of later suspicious deaths, in which far more evidence is available, that I have come to the conclusion that Shipman probably killed Miss McDonald. I cannot say that I am sure of that conclusion.

name: Edward Walker
title: Mr
place_of_death: Scaitcliffe Hall, a residential home for the elderly, Todmorden
conclusion: I am unable to reach any conclusion as to the circumstances of this death. The medical records have not survived. There are no records from Scaitcliffe Hall. There is no cremation certificate. Mrs Walker's recollection is not clear, which is not surprising as these events occurred over 27 years ago. There is no evidence that Shipman saw Mr Walker in the last hour or minutes of his life. He might have done; he might not. There is no medical evidence from which I can form any view as to the likelihood of a natural death. If this case involved any doctor other than Shipman, I would say that there was no reason to suspect foul play and it would follow that the death was almost certainly natural. However, as Shipman was to become a serial murderer, some suspicion is bound to arise in any case in which he might have had access to a patient shortly before death. Although there is no evidence that Shipman killed Mr Walker, I cannot say that he did not. I can reach no decision.

name: Hannah Helena Mottram
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 187 Talbot Road, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
I regret to say that the truth about Mrs Mottram's death is unlikely ever to be known.
There is no evidence from which I can judge the seriousness of Mrs Mottram's underlying heart condition. Nor am I able to form a clear view of her condition on the day of her death. The relatives' description of Mrs Mottram's condition on 5th
August is not what I would have expected if she had had a heart attack. Nor indeed does it sound as though she had had a stroke. There is no evidence of slurred speech or weakness down one side. At Shipman's first visit, he gave an injection but we do not know what it was. Mrs Mottram then seems to have deteriorated gradually during the day. Her level of consciousness seems to have declined and eventually her breathing became laboured. Although the witnesses do not recall the time of death, it sounds as though Mrs Mottram died in the late afternoon or early evening.
It seems likely that Shipman visited twice during that day, once in the morning and again in the afternoon. I find it very strange that he should have advised that Mrs Mottram was 'too ill to go into hospital'. I regard that opinion as a contradiction in terms. Mrs Mottram was only 69. She had been leading an active life. If she had had a heart attack, she should have been admitted. I do not know and cannot guess what drug Shipman injected during his first visit. Whatever it was, it cannot have been a lethal injection of opiate, as Mrs Mottram lived for many hours afterwards. The relatives do not mention that Shipman left a prescription or that anyone went to a pharmacy that day. It is possible that Shipman gave an injection of opiate of an amount which was not lethal or of some sedative drug, such as Largactil. If he did, it would appear that the dose was not harmful, as there is some evidence that Mrs Mottram was able to join in a conversation for some time afterwards, although later on she was asleep.
We do not know what treatment, if any, Shipman gave at his second visit. Nor is there any clear evidence of the time of this visit, save that I have the distinct impression that Mrs Mottram lived for well over an hour after Shipman's second visit. If she did, she cannot have died as the result of a lethal injection of opiate. Professor Henry McQuay and Dr John Grenville agree that if a lethal injection of opiate is given intravenously it will cause death within a few minutes; if given intramuscularly, death will follow within about an hour.
I am puzzled by the evidence that Shipman appeared to be anxious to retain control over Mrs Mottram. He was the Donneybrook doctor on duty that weekend and, provided the family only sought the help of a general practitioner, Shipman would retain control of the certification of Mrs Mottram's death. It is possible that he was concerned that the family might call an ambulance, in which case he would lose control. The fact that Shipman said that Mrs Mottram was too ill to go to hospital also suggests that he was anxious to keep her treatment under his control. These factors give rise to some suspicion that Shipman might have caused Mrs Mottram's death.
Owing to the passage of time and the loss of the documentary records, I am unable to decide whether this death was natural or was due to an unlawful act on the part of Shipman.

name: Harriet Stopford
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Yew Trees Elderly Persons Home (known as Yew Trees), Yew Tree Lane, Dukinfield
certified_cause: bronchopneumonia due to chronic obstructive airways disease
conclusion:
Mrs Eades has never had any suspicion that Shipman was unlawfully involved in her mother's death. Whilst she was aware that he had withdrawn her mother's medication in order to let her die, she believed that this was the best thing for her mother. She did not wish to see her mother's suffering prolonged unnecessarily.
I have little doubt that Professor Baker was suspicious about this death because Shipman had visited Mrs Stopford so short a time before she died. When seen in context and when explained by Mrs Eades' evidence, however, there is no reason to have suspicion about this death.
I am quite satisfied that Shipman did not kill Mrs Stopford by lethal injection or by any other means. He appears to have involved Mrs Stopford's daughter in a sensitive discussion as to whether her mother's medication should be continued or withdrawn and Mrs Stopford's daughter seems to have been fully informed when she took the decision. Once her medication was withdrawn, Mrs Stopford died of natural causes.

name: Winifred Mary Walker
title: Mrs
conclusion:
I think Shipman probably did visit Mrs Walker on Friday, 2nd
November, even though no visit is recorded in the Evaluation Sheets. I say that because I am satisfied that Shipman was taking a week's leave, starting on the Saturday. Friday would be his last chance to visit Mrs Walker, who he knew was close to death. He had promised to visit on the Friday. Mr Geoffrey Walker, whose evidence I found the most reliable of all the family witnesses, said that Shipman visited that day. Initially he had not said that Shipman gave an injection although later he was to assert that an injection was given. I think it is unlikely although possible that Shipman gave Mrs Walker an injection on that day. She had quite large quantities of morphine elixir and there is no evidence that she was suffering from breakthrough pain. If he did give an injection, it is plain that it did not cause Mrs Walker's death, as she lived for about 36 hours afterwards.
I find that Shipman probably did not visit Mrs Walker on Saturday, 3rd
November. For one thing, he was on leave, although probably spending it at home. It would have been possible for him to visit. More importantly, I find the evidence of the family unsatisfactory. They have clearly persuaded themselves and each other that Shipman visited that day. Their accounts have changed considerably over the course of the two investigations and the hearing.
Even if Shipman did attend on Saturday, 3rd
November and even if he gave an injection, it is quite clear that that injection did not cause Mrs Walker's death. Mrs Walker lived for about 12 hours after that injection was given, if it ever was. Dr Grenville and Professor Henry McQuay have said in their generic evidence that, if a lethal dose of strong opiate is given intravenously, the patient will be unconscious within a few seconds and will be dead within about five minutes. If a lethal dose is given intramuscularly, the patient will be dead within about an hour. Dr Grenville has also said that Mrs Walker's state of confusion on the Saturday afternoon was not indicative of or compatible with an overdose of opiate.
I have considered the possibility that Shipman gave a massive dose of a sedative drug such as Largactil. I rule this out as well. A massive dose of sedative would have sent Mrs Walker into a deep sleep for several hours. According to the family, she was confused and restless after the injection.
I am quite sure that Mrs Walker died a natural death.

name: Alice Brown
title: Miss
place_of_death: her home, 11 Pexwood Place, Todmorden
conclusion:
Mrs Hepworth and Mrs Sutcliffe confirm that Miss Brown appeared to be in the terminal stages of lung cancer. It seems likely that a doctor was visiting every day during the last week or two of her life. Shipman says that he visited on 10th
March. There is no reason to suspect that he visited on the day of the death, as the death occurred at 6am. Even though it is quite likely that he administered some medication on 10th
March, it is extremely unlikely that that medication could have caused or contributed to Miss Brown's death. If a lethal dose of opiates had been administered by intramuscular injection, she would have died within an hour.
It seems highly likely that Mrs McLoughlin, who sat with Miss Brown on the night before her death, called for a duty doctor when Miss Brown deteriorated. That must be why Dr Grieve attended.
I am sure that Miss Brown's death was natural and that Shipman played no part in it.

name: Clifford Barnes Heapey
title: Mr
place_of_death: Godley Court, Hyde Nursing Home, Grange Road South, Hyde
conclusion:
There are some features of this death which are very suspicious. The first and most obvious is that the death occurred in Shipman's presence and immediately after he had administered an injection to Mr Heapey. It appears that he told Mrs Berry that the injection was of a diuretic but he did not record the fact that he had given an injection in the medical notes.
It is not possible to be certain of Mr Heapey's medical condition at the time of Shipman's arrival. It is clear that he was sufficiently unwell to need a visit from the doctor and it is possible that he was critically ill. However, I think that the nursing home staff would have recognised if Mr Heapey was seriously ill and would have conveyed a sense of urgency to the surgery staff, who would have reflected that urgency in their note in the visits book. Moreover, had the nursing home staff realised that Mr Heapey might possibly die, they would have summoned his son. Accordingly, I think it unlikely that Mr Heapey was critical at the time Shipman was summoned. There is no evidence of deterioration between the telephone call and Shipman's arrival, although I cannot rule that out. In my view, it seems likely that, at the time of Shipman's arrival, Mr Heapey was quite unwell but not in a critical state. That he should die immediately after the injection which Shipman then gave makes me think that it is highly likely that the injection Shipman gave was an opiate and that, by injecting him, Shipman intended to bring about Mr Heapey's death. I cannot say that I am sure of this conclusion but I think it highly likely that Shipman killed Mr Heapey.

name: Oscar Meredith
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 32 Hough Lane, Hyde
conclusion:
Mr Meredith had a history of stroke and was clearly very unwell before Shipman's arrival at the house at about 2pm on 12th
November. It is possible that he had had another stroke, even though pain is not usually a feature of such an event. It is also possible that Mr Meredith had some other illness, with painful symptoms, and that his son was either not aware of this or has forgotten about it. Shipman told Mr David Meredith that he had given his father something to make him more comfortable. In the light of Mr David Meredith's evidence about the empty phial of morphine, it seems likely that that was what Shipman gave on that day. If it was morphine, the dose cannot have been lethal, as Mr David Meredith lived for at least 12 hours and probably rather longer. A lethal dose of morphine would have killed within the hour. However, it is possible that Shipman gave a sub-lethal dose of morphine or a large dose of a sedative such as Largactil. If heavily sedated, Mr Meredith would be more vulnerable to bronchopneumonia, a common mechanism of death in elderly people. If Shipman did this, it would not be possible to say whether he had done it with the intention of keeping Mr Meredith comfortable or whether he used it as an indirect way of hastening his death.
What remains quite uncertain is what happened on 13th
November. It is not clear whether Shipman saw Mr Meredith alive on that day. He said that he did when completing the MCCD counterfoil. Mr Meredith's name was not in his visits book for that day but that is not conclusive either way. Mrs Meredith seems to have given her son the impression that Shipman had not visited that day. However, given the passage of time and the nature of the evidence, that does not seem conclusive either. There remains a real possibility, even a likelihood, that Shipman was at the house shortly before Mr Meredith's death.
Mr David Meredith says he found an empty phial of morphine on 13th
November and assumed it had been left on the previous day. However, it might well have been left that day and the contents might have been administered that day. I am afraid I do not know. If Shipman did give Mr Meredith an injection of morphine on that day, I am unable to say whether such a dose was justified. I do not know whether Mr Meredith was in pain. Nor do I know how large a dose it might have been or how soon before the death it was administered. It follows that I could not say whether such a dose, if given, had caused or hastened Mr Meredith's death.
I regret to say that I am unable to decide whether Shipman did or did not hasten Mr Meredith's death. If he did, I do not think he could have hastened the end by a significant period of time.

name: Margaret Smith
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Norbury House, a residential home for the elderly, Great Norbury Street, Hyde
conclusion:
I am satisfied that Mrs Smith died of natural causes. It is clear from the evidence of her daughter that Mrs Smith had lapsed into semi-consciousness the evening before her death. Whatever the precise cause of her death, it would appear that the death was not sudden or unexpected.
Apart from the ambiguous entry in the Norbury House register of residents, there is no evidence that Shipman saw or had access to Mrs Smith on the day of her death. Although this entry is ambiguous, Mrs Mackie says that the entry means that she summoned Shipman to see Mrs Smith's body after the death and had not asked him to visit her on that day while she was still alive. It would be unusual for Shipman to visit before 10.40am on a weekday. He would usually be busy in his surgery until about noon. It seems to me that I can discount the possibility that Shipman visited Mrs Smith while alive on 21st
March. I conclude that there is no cause to suspect that Shipman was in any way involved in this death.

name: Minnie Ward
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Laurel Bank, a residential home for the elderly, Knott Lane, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Ward died as the result of natural causes.
The Laurel Bank diary is plainly a contemporaneous record of events and I am confident of its accuracy. It is clear from the diary that Mrs Ward became unwell in the last week or two of her life. She had reached a very great age and had suffered from congestive heart failure for some time. When she developed a chest infection, it is not surprising that she succumbed quite quickly. Although her death seemed quite sudden, I do not think it could be said to be unexpected from a medical point of view.
It seems clear to me that Shipman last saw Mrs Ward on 11th
April, a week before her death. It is possible, but unlikely, that he made a later visit. It is clear that the staff at the home were concerned about Mrs Ward's deteriorating condition in the night before she died, but there is no evidence that Shipman was called or that he visited.
Mrs Kenworthy expressed concern that Shipman may have contributed to her mother's death by changing her medication inappropriately. The evidence of Dr Grenville, however, makes it clear that Shipman's treatment of Mrs Ward was appropriate in this case and that the change to her medication regime in no way contributed to her death.

name: Lydia Edith Butcher
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion: I am quite satisfied that Mrs Butcher died a natural death from CHF. Although there are no medical records for the period before the death, the Charnley House diary gives a very full account of Mrs Butcher's last days. The diary shows that her condition deteriorated in the days leading up to her death. Her family knew that she was close to death. Shipman visited her at 6.45pm that evening but she was plainly alive when he left because the staff were observing Mrs Butcher frequently and they did not call the duty doctor until Mrs Butcher died much later that night. Mrs Butcher's family can be reassured that her death was entirely natural.

name: Lily Crossley
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 2 Longfield Way, Todmorden
conclusion:
There is no real doubt in my mind that, shortly before her death, Mrs Crossley was in the terminal phase of lung cancer, which had spread into the tissues of her neck and shoulder. This would have been a very painful condition, which would have warranted the administration of powerful pain-relieving drugs.
On the evening of 21st
January 1975, a doctor attended Mrs Crossley. Although Mrs Gilyeat cannot identify him by name, I think it was probably Shipman. Dr Grieve says it would probably have been he or Shipman. Mrs Crossley was Shipman's patient. I know from the case of Mr Robert Lingard, who died during the same evening as Mrs Crossley, that Shipman was either present at or was called out after Mr Lingard's death, which probably took place at about 7.30pm. I am satisfied, therefore, that Shipman was on duty that evening and it seems likely that he was the doctor who attended Mrs Crossley.
Shipman gave an injection, which he said would calm Mrs Crossley down and it appeared to have that effect. We do not know what he gave or how much. Whenever Shipman gave a drug shortly before death, a suspicion arises that he might have intentionally hastened the patient's death.
Although Dr Grieve says that the usual practice of the doctors from the Abraham Ormerod Medical Centre was to give Largactil for pain relief in cases of this kind, it appears that Shipman had prescribed pethidine. Whether he gave any pethidine to Mrs Crossley or whether he kept it all for his purposes, I cannot say. If Shipman gave either Largactil or pethidine shortly before the death, those drugs might well have had the desired effect of calming Mrs Crossley, but they would be unlikely to have caused or contributed to her death within the hour. A very large dose of pethidine would have been required to kill. However, a relatively modest dose of morphine or diamorphine could have killed her. It is entirely possible that Shipman gave a much stronger opiate than pethidine. He would almost certainly have had either morphine or diamorphine in his medical bag for use in emergencies. If he gave a lethal dose of strong opiate intramuscularly, death would have followed within the hour. The evidence of Mrs Gilyeat is that Mrs Crossley died within about an hour of the doctor's visit.
There is, therefore, a real possibility that Shipman gave a lethal injection of opiate and hastened Mrs Crossley's death. I cannot say that he did, as she might have died naturally, due to her advanced cancer. The injection might have done no more than calm her. It is also possible that Shipman gave an injection of opiate in good faith, intending only that it should ease Mrs Crossley's pain but that the drug had the unintended effect of hastening her death. However, knowing what I know about Shipman's later years, and knowing that three patients of his died on 21st
January 1975, I am suspicious that he unlawfully killed Mrs Crossley. I am unable to say that he probably did so. If Shipman did kill her, I think it is clear that he hastened her death by only a short time.

name: Muriel Eveline Harrison
title: Miss
place_of_death: Hyde Nursing Home, Grange Road South, Hyde
conclusion:
I am satisfied that Shipman did not cause or contribute to Miss Harrison's death.
Miss Harrison suffered a bad fall a few days before her death. Her condition deteriorated from that time. She was seen to be unresponsive at lunchtime on the day of her death. Shipman was called but did not give any treatment. He plainly thought that Miss Harrison was dying. After he had gone, Miss Harrison seems to have had some sort of haemorrhage immediately before her death.
Although it is clear that Shipman saw Miss Harrison only about an hour or so before her death, the evidence is that he did not give any treatment and certainly did not give an injection. The way in which Miss Harrison died, following a haemorrhage, is not suggestive of a death due to opiate poisoning.
It appears to me that Miss Harrison's death was neither sudden nor unexpected. There is no reason to suspect that Shipman did anything which caused or hastened the death.

name: Cyril Mitchell
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 5 Paignton Walk, Hyde
conclusion: Nothing is known of Mr Mitchell's medical history or his state of health shortly before his death. I cannot say whether or not he was likely to suffer a fatal coronary thrombosis. Nor am I able to say whether or not the information recorded by Shipman on the counterfoil to the MCCD is correct. It is not known whether he visited Mr Mitchell on the day of his death. The lack of evidence makes it impossible to say whether this death was due to an unlawful act on the part of Shipman or whether it was a natural death.

name: Ruth Strickland
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Strickland died of natural causes. Although she had been in poor health for some time, it appears she became very unwell on 28th
November. She was chesty and ill in the day or two before her death. This description is entirely consistent with the certified cause of death, bronchopneumonia. Shipman prescribed penicillin, which would have been appropriate in the circumstances.
There is no record that Shipman gave an injection on the day of Mrs Strickland's death. Whilst it is theoretically possible that he might have administered some medication which had the effect of suppressing the breathing of his elderly patient, or otherwise hastening her death, this is highly unlikely.
The fact of Mrs Strickland's death was certified by Dr Smith. It does not, therefore, seem likely that Shipman was on call on the afternoon of Saturday, 2nd
December 1978. Nor does it seem likely that he was with Mrs Strickland shortly before her death.
I am quite satisfied that there is no cause for concern about this death.

name: Kathleen May Wass
title: Miss
place_of_death: Laurel Bank, a residential home for the elderly, Knott Lane, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Miss Wass died of natural causes, probably as the result of a chest infection or a heart attack. It appears from the Laurel Bank diary that she was unwell for a few days before her death and that her death, although quite sudden, was not inexplicable.
The Laurel Bank diary gives every appearance of being a genuinely contemporaneous record of events. It suggests that Shipman was not involved in Miss Wass' death. Shipman visited on 1st
November and gave no treatment. I am confident that, if he had given an injection, a record would have been made in the diary. No change in Miss Wass' condition is noted after his departure on that day. There is no evidence that he came to the home again until after her death.
I agree with Dr Grenville and Professor Baker that the certified cause of death was not appropriate. However, it does not seem to me that this factor gives rise to any suspicion that Shipman caused Miss Wass' death.

name: Mary Louisa Boardman
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Laurel Bank, a residential home for the elderly, Knott Lane, Hyde
conclusion:
It seems to me highly likely that Mrs Boardman's death was entirely natural. The course of her decline is well described in the daily diary and her death on 11th
January was neither sudden nor unexpected.
The only cause for concern and suspicion is that Shipman claims to have visited Mrs Boardman between 10.30pm and 11pm on 10th
January. The Laurel Bank diary makes no mention of this visit; nor does it suggest that there was any reason for the doctor to be called. The diary only records the death, at 1.50am on 11th
January. If Shipman really did visit Mrs Boardman very late at night and if the staff did not record the visit, I would be concerned that he might have given her a drug which caused or hastened her death. That is a possibility. However, I think it is highly unlikely that Shipman visited Laurel Bank that night. He had said that nature was to take its course. Mrs Boardman was beyond treatment. It would be very strange and quite uncharacteristic for him to make a visit at this hour unless summoned in an emergency. There seems to be no suggestion even in the medical record that Mrs Boardman needed urgent medical attention. In respect of this supposed late night visit, Shipman noted only that Mrs Boardman was not yet dead. I think the most likely explanation is that Shipman made a false claim for a late night visit on 10th
January, when he had made no such visit. He may well have done the same for the night of 9th
January. He was a completely dishonest man. I have come across another case, that of Mr Joseph Beech, in which I suspect he may have made a fraudulent claim for an 'out of hours' visit which did not take place. As I have some faith in the accuracy of the Laurel Bank records and as I know that Shipman did not usually visit at night save in a real emergency, I think that is a far more likely explanation than the possibility that he visited Mrs Boardman at 11pm.
I think that Shipman did not see Mrs Boardman after his daytime visit on 10th
January. Shipman cannot have given any drug at that visit which directly caused or hastened her death. She lived for many hours afterwards.
There is no evidence in this case that Mrs Boardman was heavily sedated during her last days. There is evidence that she was declining and taking very little fluid but she appears to have been at least intermittently conscious. I can therefore rule out the possibility that Shipman hastened Mrs Boardman's death by over-sedating her so as to make her vulnerable to bronchopneumonia.
My conclusion is that although I cannot absolutely rule out the possibility that Shipman visited late at night and gave a drug which hastened Mrs Boardman's death, I think it is highly likely that she died a natural death.

name: Alice Hilda Connaughton
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
Mrs Connaughton's condition in the weeks leading up to death was very poor and she was suffering from severe diarrhoea. Her condition deteriorated in the days leading up to her death and she became dehydrated, weak and bed bound. It appears that her death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
Cause for suspicion arises from the conflict between the various sources of information as to whether Shipman saw Mrs Connaughton alive on the day of her death. The daily diary suggests that he did not and had not seen her since 10th
March, although I do not think that can be a complete record of his visits. Shipman himself says on Form B and on the MCCD counterfoil that he saw Mrs Connaughton alive on the day of the death. There is some support for that in his visits book, where her name appears without a cross beside it.
Suspicion is increased by Shipman's claim that Mrs Connaughton was in a coma for 12 hours before her death. A death from 'old age' would normally be preceded by a significant period of coma. Yet, the daily diary suggests that Mrs Connaughton was not in a coma at the end of the morning shift. My concern is further increased by Shipman's failure to state on Form B at what time on the day of death he had seen Mrs Connaughton alive. He left the box blank and it was probably completed after the medical referee had spoken to a member of the surgery staff. The answer seems unlikely to be accurate.
In the light of these uncertainties and causes for suspicion, I feel unable to reach any conclusion about this death.

name: Violet Hadfield
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 5 Gloucester Road, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
It is not possible to reach any conclusion about the cause of Mrs Hadfield's death or to form any view about whether or not Shipman was unlawfully involved.
There is very little evidence as to Mrs Hadfield's state of health at the time of her death. The reason for her fortnight's stay at Charnley House is unknown. It is possible that she was convalescing after a spell in hospital. Another possibility is that Mrs Hadfield was at Charnley House to give her usual carers two weeks' respite. However, as it does not appear that Mrs Hadfield had any relatives, this seems unlikely.
Although it appears that Mrs Hadfield was in reasonable health when she left Charnley House on Sunday, 12th
May, 12 days before she died, it seems that her health soon declined.
