On the basis of Shipman's visits book, he visited her on at least four occasions between her return home and the day of her death. It would seem likely that she developed quite a serious illness and he was visiting her periodically to monitor her condition.
In many cases considered by the Inquiry, suspicion has arisen because Shipman has been present at the death or has visited the deceased on the day of the death. If the deceased had not been seen alive after his visit, a high degree of suspicion would arise. There is some cause for suspicion in this case because Shipman recorded on the MCCD counterfoil that he had last seen Mrs Hadfield alive on the day of her death. However, it is not known whether she was seen alive after his departure.
The Inquiry has seen many cases in which Shipman has killed a patient and has attributed the death to a coronary thrombosis. This was one of the most common reasons he would give for a death which he himself had caused. This factor, when considered with the evidence that Shipman saw Mrs Hadfield on the day of death, raises a small element of suspicion in my mind that he might have killed her. However, the paucity of other evidence is such that I cannot reach any conclusion.

name: Thomas Moult
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 6 Thorpe Hall Grove, Hyde
conclusion:
Very little is known about the circumstances of Mr Moult's death. However, what is known gives rise to grave suspicion that Shipman may have killed him.
As nothing is known about Mr Moult's medical history, I must assume that what Shipman said on the MCCD is or might be true, namely that Mr Moult suffered from ischaemic heart disease and chronic bronchitis. Those conditions are not incompatible with the evidence that Shipman had not visited Mr Moult during the two months before his death.
The suspicion arises from the evidence relating to the day of the death. The fact that the death occurred on a day when Shipman visited is itself a cause for suspicion, especially as Mr Moult was obviously not terminally ill. It appears from the MCCD counterfoil that Mr Moult was still alive when Shipman visited him. That rules out the possibility that Mr Moult had been found dead and Shipman had been summoned to see the body. Shipman certified that Mr Moult died of a coronary thrombosis and that he saw the body after death. That suggests either that Shipman visited Mr Moult twice that day, once when he was alive and again after his death, or that the death occurred in Shipman's presence during his only visit. Either situation is possible but both are resonant of other cases in which Shipman has killed.
It is possible that, when Shipman was asked to visit Mr Moult that morning, Mr Moult was suffering from the symptoms of a heart attack, or perhaps angina. Such a request, if it sounded serious, would have been treated as an emergency. However, it seems that Mr Moult's request was not so treated. The surgery staff say that Shipman's usual procedure whenever an emergency arose was either for him to drop everything and go immediately or to instruct the staff to call an ambulance. Here, the position of Mr Moult's name in the visits book suggests that his name was written down by the receptionist in the ordinary way and that, when Shipman finished his surgery, which at this time was usually at about 11am, he decided on the order in which he would carry out his visits. That Mr Moult was given the first position might suggest that he was the most urgent but that is not necessarily so. Even if he were the most urgent, it does not seem likely that his condition gave rise to an emergency.
In my view, it is possible, although unlikely, that Mr Moult was having a heart attack when Shipman arrived. If that had happened, it would not be surprising, nor would it give rise to any suspicion, if Mr Moult died in Shipman's presence.
If Mr Moult was not having a heart attack when Shipman arrived, his subsequent death gives rise to grave suspicion that Shipman might have caused it. If Mr Moult died during Shipman's only visit and it was a non-emergency visit, the death during that short time would be a remarkable coincidence. Dr John Grenville says that such a coincidence might occur once in a general practitioner's lifetime. Shipman would have us believe that it happened quite frequently in his professional experience. I am satisfied that it did not and that almost all of the many deaths which occurred in Shipman's presence were almost certainly caused by him.
There is another possibility, which is that Shipman visited Mr Moult twice that day and that he saw the dead body on his second visit. If that were the case, it would not follow that the death had occurred in Shipman's presence. It would be possible that he had visited for the first time, treated Mr Moult and left him at home, presumably having decided that his condition, whatever it was, did not warrant hospital admission. Mr Moult could then have died and someone might have called Shipman out to see the body. However, I have found that many of Shipman's victims were killed during his first visit to a patient on a particular day, after which he would leave and wait until the body was found. Then he would return to see the body. Sometimes, he would return of his own volition and discover the body himself. It follows that the possibility that Shipman made two visits to Mr Moult on 26th
June does not necessarily reduce my suspicion that he might have killed him.
It is, of course, possible that Mr Moult died a natural death as the result of a coronary thrombosis. However, the fact that Shipman admitted that he had seen Mr Moult alive and seen the body after death on the same day persuades me that it is likely that Shipman killed Mr Moult. I would not reach that conclusion were it not for the fact that my consideration of other cases has led me to conclude that, by 1985, Shipman had already killed about 25 patients. The frequency with which he was killing was increasing. In reaching this decision, I have not relied on the fact that he also killed Mrs Mildred Robinson on that day, though the similarities are remarkable. Both were said to have died of a coronary thrombosis and both were said to have had chronic bronchitis as a contributory cause. Both had been seen before and after death on the same day. I reached my decision in Mrs Robinson's case before considering Mr Moult's. Despite the remarkable similarities, I do not think that I could properly say that the evidence that Shipman killed Mrs Robinson is probative in respect of Mr Moult.
My conclusion is that Shipman probably killed Mr Moult although I could not say that I am sure that he did.

name: Neville Shaw
title: Mr
place_of_death: Tameside General Hospital
conclusion:
I am quite sure that Mr Shaw died a natural death. In the light of the publicity surrounding Shipman's activities, it is understandable that the families of patients who had been treated by Shipman should be anxious about the deaths of their loved ones, particularly where it is thought that Shipman used to administer injections to them.
I am able to reassure Mr Shaw's family. It is usual for patients suffering from schizophrenia to have periodic injections of antipsychotic medication while living in the community. It is quite likely that Shipman would have administered those injections to Mr Shaw at Brindle House. No concern need be felt about those injections, as Mr Shaw did not suffer any ill effect and lived for many months after he went into Tameside General Hospital, when his contact with Shipman would have ceased.
It appears that Mr Shaw's physical health declined during the last year of his life and his death was not unexpected. Although Mr Derek Shaw and Mr Oldham were not aware of the nature of any physical illness, it seems likely that Mr Shaw was suffering from heart disease. It appears that he had a fatal heart attack during the night of 26th
to 27th
May 1986. It is almost inconceivable that Shipman could have had any contact with Mr Shaw during the evening of 26th
May and the early morning of 27th
May. Tameside General Hospital has its own medical staff and does not depend on the services of local general practitioners. In any event, the physical findings on post-mortem examination were conclusive and there can be no doubt that Mr Shaw died as the result of a heart attack.

name: Ellen Frances Wharam
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Bowlacre, a residential home for the elderly, Stockport Road, Hyde
conclusion: So little is known about the circumstances of this death that I do not feel able to reach any positive conclusion. The facts that Mrs Wharam was 91 years of age and lived in a nursing home, considered in conjunction with the absence on any evidence that Shipman visited her shortly before her death, would suggest that she probably died a natural death. However, there are some causes for concern. If, as Shipman certified, Mrs Wharam was suffering from carcinoma of the ovary, it would seem likely that she would have needed regular, if not frequent, medical attention. I would have expected to see regular visits recorded in the visits book. It is possible that Mrs Wharam's care had been assigned to the district nurses, but no information is available about that. Shipman frequently lied when completing MCCDs and Forms B. When not lying, Shipman was often careless in completing these forms. I have no confidence in what he wrote there.

name: Lily Brookes
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Hyde Nursing Home, Grange Road South, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that this was a natural death. The evidence of Mrs Hodgin shows that Mrs Brookes collapsed some time before Shipman arrived at the nursing home. It appears likely that she was either dead or very close to death before Shipman arrived.
Viewed in isolation, the contemporaneous documentation does give rise to concern. In particular, the information recorded on Form B suggests that Shipman was present at the moment of death, albeit with others. It seems that Shipman was probably mistaken in recording that he was present at the death, although if he attended whilst the paramedics were still present and when they attempted resuscitation then he may have felt entitled to declare that he was present at the death. This possible inaccuracy does not give rise to any suspicion that Shipman might in some way have caused the death. He plainly did not.

name: Josephine May Carroll
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Pole Bank Hall Residential Care Home, Stockport Road, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
We now know that Shipman became a serial killer and that his favoured method of killing was by the administration of a lethal injection of opiate. His typical victims were elderly women in poor health. Mrs Carroll fell into that category, not least because she suffered from a degree of senile dementia. However, this death occurred only a matter of days after Shipman had entered practice at the Donneybrook Surgery in Hyde. He could not have been well known to the staff at Pole Bank Hall at that time. The usual practice was for a doctor to be accompanied by the matron when visiting a patient at the home. While he was so new and unknown, it seems unlikely that Shipman would have risked giving a lethal injection to Mrs Carroll, especially in the presence of a member of staff.
On the other hand, if Mrs Davies' recollection were reliable, it would appear that her mother's death was very sudden. A death from bronchopneumonia is not sudden and it is most unlikely that Mrs Carroll could have been smoking and chatting in the conservatory at 11.30am and die as the result of bronchopneumonia by 12.30pm. However, these events occurred a very long time ago and there is no contemporaneous record which can confirm Mrs Davies' account.
There is no clear evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Carroll on the day of the death. Mrs Davies says that a care assistant told her that a doctor was going to see her mother that day and that Shipman later told her that he had done. On the MCCD, he said that he last saw Mrs Carroll alive on the day before the death. I do not place much reliance on Shipman's claim on the MCCD, as I know that he often lied on such documents when it suited him to do so. However, it would be surprising if he were to lie about this on the MCCD if he had openly admitted to Mrs Davies that he had seen Mrs Carroll in the morning just before she died. It is possible that he did see Mrs Carroll on the Saturday, as Mrs Davies says that he told her. However, despite Mrs Davies' certainty, it is quite possible that when she visited him after the death, Shipman said that Mrs Carroll had been quite well when he saw her 'the other day'. It is also possible that Mrs Davies' recollection of this conversation is mistaken in other respects.
In the absence of the medical records, the cremation certificate and any daily occurrence record from the home, I am left to rely solely on Mrs Davies' evidence for an account of the circumstances surrounding the death. Even taken at its highest, her evidence does not prove that Shipman killed her mother, although it does arouse a real suspicion that he could have done. On the basis of her evidence I would say that Shipman might or might not have killed her mother. However, when I consider Shipman's situation in October 1977, as a newly arrived doctor, I think it is unlikely that he killed Mrs Carroll. My conclusion is that this was probably, although not certainly, a natural death.

name: Caroline Veronica Hammond
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, Flat 41 Chartist House, Mount Street, Hyde
conclusion:
There is no evidence from which I could conclude that Shipman was unlawfully involved in Mrs Hammond's death. There are some uncertainties, which is not surprising, given the passage of time, but nothing that arouses real suspicion.
Mrs Hammond was clearly very unwell at midday on Saturday, 17th
January. The doctor who visited had contemplated admitting her to hospital if her condition had not improved by the Monday. However, he did not seem to think it necessary to admit her that day. However, by the evening, Mrs Hammond was hallucinating and, at least with the benefit of hindsight, one can say that she must have been very ill. Her death during the night was certainly a shock to Mrs Fowden but, if she was very ill in the evening, her death during the night does not seem entirely surprising. This gradual progression through confusion to death is not typical of or consistent with death due to opiate poisoning. In short, this sounds like a natural death and not a Shipman killing.
There is no direct evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Hammond on 17th
January, except that he seems to have claimed to have done so when he completed the MCCD. Also Mrs Hammond's name appears in his visits book for that day. There are a number of possibilities. First, Mrs Fowden might be mistaken when she says it was Dr Bennett who visited at midday. It might have been Shipman. Second, Shipman might have visited in the afternoon at the request of the doctor who visited at midday. Mrs Unsworth could have let him in. This is unlikely as Shipman's calendar suggests that he was not on duty that weekend. If he did visit in the afternoon, he did not kill Mrs Hammond, as she was still alive in the evening, when her daughter visited. Third, it is possible that Shipman did not visit Mrs Hammond at all but completed the MCCD on behalf of one of the other doctors, either Dr Roberts or Dr Bennett, who might have been unavailable on the Monday. It may be that on the certificate itself, he explained that he was completing the form on behalf of a colleague. It may be that he bent the rules and completed it as if he had seen Mrs Hammond himself when he had not. These uncertainties cannot be resolved. However, none of these possibilities gives rise to any serious suspicion that Shipman killed Mrs Hammond.
I am sure that Mrs Hammond died a natural death.

name: Walter Mansfield
title: Mr
place_of_death: his daughter's home, 4 Marlborough Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I regret that I am unable to reach any positive conclusion about the circumstances of this death.
I am unable to assess the seriousness of Mr Mansfield's medical condition on the day of his death. It is possible that he was suffering from heart failure. However, he does not appear to have been unwell during the preceding weeks. That he was able to entertain a visitor and was not confined to bed suggests that his condition was not critical.
It is not known what injection Shipman gave or whether the injection was given intravenously or intramuscularly. The injection caused Mr Mansfield to lose consciousness almost immediately. That leads me to suspect that the drug might have been an opiate, given intravenously. It cannot have been an opiate given intramuscularly, as Mr Mansfield became unconscious almost immediately. If the injection was of an opiate given intravenously, it cannot have been of a lethal dose as Mr Mansfield lived for an appreciable time afterwards. However, it is possible that Shipman gave a sublethal dose, which was sufficient to make him unconscious and to depress his respiration so that he suffered brain damage due to the insufficiency of the oxygen supply to the brain. He could in those circumstances have survived for an hour or two, or longer. In 1979, Mrs Alice Maude Gorton lived for two days following a sublethal dose of opiate. In 1994, Mrs Renate Overton lived for 14 months after Shipman injected her with opiate. All three of these patients were quite heavy and it is possible that Shipman had underestimated the amount needed to have a lethal effect.
This theory could fit the facts but would mean that Shipman was prepared to give a lethal or near-lethal injection of opiate in the presence of Mr Mansfield's daughter and possibly Mr Mansfield's friend, Mr Bradley. To do this would seem to be utterly foolhardy. In general, Shipman gave lethal injections when he was alone with the patient. If Shipman did give an injection of opiate with the intention to kill, his efforts at resuscitation must have been a sham. This is not impossible. I have come across at least two cases where he made a show of attempting to resuscitate a patient to whom he had given an opiate. However, I still think it unlikely that he would have deliberately tried to kill Mr Mansfield in the circumstances which prevailed here.
I have considered what other drug Shipman might have given. He cannot have given a strong diuretic. That would have been appropriate treatment for congestive heart failure, the condition which Shipman was to give as the cause of death. However, a diuretic would not have caused Mr Mansfield to lose consciousness. It is possible that Shipman gave aminophylline or terbutaline. As Dr John Grenville explained when giving evidence in the case of Mrs Hannah Jones, these drugs were widely used in the 1980s when treating asthma. Aminophylline carries some risk of causing cardiac arrest. That is a possible explanation for events. However, if that is what happened and if Shipman had given the injection in good faith, I would have expected him to call an ambulance as soon as Mr Mansfield became unconscious. The cardiac complication is a known side effect. The equipment available on an ambulance, let alone the facilities of a hospital, might have saved Mr Mansfield's life. Instead, Shipman appears to have decided that nothing more should be done and he departed, leaving Mr Mansfield in the care of his daughter. He also advised her that 'if anything happened' she should call him rather than any other doctor. That suggests that he might not have wished his actions to come to the attention of a professional colleague.
I am puzzled by this case. If Mrs Oldham's account is accurate, it gives rise to suspicion that Shipman killed Mr Mansfield. However, there are so many uncertainties that I feel unable to reach a decision.

name: Leonard Shaw
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 3 Newton Hall Court, Hyde
conclusion: On the available evidence, it is not possible to determine whether or not Shipman played a part in Mr Shaw's death. The fact that Mr Shaw's name appears in Shipman's visits book for the day of death might indicate that he was visited by Shipman. Equally, it is possible that Shipman visited Mr Shaw on 5th January and recorded an intention to revisit, but did not actually visit Mr Shaw while he was alive on the day of his death. Although there is no positive evidence to suggest that Shipman played any part in Mr Shaw's death, in the absence of witness evidence, the possibility cannot be discounted.

name: Maud Wilkinson
title: Miss
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Miss Wilkinson died a natural death and that she was not seen by Shipman at or about the time of her death.
Mr Shaw's concern seems to have arisen because he confused Miss Wilkinson with Mrs Irene Brooder. I hope that this confusion has not caused distress to Miss Wilkinson's family and that any anxiety which they felt has now been quite allayed.

name: Norman John Bell
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 28 Stalybridge Road, Mottram
conclusion:
It seems to me that Mr Bell must have died a natural death. He and his wife were alone in the house at the time of his death and it does not appear that Shipman arrived at the house until after Mr Bell had died.
Mr Bell's death was extremely sudden and unexpected. However, people do sometimes die very suddenly as the result of a heart attack. Without the medical records, it is not possible to say whether or not Mr Bell had a significantly increased risk of a sudden cardiac death. However, in view of the facts that he was a smoker and had probably had a coronary thrombosis a few years earlier, it seems likely that this was so.
There are one or two slight mysteries surrounding the death. It is strange that Shipman should have said on the MCCD and Form B that he had last seen Mr Bell alive on 3rd
February, when his visits book suggests that he might have seen him only the day before his death. However, that entry in the visits book might have related to Mrs Bell. It would not be unusual for Shipman to claim that he had seen a patient within 14 days of death in order to avoid any risk that the registrar might refer the case to the coroner. That is not necessarily a cause for suspicion, although it is a device which Shipman used in many cases where he had killed the patient. It is also strange that Shipman should have said that Mrs Bell nursed her husband during his last illness, when Miss Jean Bell says that her father was very fit and active until the day of his death. As I say, these are mysteries, but they are not grounds to suspect that Shipman played a sinister role in Mr Bell's death.

name: Eileen Daphne Crompton
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I accept the evidence of Mrs Heyl as honest and as accurate as can be hoped for after the lapse of time. I think that she has quite a good recollection of Mrs Crompton's death because of the unusual circumstances and because the death was unexpected.
I think it likely that Mrs Crompton was quite poorly on 2nd
January. It sounds as though she was developing a chest infection and it is quite possible that the condition might have been her final illness. However, I do not think she was yet close to death. She had not yet reached the stage where the staff thought it prudent to call her sons.
As Dr Grenville has said, if his record of the consultation were genuine, Shipman might have been justified in thinking that Mrs Crompton was suffering from an overwhelming infection and that the drastic remedy of intravenous benzylpenicillin was justified. However, if his note was not genuine and if he said the things that Mrs Heyl recalls, then there is a grave suspicion that he gave not an antibiotic but an opiate.
I accept that Shipman did not carry out the examination which he claimed to have done. I am satisfied that his note is fabricated. I am also satisfied that he said to Mrs Heyl that he was going to give a 'kill or cure' injection in the hope of kick-starting Mrs Crompton's heart. In so saying, he was deceiving her. Shipman's medical note was designed to provide a plausible explanation for the death.
Shipman also lied on Form B when he said that Mrs Crompton had been in a coma for 24 hours. He knew she had not, but he said that she had as that would be consistent with the cause of death he had certified, bronchopneumonia.
It may well be that Mrs Crompton had not long to live. However, I am sure that, very shortly before her death, Shipman injected her with a strong opiate with the intention of ensuring that she died immediately.

name: Mary Jane Hett
title: Mrs
conclusion:
It appears to me that Mrs Hett must have died a natural death. She had a history of chronic bronchitis and breathing difficulties, which would have made her more susceptible to bronchopneumonia. Although she was noted to be well by her son two to three days before she died, we know from the generic evidence of Dr John Grenville that the period between the onset of bronchopneumonia and death can be as little as a few hours.
It is recorded on the MCCD counterfoil that Shipman saw Mrs Hett on the day before her death. Mr Walter Hett did not mention Shipman's visit to his son. It is unclear whether Shipman did in fact visit but, if he did, then Mr Hett obviously did not associate his wife's death with that visit.
Even if Shipman had visited Mrs Hett, the possibility that he gave her a lethal injection of opiates can be discounted. Professor Henry McQuay and Dr Grenville have given joint generic evidence to the Inquiry as to the timing and effect of opiates. If a lethal injection of opiates is administered intravenously, death follows within minutes. If administered intramuscularly, a lethal injection of opiates causes death within about an hour. Mr Walter Hett found his wife dead when he awoke on the morning of 22nd
November and told his son that she had died during the night. She must have been alive when he went to bed on the evening of 21st
November. I am satisfied that Shipman played no part in bringing about Mrs Hett's death.

name: Dora Elizabeth Smith
title: Mrs
conclusion:
The evidence suggests that Mrs Smith suffered a right-sided stroke or cerebrovascular accident in the early hours of Friday, 24th
August 1979. That morning, she was unable to eat or speak but is not described as unconscious. Shipman visited, probably in the late morning, which was his usual visiting time. It is not clear exactly when Mrs Smith became unconscious, although she was certainly unconscious from the time of Mrs Beetson's visit in the evening of 24th
August until her death in the early hours. The course of her decline over a period of 24 hours is entirely compatible with the development of a stroke followed by a natural death.
There is no evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Smith for a second time on 24th
August or in the early hours of 25th
August. It seems very unlikely that he would have visited during the night unless asked to do so by the staff and there is no record that they did. I therefore rule out the possibility that Shipman unlawfully killed Mrs Smith by administering a lethal dose of opiates, which directly caused her death.
There remains the possibility that Shipman gave Mrs Smith an injection on 24th
August, of some form of sedative drug, and that the dose was larger than was necessary or appropriate. This might have rendered Mrs Smith unconscious sooner and more deeply than would otherwise have been the case. If over-sedated, Mrs Smith would be more vulnerable to bronchopneumonia, a common mechanism of death in elderly people. Her death could have been hastened in this way. However, there is no evidence that Shipman gave any injection when he visited on 24th
August and, although I cannot absolutely rule out the possibility, I think it unlikely that he did. I would have expected a reference to it in the daily diary.
My conclusion is that it is highly likely that Mrs Smith died a natural death.

name: Sydney Walton
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 15 Rutland Street, Hyde
conclusion:
I have found this case difficult to decide. My task has been made particularly difficult by the passage of time and the absence of any medical records from which I could make a reliable assessment of Mr Walton's state of health in the weeks and days before his death.
I think it likely that all members of the family have forgotten the detail though not the essence of their father's illness. That is not surprising after the passage of more than 20 years. From the fact that he used an oxygen cylinder, I think I must assume that he was quite seriously ill with chronic bronchitis and probably emphysema. I think it likely that Shipman did visit Mr Walton on 30th April and 1st May. This evidence comes from his visits book. Although it is quite possible that Shipman had fabricated entries in his visits book, I have not found evidence that he did so, in the way that I have found evidence of the fabrication of medical records. I have the impression that the visits book was no more than an aide-memoire for Shipman. If, as I think likely, Shipman did visit on the two days preceding the death, this would indicate that Mr Walton was more seriously ill than usual. I think the family may have forgotten that. However, I accept that they did not think he was critically ill and did not expect him to die. Mrs Hurst would not have gone shopping in Hyde and Mrs Blackwell would not have gone to work, had that been the case.
I cannot say whether Mr Walton might have been suffering from bronchopneumonia. Certainly an illness lasting three days before death is consistent with the development of bronchopneumonia. However, if this was bronchopneumonia, the family would have been very worried about his condition and I do not think they were. Accordingly, I have some suspicions about the cause of death which Shipman gave.
My principal difficulty arises from the evidence of Mrs Clayton, who is the only witness who says that Shipman was present at the death or raises any suggestion that he might have given an injection of opiate. I have not had the advantage of hearing Mrs Clayton in person. I confess that I am puzzled by her claim that she never made the connection between her father's death and Shipman. I find it hard to believe that, if her present recollection of the day's events is accurate and true, she could have failed to make the connection in the three years which had elapsed between Shipman's arrest and the publication of the advertisement. Mrs Clayton claims to have known that a doctor was present at her father's death. She claims to have seen him sitting on her father's bedside, offering to give him something for his pain. She says that he died within quite a short time after that. She claims to recall that the doctor was very matter of fact in his manner. She says that her father's death was a great shock to her. I infer that she felt it was sudden and unexpected. In my view, anyone who had so clear a recollection of her father's death and who knew that Shipman was her mother's doctor, could hardly have failed to realise, when she heard accounts of Shipman's activities in the media, that Shipman might also have been her father's doctor.
I accept, however, that Mrs Clayton did not make the connection. If she had, she would have volunteered her information as soon as she could. She and her sisters are represented by experienced solicitors in connection with Mrs Moss' death. In the absence of the opportunity to hear her own account, I can only say that I cannot have confidence in Mrs Clayton's account of the circumstances of her father's death. If the doctor was not present at the death, had not offered to give Mr Walton something for the pain, had not been matter of fact in his manner, I can well understand why the news of Shipman's practices did not ring any bells in her mind. I also note that there is an important difference between the account Mrs Clayton gave to the Inquiry and the account which Mrs Blackwell says she gave to her in September 2001. To the Inquiry she suggested that the death occurred while Shipman was there and within a short time after his arrival. To Mrs Blackwell she seems to have said that there was deterioration after Shipman had gone and Mrs Walton called the ambulance. Mrs Clayton is the only witness who claims to be able to give a full account of what had occurred. Neither Mrs Hurst nor Mrs Blackwell was present. Mrs O'Gorman was only 12 and her recollection is obviously flawed. As I am not confident of the accuracy and reliability of Mrs Clayton's account, I cannot reach any conclusion as to whether Shipman gave any injection at all.
I am not even sure that Shipman was present at the house before the death. Although he noted in his visits book an intention to visit Mr Walton on 2nd
May, he claimed on the MCCD that he did not see Mr Walton alive on that day. Although I recognise that very little credence can be given to Shipman's claims, it does seem possible that he did not arrive until after the death.
Shipman did not usually kill patients in the presence of members of the family although I think, on occasions, he probably hastened the deaths of patients who were close to death, even in the presence of relatives. The family says that Mr Walton was not close to death. To kill Mr Walton while his wife and one of his daughters were in the house would have been very risky. In 1979, Shipman was not the accomplished serial killer that he later became.
I am afraid that the uncertainties in the evidence relating to Mr Walton's death mean that I am unable to reach any decision at all as to whether or not Shipman was involved.

name: Jane Bridge
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 3 Lyne View, Hyde
conclusion:
It is not possible for me to make a decision as to whether or not Mrs Bridge died a natural death. Her medical records have not survived and Mrs Lever can recall very little about the nature of her mother's final illness. That Shipman certified the cause of death as old age has not helped to throw light on the medical position. Dr John Grenville said in his generic evidence that old age is only appropriate as a cause of death where the patient has declined slowly towards death over a period of time. Usually the patient will have been confined to bed for some weeks and has gradually faded away. In such circumstances, there may be multiple organ failure and it may not be possible for the doctor to specify the precise cause of death. However, it does not appear that Mrs Bridge fell into that category. She seems to have had a relatively short illness and, at least until she became unconscious, her death was not expected. I am not in a position to say whether Mrs Bridge had a condition from which she might have died a natural death.
Mrs Lever's concern about her mother's death arises because Shipman gave her mother an injection not long before her death. It is not clear when the injection was given. According to Mrs Lever's letter to the Inquiry, Shipman gave Mrs Bridge an injection 30 hours before her mother's death. That would suggest that it was given in the early hours of the morning of 3rd
January. In her statement of evidence, Mrs Lever said that Shipman gave the injection in the late afternoon or early evening of 3rd
January. However, that time difference can make very little difference to the question of whether or not Shipman's actions caused or contributed to Mrs Bridge's death.
Assuming that an injection was given, and assuming for the sake of argument that this was a strong opiate or a very large dose of sedative, the crucial question is whether or not Mrs Bridge lapsed into unconsciousness within a fairly short period after the injection was given. The evidence on this point is not clear, although the impression is given that she 'fell asleep' not long afterwards.
Professor Henry McQuay and Dr Grenville have given joint generic evidence to the Inquiry about the timing and effect of opiates. If a lethal dose of opiate is given intravenously, the patient will become unconscious almost immediately and will die within minutes. If a lethal dose is given intramuscularly, the patient will probably be unconscious within about 15 minutes and will die within about an hour. However, in the case of Mrs Alice Maude Gorton, Dr Grenville considered what would happen if a dose of opiate were given which was almost, but not quite, enough to kill. He said that it was possible that such a dose might cause almost complete cessation of respiration leading to hypoxia and permanent brain damage. The patient might then lie unconscious until he or she died as the result of the brain damage or from bronchopneumonia or a combination of the two. Similarly, a very large dose of a sedative such as Largactil might have put Mrs Bridge into a deep sleep for a long period, during which time she would be vulnerable to bronchopneumonia.
Accordingly, it is possible that Shipman caused Mrs Bridge's death by administering an injection of opiate or sedative which was not large enough to kill her outright but was sufficient to cause prolonged loss of consciousness and eventual death. However, it is not possible on the evidence available to reach a conclusion about this. Not enough is known about Mrs Bridge's underlying state of health. It is quite possible that the passage of time has coloured Mrs Lever's recollection of the extent of her mother's illness in the days leading up to her death. This would not be surprising. It is entirely possible that Shipman acted appropriately in giving Mrs Bridge an injection to ease her pain and distress and that her loss of consciousness was due to the natural progression of her underlying disease. There are too many uncertainties in this case for me to reach any decision.

name: Frederick Coomber
title: Mr
place_of_death: Bowlacre, a residential home for the elderly, Stockport Road, Hyde
conclusion:
Nothing is known about Mr Coomber's state of health in the period before his death. I do not know whether he had developed bronchopneumonia or indeed any chest infection. I cannot say whether Mr Coomber's death was sudden or expected.
Although the evidence would suggest that Shipman did not see Mr Coomber in the last two days of his life, the only source of information is Shipman himself. His account cannot be accepted unless corroborated by other evidence. I cannot therefore say whether Shipman had access to Mr Coomber shortly before he died.
In view of the paucity of information, I am unable to reach any conclusion about Shipman's role in this death.

name: Harriet Harris
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 12 South View, Woodley, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
Mrs Harris had suffered from angina for a number of years before she died and was, therefore, at significant risk of suffering a heart attack. She was unwell in the weeks before she died, although the nature of her illness is not known. There must have been some reason for her to see a doctor while in Hertfordshire. She was very tired on her return home.
On the day of her death, Mrs Harris was still tired and reluctant to get up. Shipman visited at about lunchtime and was alone with her. However, there is no reason to think that he gave her any drug which might have caused or precipitated her death. Certainly there is no reason to think that he gave her a lethal injection of opiate. Had he done so, she would have fallen deeply asleep and died long before she got up, dressed and came downstairs. Dr John Grenville and Professor Henry McQuay, in their evidence to the Inquiry, have explained the timing and effect of opiates. A lethal dose of opiate given intravenously will cause death within a few minutes. If given intramuscularly, a lethal dose will cause death within about an hour. That Mrs Harris remained alive and conscious for at least two hours after Shipman's visit shows that he cannot have killed her by injection of opiate. From the description given by Mr Harris of the manner of her death, it sounds as though Mrs Harris had a sudden, fatal heart attack. The medical advisor to the Inquiry has advised me that he knows of no drug which Shipman could have administered which could have induced a heart attack two or three hours later.
There are two unusual features about the case. The first is that Shipman claimed that he last saw Mrs Harris alive on 8th
January 1979, when the witness evidence and Shipman's visits book suggest that he saw her alive on the day of her death. It is possible that this was a deliberate attempt to conceal from the registrar that he had seen Mrs Harris alive on the day of her death. That is unlikely because the circumstances in which he did so would have been readily capable of confirmation by Mr Harris and would not have excited any suspicion.
Second, Mr Harris believes that Shipman took his mother's wedding ring after her death. As this was not investigated at the time, I could not be confident that Mr Harris' recollection is correct.
Neither of these unusual features gives rise to any suspicion that Shipman caused Mrs Harris' death. I am quite sure that Mrs Harris died a natural death and I hope that this decision will serve to put her relatives' minds at ease.

name: Emmeline Swindells
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Swindells died of natural causes. Her gradual deterioration is clearly documented in the Charnley House diary and there is no suggestion from any source that Shipman saw her in the days leading up to her death. Mrs Swindells died in the early hours of 20th
April, which was Easter Monday, a day when Shipman was apparently not at work.

name: George Winston
title: Mr
conclusion:
Although a post-mortem examination was held, the findings were equivocal. A tumour was found in the left lung but there was no positive evidence that Mr Winston died of the tumour rather than with it. The findings certainly do not exclude the possibility that Mr Winston died as the result of a lethal injection of morphine administered by Shipman. However, all the other evidence tends to suggest that he did not.
First, the fact that Shipman referred the case to the coroner suggests that he had not caused the death. Usually (although not quite invariably), when he had killed a patient, he certified the cause of death himself and avoided a referral to the coroner.
Second, there is no evidence that Shipman saw Mr Winston shortly before his death. That is not conclusive.
Third, the circumstances of the death, as described by Mr Savill, would suggest that this was a natural death. It would appear that Mr Winston had locked the front door and had secured it with a chain at some time before his death. Usually, when Shipman had killed a patient, he would wait until the patient was dead before leaving. Thus it would be impossible for him to secure the door behind him with a chain.
Fourth, most of Shipman's victims were found sitting or lying peacefully. Mr Winston, on the other hand, seems to have 'keeled over' while trying to take his trousers off. He might have been getting ready for bed on the evening of 12th
July. He might have felt ill at some time during 13th
July and have gone upstairs to lie down. His position and appearance in death are more consistent with a sudden death from natural causes than with death following a lethal injection of opiate.
Although I cannot absolutely rule out the possibility that Shipman was involved, it seems to me highly likely that Mr Winston died a natural death.

name: Albert Brierley
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 26 Werneth Avenue, Hyde
conclusion:
Mr Brierley was 91 and, at his age, a sudden death can never be regarded as wholly unexpected. However, on the evidence now available, it does not appear that Mr Brierley was known to be suffering from any life-threatening condition. It would appear from Shipman's conversation with Mr William Brierley that Shipman was not aware that Mr Brierley was suffering from any condition which might have caused his sudden death. I do not think that old age can have been an appropriate cause of death. Mr Brierley had not deteriorated over a period of time. He was not confined to bed. Indeed, it appears that he was up and dressed on the day of his death. I cannot say why Mr Brierley died. He might have died a natural death; he could have been killed by Shipman.
Mr Brierley's position and appearance in death were not typical of those usually seen after a death from a heart attack or stroke or any of the other common causes of sudden death. They were, however, typical of those seen in many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of opiate.
I feel some concern that Shipman certified the death as due to old age, which was not appropriate. However, as Shipman was extremely casual about his duties of certification and frequently made untrue and inaccurate entries in respect of perfectly natural deaths, I cannot attach great weight to this factor.
I regret to say that the lack of evidence makes it impossible for me to decide whether this death was due to an unlawful act on the part of Shipman or whether it was due to natural causes.

name: Elsie Clayton
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charlotte House, a residential care home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
The exact nature of Mrs Clayton's final illness is not clear, but the evidence of Mr Clayton and Mrs Aldred suggests that she was very ill when they last saw her in the early evening of Friday, 18th
October. It appears that her decline had been gradual and quite prolonged. Her death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
It is possible that Shipman saw Mrs Clayton on the Friday evening, 18th
October, although I suspect that he might not have done and merely claimed that he had made a visit so that he could say that he had attended her during her last illness. That would enable him to certify the cause of her death. Possibly Dr Napier was away on holiday or otherwise not available. Shipman was quite cavalier about his duties of certification and would not have hesitated to say that he had visited Mrs Clayton when he had not, if it were convenient to do so. It is possible that he called in on the Friday evening because Dr Napier had told him that the death was expected and wished Shipman to be able to certify the cause of death. It is even possible that the staff called Shipman out on the Friday evening. However, I think that is most unlikely. I do not think there was anything which could have been done for Mrs Clayton. She seems to have been slipping quietly away and I do not think the staff would call the doctor in those circumstances. In any event, even if Shipman was called out on the Friday evening, there is no reason to think that he did anything to cause her death. He cannot have given her a lethal dose of opiate; if he had she would have been dead within the hour. It is possible that he gave Mrs Clayton an inappropriately large dose of sedative. If over-sedated, Mrs Clayton would have been more vulnerable to bronchopneumonia, a common mechanism of death in the very old. However, there is no evidence to suggest that he did any such thing.
My conclusion is that it is highly likely that Mrs Clayton died a natural death.

name: Christina Harrison
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
When Mrs Harrison was first admitted to Charnley House, she was unable to stand or walk. It is not clear whether her mobility improved after admission but she seems to have been quite agitated and to have developed heart failure. She deteriorated and, when seen by Mr Fallon two or three days before death, was sleeping a lot and seemed lifeless. It would appear that her death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
In the last few days, there are signs in the daily diary that Mrs Harrison was suffering from congestive heart failure and possibly bronchopneumonia. The fast breathing, later described as heavy, would be consistent with either or both of these conditions, which are common causes of death in the very old. The description of Mrs Harrison's decline sounds entirely typical of a natural death.
There is no evidence that Shipman had access to Mrs Harrison shortly before her death and no reason to suspect that he administered any drug which might have hastened her death. I feel some concern about Shipman's direction to withdraw Mrs Harrison's medication, at least without any discussion with Mr Fallon, who was visiting his grandmother very frequently and who would, I am sure, have been ready and willing to discuss the issue. However, Dr Esmail and Dr Grenville do not suggest that the withdrawal hastened Mrs Harrison's death.
On the evidence, I could not say that the withdrawal of the diuretic was wrong and, in any event, it seems to me that the decision could not have made a significant difference to the length of Mrs Harrison's life. I am quite satisfied that she died a natural death.

name: Louisa Stocks
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
Mrs Stocks' health had deteriorated in the days leading up to her death. She was very weak and probably dehydrated. Her death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
The daily diary shows that Shipman visited Mrs Stocks on the day of her death. We do not know at what time he visited but, as the visit is recorded in the morning report, I infer that he visited before 1pm. The daily diary suggests that Mrs Stocks died at about 7pm. If those entries are right and complete, there should be no reason to suspect that Shipman did anything directly to cause Mrs Stocks' death. A lethal dose of opiate would have resulted in death within the hour.
However, there are two causes for suspicion and concern. One is that Shipman was said to have left some night sedation for Mrs Stocks but there is no record, as there should have been, to show whether this was given. I suspect that it was, as Mrs Stocks slept all afternoon. Knowing Shipman, the 'night sedation' might well have been an opiate drug. If it was to be given orally, it might have been Oramorph. If it were to be given by injection, it could well have been morphine, pethidine, diamorphine or a sedative such as Largactil. We shall never know.
The second cause for concern is that Mrs Jackson was told that her mother died after an injection given by the doctor. As Shipman was Mrs Stocks' doctor, if a doctor did give her an injection, it was probably him. There is no record that Shipman attended a second time on 29th
March. However, there is every reason to think that he attended in the evening, as he certified the death on 29th
March and claimed that he had already seen the body. Yet that visit was not recorded in the daily diary which says only that the doctor was
'informed'
of the death. There remains a suspicion that Shipman paid a second visit to Mrs Stocks in the late afternoon or early evening, gave her a lethal injection and stayed at the home until he was
'informed'
of the death, which he then certified.
I do not feel able to reach a definite conclusion in this case. There are some indications that Mrs Stocks died a natural death. I have a suspicion (and it is no more than suspicion) that Shipman might have killed her. There is insufficient evidence to enable me to reach a conclusion. If Shipman did give Mrs Stocks an injection that hastened her death, I do not think it can have shortened her life by an appreciable period of time.

name: Edith Whittle
title: Miss
place_of_death: Pole Bank Hall Residential Care Home, Stockport Road, Hyde
conclusion:
Although Mrs Oakes says that she was surprised at Miss Whittle's death, it does appear that she had been frail for some time and I do not think it could be said that her death was wholly unexpected.
The evidence of the circumstances of the death is not wholly clear. Mrs Oakes' evidence is not entirely consistent with that of Mrs Potts. However, the essence of their evidence is that Shipman did not visit Miss Whittle either on the day before her death or during the night when she died. Shipman himself nowhere suggested that he had seen Miss Whittle shortly before she died.
The only cause for concern arises because some of Shipman's entries on Form B and the MCCD counterfoil are probably not accurate and may well be untrue. I think it unlikely that Shipman saw Miss Whittle on 5th
February. I think it more likely that he had not seen her for about a month before her death. I have come across many occasions when Shipman has filled in MCCDs and Forms B inaccurately when there is no reason to suppose that he has been involved in the death. I think he paid scant regard to his duties in connection with certification procedures.
There appears to me to be no real reason to suspect that Shipman was involved in this death. I am satisfied that Miss Whittle died of natural causes.

name: Frances Bennett
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
The daily diary reveals that Mrs Bennett declined gradually in the weeks before her death. Her death was fully expected. There is no evidence that Shipman saw her after 14th
May, except for the entry in his visits book relating to the day of her death. The overwhelming likelihood is that Shipman entered her name in the book for that day as a reminder that he was to attend Charnley House to deal with the MCCD. On the MCCD counterfoil, it appears that Shipman claimed that he had last seen Mrs Bennett on 20th
May 1981. He probably did not, as no visit is recorded in the daily diary at Charnley House. I have noticed that Shipman was often careless when completing death and cremation certificates. It seems likely that he did not take the trouble to check the date of his last visit. As he had seen the body after death and had seen Mrs Bennett on 14th
May, there could be no suggestion that he was not qualified to certify the cause of death. The fact that he entered a wrong date on the MCCD does not give rise to any suspicion.
The overwhelming likelihood is that Mrs Bennett died of natural causes.

name: Amy Chidlow
title: Miss
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am satisfied that Miss Chidlow died from natural causes.
There is clear evidence that Miss Chidlow suffered a violent choking episode soon after lunch on 2nd
November 1988. It appears that she died very shortly afterwards. I think it is unlikely that she lived until 3.15pm. I think that is probably the time at which a doctor attended to pronounce her death. I think she must have died at about 12.45pm. Due to the sudden and unusual nature of the death, the police were summoned.
There is no evidence whatsoever that Shipman was present during or immediately after this choking incident. Accordingly there is no cause for concern that Shipman might have done anything to cause or hasten Miss Chidlow's death.

name: Sarah Hawkins
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion: I am quite satisfied that Mrs Hawkins died of natural causes. It is clear from the daily diary that Mrs Hawkins was very ill and was expected to die. It appears to me that Shipman's management of her terminal phase was entirely appropriate. The drugs administered by the district nurse appeared to give substantial relief. I think it is most unlikely that Shipman would have prescribed excessive amounts of these drugs if they were to be administered by the district nurse. There is no evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Hawkins on the day of her death and the available evidence suggests that he did not come to Charnley House that day until over two hours after the death.

name: Alice Squirrell
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion: I am quite satisfied that Mrs Squirrell died a natural death. She was very poorly in the weeks and days leading up to her death. Her death was not sudden and was clearly expected by the staff. There is no evidence that Shipman gave or withdrew any treatment so as adversely to affect her condition. There is no evidence that he saw her on the day of her death. It is highly likely that he did not do so. Another doctor attended that afternoon to certify the fact of death.

name: Emily Williams
title: Mrs
place_of_death: 5 Hilda Road, Hyde, the home of her daughter, Mrs Dorothy Anne McKey
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to carcinoma of the colon
conclusion:
There is no doubt that Mrs Williams was in the terminal stage of cancer and did not have long to live. She was in great pain. I think it is likely that Mr Williams' account of the events leading to the death is accurate. I accept that Shipman visited on the day before the death and on the morning of the day of the death. It also seems highly likely that he would have given Mrs Williams a pain-relieving injection on both occasions. Those injections were probably of a strong opiate, probably diamorphine. Provided that a genuine attempt was made to estimate a suitable dose, Shipman's actions would not be unlawful. Dr John Grenville has explained that it can be very difficult for a general practitioner to estimate the appropriate dose in these circumstances. If he errs on the low side, the patient's pain is not relieved. If he errs on the high side, he might hasten the patient's death.
In this case, Mr Williams' sister told him that their mother died within a short period of time after Shipman had given an injection. We do not know what is meant by 'a short period of time'. If Mrs Williams died within a few minutes of the injection, I would have little hesitation in concluding that Shipman had probably given a lethal dose of opiates intravenously. It would be something of a coincidence if she were to die naturally within minutes. However, I cannot assume that that is what happened. Indeed, the expression 'within a short period of time' implies a period rather longer than a few minutes.
If Mrs Williams died within about an hour of the injection, a suspicion arises that the injection was of a lethal dose and was given intramuscularly. That would be the usual method of giving a pain-relieving injection which was intended to have effect over a period of several hours. If the dose were lethal, death would be expected to follow within about an hour. I think it is quite likely that Shipman gave a lethal injection, knowing and intending that it would bring Mrs Williams' life and her suffering to an end within an hour. However, as Mrs Williams was very ill indeed, it is quite possible that she died naturally within an hour. She might also have lived rather longer than an hour, in which case the injection will not have directly precipitated her death.
Thus, there is a suspicion that Shipman gave an excessive dose of opiate which brought Mrs Williams' life to an end a short time before she would have died naturally. My suspicion that this occurred is heightened by Shipman's entry on the MCCD counterfoil. On 25th
September, the very day of the death, Shipman claimed that he had last seen Mrs Williams alive three days earlier. Events were so recent that he could hardly have made a mistake about the day when he had last seen her. He must have known that he saw her that morning. That he should pretend that he had not seen her for three days raises my level of suspicion. It is, of course, possible that Mr Williams is mistaken about the course of events and that Shipman did not see Mrs Williams for three days before her death.
My suspicion is such that I cannot say that I think it is likely that Mrs Williams' death was natural. Nor is it high enough for me to say that I think it likely that Shipman killed her. I cannot say. However, I recognise that if Shipman did deliberately hasten Mrs Williams' death, he did so by only a short time and he also relieved her suffering. Her family felt that he acted with compassion.

name: Alice Bolland
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am satisfied that Mrs Bolland died of natural causes. The daily diary shows that she was very unwell in the period leading up to her death. Her death occurred before surgery hours. It would be most unusual for Shipman to visit a patient at that hour of the morning, save in an emergency. There is no suggestion that Shipman visited Mrs Bolland either on the day of the death or the previous day. The overwhelming likelihood is that on 16th
May Shipman attended at Charnley House only after the death.

name: Ida Cains
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 213 Lumn Road, Hyde
conclusion:
It is not possible to say, on the basis of the information available, whether or not Mrs Cains died a natural death.
Mrs Cains had some history of congestive heart failure, although there is no indication in the records that this was ever a serious problem. In the weeks before her death, she was being treated for a suspected stroke, although the basis for that diagnosis is quite unclear. She had also had an attack of bronchitis. Any one or more of these conditions could have developed so as to provide an explanation for a natural death. However, as there is no evidence of Mrs Cains' condition in the days shortly before her death, it is impossible to say whether any of them did so develop. It may be that Mrs Cains was well and did not need to call out Shipman, or it may be that she was unwell and chose not to call him out. It does not seem likely that she called him out, given the absence of documentary evidence to that effect.
There is no evidence whatsoever that Shipman saw Mrs Cains on the day of her death or on the days leading up to it. There is no obvious reason why Shipman should have chosen to call on her that day and she does not appear to be one of those patients upon whom he called regularly and without prior notice. Shipman could have visited her on 16th
March but there is no reason to think that he did. The fact that there is no entry in the records does not count for much, as Shipman often failed to record visits.
It appears that Shipman lied on the MCCD, and possibly in Form B in stating that he last saw Mrs Cains alive either 13 days before her death or on 3rd
or 13th
March. There is no record that he saw her in March at all. It has become clear from other cases investigated by the Inquiry that Shipman displayed a disregard for his duties in respect of the certification of deaths. There are cases in which he has falsely claimed to have seen a patient within 14 days of death, where the death was obviously natural. It is not possible to infer that he must have killed Mrs Cains simply from the fact that he made a false assertion on the MCCD. He seems to have done so on some occasions in which he had not killed the patient and I have inferred that, for the benefit of the family, he must have wished to avoid any risk that the registrar might refer the case to the coroner.
In his generic evidence to the Inquiry, Dr John Grenville explained the circumstances in which 'old age' is appropriate as a cause of death. Where there has been a prolonged period of ill health and a gradual decline towards death, it may be difficult for the doctor to determine which organ has failed so as to precipitate the death. The doctor may then properly give 'old age' as the cause. It appears unlikely that Mrs Cains was in such a condition as to fit that description. It may be that this was simply the best cause that Shipman felt able to proffer in his attempt to avoid the referral to the coroner.
With regret, I am unable to say whether or not Mrs Cains died a natural death.

name: Alline Devolle Holland
title: Ms
place_of_death: The Sycamores, a residential home for the elderly, Victoria Street, Hyde
conclusion: I regret to say that there is insufficient material upon which I can make a decision. Whilst it may be thought unlikely that Shipman would have killed one of his patients in a nursing home, the possibility cannot be ruled out.

name: Elsie Scott
title: Miss
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Shipman did not directly cause Miss Scott's death by injecting her with a lethal dose of opiate such as diamorphine. There is no evidence that he saw her within the last hour of so of her life. Indeed, it seems most unlikely that he did, as Miss Scott died in the early hours of the morning. Shipman did not usually turn out in the middle of the night. A deputising service was used. If Shipman gave Miss Scott an injection in the afternoon of 5th
February, it cannot have been a lethal dose. If it had been, she would have died within about an hour.
It appears likely that Shipman diagnosed a coronary thrombosis at his first visit of 5th
October. That probably took place in the late morning. In the absence of the medical records, I cannot say whether or not that diagnosis was well founded. I think it is likely that Shipman gave Miss Scott an injection of 100mg Largactil either then or possibly at his second visit, that afternoon. Whether or not any dose was justified, I do not know. The daily diary does not suggest that Miss Scott was in pain or distress, only that she was very poorly. Assuming that some Largactil was appropriate, it seems difficult to imagine how so large a dose could have been warranted. Shipman himself claimed that Miss Scott was in a coma for 24 hours before her death. If she was, a heavy dose of Largactil could not have been justified within that period.
If Shipman gave 100mg Largactil, as I think he probably did, I have to ask myself what he intended to achieve. It may be that Shipman believed that nothing could be done for Miss Scott and that he would make her final hours easier by giving her a substantial dose of Largactil. He might have thought that, if she continued to improve, she would become disturbed as she had been two nights earlier, and he wanted to avoid that. He might have intended to hasten her death by sedating her so heavily that she became more vulnerable to death by a respiratory illness such as bronchopneumonia. If he did so deliberately and wilfully, however, it is somewhat surprising that he should have recorded the overdose in his visits book. In any event, the generic evidence available to the Inquiry suggests that the response of any individual patient to an overdose of sedative is variable and unpredictable. Largactil would be an unlikely drug for Shipman to choose if his intention was to kill Miss Scott. It is possible, however, that he did not have an illicit supply of opiate at this time (or did not have any opiate with him) and used what was available.
I am unable to reach a decision in this case. There are too many uncertainties. I do not know whether Miss Scott had, in fact, had a heart attack on 5th
October or whether she might only have had an attack of gastroenteritis. It is possible that she was very ill indeed and the dose of Largactil had no effect on the length of Miss Scott's life. However, the dose seems to have been excessive and I suspect that Shipman took the decision to put Miss Scott to sleep for quite a long time and was reckless as to the consequences, and as to whether she lived or died.

name: Fanny Wood
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
It is clear that, from the time when she was first admitted to Charnley House, Mrs Wood was not in good health. Her condition seems to have taken a turn for the worse on the morning of Thursday, 6th
March 1980 when Dr Roberts diagnosed a slight heart attack. From that time onwards, her condition seems to have been poor and her death plainly did not come as a surprise to anyone who was involved in her care.
There is no record that Shipman visited Mrs Wood after Monday, 10th
March. Although Shipman was known to visit Charnley House unannounced and it is possible that some of his visits were not recorded, it does not seem likely that he visited Mrs Wood on the day of her death or in the few days preceding it.
Mrs Wood died at about 9pm on the evening of 14th
March. Although there might have been occasions when Shipman visited at that time of the evening, there is no evidence to suggest that he did so on this particular evening. It does not appear that Shipman was the doctor who came out to certify the fact of death, as he was to state on Form B that he saw the body more than 12 hours after death. He probably saw the body the following day at the undertakers.
In all the circumstances, I am quite satisfied that Mrs Wood died as the result of natural causes.

name: Mary Elizabeth Bowers
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Pole Bank Hall, a residential home for the elderly, Stockport Road, Hyde
conclusion:
Mrs Bowers was very weak, frail and unwell in the days leading up to her death. She was confined to bed and, shortly before her death, was drifting in and out of consciousness. It is clear that she was not expected to live long. Her death on 10th
November was neither sudden nor unexpected.
The main cause for suspicion in this case arises from the fact that, on the MCCD counterfoil, Shipman claimed that he had seen Mrs Bowers alive on the day of the death. His own visits book suggests that he intended to call at Pole Bank Hall to see her on that day, although it is not at all clear whether the request that he should attend was made for the purpose of obtaining treatment for her in life or the certification of her death.
Shipman appears to have seen Mrs Bowers on 4th
November and was entitled to certify the cause of her death, whether or not he had seen her alive on 10th
November. As Shipman had no need to tell lies in order to make it appear that he was entitled to complete the MCCD, it would seem likely that he was telling the truth when he said he had seen her alive on the day of her death.
We do not know the time of Mrs Bowers' death. If she died in the late morning or at about lunchtime, it is entirely feasible to suggest that Shipman might have visited her, found her in a very poor state, given an intravenous injection of opiate, waited the short time before she died and then certified her death. There is no evidence that he did such a thing, but the evidence is such that I cannot rule it out.
Mrs Bowers was very weak and was expected to die at any time. For that reason, my conclusion is that she probably died a natural death. However, I cannot rule out the possibility that Shipman gained access to her and gave her an injection which hastened her death. Nor can I rule out the possibility that Shipman administered an injection or a series of injections, of a sedative, in the days before Mrs Bowers died. If sedated, Mrs Bowers would be vulnerable to bronchopneumonia, a common mechanism of death in elderly people. There is, however, no evidence that Shipman saw Mrs Bowers between 4th
November and 11th
November and taking the evidence as a whole, I think it is unlikely that he did so.

name: George Charnock
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 56 Church Street, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
Little is known of Mr Charnock's medical history, as his records have not survived. He seems to have been a person who did not discuss medical matters with his family. It is quite possible that Mr Charnock had a history of heart disease, as Shipman claimed on the MCCD counterfoil. Whether or not there was any such history, it is entirely possible that he could have succumbed to a sudden death by heart attack. The position in which Mr Charnock was found, collapsed on his doorstep, is consistent with his having suffered a sudden coronary thrombosis while standing outside his house, as he was in the habit of doing.
There is no direct evidence to suggest that Shipman visited Mr Charnock on the day of his death. He probably did visit him the day before. Although it is possible that Shipman visited Mr Charnock again on the day of the death, it is very unlikely that he caused his death. Shipman's usual method of killing was to give an intravenous injection of opiate which caused death within minutes. Although it is theoretically possible that Shipman could have given Mr Charnock a lethal injection by the intramuscular route, which would take longer to act, it is most unlikely that Shipman would have given such an injection and left his patient conscious and walking about. The risk of discovery would have been enormous.
There is an inconsistency between the time that Shipman last saw Mr Charnock alive, as recorded on the MCCD counterfoil on the one hand, and what is stated within the Report of Death to the Coroner and Shipman's visits book on the other. It seems likely that what is written in his visits book and the Report of Death to the Coroner is correct and that Shipman was careless in completing the MCCD counterfoil, as he often was. This single inaccuracy does not give rise to suspicion.
I am quite satisfied that Mr Charnock died a natural death.

name: Emma Hirst
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Hirst died as a result of natural causes, as certified by Shipman.
Her deterioration during the last two weeks of life is well documented in the Charnley House daily diary and is confirmed by the recollection of Mr Knowles. It appears that she had had a stroke and this may well have been the latest of several. Her death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
There is no positive evidence that Shipman saw Mrs Hirst alive on the day of her death. Indeed the evidence strongly suggests that he did not.

name: Emma Smith
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 13 Back Bower Lane, Hyde
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to carcinoma of the left breast
conclusion:
It is clear that Mrs Smith was very ill and it appears likely that her death was imminent. I infer from Mr Parker's evidence that Mrs Smith was in pain and distress in the early evening of 24th
August. It appears that she had been unable to sleep. This is almost certainly why Shipman was summoned. In 1981, cancer patients often required periodic injections of opiate to control their pain. Syringe drivers were not then in general use. I think it likely that Shipman gave Mrs Smith an injection of opiate. If he gave this with the intention of relieving her pain and allowing her to sleep, that would be a wholly proper thing to do. If he deliberately gave her an excessive dose, intending to hasten her death, that would be unlawful. Shipman's remark to the family that they would be able to sleep that night does not provide any clue as to his intention.
It is not entirely clear to me at what time Mrs Smith died. Mr Parker says that, at some time before 8am on 25th
August, his wife went into the bedroom and reported that her mother was still asleep. Yet only a short time later, Mrs Smith was found to be dead. If Mrs Smith was still alive when her daughter went in to her, then there is no possibility that Shipman could have hastened Mrs Smith's death by giving a lethal dose of opiate. Had Shipman done that, Mrs Smith would have died within an hour of the injection. My only reservation about this case is that it seems possible to me that Mrs Parker might not have realised that her mother had already died when she went into the bedroom in the early morning. I can well imagine that, if Mrs Smith had been sleeping badly, Mrs Parker might have been anxious not to disturb her mother and might not have examined her closely. If Mrs Smith were already dead when her daughter went in, it is not known at what time she had died and the possibility that she died shortly after Shipman's visit would arise.
My conclusion is that this was probably a natural death but I cannot rule out the possibility that Mrs Smith died soon after Shipman's visit on 24th
August, in which case it is possible that he had hastened her death by injecting her with an opiate drug.

name: Lavinia Wharmby
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 20 Ward Street, Hyde
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to carcinoma of the stomach
conclusion:
It appears that Mrs Wharmby was suffering from terminal cancer. She was in pain and probably in need of pain-relieving drugs. If her pain could not be controlled by oral medication, it would have been appropriate for her to receive injections of morphine or diamorphine. If injections were given, they would probably have been given once to twice daily, by the intramuscular route, in order to spread their effect over a prolonged period. Mrs Wharmby's death was probably imminent and, since she was being visited by Shipman quite frequently, it would not be surprising if she died shortly after one of his visits.
The death is suspicious, however, because during the week before Mrs Wharmby died, Shipman apparently said that he would call on the day when Mrs Wharmby did in fact die, and that he would give her 'an extra dose' of the painkiller, which would be her 'final dose'. If this evidence is right, it suggests that Shipman might have had it in mind to give Mrs Wharmby a dose of opiates that was greater than was required to control her pain and was likely to end her life. However, it is possible that this remark was not made exactly as it is now recalled. It is quite possible that Shipman had said that he would have to increase Mrs Wharmby's dose of painkiller the following week. This is often necessary, as the pain worsens and the patient becomes habituated to the drug. It is quite possible that Shipman explained that, when he increased the dose to satisfy Mrs Wharmby's need for pain relief, the effect might be to make it her final dose. It is also quite possible that Shipman had warned that Mrs Wharmby could not be expected to live much longer and that Mrs Cowan was told to say goodbye. I find it strange that the suggestion was that Shipman would visit on a specific day the following week. If Mrs Wharmby were in such pain as required relief in the form of injections, I would have expected Shipman to visit every day. I note that Mrs Wharmby's name does not appear in the visits book every day. This raises the possibility that Mrs Wharmby's pain was being adequately controlled by oral medication and that she was not receiving regular injections. The position is far from clear. Some doubt is thrown on the accuracy of Mrs Cowan's recollection, as it would be strange if Shipman had expressed an intention to give the 'final dose' not on his next visit but on a later one.
I am satisfied that Shipman visited Mrs Wharmby on Wednesday, 18th
July. Her name is recorded in his visits book and Shipman said on the MCCD counterfoil that he had seen her alive on that day. Mrs Cowan says that someone told her that during that visit, Shipman had given Mrs Wharmby an injection. It is quite possible that he gave her an injection every time he came, if she was in severe pain. Mrs Harris does not recall that she was told that Shipman gave an injection that day, but was told that Shipman had stayed at the house until Mrs Wharmby had died.
