It is not clear for how long he stayed. Shipman would have been unlikely to stay with Mrs Wharmby for a long period, as he would have other patients to attend to. It is likely that Mrs Wharmby died within the hour. If Shipman had given a lethal dose of opiate intramuscularly, death would have followed within about an hour.
I do not think I can reach a positive decision in this case. Although there are real causes for suspicion, I think it would be unsafe for me to rely on the granddaughters' recollections of what they were told to the extent necessary for me to reach the conclusion that Shipman deliberately caused or hastened Mrs Wharmby's death.

name: Ethel Buckley
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
It seems overwhelmingly likely that Mrs Buckley died a natural death. Whether the cause of death was acute bronchitis, as Shipman certified, seems rather doubtful, as the Charnley House daily diary gives the impression of a gradual deterioration towards death rather than an acute illness. A few days before she died, Dr Moysey recognised that Mrs Buckley's condition was terminal and that the best that could be done for her was to keep her comfortable.
Although Shipman certified the cause of death, it seems that he could only have been in a position to do so had he discussed Mrs Buckley's condition with Dr Moysey. It is extremely unlikely that Shipman saw Mrs Buckley during the night before her death. The duty doctor transfer book reveals that he was not even on duty that night.
It is a matter of some concern that Shipman might have certified the cause of Mrs Buckley's death without ever having seen her alive. There is no evidence to support his claim that he saw her alive on 26th
September. However, it is possible that he saw her on 13th
September and knew enough of her condition to enable him to certify the cause of her death 16 days later. There is evidence that he saw her body after death and it is possible that he was properly qualified to certify the cause of death. However, given that the stated cause of death is not really consistent with the picture created by the Charnley House diary, I do wonder whether Shipman ever had seen Mrs Buckley. There is a good deal of evidence that Shipman was cavalier about his duties in respect of death and cremation certification. It is possible that the entries on the counterfoil were quite inaccurate. Although this gives some cause for concern, it still does not appear to me that there is any real reason to suspect that Shipman played any part in causing Mrs Buckley's death.

name: Hannah Cartwright
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
certified_cause: cardiac failure due to anaemia and a bleeding duodenal ulcer
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Cartwright died of natural causes and that Shipman played no sinister part in her death.
Mrs Cartwright was plainly quite unwell when she was last seen by Shipman on 29th
April 1980. Thereafter, but not immediately thereafter, her condition deteriorated. There is no suggestion that Shipman was present at the home on the day of Mrs Cartwright's death and it would appear that he had taken the day off work.

name: George Eric Higginbottom
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 14 Kingston Gardens, Hyde
conclusion:
It is clear that Mr Higginbottom was suffering from terminal cancer and had not long to live. His wife was nursing him with help from the district nurses. Shipman had visited quite regularly during the last two weeks of his life. It is highly likely that Mr Higginbottom was receiving pain-relieving medication at this time.
All the documentation suggests that Shipman did not visit Mr Higginbottom on 7th
March until after the death. In those circumstances, it would seem clear that Shipman could not have killed Mr Higginbottom or have done anything to hasten his death. However, as Shipman himself is the author of all the documentation, the contents cannot be accepted at face value. He is known to have made false entries on many cremation forms. It is entirely possible that Shipman called on Mr Higginbottom on the morning of 7th
March (not making any entry in his visits book) and administered an injection of opiate in sufficient quantity to ensure that Mr Higginbottom died that day. If the injection were a lethal dose, the death would have occurred within the hour.
In the absence of a witness with knowledge of the circumstances of the death, it is impossible for me to reach a decision about this case. It might be thought that it is fanciful to suggest that Shipman hastened Mr Higginbottom's death when there is no positive evidence to suggest that he did and every reason to think that Mr Higginbottom was close to a natural death. In my view, it is not fanciful, as, by 1987, Shipman was a serial killer. Many of the patients he had killed were in poor health and there were others, close to death, whose ends he had hastened.

name: Margaret Sankey
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Norbury House, a residential home for the elderly, Great Norbury Street, Hyde
conclusion:
Mrs Sankey had been in very poor health for some time before her death. It appears that she sensed that she had not long to live and there is clear evidence that she had received the last rites while conscious. Shipman had noted that she was
'very chesty'
when he visited on 30th
October, and Mrs Mackie's description of Mrs Sankey's decline over the last three days of her life is typical of that seen in cases of bronchopneumonia. It seems to me that the death on 1st
November was neither sudden, unexpected nor inexplicable.
There is conflicting evidence about Shipman's attendance on the day of the death. His visits book and the medical record made on the previous Saturday suggest an intention to visit on the Monday. He claimed on the MCCD counterfoil that he had done so. Ms Ryan says that he did not visit while she was there and she can speak of a period lasting several hours before the death. She cannot exclude a visit before her arrival. Mrs Mackie says that Shipman did not visit that day. However, I do not think her recollection can be relied on, as she also says that he had not attended for several days and in that I am sure she is mistaken. I think it likely that Shipman did visit Mrs Sankey on the day of her death, probably in the late morning, as soon as surgery finished. I think this may well have been before Ms Ryan arrived.
Having said that, I do not think that Shipman's presence indicates that he did anything to hasten Mrs Sankey's death. She lived for several hours after the visit so I can rule out the possibility that he killed her by giving a lethal injection of opiate. She would have been dead within the hour if he had done. The other possibility is that he gave her an overdose of a sedative such as Largactil, which would have made her sleep very deeply and might have accelerated the progress of her bronchopneumonia. However, there is no evidence at all that he gave such an injection and the fact that she remained intermittently conscious until the end shows that it is most unlikely that she had been over-sedated.
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Sankey died a natural death.

name: Charles Henry Wood
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 68 Marlborough Road, Hyde
conclusion:
It appears to me that this death was probably due to natural causes. Mr Wood's son lived with him and was said to be present at the death. Shipman does not appear to have visited before the death. However, in the absence of evidence from a witness with knowledge of the circumstances of death, it is impossible to exclude entirely the possibility that Shipman was involved, particularly where the information available to the Inquiry is reliant in the main on documentation completed by Shipman himself.
The absence of any reference to a visit on 18th
January in the visits book is puzzling. It is possible that Shipman visited on that day but did not record it in his book. It is also possible that he invented a visit to create the impression that he was in a position to certify the cause of death. A further possibility is that Mr Wood was seen by Shipman at the surgery, although, given his age, this seems unlikely. It is clear from many cases investigated by the Inquiry that Shipman was far from scrupulous in the way he carried out his duties of certification. However, this single factor does not give rise to suspicion that he might have caused or hastened the death.

name: Mary Alice Brown
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Pole Bank Hall, a residential home for the elderly, Stockport Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Brown died a natural death.
The evidence suggests that Mrs Brown's health had deteriorated a few days before her death. Mr Hampson was summoned to Pole Bank Hall in the early hours of 15th
May. The staff would not have called him out at that hour unless Mrs Brown had been critically ill. She was alive but very ill when he arrived and died while he was fetching his hearing aid. It appears to me that Mrs Brown's death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
There is no evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Brown in the hours leading up to her death. The duty doctor transfer book indicates that Dr Bills, who was on out of hours duty that weekend, had transferred calls to the deputising service. It think it likely that he came out to see Mrs Brown's body at some time after 8am on the Sunday morning, by which time he would have resumed weekend duty. This would explain Shipman's endorsement on the MCCD counterfoil. It would be most unusual for Shipman to turn out in the middle of the night when not on duty. I think that possibility can be entirely discounted. I, therefore, rule out the possibility that Shipman unlawfully killed Mrs Brown by administering to her a lethal dose of opiates.
When Mr Hampson last saw Mrs Brown shortly before she died, she was conscious and attempted to talk to him. I am satisfied therefore that it is extremely unlikely that Shipman had over-sedated Mrs Brown in the days before her death to the extent that might have indirectly contributed to her death.

name: Frances Clayton
title: Miss
conclusion:
It is quite clear that Miss Clayton was in a very frail physical condition in the days leading up to her death. Her death was neither sudden nor unexpected and it is very likely that she died as a result of natural causes.
There is no evidence that Shipman saw Miss Clayton in the hours immediately before her death and I therefore rule out the possibility that Shipman killed her by administering a lethal dose of opiates.
I cannot absolutely rule out the possibility that Shipman over-sedated her when he visited on the morning of 6th
January. If over-sedated, Miss Clayton would be more vulnerable to bronchopneumonia, a common mechanism of death in elderly people. If Shipman did this, it would not be possible to say whether he had done it with the intention of keeping Miss Clayton comfortable or whether he used it as an indirect way of hastening her death.
However, I note that Miss Clayton was already very sleepy before Shipman saw her on the morning of 6th
January and it seems unlikely that he would have given her any drug.
My conclusion is that Miss Clayton probably died a natural death. I cannot absolutely rule out the possibility that Shipman contributed to her death by over-sedating her. However, I think this is unlikely.

name: William Hague
title: Mr
place_of_death: Bowlacre, a residential home for the elderly, Elson Drive, Stockport Road, Gee Cross, Hyde
conclusion:
In my view it is likely that Mr Hague died a natural death. Mrs Wood recalls that he was very unwell before he died and the death was expected. Mrs Wood's description of her uncle's condition on the day before the death is entirely typical of bronchopneumonia. There is good evidence to support the cause of death certified by Shipman.
It is entirely possible that Shipman visited Mr Hague on the day of his death. He had also visited him on four other occasions in the previous week and had not administered a lethal injection. It is possible that Shipman did give an excessive dose of opiate to Mr Hague shortly before his death. However, if the system described by Mrs Holdsworth operated as it should, I think it is unlikely that Shipman would have risked giving an inappropriate injection. I cannot say that the system always operated as it should, but it seems likely that Mrs Holdsworth might have remembered if Shipman gave an injection but would not hand over the used ampoule. Although I cannot rule out the possibility that Shipman hastened Mr Hague's death by giving an inappropriate injection, I think it highly likely that the death was entirely natural.

name: May Slater
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 30 Hough Lane, Hyde
conclusion:
More than 20 years have passed since Mrs Slater died and the quality of the evidence has suffered as a result. No medical records survive and the only documentary evidence emanates from Shipman himself. It is therefore very difficult to be sure, for example, of the degree of congestive heart problems that Mrs Slater had, if any. She may have been a strong candidate for a sudden cardiac death but the evidence of her family and, to some extent, Mrs Laithwaite, would not suggest that she was. She was, however, being treated by Shipman for something, possibly phlebitis. The family recalls that Mrs Slater was unwell in the week leading up to her death, perhaps with a cold or mild chest infection.
It is not certain that the doctor who was called on the Saturday afternoon was Shipman. As he completed the MCCD counterfoil on 18th
April, I think it was probably he who answered the call. I cannot see why he would have come into the surgery on a Saturday afternoon or evening just for the purpose of completing the MCCD, when it would not be possible to register the death until after the weekend. Whether he came because he was the doctor on duty or whether he came to see his patient even though he was not on duty, I do not know. It is almost certain that Mrs Slater was registered with Shipman despite what her family remembers. If Shipman did answer the call, he completed the MCCD counterfoil on the basis that Mrs Slater was already dead when he arrived.
The question then arises as to why Shipman was called out. On this issue, Mrs Catherine Slater says that Mrs Laithwaite told the family at the time that she had called out the doctor because Mrs Slater was unwell. It is unlikely that they are mistaken about this and they would probably have remembered had they been told that she had been found dead. However, I have come across cases in which a warden has been reluctant to give the news of a death over the telephone and has asked the family to come to see her before going to the home of their elderly relative. It is possible that that is why Mr and Mrs James Slater went to see the warden rather then going straight to Mrs Slater's bungalow. It is, therefore, possible that Mrs Slater was dead before Mrs Laithwaite telephoned Mr and Mrs James Slater. It is also possible that Mrs Slater had been found dead and the doctor had been called out to confirm the death. It is possible that Mrs Laithwaite called the doctor because Mrs Slater was unwell and that seems more likely, as I do not think Mrs Laithwaite would have visited Mrs Slater at that time of day unless summoned, and would not have found her body until later. It is far more likely that Mrs Slater summoned Mrs Laithwaite by pulling her emergency cord and that Mrs Laithwaite decided to call the doctor. What is not known is whether she telephoned the family at the same time or waited until the doctor had arrived. If she was concerned about Mrs Slater, I think it likely that she would have telephoned Mr James Slater straight away. Mrs Catherine Slater gives the impression that when her husband received the call from Mrs Laithwaite, the doctor had been called but had not yet arrived.
The family arrived about ten minutes later, by which time the doctor was almost certainly with Mrs Slater. The family did not go straight to the bungalow but spoke to Mrs Laithwaite in the centre. I think this must have been either because Mrs Laithwaite had asked them to come to the centre rather than going straight to the bungalow or because Mrs Laithwaite kept a lookout for them to prevent them from going straight to the bungalow. Whichever it was, I think the explanation must be that by that time Mrs Laithwaite knew that Mrs Slater was either dead or dying. I think what must have happened is that when the doctor arrived, Mrs Laithwaite took him in and stayed while he examined Mrs Slater. It would then appear that the doctor told Mrs Laithwaite either to go to telephone the family or possibly to go to intercept the family's arrival. If that had happened and if Mrs Slater had then died in the doctor's presence and the doctor was Shipman, I would be very suspicious that Shipman had caused the death. According to Mrs Catherine Slater, the doctor gave Mrs Laithwaite the news of the death. If that is right, it seems likely that the doctor had told Mrs Laithwaite that Mrs Slater was seriously ill and close to death and that he told her of the death when he came out. He did not speak to Mr and Mrs James Slater but he might not have realised that they had arrived because they had not come by car.
I have not found this case easy to decide. I have some doubt as to whether the doctor was Shipman. However, I have come to the conclusion that he probably was. Although it is possible that Mrs Slater was already dead when Shipman arrived, I think on balance that it is more likely that she was not. Had she been dead, I think Mrs Laithwaite would probably have told the family over the telephone. I think it is more likely that Mrs Laithwaite called out Shipman because Mrs Slater was ill.
It appears likely, therefore, that Mrs Slater died in Shipman's presence. It is possible that she could have died of natural causes in his presence but knowing, as I do, that Shipman had already killed a number of patients and was later to kill many more, I have come to the conclusion that he killed Mrs Slater. I could not say that I am sure of this conclusion but I think that it is probable.

name: Olive Winston
title: Mrs
place_of_death: The Sycamores, a residential home for the elderly, Victoria Street, Hyde
conclusion:
I am satisfied that Mrs Winston died as the result of natural causes.
The evidence suggests that Mrs Winston's health deteriorated suddenly about two months before her death and that she declined gradually thereafter. It appears that, in the period preceding her death, she was very weak and her death was expected.
There is no evidence that Shipman saw Mrs Winston on the day or during the night before her death. Mrs Jeffries spent the evening of 11th
October with her mother and, when she left, Mrs Winston was still alive although deteriorating. It would be most unusual for Shipman to visit an elderly persons' home during the night. In my view there is no reason to suspect that Shipman was involved in this death.

name: Miriam Bradshaw
title: Mrs
place_of_death: The Sycamores, a residential home for the elderly, Victoria Street, Hyde
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to carcinoma of the left breast
conclusion:
Very little is known about the precise nature of Mrs Bradshaw's health. She was, however, a frail lady who had been found to have inoperable breast cancer. The evidence suggests that her health had deteriorated in the days leading up to her death, although it appears that the death was not preceded by a long period of confinement to bed.
There is evidence that Shipman attended Mrs Bradshaw two days before her death but no positive evidence that he saw her alive on the day of the death. However, that does not mean that he could not have done. He did not always make entries in his visits book, especially when called out in an emergency. It is entirely possible that Shipman was called out on the morning of 13th
January because Mrs Bradshaw had deteriorated and that he did not make an entry in his visits book. The nursing records or diary from The Sycamores have been destroyed. If Shipman did visit Mrs Bradshaw on the day of her death, it is quite possible that he gave her some form of pain relief. If she was indeed suffering carcinomatosis, as Shipman certified, it is probable that she was in quite severe pain shortly before her death. The possibility then arises that Shipman could have given a lethal quantity of strong opiate, which caused or hastened Mrs Bradshaw's death.
I feel unable to reach any conclusion in this case, even on the balance of probabilities. There is insufficient evidence. It is possible that Shipman was unlawfully involved in Mrs Bradshaw's death. However, I stress that there is no positive evidence that he was.

name: Constance Anne Couldwell
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Norbury House, a residential home for the elderly, Great Norbury Street, Hyde
conclusion: The evidence suggests that Mrs Couldwell deteriorated gradually before her death and that her son was with her at the end. This would indicate that the death was not unexpected. However, there is also evidence that Shipman saw Mrs Couldwell alive on the day of her death. Unfortunately there is no evidence at all about the purpose or circumstances of his visit. It follows that I am unable to form any view about whether Shipman unlawfully killed Mrs Couldwell or whether she died as a result of natural causes.

name: Ethel Doris Holgate
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
Mrs Holgate was clearly unwell in the weeks before her death. Her appetite was poor and she was very agitated at night. She was obviously very weak and required a high level of personal care from the staff. Her son recognised that her death was imminent. When it occurred, the death was neither sudden nor unexpected. I agree with Dr Grenville's evidence that it was not inappropriate for Shipman to certify that the death was due to senility.
Although Shipman had attended Mrs Holgate on several occasions during her final illness, there is no evidence to suggest that he visited her during the final hours and no reason to suspect that he administered any drug which might have had the effect of hastening her death.
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Holgate died of natural causes.

name: Albert Slater
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 10 Newton Hall Court, Hyde
conclusion:
Mr Slater was clearly unwell in the weeks before his death, and might have been more unwell than Mr Samuel Slater recalls. Given the passage of time, that would be perfectly understandable. That Mr Slater was confined to bed for two weeks and had been visited by Shipman several times, would suggest that he was quite seriously unwell, although not apparently suffering from a condition which Shipman thought should be treated in hospital.
In the absence of the medical records, it is difficult to know what Mr Slater was suffering from. I have the impression that the underlying illness was connected with his lungs, possibly a chest infection. If that were so, it seems likely that Shipman had been giving Mr Slater a series of antibiotic injections. It is possible that Mr Slater had developed heart failure and that this was the cause of his breathing difficulties. It might then be that Shipman gave a diuretic in an attempt to remove fluid from the lungs. However, that seems unlikely, as such injections are not usually given in the evening, as the patient is unable to sleep because of the frequency with which he or she urinates. It is unclear whether Mr Slater had suffered from angina as Shipman claimed. In any event, there does not seem to be any history from which Shipman could have diagnosed that the cause of death was a heart attack.
Some suspicion arises in this case because Shipman attended at the house on 10th
January 1979 and administered an injection to Mr Slater. That injection might have been an antibiotic, which could have done no harm to Mr Slater and might have done some good. There is no real reason to suspect that that injection was of an opiate, although suspicion that it might have been always arises, on account of Shipman's practice of killing patients by that method. However, it seems unlikely that Shipman could have caused Mr Slater's death directly by giving a lethal injection of opiate. I am satisfied that Mr Slater lived for several hours after the injection and, as Professor Henry McQuay has said, a lethal dose of opiate will kill within an hour of administration. It is possible, however, that Shipman gave a fairly small dose of opiate or other sedative, which would have impaired Mr Slater's respiratory function even more than it was already impaired. It is possible that Shipman gave an inappropriate injection with the intention of hastening Mr Slater's death.
My main cause for concern, in this case, is that Shipman certified that the cause of death was coronary thrombosis, although there does not appear to be any history of such an event. In later years, Shipman frequently certified a death as due to coronary thrombosis when he had in fact killed the patient. I think Mr Slater may have had bronchopneumonia or have been in respiratory failure and I can see a possible method by which Shipman could have hastened his death from that cause. But why, if he did that, Shipman would want to certify the death as due to coronary thrombosis I cannot imagine.
I do not feel able to reach any conclusion as to whether Mr Slater's death was due to natural causes or whether Shipman hastened his end.

name: Maureen Whittaker
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Hyde Nursing Home, Grange Road South, Hyde
certified_cause: respiratory failure due to chronic obstructive airways disease
conclusion:
I am satisfied that Mrs Whittaker died of natural causes, as certified by Shipman.
Mrs Whittaker was clearly extremely unwell for a number of years before her death. She had chronic breathing difficulties for which she required oxygen from a cylinder. According to the staff at Hyde Nursing Home, her condition deteriorated during her time there and members of her family agree that she was very ill in the days leading to her death. Her death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
The only possible cause for suspicion in this case arises from the fact that Shipman last saw Mrs Whittaker alive on the day of her death. Shipman appears to have visited at about 1.30pm. There is no evidence that he gave any medication at that time and the evidence suggests that he refused or postponed Mrs Doyle's request that he should give Mrs Whittaker some morphine. As Mrs Whittaker's respiratory function was already severely compromised, any dose of opiate would probably have had the effect of hastening her death.
It appears likely that Mrs Whittaker died before Shipman returned that day. Mrs Doyle says that Shipman was not present during the two hour period before the death. Mrs Doyle was with her mother during that time and has described Cheyne-Stokes respiration. I think the possibility that Shipman gave Mrs Whittaker a dose of an opiate drug or a strong sedative can be ruled out.

name: Bertha Bagshaw
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 12 Walker Close, Hyde
conclusion: It is impossible for me to reach any conclusion as to whether or not Shipman played a part in Mrs Bagshaw's death. The fact that he claimed a visit the day before death which was not confirmed by the visits book might raise a suspicion that he had a reason for avoiding a referral to the coroner. However, it is possible that he did visit Mrs Bagshaw on that day but failed to record his intention to do so in the visits book. The Inquiry is aware that this did happen on occasions. Without evidence from a witness with knowledge of the circumstances of the death, no conclusion can be reached.

name: Ivy Elizabeth Challinor
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion: I am quite satisfied that Mrs Challinor died of natural causes. She was in severe pain before her death and needed quite substantial amounts of diamorphine. It would appear that these injections were usually given not by Shipman but by the district nurse at Shipman's behest. The only evidence that Shipman actually visited Mrs Challinor on the day of her death comes from the MCCD counterfoil. It is possible, but unlikely, that he saw her on that day and extremely unlikely that he did so shortly before her death. Had he been on duty that evening, one would expect that it would have been he and not Dr Napier who was called out to certify the fact of death.

name: May Hurd
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion: I am quite satisfied that Mrs Hurd died of natural causes as certified by Shipman. Mrs Hurd was seen by two other doctors in the days before she died. Mr Cooper Wilson diagnosed inoperable bladder cancer and Dr Moysey, Shipman's partner at the Donneybrook Surgery, recognised her terminal illness and suggested that she be given palliative treatment only. There is no evidence that Shipman saw her in the days leading up to her death and it is extremely unlikely that he did so. Although Shipman stated that he had seen Mrs Hurd about 13 days before she died, the likelihood is that he said this in order to avoid the time and trouble involved in a referral to the coroner.

name: Florence Slater
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 10 Newton Hall Court, Hyde
conclusion:
The evidence in this case is extremely limited. However, it seems clear that Mrs Slater was in a very frail condition and probably became unconscious in the week leading up to her death. The visits book suggests that she was also receiving a high degree of medical attention at this time.
Unfortunately, however, very little is known about the circumstances surrounding Mrs Slater's death. It seems likely that Shipman saw Mrs Slater alive on the day of her death. It follows that there is a possibility that he administered a drug that hastened her death. On the other hand, it is clear that her death was neither sudden nor unexpected. It would seem unlikely that Shipman would kill an unconscious patient. Although I cannot rule out the possibility that Shipman hastened Mrs Slater's death, I think it far more likely that her death was natural.

name: Muriel Elsie Wilson
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Norbury House, a residential home for the elderly, Great Norbury Street, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Wilson died of natural causes.
Mrs Wilson had a history of heart problems but, in the weeks leading up to her death, she developed a persistent abdominal complaint, which caused her to become dehydrated and aggravated her confused state. It does not appear that the abdominal problems were ever fully investigated as Mrs Wilson's condition deteriorated to such an extent that only terminal care was appropriate. Her death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman saw Mrs Wilson in the period immediately before her death. The visits book, the MCCD counterfoil and Form B all suggest that he last saw her on 1st
July. Shipman usually carried out his routine visits between about noon and 3.30pm. As Mrs Wilson died shortly after 4am, it would appear that she lived for at least 12 hours after Shipman's last visit. He cannot have given her a lethal dose of an opioid drug at that visit, as she would have died within an hour had he done so. It is most unlikely that Shipman would have visited Mrs Wilson in the middle of the night. A deputising doctor was called out to confirm the death.
I have also considered the possibility that Shipman had over-sedated Mrs Wilson by giving her large doses of a drug such as Largactil. It does not appear to me that this could have happened. First, Shipman had prescribed Melleril which was to be administered by the staff at the home. There does not appear to have been any need or justification for further medication. Also, it does not appear that Shipman visited every day, as would have been necessary if he was to keep Mrs Wilson in an unconscious state by over-sedation.
I see no reason to suspect that Shipman was unlawfully involved in Mrs Wilson's death.

name: James Edward Barnes
title: Mr
place_of_death: Hyde Nursing Home
conclusion:
The medical records show that Mr Barnes suffered a stroke about four months before his death and the evidence suggests that he suffered a second stroke on Wednesday, 27th
October 1993. He was asleep or unconscious from the time that Mr Barnes Junior arrived at the nursing home on Thursday, 28th
October. It is entirely possible that Mr Barnes died as a result of natural causes and that Shipman played no part in hastening his death.
There is no evidence that Shipman visited after 9pm on Thursday, 28th
October. Mr Barnes lived for more than nine hours after that visit. It seems highly unlikely that Shipman would have visited during the night. I therefore rule out the possibility that Shipman gave Mr Barnes a lethal dose of opiate which directly caused his death.
However, I cannot completely rule out the possibility that Shipman over-sedated Mr Barnes during the last two days of his life and that the sedation caused or contributed to Mr Barnes' unconscious state. Shipman would have had the opportunity to administer sedative drugs when he visited on 25th
October, 27th
October and 28th
October. If deeply unconscious, Mr Barnes would be more vulnerable to bronchopneumonia, a common mechanism of death in elderly people. It is possible that Shipman's actions in this respect could have contributed indirectly to the death. However, there is no positive evidence to suggest that Shipman gave any sedative drugs during the last few days of Mr Barnes' life and no positive reason to suspect that, if he did, the doses were inappropriately large. I think it is highly likely that Mr Barnes died a natural death.

name: Alice Chappell
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 320 Market Street, Hyde
conclusion:
The Inquiry has very little evidence about this death.
The entries in Shipman's visits book strongly suggest that he was not on duty over the weekend when Mrs Chappell died. Whilst experience has shown that Shipman was at times available to visit on days when he was nominally off duty, it must make attendance by him much less likely. The MCCD was signed on the day after death, which would be entirely consistent with his having certified death on his return to work on the Monday.
In the circumstances, it appears to me that it is highly likely that Mrs Chappell died from natural causes although, in the absence of evidence from a witness with knowledge of the circumstances of the death, it is impossible to be completely sure that this was the case.

name: Alice Holt
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 147 Ashton Road, Hyde
certified_cause: heart failure due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
I regret to say that I am unable to say whether Mrs Holt's death was natural or resulted from an unlawful act on Shipman's part.
There is some evidence that Mrs Holt suffered from heart problems. Her daughter has a recollection of her saying that she had a 'faulty heart valve'. She also suffered from oedema, which may be a sign of congestive heart failure. There are, however, other explanations for oedema and it does not necessarily follow that Mrs Holt was suffering from heart failure. There is no report that she suffered from shortness of breath, which is another common symptom of congestive heart failure. However, as she led a very sedentary life, any shortness of breath might have gone unnoticed.
Congestive heart failure can lead to a sudden death. However, it does not usually do so unless the underlying chronic condition is quite severe. When Mrs Ogden last saw her mother, just before midday on 22nd
February, she was up and dressed and was not complaining of feeling unwell. Although these events occurred many years ago, Mrs Ogden is confident in saying that her mother was not unwell because, if she had been, Mrs Ogden would either have stayed with her or at the very least called in after work that day. I think it is unlikely that Mrs Holt's congestive heart failure had reached a severe stage. I think her daughter would have been aware of it. If Mrs Holt had become unwell during the day, she would have contacted her next door neighbours. It follows that Mrs Holt's deterioration and death later that day must be considered as somewhat sudden and unexpected. I could not say that such a deterioration and death could not have occurred so quickly. I accept that it could. However, it would not be typical of a death from heart failure.
It is possible that Mrs Holt had a heart attack. However, she was found sitting peacefully in a chair, with the outward appearance of being asleep. Her position and appearance in death were not typical of a death from any of the common causes of a sudden natural death. Her position and appearance are typical of those seen in many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by lethal injection of opiate.
There is no evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Holt on the day of her death. He had visited some three or four days earlier, on 19th
February. Mrs Holt's name does not appear in Shipman's visits book on either Monday, 22nd
February or Tuesday, 23rd
February. Although Mr Harrison says that his parents did not see Shipman visit Mrs Holt the day before her body was discovered, a visit cannot be ruled out. If Shipman did visit Mrs Holt and kill her, then according to what we know about her routine, the visit would have occurred some time after 6.30pm, when it would be dark. That, of course, would have been at the end of Shipman's working day. At the time, Shipman lived in Mottram and calling in to see Mrs Holt on Ashton Road would have involved only a small detour on his journey home from the Donneybrook Surgery.
There are suspicious features surrounding this death but I feel unable to make a positive decision. Had there been any cremation documents and had the medical records survived, the picture would, I think, have been clearer.

name: Kate Elizabeth Stafford
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Pole Bank Hall Residential Care Home, Stockport Road, Hyde
conclusion: There is no evidence that Shipman saw Mrs Stafford in the hours before her death and I can therefore rule out the possibility that Shipman unlawfully killed her by administering a lethal dose of an opiate, which directly caused her death. However, I cannot rule out the possibility that Shipman might have given Mrs Stafford quite large doses of a sedative over a period of four to five days with the intention of keeping her asleep. If she was sedated, Mrs Stafford would be vulnerable to bronchopneumonia, a common mechanism of death in elderly people. If Shipman did this, it would not be possible to say whether he had done it with the intention of keeping Mrs Stafford comfortable or whether he used it as an indirect way of hastening her death. I stress that there is no positive evidence to suggest that Shipman did over-sedate Mrs Stafford. My conclusion is that it is very likely that Mrs Stafford's death was entirely natural.

name: Violet Mary Whittaker
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 230 Market Street, Hyde
certified_cause: respiratory failure due to chronic bronchitis with emphysema and asthma
conclusion:
It seems to me that this was probably a natural death.
Very little is known of Mrs Whittaker's medical history but it appears that she was in poor health and probably suffered from several of the conditions mentioned on the MCCD counterfoil, any one of which could have led to her death. The evidence as to the circumstances in which she was found is not clear, but it seems quite possible that she suffered an acute respiratory episode, lay down on her bed to rest and later died.
There is no evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Whittaker in the days preceding her death. It would appear that he did not visit her at home regularly. He himself claimed that he last saw her three weeks before her death. If he did, it would appear that this was probably at a surgery appointment rather than a visit. He appears to have been familiar with her health problems, as the causes to which he attributed her death did not come as a surprise to members of her family.
It is unusual for Shipman to state on an MCCD that he had not seen a patient within 14 days before the death. Here he acknowledged that he had not seen Mrs Whittaker for over three weeks before her death. That would tend to suggest that Shipman was not anxious to avoid a post-mortem examination. It may be that he spoke to the coroner to seek permission to certify the cause of death. Shipman and other doctors, as well as some registrars and coroners, seem to have been under the impression that a doctor was not qualified to certify the cause of a death unless he or she had seen the patient within 14 days before death. That is not essential provided the doctor has attended the patient in the last illness and has seen the body after death.
Very little is known about the circumstances of this death. It is possible that Shipman was involved in the death but, in my view, it is likely that Mrs Whittaker died of natural causes.

name: Edward Buckland
title: Mr
place_of_death: Laurel Bank Residential Home
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mr Buckland died a natural death as certified by Shipman. His oesophageal cancer was diagnosed at Tameside General Hospital. The Laurel Bank diary charted his gradual decline. His death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
It appears from the Laurel Bank diary that Shipman did not visit Mr Buckland in the 12 hours before his death. Nor did he attend to certify that Mr Buckland had died. The duty doctor did this. There is no reason to suspect that Shipman gave Mr Buckland an injection of opiate which directly caused his death.
I have also considered whether Shipman might have given Mr Buckland large doses of analgesic or sedative with the intention of keeping him deeply asleep during the last few days of his life and of hastening his death. It is strange that there is no record of any medication given during this period, either in the medical records or Laurel Bank daily diary, which seems to be a comprehensive record. I would have expected that Mr Buckland would have needed some analgesia during the terminal phase of his illness. The absence of any record would lead me to suspect that Shipman might have given drugs from his own supplies rather than those which he had openly prescribed. However, the evidence suggests that Mr Buckland was not deeply asleep or in a coma during the last few days. He was said to be a little distressed during the evening before his death. He cannot have been in a coma or over-sedated. I conclude therefore that it is overwhelmingly likely that, if Shipman was giving any drug treatment, it was only that which was necessary to keep Mr Buckland comfortable and was not designed to hasten his death.

name: Wilfred Chadwick
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 73 Corporation Street, Hyde
conclusion:
It seems that Mr Chadwick's death was quite sudden and unexpected to both his daughter and Shipman. It appears that he died alone. One might have expected, in those circumstances, that Shipman would refer the death to the coroner with a view to a post-mortem examination. However, Shipman certified the cause of death as heart failure. That is not a very exact cause of death and Shipman did not specify any underlying cause. However, it does not necessarily follow that Shipman had been involved in the death. Mr Chadwick seems to have had some kind of cardiac condition, possibly angina, and may also have had a degree of congestive heart failure. As a smoker, he may well have been at increased risk of suffering a heart attack.
There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman had had access to Mr Chadwick in the period immediately preceding his death. Mrs Gratrix herself saw her father in the early evening of 24th
August. I can rule out the possibility that Shipman had visited Mr Chadwick and killed him during the early evening. It would be unusual, although not impossible, for Shipman to visit a patient on his way home from the surgery. However, it seems most unlikely that Shipman could have called then and killed Mr Chadwick, as there would, by then, have been no reason for him to change into his pyjamas. It seems highly likely that Mr Chadwick went to bed as usual and died during the night. Whether or not he had got up in the night, I could not say.
My conclusion is that it seems highly likely that Mr Chadwick died a natural death. I cannot absolutely rule out the possibility that Shipman was involved but I think it highly unlikely that he was.

name: Marion Harrison
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Norbury House, a residential home for the elderly, 70 Great Norbury Street, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
I am sure that Mrs Harrison's death was due to natural causes.
It is clear from her medical records that she was severely overweight and suffered from chronic breathing difficulties. In 1987, investigations did not reveal any cardiac problems. However, Mrs Harrison must have been at some risk of suffering a heart attack. Her death was sudden in that the staff had not anticipated that she might die and had not warned the family to expect it. However, against the background history, I do not think it could be said that her death was wholly unexpected or inexplicable.
Mrs Harrison died in the early morning, at a time when Shipman was almost certainly not at Norbury House. There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman saw Mrs Harrison in the hours or days before she died. There is therefore no reason to suspect that Shipman was in any way involved in Mrs Harrison's death.

name: Edna Shawcross
title: Miss
place_of_death: her home, 105 Stockport Road, Hyde
certified_cause: cachexia due to carcinomatosis due to carcinoma of the rectum
conclusion:
Miss Shawcross was very ill with cancer and the evidence suggests that her sister nursed her during her last illness. It is surprising that Shipman does not appear to have visited Miss Shawcross regularly during the last few days of her life. However, it may be that he did but did not enter her name in his visits book. It is possible that the district nurse was primarily responsible for the provision of pain-relieving medication.
If Shipman accurately recorded that he had last seen Miss Shawcross alive eight hours before her death, he cannot have directly caused her death. If, as seems quite possible, Shipman was on occasions giving pain-relieving drugs to Miss Shawcross, any dose that he could have given at about 6pm on 7th
January would have long since reached and passed its point of maximal effect by the time of her death.
It is possible but unlikely that Shipman was called out in the early hours of the morning of 8th
January. He was not on duty. It is possible that he gave Miss Mabel Shawcross his home telephone number and advised her to telephone him if she needed further assistance. If he did visit in the early hours, it is possible that he gave Miss Shawcross an excessive dose of opiate which caused or hastened her death. However, it seems far more likely that he visited in the early evening and did not see Miss Shawcross alive again.
Although I cannot rule out the possibility that Shipman hastened Miss Shawcross' death, I think it is far more likely that she died a natural death of the causes certified by Shipman.

name: William Hill Wareing
title: Mrs
place_of_death: his home, 41 Newton Street, Hyde
conclusion:
It is clear from the evidence of Mrs Wareing that her father had reached the terminal phase of his illness. His death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
It appears that Shipman visited very frequently in the last week of the Revd Wareing's life. It seems likely that Shipman prescribed morphine for the relief of pain and distress. That would be entirely appropriate.
Although it appears that Shipman visited the Revd Wareing on the day of his death, there is no evidence that the visit took place within the hour before the death. If he did not visit, there is therefore no reason to suspect that he administered an excessive dose of opiate with the intention of hastening the death. These events took place a long time ago and it is possible thatShipman did visit within a short time of the death and hastened the death by giving a lethal dose of morphine. However, as Mrs Wareing does not recall a visit shortly before the death, it seems to me far more likely that the Revd Wareing died a natural death due to the cause certified by Shipman.

name: Harold Bramwell
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 8 Bryce Street, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
Mr Bramwell was clearly very unwell in the weeks leading up to his death. His condition deteriorated in the week before he died and particularly on the day of the death. The fact that Shipman was called out in the late evening indicates a high degree of concern about his condition. It would appear that Mr Bramwell was facing death due to respiratory failure. His death at any time would not have been unexpected.
Nevertheless, there are strong grounds to suspect that Shipman unlawfully killed Mr Bramwell. The most suspicious feature is that Mr Bramwell died in the presence of Shipman shortly after members of his family had been asked to leave the room. On the basis of the account given by Mr Alan Bramwell, Shipman manipulated events so that he could be left alone with Mr Bramwell, although he did not say for what purpose he wished to see Mr Bramwell alone. Shortly afterwards, Shipman came downstairs and told the family that Mr Bramwell had died. It is unusual for a doctor to ask to see a patient alone in these circumstances. It is also unusual for a doctor who knows that death is imminent not to summon family members so that they can be present at the moment of death. These circumstances lead me to suspect that Shipman gave Mr Bramwell a drug that hastened his end. That is the most plausible explanation for Shipman's actions.
According to his son, Mr Bramwell was suffering respiratory distress. In those circumstances even a small dose of any drug which affected respiration would be likely to end life. Mr Bramwell was not in pain but it does appear that he was in some distress. It is possible that Shipman felt that some sedative drug was required. However, if that was his view, he should have explained his reasoning to the family and should have warned them that the possible consequence of the drug was that it might hasten the death. Shipman's secretive behaviour was not acceptable practice and leads me to the conclusion that he knew and intended that the drug would end Mr Bramwell's life.
It seems to me rather strange that Shipman should have certified that the cause of death was a heart attack. Although Mr Bramwell had a history of heart disease and must have been at risk of another heart attack, his main problem at the time seems to have been respiratory failure. It would have been a most remarkable coincidence if Mr Bramwell had suffered a fatal heart attack just as Shipman had asked the family to leave the bedroom.
Taking all the circumstances into account, I am driven to the conclusion that it is overwhelmingly likely that Shipman killed Mr Bramwell with some sort of sedative drug, probably an opiate. I think it highly likely that Mr Bramwell had not long to live. It may be that Shipman persuaded himself that he was saving Mr Bramwell and his family from further suffering. Even if he did, under the law of this country, such actions are unlawful, if they are intended to shorten life. I think the circumstances of this death show that Shipman must have intended that consequence. I feel able to say that I am sure of that conclusion.

name: Norah Cheetham
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 11 Brooks Avenue, Hyde
certified_cause: carcinoma of the stomach due to partial gastrectomy
conclusion:
I am of the opinion that Mrs Cheetham died a natural death. Her husband realised that she was very ill and sent for his son and daughter-in-law. It is clear that Shipman attended regularly and gave pain-relieving injections. It seems very likely that Mrs Cheetham was in the terminal stage of cancer. Her death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
There is no evidence that Shipman had access to Mrs Cheetham in the few hours before her death. Shipman claimed that he last saw her on Saturday, 28th
January. His visits book suggests that he last saw her on 27th
January. Mrs Carole Cheetham thinks he probably visited on Sunday, 29th
January. If Mrs Carole Cheetham is right and he visited on the Sunday, it would seem most unlikely that he visited in the evening or late at night. If he had, I think Mrs Carole Cheetham would have remembered. However, even if he had visited at 11pm and had given an intramuscular injection of an opiate, there would be no reason to suspect that he gave a lethal dose. If he had done so, Mrs Cheetham would have died within about an hour. She lived until about 4am.
I feel able to say with confidence that Shipman did not cause or hasten Mrs Cheetham's death.

name: Robert Hickson
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 61 Chartist House, Hyde
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to cancer of the stomach
conclusion:
It is clear that by the time of his death, Mr Hickson was at an advanced stage of terminal cancer. It appears that the death was not unexpected.
The evidence suggests that Shipman probably saw Mr Hickson on the day of his death. There is no evidence of the time of his visit. He usually carried out his visits between about noon and 3.30pm. We do not know how or at what time Mr Hickson died. Nor do we know how or at what time Mrs Unsworth became aware of Mr Hickson's death. If there was a close temporal association between Shipman's visit and the death, I would have a strong suspicion that Shipman had caused the death. I am satisfied that he would not have had any moral scruple about hastening the death of a patient with terminal cancer.
As the evidence is unclear on so many points, I feel unable to reach any decision. However, there is a real possibility that Shipman hastened Mr Hickson's death.

name: Robert Swann
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 57 Great Norbury Street, Hyde
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to cancer of the stomach
conclusion: I regret that I am unable to reach a positive conclusion in this case. There is insufficient evidence. Such evidence as there is suggests that the death was natural. Mr Swann was in need of periodic visits by Shipman. His daughter was with him at the death. However, there is so little information that I feel unable to say, even on the balance of probabilities, whether the death was due to natural causes or might have been caused by Shipman.

name: Mark Wimpeney
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 44 Peel Street, Hyde
conclusion: Unfortunately, it has not been possible to discover any information from members of Mr Wimpeney's family as to the circumstances of the death. The information available to the Inquiry has been insufficient for me to reach any conclusion about whether the death was natural or whether Shipman was unlawfully involved.

name: Thomas Condon
title: Mr
conclusion:
As Mr Condon's medical records are not available, it is not possible to form an accurate view of his state of health shortly before his death. Mrs Jenkinson's impression was that he was recovering from his recent attack of influenza. He seems to have been up and dressed on the Friday and Saturday. If he were, it would not appear that he was about to succumb to bronchopneumonia. Dr John Grenville says that a patient is usually very weak and ill for a day or two before death from that cause. That Shipman had not visited since 30th
April would also tend to suggest that Mr Condon's health was improving and that he had not suffered a reverse. I also recognise that it is entirely possible that a man of Mr Condon's age might die quite suddenly following a serious attack of influenza.
Shipman was on out of hours duty that weekend. Although there is no evidence that Shipman did in fact call on Mr Condon, I cannot rule out the possibility that he did. He had seen him the previous week and might have called on the pretext of checking his progress. I have come across another case, that of Joseph Bardsley, who died only three weeks before Mr Condon, where Shipman made an unsolicited call while on duty on a Sunday and killed the patient. It is also possible that Mr Condon felt ill and called a doctor on the afternoon or evening of 5th
May, in which case it would have been Shipman who visited.
There is no positive evidence to suggest that Shipman caused Mr Condon's death. However, in the light of the factors I have mentioned above, I cannot rule it out. I regret to say that I am unable to determine whether Mr Condon probably died of natural causes or as the result of an unlawful act of Shipman.

name: Janet Hallsworth
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Hallsworth died as the result of natural causes and that it was entirely appropriate for Shipman to certify that her death was due to old age. She had deteriorated gradually over a period of at least a week. Her death was expected.
There is evidence that Shipman saw Mrs Hallsworth on 19th
December 1994. There is no evidence that he saw her again until after her death, when he attended to confirm that she had died. There is no reason to suspect that Shipman was unlawfully involved in Mrs Hallsworth's death.

name: Susan Eveline Shaw
title: Mrs
place_of_death: The Sycamores, a residential home for the elderly, Victoria Street, Hyde
conclusion:
I agree with Professor Baker that the medical records are quite inadequate to support a diagnosis of cancer of the stomach as the cause of death. Shipman noted only an abdominal swelling and loss of weight. While those signs are consistent with the diagnosis, they do not form a satisfactory basis for it. The reports that Mrs Shaw deteriorated quickly, was in a coma and did not appear to be in pain are also non-specific. I cannot feel any great confidence that the true cause of death was as certified by Shipman. It might have been; it might not.
Having said that, there is no real reason to suspect that Shipman caused or hastened Mrs Shaw's death. There is no evidence that he saw her on the day of her death. The rota shows that Dr Carroll was the Donneybrook doctor on duty that evening. It seems unlikely that Shipman would have called at The Sycamores that evening.
My conclusion is that it is highly likely that Mrs Shaw died of natural causes. I cannot absolutely exclude the possibility that Shipman called at The Sycamores on the evening of 21st
September and administered something which hastened Mrs Shaw's death, but that possibility seems extremely remote.

name: Jessie Irene Wagstaff
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 97 Two Trees Lane, Denton
certified_cause: cardiac failure due to coronary thrombosis
conclusion:
As the medical records have not survived, I am unable to discover the nature of Mrs Wagstaff's illness. It appears that she was very unwell and was spending virtually all her time in bed. That the bed had been brought downstairs suggests a high degree of dependency.
It is quite possible that she was suffering from some form of cancer but that her husband did not speak openly about it to the rest of the family. If she were, that would explain why she needed twice daily injections. They would have been for the relief of pain. It would also explain why the call for the doctor was not treated as an emergency. Had Mrs Wagstaff's pain been of sudden onset, one would have expected the doctor to attend quickly or to send an ambulance. I think it very unlikely that the daily injections were of a diuretic. Such medication is given orally save in an emergency. Whatever the nature of the underlying condition, the witness evidence suggests that Mrs Wagstaff's condition deteriorated quite noticeably on the day of her death. She was complaining of chest pain and looked pale. It is possible (although I think unlikely) that she was suffering a heart attack.
It appears likely that the doctor who attended was Shipman. He was the Donneybrook doctor on duty that day. He signed the MCCD, saying that he had seen Mrs Wagstaff alive on the day of her death. As she was another doctor's patient, it seems most unlikely that Shipman would have signed the certificate if he had not seen her shortly before her death.
It appears that, for whatever reason, Mrs Wagstaff was in pain when Shipman arrived. It would have been quite appropriate for him to give some pain-relieving drug. Valium is usually given orally and helps a distressed patient to relax and sleep. In the early 1980s, Valium was sometimes given by intramuscular injection. It is not usually given intravenously, as it irritates the vein. We do not know how Shipman gave the injection on this occasion. Nor do we know what Mrs Wagstaff's usual injection contained. It is known that Shipman sometimes used a strong opiate such as morphine or diamorphine to kill his patients. A lethal dose of strong opiate given intravenously will usually kill within minutes. If given intramuscularly, a lethal dose will kill in about an hour.
I cannot reach any conclusion about whether Shipman caused or hastened Mrs Wagstaff's death. I do not know what was her underlying condition. It might well have been a terminal condition. I do not know how close she was to a natural death. I do not know what the injection contained. That Shipman said that it contained Valium does not help a great deal. He might have been telling the truth; he might not. If Mrs Wagstaff's underlying condition were cancer, I would be very suspicious about her sudden death certified by Shipman as due to cardiac failure due to a coronary thrombosis. I have come across other cases where Shipman has hastened the death of a patient who was seriously ill with cancer (although not yet in the terminal stages) and has passed the death off as due to a heart attack.
I regret that I cannot make any decision about this case. There are too many uncertainties.

name: William Baxter
title: Mr
conclusion:
It is clear that Mr Baxter had terminal cancer and had not long to live. He was confined to bed and was in some pain and distress. He did not like taking the analgesic syrup, which Shipman had prescribed for him. In those circumstances, it would have been entirely appropriate for Shipman to prescribe an opiate to be given by injection. Provided Shipman gave a dose which was genuinely intended to relieve Mr Baxter's pain and was not intended to shorten his life, the administration of such an injection would be lawful and quite proper.
The difficulty in this case is that we do not know how large a dose Shipman gave or how long Mr Baxter lived after he had received it. A suspicion might arise that the dose might have been excessive and that Mr Baxter might have died very soon afterwards. Professor Henry McQuay and Dr John Grenville have explained that a lethal dose of opiate will kill within a few minutes if the dose is given intravenously. The usual site for an intravenous injection would be into a vein in the crook of the arm or on the hand. If a lethal dose is given intramuscularly, the drug will reach its maximal effect within about 30 to 60 minutes and death will occur within about an hour. The usual sites for an intramuscular injection are the thigh or upper arm. If Mr Baxter died very soon after the injection, there would be grave cause for suspicion that Shipman had given a lethal dose. Having said that there is a suspicion that Mr Baxter might have died very soon after the injection, I do not believe that he did. Mrs Barnhill sat with her father during the evening and I would have thought she would have realised if he had stopped breathing.
A further difficulty arises because, even if it were clear that Mr Baxter had died within an hour of the injection, I would not be able to say with confidence that Shipman had deliberately and unlawfully hastened Mr Baxter's death. As Dr Grenville has explained, it can be difficult for a doctor to assess the optimum quantity of opiate to give to a patient like Mr Baxter. If the doctor errs on the low side, the patient's pain will not be relieved and he or she will suffer. If the doctor errs on the high side, the pain might be quelled but the drug might also shorten life. The appropriate dose cannot be precisely calculated. The effect of a particular dose will vary from patient to patient, depending, for example, on body weight and general condition. A patient with impaired respiratory function should usually not have opiate drugs at all, as they depress respiration. But if the pain is severe, the doctor may take the view that he or she must relieve it even if the consequence is to hasten the death. Mr Baxter may have had impaired respiratory function. Shipman seemed to think he had, as he certified that chronic bronchitis had contributed to the death. It is possible that Shipman gave an injection of opiate intending it to end Mr Baxter's life but it is also possible that he decided to give an opiate injection because it was the only way to relieve Mr Baxter's suffering, even though it might also shorten his life. I would add that a doctor who faces that dilemma should discuss the situation with family before proceeding.
I regret that I am unable to reach a positive conclusion about this case. It is possible that Shipman deliberately gave a lethal injection and Mr Baxter died soon afterwards. It is possible that he gave a proper therapeutic dose and Mr Baxter died some time later due to the natural progression of his disease. It is also possible that Shipman gave a dose which he genuinely considered was appropriate, but which had the unintended effect of hastening Mr Baxter's death.

name: Annie Campbell
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 20 Rydal Avenue, Hyde
conclusion:
The evidence of Mrs Campbell's family members is not entirely consistent. Given the passage of time, this is understandable. The only person who had contact with Shipman on the day of the death was Mrs Pragnall and she has since died. I remind myself that I must be cautious before accepting hearsay evidence as accurate, especially when it relates to events which occurred over 20 years ago. I am inclined to attach greater weight to the evidence of Mr George Pragnall than to that of his children. He was more closely involved with the event.
It is clear that Shipman came to Mrs Campbell's house on the day of her death. Whether he visited in response to a request made by Mrs Pragnall or as a matter of routine does not greatly matter. I am inclined to think that his visit was routine because, if Mrs Campbell had been ill, I think it likely that Mrs Pragnall would have told her husband and the death would not have come as so much of a surprise as it appears to have done. Even if Mrs Campbell was unwell that morning, I do not think she can have been suffering from any worrying symptoms, such as chest pain. Otherwise Mrs Pragnall would not have left her alone, as I am satisfied that she did.
I accept Mr Pragnall's evidence that Shipman called at the Pragnall home to say that he had found Mrs Campbell dead. That in itself is a highly suspicious circumstance. Either Shipman killed Mrs Campbell or she died naturally in the quite short interval between Mrs Pragnall's departure, after which Mrs Campbell apparently ate her lunch, and Shipman's arrival. That is of course possible, although something of a coincidence. An elderly woman such as Mrs Campbell could die quite suddenly from cardiac causes without any warning. As there are no medical records, I am unable to assess the extent of Mrs Campbell's risk of such a sudden death. However, this kind of coincidence seemed to occur very frequently in Shipman's professional career. Knowing what is now known about Shipman, I think it is far more likely that Shipman found Mrs Campbell alone and took the opportunity to kill her than that he found her dead.
It is slightly strange that Shipman stated on the MCCD counterfoil that he saw Mrs Campbell alive on the day of her death, as well as seeing the body afterwards. This is not consistent with the story that he found her dead when he arrived. It would, however, be typical of one of his favoured explanations for a death which he had caused, namely that he had arrived to find the patient breathing her last. I am always suspicious in cases where Shipman has seen the patient alive on the day of the death. Unless there is eyewitness evidence of the time or times of his visit or visits, I cannot tell whether he has been present at the death. In the present case, I suspect that there was only one visit and that Shipman's official account, which he would have advanced on cremation Form B had there been one, was that he had found Mrs Campbell close to death, exhibiting symptoms from which he was able to diagnose that the cause of death was a coronary thrombosis.
The close temporal link between Shipman's presence at the flat and Mrs Campbell's sudden death persuades me that he was responsible for her death.
The position in which Mrs Campbell was found, sitting upright in a chair, is not typical of that seen in deaths due to coronary thrombosis but is typical of that in which many of Shipman's victims were found.
Notwithstanding the lack of direct evidence and the loss of the medical records, I feel able to say that I am sure that Shipman killed Mrs Campbell.

name: Leonora Hamblett
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 9 St Michael's Road, Hyde
certified_cause: congestive heart failure due to myocardial degeneration
conclusion:
As the medical records have not survived, it is not possible to discover the true nature of Mrs Hamblett's last illness. The family was aware that she had respiratory problems and thought these were due to bronchitis and emphysema. Shipman certified that the cause of death was congestive heart failure due to myocardial degeneration. In other words, he certified that the death was due to a cardiac condition. However, the symptoms of weakness and breathlessness noted by the family would be consistent with a death from either a respiratory or cardiac cause. It does not appear that Mrs Hamblett's death was either sudden or unexpected.
The cause for suspicion in this case arises from the fact that the district nurse apparently summoned Shipman whilst Mrs Hamblett was still alive and that Shipman may have arrived at the house before Mrs Hamblett died. The documentary evidence suggests that Shipman did not arrive until after the death. However, as Shipman is the author of the documents, they cannot be relied on as truthful or accurate. Shipman often made false entries on such documents when he wished to conceal his role in causing a death.
Mrs Bennett believes that Mr Hamblett would not have left his wife alone with Shipman during a visit. The death certificate records that he was present at the moment of his wife's death. Mr Hamblett did not apparently mention to the family that Shipman had given his wife an injection shortly before the death. These factors would tend to suggest that Shipman did not do anything to cause or hasten Mrs Hamblett's death.
My conclusion is that Mrs Hamblett probably died a natural death, but I cannot rule out the possibility that Shipman visited shortly before the death and administered something which hastened her death by a short time.

name: Kenneth Harry Simpson
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 29 Dowson Road, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mr Simpson died of natural causes as certified by Shipman.
It is clear that Mr Simpson was seriously ill and had reached the terminal phase. His death was neither sudden nor unexpected.
Shipman attended Mr Simpson several times in the days before his death. It is likely that Shipman, and possibly the district and Macmillan nurses, were giving him pain-relieving injections, probably of a strong opiate. Shipman last saw Mr Simpson alive at about 6pm and gave him an injection. Miss Simpson says that he lived for about another four hours after that. It seems to me highly unlikely that that injection caused or hastened Mr Simpson's death. Professor Henry McQuay and Dr John Grenville have given joint generic evidence to the Inquiry as to the timing and effect of opiates. If a lethal injection of opiates were administered intravenously, then death would follow within minutes. If administered intramuscularly, a lethal injection of opiates would cause death within about an hour. It appears to me that Shipman's treatment of Mr Simpson was entirely appropriate.

name: Annie Watkins
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 46 Carter Place, Hyde
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to carcinoma of the right breast
conclusion:
It seems clear that Mrs Watkins' cancer had metastasised or spread. It is quite possible that her gradual decline in health in the weeks before her death was the result of the spread of cancer to one or more of her vital organs. If so, there would be a sound basis for certifying that the immediate cause of her death was carcinomatosis. It certainly seems that Mrs Watkins was in pain over the weekend before she died.
On the day of her death, it appears that Mrs Watkins was very ill but conscious in the morning, when Mrs Davies visited her. By early afternoon, she was unconscious. It is not known whether or at what time Shipman visited during the day. It seems likely that he did, as Mrs Watkins' name was in his visits book. That would suggest that he would probably visit her in the late morning or early afternoon. I suspect that Mrs Holt may be mistaken in thinking that Shipman visited at about 6pm. I think it more likely that he visited in the early afternoon. If he did visit during the day, as opposed to the evening, as I think likely, it seems likely that he gave an injection. It is possible that he found Mrs Watkins half awake but in pain and distress and gave her the dose of Largactil, which Miss Holt saw recorded in the medical notes. That might well have caused Mrs Watkins to fall into a deep sleep or unconsciousness. It is also possible that he gave a different drug, not the Largactil as recorded or that he gave more than he recorded. We do not know.
Mrs Holt suggests that Shipman gave an injection at about 10pm. She may well be right. Shipman himself said on Form B that he last saw Mrs Watkins alive at about 9pm but he might well be wrong about the time. So, of course, might Mrs Holt. I think Shipman probably gave an injection in the late evening. That was probably the second injection of the day. However, I cannot be sure of this. The evening injection, if there was one, might have been Largactil or it might have been something else. Whatever it was, it is hard to see why it was necessary, as it appears that Mrs Watkins was in a coma. It may be that Shipman thought that the effect of the lunchtime injection would expire and Mrs Watkins would have a bad night if he did not give some more sedative. However, a suspicion must arise that the evening injection was given not for the relief of pain or distress but in order to hasten the death. If the evening injection were of Largactil, it could have hastened the death if the dose was large and Mrs Watkins' respiratory drive was already diminished, as seems likely. A dose of opiate would probably have hastened the death. It is also possible that the injection was of something else entirely, such as a diuretic, to help Mrs Watkins' breathing, although this seems unlikely, as Miss Holt would probably have noticed this on the medical record.
It is clear that in the late evening Shipman did not give Mrs Watkins an intravenous injection of a lethal dose of opiate. I say that because Mrs Watkins lived for some time afterwards. A lethal injection given intravenously would have killed her within a few minutes. However, Shipman might have given a lethal injection of opiate intramuscularly, which would have caused death within about an hour. Alternatively, he could have given a sub-lethal dose of an opiate or a large dose of Largactil, either of which might well have depressed Mrs Watkins' respiration sufficiently to hasten her death. If he gave her any form of sedative, I would be suspicious that he did so with the intention of hastening the death rather than merely keeping Mrs Watkins comfortable. I say that particularly because Miss Holt did not think that any sedation was necessary. However, it is also possible that Mrs Watkins' death was unaffected by any drug she had been given. A further possibility is that Shipman gave a small dose of opiate or a modest dose of sedative (in good faith believing it to be the best way of ensuring that Mrs Watkins did not suffer during the night), which had the side effect of hastening her death. Such an action would not have been unlawful.
From this discussion, it will be apparent that, although I am suspicious, there are too many uncertainties in the evidence for me to be able to say whether Mrs Watkins' death was natural or whether it was hastened by an unlawful act of Shipman. In any event, it is clear that Mrs Watkins would not have lived much longer.

name: Kathleen May Boardman
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 73 Harbour Farm Road, Newton, Hyde
conclusion:
I have no doubt that this was a natural death.
Mrs Boardman had a history of heart disease and there were clear signs that she was suffering from angina two days before her death. She must have been at real risk of suffering a fatal heart attack.
The history of the onset of pain in the late afternoon and later collapse and cardiac arrest in the early evening of 17th
December sounds quite typical of a heart attack. The post-mortem examination showed that Mrs Boardman had severe ischaemic heart disease and it is clear that the death was due to a cardiac event.
There is no reason to suspect that Shipman saw Mrs Boardman on the day of her death or that the death was caused by an unlawful act on his behalf. Whether Shipman ought to have admitted Mrs Boardman to hospital on 15th
December when she complained of chest pain and whether the outcome would have been different if he had, I cannot say. Questions of negligence are outside the Inquiry's Terms of Reference.
Mrs Layton was concerned about her mother's death because she had died suddenly and Shipman was her general practitioner. I hope this decision will put her mind at rest in that she can at least be assured that Shipman did not murder her mother.

name: Hilda Hulme
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
As Professor Baker has observed, the diagnosis of cancer of the bowel on 20th
March was somewhat tentative and carcinoma of the ascending colon was one of a number of potential causes of death. Having said that, Mrs Hulme's condition was very poor in the days leading up to her death. She was not eating and taking only a little fluid. She was confined to bed and suffering a great deal of pain. Her death does not appear to have been either sudden or unexpected.
