It appears that the prescribed dose of Cyclimorph would be appropriate for the relief of Mrs Hulme's pain. It appears also that this drug was administered by the Charnley House staff and not by Shipman. There is therefore no reason to suspect that an excessive amount would be given deliberately. In any event, it appears that Mrs Hulme lived for about nine hours after the second dose was given. That dose could not have had any direct effect on the timing of her death.
There is no record that Shipman saw Mrs Hulme shortly before her death. It seems likely that she died at about 5.40am. It is extremely unlikely that Shipman would have come to the home at that hour of the day. I think I can safely rule out that possibility.
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Hulme died a natural death, probably of the cause certified by Shipman.

name: Florence Sidebotham
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Yew Trees, a residential home for the elderly, Yew Tree Lane, Dukinfield
certified_cause: senility due to generalised cerebral arteriosclerosis
conclusion:
The evidence suggests that Mrs Sidebotham suffered from severe senile dementia. There is also evidence that she suffered fits in the last two years of her life. This picture is consistent with the cause of death certified by Shipman. Her death was not unexpected.
Unfortunately, very little is known about the circumstances immediately surrounding Mrs Sidebotham's death. Her son lived away from the area and her granddaughter, who saw her quite often, was away on holiday at the time of her death. There are no surviving records from Yew Trees. Thus, it is impossible to say whether Shipman visited Mrs Sidebotham shortly before her death. The only evidence suggesting that he may have visited her before her death is the appearance of her name in the visits book for the day of her death. This could have been a reminder to Shipman to attend to certify the death. On the other hand, it could represent an intention to visit while she was alive. It is possible that Shipman's claim that he had last seen Mrs Sidebotham alive on 25th
June was false, as her name does not appear in his visits book for that day.
I regret to say that I am unable to determine whether Mrs Sidebotham's death was natural or was caused by an unlawful act on the part of Shipman.

name: Annie Wilkinson
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 30 Rydall Avenue, Hyde
conclusion: So little is known about the circumstances of Mrs Wilkinson's death that I hesitate to reach any conclusion about whether Shipman was involved in the death. There is no positive evidence that he caused it and nothing to show that he did not. As Mrs Wilkinson's husband was present at the time of her death, it might appear less likely that anything untoward could have happened. In 1979, Shipman had already killed a number of patients but he was not so frequent a killer as he became in later years. I think I am able to say that it is likely that Mrs Wilkinson died a natural death. However, the possibility must remain open that she died at his hand.

name: Squire Barber
title: Mr
place_of_death: Hyde Nursing Home, Grange Road South, Hyde
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mr Barber died of natural causes as certified by Shipman. It is clear that he had terminal cancer and had reached the final phase of his illness. He required large amounts of diamorphine to relieve his pain. This was provided by a syringe driver. The dose prescribed was appropriate. Mr Barber's death on 20th
March 1997 was neither sudden nor unexpected.
Although there is some uncertainty about the time of Shipman's last visit to Mr Barber, there is no real reason to doubt the truth of his claim that he visited in the afternoon of 20th
March. There is no evidence that Shipman administered any additional medication during that visit. Even if there were evidence that he had done so, I would conclude that the medication had not caused the death. Mr Barber lived for about eight hours after that visit. For Shipman to have caused Mr Barber's death, he would have had to visit again much later in the evening of 20th
March. There is no evidence that he did so.

name: Mary Elizabeth Haslam
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 38 Mansfield Road, Hyde
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to carcinoma of the large bowel
conclusion: I am sure that Mrs Haslam was very poorly in the days leading up to her death and that it is most probable that she was suffering the terminal stages of cancer. The only real bases for any suspicion are that she was being treated by Shipman and that he was treating her with morphine. The possibility that he administered a lethal dose of diamorphine or morphine can be discounted because of the interval between his last visit and the time of death. The possibility that he may have given a sub-lethal dose, intending to render Mrs Haslam more vulnerable to the effects of her disease and any possible secondary bronchopneumonia, cannot be discounted. However, taking into account that the progression of her illness is exactly as would normally be expected, I believe that this was very probably a natural death.

name: Eric Wardle
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 29 Strines Court, Hyde
conclusion:
The evidence in this case is inconclusive. Mrs Parr and Mrs Tunnicliffe recall different conversations with their mother. If Mrs Parr is right, the doctor could not have seen Mr Wardle alive. If Mrs Tunnicliffe is right, he did. Shipman said that he saw Mr Wardle alive that day. Although Shipman's claims should never be taken at face value, it seems likely that Shipman did see Mr Wardle alive on 9th
January and, if he did, it might well have been very shortly before death.
That possibility gives rise to cause for concern. There is no evidence that Shipman injected Mr Wardle or treated him in any way. However, it is possible that he did so. He might well have been alone with Mr Wardle for some time. I note that there is some evidence that an ambulance attended the flat but it appears that Mr Wardle was already dead.
I note that Shipman certified that Mr Wardle died of a right-sided cerebrovascular accident. As Dr John Grenville has said in his generic evidence, a stroke which affects one side of the body is usually caused by the occlusion of a blood vessel in the cortical region of the brain. It does not usually lead to sudden death. Such strokes are not usually fatal, although they can be. If they are to be fatal, death usually follows the development of the stroke over a period of at least several hours and more often two to three days. During this time, the patient's level of consciousness sinks gradually.
There are features of this case which are similar to later cases in which I have found that Shipman has killed. The suddenness of the death and Shipman's possible presence at or shortly before the death give rise to suspicion. Another suspicious feature is the calling of an ambulance which arrives too late to take the patient to hospital. A sudden death supposedly from a right-sided stroke gives rise to suspicion.
I regret to say that I will be unable to reach a positive conclusion in this case. As I have indicated there are causes for suspicion. However, the circumstances of the death are not sufficiently clear for me to be able to say, even on the balance of probabilities, whether this was a natural death or whether Shipman was unlawfully involved.

name: William Henry Brown
title: Mr
place_of_death: The Sycamores, a residential home for the elderly, Victoria Street, Hyde
conclusion:
There is very little evidence about the circumstances of Mr Brown's death. If the evidence of Mrs Izyckyj is correct, he died between 8pm and 8am. However, we do not know whether he died in the early morning of 24th
February or in the late evening of 23rd
February. Shipman claimed on the MCCD counterfoil that he had last seen Mr Brown alive the day before he died. If Shipman visited in the middle of the day (as was usual) on 23rd
February, this would be at least 12 hours before the death and possibly as much as 36 hours. Although it is possible that Shipman saw Mr Brown after this visit during the evening or night of his death, this seems unlikely. There is no positive evidence to suggest that he did so. It follows that I think it very unlikely that Shipman caused Mr Brown's death directly by giving him a lethal dose of opiate. Mr Brown lived for an appreciable period after Shipman's last visit. In any event, I think it extremely unlikely that Shipman would have risked abusing opiate drugs in an institution so soon after his arrival in Hyde.
However, I cannot discount the possibility that Shipman over-sedated Mr Brown in the last day or so of his life. If over-sedated, Mr Brown would have been very vulnerable to bronchopneumonia, a common mechanism of death in the elderly. It is possible that Shipman indirectly hastened Mr Brown's death in this way.
My conclusion is that I think it likely that Mr Brown's death was natural but I cannot completely rule out the possibility that Shipman was unlawfully involved.

name: Samuel Harrison
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 162 Lodge Lane, Newton, Hyde
certified_cause: cardiogenic shock due to coronary thrombosis
conclusion:
I regret I am unable to reach a positive conclusion about this case.
I am inclined to the view that Mrs Morrison is probably right in her recollection that Mr Harrison was really quite ill, at least for a short time before his death. I do not think that the district nurses would have been attending, as it appears they probably were, twice a day, unless there was something seriously amiss. I do not accept Mrs Green's explanation that they only came once a day, late at night, for the sole purpose of giving an injection to help Mr Harrison to sleep. That would not account for the arrival of the district nurse on the Saturday morning. I do not accept Mrs Taylor's suggestion that Shipman arranged the nurse's attendance that morning by telephone. I think the district nurse arrived as a matter of routine.
I also accept Mrs Morrison's account of how she came to be present on the Saturday morning. I think she was working overtime because Mr Harrison was ill. I do not accept that she 'popped in' or was 'coming and going' as Mrs Green suggested. I think she was there throughout. As I think she is honest and that she would have remembered Mrs Taylor if she had been there, I am doubtful as to whether Mrs Taylor was there that morning at all.
There are at least two other reasons why I am doubtful about Mrs Taylor's evidence. Mrs Taylor claims that Shipman arrived at about 8.30am or 8.45am. I know that it was Shipman's practice to hold a short surgery on Saturday mornings from about 8.30am until 10am. He would only have gone out on a visit in an emergency. I have the impression that this was not an emergency and that Shipman probably arrived some time after 10am. I am satisfied that it was he and not any other doctor. He said on the MCCD counterfoil that he had seen Mr Harrison alive on the day of the death.
Mrs Taylor gave a graphic account of Shipman giving an intravenous injection into Mr Harrison's left arm. Although her account was very detailed, I am doubtful that it occurred. I felt her account was too colourful and too dramatic to be true. If she had really witnessed and been a part of this event, I am quite sure she would have told the police all she knew as soon as the news about Shipman broke. She never did so and has advanced her story only when approached by the Inquiry.
Mrs Taylor and Mrs Green have advanced a similar account about the giving of the injection. Mrs Green says she was not there but was told about it that day. These two witnesses gave very different accounts of the sequence of events. Mrs Taylor says that Mr Harrison went stiff and grey and then fell into a coma. She says she believes he was dead by about 10am. As the injection she says she witnessed was given intravenously before 9am, it could not have been a lethal injection. Mr Harrison would have been dead within minutes if he had had a lethal injection. Mrs Green says that her father died at about 1pm, which would have been about four hours after the injection, if one was given in the circumstances described by Mrs Taylor. If he lived until 1pm, his death cannot have been caused or contributed to by the injection given before 9am.
The only witness who gives an account which could possibly lead to the conclusion that Shipman was unlawfully involved in this death is Mrs Morrison. She is not sure that an injection was given. If it was, she does not know what the injection was or how it was given. It might have been given intravenously or intramuscularly. She has the impression that Mr Harrison died quite soon after Shipman's visit, before Mrs Green and Cilla had returned from the kitchen. On her account some suspicion arises that Shipman might have hastened Mr Harrison's death.
I am unable to reach any definite conclusion. I say only that there are some grounds to suspect that Shipman might have hastened the death.

name: Edith Wibberley
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 19 Cheetham Fold Road, Hyde
conclusion:
Mrs Wibberley was unwell in the days before her death. It appears that she had suffered a series of minor strokes. She must have been at considerable risk of suffering a fatal stroke. However, on the morning of 18th
December, her condition was unexceptional. I do not think her daughter-in-law would have left her if she had the impression that her condition had deteriorated. Shipman was expected, but only because he had said he wanted to take a blood sample. It would have been a remarkable coincidence if Mrs Wibberley had suffered a sudden fatal stroke just at the time of Shipman's visit. It would also be remarkable if she had suffered a stroke while alone during the morning and had died just at the time when Shipman called to take a blood sample. Dr John Grenville said in his generic evidence that such a coincidence might occur perhaps once in a general practitioner's professional lifetime. With Shipman, it seems to have happened time and time again. I am satisfied that events such as this were not coincidences: they were killings. The notion that Mrs Wibberley's death occurred in Shipman's presence, but without his involvement, is so inherently implausible that I discount it. I am sure that he killed her.
This case represents an early example of Shipman having given a lethal injection under the pretext of taking a blood sample. It was a device he was to use on many occasions thereafter. Taking a blood sample gave him the opportunity to introduce a needle into the patient's vein. Most patients do not watch such a procedure and even those who do would not necessarily realise that they were being injected. It appears to me that, when Shipman visited Mrs Wibberley on 17th December, he must have decided to kill her. I think perhaps that he did not have any or enough opiate with him to inject her that day and made an arrangement to return the next day, ostensibly to take a blood sample but, in fact, to kill her. I think Mrs Julia Wibberley was right to be puzzled about Shipman's wish to take a blood sample. It is hard to think what genuine purpose it could serve.

name: Mary Ivy Birchall
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 170 Lower Bennett Street, Hyde
certified_cause: carcinomatosis due to squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder
conclusion:
I am entirely satisfied that Mrs Birchall died a natural death of the causes certified by Shipman. Although the witness accounts differ in some respects, all the witnesses say that she was suffering from terminal cancer and that her life expectancy was short. Mr Brian Birchall now recalls that his mother's death was sudden, in that he had expected her to live longer, even though he knew that she was terminally ill. From the description given by Ms Edwards, it would appear that Mrs Birchall was known to be quite close to death.
The evidence suggests that Shipman last saw Mrs Birchall alive on Wednesday, 31st
May. That is what he stated on the MCCD counterfoil and Ms Edwards agrees. Shipman cannot have given Mrs Birchall a lethal injection of opiates on that day, as, if he had done so, she would not have survived until Sunday morning. Although it is possible that Shipman administered an injection of a sedative on that day, for example Largactil, which could have indirectly hastened her death, in the circumstances it is extremely unlikely that he did so.
Mr Brian Birchall recalls that his brother told him that a doctor had been called out on the day of the death and had given an injection, after which Mrs Birchall died. This is a hearsay account of an event that is said to have occurred about 17 years ago. It is not consistent with the evidence of Ms Edwards, who was present at the house when Mrs Birchall died. On her account, neither Shipman nor any other doctor attended in the hours before Mrs Birchall died. In any event, it appears that Shipman was not on weekend duty on 3rd
June. I think it unlikely that any doctor attended that morning and there is no evidence at all that Shipman was there.

name: Gladys Heapey
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 15 Acorn Avenue, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
It appears that Mrs Heapey suffered from angina, although her son does not recall her ever complaining of symptoms. If she did, she would have been at an increased risk of suffering a heart attack. Mrs Heapey was apparently well during the days before her death but it seems that she undertook some strenuous activity on the day she died and this might well have put a strain on her heart. It is therefore quite possible, even likely, that Mrs Heapey died a natural death from the cause certified by Shipman.
There are, however, some significant gaps in the evidence. First, we have no account of the death itself. If Mr Heapey had been present when his wife had a heart attack, I would expect him to tell his son about it and I would expect the son to have some recollection of the account. It seems possible, therefore, that Mr Heapey was not present at the time of the death, and found Mrs Heapey dead in her chair. That seems consistent with Mr Brian Heapey's recollection that his father telephoned to say that he thought Mrs Heapey had died. If that is what happened, and Mr Heapey was out of the house at the time of the death, there is a possibility that Shipman had visited during his absence. Mrs Heapey's name is in the visits book and, although it might have been entered after her death, it is also quite possible that the entry reflects Shipman's intention to visit on his rounds. On the other hand, if Shipman had visited Mrs Heapey when she was still alive, I would have expected her husband to mention it.
The fact that Mrs Heapey may have been found dead sitting in her chair excites a degree of concern. In his generic evidence, Dr John Grenville says that a patient who has died of a heart attack is not usually found sitting in a chair. He or she is more likely to be found collapsed in circumstances which suggest an attempt to call for help. On the other hand, I have already noted the very real possibility that Mrs Heapey died a natural death.
I am afraid I am unable to decide whether Mrs Heapey died a natural death or whether she was killed by Shipman.

name: Annie Wood
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Charnley House, a residential home for the elderly, Albert Road, Hyde
conclusion:
Mrs Wood had become very frail in the weeks before her death. She seems to have been very unwell during the night before she died. The daily diary entry suggests that she was suffering from a fever. On the day of her death, it appears that she stayed in bed but was well enough to eat a little breakfast and lunch. There was some concern for her health, however, as Shipman was sent for at 8.30am, which is about the time that the surgery opened. If Mrs June Wood's recollection is right, her mother-in-law was seen by another doctor that morning. That is possible, as it is clear that Dr Moysey and Dr Beenstock were at Charnley House at some stage. If another doctor saw her, the fact was not noted in the daily diary. I do not think there can have been any serious concern for Mrs Wood's health, as it was the practice at Charnley House to warn relatives if a resident was expected to die. Mrs June Wood says that the death came as a great surprise to her and her husband. It does appear to me that Mrs Wood's death was quite sudden and unexpected.
The evidence given by members of Charnley House staff suggests that Shipman usually visited at about lunchtime. Residents took lunch at about midday and there would be a shift change at 1pm. According to Mrs Stansfield's diary entry, which she would usually make at the end of her shift, Mrs Wood died suddenly at about 12.30pm. That would be after lunch but before the end of the morning shift. It would also be at about the time when Shipman might well be expected to visit. I know from other cases I have examined that the Charnley House diaries are not always complete and wholly accurate. I am also aware of evidence to suggest that during this period, the doors to the home were not kept locked and there was not a strict rule that a doctor must always be accompanied by a member of staff while seeing a patient. I cannot rule out the possibility that, unbeknown to Mrs Stansfield, Shipman visited Charnley House before Mrs Wood's death on 26th
March 1984. I say that notwithstanding the fact that Shipman's claim that he had last seen Mrs Wood alive on 23rd
March is consistent with the Charnley House diaries.
Mrs Wood's death was quite sudden and it appears to me that Shipman ought not to have certified the cause as 'old age'. If the death really did occur suddenly but naturally at 12.30pm, Shipman could not have known the cause of the sudden death and he should have referred the death to the coroner with a view to a post-mortem examination.
I regret to say that there is insufficient evidence for me to determine whether Mrs Wood died of natural causes or was killed by Shipman.

name: Doris Bridge
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 20 Gower Road, Hyde
certified_cause: coronary thrombosis, due to ischaemic heart disease and hypertension
conclusion:
Mrs Bridge had a history of angina and was at increased risk of heart attack. The evidence suggests that she may well have been suffering chest pain on the morning of her death, although she herself does not seem to have been unduly alarmed about her symptoms. I think, however, that Mrs Sleigh must have been quite worried, as she appears to have given an account to the receptionists which resulted in a personal telephone conversation with Shipman. That was quite unusual. It is quite possible that Mrs Bridge could have died of a heart attack that morning.
On the other hand, there are some causes to suspect that Shipman might have been involved in the death. Mrs Sleigh obviously told Shipman that her aunt had chest pain. I think there was then a discussion about how long it would take for Mrs Sleigh to reach her aunt's house. It sounds as though she estimated that it would take about half an hour. Shipman then said that, if Mrs Bridge were only suffering an angina attack, it would be over within half an hour. If it were a heart attack, it would still be happening when Mrs Sleigh arrived. What he does not seem to have suggested is that, in case Mrs Bridge were having a heart attack, it would be prudent to call an ambulance or at least arrange for someone to sit with her so that an ambulance could be called if necessary. If Shipman had it in mind to kill Mrs Bridge, as he could have done after this conversation, he would have known for how long Mrs Bridge would be alone. Shipman would have had time to visit in the half hour before Mrs Sleigh could arrive but it would be most inconvenient for him to do so, as he would usually be very busy at that time of the morning. It is possible that he would have felt able to justify the disruption of his surgery appointments on the ground that he had to deal with an emergency. In their generic evidence, the Market Street Surgery staff say that if they received a telephone call of a report of something sounding like a heart attack, Shipman would either attend immediately or instruct them to call an ambulance. When he gave evidence at the trial, Shipman said that, in an emergency, he would leave patients to wait in the surgery. It does not appear that, in this case, there was ever any question of calling an ambulance. It is possible that Shipman 'dropped everything' and went to Mrs Bridge's house. She could have let him in. He could have given her an injection, supposedly to relieve her chest pain and, if the injection were a lethal dose of opiate given intravenously, she would have been dead within a few minutes. Shipman could then have left the house, closing the door behind him, and returned to continue his surgery appointments. What militates against this theory is that he would have had to give some account to the staff when he returned. He obviously could not have said that he had found Mrs Bridge dead. If he wanted to say that, he would have had to stay at the house until Mrs Sleigh arrived. He could not return to say that Mrs Bridge was very ill but still alive, as it would obviously not have been right to leave her. If he had returned to say that she was in a satisfactory state and within a short time Mrs Sleigh had telephoned to say that she had found Mrs Bridge dead, the staff might have been suspicious. However, it must be said that Shipman appears to have had the complete confidence of his staff. The Market Street staff do not appear to have suspected him even when he had killed several patients in the surgery.
Mrs Sleigh's recollection of her aunt's appearance in death is consistent with her having died a natural death due to coronary thrombosis, although it certainly does not exclude death by lethal injection of opiate. Mr Sleigh's recollection is that Mrs Bridge looked as though she was asleep and this suggests that death by intravenous injection is more likely. The evidence as to Mrs Bridge's appearance in death is, therefore, inconclusive.
The history of sudden onset of probable chest pain indicates that this could well have been a natural death. However, the circumstances in which Shipman was alerted to Mrs Bridge's acute condition, and the fact that he had the opportunity to visit her and that she died so quickly, are suspicious features. Although this case gives rise to suspicion, I do not feel able to say whether it is likely that Shipman killed Mrs Bridge or that she died a natural death.

name: Charles Harris
title: Mr
place_of_death: his home, 51 Corporation Street, Hyde
conclusion:
There is no direct witness evidence as to the circumstances of Mr Harris' death. Mrs Schofield's hearsay account is extremely vague. There is a suggestion that Mr Harris was suffering from cancer, but it does not appear that he had yet reached the terminal phase. He was up and dressed at the time of his death. Shipman did not certify that the death was due to cancer.
It would appear that Shipman visited Mr Harris on the day before he died. It is reasonable to infer that Mr Harris was unwell that day and that Shipman decided to visit again the following day. However, it does not appear that Mr Harris' condition on 22nd
November gave rise to any need for him to be admitted to hospital. If Mr Harris was suffering from a chest infection of such severity that he was to die of bronchopneumonia the following day, one might have expected him to be admitted to hospital, especially as he lived alone and had no full-time carer. I do, therefore, find myself somewhat suspicious that Mr Harris should have been found dead the following day, sitting on a sofa, fully dressed. In his generic evidence to the Inquiry, Dr John Grenville said:
'Patients dying of bronchopneumonia are usually weak and become exhausted. They usually lapse into unconsciousness and the respiration becomes increasingly rattly.
It follows from the description of bronchopneumonia and lobar pneumonia that it is inconsistent for a patient dying of these conditions to be found sitting in a chair looking peaceful and appearing to be asleep'
.
In my view, that Mr Harris was found sitting on the sofa dressed in day clothes, is inconsistent with a death from bronchopneumonia. If it had been from bronchopneumonia, I doubt that he would have got up and dressed himself.
A further cause for suspicion arises from Shipman's reported conversation with Mrs Schofield about the need for a post-mortem examination. The decision as to whether there will be a post-mortem is for the coroner. It is the doctor's duty to decide whether he or she ought to refer the case to the coroner if he or she is insufficiently sure of the cause of death to sign the MCCD. It is not a matter for the relatives to decide. I have come across many cases in which Shipman has suggested to relatives that it is for them to say whether there will be post-mortem examination. Most relatives, given an apparent choice, will say that they do not want a post-mortem. In this way, Shipman creates the impression that it is not he who has sought to avoid referral to the coroner. He creates the impression that he is being considerate of the family's wishes. I regard this as quite sinister.
I have real suspicions that Shipman might have killed Mr Harris. However, bearing in mind the lack of evidence about the circumstances, I do not feel able to decide whether the death was natural or was caused by Shipman.

name: Ellen Walker
title: Miss
place_of_death: The Sycamores, a residential home for the elderly, Victoria Street, Hyde
conclusion:
It appears likely that Miss Walker died of natural causes, as certified by Shipman.
The diagnosis of pancreatic cancer was properly established by hospital investigation. This is an untreatable condition and is invariably fatal. Miss Walker's death was expected and wholly explicable.
There is no evidence to suggest that Shipman saw Miss Walker shortly before her death, at a time when he might have given her a drug which directly caused or hastened her death. The strange feature of this case is that there is no record of a prescription for any pain-relieving medication and it would seem likely that Miss Walker would have required some form of sedative or analgesia. If there were a record of the giving of analgesic or sedative drugs, I would have no concerns at all about this death. It is only because there is no record of any such drug that I suspect that Shipman might have given unrecorded doses of sedative or pain-relieving drugs on 27th
February and 1st
March and even on 2nd
March. It is possible that those doses were larger than appropriate and had the effect making Miss Walker deeply unconscious. I have come across one case where Shipman made a note in his visits book that he had given a very elderly patient an injection of 100mg of Largactil. That is a very large dose and would send a frail and elderly patient into a deep coma. In that state, the patient is vulnerable to bronchopneumonia and death. There is a possibility that Shipman did something of that kind in the present case, with the intention of hastening Miss Walker's death.
However, there is no evidence that he did so and I consider that it is likely that Miss Walker's death was entirely natural.

name: Edith Brierley
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Hyde Nursing Home, Grange Road South, Hyde
conclusion:
Mrs Brierley was of advanced years and had become very frail. Her gradual deterioration in the days leading up to her death is documented in the Hyde Nursing Home notes as well as the medical records completed by Shipman. Her death was not unexpected.
It is not known at what time Shipman visited Mrs Brierley on 10th
February 1998. However, the note recording his attendance in the care assistant notes kept by the home comes before an entry timed at 9.45pm, which would suggest that Shipman must have visited before that time. The possibility that Shipman administered a lethal dose of opiates during his visit on 10th
February can be ruled out. Professor Henry McQuay and Dr John Grenville have given joint generic evidence to the Inquiry as to the timing and effect of opiates. If a lethal injection of opiates were administered intravenously then death would follow within minutes. If administered intramuscularly, a lethal dose of opiates would cause death within about an hour. Mrs Brierley did not die until 2.45am on 11th
February, at least 12 hours after Shipman's visit and probably longer. There is no evidence that Shipman visited Mrs Brierley again either later in the day or in the early hours of 11th
February.
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Brierley died of natural causes, almost certainly of a cerebrovascular accident as certified by Shipman.

name: Ellen Hennefer
title: Mrs
place_of_death: Norbury House, a residential home for the elderly, Great Norbury Street, Hyde
conclusion:
It appears to me that Mrs Hennefer very probably died as the result of natural causes.
The evidence shows that Mrs Hennefer declined gradually before her death, so that when the time came, her death was not unexpected.
Shipman claimed that he last saw Mrs Hennefer three days before her death. There is no evidence to suggest that he visited her after that. As the medical records and nursing notes are not available, I cannot say with certainty that Shipman did not visit Mrs Hennefer on one or more later occasions. If he did, it is possible that he might have done something to hasten her death. However, there is no evidence that he did.
In these circumstances, it seems highly likely that the death was natural.

name: Elizabeth Mary Burke
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 44 Carter Place, Hyde
certified_cause: left ventricular failure due to coronary thrombosis
conclusion:
The circumstances of Mrs Burke's death give rise to strong suspicion that Shipman killed her.
Shipman appears to have been present at the death. He said on the MCCD counterfoil that he had seen Mrs Burke alive on the day of the death and that he had examined her body after death. From the telephone call to Mr Pritchard, it appears highly likely that he was present at the death. That factor in itself gives rise to a strong suspicion that Shipman caused this death. Dr John Grenville has said that it is most unusual for a patient to die during a general practitioner's home visit, unless the patient is known to be terminally ill, or the doctor has been called out in an emergency where it appears that the patient is suffering from symptoms of a life-threatening condition such as heart attack or stroke. Here, there is no history of terminal illness or an emergency call. Indeed, the entry in Shipman's visits book is typical of what is seen when he is responding to a non-urgent call. I think it likely that Mrs Burke asked Shipman to visit, either because she was concerned about her swollen ankles or because she had a cold, or possibly both. That she should die during his visit is highly suspicious.
Mrs Burke's peaceful appearance in death does not suggest that she died as a result of left ventricular failure. In giving his generic evidence to the Inquiry, Dr Grenville said:
'When the left ventricle fails acutely blood from the left ventricle is not pumped out into the rest of the body. The right ventricle continues to pump blood into the lungs but it cannot progress from there into the left side of the heart. Blood therefore accumulates rapidly in the small blood vessels of the lungs. The pressure in these small blood vessels increases and they rupture into the air spaces of the lungs. This causes sudden severe breathlessness. Air cannot be moved into the air spaces of the lungs since they become full of fluid and blood is no longer circulating through the lungs and into the rest of the body so death ensues due to lack of oxygenated blood to the vital organs. The severe breathlessness of acute left ventricular failure is usually accompanied by the appearance of foam, often blood stained at the mouth and nose. This is the fluid which has been released into the lungs and which then rises up through the airways. The mechanism of death in acute left ventricular failure is analogous to drowning or suffocation and the patient is usually extremely distressed. Patients in acute left ventricular failure feel slightly less uncomfortable sitting upright or standing and they often try to get more air by loosening their clothing and opening doors and windows because of the feeling of suffocation'
.
It follows that Mrs Burke's position and appearance in death were not typical of what is seen following death due to left ventricular failure. They were, however, entirely typical of many of Shipman's victims who had been killed by intravenous injection of a lethal dose of strong opiate.
It seems to me highly likely that Shipman killed Mrs Burke. I stop short of saying that I am sure that he did only because I am not quite sure that Shipman was present at the death. However, it seems most likely that he was and, if he was, I am satisfied that he killed her.

name: Clara Hackney
title: Miss
place_of_death: her home, 6 Farm Lane, Hyde
certified_cause: congestive heart failure due to ischaemic heart disease
conclusion:
I am satisfied that Miss Hackney died of natural causes.
Very little is known about Miss Hackney's health in the period before her death. However, it appears that she was known to have some sort of heart condition and was generally rather frail. She was able to cope at home only because she had such excellent support. Although her death appeared quite sudden to Mrs Swindells, I do not think it was wholly unexpected.
Miss Hackney was alive when Mrs Swindells left the house at about 9pm on 20th
September 1990. She was discovered dead in bed, early the following morning. It is extremely unlikely that Shipman would have visited her during that time. Had she requested a visit after Mrs Swindells left, which is most unlikely in itself, it would not have been Shipman who attended. There is no reason to suspect that Shipman was in any way involved in Miss Hackney's death.

name: Edith Annie Bill
title: Mrs
place_of_death: her home, 60 Mark Lane, Todmorden
conclusion:
I am quite satisfied that Mrs Bill's death was entirely natural.
Mrs Bill had a history of ankle oedema, which is often a sign of heart failure. She was clearly unwell and complaining of ankle oedema on the morning of the day before her death. Shipman visited her and prescribed medication, probably at about lunchtime. That medication cannot have caused or hastened Mrs Bill's death. Mrs Bill was still conscious in the small hours of the morning when she spoke to Mr Hartley. That was more than 12 hours after Shipman's visit. Professor McQuay and Dr John Grenville have said in their generic evidence that, if an opiate is injected intravenously, it reaches maximal effect within minutes. If administered intramuscularly, the maximal effect occurs within 30-60 minutes. A lethal injection of an opiate would cause death within one hour of being administered. Nothing that Shipman might have done at lunchtime on 21st
June could have caused or contributed to the death which occurred in the early hours of 22nd
June, given the evidence that Mrs Bill was conscious several hours after his departure.
The post-mortem findings of Dr Edwards confirmed that Mrs Bill had suffered a recent myocardial infarction. Her underlying conditions included severe occlusive atheroma. Professor Whitwell, having examined the report prepared by Dr Edwards, is satisfied that the findings are consistent with a death due to myocardial infarction.
All the evidence points to a natural death.

name: Phyllis Cooling
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
certified_cause: ventilatory failure due to chronic bronchitis and emphysema
conclusion:
In the absence of the medical records, it is not possible to discover the nature or gravity of Mrs Cooling’s medical condition at the time of her admission to hospital. In the absence of witness evidence or cremation forms, nothing is known about the immediate circumstances of the death. It is clear, however, that her death was sudden and wholly unexpected to her sons. Whatever had happened, the death should have been reported to the coroner, if only because Mrs Cooling had been in hospital for only about two hours. There may have been another reason why the death should have been reported to the coroner. The Indian doctor who spoke to Mrs Cooling’s sons said that Mrs Cooling
‘had not responded’
to the injection. I find that an odd expression. If Mrs Cooling had been on the verge of death and the treatment had failed to save her life, one might say that she had not responded to the treatment. However, there was no suggestion that Mrs Cooling was on the verge of death when admitted. It is clear that the Indian doctor knew that an injection had been given and that it had been closely associated with the death. I think it likely that she knew that the injection had caused the death but believed that whatever drug had been given had been administered in good faith. I think the expression
‘had not responded’
was a euphemism and that what she really thought was that the injection had had unforeseen and tragic results. Such a death should have been reported to the coroner. Yet, it is clear that Shipman was prepared to certify the cause of death. He plainly should not have done. As I have explained in
Chapter Seven
, I believe that Shipman sometimes sought to avoid reporting a death to the coroner in cases where he had not been guilty of any criminal activity, possibly for selfish financial reasons or so as to avoid the need for further formalities. However, on this occasion, the need for a report was so obvious that it appears to me likely that Shipman had a pressing reason not to report the death. I think it likely that Shipman did not wish his actions to be scrutinised at an inquest.
The causes for concern in this case are, therefore, as follows. First, Shipman must have been involved in the treatment of Mrs Cooling before her death; otherwise he would not have been in a position to certify the cause of death. I infer that it was probably Shipman who gave the injection that preceded death. Second, Shipman certified the death when it ought clearly to have been reported to the coroner. Third, by this time, Shipman had been the SHO on the medical wards for four months and, during that time, I am satisfied that he had killed at least three patients, possibly more. These factors give rise to some suspicion that Shipman might have killed Mrs Cooling.
However, just because Shipman wished to avoid an inquest is not to say that he had killed Mrs Cooling deliberately. If Mrs Cooling was suffering from breathlessness when she was admitted, it would have been standard treatment at PGI for her to be given an injection of aminophylline. That drug should be administered very slowly by the intravenous route. It is well recognised that there is a small risk that, even if given properly, the drug can cause irregularity of the heartbeat which can be fatal. Collapse and death can occur almost immediately. It is said that the patient dies ‘on the end of the needle’. This risk is much increased if the drug is given too quickly. It is quite possible that Mrs Cooling’s death resulted from an injection of aminophylline, given either in good faith at a proper rate or carelessly or recklessly at too fast a rate. The Inquiry has received evidence of an occasion when Shipman gave an injection too quickly and caused the collapse of the patient. It is possible that Mrs Cooling was the patient involved on that occasion. To a large extent, this is speculation, but the explanation I have suggested would readily explain why Shipman would have wished to avoid a coroner’s inquest; even if he had acted in good faith, he would have faced potential criticism.
There is another factor that militates against the conclusion that Shipman deliberately killed Mrs Cooling. I have formed the impression that, during this period, Shipman was more likely to kill a patient whose death was inevitable than one who had reasonable prospects of recovering and leaving hospital. The evidence of her sons suggests that Mrs Cooling was not seriously ill and had every prospect of receiving successful treatment. Although this factor is not determinative, in my view, it shifts the balance slightly towards the conclusion that the death was more likely to have been the result of an error on Shipman’s part rather than an act done with the intention to kill.
That said, the probability is that Mrs Cooling died soon after being given an injection by Shipman. In the light of my findings that he had already killed at least three patients at PGI and was to become a prolific killer, some suspicion must attach to the circumstances of this death.
I very much regret that I have had to raise these doubts so many years after the death and I am sorry for the distress this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.

name: Alice Smith
title: Mrs
place_of_death: on Ward 1, at Pontefract General Infirmary (PGI)
conclusion:
In the absence of medical records and cremation certification, there is very little evidence upon which to base a conclusion. From Mrs Butterworth’s description of her mother’s decline, it is entirely possible that she died a natural death on 14th
April 1972. The only reasons why one might harbour any suspicions about the death are that Shipman was clearly on duty and involved with patients on the ward, the family had not been warned that Mrs Smith’s death was imminent and the death occurred during the evening. An abnormally large proportion of deaths whose cause was certified by Shipman occurred between the hours of 6pm and midnight and any death certified by him which occurred during this period is to some extent suspicious. That would be the period during which it would be relatively easy for him to gain access to a patient in the absence of a nurse. On this particular evening, at 10.15pm and 10.30pm, he also claimed to have been present at two other deaths on the ward about which I am suspicious. I conclude that, although Mrs Smith might well have died a natural death, there is some cause to suspect that Shipman might have caused it.
I very much regret that I have had to raise these doubts so many years after the death and I am sorry for the distress this must have caused. As I explained in
Chapter One
, however, it would have been wrong for me to ignore or dismiss the concerns that were raised about Shipman’s conduct at PGI, once those concerns had been communicated to the Inquiry.
